title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
About this lecture

Differential accessibility gave us thousands of peaks that are more open in B cells than in CD4 T cells, and the reverse. A list of peaks is not yet biology: which transcription factors (TFs) open these regions?

Motif enrichment: which TF motifs are over-represented in a set of peaks (a 2×2 test, and the choice of background).
chromVAR: how open the peaks with a given motif are, per sample (or per cell).
Footprinting: whether a TF actually sits on its site, from the pattern of Tn5 insertions.


This is the last unit of the ATAC-seq block. The running example continues from Differential accessibility: the Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis ATAC-seq data, B cells versus CD4 T cells from the same three donors. Of 211 824 peaks tested, 19 404 are more open in B cells (B-up) and 16 897 more open in CD4 T cells (T-up), at adjusted p below 0.05 and an absolute apeglm-shrunken log2 fold change above 1. The exercise reads the saved differential_peaks.tsv table from that analysis; the remaining 175 523 ns peaks form the background for both differential groups. The question for this unit is which TFs are behind those differences. Three ideas, in increasing resolution: enrichment over a set of peaks, accessibility per sample, and protection of single sites. The motif sequences in the middle panel are real consensus sites (PU.1, OCT, IRF in blue; RUNX, TCF/LEF, ETS1 in orange); the lists on the right are what we actually find later in this lecture.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Recap: a PWM finds motif matches
text:
Recap: a PWM finds motif matches


A position weight matrix (PWM) gives a log-odds score for each base at each position (from Gene regulation). The score of a window is the sum; scan both strands.
A match is a window whose score is unlikely in random sequence: here p < 5 \times 10^{-5} (the motifmatchr default).
Short motifs match by chance everywhere. A 500-bp peak has ~1000 windows, so about 5% of peaks match any given motif by chance alone.


Only a recap: Gene regulation introduced counts, frequencies, log-odds and logos. What matters here is the threshold. Tools convert the score into a p-value: the probability that a random window with the background base composition scores at least this high. With p = 5e-5 and 1000 windows per peak, the expected number of chance matches is 0.05 per peak. In our 211 824 Corces peaks, the median JASPAR motif matches 6.4% of peaks, close to that expectation. This is why “my peak has a GATA motif” means very little on its own; the question is always whether there are more matches than expected.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Motif databases, and TF families


JASPAR 2024 (open, curated; 879 vertebrate CORE motifs), CIS-BP (motifs inferred for ~1600 human TFs), HOCOMOCO (from ChIP-seq). HOMER and MEME ship their own collections.
TFs of one family share a DNA-binding domain and bind almost the same motif. A motif hit names a family, not a TF.
Matrices for the same TF differ between databases and versions. JASPAR’s PAX5 matrix is only the 8-bp core; its PAX2 and PAX8 matrices are longer.


The logos are JASPAR 2024 matrices, aligned (RC = shown as reverse complement). PU.1 (SPI1) and SPIB are almost identical, and both share the GGAA core with ETS1 and GABPA; the flanks differ (an A-rich 5’ flank for PU.1/SPIB, CCGGAAGT for ETS1/GABPA), and this turns out to matter for B vs T cells. RUNX1, 2 and 3 all bind TGTGGT. TCF7, LEF1 and TCF7L2 all bind CTTTGAT. Humans have about 1600 TFs but only a few hundred distinct motifs, so a large motif collection is highly redundant: 28 of the 879 JASPAR motifs are ETS. Pick the TF within a family with other evidence: is it expressed (RNA-seq), is there ChIP-seq. The PAX example is real and will come back: a short matrix can fail where the family’s longer matrices work.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Motif enrichment is a 2×2 table


Count target and background peaks with and without a match. Effect size: the odds ratio; with 42% vs 20%, OR = 2.95.
p-value: Fisher’s exact test, which is the hypergeometric test: how surprising is it to draw this many motif peaks if the 19 404 B-up peaks were a random draw from B-up plus ns peaks?
Expected matches in B-up under the null: 19 404 × 43 302 / 194 927 ≈ 4310. Observed: 8227.


The numbers are real: SPIB in B-up peaks. a = 8227 of 19 404 B-up peaks contain a SPIB match, against c = 35 075 of the 175 523 ns peaks. The odds ratio (a·d)/(b·c) is 2.95. The one-sided hypergeometric p-value is about 10^-966, which R can only represent on the log scale. The null draws the B-up group from the combined B-up and ns pool; the 16 897 T-up peaks are excluded. HOMER reports this hypergeometric p-value (or a binomial approximation); MEME’s SEA uses Fisher’s exact test as well. The background contains tested peaks that did not meet the differential thresholds, rather than random genomic DNA. Students did the same kind of 2×2 table for gene-set enrichment in RNA-seq; here genes are peaks and the gene set is “has a motif”.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Choosing the background


The background decides the question. Here each differential group is compared with the tested ns peaks, excluding both B-up and T-up from the background.
GC content is the classic confounder: motifs differ in GC, and so do peak sets (promoters are GC-rich, distal enhancers AT-richer).
The random-genome background is the motif version of the naive shuffle in Genomic intervals: it answers “open vs closed DNA”, not “B vs T”.


Three choices. (1) The ns peaks: what distinguishes B-up or T-up regions from peaks that are not differential by the course thresholds. We use the same background for both groups, excluding the opposite differential group. The ns label includes peaks with insufficient evidence or a small effect; it does not prove that accessibility is identical. Features common to open chromatin tend to cancel. (2) GC-matched: draw background regions with the same GC distribution as the target, so motifs that are GC-rich or AT-rich do not win simply because the target is GC-rich or AT-rich. HOMER does this by default, from random genomic regions (findMotifsGenome.pl), and normalises k-mer content as well. chromVAR, later, matches on both GC and average accessibility. (3) Random genome or shuffled sequence: the target is compared with closed, AT-rich DNA, so every motif of open chromatin looks enriched. Same lesson as the shuffle test in Genomic intervals: the null decides the answer. Shuffled sequences (preserving dinucleotide content) are what MEME tools use by default when no background is given.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: the background changes the answer
text:
Real data: the background changes the answer


B-up peaks are AT-richer than ns peaks (mean GC 0.48 vs 0.51) but GC-richer than random DNA (0.41).
Against ns peaks, GC-rich motifs (SP1, KLF4, NRF1) look depleted; GC matching removes most of this. EBF1 (GC-rich) gains: OR 1.13 → 1.44.
Against random genome, SPIB looks more enriched (OR 4.89 versus 2.95 against ns) and CTCF flips from depleted to enriched.


Real numbers from make-motifs-figs.R. For the GC-matched background, we sampled ns peaks without replacement in the same 2%-GC bins as B-up peaks, taking at most one partner per target. Bins with insufficient ns peaks contribute fewer partners; report the resulting background size and GC distribution. Here all 19 404 targets find partners: both the target and the GC-matched background have mean GC 0.477, versus 0.513 in all ns peaks. For the random background, 19 404 random 500-bp windows from chr1–22 and X without Ns or blacklisted regions. Read the plot motif by motif. SPIB: enriched against any background, the robust finding. CTCF: depleted against peaks (many CTCF sites are shared across cell types, so they are not B-specific), but enriched against random DNA (CTCF sites are open chromatin). SP1, KLF4, NRF1: their apparent depletion against ns peaks is mostly GC: B-up peaks are distal, AT-richer elements, while the background contains GC-rich promoters. EBF1 is the reverse: its motif is GC-rich, so the AT-rich target hides its enrichment until GC is matched. Always report which background you used.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: motifs in B-up and T-up peaks
text:
Real data: motifs in B-up and T-up peaks


B-up: PU.1 / SPIB / SPIC (ETS), IRF and STAT, OCT (POU2F2 = OCT2), IKZF1, MEF2, NF-κB. T-up: ETS1 / GABPA / ERG-type ETS, RUNX, TCF7/LEF1, BCL11B, GATA3 (OR 1.5).
EBF1 is only weakly enriched (OR 1.13) and PAX5’s JASPAR matrix not at all, although both are B-cell master regulators. EBF is clearly depleted in T-up peaks (OR 0.51).


Each point is one of 879 JASPAR motifs, B-up or T-up compared with the same ns background; the dashed line is the Bonferroni threshold. The B-cell list is textbook: PU.1 and SPIB, the ETS–IRF composite elements bound by PU.1 or SPIB with IRF4/IRF8, OCT2 with its coactivator OBF1, IKAROS, MEF2C, and NF-κB. The T-cell list: RUNX1/3 with CBFβ, TCF1 (TCF7) and LEF1, the ETS factors ETS1 and GABPA, BCL11B and GATA3. Where expectations fail is instructive. EBF1 is enriched only weakly with this matrix and background (better with GC matching, previous slide). PAX5, the B-cell identity factor, is not enriched with JASPAR MA0014.4, while the longer PAX2/PAX8 matrices give OR about 1.86: matrix choice and background can mask a known regulator. And a motif being absent from the list does not mean the TF does not act there: TFs bind as partners, and many sites are weak matches below the threshold.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
One family, two lineages


Each point is a motif: enrichment in B-up (x) against enrichment in T-up (y).
The ETS family splits: PU.1/SPIB motifs (A-rich flank) go with B cells, ETS1/GABPA motifs (CCGGAAGT) with T cells. The flanks seen in the logos carry the lineage information.
CTCF and GC-rich promoter motifs (SP1, KLF4) are below 1 in both: constitutively open, not lineage-specific.


Points on the diagonal are enriched in both, points in the lower right only in B, upper left only in T. RUNX and TCF/LEF are T-specific, EBF is depleted in T-up, the POU and IRF motifs are positive in both sets (both are lymphoid, and the ns background includes peaks accessible in either cell type that did not meet the differential thresholds). This plot is a good way to see the redundancy problem: you cannot tell from the motif alone whether PU.1 or SPIB is the factor in B cells; both are expressed in B cells. To name the TF, combine motif enrichment with expression (RNA-seq of the same cells), with ChIP-seq, or with perturbation. This is the logic of Heinz et al. 2010 (key papers): a few lineage-determining TFs, PU.1 with C/EBP or with E2A/EBF/OCT, select the enhancers of a cell type.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Hundreds of motifs: p-values and effect sizes
text:
Hundreds of motifs: p-values and effect sizes




B-up
T-up




motifs tested
879
879


enriched at BH FDR 5% (OR > 1)
511
507


enriched at Bonferroni 5% (p < 0.05 / 879 = 5.7 × 10⁻⁵)
361
432


strongest odds ratio
2.95 (SPIB)
2.89 (BCL11B)




With ~19 000 target peaks, tiny effects are significant. Half of all motifs pass FDR 5%; most are family members of a few real signals, or GC.
Correct for the number of motifs (BH or Bonferroni, as for genes in RNA-seq), then rank by effect size (odds ratio, or fraction of target vs background), and group motifs by family.
With few target peaks (say 200), the opposite problem: little power, and multiple testing matters more.


The multiple-testing part is the same as in RNA-seq: 879 tests, so a nominal p of 0.05 would give about 44 false positives. BH controls the false discovery rate; Bonferroni the family-wise error rate (threshold 0.05/879). But with nearly 20 000 peaks in the target set, statistical significance is almost guaranteed for any motif with even a few percent difference, as with a huge RNA-seq experiment where every gene is “significant”. So report the odds ratio and the two fractions (42% vs 20% for SPIB), not only −log10 p, and look at the top of the list by effect size. Correlated tests: motifs of the same family give nearly the same answer, so “511 significant motifs” is many fewer independent findings. For this reason many analyses first cluster similar motifs into non-redundant ‘archetypes’ and report one per cluster.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Known motifs vs de novo discovery
text:
Known motifs vs de novo discovery


Known-motif enrichment tests each database motif: fast, names come for free, but limited to the database and to the quality of each matrix (PAX5 above).
De novo discovery finds the words that best separate target from background, builds a PWM, then compares it with the database: “looks like EBF1”.
Both give a motif, not a TF: the family problem remains.


HOMER (Heinz et al. 2010) does both in one run: known motifs first, then de novo motifs of length 8, 10, 12, then matches each new motif to its database. The MEME suite (Bailey et al. 2015) has separate tools: SEA or AME for known motifs (enrichment), STREME and MEME for discovery, Tomtom for comparing a new motif with a database. De novo results are useful when the TF is unknown, when the cell type uses an unusual variant, or for composite elements such as the ETS–IRF composite in B cells, which appears as one longer motif. Newer approaches train a neural network on the sequence of peaks (chromBPNet) and extract the learned motifs (TF-MoDISco): see the machine-learning units.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: HOMER and MEME on the command line
text:
HOMER and MEME on the command line
# HOMER: known + de novo motifs, 200 bp at the peak centre,
# GC-matched random genomic background (default) ...
findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa homer_b_up/ -size 200 -p 8
# ... or the saved ns peaks as background for differential peaks
findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa homer_bg/ -size 200 -bg ns.bed -p 8

# MEME suite: known motifs (SEA) and de novo (STREME) vs the saved ns peaks
bedtools getfasta -fi hg38.fa -bed b_up.bed   > b_up.fa
bedtools getfasta -fi hg38.fa -bed ns.bed > ns.fa
sea    --p b_up.fa --n ns.fa --m JASPAR2024_CORE_vertebrates.meme
streme --p b_up.fa --n ns.fa --dna

Not installed in this course: the exercise does the known-motif test in R (motifmatchr + Fisher), which shows every step.


These are the commands a student would run on a cluster with HOMER or the MEME suite installed (both are in Bioconda). HOMER’s -size 200 uses 200 bp around the peak centre: for summit-centred TF peaks, a narrow window raises the signal-to-noise ratio, because the motif sits near the summit. Our Corces peaks are fixed 500-bp windows around summits. Without -bg, HOMER picks GC-matched random genomic regions as background, which is the “random genome” question with GC matching. With -bg ns.bed it asks what distinguishes B-up from the tested ns peaks, as in our exercise. SEA wants a motif file in MEME format, which JASPAR provides for download. The output in each case is a ranked table like ours: motif, fraction of target and background with a match, p-value, q-value.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
chromVAR: motif accessibility per sample


Enrichment needs a set of peaks. chromVAR asks the question per sample: are the peaks with motif X more open in this sample than in the average sample?
Compare with background peaks matched for GC content and average accessibility, so technical differences between samples (GC bias, signal-to-noise) cancel.
Output: a deviation z-score per motif and sample, and the variability of each motif across samples.


chromVAR (Schep et al. 2017) starts from the peak-by-sample count matrix, the same matrix used for DESeq2. For each motif and sample: observed = reads in peaks with the motif divided by all reads in peaks; expected = the same fraction in the pooled data. The raw deviation is (observed − expected)/expected. The same is computed for many background peak sets: for each motif peak, a background peak with similar GC and similar mean accessibility, sampled 50 times. The z-score says how many standard deviations the motif’s deviation lies away from those background sets. It is robust to sample-level biases: if one library has more GC-rich fragments, all GC-rich peak sets go up, background included, so the z-score does not. Variability is the standard deviation of the z-scores across samples: high for motifs whose accessibility differs between cell types.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: chromVAR across haematopoiesis


13 cell types, 47 donor × cell-type samples from Corces et al. 2016; the 100 000 most-read peaks; 879 JASPAR motifs.
Motifs of 26 known regulators. GATA in MEPs and erythroblasts (and rising from HSC to MPP to CMP); CEBP in GMPs and monocytes; PU.1/SPIB in LMPPs, GMPs, monocytes and B cells; EBF1 in CLPs (less in B cells); the E-box (TCF3, E2A) in LMPPs, CLPs, B and T cells; POU2F2 and NF-κB in B cells; TCF7/LEF1 in CD4 and CD8 T cells; T-box (TBX21, EOMES) and ETS1 in NK and CD8 T cells.
The motif called Gata3 behaves exactly like GATA1: it is highest in erythroid cells, not in T cells. Same family, same motif.


Each column is one donor and cell type (technical replicates summed), 47 columns over 13 cell types; z-scores capped at ±15 for colour. The data are the Corces et al. 2016 count matrix lifted to hg38, the 100 000 peaks with the most reads, 879 JASPAR motifs, 50 background iterations; the whole computation takes under a minute after motif matching. This is essentially the analysis of the chromVAR paper, which used the same haematopoiesis data. The picture recovers the textbook regulators of each lineage without any differential analysis: GATA1/TAL1 along the erythroid branch, C/EBP along the myeloid branch, PU.1 in myeloid and B cells, EBF in common lymphoid progenitors, E2A across lymphoid cells, TCF1/LEF1 in T cells, T-bet and Eomes in NK and CD8 T cells. Point at the Gata3 row: chromVAR cannot know that GATA3 is the T-cell GATA factor; the motif is the motif. HLF and HOXA9, HSC regulators, do not stand out here: their motifs are weak or shared with other factors. The z-scores of the same cell type from different donors agree well, which is what you want before trusting a difference.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Variability, and single cells


Variability ranks motifs by how much their accessibility differs between samples: an unsupervised way to find the TFs that distinguish cell types.
The top of the list is dominated by families, often under unexpected names: FIGLA, ASCL1, BHLHE22 are E-box motifs (E2A/TCF3 in lymphoid cells), TBR1 is a T-box motif (T-bet, Eomes), MAFG::NFE2L1 is the erythroid NFE2 motif.
chromVAR was built for single-cell ATAC-seq, where each cell has a few thousand fragments: no single peak is informative, but summed over the thousands of peaks with a motif, each cell gets a z-score (ArchR, Signac).


Left: the 15 most variable motifs, keeping one motif per group of motifs whose z-scores correlate above 0.9; the label in brackets says what kind of motif it is. GATA is far ahead (variability 33): erythroid and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors differ most from everything else. Right: one dot per donor for five motifs, along the haematopoietic tree. GATA1 rises from HSC (about 0) through MPP and CMP to MEP (about 65); PU.1 is high in LMPP, GMP, monocytes and B cells and negative in erythroid, T and NK cells; EBF1 peaks in CLPs, TCF7 in T cells, CEBPA in GMPs and monocytes. The names on the left are a lesson in the family problem: JASPAR names a matrix after the protein it was measured for, which is often not the factor active in blood. In single cells, chromVAR z-scores are used to cluster cells, to annotate clusters, and to follow TF activity along differentiation trajectories; the Schep et al. paper did this for single-cell ATAC-seq of the same haematopoietic populations.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Footprints: a bound TF protects its site
text:
Footprints: a bound TF protects its site


Tn5 cannot insert where a protein sits. A TF bound for long enough leaves a dip of insertions over its motif (the footprint), flanked by high insertion rates in the free DNA next to it.
Footprinting needs base-resolution insertion sites (the +4/−5 shifted read ends of ATAC-seq processing and peak calling), not coverage, and deep sequencing: ~10⁸ reads for single sites.


The idea is old: DNase I footprinting on gels since 1978, then genome-wide with DNase-seq, and with ATAC-seq: the first ATAC-seq paper (Buenrostro et al. 2013) already showed an aggregate CTCF footprint. The two features: the flanks are high because the TF keeps the neighbourhood free of nucleosomes, and the centre is low because the protein blocks Tn5. For a single site you need many insertions within ±100 bp, so footprinting individual sites requires very deep libraries; aggregating over thousands of sites of the same motif (next slide) works with ordinary depth.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: From reads to an aggregate footprint
text:
From reads to an aggregate footprint


Each read end is one Tn5 insertion: in BED coordinates, start + 4 for reads on +, end − 5 for reads on −. In 1-based R coordinates, use start + 4 and end − 4.
Take every motif match, cut a window of ±100 bp around its centre, flip sites on the − strand, and average the insertion counts position by position.


The +4/−5 shift comes from the 9-bp duplication Tn5 creates when it inserts: the two strands are cut 9 bp apart, so the two read ends of a fragment are offset; shifting puts both on the centre of the insertion event (ATAC-seq processing unit). Orientation matters because motifs are not palindromic: the protein’s contacts, and Tn5’s sequence preference, are asymmetric relative to the motif. Without flipping, the footprint of a non-palindromic motif is smeared. In R this is coverage() on single-base GRanges, a Views/matrix of windows, and colMeans. deepTools computeMatrix on a bigWig of insertions does the same on the command line.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: CTCF footprint in GM12878
text:
Real data: CTCF footprint in GM12878


Bound sites (motif in a ChIP peak, n = 400): high flanks peaking at about −23 and +34 bp, and a dip over the motif. Open but unbound motif sites (n = 427): flat, no flanks, no dip. Closed sites: almost no insertions.
The narrow spike at the motif centre appears in bound and unbound sites: it is Tn5’s sequence preference, not protein.


Real data from the exercise: GM12878 ATAC-seq replicate 1, chr21 only, 505 000 insertions after removing duplicates. CTCF motif matches on chr21 at p < 1e-4 (JASPAR MA0139.2), oriented by motif strand, averaged per site; thin lines are 1-bp values, thick lines a 5-bp running mean. Bound sites: insertions rise to about 0.7 per site at the flanks and fall to about 0.2 on either side of the centre; averaged over ±10 bp the centre is 0.34 against 0.48 at 30–60 bp, a ratio of 0.69. Three lessons. The flanks: CTCF positions nucleosomes and keeps the neighbourhood open. The dip: the protein blocks Tn5 over roughly 20–40 bp, wider than the 15-bp motif because CTCF’s zinc fingers and the protein bulk cover more DNA. The spike at the centre: the unbound open sites have it too, so it comes from the motif sequence itself, which Tn5 prefers to cut (next slide). With one chromosome and 400 sites the profile is noisy; genome-wide it is very clean.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Tn5 has a sequence preference


Base composition around 200 000 insertion sites in the GM12878 reads, relative to the same reads 20–30 bp away. Within ±10 bp of the insertion, bases are up to 1.8-fold enriched or 2.6-fold depleted, in a structured pattern around the 9-bp duplication.
Tn5 does not cut at random: some sequences are cut more often whatever is bound. A motif has nearly the same sequence at every site, so this preference repeats at every site and does not average out.


The +4/−5 shift puts position 0 at the centre of the 9-bp target-site duplication. The pattern is a weak, roughly palindromic preference, as expected for an enzyme that binds DNA as a dimer. The same kind of bias exists for DNase I, MNase and the restriction enzymes: every enzyme has a sequence preference. Comparing with positions 20–30 bp away removes the general GC richness of open chromatin, which would otherwise dominate. The consequence for footprinting: averaged over thousands of copies of the same motif, Tn5’s preference for the motif’s own sequence produces a reproducible shape, a spike or a dip, that has nothing to do with binding. The central spike in the CTCF footprint is an example.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Correcting for Tn5 bias


Observed insertions = Tn5 sequence preference × protection. Inside a motif the sequence is the same at every site, so the bias is the same at every site and adds up in the aggregate: it can create a fake footprint, or hide a real one.
Correct by comparing with insertions expected from sequence alone: Tn5 on naked DNA, a k-mer model (TOBIAS ATACorrect), or a neural network bias model (chromBPNet).


Sung et al. 2014 showed for DNase-seq that much of the fine structure inside “footprints” comes from the enzyme’s sequence preference, not from protein contacts; Tn5 has the same problem. TOBIAS (Bentsen et al. 2020) estimates Tn5’s preference from the data with a position-weight model around insertion sites, computes the expected insertions at every position, and subtracts them (ATACorrect); then it scores footprints (ScoreBigwig) and compares conditions per site (BINDetect). chromBPNet (Kundaje lab) trains a small network on insertions in closed regions to learn the bias, and a second network for the rest; the bias-corrected predictions show footprints. Commands in the exercise “Where this leads”. The key point for the exam: an aggregate dip is evidence of binding only after bias correction, or with a control set of unbound sites with the same motif.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Which TFs leave footprints?


Footprint depth reflects how long the TF stays on DNA (residence time), not just whether it binds.
CTCF (minutes) footprints well. Many TFs exchange within seconds and leave little or no footprint even where ChIP-seq shows binding (Sung et al. 2014).
“No footprint” is therefore not evidence of no binding; compare conditions (TOBIAS BINDetect) rather than reading single sites.


Live-cell imaging measures residence times: about 10 seconds for the glucocorticoid receptor, two orders of magnitude longer for CTCF. Sung et al. 2014 compared DNase-seq footprints with these kinetics: GR and SOX2 showed little or no protection at sites bound in ChIP-seq, AP-1 and CREB1 were intermediate, CTCF strong; the same logic applies to Tn5. In a 30-minute tagmentation, a site with a short residence time is free most of the time, so Tn5 cuts it almost as often as the flanks. The TF still opens the chromatin (high flanks), but leaves no dip. This is why footprinting works beautifully for CTCF and a few others, and poorly for many important regulators. A practical consequence: compare the same motif between conditions (B vs T), where bias and residence time cancel, rather than claiming binding at individual sites.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: A motif is not a binding event
text:
A motif is not a binding event


Of 15 684 CTCF motif matches on chr21, only 400 (2.6%) lie in a CTCF ChIP-seq peak; 95% are in closed chromatin. Conversely, 82% of the 405 chr21 CTCF ChIP peaks contain a match.
CTCF has one of the longest, most informative motifs. For short motifs (GATA: WGATAR) the fraction bound is far smaller. A match says where a TF could bind; chromatin and partners decide where it does (Gene regulation).


Real numbers from the exercise. Motif matches at p < 1e-4 on chr21, after removing blacklisted regions; ChIP peaks are the ENCODE conservative IDR peaks for GM12878 CTCF. Even for CTCF, which binds a long motif with high specificity and is bound at about 44 000 sites in this GM12878 ChIP-seq experiment (all chromosomes), the vast majority of motif matches in the genome are not bound: most lie in closed chromatin, in DNA methylated at the motif’s CpGs, or are weak matches. The 18% of ChIP peaks without a match are weaker motifs below the threshold, indirect binding, or noise. This is why enrichment, chromVAR and footprinting all restrict motif analysis to open chromatin, and why the step from motif to binding needs direct evidence. The 427 open but unbound sites in the previous figure show no footprint: being in open chromatin is not enough either.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Three questions, three tools


Enrichment for a set of peaks (differential peaks, a cluster); chromVAR for samples or single cells; footprinting for sites, with deep data and bias correction.
All three start from motifs, so all three inherit the motif’s limits: family redundancy, imperfect matrices, and motif ≠ binding.


A map for choosing. If you have a list of differential peaks: enrichment. If you have many samples or cells and want a per-sample activity score, for clustering or for plotting along a trajectory: chromVAR. If you want to know which sites are occupied, or how occupancy changes between conditions: footprinting, with deep data and a bias-corrected tool. Each answer is still about a motif, and naming the TF needs other evidence: expression, ChIP or CUT&RUN for the candidate TF, or perturbation. The ChIP and CUT&RUN units come next.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




motif match
PWM log-odds score above a p-value threshold; ~5% of 500-bp peaks match any motif by chance


databases
JASPAR, CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO; families share motifs, so a motif names a family


enrichment
2×2 table: target vs background × match vs no match; odds ratio; Fisher = hypergeometric


background
decides the question; tested ns peaks for differential sets; match GC; random genome inflates


multiple testing
~900 motifs: BH or Bonferroni, then rank by effect size and group by family


de novo
find enriched words, build a PWM, compare with the database (HOMER, STREME, Tomtom)


chromVAR
per-sample deviation of motif peaks vs GC/accessibility-matched background; z-score; variability; single cells


footprint
dip of Tn5 insertions at a bound motif, high flanks; aggregate over oriented sites


caveats
Tn5 sequence bias makes fake footprints (correct: TOBIAS, chromBPNet); short residence time leaves none




Students should leave able to fill in and evaluate a 2×2 motif table by hand, explain why the background matters, read a chromVAR heatmap, read an aggregate footprint and say what the flanks and the dip mean, and explain why neither a motif match nor a missing footprint settles whether a TF binds. Next: ChIP-seq, which measures the binding of one TF directly.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities. HOMER, and PU.1 with partners selecting cell-type enhancers.
Bailey et al. 2015, Nucleic Acids Res. The MEME Suite. The other standard motif toolkit (MEME, STREME, SEA, Tomtom).
Rauluseviciute et al. 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles. The motif database we use.
Schep et al. 2017, Nat Methods. chromVAR: inferring transcription-factor-associated accessibility from single-cell epigenomic data. chromVAR, demonstrated on the same Corces haematopoiesis data.
Sung et al. 2014, Mol Cell. DNase footprint signatures are dictated by factor dynamics and DNA sequence. Why many bound TFs leave no footprint, and why enzyme bias shapes the ones you see.
Bentsen et al. 2020, Nat Commun. ATAC-seq footprinting unravels kinetics of transcription factor binding during zygotic genome activation. TOBIAS: bias correction and differential footprinting.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Quiz: what people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Short questions on prediction tasks in epigenomics and on judging an evaluation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. For each task, name the input, where the labels come from, and what the test set should contain: (a) predicting DNase accessibility in 100 cell types from 1 kb of sequence; (b) predicting a person’s age from blood methylation; (c) predicting which enhancer regulates which gene.






Answer






Reference sequence windows; DNase-seq peaks in each cell type; held-out chromosomes (and, if the claim is about new cell types, cell types not used in training). (b) CpG methylation (β values from arrays) of a blood sample; the donor’s chronological age; people from independent cohorts, ideally other labs. (c) Features of (enhancer, gene) pairs such as activity, contact and distance; CRISPRi screens (or eQTLs, loops); pairs whose genes and enhancers are not in the training set, e.g. held-out chromosomes.





Q2. How is the effect of a non-coding variant predicted with a sequence model? A model predicts P(bound) = 0.72 for the reference and 0.69 for the alternative allele, and 0.80 vs 0.15 for a second variant. Which variant would you test first, and why?






Answer





Predict the reference and the alternative sequence with the same trained model and take the difference. Effects: −0.03 and −0.65. Test the second: the predicted effect is large, typical of a variant that destroys a strong motif. A difference of 0.03 may be harder to validate, but its uncertainty must be measured; probability differences alone do not establish a model’s resolution.




Q3. A group makes 10 shifted copies of each peak window (shifts of 0–90 bp) to enlarge its training set, then splits all windows at random into 80% training and 20% test. Its CNN reaches AUC 0.97. Why is this number not trustworthy, and how should the split be done?






Answer





Shifted copies overlap almost completely, so nearly every test window has near-copies in the training set: a flexible model can recognise them without learning anything general (leakage). Split first, by peak or better by chromosome, and make shifted copies only within the training set.




Q4. In the lecture, a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier reached 96% accuracy with a random split of windows and 65% with whole regions held out, while a GC-only logistic regression changed little. Why does leakage inflate the nearest-neighbour model so much more?






Answer





The nearest-neighbour model memorises: it copies the label of the most similar training example, and with a random split that example is usually a shifted copy of the test window itself (87% of the time here). The GC model has two parameters and cannot memorise individual windows; it can only learn the general GC trend, which is the same whatever the split.




Q5. Why is holding out whole chromosomes the standard in genomics? Name one kind of leakage it does not prevent.






Answer





Neighbouring and overlapping windows, multiple summits of one peak, and regions in the same domain are related; putting a whole chromosome in the test set keeps all of them on one side. It does not prevent leakage through similar sequences on different chromosomes: repeat families, segmental duplications, paralogous genes.




Q6. A model distinguishes CTCF peaks from random genomic windows with ROC AUC 0.85. A logistic regression on GC content alone reaches 0.71 on the same data. With GC-matched negatives, the GC model drops to 0.49. What does this tell you about the first number, and which negatives would you use to claim that the model learned CTCF’s binding rules?






Answer





Part of the 0.85 comes from GC content, which separates peaks from random genome but says nothing about CTCF specifically. With GC-matched negatives GC is useless (0.49 = chance), so whatever the model achieves there comes from other sequence features. To claim it learned CTCF’s rules, use GC-matched negatives, or accessible-but-unbound negatives, and compare with a single CTCF PWM as a baseline.




Q7. TargetFinder predicted enhancer–promoter interactions with F1 ≈ 0.83 using random cross-validation over pairs, and 0.13 when pairs were split by chromosome (the random-guess F1 was about 0.09). Explain what happened.






Answer





Most pairs shared their promoter (and overlapping “window” features) with other pairs. With a random split, pairs of the same promoter were in both training and test sets, so the model learned which promoters have many interactions and applied that to the test pairs. Split by chromosome, the promoters in the test set were new, and the model was barely better than guessing.




Q8. Expression models such as Enformer correlate well with measured expression across genes (r ≈ 0.55–0.6), but poorly across individuals for the same gene. Why are these different questions, and which one matters for interpreting a patient’s genome?






Answer





Across genes, the model must tell highly from lowly expressed genes, which depends on large differences in promoters and regulatory landscape. Across individuals, it must predict the small effect of each person’s own variants on one gene. Training on the reference genome across genes teaches the first, not the second; predicted effects often have the wrong sign (Sasse et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023). The second question is the one that matters for a patient.




Q9. A model of open chromatin is trained in GM12878 (a B-cell line) and tested in K562 (an erythroleukaemia line). Which regions do you expect it to predict well, and which badly?






Answer





Well: regions open in both cell types, such as CpG-island promoters and many CTCF sites, whose sequence features (GC, CpG, CTCF motifs) are shared. Badly: regions open only in K562, which depend on erythroid TFs (GATA1, TAL1) whose motifs the B-cell model has no reason to favour. Regions open only in GM12878 would be predicted as open even in K562: false positives.




Q10. A paper reports: “Our deep model achieves 94% accuracy in predicting TF binding sites genome-wide.” List three things you would want to know before believing that it is a good model.






Answer





Any three of: the class balance of the test set (binding sites are rare, so 94% may be below “always unbound”); a threshold-free metric with prevalence (PR AUC); how the data were split (chromosomes, no overlapping windows); what the negatives were (random genome or matched); the baselines (GC, k-mers, the known motif); whether the test set was used to choose the model; whether it was tested in another cell type or data set.

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Describe a prediction task in epigenomics by its input, its labels, its intended use, and the test that matches that use.
Recognise leakage in a data split, and show with real data how much it inflates a memorising model (k-nearest neighbours) compared with simpler ones.
Explain why the negatives define the question, and show that a GC-only model is at chance once negatives are GC-matched.
Use a known motif and k-mer counts as baselines for a TF-binding model.
Test whether a model trained in one cell type works in another, and say which regions it gets wrong.

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Background
Leakage. A test set is meant to be new. In genomic data many examples are related: shifted or overlapping windows, several summits of one peak, neighbouring regions in the same domain, copies of a repeat. If related examples fall on both sides of a split, the test set partly repeats the training set, and models that can memorise look much better than they are. Split by group (region, gene, chromosome), and do augmentation after the split.
Negatives. A classifier learns whatever separates positives from negatives. Peaks are GC-rich; random genome is not. With random negatives GC content alone scores well; with GC-matched negatives (same GC distribution as the positives) it cannot, and only sequence information beyond GC helps. Accessible negatives (open regions without the TF) ask what makes a site bound rather than merely open.
Baselines. Report the simple models next to the complex one: GC content, k-mer counts, the known motif (a PWM), nearest gene. A complex model is interesting by how much it adds.
Generalisation. A held-out chromosome tests new regions in the same cell type. New cell types and new individuals are harder, and are the tests that matter for many uses.

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Data
The same files as Machine learning from scratch, plus the GM12878 CTCF peaks and the K562 ATAC-seq peaks (ENCODE ENCSR483RKN, IDR thresholded peaks ENCFF925CYR, GRCh38; the same lab and pipeline as the GM12878 ATAC data). From the course repository:
data/download.sh ml-prediction-tasks
cd ~/epi/ml                         # where ml_atac.rds from Machine learning from scratch R1 is
You need ml_atac.rds, the open/closed data set made in R1 of the Machine learning from scratch exercise; run that step first if you do not have it. Packages: as in that exercise, plus class (k-nearest neighbours; installed with R). Runtimes on one core: R1 about 10 minutes (k-nearest neighbours is slow), R2 about 5 minutes, R3 about 3 minutes.
Simplifications. The models here are small (k-NN, logistic and ridge regression on 4-mer counts), so that each trap shows clearly in minutes. The traps are the same for deep networks, and usually worse, because deep networks memorise more easily.

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
By hand
B1. Name the task. For each study give the input, the source of the labels, the intended use, and what the test set must contain to support that use.

A CNN predicts H3K27ac peaks in 50 tissues from 2 kb of sequence; the authors want to interpret GWAS variants.
An elastic net predicts gestational age from cord-blood methylation; the authors want a tool for other hospitals.
A model predicts Hi-C contact maps of a new cell type from its ATAC-seq and CTCF ChIP-seq.

B2. Which split leaks? Say for each whether information can leak from test to training, and why.

Peaks are cut into 200-bp bins with 1000 bp of input each (neighbouring inputs overlap by 800 bp); bins are split 80/20 at random.
The same, but chromosomes 8 and 9 are the test set.
Each peak window and its reverse complement are added as separate examples, and examples are split at random.
Feature selection (keep the 500 k-mers most different between bound and unbound) is done on all data; then a classifier is cross-validated on those 500 k-mers.
A methylation age clock is trained on 2000 blood samples from one cohort and tested on 500 other samples of the same cohort, which include siblings of people in the training set.

B3. A nearest-neighbour classifier by hand. Windows are described by two features, (GC, CpG o/e). Training windows: A = (0.62, 0.70) open; B = (0.38, 0.15) closed; C = (0.45, 0.30) open; D = (0.41, 0.22) closed. Test window T = (0.43, 0.24).

Compute the Euclidean distance from T to each training window. What does the 1-nearest-neighbour classifier predict?
T is in fact a copy of D shifted by 100 bp, so its true label is closed. What does a random split risk doing with such copies?

B4. GC matching. Positives (CTCF peaks) and a pool of random windows have these counts per GC bin:



GC bin
0.30–0.40
0.40–0.50
0.50–0.60
0.60–0.70




positives
200
400
300
100


random pool
40 000
30 000
8 000
1 000




What fraction of the positives and of the pool have GC above 0.5? Would a GC-only model separate positives from 1000 random windows drawn from the pool?
How many negatives do you draw from each bin to make 1000 GC-matched negatives? Is the pool large enough?
With GC-matched negatives, what ROC AUC do you expect for the GC-only model? Explain.

B5. Judge the baselines. A paper reports, for CTCF peaks vs GC-matched negatives on held-out chromosomes: CNN ROC AUC 0.94; CTCF PWM best-match score 0.91; GC content 0.50.

What does the GC result tell you about the negatives?
How much does the CNN add over the motif? What could the extra 0.03 come from?
A second paper reports CNN AUC 0.97 with random genomic negatives and no baselines. Can you say which CNN is better?
A third paper reports the same PWM baseline at only 0.83. Its methods say the best-match score was taken from a scan at p < 5 × 10⁻⁵, with score 0 for windows without a match; 91% of the negatives and 28% of the peaks have no match. Why is its baseline lower, and is the comparison with its CNN fair?

B6. A random-guess F1. An enhancer–promoter data set has 1 positive pair for every 20 negative pairs. A “classifier” calls every pair positive.

What are its precision and recall? Compute \(F_1 = 2PR/(P + R)\).
TargetFinder had F1 0.83 with random cross-validation and 0.13 with chromosome-split cross-validation. Compare both with (a).

B7. Across genes, across people. A model predicts, for gene X, that the alternative allele of an eQTL SNP lowers expression. In 400 people, carriers of the alternative allele have higher measured expression of X.

Across these people, is the correlation between predicted and measured expression of X positive or negative?
The same model correlates well with expression across 10 000 genes in the reference genome. Explain how both results can be true.

B8. Another cell type. A model of open chromatin is trained in GM12878 (B cells; motifs of PU.1, EBF1, IRF and CTCF) and tested in K562 (erythroid; GATA1, TAL1, CTCF).

Rank, from best to worst predicted, K562 regions that are: open in both cell lines; open only in K562.
Will GM12878-only regions give false positives or false negatives when the model is used in K562?

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Explore: leakage in data splits
The demo rebuilds R1 with simulated data, so that you can turn each source of leakage on and off. It has 300 regions on 10 chromosomes, half open and half closed, each cut into 3 windows of 200 bp. Window overlap sets how much neighbouring windows of a region share (70% is like the ±150-bp shifts of 500-bp windows in R1). True signal is the difference in mean GC content between open and closed regions; at 0, the label has nothing to do with the sequence. Regions that are copies makes a fraction of regions near-identical copies (98% identity, same label) of a region on another chromosome, like a segmental duplication or a repeat family. The classifier is k-nearest neighbours on 4-mer counts, as in R1: the bars give 1-NN accuracy and the ROC AUC of a 15-NN vote. The third bar, the GC score, uses the GC content of each window directly as its score, so it trains nothing and cannot memorise. The three groups are three test sets: 20% of windows at random, 20% of regions, and chromosomes 9 and 10. Under each group you can read how often the nearest training window of a test window is a shifted copy from the same region, or a homologous copy. The map shows the test windows (orange) of the split you choose; purple boxes are copies, and a dark purple line joins a test region to a copy in the training set.



E1. (links to R1b, R1c) At the default settings, write down the three bars for each split and compare them with the table of R1. Which model gains most from the random split, and why? Press new random genome a few times: is the pattern stable?
E2. Click no signal at all. Now nothing can be predicted. Which numbers are leakage? How far from 0.5 are the numbers of the honest splits and of the GC score, and what does that tell you about a test set of this size?
E3. (links to B2a) With no signal, set the window overlap to 0, 25%, 50% and 90% in turn, and note the random-split 1-NN accuracy and how often the nearest training window comes from the same region.
E4. (links to B2b) Click 30% copies, no signal (no overlap) and show the test set of whole chromosomes. Is the chromosome split honest here? What would you do instead?
E5. Click unit R1: 70% overlap, then raise the true signal to 0.12. How do the random-split and chromosome-split 1-NN accuracies change, compared with signal 0.08 and signal 0? What does the leaky number tell you about how much signal there is?






Solutions (E1–E5)





E1. 1-NN accuracy, 15-NN AUC and GC AUC: random windows 1.00, 0.91, 0.90; whole regions 0.68, 0.83, 0.87; whole chromosomes 0.68, 0.78, 0.87. For 99% of the random-split test windows, the nearest training window is a shifted copy of the same region. This is the R1 pattern (0.959 against 0.648 and 0.636). 1-NN gains most because it copies the label of a single neighbour. The 15-NN vote gains less, because at most two of its 15 neighbours are copies. The GC score cannot memorise and hardly changes. Over the first five genomes, the 1-NN accuracy averages 0.99, 0.65 and 0.65.
E2. Random split: 1-NN accuracy 1.00 and 15-NN AUC 0.77. Both are pure leakage, because there is nothing to learn. Region and chromosome splits: 1-NN 0.49, 15-NN AUC 0.45 and 0.46, i.e. chance. The GC score gives 0.58 to 0.62 without any training, so this is not leakage but chance. The test set holds only about 60 regions, whose 3 windows are strongly correlated, so values up to about ±0.1 from 0.5 can arise by chance. A value of 1.00 cannot.
E3. Overlap 0: 1-NN accuracy 0.50, nearest neighbour from the same region 0%. Overlap 25%: 0.69 and 34%. Overlap 50%: 0.97 and 93%. Overlap 90%: 1.00 and 100%. Even a 25% overlap leaks. At overlap 0 the windows of a region share only their GC content in this simulation. In a real genome, adjacent windows also share repeats and chromatin domains, so they leak somewhat even without overlap.
E4. No. With no signal, 1-NN accuracy is 0.64 (random windows), 0.72 (regions) and 0.67 (chromosomes), and for 27% of the chromosome-split test windows the nearest training window is a homologous copy on a training chromosome. Splitting by chromosome removes the leakage from overlap, but not from homology between chromosomes: segmental duplications, repeat families and paralogous genes. Cluster the regions by sequence similarity and keep each cluster on one side of the split, or remove test regions that have a close match in the training set. The 15-NN vote leaks less (AUC 0.53 for chromosomes), because only a few of its 15 neighbours are copies.
E5. Random split: 1.00 at signal 0, 0.08 and 0.12. Chromosome split: 0.49, 0.68 and 0.76. The honest number follows the true signal; the leaky number is about 1 whatever the signal, so it says nothing about how predictable the label is. Note also that the GC score (AUC 0.94 at signal 0.12) beats the 15-NN vote (0.88): a simple baseline that encodes the real cause is hard to beat (compare R2).

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
In R

R0 — Set up
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
  library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite); library(motifmatchr)
  library(glmnet); library(class)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
fa   <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))
auto <- paste0("chr", 1:22)
bl   <- import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz"))
auc_roc <- function(score, label) {               # ROC AUC with ties handled, as in R6 of
  o  <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)            # Machine learning from scratch
  s  <- score[o]; l <- label[o]; k <- c(diff(s) != 0, TRUE)
  tpr <- cumsum(l)[k] / sum(l); fpr <- cumsum(1 - l)[k] / sum(1 - l)
  sum(diff(c(0, fpr)) * (tpr + c(0, head(tpr, -1))) / 2)
}
kmers   <- function(gr) oligonucleotideFrequency(getSeq(fa, gr), 4, as.prob = TRUE)
dat <- readRDS("ml_atac.rds")        # open/closed windows from Machine learning from scratch, R1
dim(dat)
The helper auc_roc is the tie-aware ROC AUC from R6 of Machine learning from scratch; kmers returns the frequencies of the 256 4-mers in each window.


R1 — Leakage through overlapping windows
set.seed(4)
reg <- dat[c(sample(which(dat$open == 1), 3000), sample(which(dat$open == 0), 3000)), ]
reg$region <- seq_len(nrow(reg))
# three windows per region, shifted by -150, 0 and +150 bp: a common "augmentation"
win <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(-150, 0, 150), function(o)
  transform(reg, start = start + o, end = end + o, shift = o)))
gr  <- GRanges(win$chrom, IRanges(win$start + 1, win$end))
X   <- kmers(gr)
win$gc <- letterFrequency(getSeq(fa, gr), "GC")[, 1] / width(gr)
y   <- win$open
dim(X)

set.seed(5)
splits <- list(random     = runif(nrow(win)) < 0.2,                          # windows at random
               region     = win$region %in% sample(reg$region, 0.2 * nrow(reg)),  # whole regions
               chromosome = win$chrom %in% c("chr8", "chr9"))                # whole chromosomes
sapply(splits, sum)                  # test windows in each split
evaluate <- function(te) {
  set.seed(1)
  nn1  <- knn(X[!te, ], X[te, ], factor(y[!te]), k = 1)
  nn25 <- knn(X[!te, ], X[te, ], factor(y[!te]), k = 25, prob = TRUE)
  p25  <- ifelse(nn25 == "1", attr(nn25, "prob"), 1 - attr(nn25, "prob"))
  rdg  <- cv.glmnet(X[!te, ], y[!te], family = "binomial", alpha = 0, nfolds = 5)
  gcm  <- glm(y ~ gc, binomial, data.frame(y = y, gc = win$gc)[!te, ])
  c(knn1_accuracy = mean(as.character(nn1) == y[te]),
    knn25_AUC = auc_roc(p25, y[te]),
    ridge_AUC = auc_roc(as.numeric(predict(rdg, X[te, ], s = "lambda.min")), y[te]),
    gc_AUC    = auc_roc(predict(gcm, data.frame(gc = win$gc[te])), y[te]))
}
leak <- sapply(splits, evaluate)
round(leak, 3)
# why: for a random split, who is the nearest training window?
te <- splits$random
nn <- knn(X[!te, ], X[te, ], factor(win$region[!te]), k = 1)
mean(as.character(nn) == win$region[te])        # fraction whose nearest neighbour is a shifted copy

How many windows are there, and how many test windows does each split give? Why does the chromosome split give fewer?
Fill in a table of the four measures for the three splits. Which model gains most from the random split, and which hardly at all? Why?
What fraction of test windows in the random split have a shifted copy of themselves as nearest training window? Relate this to the 1-NN accuracy.
The GC model’s AUC differs between the region split and the chromosome split, although GC cannot memorise anything. What else differs between these two test sets?



R2 — The negatives decide what is learned: CTCF peaks
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
ctcf <- ctcf[seqnames(ctcf) %in% auto]
pos  <- resize(GRanges(seqnames(ctcf), IRanges(start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak, width = 1)), 500, fix = "center")
pos  <- pos[!overlapsAny(pos, bl) & countOverlaps(pos, pos) == 1]
set.seed(1)
pos  <- sort(pos[sample(length(pos), 10000)])

gc_of <- function(gr) { s <- getSeq(fa, gr); f <- letterFrequency(s, c("G", "C", "N"))
  data.frame(gc = (f[, 1] + f[, 2]) / width(s), n = f[, 3]) }
pos$gc <- gc_of(pos)$gc

# a pool of random windows away from CTCF peaks
len <- seqlengths(seqinfo(fa))[auto]
set.seed(2)
chr  <- sample(auto, 300000, replace = TRUE, prob = len)
pool <- GRanges(chr, IRanges(floor(runif(300000, 1, len[chr] - 500)), width = 500))
pool <- pool[!overlapsAny(pool, ctcf, maxgap = 500) & !overlapsAny(pool, bl)]
g    <- gc_of(pool); pool <- pool[g$n == 0]; pool$gc <- g$gc[g$n == 0]

# negative set 1: random windows
rnd <- pool[1:10000]
# negative set 2: GC-matched, the same number of windows per 2%-GC bin as the positives
bin  <- function(x) cut(x, seq(0, 1, 0.02), include.lowest = TRUE)
need <- table(bin(pos$gc))
set.seed(3)
idx <- unlist(lapply(names(need)[need > 0], function(b) {
  w <- which(bin(pool$gc) == b); w[sample.int(length(w), min(need[b], length(w)))] }))
gcm <- pool[idx]
# negative set 3: open but not CTCF-bound: GM12878 ATAC summits away from CTCF peaks
atac <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
atac <- atac[seqnames(atac) %in% auto]
aw   <- resize(GRanges(seqnames(atac), IRanges(start(atac) + atac$peak, width = 1)), 500, fix = "center")
aw   <- unique(aw[!overlapsAny(aw, ctcf, maxgap = 500) & !overlapsAny(aw, bl)])
set.seed(4)
acc  <- aw[sample(length(aw), 10000)]; acc$gc <- gc_of(acc)$gc
round(c(positives = mean(pos$gc), random = mean(rnd$gc), gc_matched = mean(gcm$gc),
        accessible = mean(acc$gc)), 3)
jdb <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf_pwm <- getMatrixByID(jdb, "MA0139.2")
feat <- function(gr) {
  s  <- getSeq(fa, gr)
  sc <- matchMotifs(ctcf_pwm, s, p.cutoff = 1, bg = "even", out = "scores")      # every window: its best score
  ht <- matchMotifs(ctcf_pwm, s, p.cutoff = 5e-5, bg = "even", out = "scores")   # strict: is there a match?
  list(chrom = as.character(seqnames(gr)), gc = letterFrequency(s, "GC")[, 1] / width(s),
       motif = as.numeric(motifScores(sc)[, 1]), hit = as.numeric(motifCounts(ht)[, 1]) > 0,
       k4 = oligonucleotideFrequency(s, 4, as.prob = TRUE))
}
fp <- feat(pos)
neg_res <- sapply(list(random = rnd, gc_matched = gcm, accessible = acc), function(ng) {
  fn <- feat(ng)
  y  <- rep(1:0, c(length(pos), length(ng)))
  te <- c(fp$chrom, fn$chrom) %in% c("chr8", "chr9")
  d  <- data.frame(y = y, gc = c(fp$gc, fn$gc), motif = c(fp$motif, fn$motif))
  K  <- rbind(fp$k4, fn$k4)
  m_gc  <- glm(y ~ gc, binomial, d[!te, ])
  m_mot <- glm(y ~ motif, binomial, d[!te, ])
  fold  <- match(c(fp$chrom, fn$chrom), auto) %% 5 + 1          # chromosome-grouped folds
  m_k4  <- cv.glmnet(K[!te, ], y[!te], family = "binomial", alpha = 0, foldid = fold[!te])
  c(gc_AUC    = auc_roc(predict(m_gc, d[te, ]), y[te]),
    motif_AUC = auc_roc(predict(m_mot, d[te, ]), y[te]),
    kmer_AUC  = auc_roc(as.numeric(predict(m_k4, K[te, ], s = "lambda.min")), y[te]),
    motif_in_negatives = mean(fn$hit))
})
round(neg_res, 3)
mean(fp$hit)                         # fraction of CTCF peaks with a motif match

What is the mean GC of the positives and of each negative set? Was the matching successful?
Fill in the table of AUCs (three models × three negative sets). Which model depends on the choice of negatives, and which does not?
The 4-mer ridge model is worse than the single PWM score against GC-matched negatives, although it has 256 parameters. Explain.
What fraction of CTCF peaks, and of each negative set, has a motif match? Think of two reasons why a GC-matched window can contain a CTCF motif without being a CTCF peak.
The code scans twice: with p.cutoff = 1 for the score and p.cutoff = 5e-5 for presence. Change the first to 5e-5 and rerun the motif model against GC-matched negatives. What happens to the AUC, and why? (Hint 2.)



R3 — Does a GM12878 model work in another cell type?
k562 <- import(file.path(D, "k562_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
gm   <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
summits <- function(pk) {
  pk <- pk[seqnames(pk) %in% auto]
  pk <- pk[order(-pk$signalValue)]
  pk <- pk[!duplicated(paste(seqnames(pk), start(pk), end(pk)))]
  w  <- resize(GRanges(seqnames(pk), IRanges(start(pk) + pk$peak, width = 1)), 500, fix = "center")
  w[!overlapsAny(w, bl) & countOverlaps(w, w) == 1]
}
gm_w <- summits(gm); k5_w <- summits(k562)

# closed in both cell types: the closed windows of ml_atac.rds that are also far from K562 peaks
neg <- with(dat[dat$open == 0, ], GRanges(chrom, IRanges(start + 1, end)))
neg <- neg[!overlapsAny(neg, k562, maxgap = 500)]
test_chr <- c("chr8", "chr9")
is_test  <- function(gr) as.character(seqnames(gr)) %in% test_chr

# train one model per cell type: 4-mer ridge regression, training chromosomes only
train_model <- function(open_w) {
  set.seed(8)
  p <- open_w[!is_test(open_w)]; p <- p[sample(length(p), 15000)]
  n <- neg[!is_test(neg)]
  fold <- match(c(as.character(seqnames(p)), as.character(seqnames(n))), auto) %% 5 + 1
  cv.glmnet(rbind(kmers(p), kmers(n)), rep(1:0, c(length(p), length(n))),
            family = "binomial", alpha = 0, foldid = fold)
}
fit_gm <- train_model(gm_w); fit_k5 <- train_model(k5_w)

# test windows on chr8 and chr9, split into shared and cell-type-specific open regions
t_gm <- gm_w[is_test(gm_w)]; t_k5 <- k5_w[is_test(k5_w)]
tests <- list(GM12878_only = t_gm[!overlapsAny(t_gm, k562)],
              shared       = t_gm[overlapsAny(t_gm, k562)],
              K562_only    = t_k5[!overlapsAny(t_k5, gm)])
t_neg <- neg[is_test(neg)]
sapply(tests, length); length(t_neg)
Kneg <- kmers(t_neg)
cross <- sapply(tests, function(w) {
  K <- rbind(kmers(w), Kneg); y <- rep(1:0, c(length(w), length(t_neg)))
  c(trained_on_GM12878 = auc_roc(as.numeric(predict(fit_gm, K, s = "lambda.min")), y),
    trained_on_K562    = auc_roc(as.numeric(predict(fit_k5, K, s = "lambda.min")), y))
})
round(cross, 3)

How many test windows are in each group?
Fill in the 2 × 3 table of AUCs. Which regions are easy for both models? Which model is better on each cell-type-specific set?
The GM12878 model still reaches 0.82 on K562-only regions. What has it learned that transfers? What would you expect for a model trained against GC-matched negatives?

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — leakage (B2, B3, R1)





Ask of every pair of examples on opposite sides of a split: do they share sequence, a peak, a promoter, a person, or a decision? knn from the class package gives each test example the majority label of its k nearest training examples (Euclidean distance on the features); with prob = TRUE it also returns the fraction of neighbours that voted for the winning class. The review by Whalen et al. 2022 lists the common forms of leakage in genomics.









Hint 2 — negatives and baselines (B4, B5, R2)





GC matching means: the same number of negatives as positives in every GC bin, so the two GC distributions are identical. A model of one feature cannot separate two classes whose distributions of that feature are identical. matchMotifs(..., out = "scores") returns, per window, the best match score (motifScores) and the number of matches (motifCounts). Careful: a window with no match passing p.cutoff gets score 0, so with the usual cutoff (5 × 10⁻⁵) most windows tie at 0 and the score loses its ranking. For a continuous score use p.cutoff = 1 (every window keeps its true best score); for counts or presence keep a strict cutoff. How a CNN reads DNA meets the same trap. Motif background and GC matching are also discussed in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting.









Hint 3 — F1 and correlations (B6, B7)





Calling everything positive gives recall 1 and precision = fraction of positives. A correlation across people is positive when people with higher predicted expression tend to have higher measured expression. See Sasse et al. 2023 and Huang et al. 2023.









Hint 4 — cross-cell-type (B8, R3)





Which TFs open chromatin in each cell type? PU.1 (SPI1), EBF1 and IRF4 in B cells; GATA1 and TAL1 in erythroid cells; CTCF and CpG-island promoters everywhere. overlapsAny splits the peaks into shared and specific.

title: Exercise: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Input: 2 kb of reference sequence; labels: H3K27ac peaks per tissue (ChIP-seq); use: predict the effect of GWAS variants, i.e. of sequence changes. The test must contain held-out chromosomes, and, for the variant claim, a comparison of predicted effects with measured allelic effects (allele-specific H3K27ac, QTLs, reporter assays). (b) Input: CpG methylation of cord blood; labels: gestational age from clinical records; use: other hospitals. Test on independent cohorts measured in other labs and, ideally, on other array versions: batch effects between labs are the main threat. (c) Input: ATAC-seq and CTCF ChIP-seq tracks (plus sequence); labels: Hi-C maps; use: new cell types. Test on cell types not used in training, not only on held-out regions of training cell types.
B2. (a) Leaks: neighbouring bins share 800 of their 1000 input bases and usually the same peak, and random splitting puts neighbours on both sides. (b) Does not leak through overlap (each chromosome entirely on one side); similar sequences on other chromosomes can still leak a little. (c) Leaks: a window and its reverse complement carry identical information, so the test set contains reverse-complement copies of training examples. (d) Leaks: the selection used the labels of the examples that later serve as cross-validation test folds. Select features inside each fold. (e) Leaks, mildly: siblings share half their genome and often their environment, so their methylation is correlated. Split by family.
B3. (a) Distances: A \(\sqrt{0.19^2 + 0.46^2} = 0.50\); B \(\sqrt{0.05^2 + 0.09^2} = 0.10\); C \(\sqrt{0.02^2 + 0.06^2} = 0.063\); D \(\sqrt{0.02^2 + 0.02^2} = 0.028\). Nearest is D: predicted closed. (b) The prediction is right, but only because a copy of T was in the training set. With a random split many test windows have such copies, and accuracy measures memory, not generalisation.
B4. (a) Positives: 400/1000 = 40% above 0.5; pool: 9000/79 000 = 11%. Random negatives would be mostly AT-rich, and GC alone would separate them from peaks fairly well. (b) 200, 400, 300 and 100: the same counts as the positives. The smallest bin of the pool (1000 windows at 0.6–0.7) is enough for 100. (Matching gets hard for very GC-rich positives, where the pool is thin.) (c) About 0.5: the GC distributions are identical by construction, so GC carries no information about the label.
B5. (a) The matching worked: GC carries no information (0.50 = chance). (b) 0.03 of AUC. It could come from flanking sequence around the motif, weaker or non-canonical CTCF motifs below the PWM threshold, the number and arrangement of motifs, or sequence features of open chromatin (CTCF binds mostly in accessible DNA). (c) No: different negatives make different questions, and random negatives are easier (GC helps). Without a baseline on the same data, 0.97 cannot be compared with 0.94. (d) All windows without a significant match tie at score 0, so the baseline cannot rank 91% of the negatives and 28% of the peaks among themselves; it degenerates to little more than “is there a match?”. The CNN is compared with a crippled baseline, and its advantage is overstated. Scan with p.cutoff = 1 to keep every window’s best score (R2e; How a CNN reads DNA).
B6. (a) Precision \(= 1/21 = 0.048\), recall 1; \(F_1 = 2 \times 0.048 \times 1 / 1.048 = 2/22 = 0.091\). (b) 0.83 is far above it, but 0.13 is barely above the 0.09 of calling everything positive: with new promoters the model had little real skill.
B7. (a) Negative: people the model predicts to have lower expression (carriers) have higher measured expression. (b) Across genes, the model needs to rank genes by expression, which depends on large differences (promoter strength, CpG islands, chromatin context) that it learned from the reference genome. Across people, it must predict the small effect of a single base change on one gene, which it was never trained on directly; the sign of such small effects is often wrong (Sasse et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023).
B8. (a) Open in both (promoters, CTCF sites: sequence features common to both cell types), then K562-only (needs erythroid motifs the model did not learn). (b) False positives: the model predicts them open because they look like GM12878 open regions, but they are closed in K562.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 6000 regions × 3 shifts = 18 000 windows. Test windows: 3590 (random), 3600 (whole regions, 20% of 6000 × 3) and 1746 (chr8 + chr9, about 10% of the genome). (b)

The 1-NN classifier gains most (+0.31): it memorises. The 25-NN model averages over 25 neighbours, of which at most two are copies, so it gains less (+0.06). Ridge regression (+0.03) and GC (+0.01) cannot memorise individual windows. (c) 0.87: for 87% of test windows the nearest training window is one of its own shifted copies, so the 1-NN classifier copies the right label. Accuracy 0.96 is what memory gives; 0.65 is what the model has learned. (d) The test windows themselves: the region split samples regions from the whole genome, the chromosome split only chr8 and chr9, which differ in GC composition and in their mix of promoters and distal sites. GC depends entirely on the negatives; the PWM score much less (0.94 → 0.91). The 4-mer model loses 0.09: part of what it had learned was GC. (c) 0.70 against 0.91. The CTCF matrix used here (MA0139.2) spans 15 bp, and 4-mer counts cannot represent its full pattern: they count short words anywhere in the window, losing their order and the motif’s long-range pattern. One well-chosen feature that encodes biology beats many generic ones. A CNN can learn long motifs from the sequence itself, which is the subject of How a CNN reads DNA. (d) 71.7% of CTCF peaks have a match; 5.0% of random, 9.3% of GC-matched and 8.2% of accessible windows. (e) With p.cutoff = 5e-5 for the score, every window without a significant match gets score 0: 91% of the GC-matched windows and 28% of the peaks tie at 0, the ranking within them is lost, and the AUC against GC-matched negatives falls from 0.905 to 0.834. A continuous score needs p.cutoff = 1.
