title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
Background
Data. For CpG \(i\) and sample \(j\): \(X_{ij}\) methylated reads out of \(N_{ij}\) reads. The level is \(\beta_{ij} = X_{ij}/N_{ij}\); Δβ = mean β of group 2 − mean β of group 1.
Binomial (sampling only): \(\text{Var}(X) = N p (1-p)\). Beta-binomial (sampling + biological variation between samples with overdispersion \(\varphi\)):
\[ \text{Var}(X) = N p (1-p)\,[1 + (N-1)\varphi], \qquad \text{SD}(\hat\beta) = \sqrt{p(1-p)\,[1 + (N-1)\varphi]/N}. \]
This is the methylation counterpart of the negative binomial of RNA-seq (Poisson + gamma).
Comparing two replicates. With pooled level \(p\), \(z = (\hat\beta_1 - \hat\beta_2)\,/\,\sqrt{p(1-p)(1/N_1 + 1/N_2)}\) has variance about 1 if the replicates differ only by sampling.
DSS fits a beta-binomial per CpG, shrinks \(\varphi\) across CpGs (empirical Bayes, like DESeq2’s dispersions), optionally smooths each sample over neighbouring CpGs (500-bp window), and uses a Wald test. callDML reports differential CpGs (DMLs); callDMR merges significant CpGs less than 100 bp apart into regions of at least 3 CpGs and 50 bp in which at least 50% of CpGs are significant.

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
Data
From the course repository:
data/download.sh methylation-differential     # about 80 MB (plus the GTF if not yet present)
mkdir -p ~/epi/diffmeth && cd ~/epi/diffmeth
D=/path/to/course/data                        # where download.sh put the files

gm12878_wgbs_rep{1,2}_chr21.bed.gz, k562_wgbs_rep{1,2}_chr21.bed.gz: ENCODE WGBS per-CpG calls, chr21, two replicates per cell line (GM12878 ENCSR890UQO, K562 ENCSR765JPC). Format as in DNA methylation biology (column 10 coverage, 11 % methylated rounded down, 13 called genotype).
hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz, gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz: CpG islands and genes.
gm12878_rna_rep{1,2}_genes.tsv, k562_rna_rep{1,2}_genes.tsv: ENCODE total RNA-seq gene quantifications (TPM).

Shortcuts, said plainly. One chromosome; per-CpG calls from ENCODE’s pipeline rather than our own alignment (Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing shows they agree closely). The “replicates” are independent cultures of two cell lines from two different people, so this is a demonstration of the method, not a comparison of B cells and erythroid cells in a population (B7).
Install DSS with BiocManager::install("DSS") (it brings bsseq). The R part runs in about 3 minutes and needs about 4 GB of memory.

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Sampling vs biology. A CpG has true mean level \(p = 0.5\).

With \(N = 20\) reads, what is the SD of \(\hat\beta\) under the binomial? Under the beta-binomial with \(\varphi = 0.1\)?
Repeat for \(N = 200\). By what factor did the SD fall in each model?
You can afford 400 reads per CpG in total for each group. Is it better to sequence 2 samples at 200x or 20 samples at 20x? Why?

B2. One CpG, two groups. Group A (GM12878): replicate 1 has 9/10 methylated reads, replicate 2 has 16/20. Group B (K562): 2/10 and 5/20.

Compute β per sample, the mean β per group (average of the samples), and Δβ (B − A).
Pool the reads per group and write the 2 × 2 table that Fisher’s exact test would use. What does this test assume about the reads?
Use the \(z\) formula of the Background to compare the two A replicates. Is their difference compatible with sampling noise alone?

B3. Overdispersion in real data. For CpGs with ≥ 10 reads in both replicates, the variance of \(z\) is 1.05 for the two K562 replicates and 3.44 for the two GM12878 replicates.

What would you expect under pure binomial sampling? (b) Which pair behaves like two sequencing runs of one sample? (c) Give two biological reasons why two cultures of the same cell line can differ. (d) Pooled-read Fisher tests on GM12878 rep1 vs rep2 give \(p < 0.05\) for 17% of CpGs. What should that fraction be?

B4. Merge DMLs into DMRs. Significant CpGs (all with Δβ of the same sign) at positions: 5000, 5060, 5110, 5150, 5400, 5430, 5470, 5900, 6000, 6080, 6150, 6230, 6260, 6290. Non-significant CpGs lie between 5150 and 5400 (at 5200, 5250, 5300, 5350) and nowhere else.

Apply: merge significant CpGs less than 100 bp apart; keep regions with ≥ 3 CpGs and ≥ 50 bp. Which regions do you get?
Would the first two regions merge if the gap rule were 300 bp? What would the “fraction significant” of that merged region be, counting the four non-significant CpGs?

B5. Multiple testing. (a) A WGBS study tests 25 million CpGs. How many have \(p < 10^{-3}\) by chance if nothing differs? (b) DSS calls 5 061 DMRs at a CpG-level threshold. Why is “5 061 DMRs at FDR 5%” not a correct statement? (c) How does dmrseq obtain region-level inference even with only 2 vs 2 samples, where a separate permutation test for each region would have very coarse p-values?
B6. Read the results. Use the lecture figures.


How many DMRs are lower and how many higher in K562? (b) Where are the losses, and where are the gains enriched, relative to all tested CpGs (CGI 7.1%, promoter 4.9%, K562 low domain 46.5%)? (c) Why might counting DMRs overstate the number of “events” for the losses?

B7. Judge the design. (a) In our data, what population do the two groups represent? What does a significant DMR tell you? (b) A study compares blood WGBS of 4 smokers and 4 non-smokers and reports DMRs at genes of the immune response. Name four confounders or artefacts to rule out. (c) Methylation differences between cell types are often Δβ 0.3–1, between exposed and unexposed people often 0.01–0.05. What does that mean for the number of samples and for the choice of platform?
B8. Expression. Of 11 chr21 genes whose promoter is more methylated in K562, 5 are expressed more than 2-fold lower in K562 and 1 higher. Of 63 genes whose promoter is less methylated in K562, 7 are higher and 7 lower. Explain the asymmetry, and say what experiment would test whether methylation of the ITGB2 promoter silences it in K562.

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
On the command line

C1 — Input tables for DSS
DSS wants, per sample, a table with columns chr pos N X (position of the CpG, reads, methylated reads). Combine the two strands as in DNA methylation biology and drop CpGs with a SNP:
for s in gm12878_wgbs_rep1 gm12878_wgbs_rep2 k562_wgbs_rep1 k562_wgbs_rep2; do
  zcat $D/${s}_chr21.bed.gz \
    | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$13 == "CG" { p = ($6 == "+") ? $2 + 1 : $2
          N[p] += $10; X[p] += int($10 * $11 / 100 + 0.5) }
        END { print "chr", "pos", "N", "X"; for (p in N) print "chr21", p, N[p], X[p] }' \
    | (read h; echo "$h"; sort -k2,2n) > $s.dss.txt
  echo "$s $(tail -n +2 $s.dss.txt | wc -l) CpGs, methylation $(awk 'NR > 1 { n += $3; x += $4 } END { printf "%.3f", x / n }' $s.dss.txt)"
done
head -3 gm12878_wgbs_rep1.dss.txt

Why is pos the start + 1 for the + strand line and the start for the − strand line? (b) Compare the overall methylation of the four samples. What stands out?



C2 — How many CpGs are well covered in all samples?
for s in gm12878_wgbs_rep1 gm12878_wgbs_rep2 k562_wgbs_rep1 k562_wgbs_rep2; do
  awk 'NR > 1 && $3 >= 10 { print $2 }' $s.dss.txt > $s.cov10
done
sort gm12878_wgbs_rep1.cov10 gm12878_wgbs_rep2.cov10 k562_wgbs_rep1.cov10 k562_wgbs_rep2.cov10 | uniq -c \
  | awk '{ n[$1]++ } END { for (k = 1; k <= 4; k++) print k, "samples:", n[k] }'
How many CpGs have at least 10 reads in all four samples? Why would a per-CpG test that requires 10 reads everywhere lose many CpGs, and how does smoothing help?

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
section: Explore: why pooling reads gives false DMLs
text:
Explore: why pooling reads gives false DMLs
The demo simulates 5 000 CpGs in two groups of replicates. Every replicate has its own true level, drawn from a beta distribution around the group mean with overdispersion φ (the beta-binomial of the Background), and its reads are a binomial draw from that level. By default nothing differs between the groups; differential CpGs and their true Δβ make a fraction of CpGs truly different. Three tests are run on every CpG: Fisher’s exact test on reads pooled per group (it ignores the replicates), a beta-binomial Wald test with one φ estimated from the replicates of all CpGs (what DSS does, without its per-CpG part), and a t-test on the per-sample β values. (a) shows the p-values of one test, with the CpGs that truly differ stacked in orange; for CpGs that do not differ, a valid test gives a flat histogram. (b) shows how many CpGs each test calls at a Benjamini–Hochberg FDR of 5%, split into true and false calls.



E1. (links to B3) With the defaults (20 reads, 3 vs 3 samples, φ = 0.1, nothing differs): how many CpGs does Fisher’s test call at FDR 5%, and what fraction of CpGs get \(p < 0.05\)? Describe the p-value histogram. Switch the histogram to the beta-binomial and the t-test: what do they give? Scale Fisher’s result up to the 28 million CpGs of a genome.
E2. Set φ to 0, then 0.02 and 0.2, and note Fisher’s calls and its fraction of \(p < 0.05\). Then return to φ = 0.1 and set the reads to 5, 50 and 100. Why does the problem of the pooled test grow with sequencing depth? Use \(\text{Var}(X) = Np(1-p)[1 + (N-1)\varphi]\).
E3. (links to B1) Set φ = 0.05 and click 10% differ (Δβ = 0.2; 453 CpGs truly differ). With 3 vs 3 samples at 20 reads, how many true CpGs does the beta-binomial test find, and how many of Fisher’s calls are false? Raise the reads to 100. Then go back to 20 reads and raise the replicates to 6 and to 8. Which helps more, and why? Compare the total reads per group.
E4. Still at φ = 0.05, 10% differ, 20 reads: (a) set the replicates to 1. Which tests can still be run, and can you trust Fisher’s list? (b) Set 6 replicates and compare the beta-binomial with the t-test. Both are valid (few false calls); why does the t-test find fewer CpGs?






Solutions (E1–E4)





E1. Fisher calls 340 CpGs, all false, and 21.6% of CpGs have \(p < 0.05\) instead of 5%. The histogram piles up near 0 instead of being flat; the spike at \(p = 1\) comes from CpGs near 0 or 100% methylation, where Fisher’s discrete test can rarely give anything else. The beta-binomial test gives 0 calls with 4.0% below 0.05, the t-test 0 calls with 4.2%: both use the variation between replicates, and both have flat histograms. 340 of 5 000 is 6.8%; over 28 million CpGs that is about 1.9 million false DMLs. The real GM12878 replicates of the lecture behave the same way (20 902 Fisher calls on chr21 between two replicates, 17% with \(p < 0.05\) in B3).
E2. φ = 0: Fisher gives 0 calls and 3.7% below 0.05 (slightly conservative, as discrete tests are): without biological variation, reads really are independent draws and pooling is fine. φ = 0.02: 0 calls, 7.0%. φ = 0.2: 1 050 calls, 32.6%. At φ = 0.1 with 5 reads: 0 calls (4.8%); 50 reads: 1 525 calls (40.3%); 100 reads: 2 406 calls (54.1%). The pooled test assumes the binomial variance \(Np(1-p)\), so its standard error of β shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{N}\). The real variance is larger by the factor \(1 + (N-1)\varphi\), which grows with \(N\): at 5 reads it is 1.4, at 100 reads 10.9. With more reads the biological differences between replicates become “significant”, although they are the same in both groups. Depth cannot remove biological variation; only a test that measures it can.
E3. 3 vs 3 at 20 reads: the beta-binomial finds 4% of the 453 differential CpGs (22 calls, 2 false); Fisher makes 305 calls of which 116 (38%) are false. At 100 reads: beta-binomial 25%; Fisher finds 94% but 1 470 of its 1 895 calls (78%) are false. At 20 reads with 6 replicates: beta-binomial 43% (201 calls, 8 false); with 8 replicates 58%. Six samples at 20 reads (120 reads per group) beat three samples at 100 reads (300 reads per group): each extra replicate gives an independent draw of the biological level, while extra reads only measure the same three samples more precisely (B1(c)).
E4. (a) With one sample per group only Fisher can run: there is no replicate to estimate φ or a variance from. Its 43 calls contain 19 false (44%), and nothing in the data tells you which. A 1 vs 1 comparison can say that two samples differ, not that two groups do. (b) At 6 vs 6 the t-test finds 10% (46 calls, 0 false), the beta-binomial 43%. The t-test estimates the variance of each CpG from only 12 values (10 degrees of freedom) and ignores how many reads each β is based on; the beta-binomial uses the read counts and borrows φ from all CpGs, as DSS (and DESeq2 for RNA-seq) shrink dispersions towards a common value.

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
In R
You need data.table, GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, DSS and ggplot2 (see Install the software you need). Run R in the folder where C1 wrote the .dss.txt files.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(DSS); library(ggplot2)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Read the samples
samples <- c(gm1 = "gm12878_wgbs_rep1", gm2 = "gm12878_wgbs_rep2", k1 = "k562_wgbs_rep1", k2 = "k562_wgbs_rep2")
dat <- lapply(samples, function(s) fread(paste0(s, ".dss.txt")))
sapply(dat, function(x) c(CpGs = nrow(x), median_N = median(x$N), meth = sum(x$X) / sum(x$N)))
bs <- makeBSseqData(lapply(dat, as.data.frame), names(samples))
bs
How many CpGs does the BSseq object contain, and why more than any single sample?


R2 — Are the replicates overdispersed?
zrep <- function(a, b, minN = 10) {
  m <- merge(a, b, by = c("chr", "pos"))[N.x >= minN & N.y >= minN]
  p <- (m$X.x + m$X.y) / (m$N.x + m$N.y)
  m <- m[p > 0 & p < 1]; p <- p[p > 0 & p < 1]
  m[, z := (X.x / N.x - X.y / N.y) / sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / N.x + 1 / N.y))][]
}
zg <- zrep(dat$gm1, dat$gm2); zk <- zrep(dat$k1, dat$k2)
c(GM12878 = var(zg$z), K562 = var(zk$z))
c(GM12878 = mean(abs(zg$z) > 1.96), K562 = mean(abs(zk$z) > 1.96))

Compare the variances with 1. (b) What fraction of CpGs has \(|z| > 1.96\) in each pair, and what would you expect without overdispersion?



R3 — The price of pooling reads
Fisher’s exact test between the two GM12878 replicates, on 50 000 random CpGs with ≥ 5 reads in both (there is no group difference here):
set.seed(1)
nul <- merge(dat$gm1, dat$gm2, by = c("chr", "pos"))[N.x >= 5 & N.y >= 5][sample(.N, 50000)]
nul[, p := mapply(function(a, n1, b, n2) fisher.test(matrix(c(a, n1 - a, b, n2 - b), 2))$p.value, X.x, N.x, X.y, N.y)]
sum(p.adjust(nul$p, "BH") < 0.05)
mean(nul$p < 0.05)
How many “significant” CpGs at FDR < 0.05? What fraction has \(p < 0.05\)? What does this say about tests that pool reads over replicates?


R4 — DSS: differential CpGs
dml <- DMLtest(bs, group1 = c("gm1", "gm2"), group2 = c("k1", "k2"), smoothing = TRUE, ncores = 4)
head(dml, 3)
summary(dml$phi1); summary(dml$phi2)
dmls <- callDML(dml, delta = 0.2, p.threshold = 1e-5)
nrow(dmls); table(dmls$diff > 0)
ggplot(dml[sample(nrow(dml), 50000), ], aes(-diff, -log10(pval))) + geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.2, 0.2), linetype = 2) + labs(x = "Δβ (K562 − GM12878)", y = "−log10 p")

What are mu1, mu2, diff and phi1/phi2? (b) Compare the median dispersion of the two groups with your answer to R2. (c) How many DMLs, and in which direction? (On 4 cores about 1 minute.)



R5 — DSS: differential regions
dmrs <- as.data.table(callDMR(dml, delta = 0.2, p.threshold = 1e-5))
nrow(dmrs)
dmrs[, dir := ifelse(diff.Methy > 0, "lower in K562", "higher in K562")]
dmrs[, .(n = .N, median_bp = median(length), median_CpGs = median(nCG), total_kb = sum(length) / 1e3), by = dir]
head(dmrs[, .(chr, start, end, length, nCG, meanMethy1, meanMethy2, diff.Methy, areaStat)], 5)

How many DMRs in each direction, how long, and how much of chr21 do they cover? (b) What do the top five by areaStat have in common? Look up their positions in the PMD plot of DNA methylation biology.



R6 — Where are the DMRs?
cgi <- fread(file.path(D, "hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz"), header = FALSE)[V2 == "chr21"]
cgi <- GRanges(cgi$V2, IRanges(cgi$V3 + 1, cgi$V4))
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
genes <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
prom <- promoters(genes, 1000, 1000)
kb <- dat$k1[, .(m = sum(X) / sum(N), n = .N), by = .(bin = pos %/% 1e5)][n >= 50]
low <- reduce(GRanges("chr21", IRanges(kb[m < 0.1]$bin * 1e5 + 1, width = 1e5)))
dg <- GRanges(dmrs$chr, IRanges(dmrs$start, dmrs$end))
dmrs[, `:=`(cgi = overlapsAny(dg, cgi), promoter = overlapsAny(dg, prom), k562_low = overlapsAny(dg, low))]
dmrs[, .(n = .N, cgi = mean(cgi), promoter = mean(promoter), k562_low = mean(k562_low)), by = dir]
bg <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(dml$pos, width = 1))
c(cgi = mean(overlapsAny(bg, cgi)), promoter = mean(overlapsAny(bg, prom)), k562_low = mean(overlapsAny(bg, low)))

Compare each direction with the background of tested CpGs. Which features are enriched for losses, which for gains? (b) Why do we compare with all tested CpGs rather than with the whole chromosome?



R7 — Promoter DMRs and expression
tpm <- function(f) { x <- fread(file.path(D, f))[grepl("^ENSG", gene_id)]; setNames(x$TPM, sub("\\..*", "", x$gene_id)) }
id <- sub("\\..*", "", genes$gene_id)
ex <- data.table(id, gene = genes$gene_name,
                 gm = (tpm("gm12878_rna_rep1_genes.tsv")[id] + tpm("gm12878_rna_rep2_genes.tsv")[id]) / 2,
                 k5 = (tpm("k562_rna_rep1_genes.tsv")[id] + tpm("k562_rna_rep2_genes.tsv")[id]) / 2)
ex[, lfc := log2((k5 + 1) / (gm + 1))]
po <- findOverlaps(prom, dg)
pd <- data.table(id = id[queryHits(po)], dB = -dmrs$diff.Methy[subjectHits(po)], cgi = dmrs$cgi[subjectHits(po)])
pd <- pd[, .SD[which.max(abs(dB))], by = id]
ex <- merge(ex, pd, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
ex[, cls := ifelse(is.na(dB), "none", ifelse(dB > 0, "higher in K562", "lower in K562"))]
ex[!is.na(lfc), .(genes = .N, median_lfc = median(lfc), down = sum(lfc < -1), up = sum(lfc > 1)), by = cls]
ex[cls == "higher in K562"][order(lfc), .(gene, gm = round(gm, 1), k5 = round(k5, 1), lfc = round(lfc, 2), dB = round(dB, 2), cgi)]
cor(ex$dB, ex$lfc, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

Fill in the table of B8 from the output. (b) Which genes lose expression with a promoter gain? Are they plausible B-cell genes? (c) What is the overall correlation, and why is it weak?



R8 — How much do the choices matter?
dml0 <- DMLtest(bs, group1 = c("gm1", "gm2"), group2 = c("k1", "k2"), smoothing = FALSE)
c(smoothed = sum(dml$fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), not_smoothed = sum(dml0$fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
nrow(callDMR(dml0, delta = 0.2, p.threshold = 1e-5))
nrow(callDMR(dml, delta = 0.4, p.threshold = 1e-5))
fwrite(dmrs[, .(chr, start = start - 1, end, name = dir, score = round(1000 * abs(diff.Methy)))],
       "dmrs_gm12878_vs_k562.bed", sep = "\t", col.names = FALSE)

How do smoothing and the delta threshold change the results? (b) Why do we subtract 1 from start when writing BED?

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — variances (B1, B3, R2)





Plug into \(\text{SD}(\hat\beta) = \sqrt{p(1-p)[1+(N-1)\varphi]/N}\). As \(N \to \infty\) the beta-binomial SD tends to \(\sqrt{p(1-p)\varphi}\). Under the binomial, about 5% of \(|z|\) exceed 1.96. The DSS model is in Feng, Conneely & Wu 2014.









Hint 2 — tests and pooling (B2, R3)





fisher.test takes a 2 × 2 table of methylated and unmethylated reads in two groups. Pooling makes every read an independent observation; replicates disappear. Compare with pseudo-replication in Differential accessibility.









Hint 3 — DSS (R1, R4, R5, R8)





The DSS vignette explains makeBSseqData, DMLtest, callDML, callDMR and their columns (mu1, mu2, diff, phi1, phi2, areaStat). diff is group 1 − group 2, here GM12878 − K562.









Hint 4 — regions and multiple testing (B4, B5)





Walk along the positions and start a new region whenever the gap is ≥ 100 bp. Expected false positives = number of tests × threshold. Region-level FDR: dmrseq (Korthauer et al. 2019) permutes sample labels; with 2 + 2 samples there are only 3 distinct splits.









Hint 5 — annotation and expression (B6, B8, R6, R7)





overlapsAny, findOverlaps and promoters are as in Genomic intervals. A DMR in a domain that is silent in both cell lines cannot change expression. dCas9 fused to TET1 or DNMT3A edits methylation at one locus.









Hint 6 — design (B7)





Think of everything that differs between the groups besides the variable of interest: cell-type composition, age, sex, genotype, batch, conversion, coverage. Methylation arrays covers composition in blood (Jaffe & Irizarry 2014).

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Binomial: \(\sqrt{0.25/20} = 0.112\). Beta-binomial: \(\sqrt{0.25 \times (1 + 19 \times 0.1)/20} = \sqrt{0.25 \times 2.9/20} = 0.190\). (b) \(N = 200\): binomial \(\sqrt{0.25/200} = 0.035\) (3.2-fold lower); beta-binomial \(\sqrt{0.25 \times 20.9/200} = 0.162\) (only 1.2-fold lower). (c) 20 samples at 20x: the biological variance (\(\approx p(1-p)\varphi = 0.025\) per sample) shrinks only with the number of samples. The SD of a group mean is about \(0.19/\sqrt{20} = 0.042\) with 20 samples at 20x versus \(0.16/\sqrt{2} = 0.11\) with 2 samples at 200x; and with 2 samples φ itself can hardly be estimated.
B2. (a) A: 0.90 and 0.80, mean 0.85. B: 0.20 and 0.25, mean 0.225. Δβ $= 0.225 - 0.85 = $ −0.625. (b) Pooled: A 25 methylated, 5 unmethylated; B 7 methylated, 23 unmethylated. Fisher assumes all 60 reads are independent draws from two binomial populations, one per group: it ignores that reads come in samples with their own levels. (c) Pooled \(p = 25/30 = 0.833\); \(z = (0.90 - 0.80)/\sqrt{0.833 \times 0.167 \times (1/10 + 1/20)} = 0.10/\sqrt{0.0208} = 0.10/0.144 = 0.69\): compatible with sampling noise.
B3. (a) 1. (b) K562. (c) The two cultures had different numbers of divisions since thawing (methylation in partially methylated domains drifts with divisions), and subclones can take over a culture (different epialleles, copy-number changes); EBV-transformed lines are oligoclonal. (Different handling and DNA extraction add technical variation.) (d) 5% (by definition of a valid test under the null); 17% means the test is badly anticonservative.
B4. (a) Gaps: 60, 50, 40, | 250 |, 30, 40, | 430 |, | 100 |, 80, 70, 80, 30, 30. Regions: {5000–5150}: 4 CpGs, 150 bp → DMR; {5400–5470}: 3 CpGs, 70 bp → DMR; {5900}: 1 CpG → rejected (the gap to 6000 is exactly 100, not less than 100); {6000–6290}: 6 CpGs, 290 bp → DMR. (b) Yes: with a 300-bp rule 5150 and 5400 (gap 250) merge into 5000–5470 with 7 significant and 4 non-significant CpGs: 7/11 = 64% significant, above DSS’s 50% rule, so one region. The rules decide whether one long or two short regions are reported.
B5. (a) \(25 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-3} = 25\,000\). (b) DSS’s threshold is applied to CpGs; DMRs are built afterwards from the significant CpGs, so the proportion of false DMRs is not controlled (one false region can contain many correlated false CpGs, and region boundaries are chosen after seeing the data). (c) dmrseq scores candidate regions with generalised least squares on transformed proportions, accounting for spatial correlation. It pools null statistics across regions and label permutations rather than testing each region against its own few permutations. This supports region-level inference with at least two samples per group; more replicates improve power and robustness. See the dmrseq documentation.
B6. (a) 4 803 lower, 258 higher in K562. (b) Losses: 68% overlap K562 low domains (background 46.5%); depleted at CGIs (2.0% vs 7.1%) and promoters (1.8% vs 4.9%). Gains: enriched at CGIs (9.7%) and promoters (6.6%), almost absent from low domains (3.1%). (c) A low domain of several hundred kb is one event (one region that lost methylation), but the merging rule cuts it into many DMRs wherever two significant CpGs are 100 bp or more apart.
B7. (a) Each group is one cell line; the replicates are cultures of the same cells. A significant DMR means that the two cultures differ more than replicate cultures do; it says nothing about B cells vs erythroid cells in general, or about which of the many differences between the lines (donor, lineage, EBV, leukaemia, karyotype) causes it. (b) Blood cell-type composition (smoking raises neutrophils), age, sex, genotype at CpG-SNPs/meQTLs, batch/processing day, conversion and coverage differences, and with 4 vs 4 the weak region-level error control. (c) Small effects need many samples (hundreds) for power, which favours cheap per-sample platforms (arrays, targeted methods) over WGBS; large cell-type effects are found with a few samples.
B8. Gains of methylation at CpG-island promoters go with silencing: once a CGI promoter is methylated it is stably off (or it was silenced first and then methylated). Most losses of promoter methylation lie in large domains that lost methylation in K562 at genes silent in both lines; losing methylation does not activate a gene without the right transcription factors. To test ITGB2 in K562: demethylate its promoter with dCas9-TET1 (or treat with decitabine, less specific) and measure expression; conversely methylate it in GM12878 with dCas9-DNMT3A(-3L) and see if expression drops.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) The file is BED (0-based start) and lists each strand’s C. The + strand C at 0-based start \(s\) is at 1-based position \(s+1\); the − strand C of the same CpG is one base to the right, at 0-based \(s+1\), so its start is already the 1-based position of the + strand C. Both get the same pos. (b) GM12878 rep1 350 466 CpGs, 0.458; rep2 349 682, 0.511; K562 rep1 346 903, 0.230; rep2 350 620, 0.256. K562 is half as methylated as GM12878; the GM12878 replicates differ by 0.05 overall, the K562 replicates by 0.03. (17 s.)
C2. 168 666 CpGs have ≥ 10 reads in all four samples (31 710 in only one, 44 932 in two, 68 990 in three). A per-CpG test requiring 10 reads everywhere discards about half of the CpGs. Smoothing uses the reads of neighbouring CpGs, so CpGs with few reads still contribute to a regional estimate.









Solutions — R





R1. 366 640 CpGs: the union of all CpGs covered in at least one sample (samples with 0 reads at a CpG get N = 0).
R2. (a) GM12878 3.44, K562 1.05. (b) \(|z| > 1.96\): GM12878 30%, K562 3% (expected 5%; slightly below because small integer counts make the test conservative).
R3. 3 569 of 50 000 CpGs at FDR < 0.05 (7%), and 17% with \(p < 0.05\), between two replicates of the same cell line. Pooling turns sample-to-sample variation into “significance”; a model with a dispersion parameter and samples as replicates is needed.
R4. (a) mu1, mu2: smoothed mean levels of group 1 (GM12878) and 2 (K562); diff = mu1 − mu2; phi1, phi2: estimated (shrunken) dispersions per group. (b) Median φ 0.15 for GM12878 and 0.05 for K562: GM12878’s replicates are more variable, as in R2. (c) 87 108 DMLs (|Δβ| > 0.2, p < \(10^{-5}\)); 82 788 lower in K562 (diff > 0), 4 320 higher. About 1 minute on 4 cores.
R5. (a) 5 061 DMRs: 4 803 lower in K562 (median 416 bp, 10 CpGs, 3.25 Mb in total) and 258 higher (median 495 bp, 7 CpGs, 0.19 Mb). (b) All five are long (9–25 kb, 187–337 CpGs) and lower in K562 (≈ 0.9 in GM12878 vs 0.03–0.14 in K562): stretches near 36.2 Mb and 41.4 Mb, in domains that K562 lost almost completely.
R6. (a) Losses: CGI 2.0%, promoter 1.8%, low domain 68% vs background 7.1%, 4.9%, 46.5%: enriched in low domains, depleted at islands and promoters. Gains: CGI 9.7%, promoter 6.6%, low domain 3.1%: enriched at islands and promoters, nearly absent from low domains. (b) Only tested CpGs could become DMRs; the tested set is not uniform over the chromosome (coverage, CpG density), so the fair comparison is with what could have been found.
R7. (a) No DMR: 143 genes, median log2 FC 0.02, 2 down and 26 up. Lower in K562: 63 genes, median 0, 7 down and 7 up. Higher in K562: 11 genes, median 0, 5 down and 1 up. (b) ITGB2 (16.8 → 0.2 TPM; CD18, a leukocyte integrin expressed in B cells), IFNGR2, CBR3, CBR1, MAP3K7CL; ITGB2, CBR1 and CBR3 have CGI promoters. Five other genes with promoter gains (e.g. OLIG1, RIPK4) are silent in both lines. (c) Spearman 0.14 between promoter Δβ and expression change: most promoter DMRs are at genes silent in both lines, and expression has many other determinants.
R8. (a) FDR < 0.05: 255 128 CpGs with smoothing vs 125 863 without; DMRs without smoothing: 2 127 (instead of 5 061); with delta 0.4: 1 880. Smoothing roughly doubles the power on 10–20x data; a stricter delta keeps the large differences. The direction and location of the main changes do not depend on these choices. (b) DSS reports 1-based positions; BED starts are 0-based.

title: Exercise: Differential methylation
text:
Where this leads

Methylation arrays uses the same ideas with a linear model on M-values (limma) and region finders such as DMRcate; cell-type composition is handled there.
Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers uses many small, consistent differences (age, disease) rather than DMRs.
Epigenetics in disease and therapy returns to CpG-island hypermethylation and domain hypomethylation in cancer.
Linking regulatory elements to genes asks which distal DMRs (enhancers) regulate which genes.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
About this lecture
DNA methylation biology showed per-CpG methylation levels of GM12878. This lecture shows how such numbers are made, and what can go wrong on the way.

Bisulfite chemistry: unmethylated C becomes T; 5mC (and 5hmC) stay C.
Libraries and alignment: four strands, directional libraries, alignment in a three-letter alphabet with Bismark.
Quality control: M-bias, conversion efficiency, duplicates, coverage.
From reads to per-CpG calls, and how they compare with ENCODE’s.
Pitfalls: SNPs that look like unmethylated CpGs.
The alternatives: RRBS, EM-seq, TAPS, and where arrays and long reads fit.


This is the processing unit of the methylation block, the counterpart of From reads to coverage for enrichment assays for ChIP and ATAC. Everything shown on the real-data slides comes from the exercise: 360 142 reads from ENCODE’s GM12878 whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), the reads that ENCODE aligned to a 2 Mb region of chr21, processed end to end with fastp and Bismark in about five minutes. The general logic (trim, align, deduplicate, count) is the one students know from enrichment assays; spend the time on what is different: the chemistry, the three-letter alignment, and the QC plots specific to bisulfite.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
5mC is invisible to sequencing


Polymerases copy 5mC as C, and sequencers read it as C: the methylation of a molecule is lost in PCR and in sequencing.
Either turn methylation into a sequence difference first (bisulfite, enzymes), or read the native molecule (nanopore, PacBio: Methylation and chromatin from long reads).
Older methods used methylation-sensitive restriction enzymes or antibodies against 5mC (MeDIP); they give regional, not single-base, information.


The problem in one picture. The two molecules have the same sequence and differ only in the methyl group at one CpG; after PCR the information is gone. After bisulfite treatment the unmethylated molecule has a T where the methylated one keeps a C. Methylation-sensitive restriction (HpaII vs its methylation-insensitive isoschizomer MspI) was the first genome-scale approach; MeDIP (immunoprecipitation with an anti-5mC antibody) is like ChIP for methylated DNA and was used before WGBS became affordable. Both survive in niche uses; WGBS is the reference method, arrays are the workhorse of population studies (Methylation arrays).

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Bisulfite chemistry


Bisulfite adds to C; the adduct deaminates to uracil-sulfonate; alkali removes the sulfonate; PCR copies U as T.
5mC reacts about 100 times more slowly and stays C. 5hmC forms a stable adduct (CMS) and also reads as C.
Harsh conditions (low pH, heat, hours): most of the DNA is fragmented and lost, and conversion must be > 99% to be useful.


Frommer et al. 1992 (key paper) introduced bisulfite genomic sequencing. Conditions differ between kits, but typically DNA is denatured and incubated with sodium bisulfite at pH 5 and 50–65 °C for hours. The damage is real: depurination and strand breaks destroy 80–95% of input DNA, which is why bisulfite libraries need more input or post-bisulfite adapter tagging (PBAT), and why enzymatic alternatives were developed. Two consequences for data analysis follow from this slide. Incomplete conversion turns unmethylated C into apparent methylation, so it must be measured (conversion slide). And 5hmC is counted as methylated (DNA methylation biology); 5fC and 5caC convert like C.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
One molecule, four strands


After conversion the two strands are no longer complementary: each is its own template.
PCR makes a complementary copy of each: four possible strands in the library.
Standard WGBS kits are directional: read 1 always comes from OT or OB, which halves the alignment work.


This slide explains Bismark’s default directional mode versus –non_directional and –pbat. In a directional library methylated adapters are ligated before bisulfite treatment, so the adapter orientation records which original strand a fragment came from; read 1 reads OT or OB, read 2 reads the complementary strands. A non-directional library can yield all four strands. Standard post-bisulfite adapter tagging (PBAT) instead yields read 1 from CTOT or CTOB, and Bismark’s –pbat mode searches those two strands. Some modified PBAT protocols yield non-directional libraries: choose the mode from the actual protocol, not just when adapters were added. Aligning a four-strand non-directional library as directional loses roughly half the reads; using directional mode on a standard PBAT library can lose nearly all. See Bismark’s library options. Our exercise reads are read 1 of a directional library: Bismark finds only OT and OB alignments, as expected (158 877 and 157 074).

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Reading a converted read


Compare each read with the reference: where the reference has a C, a C in the read means methylated, a T means unmethylated.
Bismark writes one symbol per base in the XM tag of the BAM file; upper case = methylated.
The level of a CpG is the fraction of reads with C: \beta = M / (M + U).


This is the core of every by-hand question in this unit: given a reference and some aligned reads, count C and T at each CpG. The XM string is a compact record of every call in a read: z/Z for CpG, x/X for CHG, h/H for CHH, u/U for unknown context, a dot for non-C positions. Note that a T can also be a C-to-T SNP or a sequencing error, and a C at a non-CpG position is usually a failure of conversion rather than methylation in mammals. For reads from the bottom strand (OB), the comparison is done on the bottom strand: Bismark handles that and reports the call at the genomic position.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Bisulfite reads look strange


Our 360 142 reads (GM12878, read 1): 1.5% C and 48.5% T, against 20.4% C and 29.6% T in the genome.
Almost all remaining Cs are in CpG context: the methylated ones.
Low complexity breaks normal tools: quality metrics complain, and a normal aligner sees many mismatches.


A quick check that every student should do on any bisulfite FASTQ (exercise C1). Read 1 of a directional library comes from OT or OB, which are both C-depleted; G content stays near the genome’s. Read 2 would show the complement: few G, many A. If a “bisulfite” FASTQ has normal base composition, it was not converted, or it is read 2 of the complementary strands. FastQC flags these libraries as failing per-base content; that is expected. The low complexity also means that fewer reads align uniquely than in a normal library: two regions that differ only at C positions become identical after conversion.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Alignment in three letters


Convert all C to T in the read, and make two converted copies of the genome (C→T and G→A).
Align with a normal aligner (bowtie2) to both; keep the read only if it has a unique best alignment.
Then compare the original read with the original genome to call methylation.


This is the Bismark strategy (Krueger & Andrews 2011, key paper). By converting both sides, methylation no longer causes mismatches, so the aligner is unbiased between methylated and unmethylated reads. The cost is a reduced alphabet, more multi-mapping reads, and twice the index (two converted genomes; four alignments for non-directional libraries). An alternative family of aligners (bwa-meth, BSMAP, gemBS which ENCODE used for these data) use similar in-silico conversion with different aligners or seeding tricks. bwa-meth is often faster and maps a few % more reads; in practice results are very similar, as the comparison with ENCODE later in this lecture shows.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
section: Bismark: from FASTQ to per-CpG calls
text:
Bismark: from FASTQ to per-CpG calls

bismark_genome_preparation genome                  # once per genome
bismark --genome genome trimmed.fastq.gz
deduplicate_bismark --bam trimmed_bismark_bt2.bam
bismark_methylation_extractor --gzip --bedGraph trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated.bam
coverage2cytosine --merge_CpG --genome_folder genome -o gm_cpg *.bismark.cov.gz

The whole exercise pipeline. Run times on 8 server threads for our 360 000 reads: index 48 s, alignment 59 s, deduplication 11 s, extraction 26 s, strand merging 69 s; a laptop is two to three times slower. A full human WGBS sample (300–600 million read pairs) takes one to two days on a node with Bismark, which is why production pipelines (later slide) parallelise over chunks. The extractor writes one file per context and strand, an M-bias table, a splitting report with conversion statistics, and a coverage file (chromosome, position, % methylated, count methylated, count unmethylated). coverage2cytosine with –merge_CpG adds up the two strands of each CpG. The trimming step comes first and is shown in the exercise (fastp with the Illumina adapter).

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
What happened to our reads


fastp removed 6% (low quality), and trimmed adapters from 36 808 reads.
Bismark aligned 93.5% uniquely; only 379 reads were ambiguous.
19.4% were duplicates (same start and strand); 254 533 reads remain.


Honesty about the shortcut: 93.5% is much higher than a real WGBS library (typically 60–80% unique alignment to the whole genome), because these reads were selected as the ones ENCODE had already aligned to this region, and we align them to chr21 only. Reads from elsewhere in the genome are not in our file, so they cannot mis-align to chr21; in a real analysis always align to the whole genome. The duplicate rate is also inflated: the region is small and deeply covered, so independent fragments share start positions by chance more often than across the whole genome. The 21 757 reads with no alignment are reads that ENCODE’s aligner (GEM3) placed, often with MAPQ 0, but bowtie2 under Bismark’s stricter scoring did not.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Duplicates


In WGBS, reads with the same start and strand are probably PCR copies of one molecule: keep one (deduplicate_bismark).
In RRBS (and amplicon methods), fragments start at the same restriction site by design: do not deduplicate.
Duplicates inflate coverage without adding information: a CpG seen 20 times in one molecule’s copies has really one observation.


The same logic as in From reads to coverage for enrichment assays, with one twist: deduplication matters more for methylation than for coverage tracks, because the statistic is a proportion. Ten PCR copies of one methylated molecule look like ten independent methylated reads and give false confidence (a β of 1 with “20 reads” instead of 2). For paired-end data, both ends define a duplicate, which is more reliable. Unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) solve the RRBS problem in some protocols.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Where M-bias comes from


Sheared fragments are end-repaired before adapter ligation; the polymerase fills gaps with unmethylated dCTP.
The filled-in bases are read at the start of read 2: their CpGs look unmethylated.
Other read-end artefacts: adapter remnants, random-primer bias (PBAT), low quality at 3’ ends.


Methylation of a CpG cannot depend on where in the read it is observed, so any trend of methylation along the read is a technical artefact: that is the idea of the M-bias plot (Hansen et al. 2012 introduced it with BSmooth; Bismark computes it). The end-repair artefact is the classic one: fragment ends are blunted by a polymerase that synthesises new DNA, and new DNA is unmethylated; in a directional library this new DNA sits at the start of read 2. The fix is to ignore those positions when calling methylation, not to throw away the reads.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Reading an M-bias plot


ENCODE paired-end data (left): read 2 positions 2–4 are at 40–43% vs a plateau of 48%; position 1 jumps to 66%. Read 1 is nearly flat.
Our single-end read 1 (right): flat at about 61% (this region is more methylated than the genome average).
Fix: ignore the biased positions at extraction, e.g. --ignore_r2 4, and check the plot again.


The left plot uses about 3 million random read pairs from ENCODE’s older Bismark alignment of the same GM12878 replicate (the first 800 MB of a 121 GB BAM; data file gm12878_wgbs_pe_mbias.txt). The curve of read 2 drops towards the end because few reads are that long after ENCODE’s trimming, so the estimate gets noisy. The lesson for reading an M-bias plot: find the plateau, find where the curve departs from it, and ignore those positions in both reads. Typical choices are 2–10 bp at the 5’ end of read 2 and sometimes a few at the 3’ end of both. Also check the CHH curve: it should be flat near 0; a rise at the read ends signals the same artefact. Do not trim for wiggles in the middle of the read: with few calls per position they are sampling noise, not bias.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Conversion efficiency





In most mammalian cells non-CpG methylation is near 0. So methylated CHH calls measure failed conversion: here 0.66%, a conversion rate of 99.34%.
A spike-in of unmethylated lambda phage DNA measures it directly, also where CpH methylation is real (neurons, ES cells, plants).
Effect: an unmethylated CpG appears 0.7% methylated; β = 0.5 appears 0.503. ENCODE requires conversion ≥ 98%.



The splitting report gives the numbers: 30 824 methylated of 4 644 038 CHH calls. Incomplete conversion adds a small upward bias to every β: observed = β + (1 − β) × non-conversion rate. At 99.3% this is negligible for most purposes; at 95% (a failed batch) every unmethylated CpG island looks 5% methylated, which can create false differences between batches. Caution: non-CpG methylation is real and abundant in neurons (mCA, written by DNMT3A) and in embryonic stem cells, and of course in plants (CHG, CHH), so there the CHH estimate is not a conversion estimate; use lambda or another unmethylated spike-in. A methylated control (e.g. fully methylated pUC19) checks the opposite error, over-conversion of 5mC.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Coverage and precision


After merging strands, 24 675 CpGs; median 14 reads, 75% with at least 10.
With 14 reads a CpG at β = 0.5 has a 95% interval of about ± 0.26: single CpGs are imprecise.
Remedies: more depth, more replicates, or averaging neighbouring CpGs (Differential methylation).


The binomial standard error is sqrt(β(1 − β)/N); at N = 14 and β = 0.5 that is 0.13, so the 95% interval spans about 0.24 to 0.76. ENCODE’s standard for WGBS is at least 30x coverage per replicate (both strands combined), which halves the interval width compared with 14 reads. Strand merging is valid for CpGs because they are symmetrically methylated almost everywhere; it doubles the reads per site. Never merge strands for non-CpG contexts. A few CpGs have unusually high coverage (copy number gains, repeats, PCR jackpots); analyses often remove the top 0.1% of coverage.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
section: Do our calls agree with ENCODE’s?
text:
Do our calls agree with ENCODE’s?





Same reads, different pipelines: ENCODE used gemBS (GEM3 aligner, its own caller), we used fastp + Bismark.
23 567 CpGs in both; 17 483 with ≥ 10 reads in both: r = 0.997, mean |Δβ| = 0.016.
Only 28% of CpGs have identical counts: trimming, duplicate removal and alignment filters differ slightly.



A reassuring and realistic result: pipelines agree closely on well-covered CpGs, and differences come from details (which reads were filtered as low quality, which duplicates were removed, how soft-clipped ends and MAPQ 0 reads are treated, how the first and last bases are used). Mean read coverage is nearly the same (13.9 vs 14.2 per CpG). The comparison is fair because ENCODE’s per-CpG file for this replicate was made from the same read-1 FASTQ. In a methods section, say which pipeline and which filters you used, and do not mix calls from different pipelines in one differential analysis without checking for a pipeline effect.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
section: SNPs at CpGs look like unmethylated Cs
text:
SNPs at CpGs look like unmethylated Cs


On the strand with the C, a C→T SNP gives exactly the same read as an unmethylated C.
On the other strand the same site is G vs A, which bisulfite does not change: the genotype is visible there.
Tools that use both strands can call SNPs and methylation together (Bis-SNP, gemBS, BISCUIT).


This is the most important bisulfite-specific pitfall for differential analyses between individuals: a CpG that carries a C/T SNP in some people looks partially or fully unmethylated in them, and appears as a “differentially methylated” site that is really a genotype difference. CpG-SNPs are common because CpG is the most mutable dinucleotide in the genome. Practical remedies: remove CpGs that overlap known SNPs (dbSNP above some frequency) or that are called as SNPs in the samples themselves (ENCODE’s gemBS output contains the genotype; column 13 of our per-CpG file); for arrays, manufacturers flag probes over SNPs (Methylation arrays). meQTL studies (Epigenomics and genetic variation) deliberately model genotype effects on methylation.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
SNPs in real data


ENCODE called the genotype of GM12878 at every CpG. In our Bismark calls, CpGs with a heterozygous C/T SNP average 0.38 (vs 0.63), and homozygous C>T sites 0.01.
Other SNPs (C/A, C/G, G/T) change the base to one bisulfite cannot produce, so they are seen as mismatches, not as unmethylated.


Real numbers from the exercise region (CpGs with at least 8 reads). The homozygous sites are not CpGs in this genome at all: there is no cytosine to methylate, yet a naive analysis reports “unmethylated”. The heterozygous sites lose roughly half their methylation signal (0.63 to 0.38; a bit more than half remains because the reference allele reads are unaffected). In a comparison of GM12878 with another person’s cells, all these sites would appear as differences. This is exercise R5.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Reduced representation bisulfite sequencing (RRBS)


MspI (C^CGG) cuts regardless of methylation; short fragments come from CpG-dense DNA: islands and promoters.
Cheap and deep for 1–3 million CpGs, ideal for many samples; blind to most enhancers, gene bodies and PMDs.
Analysis differences: Trim Galore --rrbs, no deduplication, and only regions covered in all samples can be compared.


RRBS (Meissner et al. 2005, key paper) enriches CpG-rich sequence with a restriction enzyme whose site contains a CpG; size selection of 40–220 bp keeps the fragments from dense regions. A small fraction of the sequencing cost of WGBS for 5–10% of CpGs, but those include most CpG-island promoters, which is why RRBS was used in many cancer and mouse studies, and in ENCODE’s early phase (GM12878 and K562 have RRBS data too). Its main limitations: low coverage of the regulatory regions that differ most between cell types (distal enhancers are CpG-poor), and fragment-start artefacts handled by the –rrbs trimming mode. Enhanced RRBS uses several enzymes for broader coverage.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
EM-seq and TAPS: without bisulfite


EM-seq: TET2 and T4-BGT protect 5mC and 5hmC; APOBEC3A deaminates the unprotected C. Same readout as bisulfite, so the same pipeline (Bismark works unchanged).
TAPS: only modified Cs change (to T). Reads keep four letters: better alignment, less sequencing wasted.
Both damage DNA much less: lower input, more uniform coverage, fewer duplicates.


EM-seq (Vaisvila et al. 2021, key paper) is now widely used where input is limited (cell-free DNA, clinical samples, single cells) and is a drop-in replacement for bisulfite in analysis. TAPS (Liu et al. 2019, key paper) reverses the logic: TET oxidation of 5mC and 5hmC to 5caC, then pyridine borane reduction to dihydrouracil, which polymerases read as T. Because only the 2–5% of cytosines that are modified change, the reads stay close to the reference; variants (TAPSβ, CAPS) separate 5mC from 5hmC. Newer “6-base” methods read A, C, G, T, 5mC and 5hmC in one library. Whatever the chemistry, per-CpG output is the same table of methylated and unmethylated counts.

More replicates usually beat more depth: biological variation between samples is larger than sampling noise at 10–15x.


Help students match questions to assays; it is a classic exam question (“you have 2 ng of cell-free DNA from 200 patients…”). WGBS is the only unbiased method; RRBS and arrays answer most questions about promoters and CpG islands cheaply; arrays dominate population studies (Methylation arrays, Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers). The format zoo is a practical source of errors. The Bismark coverage file is 1-based and has no strand column; the merged file with –zero_based is BED-like; ENCODE’s bed9+ is BED (0-based start) per strand, and the percentage is an integer rounded down, so counts are recovered as round(N × pct / 100), exact for coverage below 50 (DNA methylation biology exercise). Most R packages (bsseq, DSS, methylKit) want, for each CpG and sample, the number of methylated reads and the total: everything else is bookkeeping.

title: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq)
text:
Production pipelines and QC

nf-core/methylseq: trimming, Bismark or bwa-meth + MethylDackel, deduplication, M-bias, MultiQC report; runs on SLURM.
gemBS (used by ENCODE for these data), BISCUIT: fast, call SNPs and methylation together.
QC numbers to report: reads, unique alignment rate, duplication, conversion rate, M-bias decision, mean coverage per CpG, fraction of CpGs ≥ 10x.

nextflow run nf-core/methylseq -profile singularity --input samples.csv --genome GRCh38 --outdir results

After doing every step by hand on 360 000 reads, students should know what the pipeline does with 500 million. nf-core/methylseq is the standard: its default aligner is Bismark (as in the exercise); bwa-meth with MethylDackel is a faster alternative that also produces M-bias plots and lets the user set inclusion bounds per read position. The QC list is the bisulfite equivalent of the enrichment-assay QC in Experimental design and QC for epigenomic assays. For our exercise: 93.5% unique (inflated by preselection), 19.4% duplicates, 99.34% conversion, no M-bias trimming needed for read 1, median 14 reads per CpG.

title: Quiz: DNA methylation biology
text:
Short questions on the enzymes, reprogramming, the methylation landscape, imprinting, X inactivation and plants. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Which enzyme copies a methylation pattern after DNA replication, which protein brings it to the right place, and what does that protein recognise?






Hint





After replication the new strand is unmethylated.









Answer





DNMT1, brought by UHRF1. UHRF1 recognises a hemimethylated CpG (5mC on the old strand, C on the new strand) with its SRA domain, and H3K9me2/3 with its TTD domain; it ubiquitylates histone H3, which recruits and activates DNMT1. DNMT3A and DNMT3B methylate de novo.




Q2. A study of mouse cerebellum uses whole-genome bisulfite sequencing and reports that a set of neuronal genes is “highly methylated in their gene bodies”. What is the problem, and how would you address it?






Answer





Bisulfite cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC: both read as C. Neurons have a lot of 5hmC, especially in the bodies of active genes, so part of the “methylation” is probably 5hmC. Use a method that separates them: oxidative bisulfite (oxBS: 5hmC then reads as T, so BS − oxBS = 5hmC), TAB-seq, or long-read sequencing that calls 5mC and 5hmC separately.




Q3. A cell population is 80% methylated at a set of CpGs. Maintenance stops completely. What is the level after 3 divisions? What if DNMT1 still copies with efficiency 0.9?






Hint





Each division multiplies the level by \((1+e)/2\).









Answer





Without maintenance: \(0.8 \times 0.5^3 = 0.10\). With \(e = 0.9\): \(0.8 \times 0.95^3 = 0.8 \times 0.857 = 0.69\).




Q4. Most of the genome is demethylated in the mouse blastocyst. Name two kinds of sequence that stay methylated, and for one of them the mechanism.






Answer





Imprinting control regions (germline DMRs): ZFP57 (ZNF445 in human) binds the methylated allele and recruits KAP1, SETDB1 (H3K9me3) and DNMT1/UHRF1, protecting it. Some young retrotransposons (e.g. mouse IAP elements) also partly resist, through KRAB zinc-finger proteins and KAP1/SETDB1. Imprints are erased in primordial germ cells; some IAP copies partly resist that second wave too, as shown in the mouse PGC methylome study.




Q5. A 300-bp sequence has 80 C, 84 G and 20 CpG. Is it a CpG island by the classic criteria?






Answer





GC \(= 164/300 = 54.7\%\) (> 50%). CpG o/e \(= 20 \times 300 / (80 \times 84) = 6000/6720 = 0.89\) (> 0.6). Length ≥ 200 bp. Yes.




Q6. Across genes in a cell type, is DNA methylation positively or negatively correlated with expression? Answer separately for CpG-island promoters and for gene bodies, and give a mechanism for each.






Answer





Promoters: negative. Active CGI promoters carry H3K4me3, which blocks the ADD domain of DNMT3A/B, and are bound by CXXC proteins and TFs; a methylated CGI promoter is stably silent (methylation blocks methyl-sensitive TFs and recruits MBD proteins). Gene bodies: positive. Transcription leaves H3K36me3 (SETD2), which recruits DNMT3B through its PWWP domain. In the GM12878 chr21 data, body methylation is 0.82–0.84 in expressed genes and 0.46 in silent ones.




Q7. What are partially methylated domains (PMDs)? In which of these samples do you expect the deepest PMDs: sperm, a blood sample, a long-term cultured cancer cell line? Why?






Answer





Large (100 kb to Mb) late-replicating, lamina-associated, gene-poor domains where CpGs are partially and variably methylated, because maintenance is less efficient there and methylation is lost a little with every division. Deepest in the cancer cell line, which has gone through the most divisions (K562: many chr21 domains below 0.1). Sperm has essentially no PMDs; blood has shallow ones.




Q8. At the H19/IGF2 locus, a child inherits a maternal allele whose imprinting control region is methylated. Predict the expression of both genes from both alleles and the phenotype.






Answer





The methylated maternal ICR cannot bind CTCF, so it behaves like the paternal allele: the enhancers reach IGF2, and H19 is silenced. Both alleles express IGF2 and neither expresses H19: double IGF2 dosage, overgrowth (Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome).




Q9. In Arabidopsis, why does CHH methylation disappear quickly when the RdDM pathway and CMT2 are lost, while CG methylation stays?






Answer





CHH is asymmetric: the other strand has no cytosine at the mirrored position, so replication leaves no methylated template to copy. CHH must be re-established after every replication by targeted enzymes (DRM2 guided by 24-nt siRNAs, or CMT2 guided by H3K9me2). CG is symmetric and copied by MET1 from the old strand, like DNMT1 in mammals.




Q10. What methylation level do you expect at the CpG-island promoter of an X-linked gene that is subject to X inactivation, in female cells and in male cells? And for a gene that escapes X inactivation?






Answer





Female: about 0.5, because the island is methylated on the inactive X and unmethylated on the active X. Male (one active X): about 0. An escape gene is unmethylated on both X chromosomes: about 0 in both sexes. This difference is why X-linked CpG islands separate males from females in methylation data.

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Background
Methylation level. At one cytosine, bisulfite sequencing gives \(M\) reads with a C (methylated) and \(U\) reads with a T (unmethylated). The level, often called β, is
\[ \beta = \frac{M}{M + U} = \frac{M}{N}, \]
a number between 0 and 1 (or a percentage). A CpG is palindromic, so it has a C on each strand; in mammals both are usually in the same state, and the counts of the two strands are often added. How the reads are made and counted is the topic of Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq).
Precision. If the true level is \(p\) and we observe \(N\) reads, the number of methylated reads is roughly binomial, with standard error of \(\hat\beta\) equal to \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}\).
Passive dilution. Without maintenance, each replication halves the fraction of methylated strands: after \(n\) divisions a fully methylated site is at \(0.5^n\). If maintenance copies a methylated site onto the new strand with probability \(e\), the level is multiplied by \((1+e)/2\) per division.
CpG island (Gardiner-Garden & Frommer 1987): at least 200 bp with GC content above 50% and an observed/expected CpG ratio above 0.6, where
\[ \text{CpG o/e} = \frac{\#\text{CpG} \times \text{length}}{\#\text{C} \times \#\text{G}}. \]
Plant contexts. For a C on one strand, look at the next two bases on the same strand: CG; CHG; CHH (H = A, C or T).

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Data
From the course repository:
data/download.sh methylation-biology            # about 30 MB (plus the GTF and H3K4me3 bigWig if not yet present)

D=/path/to/course/data                          # where download.sh put the files

gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz, k562_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz: ENCODE whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), per-CpG calls for chr21 (GRCh38), GM12878 (ENCSR890UQO, file ENCFF570TIL) and K562 (ENCSR765JPC, ENCFF660IHA). One line per cytosine of a CpG per strand. Columns: 1–3 position (BED, 0-based start), 6 strand, 10 number of reads, 11 percent methylated (an integer, rounded down), 12 reference context, 13 context called in this genome (not CG where the cell line has a SNP).
hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz: UCSC CpG islands; columns 2–4 are chromosome, start (0-based), end.
gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz: gene annotation; gm12878_h3k4me3_fc.bigWig: H3K4me3 fold enrichment over input (both used since What is epigenetics?).
gm12878_rna_rep1_genes.tsv: ENCODE RNA-seq gene quantifications for GM12878 (columns gene_id, TPM, …).

Shortcuts, said plainly. We start from ENCODE’s methylation calls, not from reads (the reads are processed in Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing), and we use one chromosome. GM12878 and K562 are cell lines: both carry large hypomethylated domains that a primary tissue would not have, which is part of what this exercise is about.
The R part runs in about 1–2 minutes and needs about 2 GB of memory.
