B6. Read the figures. Use the lecture plots of promoter methylation against H3K4me3 and the PFKL locus.


How many promoters with methylation above 0.6 have strong H3K4me3? What does that suggest?
Give two reasons why a promoter can be unmethylated and still have no H3K4me3.



AIRE is silent in B cells, yet the CpGs around it are not unmethylated. PFKL is active, yet its body is highly methylated. Explain both.
Many dots around AIRE sit at 0.3–0.7. Give a biological and a technical reason for intermediate values.

B7. Judge the claim. A paper reports: “In tumours the promoter CpG island of gene X is methylated (β = 0.7 vs 0.1 in normal tissue) and X is expressed 10-fold less. Methylation silences X and drives tumour formation.”
Give three reasons why the data do not show this, and describe one experiment for each of the two halves of the claim (silencing; driving the tumour).
B8. Plants, mammals, flies. (a) Why can an epiallele in Arabidopsis last for many generations, while a methylation change in a mouse rarely reaches the grandchildren? (b) Fruit flies have essentially no DNA methylation. How do they keep a gene silent through cell divisions?

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
On the command line
You need bedtools (see Install the software you need).

C1 — Look at the per-CpG file
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz | head -3
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz | cut -f6 | sort | uniq -c
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz | awk -F'\t' '$13 != "CG"' | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz | awk -F'\t' '{ n++; s += $10 } END { print n, s / n }'

How many lines are there, and how many per strand? Why does the − strand line of a CpG start 1 bp after the + strand line?
How many lines have a called context other than CG? What could that mean?
What is the mean number of reads per line? Is that enough to measure a single CpG well (B1d)?



C2 — One line per CpG
Combine the strands: the − strand C at position \(s\) belongs to the CpG that starts at \(s-1\).
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz \
  | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$13 == "CG" { s = ($6 == "+") ? $2 : $2 - 1
        N[s] += $10; M[s] += int($10 * $11 / 100 + 0.5) }
      END { for (s in N) print "chr21", s, s + 2, M[s], N[s] }' \
  | sort -k2,2n > gm12878_cpg.bed
head -3 gm12878_cpg.bed; wc -l < gm12878_cpg.bed
awk '{ m += $4; n += $5 } END { printf "read-weighted methylation %.3f\n", m / n }' gm12878_cpg.bed
awk '$5 >= 10 { k++; b = $4 / $5; if (b < 0.2) lo++; else if (b > 0.8) hi++; else mid++ }
     END { printf "CpGs with >= 10 reads: %d  low %.3f  mid %.3f  high %.3f\n", k, lo/k, mid/k, hi/k }' gm12878_cpg.bed

How many CpGs are left? What is the overall methylation of chr21 in GM12878?
What fraction of well-covered CpGs is below 0.2, between, and above 0.8?



C3 — Inside and outside CpG islands
zcat $D/hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$2 == "chr21" { print $2, $3, $4 }' \
  | sort -k2,2n > cgi_chr21.bed
wc -l < cgi_chr21.bed
awk '{ print $3 - $2 }' cgi_chr21.bed | sort -n | awk '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print "median length", a[int(NR/2)], "min", a[1], "max", a[NR] }'
bedtools intersect -u -a gm12878_cpg.bed -b cgi_chr21.bed \
  | awk '$5 >= 10 { m += $4/$5; k++ } END { printf "in CGIs: %d CpGs, mean %.3f\n", k, m/k }'
bedtools intersect -v -a gm12878_cpg.bed -b cgi_chr21.bed \
  | awk '$5 >= 10 { m += $4/$5; k++ } END { printf "outside: %d CpGs, mean %.3f\n", k, m/k }'

How many CpG islands are on chr21, and how long are they?
Compare the mean methylation in and outside islands. Is the difference as large as you expected? (R2 explains why not.)

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
In R
You need data.table, GenomicRanges, rtracklayer and ggplot2 (see Install the software you need).
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(ggplot2)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Read the calls and combine the strands
read_cpg <- function(file) {
  x <- fread(file, header = FALSE, select = c(1, 2, 6, 10, 11, 13),
             col.names = c("chr", "start", "strand", "N", "pct", "call"))
  x <- x[call == "CG"]
  x[, M := round(N * pct / 100)]
  x[, pos := ifelse(strand == "+", start + 1L, start)]      # 1-based C of the + strand
  x[, .(N = sum(N), M = sum(M)), by = .(chr, pos)]
}
gm <- read_cpg(file.path(D, "gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz"))
nrow(gm)
summary(gm$N)
mean(gm$N >= 10)
sum(gm$M) / sum(gm$N)
gm10 <- gm[N >= 10][, beta := M / N]
mean(gm10$beta)

Why is round(N * pct / 100) exact here for coverage below 50, even though the percentage was rounded down?
How many CpGs, what median coverage, and what fraction with at least 10 reads? Compare the read-weighted level (sum(M)/sum(N)) with the mean of β over well-covered CpGs. Why can they differ?



R2 — CpG islands
cgi <- fread(file.path(D, "hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz"), header = FALSE)[V2 == "chr21"]
cgi <- GRanges(cgi$V2, IRanges(cgi$V3 + 1, cgi$V4))
gr <- GRanges(gm10$chr, IRanges(gm10$pos, width = 2), beta = gm10$beta)
gr$cgi <- overlapsAny(gr, cgi)
table(gr$cgi)
tapply(gr$beta, gr$cgi, mean)
ggplot(as.data.frame(mcols(gr)), aes(beta)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05)) +
  facet_wrap(~ cgi, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both)
ov <- findOverlaps(cgi, gr)
cgi_meth <- tapply(gr$beta[subjectHits(ov)], queryHits(ov), mean)
length(cgi_meth)
summary(cgi_meth)
mean(cgi_meth < 0.2); mean(cgi_meth > 0.6)

Describe the two histograms. (b) How many islands have a mean below 0.2, and how many above 0.6? Why might so many chr21 islands be methylated? (Think about where they lie; R3 helps.)



R3 — Promoters, gene bodies, intergenic DNA
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
genes <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
prom <- promoters(genes, upstream = 1000, downstream = 1000)
length(genes); sum(overlapsAny(prom, cgi))
gr$region <- "intergenic"
gr$region[overlapsAny(gr, genes)] <- "gene body"
gr$region[overlapsAny(gr, prom)] <- "promoter"
tab <- as.data.table(mcols(gr))
tab[, .(n = .N, mean = mean(beta), median = median(beta)), by = .(region, cgi)][order(region, cgi)]

What fraction of chr21 protein-coding genes has a CGI promoter? (b) Rank the six groups by median methylation. Which group is lowest, which highest? (c) Which group would you expect to be the most methylated in a primary tissue, and why is it not here?



R4 — Promoter methylation and H3K4me3
pm <- findOverlaps(prom, gr)
prom$meth <- NA_real_; prom$ncpg <- 0L
m <- tapply(gr$beta[subjectHits(pm)], queryHits(pm), mean)
n <- tapply(gr$beta[subjectHits(pm)], queryHits(pm), length)
prom$meth[as.integer(names(m))] <- m
prom$ncpg[as.integer(names(n))] <- n
pr <- prom[prom$ncpg >= 5]
pr$cgi <- overlapsAny(pr, cgi)
k4 <- rtracklayer::summary(BigWigFile(file.path(D, "gm12878_h3k4me3_fc.bigWig")), pr, type = "mean")
pr$k4 <- sapply(k4, function(z) z$score)
length(pr)
cor(pr$meth, pr$k4, method = "spearman")
table(methylated = pr$meth > 0.6, H3K4me3 = pr$k4 > 5)
ggplot(as.data.frame(mcols(pr)), aes(meth, k4 + 1, colour = cgi)) + geom_point() + scale_y_log10()

What is the Spearman correlation? Fill in the 2 × 2 table in words. (b) Why do we require at least 5 covered CpGs per promoter?



R5 — Gene bodies and expression
rna <- fread(file.path(D, "gm12878_rna_rep1_genes.tsv"))[grepl("^ENSG", gene_id)]
rna[, id := sub("\\..*", "", gene_id)]
body <- genes[width(genes) > 5000]
body <- resize(body, width(body) - 2000, fix = "end")     # drop the first 2 kb
body$tpm <- rna$TPM[match(sub("\\..*", "", body$gene_id), rna$id)]
bo <- findOverlaps(body, gr)
body$meth <- NA_real_
bm <- tapply(gr$beta[subjectHits(bo)], queryHits(bo), mean)
body$meth[as.integer(names(bm))] <- bm
b <- as.data.table(mcols(body))[!is.na(tpm) & !is.na(meth)]
b[, expr := cut(tpm, c(-Inf, 0.5, 10, Inf), labels = c("off", "low", "high"))]
b[, .(genes = .N, body_meth = mean(meth)), by = expr][order(expr)]
cor(b$meth, log1p(b$tpm), method = "spearman")

Is body methylation higher or lower in expressed genes? Give the correlation. (b) Why do we drop the first 2 kb of each gene? (c) Does this show that gene-body methylation activates genes?



R6 — Partially methylated domains
k5 <- read_cpg(file.path(D, "k562_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz"))
sum(k5$M) / sum(k5$N)
bins <- rbind(gm[, .(meth = sum(M) / sum(N), n = .N), by = .(bin = pos %/% 1e5)][, cell := "GM12878"],
              k5[, .(meth = sum(M) / sum(N), n = .N), by = .(bin = pos %/% 1e5)][, cell := "K562"])[n >= 50]
ggplot(bins, aes(bin / 10, meth, colour = cell)) + geom_point(size = 0.8) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "chr21 (Mb)", y = "mean methylation per 100 kb")
w <- dcast(bins, bin ~ cell, value.var = "meth")[!is.na(GM12878) & !is.na(K562)]
nrow(w); sum(w$K562 < 0.1)
w[, .(GM12878 = mean(GM12878)), by = .(K562_low = K562 < 0.1)]
cor(w$GM12878, w$K562)
genes$bin <- start(genes) %/% 1e5
genes$tpm <- rna$TPM[match(sub("\\..*", "", genes$gene_id), rna$id)]
g <- as.data.table(mcols(genes))[, .(bin, tpm)][w, on = "bin", nomatch = 0]
g[, .(genes = .N, median_tpm = median(tpm, na.rm = TRUE), expressed = mean(tpm > 1, na.rm = TRUE)),
  by = .(K562_low = K562 < 0.1)]

What is the overall methylation of chr21 in K562? (b) How many 100-kb bins are below 0.1 in K562, and how methylated are the same bins in GM12878? (c) Are genes in those domains expressed in GM12878? What does that suggest about the domains? (d) Name two properties of partially methylated domains that are not in these data.

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — levels, strands and precision (B1, C2, R1)





β = methylated / all reads. A percentage rounded down hides at most 1 percentage point, so \(N \cdot \text{pct}/100\) is within \(N/100\) of the true count. The binomial standard error is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}\). The ENCODE WGBS pipeline describes the files; data.table’s fread reads gzipped files directly.









Hint 2 — dilution (B2)





Each division multiplies the level by \((1+e)/2\). So after \(n\) divisions: \(\beta_n = \beta_0 \left(\frac{1+e}{2}\right)^n\), and \(x^n = e^{n \ln x}\). The lecture slides on maintenance and on partially methylated domains give the biology.









Hint 3 — CpG islands and contexts (B3, B4)





Expected CpGs = #C × #G / length. The criteria are from Gardiner-Garden & Frommer 1987; UCSC’s CpG island track explains its variant. For a C, read the next two bases on the same strand, 5’ to 3’. The plant enzymes are reviewed in Law & Jacobsen 2010.









Hint 4 — imprinting (B5)





Draw the two alleles as in the lecture and ask, for each: is the ICR methylated, does CTCF bind, which gene do the enhancers reach? UPD = both copies from one parent. Bell & Felsenfeld 2000 is short and readable.









Hint 5 — intervals in R (R2–R6)





overlapsAny, findOverlaps and promoters are explained in the GenomicRanges vignette and in Genomic intervals. The UCSC table has a 0-based start; add 1 for GRanges. rtracklayer::summary on a BigWigFile returns the mean signal in each range. bedtools intersect -u/-v keeps features with/without an overlap (manual).









Hint 6 — interpretation (B6, B7, R5, R6)





Correlation across genes is not cause. For each claim ask: what came first, is there a confounder (cell type, tumour purity, proliferation), and which perturbation would test it (demethylating drugs, dCas9-TET1, dCas9-DNMT3A)? Partially methylated domains: Lister et al. 2009, Zhou et al. 2018.

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) + strand \(9/12 = 0.75\); − strand \(5/8 = 0.625\); combined \(14/20 = 0.70\). (b) \(7 \times 0.42 = 2.94\), so 3 methylated reads (\(3/7 = 42.9\%\), rounded down to 42). (c) Hemimethylation (e.g. just after replication, or where maintenance failed), and a SNP that destroys the CpG on one allele or one strand (the C/T or G/A change then looks like a methylation call). Also non-CpG contexts in plants, which are not symmetric. (d) \(\sqrt{0.5 \cdot 0.5/14} = 0.134\). A 95% interval of about ±0.26 around 0.5 reaches 0.76: a single CpG at 14 reads cannot reliably tell 0.5 from 0.8. This is why analyses average over neighbouring CpGs (Differential methylation).
B2. (a) 37.5%, 18.8%, 9.4%, 4.7%: 4 divisions. Mouse PGCs divide several times between E7.5 and E13.5, so passive dilution alone can explain most of the erasure; TET1/2 finish specific regions such as imprints. (b) Factor per division \((1 + 0.95)/2 = 0.975\). After 20: \(0.975^{20} = e^{-0.506} = 0.60\), so $0.8 = $ 0.48. After 50: \(e^{-1.27} = 0.28\), so 0.23. (c) \((1.999/2)^{50} = 0.9995^{50} \approx 0.975\): 0.78. Real tissues stay methylated because maintenance is very accurate in most of the genome, and DNMT3A/3B re-methylate sites that maintenance missed. Slow loss shows first where maintenance is least efficient: late-replicating heterochromatin, i.e. partially methylated domains, which deepen with the number of divisions.
B3. (a) A: GC \(= 216/400 = 54\%\); o/e $= 30 /(110 ) = 12,000/11,660 = $ 1.03: an island. B: GC \(= 182/400 = 45.5\%\); o/e $= 8 /(90 ) = 3200/8280 = $ 0.39: not an island (fails both criteria). (b) \(90 \times 92/400 = 20.7\) expected, 8 observed. Methylated CpGs mutate to TpG (and CpA on the other strand) by spontaneous deamination of 5mC to T, which repair does not always fix; over evolutionary time CpGs that were methylated in the germ line are lost. Islands were unmethylated in the germ line and kept theirs.
B4. (a) C2: CG (CGT); C6: CHG (CAG); C9: CHH (CCA); C10: CHH (CAT); C14: CG (CGC); C16: CHG (CAG). (b) C2 and C14: MET1; C6 and C16: CMT3 (with H3K9me2); C9 and C10: DRM2 (RdDM) or CMT2. (c) C9 and C10 (CHH). A CHH site has no C on the opposite strand at the mirrored position (the complement of HH is DD, never a G-paired C), so after replication there is no methylated template strand to copy: the mark must be re-made by targeting (siRNAs for DRM2, H3K9me2 for CMT2) every cycle. CG and CHG are symmetric and copied from the old strand.
B5. (a) Both alleles now look paternal: no CTCF, enhancers reach IGF2 on both, H19 silent on both. Two active IGF2 copies: overgrowth (a cause of Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome). (b) The same: two paternal copies, biallelic IGF2, no H19: overgrowth (paternal UPD of 11p15 is a common cause of Beckwith–Wiedemann). (c) On the paternal allele the ICR is methylated and CTCF does not bind anyway, so deleting its sites changes nothing. On the maternal allele CTCF binding is what insulates IGF2; without the sites the enhancers reach IGF2, which is now expressed from both alleles. (d) The paternal ICR becomes unmethylated, CTCF binds it, and the paternal allele behaves maternally: Igf2 is silenced on both alleles (and H19 expressed from both), giving growth restriction (a Silver–Russell-like pattern).
B6. (a) None of the 28 promoters above 0.6 has H3K4me3 enrichment above 5. Promoter methylation and H3K4me3 are mutually exclusive, consistent with H3K4me3 blocking DNMT3 and methylation excluding CFP1/SET1, but the plot alone does not say which comes first. (b) A silent CpG-island promoter covered by Polycomb (H3K27me3, unmethylated thanks to KDM2B/TET); a non-CGI promoter that is simply inactive; an alternative promoter of a gene that uses another TSS. (c) AIRE/DNMT3L lie in a partially methylated domain: late-replicating, inactive DNA where maintenance slowly fails, giving scattered intermediate levels rather than “unmethylated”. PFKL is transcribed: H3K36me3 from elongation recruits DNMT3B and the body is methylated; only its promoter island is unmethylated. (d) Biological: cells in the population differ (heterogeneity), allele-specific methylation, or partial loss in a PMD. Technical: few reads (with 10–20 reads, 0.3–0.7 is within sampling error of each other; B1d), and mapping errors.
B7. Reasons: (1) correlation only: methylation may follow silencing (e.g. the gene was already Polycomb-repressed in the cell of origin; CGI methylation often comes last); (2) confounding by cell composition: the tumour and the normal tissue contain different cell types and different tumour purity, so methylation and expression differences may both reflect composition; (3) the gene may be silenced by other means (deletion, mutation, a transcription factor lost), and methylation is a passenger; (4) with one gene and many tested, selection bias. Experiments: for silencing, demethylate the promoter in tumour cells (decitabine, or targeted dCas9-TET1) and see if X comes back, or methylate it in normal cells (dCas9-DNMT3A) and see if X goes off; for driving the tumour, restore X in tumour cells (or knock it out in normal cells) and measure growth, ideally in vivo.
B8. (a) Mammals erase almost all methylation twice per generation (early embryo, germ line), so a change rarely survives; Arabidopsis maintains CG methylation through meiosis and gametogenesis and reinforces non-CG methylation by RdDM, so an epiallele can persist (and occasionally revert). (b) By Polycomb repression (H3K27me3 written by PRC2, read and spread by the read–write loop), by H3K9 methylation and HP1 heterochromatin, and in the germ line by small RNAs (piRNAs).









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 711 175 lines: 355 322 on +, 355 853 on −. A CpG is 5’-CG-3’ on the top strand; on the bottom strand the C pairs with the G, which is 1 bp to the right (also 5’-CG-3’ when read on that strand). (b) 29 999 lines have another called context (e.g. CR, YG, CA, TG): the cell line carries a SNP at that CpG on one or both alleles. A C→T SNP looks exactly like an unmethylated C in bisulfite data (Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing), so these are best removed. (c) 7.3 reads per line, i.e. about 14 per CpG after combining strands: enough for broad patterns, not for precise single-CpG values.
C2. (a) 350 466 CpGs; read-weighted methylation 0.458 (a typical somatic tissue is 0.7–0.8; this cell line is low). (b) 260 663 CpGs with ≥ 10 reads: 38.5% low, 27.4% intermediate, 34.2% high.
C3. (a) 446 islands on chr21, median 476 bp (202 bp to 9 174 bp). (b) In islands 6 130 CpGs with mean 0.350; outside 254 533 CpGs with mean 0.469. The difference is smaller than the textbook picture because many chr21 islands are not at promoters and are methylated, and because much of the DNA outside islands is in hypomethylated domains.









Solutions — R





Run time about 1 minute on one core.
R1. (a) The stored percentage is \(\lfloor 100 M/N \rfloor\), so \(N \cdot \text{pct}/100\) lies in \((M - N/100, M]\); for \(N < 50\) that interval is narrower than 0.5 and rounding recovers \(M\) exactly. (b) 350 466 CpGs; coverage median 14 (range 1–143); 74% have ≥ 10 reads. Read-weighted level 0.458; mean β over CpGs with ≥ 10 reads 0.466. The first weights each CpG by its coverage, the second weights all well-covered CpGs equally; they differ if coverage correlates with methylation (e.g. GC-rich, unmethylated islands are covered differently).
R2. (a) Outside islands: a peak at 0, a broad shoulder of intermediate values and a peak near 1. Inside islands: a tall peak at 0 and a smaller one near 1. (b) Of 308 islands with covered CpGs, 39% have a mean below 0.2 and 45% above 0.6 (median 0.52). Many chr21 islands are not at promoters: 126 of 446 overlap a protein-coding promoter. Others are intragenic, intergenic or in repeats near the centromere, and such “orphan” islands are often methylated, especially in cell lines.
R3. (a) 126 of 220 = 57%. (b) Median: CGI promoter 0.00 < non-CGI promoter 0.11 < intergenic non-CGI 0.29 < gene body CGI 0.60 ≈ intergenic CGI 0.62 < gene body non-CGI 0.69. (c) In a primary tissue intergenic DNA is as high as gene bodies (about 0.8). Here it is low because much of chr21’s intergenic DNA lies in partially methylated domains (R6).
R4. (a) 208 promoters, Spearman −0.60. Of promoters with methylation ≤ 0.6, 73 have strong H3K4me3 and 107 do not; of the 28 above 0.6, none has strong H3K4me3. (b) A promoter mean over 1–4 CpGs, each with 10–20 reads, is very noisy (B1d); and promoters with few CpGs are mostly non-CGI, where the averaging also mixes very different sites.
R5. (a) Higher: off 0.46 (57 genes), low 0.82 (74), high 0.84 (19); Spearman +0.69 between body methylation and log expression. (b) The first 2 kb contain the promoter and the unmethylated start of the gene, which go the opposite way and would dilute the body signal. (c) No: body methylation follows transcription (H3K36me3 recruits DNMT3B). Also, many silent genes lie in hypomethylated domains (R6), which is a third factor behind the correlation.
R6. (a) 0.230. (b) 203 of 374 bins are below 0.1 in K562; the same bins average 0.32 in GM12878 vs 0.52 in the others (correlation between the cell lines across bins 0.66). (c) No: 94 genes lie in these bins, median TPM 0, only 7% with TPM > 1, against 68% of 126 genes elsewhere. The domains are gene-poor, inactive heterochromatin, and both cell lines lost methylation there, K562 much more. (d) They replicate late in S phase, are associated with the nuclear lamina, carry H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, and get deeper with the number of cell divisions (Zhou et al. 2018).

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Where this leads

Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (WGBS, RRBS, EM-seq) makes per-CpG calls like these from raw reads, and shows why a C→T SNP looks like an unmethylated C.
Differential methylation compares the two GM12878 and two K562 replicates statistically and finds the regions that differ.
Methylation arrays measure 450 000–900 000 selected CpGs cheaply in thousands of people; Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers uses the slow drift of B2.
Methylation and chromatin from long reads reads 5mC (and 5hmC) on single molecules, which separates alleles and cells where bulk β cannot.

title: Exercise: DNA methylation biology
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Okano et al. 1999, Cell. DNA methyltransferases Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are essential for de novo methylation and mammalian development.
Tahiliani et al. 2009, Science. Conversion of 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine in mammalian DNA by MLL partner TET1.
Bell & Felsenfeld 2000, Nature. Methylation of a CTCF-dependent boundary controls imprinted expression of the Igf2 gene.
Domcke et al. 2015, Nature. Competition between DNA methylation and transcription factors determines binding of NRF1.
Smith & Meissner 2013, Nat Rev Genet. DNA methylation: roles in mammalian development.
Law & Jacobsen 2010, Nat Rev Genet. Establishing, maintaining and modifying DNA methylation patterns in plants and animals.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
About this lecture
Most human DNA methylation data do not come from sequencing but from Illumina Infinium arrays: hundreds of thousands of preselected CpGs, measured cheaply in thousands of people. Epidemiology, biobanks, epigenetic clocks and tumour classification all run on them.

The chemistry: bisulfite, Infinium I and II probes, two colours.
The numbers: β and M values, detection p-values, quality control.
Normalisation (noob, SWAN, BMIQ, functional normalisation) and probe filtering.
Cell composition: blood is a mixture, and the mixture changes with disease. Estimating it, and adjusting for it.
The epigenome-wide association study (EWAS): limma with covariates, genomic inflation, a positive control.
Running example: GSE42861, blood of rheumatoid arthritis patients and controls on the 450k array (151 samples).


Students know from Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing how bisulfite turns methylation into a C/T difference, and from RNA-seq how a linear model per feature with a design matrix works. This lecture puts the two together. The array is the most used methylation assay in human studies by far: GEO holds more than 230 000 450k and EPIC samples, cohorts like Framingham, Generation Scotland or the Swedish twin registries have tens of thousands, and the brain tumour classifier used in clinical neuropathology runs on EPIC arrays. The analysis is quite different from sequencing: no reads, no alignment, but two fluorescence intensities per CpG, with their own artefacts. The second half is about the single most important confounder in blood studies: cell composition. The data are real: a subset of the 689-sample rheumatoid arthritis study of Liu et al. 2013.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Why arrays?


About 1.7% (450k) to 3.3% (EPIC v2) of the ~28 million CpGs, chosen in advance: promoters and CpG islands (450k), plus enhancers (EPIC).
In exchange: low cost per sample, 250–500 ng DNA, a few days from DNA to data, and highly standardised data across labs and decades.


Four generations: 27k (2008, almost only promoter CpG islands), 450k (2011, 485 577 probes covering 99% of RefSeq genes and 96% of CpG islands, with several probes per island including the shores), EPIC (2016, 866 895 probes, adding about 350 000 enhancer CpGs from ENCODE and FANTOM5), EPIC v2 (2023, about 935 000, with problematic probes removed and more enhancers). Most probes are shared between generations, which is why clocks trained on 450k data still run on EPIC. The cost of an array is a fraction of a deep WGBS genome, and the output is a fixed table: CpG × sample, no alignment decisions. The price: you only see the CpGs on the array, mostly in regions that are either fully methylated or unmethylated in most tissues, and the probe design brings its own artefacts, which is what most of this lecture is about.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Bisulfite turns methylation into a C/T “genotype”
text:
Bisulfite turns methylation into a C/T “genotype”


After bisulfite conversion and amplification, each CpG of each molecule reads C (was methylated) or T (was unmethylated).
The array measures the C and T signals of millions of molecules together: the result is a proportion per CpG, not a per-molecule state.


Recap from Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing: sodium bisulfite deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil, which PCR copies as thymine; 5-methylcytosine (and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine) is protected. So a CpG becomes a SNP-like site: C/T. The Infinium assay was developed for SNP genotyping, and the methylation array is that genotyping assay applied to bisulfite-converted DNA. Two consequences. First, the readout is the fraction of methylated copies in the sample: for blood, that is averaged over all the white blood cells in the tube. Second, like bisulfite sequencing, the array cannot tell 5mC from 5hmC. Non-CpG Cs are converted almost always; that is also how the array checks the completeness of the conversion (bisulfite conversion control probes).

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Infinium I and Infinium II probes
text:
Infinium I and Infinium II probes


450k: 135 476 Type I and 350 036 Type II probes; EPIC: 142 262 and 724 574.
The two designs have different dynamic ranges: a source of technical variation that normalisation must handle.


Each probe is a 50-nucleotide oligo on a bead; the bisulfite-converted, amplified DNA hybridises, and a single labelled base is added to the probe’s 3’ end. Infinium I uses two bead types per CpG: the U bead’s probe ends with a base that matches the converted (T) version, the M bead’s probe ends with a base that matches C; only a perfectly matched 3’ end is extended. Both report in the same colour, set by the base after the CpG (A or T: red; C or G: green). Infinium II uses one bead per CpG: the probe ends right before the CpG C, and the added base itself reports the state: G (green) for C, A (red) for T. Type II needs half the beads, so most probes are Type II, but it has a compressed range (fully methylated CpGs give lower β than with Type I) and is more sensitive to dye bias. Another difference: Type I probes assume that the other CpGs under the probe have the same state as the target (the probe sequence is written for all-methylated or all-unmethylated); Type II uses a degenerate base (R = A/G) for up to three other CpGs. These counts are from the minfi manifests.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: From IDAT files to β values
text:
From IDAT files to β values
library(minfi)
targets <- read.delim(file.path(D, "gse42861_samples.tsv"))
targets$Basename <- file.path(D, "gse42861_idat", targets$basename)
rg   <- read.metharray.exp(targets = targets)    # RGChannelSet: red and green intensities per bead type
mset <- preprocessRaw(rg)                         # MethylSet: M and U per CpG
beta <- getBeta(mset, offset = 100)               # beta = M / (M + U + 100)








object
rows
contains




IDAT files
—
two binary files per array (Grn, Red): mean intensity per bead type


RGChannelSet
622 399 addresses
raw red and green intensities, including control probes


MethylSet

An IDAT file is the scanner’s output: for every bead type (address), the mean and SD of its intensity in one colour. minfi reads them into an RGChannelSet, the most raw object, which also holds about 850 control probes (staining, extension, hybridisation, bisulfite conversion, negative controls). preprocessRaw maps bead addresses to CpGs: for a Type I probe, M and U are the two beads in the probe’s colour; for Type II, M is the green and U the red signal of the one bead. Reading 151 450k arrays takes about 4 minutes. The objects behave like the SummarizedExperiment you know from DESeq2: assays, colData (the sample table) and rowData. sesame (Zhou et al.) is the main alternative to minfi, with its own preprocessing (openSesame) and probe masks; its defaults are well suited to EPIC v2.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
β values and M values

 \beta = \frac{M}{M + U + 100} \qquad\qquad M\text{-value} = \log_2 \frac{M + 1}{U + 1} \approx \log_2 \frac{\beta}{1 - \beta} 

β: interpretable (a proportion, 0–1), but its variance depends on the mean: little room near 0 and 1.
M-value: unbounded, roughly constant variance: better for linear models. Report effects in β, test on M.


The offset of 100 in β protects against division by tiny numbers when both signals are near background. The M-value is a log ratio, like a log fold change of methylated over unmethylated signal; M = 0 means β = 0.5, M = 2 means β = 0.8, M = −2 means β = 0.2. The middle and right panels are real: across the 151 arrays, the SD of β is small for CpGs near 0 or 1 and largest for intermediate CpGs, while the SD of M is more even (it is inflated at the extremes instead, where tiny differences in U or M signal become large log ratios). Du et al. 2010 showed that tests on M-values have better statistical properties; limma assumes roughly constant variance. The convention in EWAS papers: test on M, report the difference in β (Δβ), because “2% more methylated” means something to a reader and “0.1 more in M” does not. By hand: β = 0.8 gives M = log2(0.8/0.2) = 2.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Quality control: detection p-values and sex
text:
Quality control: detection p-values and sex


Detection p-value: is M + U of a probe above the background of ~600 negative control probes? Here 0.08% of probes fail (p > 0.01) in a typical array, 3.9% in the worst; 3 784 probes fail in > 5% of arrays.
Sex check: median signal of chrX vs chrY probes. All 151 arrays agree with the records; a mismatch means a sample swap.


minfi’s detectionP compares the total signal of each probe with the distribution of the negative control probes of the same array (sesame’s pOOBAH uses out-of-band Type I signal instead). Common rules: drop arrays with more than 1–5% failed probes, and drop probes that fail in more than a few percent of arrays. Here 4 of 151 arrays exceed 1% failed probes and none exceeds 5% (the worst: 3.9%); with the more lenient cut-off we keep all of them, and note the four in the methods. The sex check is the cheapest sample-identity test there is: women have two X chromosomes and no Y, so chrY probes give background signal; men have one X. Here 107 women and 44 men, all matching the GEO annotation. Other QC: bisulfite conversion controls (incomplete conversion makes everything look methylated), the overall β distribution (should be bimodal), and for repeated samples, SNP probes (59–65 rs probes on the array give a genotype fingerprint).

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Background and dye bias: noob


Fluorescence = background (normal) + signal (exponential); the Type I “wrong colour” channel estimates the background on every array.
Dye bias: the red and green channels have different gains; control probes with equal target let us rescale.


noob (normal-exponential using out-of-band probes, Triche et al. 2013) is a within-array correction and the recommended first step in most pipelines. It models the observed intensity of each probe as background plus signal; the out-of-band intensities of Type I probes (the colour they are not designed for) are pure background and give its mean and spread. The corrected value is the expected signal given the observed one, which is always positive and shrinks low values towards zero. Dye-bias correction rescales one channel so that control probes (NORM_A/T in red and NORM_C/G in green, which should give equal signal) agree. Because each array is corrected on its own, noob is safe when global methylation differs between groups (a property between-array methods do not have, see the next slides).

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Type I vs Type II, and what normalisation does
text:
Type I vs Type II, and what normalisation does


Raw data: the methylated peak sits at β ≈ 0.95 for Type I probes and 0.84 for Type II. After noob, SWAN or functional normalisation the gap shrinks to ~0.04.
Between-array methods (quantile, functional normalisation) also align arrays to each other.


Four arrays from two BeadChips, densities of β by probe design. In the raw data the Type II distribution is compressed: methylated CpGs read lower and unmethylated CpGs higher than with Type I. noob (within-array) and SWAN (subset-quantile within-array normalisation, Maksimovic 2012: quantile-normalise Type I and II probes against each other on a subset matched for CpG content) reduce the gap; BMIQ (Teschendorff 2013) fits a three-component beta mixture to each design and maps Type II onto the Type I distribution. Functional normalisation (Fortin et al. 2014) is a between-array method: it quantile-normalises arrays but uses the first principal components of the control probes to decide how much of the difference between arrays is technical. These peak positions are from the real data and printed by make-arrays-figs.R.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Which normalisation, when?








method
type
assumption / use




noob

background + dye bias; safe default; first step of most pipelines


SWAN, BMIQ
within array
Type I vs II design bias


quantile (preprocessQuantile)

all arrays have the same β distribution: same tissue, small effects


functional normalisation
between arrays
technical variation captured by control probes; keeps real global differences (e.g. tumour vs normal)


sesame (openSesame)
within array
pOOBAH detection, noob, dye bias, masking; the default for EPIC v2




As in RNA-seq: a normalisation is an assumption. Quantile normalisation would erase a true global loss of methylation (cancer).
On these 151 arrays: noob 2.7 min, SWAN 2.0, funnorm 6.5 (16 GB RAM), quantile 1.8.


There is no universally best method, and benchmark papers disagree because they measure different things (replicate agreement, preservation of known differences, removal of batch effects). A sensible default for blood EWAS is noob (perhaps followed by BMIQ for analyses that mix Type I and II probes, like clocks), with batch handled in the model. Quantile normalisation forces all arrays to have identical β distributions; that is fine for a study of one tissue with small expected effects, and wrong for tumour vs normal, where tumours lose methylation globally: the same issue as global changes in ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq (Differential accessibility). Functional normalisation was designed for exactly that case. Run times are for one CPU core on a server; funnorm needed 16 GB of memory for 151 arrays, which is why the exercise compares methods on 24 arrays.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Probes that measure something else


Here: 485 512 → 481 728 (detection) → 452 974 (Zhou et al. general mask: 20 010 non-unique probes, common SNPs at the target or extension base) → 442 415 (drop chrX, chrY).


Three classic problems. A: a SNP at the CpG (or at the extension base of a Type I probe) makes the probe report genotype: people cluster at β ≈ 0, 0.5 and 1 by genotype. A real example is visible as trimodal β distributions in any EWAS. These probes create false associations with ancestry and with any trait correlated with ancestry. B: cross-reactive probes. After bisulfite conversion the genome is mostly a three-letter alphabet, so many 50-mers match several places; the signal mixes loci. Chen et al. 2013 listed about 6% of 450k probes; Pidsley et al. 2016 did the same for EPIC; Zhou et al. 2017 provide masks per array and genome build, which we use (the M_general column). C: sex chromosomes: in women one X is inactivated and its CpG-island promoters methylated, so chrX probes differ hugely by sex, and chrY probes are empty in women. Most EWAS of autosomal traits drop chrX and chrY or analyse them separately with sex in the model. Filtering removes 9% of probes here; all filtering choices go in the methods section.

Peripheral blood leukocytes, 450k array, Liu et al. 2013 (689 samples in total, Sweden).
In the full study many BeadChips carry only patients or only controls: chip and disease are confounded. We took the 14 chips with both.


The full study (Liu et al. 2013) used 354 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 335 controls from the Swedish EIRA study, and asked whether methylation mediates genetic risk in the MHC region. For teaching we use 151 samples, which runs on a laptop. A design point: in the full GEO series, 36 of the 72 BeadChips contain only patients or only controls. Any chip effect (and chip effects are real: hybridisation, scanning, reagent batch) would then look like a disease effect, and no statistics can separate the two afterwards. Randomising samples over chips and positions before hybridisation is the cheapest protection there is. Our subset is balanced per chip, but not perfectly; we will still include the chip in the model. Note also the covariates: RA is more common in women and in smokers, and both sex and smoking change blood methylation.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
What drives the variation?


PCA of the 20 000 most variable autosomal CpGs (M-values after noob). PC1 (25%) is a batch: four BeadChips of one older lot (5730053…) vs the other ten; the slide explains 85% of PC1.
PC2 (11%) is cell composition (r = −0.80 with the granulocyte fraction), and patients sit at the high-granulocyte end. Disease itself is not a principal component.


Left: the 151 arrays on the first two principal components, coloured by the series of the BeadChip. The four 5730053… chips (36 samples) are separated from the rest along PC1, even after noob normalisation; these chips also have more failed probes (PC1 correlates 0.58 with the failed-probe fraction), so this is a technical batch: an older lot of chips, processed at a different time. Because we chose chips with both patients and controls, the batch is not confounded with disease here; it adds noise, and putting the chip in the model removes it. In the full study, where many chips hold only one group, the same batch would be a disaster. Right: PC2 against the estimated granulocyte fraction (estimated on a later slide): almost a straight line. Neutrophils and lymphocytes differ at tens of thousands of CpGs, and the neutrophil share of blood varies between people (more with inflammation, infection, stress, steroids). RA patients (orange) sit at the high-granulocyte end. This is the RNA-seq lesson “look at the PCA before you test”, with two very specific answers for blood arrays: batch and cell composition.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Blood is a mixture, and the mixture changes
text:
Blood is a mixture, and the mixture changes


A CpG that differs between cell types changes its bulk β whenever the proportions change, even if no cell changed anything.
Inflammatory disease, age, smoking, sex, stress and drugs all change blood composition: cell composition is a confounder in almost every blood EWAS.


Panel B is a by-hand calculation: β = 0.9 in neutrophils and 0.1 in lymphocytes, in every person. Control: 60% neutrophils gives 0.58; patient: 70% gives 0.66. A difference of 0.08 in β is a typical EWAS effect size, and it would appear at every one of the tens of thousands of CpGs that differ between neutrophils and lymphocytes, with tiny p-values in a large study. Whether that is “wrong” depends on the question: the association with disease is real, but it is not evidence that the disease changes methylation inside cells. Jaffe and Irizarry (2014) showed that a large fraction of published blood EWAS hits (for age and other traits) could be explained this way. In the language of linear models (which students know from RNA-seq design formulas): composition is a variable that affects the outcome and is associated with the exposure, so it belongs in the model.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Estimating the fractions: reference-based deconvolution


A reference of sorted cells gives β of marker CpGs per cell type; each sample is fitted as a non-negative mixture (Houseman et al. 2012).
minfi: estimateCellCounts(rg, compositeCellType = "Blood"); EpiDISH and sesame offer the same idea with other references.


Houseman’s method has two steps. In a reference data set (here Reinius et al. 2012: blood of 6 men, sorted by FACS into granulocytes, monocytes, B cells, CD4 and CD8 T cells and NK cells, each on a 450k array), select the CpGs that best separate the cell types (minfi picks the 50 most hypo- and 50 most hypermethylated CpGs per cell type, about 600 in total). Then for every sample, solve a constrained least-squares problem: find non-negative fractions w so that the reference profiles times w best match the sample’s β at those CpGs. This is the same linear algebra as fitting a design matrix, with the reference as the design and the constraint that fractions are non-negative and (in Houseman’s formulation) sum to at most one; minfi enforces only non-negativity by default, so its estimates can sum to slightly more than one (0.98–1.05 here). minfi normalises the samples together with the reference (quantile normalisation) before fitting. Newer references (FlowSorted.Blood.EPIC, Salas et al. 2018; and a 12-cell-type version in 2022) use EPIC arrays and more cell types, including neutrophils separately from eosinophils and naive vs memory lymphocytes. Reference-free methods (RefFreeEWAS, ReFACTor, surrogate variable analysis) estimate hidden structure without a reference.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: The reference: marker CpGs of sorted cells
text:
The reference: marker CpGs of sorted cells


Each cell type has CpGs that are unmethylated only in it (its enhancers and lineage genes): the dark/light blocks.
Granulocytes (neutrophils) and lymphocytes differ the most; CD4 and CD8 T cells the least.


The heat map shows the reference profiles that estimateCellCounts selected (rows: marker CpGs, columns: sorted cell types, colour: mean β in the reference). Cell-type-specific unmethylation is the typical pattern: a CpG in an enhancer of a myeloid gene is unmethylated in granulocytes and monocytes and methylated in lymphocytes. This is the same biology as the cell-type-specific open chromatin of Differential accessibility: lineage-specific enhancers are open, bound by TFs and unmethylated. Hard pairs (CD4 vs CD8 T cells, NK vs CD8) have fewer and weaker markers, so their estimates are noisier. A practical point: if the samples are from a tissue the reference does not cover (cord blood, saliva, tumour), the estimates are biased; use a matching reference.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Estimated fractions: patients have more granulocytes
text:
Estimated fractions: patients have more granulocytes


Granulocytes 70% in RA vs 58% in controls (p ≈ 10⁻¹³); every lymphocyte type is lower in patients.
Exactly the situation of the toy example, at real scale.


Mean estimated fractions: RA patients 70% granulocytes, 9% CD4 T cells, 6% CD8 T cells, 5% NK, 4% B cells, 7% monocytes; controls 58%, 14%, 9%, 9%, 6%, 6%. Systemic inflammation and treatment (glucocorticoids raise neutrophil counts and lower lymphocytes) both shift the blood towards granulocytes. The fractions sum to about one, so they are not independent: when modelling, leave one out (here granulocytes) to avoid a design matrix that is not of full rank, just as you drop one level of a factor. With the fractions in hand, adding them to the model is a one-line change, next slide.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: An EWAS is a linear model per CpG
text:
An EWAS is a linear model per CpG
library(limma)
M <- log2(beta / (1 - beta))                         # M-values, CpGs x samples (after filtering)
design <- model.matrix(~ status + age + sex + smoking + CD8T + CD4T + NK + Bcell + Mono, data = samples)
fit <- eBayes(lmFit(M, design))
res <- topTable(fit, coef = "statusRA", number = Inf)

The same machinery as limma for RNA-seq: one linear model per CpG, the same design matrix for all, moderated t-statistics, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR.
Covariates: age, sex, smoking, cell fractions (one left out), batch (chip). The coefficient of statusRA is the RA effect at fixed composition.


This is exactly the limma students know (limma-voom for RNA-seq), with M-values instead of log-CPM and no voom weights needed (M-values are roughly homoscedastic). Each CpG gets its own coefficients; eBayes borrows variance information across CpGs, which matters for small studies. Reading the design formula: the RA coefficient now compares patients and controls with the same age, sex, smoking status and cell composition. Factor smoking has four levels (never, ex, occasional, current), so it uses three columns. With 149 samples and up to 27 columns (with chip), the residual degrees of freedom drop from 147 to 124, which is fine at this sample size but would not be in a study of 20 people. Two samples without smoking status are dropped. An alternative to M-values is a beta regression per CpG; in practice limma on M-values is the standard.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
section: Genomic inflation: read the QQ plot
text:
Genomic inflation: read the QQ plot


\lambda = \dfrac{\text{median}(\chi^2_1 \text{ of the observed } p)}{0.455}: 1 if most CpGs follow the null. RA: 4.27 → 3.53 → 2.27 → 1.64 as covariates are added.
CpGs at FDR 5%: 102 938 → 98 983 → 2 159 → 0. Most of the “RA signal” was cell composition (and chip).


A QQ plot compares the observed −log10 p-values with those expected if no CpG were associated. In a genome-wide test where most features are null, the bulk of the points should lie on the diagonal and only the top deviate; a cloud that rises everywhere means the test statistics are inflated, by confounding, batch effects, or a truly genome-wide effect. λ condenses this into one number: the median chi-square statistic divided by its expected value (0.455). Here, status alone gives λ = 4.3 and over 100 000 “significant” CpGs: a quarter of the array. Adding age, sex and smoking barely helps. Adding the five cell fractions removes 98% of the hits. Adding the chip removes the rest at this sample size. With 151 people we lack the power of the full study; Liu et al. used all 689 samples. Should λ be 1 after adjustment? Not necessarily: a disease that truly changes methylation at many CpGs inflates λ legitimately, which is why some authors use the bacon method (van Iterson 2017) to estimate the null distribution empirically rather than dividing by λ.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
A positive control: smoking


Same model, coefficient current vs never smokers (37 vs 43 people): 13 CpGs at FDR 5%, λ = 1.95.
Top hits are the textbook smoking CpGs: AHRR cg05575921 (β 0.85 never → 0.66 current; rank 2), 2q37.1 (ALPPL2), F2RL3, 6p21.33.


Before believing a new result, reproduce an old one. Smoking has the most replicated EWAS signature there is (Joehanes et al. 2016: thousands of CpGs in a meta-analysis of 16 000 people), and the top CpGs reappear here with only 80 people in the comparison: AHRR cg05575921 is hypomethylated in smokers (the aryl hydrocarbon receptor repressor responds to the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke), as are CpGs at 2q37.1, F2RL3 and 6p21.33. The AHRR CpG is so reliable that it is used as a biomarker of smoking exposure (and partly recovers after quitting: note the ex-smokers in the middle). Seeing these in the top ten tells us that the pipeline (normalisation, filtering, model) works. If your own EWAS cannot find AHRR in smokers, look for a bug before you look for biology.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Interpreting EWAS hits

Effect sizes are small: typical Δβ of 1–5%. Real, but often less than the technical noise of a single array: replicate in an independent cohort.
Direction of causation: disease → methylation is as plausible as the reverse. RA treatment (methotrexate, steroids) changes both cell composition and methylation.
Genetics: many CpGs are controlled by nearby SNPs (meQTLs, Epigenomics and genetic variation); a disease-associated SNP can drive both. Mendelian randomisation can test the direction.
Tissue: blood is accessible, not necessarily relevant (the joint synovium is where RA happens).
450k covers about 1.7% of CpGs; EPIC about 3%: “no hit” does not mean “no methylation change”.


EWAS results are associations, like GWAS results but with an extra problem: methylation can be a consequence of the disease, its treatment or its lifestyle correlates. For RA: patients take drugs (methotrexate is a folate antagonist and affects one-carbon metabolism, which supplies methyl groups), have chronic inflammation and smoke more. Liu et al. 2013 addressed direction by asking whether methylation mediates the effect of MHC risk SNPs. Good practice: pre-register covariates, report λ and QQ plots, include a positive control, replicate, and say clearly whether cell composition was adjusted for. Note also the difference between statistical and biological significance: with 10 000 people a Δβ of 0.5% can be significant, but significance alone does not show a functional effect. A small bulk difference can also reflect a larger change in a small cell population; functional claims need further evidence.

A map of the ecosystem so that students can read methods sections. ChAMP and meffil are pipelines that wrap many of these steps; meffil is built for very large cohorts (it normalises on summary statistics instead of loading every array into memory). DMRcate and bumphunter find differentially methylated regions from array data, the counterpart of the DMR callers in Differential methylation. For EPIC v2 several probes have duplicates (replicate probes with suffixes in their names) and the manifest differs; sesame handles it natively. Whatever the tools, the decisions are the same: which normalisation, which probes, which covariates, which test, and how to check that it worked.

Next: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers uses the same arrays to predict age and asks what such predictors mean.

title: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Bibikova et al. 2011, Genomics. High density DNA methylation array with single CpG site resolution. The 450k array.
Du et al. 2010, BMC Bioinformatics. Comparison of Beta-value and M-value methods for quantifying methylation levels by microarray analysis. Why to test on M-values.
Houseman et al. 2012, BMC Bioinformatics. DNA methylation arrays as surrogate measures of cell mixture distribution. Reference-based deconvolution.
Jaffe & Irizarry 2014, Genome Biol. Accounting for cellular heterogeneity is critical in epigenome-wide association studies. How composition fakes EWAS hits.
Zhou, Laird & Shen 2017, Nucleic Acids Res. Comprehensive characterization, annotation and innovative use of Infinium DNA methylation BeadChip probes. Probe masks; the annotation we use.
Liu et al. 2013, Nat Biotechnol. Epigenome-wide association data implicate DNA methylation as an intermediary of genetic risk in rheumatoid arthritis. The dataset of this unit.

title: Quiz: methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Short questions on modified-base calling, modBAM files, haplotype-resolved methylation and single-molecule accessibility. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Name two things a nanopore read can tell you about DNA methylation that a WGBS read cannot.






Hint





Think about conversion, read length and what else sits on the same molecule.









Answer





Any two of: it separates 5mC from 5hmC (bisulfite reads both as C); it reads tens of kilobases of one molecule, so many CpGs and usually heterozygous SNPs on the same read (haplotype-resolved methylation, co-methylation patterns); it maps into repeats that short converted reads cannot place; and other modifications on the same molecule (6mA from a methyltransferase, i.e. accessibility) are read at the same time. Also: no bisulfite damage and a four-letter alignment.




Q2. A read has MM:Z:C+m?,1,0; and ML:B:C,20,235. The read’s Cs are, in order, in contexts CG, CG, CG. Which Cs have calls, and what are the probabilities of 5mC?






Answer





Skip 1 C, call the second C; skip 0, call the third. Probabilities ≈ (ML + 0.5)/256: second C 0.08 (likely unmethylated), third C 0.92 (likely methylated). The first C has no call; because of ? it is unknown, not unmethylated.




Q3. At one CpG, modkit reports N_valid = 40, N_mod (5mC) = 26, N_other (5hmC) = 2, N_fail = 4. What is the 5mC level? What would WGBS report (in expectation)?






Answer





5mC level = 26/40 = 0.65. N_valid includes the 5hmC calls (C = 40 − 26 − 2 = 12); failed calls are not counted. WGBS reads 5mC and 5hmC as C: (26 + 2)/40 = 0.70.




Q4. Why does modkit drop calls below a threshold, and why is the threshold for 6mA (0.97) much higher than for 5mC at CpG (0.87) in the same data?






Answer





Low-confidence calls (probability of the best state only slightly above the others) are often wrong; dropping the least confident 10% removes them at a small cost in coverage. The threshold is the 10th percentile of the confidence values of all calls of that base. Almost all adenines are confidently unmodified (human DNA has no natural 6mA and even treated DNA is marked sparsely), so their confidences are very high and so is the 10th percentile; CpG calls are more often uncertain.




Q5. A child is A/G at a SNP; her father is G/G and her mother A/G. Which allele is paternal? A nanopore read carries G at this SNP and is methylated at an imprinting control region nearby. Which ICR could this be: H19 or the PWS-IC (SNRPN)?






Answer





The father can only pass G, so G is paternal and A maternal. The read is paternal and methylated at the ICR: consistent with the H19 ICR (paternally methylated), not with the PWS-IC (maternally methylated).




Q6. In whole-blood WGBS a CpG at a known imprinting control region reads 0.5. In a woman’s blood, a promoter CpG island on chrX also reads about 0.5. Explain both, and say what haplotype-resolved data would show in each case.






Answer





ICR: every cell has one methylated (imprinted) parental copy and one unmethylated copy; haplotype-resolved data show one haplotype at ~1 and the other at ~0, the same parent in every person. chrX: every cell has one inactive X with a methylated promoter, but in blood (a mixture of clones) half the cells inactivated the paternal X and half the maternal X; each haplotype is ~0.5 methylated (unless X inactivation is skewed). In a clonal cell line such as GM12878 the chrX island would look like the ICR: one haplotype methylated.




Q7. In haplotype-resolved data from one person, a CpG is 0.9 methylated on haplotype 1 and 0.05 on haplotype 2. Give three possible explanations and one observation that would distinguish them.






Answer





Imprinting (parent-of-origin), X inactivation (if on chrX, in a clonal population), or sequence-dependent allele-specific methylation (a SNP in the region, an meQTL). Distinguish with parents (does the methylated allele always come from the same parent?) and with other people (does methylation follow a particular SNP allele regardless of parent?). Location (chrX vs an autosome, a known ICR) is also a strong hint.




Q8. In a Fiber-seq-type experiment, 4.8% of adenines in accessible regions and 0.37% elsewhere are called m6A; in untreated DNA of the same cells, 0.02–0.04%. What is the enrichment, and why do you need the untreated control?






Answer





4.8/0.37 ≈ 13-fold. The untreated control measures the false-positive rate of the 6mA model (and any natural 6mA): here about 0.02–0.04%, small compared with the treated signal, so most calls in the treated sample come from the enzyme. Without the control you could not tell enzyme marks from model errors, and you could not claim (or refute) natural 6mA.




Q9. A nucleosome-free region of 300 bp has about 75 adenines on one strand, and about 13% of them are marked on an open fibre. How many marks do you expect, and what is the chance (Poisson) of seeing none? What does a fibre without marks over this region most likely mean?






Answer





λ = 0.13 × 75 ≈ 9.8 marks; P(0) = e^{−9.8} ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁵. A fibre without marks is almost certainly closed (nucleosome-covered) on that molecule, or a molecule the enzyme did not reach; it is not an open fibre that was missed by chance.




Q10. A study compares nanopore methylation of 20 patients, basecalled in 2024, with 20 controls basecalled in 2022 with an older model, and reports 1 200 differentially methylated regions. What is your main concern, and how would you fix it?






Answer





The basecaller and modification model are perfectly confounded with disease: model versions differ in calibration and context accuracy, so methylation levels shift systematically. Re-basecall all raw data (POD5) with the same model, or, if the raw data are gone, at least show that the DMRs are not explained by model differences (e.g. by re-calling a few controls with both models). Ideally also randomise sequencing runs across groups.

title: Exercise: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Background
Modified-base calls in a BAM. Each read carries an MM tag (which bases have calls) and an ML tag (one probability per call). MM:Z:C+m?,3,0,1; means: modification m (5mC) on base C of the read’s top strand; the numbers are how many Cs to skip before the next call (3: skip three Cs, call the fourth; 0: call the next C; and so on). ? means Cs without a call are unknown; . would mean they are unmodified. ML:B:C,... holds one byte per call: probability ≈ (ML + 0.5) / 256. Nanopore reads called with a 5mC+5hmC model carry two lists, C+h? and C+m?, each with its own ML values; P(C) = 1 − P(5mC) − P(5hmC).
From calls to a level. For every call the most likely state is taken (C, 5mC or 5hmC). modkit estimates a threshold (the 10th percentile of the confidence of all calls) and drops calls below it as fail. The level at a CpG is then a count, like C/(C+T) in WGBS:
\[ \text{5mC level} = \frac{N_\text{5mC}}{N_\text{valid}}, \qquad N_\text{valid} = N_\text{5mC} + N_\text{5hmC} + N_\text{C} \]
Bisulfite and EM-seq read both 5mC and 5hmC as C, so compare them with \((N_\text{5mC} + N_\text{5hmC}) / N_\text{valid}\).
Phasing by transmission. A child receives one allele of each SNP from each parent. When a parent is homozygous, we know which allele that parent passed on, and the other allele of the child came from the other parent. If both parents are heterozygous the SNP is not informative. On chrX a father has only one allele (hemizygous) and passes his X to a daughter.
Haplotagging. WhatsHap compares each read with the phased heterozygous SNPs it covers and writes HP:i:1 or HP:i:2 into the read; reads without informative SNPs stay untagged. In our VCF the first allele of every genotype is the paternal one, so HP 1 = paternal, HP 2 = maternal.
Imprinting control regions in this exercise (DNA methylation biology): the H19 ICR (chr11) is methylated on the paternal allele; KvDMR (the KCNQ1OT1 promoter, chr11) and the PWS-IC (the SNURF/SNRPN promoter, chr15) on the maternal allele.
Fiber-seq-style accessibility. Nuclei are treated with an adenine methyltransferase (here EcoGII) that methylates A wherever DNA is not protected by nucleosomes or bound proteins. Human DNA has essentially no 6mA of its own, so m6A calls mark accessible DNA. An untreated sample measures the false-positive rate of the 6mA model.

text:
Data
All files are made by data/prepare-meth2.sh longreads (see data/README.md); you also need hg38.fa.bgz, the GENCODE GTF and the GM12878 ATAC-seq peaks from data/download.sh.
mkdir -p ~/epi/longread && cd ~/epi/longread
D=/path/to/course/data                     # where the course data are







file
what




hg001_ont_regions.bam
HG001 (= NA12878, the donor of GM12878) nanopore R10.4.1 reads with 5mC and 5hmC calls, 4 flow cells (ONT open data giab_2023.05), cut to 5 regions: chr11:1.96–2.05 Mb (H19), chr11:2.69–2.71 Mb (KvDMR), chr15:24.94–24.97 Mb (SNRPN), chrX:53.15–53.34 Mb (KDM5C), chr21:33–34 Mb


longread_regions.bed
the 5 regions

SNP genotypes of NA12878, her father NA12891 and her mother NA12892 in the regions (1000 Genomes 30×, 2022 release)


gm12878_wgbs_regions.bed.gz, gm12878_wgbs_rep2_regions.bed.gz
ENCODE WGBS of GM12878, replicates 1 and 2 (ENCFF570TIL, ENCFF614QHA), the same regions; one row per CpG and strand; column 10 coverage, 11 percent methylated


hg001_hp1_chrX_chr20_5mc.bed.gz, ..._hp2_...
ONT’s own haplotype-resolved 5mC pileups of HG001 (giab_2025.01, wf-human-variation, read-based phasing) for chrX and chr20: chrom, start, end, valid calls, 5mC calls


hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz
UCSC CpG islands, hg38


hg002_ecogii_regions.bam, hg002_native_regions.bam
HG002 nanopore reads, chr21:33–34 Mb, from nuclei treated with EcoGII and from untreated DNA (ONT chrom_acc_2025.06), with 5mC, 5hmC and 6mA calls



Shortcuts, said plainly. The reads were basecalled and aligned by ONT; we start from the modBAM (basecalling needs the raw signal and GPUs). We cut 1.35 Mb out of genome-wide files by indexed remote access. The haplotypes of the chrX/chr20 pileups come from ONT’s pipeline (read-based phasing), not from our trio. The chromatin data are from HG002, a different person than GM12878 (both are lymphoblastoid cell lines), so GM12878 ATAC peaks are only a guide.
You need samtools (≥ 1.15), bcftools, tabix, modkit (≥ 0.6) and WhatsHap (≥ 2.0); see Install the software you need (conda install -c bioconda ont-modkit whatshap). The command-line part takes about 5 minutes, the R part about 3 minutes.

B5. X inactivation in a cell line and in a tissue. Look at the chrX panel of the lecture figure:


Why do most chrX promoter CpG islands sit near the top-left of the panel, while chr20 islands sit near the origin?

title: Exercise: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the modBAM
samtools view -H $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam | grep '^@PG' | cut -c1-120 | head -3
samtools flagstat $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam | head -4
samtools view -F 0x904 $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam | awk '{ n++; s += length($10) } END { print n, "primary reads, mean length", s / n }'
samtools view -F 0x904 $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam chr11:2000000-2000100 | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | grep -E '^(MM|ML)' | cut -c1-80

Which programs made this file? How many primary reads are there, and how long are they on average?
What do the flags -F 0x904 remove?
Look at the MM tag of the first read: which modification lists does it have?



C2 — A bedMethyl table with modkit
modkit and WhatsHap read many random positions of the reference; an uncompressed reference of the four chromosomes is much faster than the bgzipped genome.
samtools faidx $D/hg38.fa.bgz chr11 chr15 chr21 chrX > hg38_lr.fa
samtools faidx hg38_lr.fa
modkit pileup $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam hg001_cpg.bed --ref hg38_lr.fa \
  --cpg --modified-bases 5mC 5hmC --combine-strands \
  --include-bed $D/longread_regions.bed --sampling-frac 1 -t 4 --log-filepath pileup.log
grep 'setting threshold' pileup.log | sed 's/.*INFO\] //'
grep -w m hg001_cpg.bed | head -3
awk '$4 == "m" { n++; v += $10; m += $12; o += $14 } END { print n, "CpGs; mean valid calls", v / n, "; 5mC", m / v, "; 5hmC", o / v }' hg001_cpg.bed

What threshold did modkit use? What fraction of calls did it drop?
For the first CpG: how many calls are valid, methylated, unmethylated and failed? Check the percentage.
How many CpGs, what mean coverage, and what fractions of all valid calls are 5mC and 5hmC?



C3 — Phase the SNPs by transmission and tag the reads
bcftools query -l $D/hg001_trio_regions.vcf.gz
bcftools query -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT[\t%GT]\n' $D/hg001_trio_regions.vcf.gz \
| awk 'BEGIN { OFS = "\t"
         print "##fileformat=VCFv4.2"
         print "##FORMAT=<ID=GT,Number=1,Type=String,Description=\"Genotype, paternal|maternal\">"
         print "##contig=<ID=chr11,length=135086622>"; print "##contig=<ID=chr15,length=101991189>"
         print "##contig=<ID=chr21,length=46709983>";  print "##contig=<ID=chrX,length=156040895>"
         print "#CHROM", "POS", "ID", "REF", "ALT", "QUAL", "FILTER", "INFO", "FORMAT", "NA12878" }
       { gsub(/\|/, "/", $5); gsub(/\|/, "/", $6); gsub(/\|/, "/", $7)   # ignore the panel phase
         if ($5 != "0/1" && $5 != "1/0") next                            # child must be heterozygous
         f = $6; m = $7; pat = ""
         if (f == "0/0" || f == "0") pat = 0; else if (f == "1/1" || f == "1") pat = 1
         else if (m == "0/0") pat = 1; else if (m == "1/1") pat = 0       # mother passed the other allele
         if (pat == "") next                                              # both parents het: uninformative
         print $1, $2, ".", $3, $4, ".", "PASS", ".", "GT", pat "|" 1 - pat }' > trio_phased.vcf
grep -vc '^#' trio_phased.vcf
bgzip -f trio_phased.vcf && tabix -f -p vcf trio_phased.vcf.gz
whatshap haplotag --ignore-read-groups --reference hg38_lr.fa --output-haplotag-list haplotags.tsv \
  -o hg001_tagged.bam trio_phased.vcf.gz $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam 2> haplotag.log
samtools index hg001_tagged.bam
tail -4 haplotag.log
cut -f 2 haplotags.tsv | sort | uniq -c

In which order are the samples in the VCF? Why do we replace | by / before using the genotypes?
How many SNPs are informative? How many reads got a haplotag, and how many per haplotype?
Look at awk '$1 == "chr11" && $2 > 1980000 && $2 < 2010000' <(zcat trio_phased.vcf.gz). How far is the nearest informative SNP from the H19 ICR (chr11:1 998 000–2 003 000)? What does that mean for reads of 5 kb?



C4 — Methylation per haplotype
modkit pileup hg001_tagged.bam phased/ --phased --ref hg38_lr.fa \
  --cpg --modified-bases 5mC 5hmC --combine-strands \
  --include-bed $D/longread_regions.bed --sampling-frac 1 -t 4 --log-filepath phased.log
ls phased/
for icr in "chr11 1998000 2003000 H19_ICR" "chr11 2699000 2701000 KvDMR" "chr15 24954000 24957000 PWS-IC"; do
  set -- $icr
  for hp in hp1 hp2; do
    awk -v c=$1 -v s=$2 -v e=$3 -v name=$4 -v hp=$hp '$4 == "m" && $1 == c && $2 >= s && $2 <= e && $10 >= 5 {
          n++; f += $12 / $10 } END { printf "%s %s: %d CpGs, mean 5mC %.2f\n", name, hp, n, f / n }' phased/$hp.bedmethyl
  done
done

Which haplotype is methylated at each ICR? Does it match the expectation in the Background?
Why do we require at least 5 valid calls per CpG per haplotype?



C5 — Per-read calls for single-molecule plots
modkit extract calls hg001_tagged.bam h19_calls.tsv --region chr11:1997000-2004000 \
  --reference hg38_lr.fa --mapped-only --cpg --sampling-frac 1 -t 4 --log-filepath extract.log
head -2 h19_calls.tsv | cut -f 1-4,13,14,20
awk 'NR > 1 { n++; f += ($20 == "true") } END { print n, "calls,", f / n, "failed" }' h19_calls.tsv

What is one row of this table? (b) What fraction of calls failed the threshold?



C6 — m6A in treated and untreated chromatin
for s in ecogii native; do
  modkit pileup $D/hg002_${s}_regions.bam m6a_$s.bed --ref hg38_lr.fa --modified-bases 6mA \
    --region chr21:33000000-34000000 --sampling-frac 1 -t 4 --log-filepath m6a_$s.log
  grep 'setting threshold' m6a_$s.log | sed 's/.*INFO\] //'
  awk -v s=$s '{ v += $10; m += $12 } END { printf "%s: %d A positions, %.4f%% m6A\n", s, NR, 100 * m / v }' m6a_$s.bed
done

What fraction of adenines is called m6A in each sample? (b) What is the threshold for A, and why is it higher than for C?

title: Exercise: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
In R
You need data.table, ggplot2, GenomicRanges and rtracklayer.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/longread")          # where you ran the command-line part
cols <- c("chrom", "start", "end", "code", "score", "strand", "s2", "e2", "color",
          "nvalid", "pct", "nmod", "ncanon", "nother", "ndel", "nfail", "ndiff", "nnocall")
readbm <- function(f) { x <- fread(f, header = FALSE); setnames(x, cols[seq_len(ncol(x))]); x }

R1 — Nanopore vs WGBS
a <- readbm("hg001_cpg.bed")
ont <- merge(a[code == "m", .(chrom, start, nvalid, m = nmod)], a[code == "h", .(chrom, start, h = nmod)],
             by = c("chrom", "start"))
rdw <- function(f) {
  w <- fread(file.path(D, f), header = FALSE)
  w[, pos := ifelse(V6 == "+", V2, V2 - 1)]               # the C of the - strand is 1 bp to the right
  w[, .(cov = sum(V10), meth = sum(V10 * V11 / 100)), by = .(chrom = V1, pos)]
}
wg <- merge(rdw("gm12878_wgbs_regions.bed.gz"), rdw("gm12878_wgbs_rep2_regions.bed.gz"),
            by = c("chrom", "pos"), suffixes = c("1", "2"))
j <- merge(ont, wg, by.x = c("chrom", "start"), by.y = c("chrom", "pos"))
j[, `:=`(ont = (m + h) / nvalid, wgbs = (meth1 + meth2) / (cov1 + cov2), rep1 = meth1 / cov1, rep2 = meth2 / cov2)]
k <- j[nvalid >= 10 & cov1 >= 10 & cov2 >= 10]
nrow(k); cor(k$ont, k$wgbs); median(abs(k$ont - k$wgbs))
cor(k$rep1, k$rep2); cor(k$ont, k$rep1); cor(k$ont, k$rep2)
ggplot(k, aes(wgbs, ont)) + geom_bin2d(bins = 40) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  geom_abline(colour = "red") + coord_equal() + labs(x = "WGBS", y = "nanopore 5mC + 5hmC")

How many CpGs are compared, and how well do they agree?
Compare the two WGBS replicates with each other and with the nanopore data. Which data set is the noisiest? What does this tell you about interpreting a correlation between two assays?
Why do we combine the two strands of the WGBS data, and why is the − strand position shifted by one?



R2 — Methylation per parental allele
hp <- merge(readbm("phased/hp1.bedmethyl")[code == "m", .(chrom, start, n1 = nvalid, pat = nmod / nvalid)],
            readbm("phased/hp2.bedmethyl")[code == "m", .(chrom, start, n2 = nvalid, mat = nmod / nvalid)],
            by = c("chrom", "start"))[n1 >= 5 & n2 >= 5]
hp[chrom == "chr11" & start >= 1998000 & start <= 2003000, .(CpGs = .N, pat = mean(pat), mat = mean(mat))]
hp[chrom == "chr11" & start >= 2699000 & start <= 2701000, .(CpGs = .N, pat = mean(pat), mat = mean(mat))]
hp[chrom == "chr15" & start >= 24954000 & start <= 24957000, .(CpGs = .N, pat = mean(pat), mat = mean(mat))]
h19 <- melt(hp[chrom == "chr11" & start >= 1994000 & start <= 2006000], id.vars = "start",
            measure.vars = c("pat", "mat"), variable.name = "allele", value.name = "f")
ggplot(h19, aes(start, f, colour = allele)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, geom = "line", binwidth = 400, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1998000, xmax = 2003000, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "chr11", y = "5mC", title = "H19: paternal vs maternal")

Report the three ICRs. (b) Plot the SNRPN region (chr15:24 948 000–24 966 000) the same way. What happens downstream of the PWS-IC on the paternal allele, and why?



R3 — Single molecules
ex <- fread("h19_calls.tsv")
ht <- fread("haplotags.tsv")[, .(read_id = `#readname`, haplotype)]
r <- merge(ex[fail == FALSE & ref_position >= 1997000 & ref_position <= 2004000 &
              alignment_start <= 1999000 & alignment_end >= 2001500], ht, by = "read_id")[haplotype != "none"]
r[, y := as.integer(factor(read_id, levels = unique(read_id[order(haplotype)])))]
r[, .(reads = uniqueN(read_id), methylated = mean(call_code %in% c("m", "h"))), by = haplotype]
ggplot(r, aes(ref_position, y, fill = call_code %in% c("m", "h"))) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 1.8) + scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white"), name = "5mC/5hmC") +
  facet_grid(haplotype ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") + labs(x = "chr11", y = "read")

How many reads per haplotype span the ICR? Why so few, given ~80× coverage? (Hint: C3c.)
Are there unmethylated reads on the paternal side or methylated reads on the maternal side? How would you decide whether they are real?



R4 — X inactivation from haplotype-resolved pileups
rd <- function(f) setnames(fread(f), c("chrom", "start", "end", "n", "m"))
h1 <- rd(file.path(D, "hg001_hp1_chrX_chr20_5mc.bed.gz")); h2 <- rd(file.path(D, "hg001_hp2_chrX_chr20_5mc.bed.gz"))
cgi <- fread(file.path(D, "hg38_cpgIslandExt.txt.gz"))[V2 %in% c("chrX", "chr20")]
cg <- GRanges(cgi$V2, IRanges(cgi$V3 + 1, cgi$V4))
genes <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), feature.type = "gene")
genes <- genes[genes$gene_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(genes) %in% c("chrX", "chr20")]
tss <- promoters(genes, upstream = 1000, downstream = 1000)
pcg <- cg[overlapsAny(cg, tss)]
o <- findOverlaps(pcg, tss); pcg$gene <- NA_character_; pcg$gene[queryHits(o)] <- tss$gene_name[subjectHits(o)]
agg <- function(h) {
  ov <- findOverlaps(GRanges(h$chrom, IRanges(h$start + 1, width = 1)), pcg)
  data.table(i = subjectHits(ov), n = h$n[queryHits(ov)], m = h$m[queryHits(ov)])[n >= 5, .(f = sum(m) / sum(n), k = .N), by = i]
}
x <- merge(agg(h1), agg(h2), by = "i", suffixes = c("1", "2"))[k1 >= 5 & k2 >= 5]
x[, `:=`(chrom = as.character(seqnames(pcg))[i], gene = pcg$gene[i], hi = pmax(f1, f2), lo = pmin(f1, f2))]
x[, .(CGIs = .N, one_methylated = mean(hi - lo > 0.5), both_unmethylated = mean(hi < 0.2)), by = chrom]
x[chrom == "chrX" & hi < 0.2, sort(unique(gene))]
x[chrom == "chr20" & hi - lo > 0.5, gene]
ggplot(x, aes(lo, hi)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_abline(linetype = 2) + facet_wrap(~ chrom) + coord_equal()

What fraction of promoter CpG islands is methylated on one haplotype only, on chrX and on chr20?
Which chrX genes have islands unmethylated on both haplotypes? Look up two of them: do they escape X inactivation?
Why can we not say from these files whether the paternal or the maternal X is inactive in GM12878? What would you need?



R5 — Accessibility: m6A at ATAC peaks
rdA <- function(f) setnames(fread(f, header = FALSE, select = c(1, 2, 10, 12)), c("chrom", "pos", "nvalid", "nmod"))
e6 <- rdA("m6a_ecogii.bed"); n6 <- rdA("m6a_native.bed")
atac <- fread(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"))[V1 == "chr21" & V2 >= 33e6 & V3 <= 34e6]
pk <- reduce(GRanges("chr21", IRanges(atac$V2 + 1, atac$V3)))
frac <- function(x) {
  i <- overlapsAny(GRanges(x$chrom, IRanges(x$pos + 1, width = 1)), pk)
  c(in_peaks = sum(x$nmod[i]) / sum(x$nvalid[i]), outside = sum(x$nmod[!i]) / sum(x$nvalid[!i]))
}
round(100 * rbind(EcoGII = frac(e6), untreated = frac(n6)), 3)
summits <- atac$V2 + atac$V10
prof <- rbindlist(lapply(summits, function(cc) e6[pos >= cc - 1000 & pos <= cc + 1000, .(d = pos - cc, nvalid, nmod)]))
prof[, bin := floor(d / 25) * 25][, .(m6A = 100 * sum(nmod) / sum(nvalid)), by = bin][order(bin)] |>
  ggplot(aes(bin, m6A)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "distance to ATAC summit (bp)", y = "% m6A")

Report the m6A fractions and the enrichment in peaks. (b) Describe the profile around summits. What could the shoulders at ±200–400 bp be?

title: Exercise: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — MM/ML tags (B1, C1)





The SAM tags specification, section “Base modifications”, defines MM and ML with worked examples. Count Cs in the read sequence from the left (for a reverse-strand alignment the stored SEQ is reverse-complemented, and tools undo that for you). The 5mCG model only calls Cs followed by G. pysam gives the calls in Python with read.modified_bases.









Hint 2 — modkit (B2, C2, C4, C5, C6)





modkit pileup documents the bedMethyl columns and the threshold (filtering); --phased needs HP tags. modkit extract writes one row per call: call_code is m, h, a or - (canonical), fail marks calls below the threshold. --sampling-frac 1 uses all reads to estimate the threshold, so that the result is the same every time.









Hint 3 — phasing and haplotags (B3, C3)





Mendelian logic: a homozygous parent can only pass on that allele. On chrX a father is hemizygous (one allele) and gives his X to every daughter. WhatsHap haplotag uses the first allele of a phased genotype as haplotype 1. bcftools query prints genotypes; -l lists sample names. SAM flag 0x904 = secondary (0x100) + QC fail (0x200) + supplementary (0x800): the SAM flags explainer decodes it.









Hint 4 — binomial noise and levels (B2, B4)





A level from \(n\) calls with true value \(p\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). With 12 calls and \(p = 0.6\) that is about 0.14.









Hint 5 — imprinting and X inactivation (B4, B5, R2, R4)





Recap in DNA methylation biology. Lists of genes that escape X inactivation: Tukiainen et al. 2017. Pseudoautosomal regions (PAR1, PAR2) are shared between X and Y. GNAS is a complex imprinted locus with maternal and paternal DMRs; MCTS2 (a retrogene in an intron of HM13) is imprinted too.









Hint 6 — R (R1–R5)





data.table::fread reads gzipped files; merge, .N and by = are in the data.table intro. GenomicRanges: overlapsAny, findOverlaps, reduce, promoters, as in Genomic intervals. BED and bedMethyl starts are 0-based: add 1 for a GRanges.









Hint 7 — Poisson (B6)





If a fibre has on average \(\lambda\) marks in a region, the chance of zero marks is \(e^{-\lambda}\).
