title: Exercise: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Cs at read positions 2, 5, 9, 11, 15 (C1–C5). Skip counts 0,0,1,0: call C1 (pos 2, CG), call C2 (pos 5, CG), skip C3 (pos 9, followed by A: not a CpG, the 5mCG model does not call it), call C4 (pos 11, CG), call C5 (pos 15, CG). (b) P(5mC) ≈ (ML + 0.5)/256: 0.98, 0.04, 0.94, 0.47. (c) With P(5hmC) = 0, P(C) = 1 − P(5mC): C1 5mC with confidence 0.98 (pass); C2 C with 0.96 (pass, unmethylated); C4 5mC with 0.94 (pass); C5: most likely C with 0.53 < 0.87: fail, dropped. (d) . would mean the skipped C (pos 9) is called unmodified (with high confidence), instead of “no information”.
B2. (a) N_valid = 7 + 3 + 1 = 11 (the failed call is excluded); 5mC = 7/11 = 0.64; 5hmC = 1/11 = 0.09. (b) WGBS reads 5mC and 5hmC as C: (7 + 1)/11 = 0.73. (c) \(\sqrt{0.64 \cdot 0.36 / 11} \approx 0.14\). A difference of 0.1 is smaller than the noise of a single CpG; average over a region or use many CpGs (Differential methylation).
B3. (a) s1: father C/C passed C (0); the child’s T (1) is maternal: 0|1. s2: father A/A passed A (1); maternal G (0): 1|0. s3: both parents T/C: not informative. s4: mother G/G passed G (1), so the child’s A (0) is paternal: 0|1. s5 (chrX): the father has only T (1) and gives his X to his daughter: 1|0. (b) Read 1: C at s1 and A at s2 are both paternal: HP 1. Read 2: T at s1 and G at s2 are both maternal: HP 2. Read 3 mixes a maternal allele (T at s1) with a paternal one (A at s2). Within one person the two homologues do not mix, so this is most likely a sequencing error at one of the two SNPs (or, if many reads show it, a wrong genotype). WhatsHap assigns such a read by the majority of its SNP alleles (weighted by quality) or leaves it untagged. (c) Males have one X (hemizygous): his single allele is shown as a haploid genotype.
B4. (a) Paternal 1/22 = 0.05; maternal 19/20 = 0.95; untagged 9/18 = 0.50; all reads (1 + 19 + 9)/(22 + 20 + 18) = 29/60 = 0.48. (b) Maternal methylation: KvDMR or the PWS-IC; not the H19 ICR, which is paternally methylated. (c) Every cell could carry one methylated (maternal) and one unmethylated (paternal) copy: allele-specific methylation, not a mixture of cells. Test: haplotype-resolved data (long reads with SNPs, or bisulfite reads that overlap a heterozygous SNP), or sorted cell types (if methylation were cell-type specific, sorted cells would be near 0 or 1).
B5. (a) In GM12878 nearly all cells inactivated the same X (a clonal line), so at most chrX promoter CGIs one haplotype (the inactive X) is methylated and the other (active X) unmethylated: top-left. Autosomal promoter CGIs are unmethylated on both copies: origin. (b) Whole blood of a woman: different clones inactivated different X chromosomes, so each haplotype is a mixture: both near 0.5 (on the diagonal at ~0.5), or skewed if XCI is skewed (common in older women). A man has one X: no second haplotype; the active X promoter CGIs are unmethylated. (c) Both copies unmethylated: the gene is expressed from both X chromosomes, it escapes X inactivation (KDM5C, KDM6A, DDX3X, EIF2S3, ZFX, USP9X, STS…). PAR1 genes have a copy on the Y and pair with it in meiosis; they behave like autosomal genes and are not silenced. (d) Imprinting (both are known imprinted loci). Check which parent carries the methylated allele (trio phasing as in C3) and whether the same allele is methylated in other people with different SNP alleles.
B6. (a) Inside 12 778/264 993 = 4.82%; outside 33 840/9 078 130 = 0.373%; enrichment 12.9-fold. (b) Untreated: 0.039% inside and 0.021% outside. Background-subtracted: 4.78% and 0.352%, 13.6-fold: hardly different, because the model background is small compared with the treated signal. The control is essential to know the false-positive rate (it would matter for a weak treatment or for low-accessibility regions) and to show that m6A is not a natural mark here. (c) λ = 0.13 × 50 ≈ 6.5 marks; P(0) = e^{−6.5} ≈ 0.0015. Nearly every open fibre is detected; a fibre without marks over an NDR is most likely closed (or the enzyme failed on that molecule).
B7. (a) 0.03% is the false-positive rate of the 6mA model on untreated human DNA (0.02–0.04% here). Without an untreated or 6mA-free control (whole-genome amplified DNA), bacterial contamination and RNA controls, this is indistinguishable from noise. (b) Basecaller and model differ completely between groups: any difference can be technical. Re-basecall both groups from the raw signal with the same model, or treat it as a batch effect that cannot be separated from disease. (c) 50% in every person is also what a CpG that is 50% methylated in every cell, a mixture of two cell types in stable proportions, or a sequence-dependent ASM in people who are all heterozygous would give. Imprinting requires showing that the methylated allele is the one from the same parent in every person.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) minimap2 (2.24) aligned the reads, samtools 1.17 sorted and split them into pass/fail (q ≥ 10), and samtools merged our slices. 11 748 records, 10 462 primary reads (249 secondary, 1 037 supplementary), mean length about 11 300 bases (median 4.6 kb: many short reads, a few very long). (b) Secondary (0x100), QC-fail (0x200) and supplementary (0x800) records: each read is counted once, and secondary records have no sequence. (c) Two lists: C+h? (5hmC) and C+m? (5mC).
C2. (a) setting threshold 0.8652344 (qual: 221) for base C, percentile 10, 1357745 total probabilites: the least confident 10% of calls are dropped. (b) First line: chr11 1960033 ... m 45 ... 45 13.33 6 39 0 1 3 1 2: 45 valid, 6 5mC, 39 C, 0 5hmC (column 14), 1 deletion, 3 failed; 6/45 = 13.33%. (c) 20 367 CpGs, mean 60 valid calls, 5mC 0.549 and 5hmC 0.0074 of all valid calls.
C3. (a) NA12878, NA12891 (father), NA12892 (mother). The 1000 Genomes panel is statistically phased; we want to derive the phase ourselves from transmission, so we treat the genotypes as unphased. (b) 562 informative SNPs (508 on chr21, 29 near H19/KvDMR, 2 at SNRPN, 23 on chrX). 5 575 of 11 748 alignments tagged (Alignments that could be tagged: 5575); uniq -c on the haplotag list (primary reads) gives 2 880 H1, 2 695 H2 and 4 887 none (plus one header line). (c) The nearest informative SNPs are at 1 983 675 and 1 992 105 on the left and 2 041 821 on the right: 6 kb and 39 kb from the ICR. A 5-kb read inside the ICR covers no informative SNP and stays untagged.
C4. (a) H19_ICR: hp1 (paternal) 200 CpGs, 0.71; hp2 153 CpGs, 0.01. KvDMR: hp1 0.00, hp2 0.90 (177 CpGs each). PWS-IC: hp1 0.04, hp2 0.75. (The CpG counts differ between haplotypes because the ≥ 5 call filter is applied to each haplotype separately; R2 requires both.) As expected: H19 paternal; KvDMR and PWS-IC maternal. (b) With fewer calls a single CpG’s level is very noisy (B2c); 5 is a minimum, more is better.
C5. (a) One CpG call on one read: read id, position in the read, reference position, chromosome, probability of the call, call code (m, h, -), and whether it failed. (b) About 197 000 calls (all CpGs of every read that overlaps the window, including parts outside it), about 10% failed (the threshold is the 10th percentile).
C6. (a) EcoGII: 0.50% of adenines (561 337 A positions); untreated: 0.021%. (b) Thresholds 0.975 (EcoGII) and 0.982 (untreated) for A, vs 0.865 for C: almost all A calls are confidently “unmodified”, so the 10th percentile of confidence is very high. The same rule (drop the least confident 10%) gives very different thresholds for different modifications.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 9 779 CpGs with ≥ 10 calls in the nanopore data and in each WGBS replicate; r = 0.92 with the pooled WGBS, median absolute difference 0.05. (b) The WGBS replicates agree with each other at r = 0.80; nanopore agrees with replicate 2 at r = 0.94 and with replicate 1 at r = 0.82, so replicate 1 is the noisiest data set. A correlation between two assays is limited by the noisier one; a replicate-vs-replicate comparison shows what agreement to expect. (c) CpG methylation is almost always symmetric, so adding strands doubles the coverage. bedMethyl gives the position of the C; on the − strand the C of a CpG is the second base, one to the right of the + strand C.
R2. (a) As in C4: H19 paternal 0.72 / maternal 0.01; KvDMR 0.00 / 0.90; PWS-IC 0.04 / 0.75. (b) Downstream of the PWS-IC the paternal allele becomes highly methylated (~1.0) over the gene body while the maternal allele stays low. The paternal SNRPN copy is transcribed, and gene-body methylation follows transcription (H3K36me3 recruits DNMT3B).
R3. (a) 9 paternal and 6 maternal reads that span the central 2.5 kb and carry an informative SNP; few, because the nearest informative SNP is 6 kb away (C3c), so only reads longer than ~6–10 kb are tagged. Paternal reads: 67% of calls methylated; maternal: 8%. (b) Yes, a few isolated calls. Compare with the false-positive rate of the model (unmethylated control DNA), check whether they cluster at the ICR edges (where methylation changes), and check the call probabilities.
R4. (a) chrX: 62% of 399 promoter CGIs methylated on one haplotype only; chr20: 1.5% of 330. (b) 37 chrX CGIs: GTPBP6, PPP2R3B, SHOX, SLC25A6, ASMTL, P2RY8, AKAP17A, ZBED1, CD99 (all PAR1), and STS, PRKX, KDM6A, KDM5C, DDX3X, EIF1AX, EIF2S3, ZFX, USP9X, RPS4X, TXLNG, … known escapees. (c) The haplotypes in these files come from read-based phasing within phase blocks; hp1 in one block is unrelated to hp1 in the next, and none carries a parental label. You would need trio phasing of SNPs along the whole X (as in C3) or a haplotype-resolved assembly with parental data.
R5. (a) EcoGII 4.82% in peaks, 0.37% outside (13-fold); untreated 0.04% and 0.02%. (b) A sharp peak of ~8.5% within ±50 bp of the summit, then a plateau of ~3–3.7% out to ±400 bp and a decline to ~1.5–2.5% at ±1 kb: the summit is the nucleosome-free core; the plateau is the wider open region with linker DNA between positioned nucleosomes; far away the chromatin is closed.

title: Quiz: linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Short questions on nearest genes, correlation, the activity-by-contact model and how to evaluate enhancer–gene predictions. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Give two reasons why the nearest gene of a distal ATAC peak is often not the gene it regulates.






Hint





Think about 3D structure, and about whether the nearest gene is even expressed.









Answer






Enhancers act through 3D contact, which can skip genes: the element may be in the same domain as a gene further away and separated from the nearest gene by a boundary (examples: the ZRS acting on SHH 1 Mb away, the FTO intron acting on IRX3). (2) The nearest gene may be silent in the cell type, or expressed from its own promoter without needing this element. Also: one element can regulate several genes. In the K562 CRISPRi benchmark the nearest protein-coding gene is right for about half the links (precision 0.41, recall 0.54).





Q2. Gene G has three elements besides its promoter. Promoter: activity 10 at distance 0; E1: activity 4 at 10 kb; E2: activity 8 at 40 kb; E3: activity 1 at 100 kb. With contact \(C = 1/\max(d, 5\text{ kb})\), compute the ABC score of E2. Is it predicted to regulate G at a threshold of 0.02?






Hint





\(A \times C\): promoter \(10/5\), E1 \(4/10\), E2 \(8/40\), E3 \(1/100\).









Answer





\(A \times C\): promoter 2.0, E1 0.4, E2 0.2, E3 0.01; sum 2.61. ABC(E2) = 0.2/2.61 = 0.077: yes, above 0.02. (E1 0.15, E3 0.004, the promoter 0.77.)




Q3. In Q2, gene G’s promoter becomes silent (activity 0). What happens to the ABC scores of the enhancers, and why is this a problem?






Answer





The sum drops to 0.61 and every enhancer’s share rises (E2: 0.2/0.61 = 0.33). ABC is a relative measure and does not know that the gene is off: a silent gene gets large ABC scores from any active element nearby. Predictions should be restricted to expressed genes (or reported with expression), as the published ABC does.




Q4. Why is activity computed as \(\sqrt{\text{ATAC} \times \text{H3K27ac}}\) rather than as ATAC alone?






Answer





Accessibility alone does not distinguish active enhancers from other open sites (CTCF sites, repressor-bound or poised elements); H3K27ac marks active elements. The geometric mean requires both to be high: an element with no acetylation (or no accessibility) gets a low score. It also damps noise: a factor 4 error in one assay changes the activity by a factor 2.




Q5. A method calls 200 enhancer–gene links; 120 are confirmed by CRISPRi. The screen contains 300 true links among 6000 tested pairs. Compute precision and recall. What precision would a random set of 200 pairs have?






Answer





Precision 120/200 = 0.60; recall 120/300 = 0.40. A random set has, on average, the fraction of positives: 300/6000 = 0.05.




Q6. On a benchmark with 4.5% positives, a predictor has a false positive rate of 0.04 and a true positive rate of 0.55. A colleague says “it is excellent, the ROC point is near the top-left corner”. What is its precision? Comment.






Hint





Take 10 000 pairs: 450 positives, 9550 negatives.









Answer





TP = 0.55 × 450 ≈ 248; FP = 0.04 × 9550 = 382. Precision = 248/630 ≈ 0.39: most calls are wrong, although the ROC point looks good. With rare positives, the many negatives make the false positive rate small even when false positives outnumber true ones. Use precision–recall curves and compare with a baseline such as distance.




Q7. Accessibility of an element and expression of a gene on another chromosome correlate at r = 0.95 across 6 samples (3 B-cell, 3 T-cell). Is this evidence for regulation? What would make a correlation-based link more convincing?






Answer





No. With two groups, any B-specific element correlates with any B-specific gene, anywhere in the genome: the correlation reflects the cell-type programme, not regulation, and \(r\) is easily near ±1 with 6 points in 2 groups. More convincing: restrict to cis pairs (e.g. within 500 kb), use many diverse samples (dozens of cell types, hundreds of individuals, or thousands of single cells), compare with a null (random or trans pairs), combine with distance or contact, and validate by perturbation.




Q8. Read the figure: in the K562 benchmark, what are the AUPRCs of “1 / distance”, “activity only” and ABC? What do they say about where the information in ABC comes from?







Answer





1/distance 0.44, activity only 0.10, ABC 0.48 (ATAC) and 0.52 (DNase); random 0.045. Most of the information is in distance (contact): real links are mostly close. Activity alone is nearly useless because an element’s activity is the same for every gene it is tested against. Combined and normalised per gene, activity improves on distance, mainly in the top of the ranking (higher precision at low and moderate recall).




Q9. A CRISPRi screen silences an enhancer predicted by ABC and finds no significant change in the target gene. Give three possible explanations other than “the prediction is wrong”.






Answer






Insufficient power: real effects are often 5–20%, and too few cells or guides miss them. (2) Redundancy: other enhancers of the same gene compensate (shadow enhancers). (3) Incomplete silencing: the guides did not cover the functional part of the element, or KRAB did not silence it fully. Also: the effect exists only in another state (stimulation, another cell type), or the gene is measured poorly (low expression).





Q10. Your study finds 5000 peaks more open after a drug treatment. Outline how you would go from these peaks to candidate target genes, and how RNA-seq from the same samples can test whether your links are reasonable.






Answer





Link each peak to genes with an ABC-type score (activity from ATAC + H3K27ac in the treated cells, contact from Hi-C or a power law), restricted to expressed genes; keep the score and the distance in the table and treat nearest gene only as a labelled fallback. Then test concordance: genes linked to opening peaks should go up after treatment more often than genes linked to unchanged peaks (or than the nearest genes of random peaks). Concordance supports the links on average; for the key pairs, validate by CRISPRi or deletion of the element.

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Assign an element to its nearest gene and say how often that is right, using CRISPRi screens as the ground truth.
Compute an activity-by-contact (ABC) score by hand, and explain what the normalisation per gene does.
Compute precision and recall from a confusion matrix, read a precision–recall curve, and know why the baseline is the fraction of positives.
Explain why correlation of accessibility and expression across a few cell types links unrelated genes, and how a null distribution helps.
In R: score ten thousand CRISPRi-tested element–gene pairs in K562 by distance, activity, correlation (Corces et al. 2016 cell types) and ABC; compare them; then build ABC from the course GM12878 ATAC and H3K27ac tracks and test it on the GM12878 CRISPRi pairs.

text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Assign an element to its nearest gene and say how often that is right, using CRISPRi screens as the ground truth.
Compute an activity-by-contact (ABC) score by hand, and explain what the normalisation per gene does.
Compute precision and recall from a confusion matrix, read a precision–recall curve, and know why the baseline is the fraction of positives.
Explain why correlation of accessibility and expression across a few cell types links unrelated genes, and how a null distribution helps.
In R: score ten thousand CRISPRi-tested element–gene pairs in K562 by distance, activity, correlation (Corces et al. 2016 cell types) and ABC; compare them; then build ABC from the course GM12878 ATAC and H3K27ac tracks and test it on the GM12878 CRISPRi pairs.

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Background
Nearest gene. Assign each element to the gene with the closest TSS (often only protein-coding genes, sometimes only expressed ones). Free and always available; wrong for a large fraction of enhancers.
Activity-by-contact (ABC) (Fulco et al. 2019). For element \(E\) and gene \(G\),
\[ \text{ABC}(E, G) = \frac{A_E \cdot C_{E,G}}{\sum_{e} A_e \cdot C_{e,G}} \]
where the sum runs over all candidate elements \(e\) within 5 Mb of \(G\)’s TSS, including \(G\)’s own promoter. Activity \(A = \sqrt{\text{accessibility} \times \text{H3K27ac}}\) (accessibility from DNase-seq or ATAC-seq). Contact \(C\) comes from Hi-C or from a power law of distance, \(C \propto d^{-\gamma}\) with \(\gamma \approx 1\), held constant below 5 kb. A link is predicted when ABC ≥ about 0.02. In the by-hand questions we use \(C = 1 / \max(d, 5\ \text{kb})\), with \(d\) in kb.
CRISPRi screens. dCas9-KRAB silences an element; if a gene’s expression drops significantly, the pair is positive. Not significant (with enough power) = negative.
Precision and recall. For a set of predicted links: precision \(= TP / (TP + FP)\), recall \(= TP / (TP + FN)\). Ranking all pairs by a score and lowering the threshold traces the precision–recall (PR) curve; its area is the AUPRC. A random score has precision equal to the fraction of positives at every recall.
Correlation across samples. Pearson’s \(r\) between an element’s accessibility and a gene’s expression across samples (cell types, individuals, single cells). With \(n\) independent samples and no true correlation, \(r\) exceeds \(t / \sqrt{t^2 + n - 2}\) with the one-sided probability of \(t\) under a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom. Cell types are not independent samples, so an empirical null (random pairs) is safer.

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Data
All from the course data folder (data/download.sh integration-rnaseq; the K562 element table is made by data/prepare-integ.sh):
mkdir -p ~/epi/linking && cd ~/epi/linking
D=/path/to/course/data

crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz: the K562 CRISPRi benchmark of Gschwind et al. 2023 (source): 10 356 element–gene pairs from Fulco et al. 2016 and 2019 (re-processed by Nasser et al. 2021), Gasperini et al. 2019 and Schraivogel et al. 2020, GRCh38. Key columns: chrom chromStart chromEnd (the element, 0-based starts), measuredGeneSymbol, startTSS, EffectSize (relative change of expression), Regulated (TRUE = significant decrease), distanceToTSS, Dataset.
crispr_benchmark_heldout.tsv.gz: the same format for five other cell types; we use its 68 GM12878 pairs.
k562_abc_elements.tsv.gz: 60 956 candidate elements in K562 (ATAC peak summits ± 250 bp, merged, plus all protein-coding promoters) with mean signal of ENCODE K562 ATAC-seq (fold change), DNase-seq (read-depth normalised) and H3K27ac (fold change, in a window 250 bp wider on each side).
k562_rna_rep1_genes.tsv, gm12878_rna_rep1_genes.tsv: ENCODE RNA-seq gene quantifications (RSEM, TPM).
From earlier units: gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz, gm12878_atac_fc.bigWig, gm12878_h3k27ac_fc.bigWig, gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz, hg38_blacklist.bed.gz, corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz, corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz, hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz.

Shortcuts, said plainly. The ground truth is in K562 (an erythroleukaemia line), because that is where the large CRISPRi screens were done; GM12878 has only 68 tested pairs. Our ABC is a simplified re-implementation: ENCODE fold-change tracks instead of read counts, no quantile normalisation, the power law instead of Hi-C, and ATAC peaks (not DNase peaks) as candidates. Correlation uses normal blood cell types (Corces et al.) to predict links in K562, a different cell. The numbers are therefore lower than the published ones; the comparisons between methods are fair, because every method is scored on the same pairs.
The R part runs in about 5 minutes and needs about 6 GB of memory (the GM12878 bigWigs in R7). On the cluster, run it in an interactive job or with Rscript in an sbatch script.

B3. Activity. Three elements have (ATAC, H3K27ac) = (16, 1), (4, 4) and (1, 25).

Why a geometric mean, rather than the sum or either mark alone?

B4. Precision and recall. On the K562 benchmark (471 positive pairs out of 10 356), “the element regulates its nearest protein-coding gene” makes 630 calls, 256 of them correct.

Fill in the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN). Compute precision and recall.
What precision does a random choice of 630 pairs have, on average?
Method X calls 100 links with 70 correct. Compute its precision and recall. Is X better than the nearest gene? For what purpose would you prefer each?

Without computing, what are \(r(E, F)\) and \(r(E, K)\)? Why?

B7. Judge the claims.

“We silenced 200 candidate enhancers by CRISPRi; 170 had no significant effect on their nearest gene, so most predicted enhancers are not functional.”
“Across 6 samples (3 treated, 3 control), 2 000 peaks correlate with 800 genes within 1 Mb at r > 0.95; we propose these as enhancer–gene links.”

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
On the command line

C1 — The benchmark
zcat $D/crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | cat -n | head -25
zcat $D/crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz | awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 { n[$22]++; p[$22] += ($21 == "TRUE") }
  END { for (d in n) print d, n[d], p[d] }'
for r in TRUE FALSE; do
  zcat $D/crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz | awk -F'\t' -v r=$r 'NR > 1 && $21 == r { print $23 }' \
    | sort -n | awk -v r=$r '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print r, "pairs", NR, "median distance", a[int((NR + 1) / 2)] }'
done

Which columns hold the gene, the effect size, the “Regulated” call and the distance?
How many pairs and positives does each dataset contribute?
What is the median distance from element to TSS for positive and for negative pairs?



C2 — Nearest gene with bedtools
zcat $D/gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz \
  | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$3 == "gene" && $9 ~ /gene_type "protein_coding"/ {
      match($9, /gene_name "[^"]+"/); g = substr($9, RSTART + 11, RLENGTH - 12)
      tss = ($7 == "+") ? $4 - 1 : $5 - 1; print $1, tss, tss + 1, g }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > tss_pc.bed
zcat $D/crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz \
  | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 && $21 == "TRUE" { m = int(($2 + $3) / 2); print $1, m, m + 1, $9 }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > positives_mid.bed
wc -l < tss_pc.bed
wc -l < positives_mid.bed
bedtools closest -a positives_mid.bed -b tss_pc.bed -d -t first | awk '$4 == $8' | wc -l
bedtools closest -a positives_mid.bed -b tss_pc.bed -d -k 3 | awk '$4 == $8' | wc -l

How many of the 471 positive elements have their target as the nearest protein-coding TSS? Among the 3 nearest?
What does -t first do, and why is it needed?
This counts recall only. What would you need to compute the precision of the nearest-gene rule on the command line?



C3 — Candidate elements for ABC
zcat $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ s = $2 + $10; print $1, s - 250, s + 250 }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge > gm12878_elements.bed
zcat $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz | wc -l
wc -l < gm12878_elements.bed
awk -v OFS='\t' '$4 == "PPIF"' tss_pc.bed > ppif_tss.bed
for w in 100000 1000000 5000000; do
  echo $w $(bedtools window -a ppif_tss.bed -b gm12878_elements.bed -w $w | wc -l)
done

How many peaks, and how many merged 500-bp elements? Why are there fewer elements than peaks?
How many elements enter the ABC denominator of PPIF (within 5 Mb)? How many lie within 100 kb?
Column 10 of a narrowPeak file is the summit offset. Why do ABC and many other tools re-centre peaks on summits and give them a fixed width?

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
In R
You need data.table, GenomicRanges, rtracklayer and ggplot2 (see Install the software you need).
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(ggplot2)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — The CRISPRi benchmark
cr <- fread(file.path(D, "crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz"))
dim(cr)
table(cr$Dataset, cr$Regulated)
cr[, .(pairs = .N, elements = uniqueN(paste(chrom, chromStart)), genes = uniqueN(measuredGeneSymbol),
       positives = sum(Regulated))]
cr[, .(median_kb = median(distanceToTSS) / 1000, q90_kb = quantile(distanceToTSS, 0.9) / 1000), by = Regulated]
summary(cr$EffectSize[cr$Regulated])
ggplot(cr, aes(distanceToTSS / 1000, fill = Regulated)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) + scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ Regulated, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "distance to TSS (kb)")

How many pairs, elements, genes and positives? What fraction of pairs is positive?
Compare the distances of positive and negative pairs.
What is the median effect of a positive element? What does an EffectSize of −0.10 mean?



R2 — The nearest gene
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), feature.type = "gene")
pc  <- gtf[gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding"]
tss <- resize(pc, width = 1, fix = "start")
tss$ensg <- sub("\\..*", "", tss$gene_id)
rna <- fread(file.path(D, "k562_rna_rep1_genes.tsv"))
tss$tpm <- rna$TPM[match(tss$ensg, sub("\\..*", "", rna$gene_id))]
expr <- tss[!is.na(tss$tpm) & tss$tpm >= 1]
c(protein_coding = length(tss), expressed = length(expr))
mid <- resize(GRanges(cr$chrom, IRanges(cr$chromStart + 1, cr$chromEnd)), width = 1, fix = "center")
cr[, nearest_pc   := tss$gene_name[nearest(mid, tss)]  == measuredGeneSymbol]
cr[, nearest_expr := expr$gene_name[nearest(mid, expr)] == measuredGeneSymbol]
pr_point <- function(pred, truth) c(TP = sum(pred & truth), FP = sum(pred & !truth), FN = sum(!pred & truth),
                                    precision = sum(pred & truth) / sum(pred), recall = sum(pred & truth) / sum(truth))
rbind(nearest_pc = pr_point(cr$nearest_pc, cr$Regulated), nearest_expr = pr_point(cr$nearest_expr, cr$Regulated))
mean(cr$Regulated)

Why resize(..., fix = "start") for the TSS, and why does it give the right position for genes on the minus strand?
What are the precision and recall of the two nearest-gene rules? Explain why restricting to expressed genes raises recall but lowers precision.
Compare with C2: do you get the same number of correct positives? If not, why might they differ?



R3 — Distance as a score; the PR curve
pr_curve <- function(score, truth) {
  o <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)
  tp <- cumsum(truth[o])
  # A threshold includes every pair with the same score: never split a tie.
  last <- !duplicated(score[o], fromLast = TRUE)
  k <- which(last)
  data.frame(threshold = score[o][k], recall = tp[k] / sum(truth), precision = tp[k] / k)
}
auprc <- function(score, truth) { p <- pr_curve(score, truth); sum(diff(c(0, p$recall)) * p$precision) }
prec_at_recall <- function(score, truth, r = 0.7) { p <- pr_curve(score, truth); p$precision[which(p$recall >= r)[1]] }
cr[, inv_dist := 1 / distanceToTSS]
c(AUPRC = auprc(cr$inv_dist, cr$Regulated), prec70 = prec_at_recall(cr$inv_dist, cr$Regulated))
p <- pr_curve(cr$inv_dist, cr$Regulated)
p[which(p$recall >= 0.5)[1], ]

Explain pr_curve line by line. Why must all pairs with the same score enter together?
What is the AUPRC of 1/distance, and its precision at 70% recall? At what distance threshold does it reach 50% recall, and with what precision?
Is 1/distance better than the nearest gene? Compare at the nearest gene’s recall (0.54).



R4 — Candidate elements and activity
el <- fread(file.path(D, "k562_abc_elements.tsv.gz"))
el
el[, .(n = .N, median_width = median(end - start)), by = promoter]
el[, activity := sqrt(dnase * h3k27ac)]
el[, activity_atac := sqrt(atac * h3k27ac)]
cor(el[, .(atac, dnase, h3k27ac)], method = "spearman")
elg <- GRanges(el$chr, IRanges(el$start + 1, el$end))
tested <- GRanges(cr$chrom, IRanges(cr$chromStart + 1, cr$chromEnd))
h <- findOverlaps(tested, elg)
c(tested_overlapping = mean(seq_along(tested) %in% queryHits(h)),
  positives_overlapping = mean(which(cr$Regulated) %in% queryHits(h)))
best <- function(v) { s <- numeric(length(tested)); m <- tapply(v[subjectHits(h)], queryHits(h), max); s[as.integer(names(m))] <- m; s }
cr[, `:=`(A = best(el$activity), A_atac = best(el$activity_atac))]
sapply(cr[, .(A, A_atac)], auprc, truth = cr$Regulated)

How many candidate elements are there, and how many are promoters? Why are promoters included even when they are closed?
How well do ATAC, DNase and H3K27ac agree (Spearman)? Which pair agrees best?
What fraction of tested elements, and of positive elements, overlaps a candidate? What score does a pair get when it overlaps none?
What is the AUPRC of activity alone? Why is it so low, although enhancers are, by definition, active?



R5 — ABC
el[, mid := (start + end) %/% 2]
genes <- cr[, .(chr = chrTSS[1], tss = startTSS[1] + 1), by = .(gene = measuredGeneSymbol)]   # one TSS per gene
win <- GRanges(genes$chr, IRanges(pmax(genes$tss - 5e6, 1), genes$tss + 5e6))
hw  <- findOverlaps(win, elg)
abc <- data.table(gene = genes$gene[queryHits(hw)], e = subjectHits(hw))
abc[, d := abs(el$mid[e] - genes$tss[queryHits(hw)])]
abc[, C := (pmax(d, 5000) + 1)^-1.024]
abc[, ABC := el$activity[e] * C / sum(el$activity[e] * C), by = gene]
abc[, ABC_atac := el$activity_atac[e] * C / sum(el$activity_atac[e] * C), by = gene]
nrow(abc); abc[, .N, by = gene][, summary(N)]
hm <- data.table(pair = queryHits(h), e = subjectHits(h), gene = cr$measuredGeneSymbol[queryHits(h)])
hm <- merge(hm, abc[, .(gene, e, ABC, ABC_atac)], by = c("gene", "e"))
s <- hm[, .(ABC = max(ABC), ABC_atac = max(ABC_atac)), by = pair]
cr[, `:=`(ABC = 0, ABC_atac = 0)]
cr[s$pair, `:=`(ABC = s$ABC, ABC_atac = s$ABC_atac)]
res <- sapply(cr[, .(inv_dist, A, ABC_atac, ABC)], function(v)
  c(AUPRC = auprc(v, cr$Regulated), prec_at_70 = prec_at_recall(v, cr$Regulated)))
round(res, 3)
cr[, .(called = sum(ABC >= 0.02), TP = sum(ABC >= 0.02 & Regulated),
       precision = sum(ABC >= 0.02 & Regulated) / sum(ABC >= 0.02), recall = sum(ABC >= 0.02 & Regulated) / sum(Regulated))]
curves <- rbind(data.frame(pr_curve(cr$inv_dist, cr$Regulated), score = "1 / distance"),
                data.frame(pr_curve(cr$A, cr$Regulated), score = "activity only"),
                data.frame(pr_curve(cr$ABC, cr$Regulated), score = "ABC"))
ggplot(curves, aes(recall, precision, colour = score)) + geom_path() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(cr$Regulated), linetype = 2)

Explain each line of the ABC computation. Where is the sum over all elements of a gene, and why by = gene?
How many element–gene pairs are scored, and how many elements does a typical gene have within 5 Mb?
Fill in the table: AUPRC and precision at 70% recall for 1/distance, activity, ABC with ATAC and ABC with DNase. Which input works better, and why might ATAC fold change be worse than DNase read-depth signal?
At ABC ≥ 0.02: how many calls, precision, recall? Compare with the nearest gene (R2).



R6 — Correlation across 13 blood cell types
atac <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz"))
code2type <- c(`1` = "HSC", `2` = "MPP", `3` = "LMPP", `4` = "CMP", `5` = "GMP", `6` = "MEP", `7` = "Mono",
               `9` = "CD4", `10` = "CD8", `11` = "NK", `13` = "Bcell", `14` = "CLP", `15` = "Ery")
healthy <- grep("^(Donor)?[0-9]+-", names(atac), value = TRUE)
re <- "^(?:Donor)?([0-9]+)-(?:[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*-)?([0-9]+)([A-C]?)(?:-[0-9]+)?$"
ct <- code2type[sapply(regmatches(healthy, regexec(re, healthy, perl = TRUE)), `[`, 3)]
cpm_by_type <- function(m, type) sapply(split(seq_along(type), type), function(i)
  log2(rowMeans(sweep(m[, i, drop = FALSE], 2, colSums(m[, i, drop = FALSE]), "/")) * 1e6 + 1))
A <- cpm_by_type(as.matrix(atac[, ..healthy]), ct)
chainf <- tempfile(fileext = ".chain")
writeLines(readLines(gzfile(file.path(D, "hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz"))), chainf)
lo <- liftOver(GRanges(atac$Chr, IRanges(atac$Start + 1, atac$End)), import.chain(chainf))
one <- lengths(lo) == 1
peaks38 <- unlist(lo[one]); A <- A[one, ]
rna <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz"))
rcol <- grep("^[0-9]+-", names(rna), value = TRUE)
rtype <- sub("^NKcell$", "NK", sub("Tcell$", "", sub("^[0-9]+-", "", rcol)))   # CD4Tcell -> CD4, NKcell -> NK
R <- cpm_by_type(as.matrix(rna[, ..rcol]), rtype); rownames(R) <- rna[[1]]
R <- R[, colnames(A)]
dim(A); dim(R); colnames(A)
h2 <- findOverlaps(tested, peaks38)
g  <- match(cr$measuredGeneSymbol, rownames(R))
r  <- mapply(function(q, s) if (is.na(g[q])) NA else cor(A[s, ], R[g[q], ]), queryHits(h2), subjectHits(h2))
best_r <- tapply(r, queryHits(h2), max, na.rm = TRUE)
cr[, r := NA_real_]; cr[as.integer(names(best_r)), r := best_r]; cr[!is.finite(r), r := NA]
cr[, .(with_r = sum(!is.na(r)), median_r = median(r, na.rm = TRUE), above_0.8 = mean(r > 0.8, na.rm = TRUE)), by = Regulated]
cr[, r_score := fifelse(is.na(r), -1, r)]
c(corr = auprc(cr$r_score, cr$Regulated), dist = auprc(cr$inv_dist, cr$Regulated))
set.seed(1); null_r <- replicate(5000, cor(A[sample(nrow(A), 1), ], R[sample(nrow(R), 1), ]))
quantile(null_r, c(0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)

What are the 13 columns of A and R, and what is one entry? Why summarise per cell type rather than per library?
What is the median correlation of positive and negative pairs? What fraction has \(r > 0.8\)?
What are the 95% and 99% quantiles of \(r\) for random pairs? Compare with B5b.
What is the AUPRC of correlation? Give two reasons why it is much worse than distance here.



R7 — ABC in GM12878 from the course tracks
prom <- resize(resize(pc, 1, fix = "start"), 500, fix = "center")
p  <- fread(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"))[V1 %in% paste0("chr", c(1:22, "X"))]
pk <- GRanges(p$V1, IRanges(p$V2 + p$V10 + 1 - 250, width = 500))
gm <- reduce(c(granges(pk), granges(prom[seqnames(prom) %in% paste0("chr", c(1:22, "X"))])), ignore.strand = TRUE)
gm <- gm[!overlapsAny(gm, import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz")))]
gm$promoter <- overlapsAny(gm, prom)
signal <- function(bw, gr) {                                    # mean bigWig value in each range
  cv <- import(bw, which = reduce(gr), as = "RleList")
  s  <- numeric(length(gr))
  for (ch in unique(as.character(seqnames(gr)))) {
    i <- which(as.character(seqnames(gr)) == ch)
    s[i] <- viewMeans(Views(cv[[ch]], ranges(gr)[i]))
  }
  s
}
system.time({
  gm$atac    <- signal(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_fc.bigWig"), gm) * width(gm) / 500
  gm$h3k27ac <- signal(file.path(D, "gm12878_h3k27ac_fc.bigWig"), resize(gm, width(gm) + 500, fix = "center")) *
                (width(gm) + 500) / 1000
})
gm$activity <- sqrt(gm$atac * gm$h3k27ac)
length(gm); table(gm$promoter)
ho <- fread(file.path(D, "crispr_benchmark_heldout.tsv.gz"))[CellType == "GM12878"]
ho[, .(pairs = .N, positives = sum(Regulated)), by = measuredGeneSymbol]
genes_gm <- ho[, .(chr = chrTSS[1], tss = startTSS[1] + 1), by = .(gene = measuredGeneSymbol)]
gmid <- (start(gm) + end(gm)) %/% 2
abc_gene <- function(chr, tss) {
  j  <- which(as.character(seqnames(gm)) == chr & abs(gmid - tss) <= 5e6)
  ac <- gm$activity[j] * (pmax(abs(gmid[j] - tss), 5000) + 1)^-1.024
  data.table(e = j, dist = abs(gmid[j] - tss), ABC = ac / sum(ac))
}
abc_gm <- genes_gm[, abc_gene(chr, tss), by = gene]
hg <- findOverlaps(GRanges(ho$chrom, IRanges(ho$chromStart + 1, ho$chromEnd)), gm)
hmg <- merge(data.table(pair = queryHits(hg), e = subjectHits(hg), gene = ho$measuredGeneSymbol[queryHits(hg)]),
             abc_gm, by = c("gene", "e"))
ho[, ABC := 0]; sg <- hmg[, .(ABC = max(ABC)), by = pair]; ho[sg$pair, ABC := sg$ABC]
table(predicted = ho$ABC >= 0.02, CRISPRi = ho$Regulated)

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — ABC and contact (B2, R5, R7)





Work in a table: one row per element, columns \(d\), \(C\), \(A \times C\). The ABC denominator is the same for all elements of one gene; the gene’s own promoter (at \(d = 0\), so \(C = 1/5\)) is usually the largest term. The formula and its validation are in Fulco et al. 2019; the code and the power-law parameters (γ = 1.024, 5 kb floor) are in the ABC repository. In data.table, abc[, x := ..., by = gene] computes within each gene (data.table intro).









Hint 2 — precision, recall, PR curves (B4, B6, R3)





Draw the 2×2 table first: rows = predicted link or not, columns = positive or negative in the screen. FN = all positives − TP; TN = all pairs − TP − FP − FN. On a PR curve, a random score sits at precision = fraction of positives. Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015 explain why PR curves beat ROC curves for imbalanced data.









Hint 3 — nearest gene (B1, C2, R2)





For a minus-strand gene the TSS is the end coordinate; resize(gr, 1, fix = "start") is strand-aware and takes the 5′ end (GenomicRanges intra-range methods). nearest returns the index of the closest range. On the command line, bedtools closest with -d reports the distance, -t first keeps one hit when several are equally close, -k reports the k nearest. bedtools window finds all features within -w bp.









Hint 4 — correlation and its null (B5, R6)





If two variables are both a linear function of the same group label, their correlation is ±1. The theoretical threshold assumes independent, normally distributed samples; cell types of one lineage (MEP, CMP, Ery) are not independent. cor computes Pearson’s \(r\); replicate repeats an expression to build a null. ArchR’s peak-to-gene linkage and Signac’s LinkPeaks are the single-cell versions.









Hint 5 — reading signal into elements (R4, R7)





import(bw, which = gr, as = "RleList") reads only the regions you ask for, as run-length encoded coverage; Views and viewMeans then average it over each range (rtracklayer). Multiplying the mean by width/500 turns a mean into an “amount” comparable between elements of different width. The benchmark’s own element annotation (columns DHS.RPM, H3K27ac.RPM) uses read counts.









Hint 6 — judging claims (B7)





For each claim ask: was regulation tested (perturbation) or predicted (proximity, contact, correlation)? Is a negative result powered? Is the correlation larger than for random pairs, with enough samples? Osterwalder et al. 2018 (Nature) showed that deleting single enhancers often has no phenotype because others compensate.

title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Distances: A 40 kb, B 30 kb, C 120 kb, D 130 kb. Nearest gene: B (30 kb). Nearest expressed: A (B has TPM 0.2). (b) Expressed genes by distance: A (40), C (120), D (130): C is 2nd. (c) The element contacts C, not A, in 3D (A may be in another domain, across a CTCF boundary); A is expressed from its own promoter or other enhancers and does not need this one; C’s promoter is compatible with this kind of enhancer (promoter–enhancer specificity); the element may regulate both but A’s effect is too small to detect.
B2. (a) \(C\): P 1/5, E3 1/8, E1 1/20, E2 1/100. \(A \times C\): P 2.4, E3 0.375, E1 0.3, E2 0.2; sum 3.275. ABC: E1 0.3/3.275 = 0.092, E2 0.061, E3 0.115 (P 0.733). All three pass 0.02. (b) Distances to H: H promoter 0, E2 50, E1 130, E3 158, P 150 kb. \(A \times C\): H promoter 2/5 = 0.4, E2 20/50 = 0.4, E1 6/130 = 0.046, E3 3/158 = 0.019, P 12/150 = 0.08; sum 0.945. ABC(E2, H) = 0.4/0.945 = 0.42. E2 is closer to H (50 vs 100 kb), and H has a weak promoter and few other elements, so E2 is a large share of H’s input; G has a strong promoter and other close elements, so E2 is a small share. ABC is relative: the same element scores differently for each gene. (c) Without H’s promoter, the sum is 0.545 and ABC(E2, H) = 0.4/0.545 = 0.73: higher still. ABC does not know whether a gene is expressed; a silent gene gets a large ABC from any nearby active element. Either restrict predictions to expressed genes, or treat links to silent genes as meaningless (the published ABC reports gene expression alongside).
B3. (a) 4, 4, 5. (b) (16, 1): open but not acetylated: e.g. a CTCF site or an element bound by a repressor or a poised factor. (4, 4): a typical active enhancer. (1, 25): acetylated but barely open: e.g. the flanks of an active region, or a broad acetylated domain without a single open site. (c) The geometric mean requires both: an element with zero of either scores zero, and it damps noise in one assay (a factor 4 error in one mark changes \(A\) by a factor 2). A sum would let a strong CTCF site look like a strong enhancer.
B4. (a) TP 256, FP 630 − 256 = 374, FN 471 − 256 = 215, TN 10 356 − 256 − 374 − 215 = 9511. Precision 256/630 = 0.41; recall 256/471 = 0.54. (b) The fraction of positives: 471/10 356 = 0.045. (c) X: precision 70/100 = 0.70, recall 70/471 = 0.15. Neither dominates: X is better for picking a short list of candidates to validate (most are real), the nearest gene finds more of the links but half its calls are wrong. Compare methods at equal recall or by the whole PR curve. (d) FPR = 374/(374 + 9511) = 0.038. A ROC point at (FPR 0.04, TPR 0.54) looks excellent, because the 9885 negatives make any number of false positives look small; but 59% of the calls are wrong. With rare positives, precision is the quantity that matters to the person following up the calls.
B5. (a) Both are 1: every vector is a linear function of the group (1 or 2), so any two such vectors are perfectly correlated, whatever their biology. Gene K is on another chromosome and still has \(r = 1\). (b) The theoretical threshold assumes 13 independent samples. The 13 cell types are related (lineages share programmes: MEP, CMP and erythroblasts; CD4, CD8 and NK), so the effective number of independent samples is smaller and large correlations between unrelated features are common: the empirical 95% quantile is 0.59, not 0.48. (c) Restrict to pairs in cis (e.g. within 500 kb) and compare against an empirical null (random or trans pairs, or permuted labels); use many diverse samples (dozens of cell types, hundreds of individuals, thousands of single cells or metacells); combine with distance or contact; validate top links by perturbation.
B6. (a) ABC (DNase × H3K27ac), AUPRC 0.52; random = 0.045. (b) About 0.80 for ABC (DNase) and about 0.65 for 1/distance. (c) Activity ranks pairs by how strong the element is, regardless of the gene: a strong element is tested against many genes in the screen and regulates only one or two of them, so most of its pairs are negative. It barely separates positives from negatives, just above the random line. (d) About one in five positive elements overlaps no candidate element (not called as an ATAC peak in our data), so they get ABC = 0 and tie with thousands of negatives at the bottom of the ranking.
B7. (a) Nearest gene is right for about half of the links; a loop shows contact, not regulation (many loops are CTCF–cohesin structural loops), and a loop anchored near the promoter may connect it to other elements. Ask for a perturbation (CRISPRi of the peak, measuring X and the other genes nearby) or at least an ABC-type score and concordant changes in expression. (b) Two problems: the test was only on the nearest gene (the elements may regulate other genes), and negatives may lack power (most real effects are 5–20%), or be masked by redundant enhancers. Ask for the power per pair and for measurement of all genes within 1 Mb (as in single-cell screens). (c) With 3 vs 3 samples the correlation is essentially a treatment effect: every peak that changes with treatment correlates with every gene that changes, near or far. \(r > 0.95\) is easy with 6 points in 2 groups. Ask for a null (pairs on other chromosomes give the false-positive rate), more and more varied samples, and a comparison with distance.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) Gene measuredGeneSymbol = column 9, EffectSize = 5, Regulated = 21, distanceToTSS = 23 (Dataset = 22). (b) Gasperini2019 5299 pairs / 360 positives; Nasser2021 3751 / 88; Schraivogel2020 1306 / 23. (c) Positives: 471 pairs, median 26 130 bp; negatives: 9885 pairs, median 386 621 bp.
C2. (a) 20 065 protein-coding TSSs, 471 positive elements. The target is the nearest TSS for 256 positives and among the 3 nearest for 368. (b) If two TSSs are at exactly the same distance (genes sharing a bidirectional promoter, or alternative TSSs at the same position), closest would report both; -t first keeps one, so each element gets one predicted gene, like nearest in R. (c) The same closest for all tested pairs (not only positives): count the pairs whose gene is the nearest (the calls, 630) and among them the positives (256); precision = 256/630.
C3. (a) 155 153 peaks; 77 690 merged elements. The IDR peak file lists several summits for the same region (one row per summit), and neighbouring summits within 500 bp merge. (b) 301 elements within 5 Mb of the PPIF TSS (75 within 1 Mb, 19 within 100 kb); these are ATAC elements only, the R version adds the promoters. (c) Re-centring on the summit puts the element where the signal is highest (the TF binding site) and fixed widths make signals comparable: a 3-kb merged peak would otherwise collect more reads just because it is wide.









Solutions — R





Run times are from one server core; a laptop is 1.5–3 times slower.
R1. (a) 10 356 pairs, 3941 elements, 2113 genes, 471 positives: 4.5%. (b) Positives: median 26 kb, 90% within 207 kb; negatives: median 387 kb, 90% within 938 kb. The screens tested most pairs at hundreds of kb, but positives are mostly close. (c) Median −0.10: silencing the element lowers the gene’s expression by 10% (EffectSize is the relative change; −0.10 = 90% of control). Effects range from −0.1% to −93%.
R2. (a) fix = "start" is strand-aware: for a minus-strand gene the “start” of the feature in transcription direction is its highest coordinate, which is where the TSS is. (b) 20 065 protein-coding genes, 9499 of them expressed (TPM ≥ 1). Nearest protein-coding: TP 256, FP 374, precision 0.41, recall 0.54. Nearest expressed: TP 284, FP 532, precision 0.35, recall 0.60. Removing silent genes lets elements skip to the correct expressed gene (recall up), but some elements that were previously assigned to a non-tested or silent gene now get an expressed gene that is tested and negative (more calls, precision down). (c) Yes, 256 in both. Small differences can arise from how the element centre is rounded and how ties are broken.
R3. (a) order(score, decreasing = TRUE) sorts pairs from the highest score down; cumsum(truth[o]) counts true positives. last keeps only the final row of each tied group, so every point corresponds to an attainable score threshold. Recall = TP/all positives, precision = TP/\(k\). Splitting ties, randomly or by file order, invents thresholds that the score cannot distinguish. Here AUPRC is computed as non-interpolated average precision (definition). (b) AUPRC 0.438, precision at 70% recall 0.316. 50% recall at a distance of about 26 kb (1/3.83 × 10⁻⁵), with precision 0.43. (c) At recall 0.54 the distance curve has precision about 0.41, the same as the nearest gene: in this benchmark the two rules are nearly equivalent; distance has the advantage of a full ranking.
R4. (a) 60 956 elements, 18 245 promoters (median width 742 and 720 bp). Promoters are included because ABC needs the gene’s own promoter in the denominator, and because promoters of other genes also act as enhancers (they compete for the gene). A closed promoter has activity 0 and does not affect the result. (b) Spearman: ATAC–DNase 0.72, DNase–H3K27ac 0.79, ATAC–H3K27ac 0.56. (c) 62.6% of tested elements and 81.5% of positive elements overlap a candidate; a pair without overlap gets 0 (it can never be predicted). (d) AUPRC 0.099 (DNase) and 0.099 (ATAC): an element’s activity is the same for every gene it is tested against, and most of those genes are not its targets.
R5. (a) For each gene, win is the 10-Mb window around its TSS; findOverlaps lists every element in it; d is the distance from the element’s centre to the TSS; C is the power-law contact; AC / sum(AC) with by = gene divides each element’s product by the sum over all elements of the same gene. The tested element is then matched to the candidates it overlaps, keeping the maximum ABC for that gene. (b) 758 316 element–gene pairs; a gene has a median of 320 elements within 5 Mb (22–849). title: Exercise: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Where this leads

Epigenomics and genetic variation uses enhancer–gene links to go from a GWAS variant in an enhancer to a candidate gene, and adds human genetics (eQTLs, colocalisation) as another kind of evidence.
3D genome organisation, Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices and Calling compartments, TADs and loops compute the contact frequencies that ABC can use instead of the power law.
What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works returns to enhancer–gene prediction as a machine-learning task, and to evaluation with PR curves and baselines.
Genome-wide ABC and ENCODE-rE2G predictions for hundreds of cell types are public (ENCODE portal); for your own cells, run the ABC pipeline on ATAC/DNase + H3K27ac (+ Hi-C).

title: Quiz: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
Short questions on the Hi-C protocol, read pairs, binning and normalisation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. DpnII cuts ^GATC (like MboI). What sequence marks a ligation junction in DpnII Hi-C reads, and why does it contain the site twice?






Answer





GATCGATC. Each cut end has a 4-nt 5′ overhang GATC; the fill-in copies it on both ends, and the blunt ligation joins the two copies.




Q2. Why are the two reads of a Hi-C pair aligned as single-end reads (bwa mem -SP) instead of as a normal pair?






Answer





A normal paired-end aligner expects the mates to face each other a few hundred bp apart and uses that to place or “rescue” them. In Hi-C the two ends come from loci that can be megabases apart or on different chromosomes, so that assumption is wrong for most pairs.




Q3. A read pair has both sides within the same restriction fragment, 280 bp apart, reads pointing towards each other. What is it, and what does it tell you about 3D structure?






Answer





A dangling end: a fragment that was never ligated (or a biotinylated end without a junction). It carries no information about contacts and is excluded (in practice by ignoring pairs closer than ~1–2 kb, or by explicit classification).




Q4. In the orientation plot, why are the four orientations equally frequent at large distances but not at short distances?






Answer





After ligation, the two fragments can join in either orientation and each can be read from either end, so all four combinations of strands are equally likely for real contacts. At short distances, artefacts with fixed orientations add to them: inward (+ −) dangling ends and re-ligations, outward (− +) self-circles.




Q5. Pair types: what do UU, UR, MU and NU mean, and which are kept?






Answer





UU: both sides uniquely mapped. UR: unique, plus a side rescued from a chimeric read explained by one ligation. MU: one side multi-mapped. NU: one side unmapped. UU, UR and RU are kept; pairs with an M or N side cannot be placed and are dropped.




Q6. Put the pairs (40 000, 160 000), (90 000, 110 000) and (250 000, 120 000) into 100-kb bins.






Answer





(0, 1), (0, 1), (1, 2) — the last pair is reordered so the smaller bin comes first. Pixel (0, 1) = 2, pixel (1, 2) = 1.




Q7. A raw 2 × 2 matrix is [[4, 6], [6, 16]]. Compute the row sums, the biases after one ICE step, and the new matrix.






Answer





Row sums 10 and 22, mean 16; biases 0.625 and 1.375. New pixels: 4/0.391 = 10.2; 6/(0.625 × 1.375) = 6/0.859 = 6.98; 16/1.891 = 8.46. New row sums 17.2 and 15.4: closer to equal; further iterations converge.




Q8. What assumption does matrix balancing make, and give one situation in which it is wrong.






Answer





That every bin would have the same total number of contacts without technical biases (equal visibility). It is wrong where copy number differs, e.g. an amplified region in a cancer genome or an aneuploid chromosome: the extra contacts are real but balancing removes them.




Q9. The expected contact frequency at 400 kb on a chromosome is 0.002 (balanced). A pixel at 400 kb has 0.007. What is its O/E? Another pixel at 20 kb has 0.03 with an expected of 0.05. Which pixel is enriched?






Answer





0.007/0.002 = 3.5: strongly enriched. 0.03/0.05 = 0.6: depleted, although its balanced value is four times higher. Only O/E compares a pixel with its distance.




Q10. Library A: 4% duplicates, 85% cis. Library B: 40% duplicates, 50% cis. Which one should be sequenced deeper, and what probably went wrong with B?






Answer





A. B has low complexity (deeper sequencing gives mostly duplicates) and many trans or random ligations (low cis fraction): typical of too little material, over-amplification, and ligation outside intact nuclei or poor crosslinking.

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
Background
Junction. A restriction enzyme with a 5′ overhang (MboI: ^GATC) leaves ends that are filled in and ligated blunt; the overhang is duplicated: GATC + GATC = GATCGATC.
Pairs. Each side of a read pair is placed by the 5′ end of its 5′-most alignment. A side is Unique (MAPQ ≥ 30), Multi-mapped, Null (unmapped), Rescued (part of a chimeric read explained by one ligation) or part of a Walk. Pair types UU, UR and RU are kept.
Artefacts. Pairs within one restriction fragment with reads pointing inward (+ −) are dangling ends; pointing outward (− +) are self-circles. At large distances the four orientations (+ −, − +, + +, − −) each make up 25%. Duplicates share both 5′ positions and strands.
Matrix. For 0-based positions, bin = ⌊position / bin size⌋; pixel (i, j) counts pairs with one side in bin i and one in bin j. The .pairs format uses 1-based positions, so its bin is ⌊(position − 1) / bin size⌋; cooler cload pairs handles that conversion by default.
Balancing (ICE). Model \(O_{ij} = b_i b_j T_{ij}\); iterate \(b_i \leftarrow\) row sum\(_i\) / mean row sum, divide pixel (i, j) by \(b_i b_j\), until row sums are equal. Expected \(E(s)\) = mean of the balanced diagonal at distance \(s\); O/E = pixel / \(E(s)\).

a    10    8    2

Compute the row sums and their mean, the bias \(b_i\) of each bin, and the matrix after one iteration (divide pixel (i, j) by \(b_i b_j\)).

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
On the command line

C1 — The reference, the reads and the junction
zcat $D/hg38_chr21.fa.gz > chr21.fa
bwa index chr21.fa 2> bwa_index.log
samtools faidx chr21.fa
cut -f1,2 chr21.fa.fai > chr21.sizes
cat chr21.sizes
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_R1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_R1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | head -200000 | grep -c GATCGATC
grep -v '>' chr21.fa | tr -d '\n' | tr acgtn ACGTN | grep -o GATC | wc -l
grep -v '>' chr21.fa | tr -d '\n' | tr acgtn ACGTN | grep -o AAGCTT | wc -l

How many read pairs are there? What fraction of read 1 contains the MboI junction?
How many MboI and HindIII sites does chr21 have? Compare with B1(b). (chr21 has 46.7 Mb including 6.6 Mb of N.)



C2 — Align and parse
bwa mem -SP5M -t 8 chr21.fa $D/gm12878_hic_R1.fastq.gz $D/gm12878_hic_R2.fastq.gz 2> bwa.log \
  | pairtools parse --min-mapq 30 --walks-policy 5unique --max-inter-align-gap 30 --drop-sam --drop-seq \
      -c chr21.sizes --output-stats parse.stats -o chr21.pairs.gz
zcat chr21.pairs.gz | grep -v '^#' | head -5
zcat chr21.pairs.gz | grep '^#columns'
grep -E '^(total|total_unmapped|total_single_sided_mapped|total_mapped|cis_1kb\+)\s' parse.stats
grep '^pair_types' parse.stats

What are the columns of the .pairs file? Which column holds the pair type?
How many pairs have both sides mapped? Which pair types are most common?
How long did the alignment take? (time in front of the command, or the timestamps in bwa.log.)



C3 — Sort, deduplicate, select
pairtools sort --nproc 4 -o chr21.sorted.pairs.gz chr21.pairs.gz
pairtools dedup --max-mismatch 3 --output-stats dedup.stats --output-dups chr21.dups.pairs.gz \
  -o chr21.nodups.pairs.gz chr21.sorted.pairs.gz
pairtools select '(pair_type == "UU") or (pair_type == "UR") or (pair_type == "RU")' \
  -o chr21.valid.pairs.gz chr21.nodups.pairs.gz
grep -E '^(total_mapped|total_dups|total_nodups|cis|cis_1kb\+|cis_20kb\+)\s' dedup.stats
zcat chr21.valid.pairs.gz | grep -vc '^#'

What fraction of mapped pairs are duplicates? (b) How many valid contacts remain? What fraction are more than 1 kb and more than 20 kb apart?



C4 — Whole-genome QC from the prepared statistics
S=$D/gm12878_hic_fullgenome_stats.txt
grep -E '^(total|total_mapped|total_dups|total_nodups|cis|trans|cis_1kb\+|cis_20kb\+)\s' $S
awk '$1 == "cis" { c = $2 } $1 == "trans" { t = $2 } $1 == "cis_20kb+" { l = $2 } $1 == "total_nodups" { n = $2 }
     END { printf "cis %.3f  trans %.3f  cis>20kb %.3f\n", c / n, t / n, l / n }' $S
grep '^pair_types' $S | sort -k2,2nr | head -6
grep -E '^dist_freq/(178-237|316-422|1778-2371|31623-42170)/' $S

Compute the cis and trans fractions and the fraction of long-range cis contacts. Does the library pass the QC thresholds of the lecture?
In the dist_freq lines, compare the four orientations at short distances (178–237 bp, 316–422 bp) and at 1.8–2.4 kb and 32–42 kb. Where do they become equal?



C5 — Bin into a matrix and balance
cooler cload pairs -c1 2 -p1 3 -c2 4 -p2 5 chr21.sizes:10000 chr21.valid.pairs.gz chr21_10kb.cool
cooler info chr21_10kb.cool | grep -E 'nbins|nnz|sum'
cooler zoomify -r 10000,50000,100000,250000,500000 --balance --balance-args '--cis-only' \
  -o chr21.mcool chr21_10kb.cool
cooler ls chr21.mcool
cooler dump -t bins chr21.mcool::resolutions/250000 | head -60 | tail -5
cooler dump -t bins chr21.mcool::resolutions/250000 | awk '$4 == "" || $4 == "nan"' | wc -l

How many bins, non-zero pixels and contacts does the 10-kb matrix have?
What is the fourth column of the bins table, and why is it empty (NaN) for some bins?



C6 — Compare with the published map
cooler dump --join -r chr21:35,000,000-35,500,000 chr21.mcool::resolutions/100000 | head -3
cooler dump --join -r chr21:35,000,000-35,500,000 $D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/100000 | head -3
How many times more contacts does ENCODE’s map have in the same pixels? Compare with the total numbers of contacts.

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
In Python
import re, numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
import cooler, cooltools
D = "/path/to/course/data"

P1 — The orientation plot
st = pd.read_csv(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_fullgenome_stats.txt", sep="\t", header=None, index_col=0)[1]
rows = [(int(m.group(1)), m.group(2), float(v)) for k, v in st.items()
        if (m := re.match(r"dist_freq/(\d+)-?(?:\d+|\+)?/(..)$", k))]
dfq = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["lo", "strand", "n"]).pivot(index="lo", columns="strand", values="n")
dfq = dfq[(dfq.index >= 1) & (dfq.index < 1e6)]
frac = dfq.div(dfq.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
print((frac * 100).round(1).iloc[::3])
frac.plot(logx=True, marker="o", ms=3); plt.axhline(0.25, ls="--", color="grey")
plt.xlabel("distance (bp)"); plt.ylabel("fraction"); plt.savefig("p1_orientation.png", dpi=120)

Which orientation dominates below 1 kb, and which artefact is it? Above which distance are all four within 0.03 of 0.25?



P2 — Raw and balanced
c = cooler.Cooler("chr21.mcool::resolutions/250000")
raw = c.matrix(balance=False).fetch("chr21").astype(float)
bal = c.matrix(balance=True).fetch("chr21")
w = c.bins().fetch("chr21")["weight"]
print(len(w), "bins;", w.isna().sum(), "masked")
cov = raw.sum(axis=0)
print("raw row sums of unmasked bins: min", cov[w.notna()].min(), "max", cov[w.notna()].max())
far = np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(len(w)), np.arange(len(w)))) >= 2   # balancing ignores 2 diagonals
print("balanced row sums:", np.round(np.nansum(np.where(far, bal, 0), axis=0)[w.notna()][:5], 3))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
for ax, M, t in zip(axs, [raw, bal], ["raw", "balanced"]):
    M = np.where(M > 0, M, np.nan)
    ax.imshow(M, cmap="Reds", norm=LogNorm(vmin=np.nanpercentile(M, 5), vmax=np.nanpercentile(M, 99.5))); ax.set_title(t)
plt.savefig("p2_balance.png", dpi=120)

How many bins are masked, and where are they? (b) How much do raw row sums vary? What are the balanced row sums?



P3 — Distance decay: ours against ENCODE’s
v = pd.DataFrame({"chrom": ["chr21"], "start": [0], "end": [46_709_983], "name": ["chr21"]})
for lab, fn in [("ours", "chr21.mcool::resolutions/10000"),
                ("ENCODE", f"{D}/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/10000")]:
    c = cooler.Cooler(fn)
    e = cooltools.expected_cis(c, view_df=v, nproc=2)
    e["s"] = e.dist * 10000
    e = e[(e.dist >= 2) & (e.s <= 2e7)]
    plt.loglog(e.s, e["balanced.avg"] / e["balanced.avg"].sum(), label=lab)
    sel = (e.s >= 1e5) & (e.s <= 1e6)
    print(lab, "slope 100 kb-1 Mb:", round(np.polyfit(np.log10(e.s[sel]), np.log10(e["balanced.avg"][sel]), 1)[0], 2))
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel("s (bp)"); plt.ylabel("P(s)"); plt.savefig("p3_ps.png", dpi=120)

Compare the two slopes. (b) Why does \(P(s)\) need so few reads while loops need billions?



P4 — Resolution against depth
for res in [10000, 50000, 100000, 250000]:
    out = []
    for fn in [f"chr21.mcool::resolutions/{res}", f"{D}/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/{res}"]:
        m = cooler.Cooler(fn).matrix(balance=False, sparse=True).fetch("chr21")
        cov = np.asarray(m.sum(axis=1)).ravel()          # symmetric matrix: row sum = contacts of the bin
        cov = cov[cov > 0]
        out.append(round(np.mean(cov >= 1000) * 100, 1))
    print(f"{res // 1000:>4} kb: ours {out[0]:5.1f}%  ENCODE {out[1]:5.1f}% of bins with >= 1000 contacts")

What is the resolution of our map, and of ENCODE’s, by Rao et al.’s 80% criterion? (b) What does this mean for which features you can analyse with our map?



P5 — Observed/expected on our map
c = cooler.Cooler("chr21.mcool::resolutions/250000")
e = cooltools.expected_cis(c, view_df=v, nproc=1).set_index("dist")["balanced.avg"]
m = c.matrix(balance=True).fetch("chr21")
n = m.shape[0]
d = np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(n), np.arange(n)))
oe = m / e.reindex(np.arange(n)).values[d]
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5.5))
plt.imshow(np.log2(oe), cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.5); plt.colorbar(label="log2 O/E")
plt.title("our chr21, 250 kb, O/E"); plt.savefig("p5_oe.png", dpi=120)
print("mean O/E 2, 10 and 40 bins from the diagonal:", [round(np.nanmean(np.diag(oe, k)), 2) for k in (2, 10, 40)])

Why is the mean O/E along each diagonal 1? (b) Can you see compartments in our 250-kb map? Compare with Calling compartments, TADs and loops.

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — junctions, pairs and artefacts (B1–B3)





Fill-in copies the 4-nt overhang onto the other end, so the junction is site-up-to-cut + overhang + overhang + rest of site. Probability of a \(k\)-mer at a position is \(4^{-k}\) (count one strand for a palindromic site). The two sides of a pair are the 5′ ends of the 5′-most alignment of each read. A pair is an artefact if both sides fall between the same two restriction sites (or adjacent fragments) with inward (+ −) or outward (− +) reads. Duplicates match at both sides and strands. See Lajoie et al. 2015 and the pairtools documentation on pair types.









Hint 2 — binning, ICE and O/E (B4–B6, B8)





For the 0-based positions in B4, bin = ⌊pos / 100 000⌋; order the two bins so i ≤ j. For ICE: \(b_i\) = row sum\(_i\) / mean of the row sums, new pixel = old pixel / (\(b_i b_j\)). \(E(s)\) = mean of one diagonal. Imakaev et al. 2012 for ICE; for resolution, Rao et al. 2014.









Hint 3 — command line (C1–C6)





bwa mem options -S (skip mate rescue), -P (skip pairing), -5 (5′-most split alignment primary), -M (mark shorter splits secondary). pairtools parse, sort, dedup, select; the .pairs format; pairtools stats output. cooler cload pairs, zoomify, balance, dump. A .mcool resolution is addressed as file.mcool::resolutions/10000.









Hint 4 — Python (P1–P5)





The stats file is two columns, key and value. cooler API: matrix(balance=False) raw counts, balance=True balanced, sparse=True a SciPy sparse matrix; bins() the bin table with weight. cooltools.expected_cis: dist in bins, balanced.avg is \(E(s)\). np.subtract.outer gives the distance of every pixel from the diagonal.

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) HindIII: A + AGCT (filled in) + AGCT + T → AAGCTAGCTT. NcoI: C + CATG + CATG + G → CCATGCATGG. (b) \(4^{-4}\): once every 256 bp; \(4^{-6}\): once every 4 096 bp (both sites are palindromes, so count one strand). chr21: 40.1 × 10⁶ / 256 ≈ 157 000 MboI sites expected (C1 counts the real number). (c) A contact is only resolved to the restriction fragments it joins; with fragments of ~4 kb on average (and many much longer), contacts within or between neighbouring fragments are blurred over several kb, and bins of 1 kb would often contain no cut site at all.
B2. (a) Side 1: the 5′ end of read 1’s first alignment, chr21:20 000 000 (+). Side 2: the 5′ end of read 2, which on the − strand is its rightmost base, near chr21:34 500 700 (the reported position is the 5′ end). (b) The 3′ part of read 1 and read 2 both map near 34.5 Mb, on the same fragment and consistent with one molecule: one ligation explains everything, so the chimeric part adds no new contact. A walk would need a third locus. (c) It would expect the mates to face each other a few hundred bp apart: it might rescue read 2 by forcing a local alignment near 20 Mb, mark the pair improper, or choose a poor alignment of the 3′ part, losing or corrupting the contact.
B3. p1: both sides in the fragment 1 000 000–1 000 310, inward (+ −): dangling end. p2: same fragment, outward (− +): self-circle. p3: + − inward across one site (1 000 310) into the next fragment, 500 bp: re-ligation of neighbours (or a dangling end over an uncut site), not a useful contact. p4: different fragments 250 kb apart: valid cis contact. p5: identical to p4 at both sides and strands: duplicate of p4, removed. p6: valid trans contact (chr21–chr19).
B4. Bins (i, j): (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 2), (0, 3), (3, 3), (1, 1), (0, 1) — the last one because 99 999 is in bin 0 and 100 000 in bin 1. Upper triangle:
      0   1   2   3
0     1   1   0   1
1         1   0   1
2             2   0
3                 1
B5. (a) Row sums 20, 34, 12; mean 22. Biases \(b\) = 0.909, 1.545, 0.545. New matrix: (a, a) = 10/0.826 = 12.1; (a, b) = 8/1.405 = 5.69; (a, c) = 2/0.496 = 4.03; (b, b) = 20/2.388 = 8.38; (b, c) = 6/0.843 = 7.12; (c, c) = 4/0.298 = 13.4. (b) New row sums: a 12.1 + 5.69 + 4.03 = 21.8; b 5.69 + 8.38 + 7.12 = 21.2; c 4.03 + 7.12 + 13.4 = 24.6. Much closer than 20, 34, 12; further iterations converge. (c) A copy-number gain (a duplicated region in this cell population), a change in mappability (different read length or aligner), or a GC/PCR bias difference between libraries. Balancing removes it as if it were a visibility bias; for a real copy-number gain that is wrong, because the extra copies really make extra contacts.
B6. (a) \(E(1)\) = (0.20 + 0.22 + 0.18 + 0.20)/4 = 0.20; \(E(2)\) = (0.08 + 0.07 + 0.09)/3 = 0.08; \(E(3)\) = (0.05 + 0.03)/2 = 0.04. (b) (1, 3) = 0.08/0.08 = 1.0; (3, 5) = 0.09/0.08 = 1.13; (1, 4) = 0.05/0.04 = 1.25; (1, 5): \(E(4)\) = 0.06 (one pixel), O/E = 1.0 by definition. (1, 4) is the most enriched. (c) No: the highest balanced values are always at short distances (the diagonal +1: 0.20–0.22). Only O/E compares a pixel with what its distance predicts. Note also that \(E(4)\) from a single pixel is meaningless: real maps average thousands of pixels per diagonal.
B7. (a) Library A: low duplicates (complex library, deeper sequencing will give new contacts), high cis and long-range cis fractions. (b) B’s 38% duplicates mean low complexity: few distinct ligation products (little input material, over-amplification); sequencing deeper would mostly give more duplicates. Its low cis fraction (52%) and low long-range cis (21%) point to many random ligations (nuclei lysed, poor crosslinking, ligation in solution) and many short-range artefacts.
B8. (a) 3.1 × 10⁹ / 5 000 = 620 000 bins; 400 M contacts × 2 sides / 620 000 ≈ 1 290 contacts per bin on average. (b) The average is barely above 1 000, so far fewer than 80% of bins pass (coverage varies a lot): 5 kb is not realistic. At 25 kb: 124 000 bins, about 6 450 contacts per bin, so 80% passing is plausible: 25 kb resolution, good for domains and strong loops (with APA), not for fine loops.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 273 200 read pairs; 30 023 of the first 200 000 read-1 sequences (15%) contain GATCGATC. (b) 91 397 MboI sites (157 000 expected for random sequence with equal base frequencies: GATC is under-represented in the human genome, about 0.6 of the random expectation) and 11 263 HindIII sites (expected 40.1 × 10⁶ / 4 096 ≈ 9 800). Building the bwa index takes about a minute.
C2. (a) readID chrom1 pos1 chrom2 pos2 strand1 strand2 pair_type; the 8th column is the pair type. Positions are the 5′ ends of the reported alignments; the side with the smaller position is side 1 (pairs are “flipped” into genomic order). (b) 221 776 of 273 200 pairs (81%) have both sides uniquely mapped; the most common types are UU (194 256), MU (24 656), NU (17 572), UR (14 014) and RU (13 506). (c) About 20 seconds (wall clock) with 8 threads; the whole genome would take hours.
C3. (a) 4 277 duplicates among 221 776 mapped pairs (1.9%). (b) 217 499 valid contacts (UU/UR/RU, deduplicated); 184 958 (85%) are > 1 kb apart and 140 644 (65%) > 20 kb apart. (These fractions are higher than genome-wide because there are no trans pairs here.)
C4. (a) cis 0.837  trans 0.163  cis>20kb 0.561; 23.8 M of 30 M pairs (79%) have both sides uniquely mapped (UU 20.7 M, RU 1.30 M, UR 1.29 M) and 1.9% of them are duplicates. The library passes easily: most pairs map uniquely, cis dominates, and long-range cis is well above 40%. (b) At 178–237 bp the counts are small and mixed; at 316–422 bp + − dominates (620 797 against about 8 000–10 000 for each other orientation: 96%): dangling ends. At 1.8–2.4 kb the four are within 6% of each other (72 171, 68 167, 68 043, 68 028) and at 32–42 kb equal (117 061–117 736): from about 1–2 kb on, pairs are genuine ligation products.
C5. (a) 4 671 bins, 123 129 non-zero pixels, 217 499 contacts. (b) The balancing weight (1/bias). It is NaN for masked bins: too few contacts (the short arm and centromere of chr21, 0–14 Mb, and repeat-rich bins), so no reliable weight can be estimated; 50 of 187 bins at 250 kb.
C6. The three pixels have 324, 104 and 54 contacts in our map and 55 048, 16 576 and 10 102 in ENCODE’s: 160–190 times more, close to the ratio of the totals on chr21 (35.2 M / 217 499 = 162).









Solutions — Python





P1. Between about 250 and 600 bp the inward orientation (+ −) dominates (96% at 316–422 bp): dangling ends and re-ligated neighbours. Below 200 bp other artefacts of very short molecules appear (outward pairs at < 20 bp, tandem pairs at 20–200 bp). From the 1–1.3 kb bin on, all four are within 0.03 of 0.25 (24.8, 27.8, 22.9, 24.6%), and within 0.01 from about 2–4 kb.
P2. (a) 50 of 187 bins are masked: the short arm and centromere (0–14 Mb) and a few bins near 43–44 Mb (segmental duplications). (b) Raw row sums of unmasked bins range from 399 to 3 587 contacts, a ninefold range; balanced row sums are all 1.0 (cooler scales them to 1), counted without the first two diagonals, which balancing ignores.
P3. (a) Ours −1.02, ENCODE −0.97: practically the same curve. (b) \(P(s)\) averages all pixels on a diagonal (thousands at each distance), so even a few hundred thousand contacts give a precise estimate; a loop is a single pixel and needs hundreds of contacts in that one pixel to stand out from its neighbours.
P4. (a) Ours: 81.5% of bins at 250 kb, 42.9% at 100 kb, 0% at 50 and 10 kb: a 250-kb map. ENCODE: 92.8% even at 10 kb (it reaches 5 kb and finer). (b) With our map: \(P(s)\), QC and coarse compartments; not domains or loops. Those need ENCODE’s map (Calling compartments, TADs and loops).
P5. (a) \(E(s)\) is defined as the mean of each diagonal, so dividing by it makes the mean O/E 1 on every diagonal (1.0 at 2, 10 and 40 bins; distances 0 and 1 are not used). (b) Yes, noisily: a checkerboard of red and blue blocks from about 14 Mb on, the same pattern as the chr21 eigenvector in Calling compartments, TADs and loops (mostly B from 16 to 32 Mb, A from 32 to 37 and 41 to 46 Mb). Compartments need few reads; this is why they were discovered first, with 1-Mb maps.

title: Exercise: Hi-C, from reads to contact matrices
text:
Where this leads

Calling compartments, TADs and loops starts from a balanced map and its expected values, as built here, and uses ENCODE’s deep map to call features.
The full pipeline for a whole Hi-C or Micro-C experiment is run with distiller, nf-core/hic or Juicer on a cluster; the steps are the ones of C1–C5.
Pairs files are also the input for single-cell Hi-C and for multi-way contact methods (Pore-C), which keep walks rather than reducing them to pairs.
