title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Background
Coordinates. BED and bedGraph count the boundaries between bases from 0, so an interval start end covers the bases after boundary start up to boundary end: length = end − start. GTF, SAM, VCF and GRanges number the bases from 1 and include both ends: length = end − start + 1. To go from 1-based [s, e] to BED: s − 1, e.
narrowPeak is BED6 + 4 columns: signalValue (enrichment), pValue and qValue (both as \(-\log_{10}\), −1 = not available), and peak, the summit as an offset from start.
Strand. The TSS of a transcript is its start on the + strand and its end on the − strand. Upstream of a − strand gene is towards higher coordinates.
Overlap counts and chance. Overlap by default means at least one shared base. Report each peak once (-u) when counting peaks. Whether an overlap is more than chance needs a null: shuffle one set to random positions (same widths) many times and compare.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Data
The exercise uses three GM12878 peak sets from ENCODE (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, CTCF; GRCh38), the GENCODE v46 basic annotation, the hg38 chromosome sizes, and the ENCODE blacklist. From the course repository:
data/download.sh genomic-intervals      # about 35 MB
mkdir -p ~/epi/intervals && cd ~/epi/intervals
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
You need bedtools and the usual Unix tools (see Install the software you need). Everything runs in seconds on a laptop or a login node; on the cluster you can also wrap the commands in an sbatch script.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Coordinates.

A VCF file reports a SNP at chr7  117559590 (1-based). Write the BED line for this single base.
A BED line reads chr2  1000  1250. Write the region as a browser would display it (1-based), and give its length.
A GTF exon is chr1  11869  12227  +. Write it as a BED line and give its length.
Two BED intervals chr1 100 200 and chr1 200 300. Do they overlap? Do they share a base?

B2. A narrowPeak line. This is the first line of the ENCODE CTCF file:
chr12  53676107  53676353  .  1000  .  497.29450  -1.00000  4.87269  126

How wide is the peak?
At which position is the summit? Give it as a one-base BED interval and as a 1-based position.
What does −1 in column 8 mean? What \(q\)-value does column 9 correspond to?
Can you use column 5 to rank peaks by strength? Which column would you use?

B3. Promoters and strand. A transcript is annotated in a GTF as chr5  1000000  1050000 on the − strand.

Where is its TSS (1-based)?
Define the promoter as 2 kb upstream to 500 bp downstream of the TSS. Give it as a 1-based interval and as a BED line.
A script computes every promoter as start − 2000 to start + 500, ignoring strand. Where does this put the window for this transcript, and what lies there?

B4. Interval operations. On a 1000 bp genome (chrT, BED coordinates):
A:  chrT 100 300    chrT 500 600    chrT 700 900
B:  chrT 250 450    chrT 850 950
Draw A and B on a ruler, then give the output of:

bedtools intersect -a A -b B (b) intersect -u (c) intersect -v (d) subtract -a A -b B
cat A B | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge (f) closest -a A -b B -d (the distance column) (g) complement -i A with the genome file chrT 1000.

B5. Counting overlaps. bedtools intersect -u -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l gives 21 390, but the same command without -u gives 63 214 lines. The H3K4me3 file has 53 912 peaks.

What fraction of the H3K4me3 peaks overlap a promoter?
How can the default output have more lines than there are peaks? Think about what a gene with many transcripts looks like in the promoter file.

B6. Overlaps by hand in R terms. Queries q1 = [1, 10], q2 = [20, 40], q3 = [50, 60]; subjects s1 = [5, 25], s2 = [35, 55] (1-based, as in GRanges). Write the result of findOverlaps(q, s) as a table of (query, subject) pairs, and give countOverlaps(q, s) and overlapsAny(q, s).
B7. Is it more than chance?

30 of your peaks overlap a set of enhancers. In 999 shuffles of the peaks, the mean overlap was 12, and 4 shuffles reached 30 or more. Compute the enrichment and the empirical \(p\)-value \((k + 1) / (N + 1)\).
In another test none of 99 shuffles reached the observed value. What is the smallest \(p\)-value you can report, and how could you report the result honestly?
A colleague shuffles peaks over the whole genome file, including chrY, unplaced contigs and the centromeres. Will the enrichment be too high or too low? Why?

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the data
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf; do
  zcat $D/gm12878_${m}_peaks.bed.gz | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > $m.bed
done
head -3 ctcf.bed
wc -l *.bed
awk '{ w = $3 - $2; s += w } END { print s / NR }' ctcf.bed      # mean width
cut -f1 ctcf.bed | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1n | head             # peaks per chromosome

How many peaks are in each file, and what is the mean width of each kind? Why are CTCF peaks so much narrower than H3K27ac peaks?
Which chromosomes appear? Is there a chrY in the CTCF file? Count the H3K27ac peaks on chrY. GM12878 comes from a woman: how do you explain what you find?



C2 — A TSS file from the GTF
zcat $D/gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz \
 | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$3 == "transcript" && $9 ~ /transcript_type "protein_coding"/ {
     match($9, /gene_name "[^"]+"/); g = substr($9, RSTART + 11, RLENGTH - 12)
     tss = ($7 == "+") ? $4 : $5
     print $1, tss - 1, tss, g, ".", $7 }' \
 | sort -u | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > tss.bed
wc -l tss.bed
grep -w APP tss.bed

Explain each part of the awk program. Why tss - 1, tss?
APP (amyloid precursor protein, chr21) is on the − strand. Check that its TSSs are at the end of the gene: compare with the gene line, zcat $D/gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3=="gene" && $9 ~ /gene_name "APP";/' | cut -f1,4,5,7. How many distinct TSSs does APP have?
Replace sort -u | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n by sort -k1,1 -k2,2n -u. How many lines do you get now? Why fewer? (Read man sort on -u with -k.)



C3 — Promoters and the fraction of peaks at promoters
bedtools slop -i tss.bed -g $D/hg38.chrom.sizes -b 1000 > promoters.bed
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf; do
  echo $m $(bedtools intersect -u -a $m.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l) $(wc -l < $m.bed)
done

What fraction of each kind of peak overlaps a promoter (±1 kb of a protein-coding TSS)? Does the order match the table of marks in What is epigenetics?
Run the same without -u for H3K4me3 (B5).



C4 — Strong peaks and weak peaks
Only about 40% of H3K4me3 peaks are at a protein-coding promoter, although H3K4me3 is “the promoter mark”. Rank the peaks by signalValue (column 7):
sort -k7,7gr h3k4me3.bed | head -10000 | bedtools intersect -u -a - -b promoters.bed | wc -l
sort -k7,7g  h3k4me3.bed | head -10000 | bedtools intersect -u -a - -b promoters.bed | wc -l

What fraction of the 10 000 strongest and of the 10 000 weakest peaks are at a promoter?
Give two reasons why a real H3K4me3 peak could be far from a protein-coding TSS. (Hint: what else has a promoter? What does the weak end of a peak list contain?)



C5 — Candidate enhancers and distances to TSSs
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k27ac.bed -b h3k4me3.bed \
  | bedtools intersect -v -a - -b promoters.bed > enhancers.bed
wc -l enhancers.bed
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf enhancers; do
  bedtools closest -a $m.bed -b tss.bed -d -t first | awk '{ print $NF }' | sort -n \
    | awk -v m=$m '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print m, "median distance", a[int(NR / 2)] }'
done

How many candidate enhancers are there, and what is their median distance to the nearest protein-coding TSS? Compare with the medians for the three peak sets.
Which gene is nearest to the enhancer that is farthest from any TSS, and how far away is it? (sort -k17,17nr | head -1 on the closest output.) Is “nearest gene” a convincing target at that distance?



C6 — Merge and Jaccard
cat h3k4me3.bed h3k27ac.bed | cut -f1-3 | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge > active.bed
wc -l active.bed
bedtools jaccard -a h3k4me3.bed -b h3k27ac.bed
bedtools jaccard -a ctcf.bed    -b h3k27ac.bed

How many merged “active” regions are there? Why fewer than the sum of the two files?
The Jaccard index is (bases in the intersection) / (bases in the union). Compare the two values. Does a small Jaccard index mean that CTCF and H3K27ac are unrelated? (Hold on to your answer for C7.)



C7 — Is the CTCF–H3K27ac overlap more than chance?
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X|Y)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > genome.txt   # main chromosomes only

bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b h3k27ac.bed | wc -l        # observed

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  bedtools shuffle -i h3k27ac.bed -g genome.txt -chrom -excl blacklist.bed -seed $i \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b - | wc -l
done > shuffled.txt

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  bedtools shuffle -i h3k27ac.bed -g $D/hg38.chrom.sizes -seed $i \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b - | wc -l
done > shuffled_naive.txt

What is the observed number of CTCF peaks that overlap an H3K27ac peak? What is the mean over the 100 restricted shuffles, the enrichment, and the empirical \(p\)-value?
Compute the same enrichment with the naive shuffle. Which is larger, and why (B7c)?
Combine with C6: the overlap is highly significant, but what fraction of CTCF peaks overlap H3K27ac? Write one sentence for a results section that reports both.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
section: Explore: the null decides the answer
text:
Explore: the null decides the answer
The demo is the shuffle test of B7 and C7 on a simulated toy chromosome of 10 Mb. It has a gap with no sequence (like an unassembled short arm), a centromere, a few blacklisted repeats, and two GC-rich, gene-dense regions. Set A (150 intervals, blue) and set B (100 intervals, orange) both prefer the GC-rich regions and never fall in the gaps or the blacklist, as real peaks do. The statistic is the C7 one: how many A intervals overlap at least one B interval (bedtools intersect -u -a A -b B | wc -l). Shuffle B places the B intervals at random positions, keeping their widths, once, 10 or 100 times, and adds the counts to the histogram of the null; the red line is the observed count. Keep out of gaps, centromere and blacklist is bedtools shuffle -excl; match GC region keeps each B interval inside its own class (GC-rich or not), a matched background. The data switches between a data set where part of B really sits on A, and one where B only shares the GC preference. Each setting keeps its own list of shuffles; clear shuffles starts it again. Do B7 first.



E1. The naive null. Data: B is placed near A; both null boxes unticked. Press shuffle B ×1 a few times and look at the shuffled B row: where do the red-outlined intervals land, and roughly how many per shuffle? Then press ×100. Read the observed count, the null mean, the enrichment and the empirical \(p\)-value. Check the \(p\)-value with \((k + 1)/(N + 1)\).
E2. Keep out of the gaps. Tick keep out of gaps, centromere and blacklist and shuffle ×100. How do the null mean and the enrichment change? About what fraction of the chromosome did the naive shuffle wrongly allow (count the red outlines, or read the hatched part)? Relate to B7(c).
E3. Match the GC region. Tick match GC region as well and shuffle ×100. Enrichment and \(p\)? Press ×100 nine more times (N = 1000): what happens to the \(p\)-value, and why could it not go below 0.0099 with 100 shuffles? Is B associated with A?
E4. No association at all. Switch the data to B only shares the GC preference (the observed count drops). Run ×100 with the naive null (both boxes unticked) and then with both boxes ticked. Write the two conclusions a reader would draw. Which one is right, and what does this tell you about C7, where the null keeps peaks on their chromosome and out of the blacklist but does not match GC content?






Solutions





E1. The shuffled intervals fall everywhere, also in the gap at the left end, the centromere and the blacklist (about 15–25 of the 100 per shuffle, red outlines): places where no real peak can be. After 100 shuffles: observed 91 of the 150 A intervals, null mean about 39 (range about 23–56), enrichment 91 / 39 ≈ 2.3; no shuffle reached 91, so \(k = 0\) and \(p = (0 + 1)/(100 + 1) = 0.0099\). (If you pressed ×1 first, your numbers differ slightly.)
E2. The null mean rises to about 47 and the enrichment falls to about 1.9 (\(p\) still 0.0099). The excluded regions are about 19% of this toy chromosome; the naive shuffle put about a fifth of B where nothing can overlap A, so the shuffled overlaps were too low and the enrichment too high (B7c).
E3. Null mean about 72, enrichment about 1.26; with 100 shuffles, \(k = 1\) and \(p = 2/101 \approx 0.02\). With 1000 shuffles, 6 of them reach 91: \(p = 7/1001 \approx 0.007\). With \(N = 100\) the smallest possible value is \(1/101 = 0.0099\), so more shuffles are needed to show a small \(p\). Yes, there is a real association (30% of B were placed on A), but it is much weaker than the naive 2.3-fold suggested: most of the naive “enrichment” came from the shared preference for GC-rich regions and from the gaps.
E4. Observed 71. Naive null: mean about 39, enrichment about 1.8, \(p = 0.0099\): “B is strongly enriched at A”. Matched null (both boxes): mean about 72, enrichment about 0.99, \(p \approx 0.59\): “no association beyond the shared GC preference”. The second is right, because in this data B was placed without looking at A. The same can happen in C7: CTCF and H3K27ac peaks both prefer gene-dense, GC-rich parts of the genome, so part of the 6.7-fold enrichment may be shared preference rather than a direct link. A GC- or distance-matched background (regioneR, LOLA; the motif units) asks the sharper question. The null decides the answer: always state it.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
In R
You need GenomicRanges and rtracklayer (see Install the software you need). Set D to the data folder:
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Import peaks and check the coordinates
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
ctcf
raw <- read.table(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), nrows = 1)
raw$V2; start(ctcf)[1]                   # start in the file vs in R
raw$V3 - raw$V2; width(ctcf)[1]          # widths
summit <- start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak        # careful: which convention?
summit[1]

By how much do the starts differ, and do the widths agree?
Is start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak the 1-based position of the summit? Compare with your answer to B2b.
Build a GRanges yourself with GRanges(raw$V1, IRanges(raw$V2, raw$V3)). What is its width, and what went wrong? Fix it.



R2 — TSSs and promoters in R
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding"]
tss <- resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start")        # fix = "start" respects strand
mcols(tss) <- mcols(tss)["gene_name"]
tss <- tss[!duplicated(paste(as.character(tss), tss$gene_name))]
length(tss)
tss[tss$gene_name == "APP"]
prom <- tss + 1000                                  # 1000 bp on each side

How many TSSs do you get? Compare with wc -l tss.bed from C2.
Check the APP TSSs against C2b. Why does resize(..., fix = "start") put the TSS of a − strand transcript at its end?
Is tss + 1000 the same set of bases as bedtools slop -b 1000 on the one-base BED TSS? Check the width.



R3 — Fractions at promoters, again
marks <- c("h3k4me3", "h3k27ac", "ctcf")
pk <- lapply(setNames(marks, marks), function(m)
  import(file.path(D, sprintf("gm12878_%s_peaks.bed.gz", m)), format = "narrowPeak"))
sapply(pk, function(p) mean(overlapsAny(p, prom, ignore.strand = TRUE)))
sapply(pk, function(p) length(findOverlaps(p, prom, ignore.strand = TRUE)))

Do the fractions agree exactly with C3? Do the pair counts agree with the default (no -u) line counts?
Why is ignore.strand = TRUE harmless here? (What strand do the peaks have?)



R4 — Distances to the nearest TSS
dist <- lapply(pk, function(p) mcols(distanceToNearest(p, tss, ignore.strand = TRUE))$distance)
sapply(dist, median)
sapply(dist, function(d) mean(d <= 1000))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (m in marks) hist(log10(dist[[m]] + 1), breaks = 60, main = m, xlab = "log10(distance + 1)")

Compare the medians with C5. They differ by a little for some peaks: test with two adjacent ranges, distance(GRanges("chr1", IRanges(1, 5)), GRanges("chr1", IRanges(6, 10))), and the same pair with bedtools closest -d. What is the rule?
Describe the three histograms in one sentence each. Which mark labels promoters, which labels promoters and enhancers, and which is mostly elsewhere?



R5 — Plot the shuffle test
obs  <- 7464                                    # your observed value from C7
shuf <- scan("shuffled.txt"); naive <- scan("shuffled_naive.txt")
hist(shuf, xlim = c(0, obs * 1.05), col = "grey", main = "CTCF peaks overlapping H3K27ac",
     xlab = "overlapping CTCF peaks")
abline(v = obs, col = "red", lwd = 3)
c(restricted = obs / mean(shuf), naive = obs / mean(naive))
What would the histogram look like if the two sets were unrelated?

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — coordinates (B1, B2, R1)





From 1-based [s, e] to BED: start − 1, end unchanged. From BED to 1-based: start + 1, end unchanged. A single base at 1-based position \(p\) is the BED line p−1  p. For the summit: start + peak is a BED boundary; the summit base is start + peak to start + peak + 1 in BED. The narrowPeak format is described on the UCSC format page.









Hint 2 — strand (B3, C2, R2)





On the − strand the gene is read from right to left: the TSS is the largest coordinate, and “2 kb upstream” means 2 kb towards larger coordinates. resize with fix = "start" and promoters use the strand for you.









Hint 3 — bedtools (B4, C3–C7)





Draw it. -u reports each A once if it overlaps anything; -v reports A that overlap nothing; subtract removes the overlapping bases. merge needs sorted input. closest -d reports 0 for overlaps; for non-overlapping intervals bedtools reports one more than the number of bases between them. complement returns the gaps. sort -k7,7gr sorts on column 7 as a general number, largest first.









Hint 4 — shuffling (B7, C7)





Enrichment = observed / mean of the shuffles. Empirical \(p = (k + 1) / (N + 1)\), where \(k\) is the number of shuffles at least as extreme as the observation and \(N\) the number of shuffles. -chrom keeps each interval on its own chromosome; -excl keeps them out of the given regions. See bedtools shuffle and the ENCODE blacklist paper.









Hint 5 — GenomicRanges (R1–R4)





import with format = "narrowPeak" reads the extra columns. overlapsAny, findOverlaps and distanceToNearest are the R versions of intersect -u, intersect and closest -d. gr + 1000 widens a range by 1000 on each side. makeGRangesFromDataFrame has an argument starts.in.df.are.0based.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) chr7  117559589  117559590. (b) chr2:1001-1250, length 250. (c) chr1  11868  12227, length \(12227 - 11868 = 359\) (in 1-based: \(12227 - 11869 + 1 = 359\)). (d) They touch but do not overlap: the first covers BED boundaries 100–200 (1-based bases 101–200), the second 200–300 (bases 201–300). They share no base, and bedtools intersect reports nothing.
B2. (a) \(53676353 - 53676107 = 246\) bp. (b) Summit boundary \(53676107 + 126 = 53676233\), so the summit base is chr12  53676233  53676234 in BED, position 53 676 234 in 1-based. (c) −1 means not available: the IDR pipeline did not report a \(p\)-value. \(q = 10^{-4.87} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-5}\). (d) No: column 5 is a display score (here 1000 for every strong peak). Rank by signalValue (column 7), or by the \(p\)/\(q\) columns when they are available.
B3. (a) The end, 1 050 000. (b) Upstream is towards larger coordinates: 1-based [1049501, 1052000] (500 bp downstream = 1 049 501 … 1 050 000, 2 kb upstream = 1 050 001 … 1 052 000); BED chr5  1049500  1052000. (c) 998000–1000500: around the annotated start, which for a − strand transcript is its 3’ end. The “promoter” is at the end of the gene, in the last exon or beyond.
B4. (a) chrT 250 300, chrT 850 900. (b) chrT 100 300, chrT 700 900. (c) chrT 500 600. (d) chrT 100 250, chrT 500 600, chrT 700 850. (e) chrT 100 450, chrT 500 600, chrT 700 950. (f) 0 for 100 300 (overlaps B1); for 500 600 the nearest is 250 450, with 50 bases between them (450–499), reported by bedtools as 51; 0 for 700 900. (g) chrT 0 100, chrT 300 500, chrT 600 700, chrT 900 1000.
B5. (a) \(21390 / 53912 = 0.40\). (b) The default reports one line per overlapping pair. A protein-coding gene often has several transcripts with nearby start sites, and each gives its own promoter window; a peak over that promoter overlaps all of them and is reported once per window.
B6. Pairs (1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2). countOverlaps = 1, 2, 1. overlapsAny = TRUE, TRUE, TRUE.
B7. (a) Enrichment \(30 / 12 = 2.5\); \(p = (4 + 1) / (999 + 1) = 0.005\). (b) \(p = (0 + 1)/(99 + 1) = 0.01\); report “empirical \(p = 0.01\) (none of 99 shuffles reached the observed value)”, together with the enrichment. Run more shuffles if you need a smaller bound. (c) Too high. Shuffled peaks land in places where no real peak can be (centromeres, gaps, unplaced contigs, chrY in a female cell line), so the shuffled overlaps are too low and the ratio observed/shuffled too high.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) H3K4me3 53 912 peaks (mean width 781 bp), H3K27ac 52 455 (1156 bp), CTCF 44 217 (181 bp; median 216, maximum 452). CTCF is a sequence-specific TF: it binds one ~20 bp motif, so its peaks are as narrow as the fragment size allows. Histone marks cover several nucleosomes, and H3K27ac spreads over whole enhancers and promoters. (b) chr1–22 and chrX. No chrY in the CTCF file; one H3K27ac peak on chrY (chrY 15882971 15883161, weak: signalValue 5). GM12878 is female, so this must be reads from elsewhere that align to chrY: sequence shared with the X chromosome, or a repeat. A good reason to check, and to exclude chrY from a female sample.
C2. (a) -F'\t' splits on tabs only (column 9 contains spaces); $3 == "transcript" keeps transcript lines; the regular expression keeps protein-coding transcripts; match/substr cut the gene name out of the attributes; the TSS is column 4 (start) on + and column 5 (end) on −; GTF is 1-based, so the one-base BED interval is tss − 1, tss. You should get 56 260 lines. (b) The APP gene is chr21 25880535 26171128 −; its TSSs are at 26 140 460 and 26 170 654 … 26 171 128 (BED end column): the large coordinates, the end of the gene. APP has 8 distinct TSSs in GENCODE basic. (c) 56 154 lines. With -k, sort -u compares only the sort keys (chromosome and start), so two TSSs at the same position are collapsed even if they belong to different genes or strands. A silent loss of data.
C3. (a) H3K4me3 21 390 / 53 912 = 39.7%, H3K27ac 14 320 / 52 455 = 27.3%, CTCF 6016 / 44 217 = 13.6%. The order matches: H3K4me3 is the promoter mark, H3K27ac marks active promoters and enhancers, CTCF binds mostly away from promoters. (b) 63 214 lines (B5).
C4. (a) Strongest 10 000: 8653 (87%); weakest 10 000: 1559 (16%). (b) Promoters of genes that are not protein-coding (lncRNAs, unannotated transcripts); bivalent or weakly active sites, and enhancers, which carry some H3K4me3 when highly active. The weak end of a peak list also contains noise. Including all GENCODE basic transcript start sites raises the fraction from 21 390 to 24 715 peaks (46%).
C5. (a) 22 330 candidate enhancers, median distance 28.6 kb to the nearest protein-coding TSS, against 2.7 kb for H3K4me3, 10.9 kb for H3K27ac and 23.8 kb for CTCF peaks. (H3K4me3’s median is above 1 kb because 60% of its peaks are not at protein-coding promoters, C4.) (b) chr21:5101753-5102097, nearest TSS TPTE at about 5.4 Mb. At that distance (in a region near the chr21 centromere with few genes) nearest-gene assignment means little; the integration unit uses contacts and activity instead.
C6. (a) 65 446 merged regions: wherever an H3K4me3 and an H3K27ac peak overlap (active promoters), merging makes one region of the two. (b) H3K4me3–H3K27ac 0.41, CTCF–H3K27ac 0.018. The CTCF Jaccard is small partly because CTCF peaks are narrow (few bases each), so even complete overlap of every CTCF peak would give a small fraction of the union. Jaccard measures shared bases, not shared sites.
C7. (a) Observed 7464. Restricted shuffles: mean about 1120 (range about 1000–1200; the exact numbers depend on the order of lines and the seeds), enrichment about 6.7, empirical \(p = 1/101 \approx 0.01\) (none of the 100 shuffles came close). (b) Naive: mean about 950, enrichment about 7.8: larger, because shuffled peaks fall into regions where no peak can be (B7c). (c) “17% of CTCF peaks (7464 of 44 217) overlapped an H3K27ac peak, 6.7 times more than expected from 100 shuffles of the H3K27ac peaks within their chromosomes outside blacklisted regions (empirical \(p = 1/101 \approx 0.01\)).” Significant but partial: most CTCF sites are not in active regulatory elements.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) R’s start is the file’s start + 1 (53 676 108 vs 53 676 107); widths agree (246). (b) Yes. start is now 1-based (file start + 1), so start + peak = 53 676 234 is the 1-based summit position: (file start + 1) + peak. The offset is unchanged when the interval start is converted to 1-based coordinates. (c) Width 247: the 0-based start was used as a 1-based start, adding a base on the left. Fix: IRanges(raw$V2 + 1, raw$V3), or makeGRangesFromDataFrame(..., starts.in.df.are.0based = TRUE).
R2. (a) 56 260, the same as C2 (with the plain sort -u). (b) The APP TSSs are the same 8 positions. fix = "start" keeps the biological start of the range, which is the end coordinate on the − strand. (c) Yes: tss + 1000 has width 2001, the TSS base plus 1000 on each side, the same bases as slop -b 1000 on the BED TSS.
R3. (a) Identical fractions: 0.397, 0.273, 0.136. The pair counts (63 214, 43 651, 15 474) equal the default bedtools line counts. (b) The peaks have strand *, which overlaps ranges on either strand anyway.
R4. (a) For non-overlapping ranges, distance() counts the bases between them (adjacent ranges: 0), bedtools reports one more (adjacent: 1). Overlaps are 0 in both. (b) H3K4me3: a large spike at 0 (promoters) plus a spread of weaker peaks; H3K27ac: a spike at 0 and a broad hump at 10–100 kb (enhancers); CTCF: mostly 1–100 kb, a small spike at 0.
R5. The red line would sit inside the grey histogram. Here it is about seven times further right than the mean of the shuffles.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Where this leads

From reads to coverage makes the peaks and bigWigs we used here from raw reads.
Differential accessibility merges peaks from many samples into a consensus set (C6) and counts reads in it.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting uses windows around summits (B2) and GC-matched backgrounds, a better null than C7.
Linking regulatory elements to genes replaces “nearest gene” (C5b) with contacts and activity.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Quinlan & Hall 2010, Bioinformatics. BEDTools: a flexible suite of utilities for comparing genomic features.
Lawrence et al. 2013, PLoS Comput Biol. Software for computing and annotating genomic ranges.
Kent et al. 2010, Bioinformatics. BigWig and BigBed: enabling browsing of large distributed datasets.
Frankish et al. 2019, Nucleic Acids Res. GENCODE reference annotation for the human and mouse genomes.
ENCODE Project Consortium 2020, Nature. Expanded encyclopaedias of DNA elements in the human and mouse genomes.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
About this lecture
The marks and peaks of the earlier units are one-dimensional: a position on a chromosome. But an enhancer can sit hundreds of kilobases from the gene it controls. This lecture is about how the genome is folded in the nucleus, and how that folding is measured.

The levels of folding: territories, A/B compartments, domains (TADs) and loops, all in real GM12878 Hi-C data.
The two mechanisms behind them: loop extrusion by cohesin, stopped by CTCF, and compartmentalisation of like with like.
What happens when CTCF or cohesin is removed.
Imaging single cells versus Hi-C on millions of cells; the 3C family of assays.
What folding means for genes: enhancer–promoter contact, and disease when a domain boundary breaks.


This is the biology unit of the 3D-genome block; Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices and Calling compartments, TADs and loops are the analysis units. Students saw the 3D teaser in What is epigenetics? and CTCF and loop extrusion in Gene regulation; here we build the full picture. Every real-data figure comes from the same experiment: in situ Hi-C of GM12878 (Rao et al. 2014), all replicates combined, as reprocessed by ENCODE on GRCh38 (experiment ENCSR410MDC). The figures are made by make-genome3d-figs.py in the unit folder. Keep in mind throughout that a Hi-C map is a population average: the last third of the lecture comes back to that.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Why folding matters


Enhancers often lie 10 kb to 1 Mb from the promoter they regulate, and often skip the nearest gene.
To act, an enhancer must (at least transiently) come close in 3D to its promoter.
So the questions are: what brings regions together, what keeps them apart, and how do we measure it?


In Gene regulation we met the ZRS enhancer of Shh, about 1 Mb away from its gene inside an intron of another gene (LMBR1), and saw that the nearest gene is often not the target. A linear genome browser cannot tell you which promoter an enhancer talks to. The 3D organisation constrains it: elements in the same domain contact each other more, elements separated by a boundary less. The figure is a cartoon: in reality the DNA is a dynamic polymer and “close” means within a few hundred nanometres, often only for part of the time. We return to how close is close enough at the end.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Folding at many scales


Territories: each chromosome occupies its own region of the nucleus.
Compartments (Mb): active (A) and inactive (B) chromatin segregate.
Domains / TADs (~0.1–1 Mb) and loops (~10 kb–1 Mb): local units made by cohesin and CTCF.
Nucleosome fibre: the 10-nm fibre of What is epigenetics?; the textbook 30-nm fibre is rare in living cells.


The sizes are typical ranges for human cells, not hard limits. The levels are not a strict hierarchy of boxes inside boxes: compartments and TADs are made by different mechanisms (later slides) and a TAD can contain both A and B chromatin in principle, although in practice domain boundaries often coincide with compartment switches. Numbers to remember: a human chromosome is 50–250 Mb; GM12878 contact domains have a median size of about 200 kb (Rao et al. 2014 reported 185 kb); loops have a median size of a few hundred kb. “TAD” (topologically associating domain, Dixon et al. 2012; Nora et al. 2012) and “contact domain” (Rao et al. 2014) are used almost interchangeably; we use TAD.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Chromosome territories


Each chromosome is a block on the diagonal: contacts within a chromosome far outnumber contacts between chromosomes.
In GM12878, 77% of contacts are within a chromosome, although only 5% of all pairs of positions are.
Small, gene-rich chromosomes (16, 17, 19, 20, 22) contact each other more and keep a smaller share of contacts to themselves: they sit together in the nuclear interior.


Territories were first seen by microscopy: chromosome painting with fluorescent probes for a whole chromosome shows compact, separate regions rather than intermingled spaghetti (Cremer and Cremer). Hi-C confirms it: the whole-genome map, 1 Mb bins, balanced, log colour scale, is dominated by blocks on the diagonal. The right panel computes, for each chromosome, the fraction of its contacts (raw counts, MAPQ ≥ 30) that land on the same chromosome. The “expected” figure is what you would get if a contact partner were picked uniformly from the genome, i.e. the sum of squared chromosome sizes over the squared genome size. In these data 77% of the 4.6 billion contacts are within a chromosome, against 5% expected at random; per chromosome (right panel; each trans contact counts for both chromosomes it joins) the share runs from 54% (chr21, chr22) to 68% (chr2) and 67% for chrX, whose inactive copy is compact. Numbers from make-genome3d-figs.py. Note that the cis fraction is also a quality metric for a Hi-C library: random ligation in solution (in the original dilution Hi-C protocol) produced many more trans contacts; we return to this in the processing unit.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Reading a Hi-C map


Both axes are the genome. Pixel (i, j) = how often bin i and bin j were found ligated together, summed over millions of cells.
The map is symmetric; browsers often show only the upper triangle, turned 45°.
Three patterns to look for: squares on the diagonal (domains), dots off the diagonal (loops), a checkerboard far from the diagonal (compartments).


Teach students to read a map before they compute anything. The diagonal is always the strongest: neighbouring bins are physically connected. A square of enriched contacts means a region whose parts touch each other more than they touch the outside: a domain. A dot is a specific pair of loci with more contacts than their neighbours: a loop with anchors at the dot’s row and column. The checkerboard means that bins far apart along the chromosome still prefer each other when they are of the same type (A with A, B with B). The triangle view is what you see in Juicebox, HiGlass or the WashU browser, with tracks such as ChIP-seq aligned underneath. Resolution: a pixel is a bin of 1 Mb in a genome-wide view, down to 1–5 kb in the deepest maps.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Contacts fall with distance


The contact probability P(s) falls roughly as a power law of genomic distance s: slope about −1 on a log–log plot between 100 kb and 1 Mb here (chr21: −0.97; chr19: −1.14).
This is the strongest signal in any Hi-C map. Everything else (domains, loops, compartments) is a deviation from this expectation.


P(s) is computed by averaging the balanced matrix along each diagonal (cooltools expected_cis, chr19 and chr21 at 5 kb); the processing unit computes it from the students’ own reads. Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009 found a slope of about −1 between 500 kb and 7 Mb and proposed the “fractal globule”, a knot-free, crumpled polymer state. Later work showed that the shape of P(s) reports on loop extrusion: removing cohesin changes the curve below about 1 Mb, and mitotic chromosomes, compacted by condensin loops, have a different slope again. For a student the practical point is the expected value: to say a contact is “enriched” we compare it with the average contact at the same distance (observed/expected), which the analysis units do.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
A and B compartments





Far from the diagonal, the map is a checkerboard: bins fall into two types that contact their own type more.
The first eigenvector (E1) of the map’s correlation matrix splits the bins: A (E1 > 0) and B (E1 < 0).
A matches active chromatin: on chr19, E1 correlates with H3K27ac (r = 0.50) and against H3K9me3 (r = −0.64).
57% of chr19 is A: it is the most gene-dense human chromosome.



Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009 discovered compartments at 1 Mb resolution. The left panel shows chr19 at 250 kb (balanced, log scale); below it E1 at 100 kb and the ENCODE fold-change tracks for H3K27ac and H3K9me3 averaged in the same bins. How E1 is computed, and how its arbitrary sign is fixed, is in Calling compartments, TADs and loops; here we oriented it so that it correlates positively with H3K27ac. A compartment is gene-rich, GC-rich, early-replicating, accessible and transcribed; B is gene-poor, late-replicating, and enriched for H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 and for contacts with the nuclear lamina. At higher resolution Rao et al. 2014 split them into six subcompartments (A1, A2, B1–B4) with distinct marks; for example B1 is H3K27me3-rich and B4 is a small subcompartment of KRAB-ZNF gene clusters on chr19, marked by H3K9me3 together with H3K36me3. Compartments change between cell types as genes are switched on and off, which makes them more than a sequence property.

title: 3D genome organisation
section: Where compartments sit in the nucleus
text:
Where compartments sit in the nucleus


B chromatin lines the nuclear lamina (lamina-associated domains, LADs) and surrounds the nucleolus (NADs).
A chromatin fills the interior, near nuclear speckles (splicing-factor-rich bodies).
So compartments are a sequencing readout of nuclear position: the periphery is mostly a repressive environment.


LADs were mapped by DamID (van Steensel lab): fuse the Dam methyltransferase to lamin B1 and map where adenine methylation lands. LADs are 0.1–10 Mb, gene-poor, late-replicating and largely overlap B. They are not absolute: genes moved to the lamina are often but not always repressed, and LADs vary between cells. Speckle-associated domains (mapped by TSA-seq or SPRITE) are the most active parts of A. This slide links the abstract checkerboard to the microscope picture: A–A and B–B contacts are enriched because A regions are together in the interior and B regions together at the periphery and around nucleoli.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Domains (TADs)


Domains are regions of about 0.1–1 Mb whose parts contact each other more than they contact the neighbouring regions: squares on the diagonal, triangles in this view.
Their edges, boundaries, are enriched for CTCF binding and active promoters.
16 domains called in this 5-Mb window of chr21 (Arrowhead, by ENCODE); 10 306 genome-wide, median size 185 kb.


Topologically associating domains were described in 2012 in mouse and human (Dixon et al., 40-kb bins, median about 880 kb) and in the mouse X-inactivation centre (Nora et al., 5C). With deeper data the big TADs split into smaller “contact domains” (Rao et al. 2014), many of which are loop domains: domains with a dot at their corner, i.e. a loop between the two boundaries (next slide). Domains are nested and their calls depend on the resolution and the caller, which is a theme of Calling compartments, TADs and loops. Many boundaries are shared between cell types, and between mouse and human at orthologous loci. The dashed triangles are ENCODE’s Arrowhead domains from the same data (chr21:37–42 Mb, 25-kb bins). Note the large block between about 39.6 and 41.2 Mb that has no call: domain callers disagree, especially about large and nested domains, a point taken up in the analysis unit.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Loops


A loop is a dot: two loci (anchors) with more contacts than their neighbourhood. Most loop anchors in GM12878 carry a CTCF peak.
ENCODE’s HiCCUPS calls 14 599 loops in GM12878, 164 on chr21; median anchor distance 330 kb.
Loops at the corners of domains are the “loop domains”.


Loops were mapped genome-wide by Rao et al. 2014 at 5–10 kb resolution with the HiCCUPS dot caller; how dots are called is in Calling compartments, TADs and loops. The window is chr21:24.75–26.25 Mb at 10 kb. Many dots sit at the apex of a triangle, and many anchors line up with CTCF peaks in the track below; 6 of these 15 loops have a CTCF peak at both anchors and 11 at one or both (exercise P4), while the strongest dot (25.50 × 25.56 Mb) has none: not every loop is a CTCF loop. Genome-wide, 64% of loop anchors overlap a CTCF peak against 13% of shuffled anchors (exercise C4). Rao et al. found that about 90% of loops with a CTCF motif at both anchors have the two motifs pointing towards each other (convergent): the convergent CTCF rule of Gene regulation. Most loops are not stable structures: live imaging (e.g. Gabriele et al. 2022) shows a given CTCF loop fully formed only a small fraction of the time; the dot is the population average of a transient event.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Loop extrusion


Cohesin, a ring-shaped SMC complex, is loaded onto DNA (with NIPBL) and extrudes a loop, reeling in DNA, using ATP.
It stops when it meets CTCF bound with its motif pointing into the loop. WAPL releases cohesin; the loop dissolves.
Loops are therefore dynamic: formed, held and released within minutes, over and over.


The idea that loops are extruded is old (Riggs 1990; Nasmyth 2001) and became a model for TADs when polymer simulations showed it reproduces domains, dots and the convergent rule (Sanborn et al. 2015; Fudenberg et al. 2016). Single-molecule experiments later watched it happen: yeast condensin extrudes loops on DNA curtains (Ganji et al. 2018), and human cohesin with NIPBL extrudes loops at roughly 0.5–1 kb per second (Davidson et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2019). Orientation dependence has a molecular explanation: the N-terminus of CTCF, which faces the loop when CTCF binds its motif, contacts the cohesin subunits SA2–SCC1 and blocks extrusion from that side (Li et al. 2020). Cohesin also holds sister chromatids together after replication; that is a different, longer-lived pool of cohesin.

title: 3D genome organisation
section: What extrusion leaves in a Hi-C map
text:
What extrusion leaves in a Hi-C map


A dot: many cells have the same loop between two convergent CTCF sites.
A domain: extrusion in progress produces contacts at all distances between the two sites.
A stripe: one anchor holds while the other side keeps being reeled in.


This is why loop extrusion explains so much at once. In a population of cells, cohesin complexes are at different stages: some have just started, some are stalled at both CTCF sites. Summed over cells, contacts are enriched everywhere inside the two sites (the domain), and most strongly at the two anchors themselves (the dot at the apex). If only one side is blocked by CTCF, the other side of the loop keeps moving, and the blocked anchor contacts a growing range of positions: a stripe (also called a flame or line) runs from the anchor along the edge of the domain (Vian et al. 2018). Stripes are common at strong CTCF sites and at active enhancers that load cohesin.

title: 3D genome organisation
section: Flip one CTCF site, move the loop
text:
Flip one CTCF site, move the loop


Inverting a single CTCF site with CRISPR loses the loop it anchored, and a new loop forms with the next site in the right orientation.
Deleting a site lets the domain merge with its neighbour.
Strong evidence that orientation, not only presence, of CTCF sites shapes the map.


De Wit et al. 2015 and Guo et al. 2015 inverted CTCF sites at several loci (the protocadherin cluster, the β-globin locus, and others) and saw loops lost and new ones formed as the convergent rule predicts; Sanborn et al. 2015 made a set of engineered changes and predicted the outcome with an extrusion model. The convergent rule only fixes which sites can stop cohesin; it does not say a loop is always there. Exercise B3 asks students to predict loops after deletions and inversions on paper. These results also explain why structural variants in patients (deletions, inversions, duplications) can change gene regulation without touching a gene: see the disease slides at the end.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Remove CTCF or cohesin


CTCF degraded (auxin degron, Nora et al. 2017): domain insulation and loops largely lost; compartments unchanged.
Cohesin removed (RAD21 degron, Rao et al. 2017; Nipbl deletion, Schwarzer et al. 2017): all loop domains vanish; compartments get stronger and finer.
WAPL removed (Haarhuis et al. 2017): cohesin stays longer, loops grow longer, compartments weaken.
Gene expression changes are surprisingly modest in the short term.


These acute depletion experiments are the main causal evidence for the model. With degrons a protein is destroyed within hours, before secondary effects accumulate; Hi-C after 6 hours (cohesin) or 1–2 days (CTCF) shows the direct consequences, and washout restores the structures. Two conclusions: loops and domains need cohesin, and CTCF positions them; compartments do not need either, so they are made by a different mechanism (next slide); in fact removing cohesin strengthens compartments, because extrusion normally mixes A and B. The expression changes were modest: a few hundred genes changed in each study, many only weakly. Why remains debated: many enhancer–promoter contacts are short-range and survive (Hsieh et al. 2022 with Micro-C), the effects may be stronger during activation of genes than in maintenance, or redundancy may buffer them. It is a good example of a striking structural change with a small functional readout.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Two mechanisms, one map


Extrusion (cohesin + CTCF) makes local loops and domains, in cis, with a motor.
Compartmentalisation separates chromatin types by affinity: like attracts like, for example HP1 bound to H3K9me3, Polycomb to H3K27me3.
They act at the same time and compete: extrusion mixes neighbouring A and B segments; affinity separates them.


Compartments are thought to form like microphase separation in a block copolymer: a chain made of A and B blocks, where A–A and B–B contacts are slightly favourable, folds so that like blocks cluster (Falk et al. 2019 argued that heterochromatin–heterochromatin attraction is the main driver, from inverted nuclei of nocturnal rodent rod cells). “Phase separation” or “condensates” (for HP1, Polycomb, transcription hubs) is one proposed physical basis; how much of compartmentalisation is liquid–liquid phase separation in the strict sense is debated, so say “affinity-driven segregation” when in doubt. The competition explains the depletion results: no cohesin, stronger compartments; more cohesin on DNA (WAPL loss), weaker compartments (Nuebler et al. 2018 simulations).

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
One cell versus millions


A Hi-C map is an average over millions of cells. In any one cell, two loci in the “same domain” may be far apart.
Imaging measures distances in single cells: DNA-FISH for a few loci, chromatin tracing (multiplexed FISH) for tens of loci along a region.
Single cells have domain-like globules with variable boundaries; CTCF sites make boundaries more likely, not certain.


Bintu et al. 2018 traced chromatin at 30-kb steps over a 2.5-Mb region in thousands of single cells: they saw TAD-like globules in individual cells, but with boundaries at different positions from cell to cell, preferentially at CTCF sites; after cohesin depletion the globules remained, but the preference for CTCF sites was lost. Single-cell Hi-C (Nagano et al. 2013; Stevens et al. 2017) reaches the same conclusion with far fewer contacts per cell. Contact frequency and distance are related but not the same thing: two loci can have a high Hi-C contact frequency but a large mean distance if they touch rarely but strongly, and FISH and Hi-C occasionally disagree (Williamson et al. 2014; Fudenberg and Imakaev 2017). When a paper says “the enhancer contacts the promoter”, ask: in what fraction of cells, for how long, and measured how?

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Proximity ligation: the principle


Crosslink chromatin with formaldehyde, cut the DNA, ligate ends that are held close together, and sequence the junctions.
Each sequenced junction is one contact between two genomic positions; counting them gives a contact map.
The chemistry has artefacts of its own (unligated ends, self-ligated fragments, PCR duplicates): the subject of Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices.


All “C” methods share this logic, introduced as 3C by Dekker et al. 2002 in yeast. Ligation favours ends that are physically close because crosslinking keeps them in the same small complex while the DNA is cut; ends from far apart rarely meet. What is measured is therefore a frequency of being crosslinkable and ligatable together, which depends on distance but also on the local chromatin (protein density, accessibility to the enzyme). The specifics (restriction enzymes, biotin fill-in, in situ ligation, how to map chimeric reads) come in the next unit.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
The 3C family


They differ in which ligation products are read: one pair (3C), one viewpoint against all (4C), a region (5C), everything (Hi-C, Micro-C), chosen baits (Capture-C), or only those near a protein (HiChIP, PLAC-seq, ChIA-PET).
Ligation-free methods (GAM, SPRITE) capture co-occurrence of many loci at once.


History in one breath: 3C (Dekker 2002), 4C (Simonis et al. 2006; Zhao et al. 2006), 5C (Dostie et al. 2006), Hi-C (Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009), in situ Hi-C (Rao et al. 2014), ChIA-PET (Fullwood et al. 2009), Capture-C (Hughes et al. 2014) and promoter Capture Hi-C (Mifsud et al. 2015), HiChIP (Mumbach et al. 2016), Micro-C (Hsieh et al. 2015 in yeast; mammalian cells 2020). The choice is about depth: a genome-wide map needs billions of reads to reach 1–5 kb resolution, so if you only care about the promoters of 20 genes, capture them and spend the reads there. HiChIP and ChIA-PET enrich for contacts at sites bound by a protein (cohesin, CTCF, H3K27ac); they are cheap but mix contact frequency with ChIP enrichment, a bias discussed in Calling compartments, TADs and loops. GAM (genome architecture mapping) sequences DNA from thin nuclear slices; SPRITE tags all DNA in a crosslinked complex with the same barcode; both see multi-way contacts and avoid ligation biases.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Does contact mean activation?


For: forcing a loop between an enhancer and a promoter can switch a gene on; expression rises nonlinearly with contact probability.
Not that simple: at Sox2 the enhancer–promoter distance does not track transcriptional bursts; at Shh activation came with a larger distance in one system.
Current view: proximity within a few hundred nm, perhaps in a hub of factors, rather than a stable direct touch.


Deng et al. 2012 tethered the self-associating protein LDB1 to the β-globin promoter with an engineered zinc finger and restored looping to the LCR enhancer and transcription in cells lacking the activator GATA1. Zuin et al. 2022 moved an enhancer to many positions around a promoter in mouse ES cells and found that expression depends on contact probability in a sigmoidal, nonlinear way, and that CTCF insulation acts by lowering contact probability. Against a simple contact model: Alexander et al. 2019 imaged the Sox2 promoter and its enhancer (about 110 kb away) live and found their distance unrelated to bursts of transcription; Benabdallah et al. 2019 found that activating the Shh enhancer during differentiation increased its distance from the gene. Kane et al. 2022 showed that cohesin is needed for the very long-range ZRS–Shh action but less for short-range enhancers. The honest summary: contact is necessary in some sense, but the timescales, distances and the role of hubs of TFs and coactivators are open questions.

title: 3D genome organisation
section: How much do domains matter for genes?
text:
How much do domains matter for genes?

Boundaries constrain enhancers: most enhancer–gene links found by CRISPR screens lie within the same domain, and insulation by CTCF lowers expression of genes across a boundary.
But redundancy is common: removing CTCF or cohesin changes few genes in the short term; in Drosophila, extensive rearrangements of domains on balancer chromosomes changed the expression of few genes.
Context matters: a domain change matters when it brings a strong enhancer to a gene that is ready to respond in the right tissue. That is the case in the disease examples that follow.


A text slide for balance before the disease examples. Evidence for constraint: CRISPRi screens of enhancers (Fulco et al. 2019, Gasperini et al. 2019) found that most functional enhancer–gene pairs are within the same domain; Zuin et al. 2022 showed insulation acts by reducing contact. Evidence for redundancy: Nora 2017 and Rao 2017 found hundreds rather than thousands of genes changed; Ghavi-Helm et al. 2019 studied Drosophila balancer chromosomes with many inversions and found most genes unchanged; Despang et al. 2019 removed CTCF sites between Sox9 and Kcnj2 and fused the domains with only modest effects, while a larger rearrangement that moved the domain boundary did cause misexpression. Students should leave with a nuanced view: domains are a regulatory constraint, not a switch, and the consequence of breaking one depends on what is on either side.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Broken boundaries cause limb malformations


At the WNT6–IHH–EPHA4–PAX3 locus, limb enhancers normally act only on EPHA4 in their own domain.
Deletions, inversions and duplications that move a boundary let the enhancers reach PAX3, WNT6 or IHH: three different malformations (Lupiáñez et al. 2015).
The rewiring happened only when the variant crossed a CTCF-associated boundary; mice engineered with CRISPR reproduced it.


This is the landmark paper linking TADs to disease. Patients with brachydactyly carried deletions that removed EPHA4 and the boundary to the PAX3 domain: the limb enhancers then contacted PAX3, which was expressed ectopically in the limb. F-syndrome patients carried an inversion that moved the enhancers next to WNT6; polydactyly patients carried duplications that included the boundary and placed a copy of IHH in a new domain with the enhancers. The mouse models (made by CRISPR in ES cells and tetraploid aggregation) reproduced the phenotypes and the ectopic contacts by capture-C. Clinical relevance: structural variants in non-coding DNA are routinely found by genome sequencing, and their pathogenicity can sometimes be predicted from whether they cross a boundary. Franke et al. 2016 extended this with duplications at SOX9–KCNJ2 that form a new domain (a “neo-TAD”).

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Boundary loss in cancer


In IDH-mutant gliomas, the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate inhibits TET demethylases and CpG sites gain methylation, including in CTCF motifs.
CTCF cannot bind methylated sites: a boundary is lost and a constitutive enhancer activates the oncogene PDGFRA (Flavahan et al. 2016).
Microdeletions of boundaries next to proto-oncogenes are also found in T-ALL and other cancers (Hnisz et al. 2016).


This example connects three units of the course: DNA methylation (DNA methylation biology), CTCF binding (Gene regulation: CTCF cannot bind a motif with a methylated CpG, as at the H19/IGF2 imprinting control region) and 3D organisation. Flavahan et al. showed reduced CTCF binding at the boundary in IDH-mutant tumours, and that demethylating treatment restored CTCF binding and lowered PDGFRA; disrupting the boundary in non-mutant glioma cells with CRISPR raised PDGFRA. Hnisz et al. 2016 found recurrent microdeletions of CTCF boundary sites near TAL1 and LMO2 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The cancer-epigenetics unit returns to IDH mutations.

text:
