CTCF loss: domains and loops go, compartments stay. Cohesin loss: all loop domains go, compartments get stronger.
A Hi-C map is an average over cells; single cells are variable. Contact is not the same as distance, nor as regulation.
Moving a boundary can rewire enhancers to new genes: limb malformations, cancer.


Students should be able to: read a Hi-C map and name the features; explain loop extrusion and the convergent CTCF rule and predict what an inversion or deletion of a CTCF site does; state what CTCF and cohesin depletion do and what that implies; explain the difference between single-cell distances and population contact frequencies; choose an assay from the 3C family for a given question; and explain how a structural variant can cause disease without touching a gene. Next: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices.

title: 3D genome organisation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Dekker et al. 2002, Science. Capturing chromosome conformation. The first C method (3C), in yeast.
Dixon et al. 2012, Nature. Topological domains in mammalian genomes identified by analysis of chromatin interactions. TADs, and their boundaries enriched for CTCF.
Fudenberg et al. 2016, Cell Rep. Formation of chromosomal domains by loop extrusion. The polymer model that explains domains, dots and the CTCF rule.
Nora et al. 2017, Cell. Targeted degradation of CTCF decouples local insulation of chromosome domains from genomic compartmentalization. CTCF degron.
Rao et al. 2017, Cell. Cohesin loss eliminates all loop domains. Cohesin degron; compartments strengthen.
Lupiáñez et al. 2015, Cell. Disruptions of topological chromatin domains cause pathogenic rewiring of gene-enhancer interactions. TAD boundaries and limb malformations.

title: Quiz: gene regulation
text:
Short questions on regulatory elements, transcription factors and motifs. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Banerji, Rusconi and Schaffner moved the SV40 72-bp element 3.3 kb downstream of the β-globin gene and flipped its orientation. Transcription stayed high. Which two properties of enhancers does this show, and what control showed that the element acts in cis?






Answer





Distance independence (it works kilobases away, upstream or downstream) and orientation independence. Acting in cis: the element had to be on the same DNA molecule as the gene; SV40 DNA supplied on a separate molecule did not enhance.




Q2. A gene’s promoter has a CpG observed/expected ratio of 0.9 and is marked by H3K4me3 in almost every tissue. A second gene’s promoter has a ratio of 0.2 and a TATA box. Which is more likely a housekeeping gene, and which a tissue-specific one?






Answer





The CpG-island promoter (o/e 0.9, marked everywhere) is typical of housekeeping (and developmental) genes; the CpG-poor promoter with a TATA box is typical of a tissue-specific gene, marked only where it is expressed.




Q3. An element 40 kb from gene A and 300 kb from gene B carries H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, has an ATAC-seq peak and produces short bidirectional RNAs. What is it, and which gene does it regulate?






Hint





Think of the ZRS and SHH.









Answer





An active enhancer (open core, H3K4me1 + H3K27ac, eRNAs). Its target cannot be read from these data: enhancers often skip the nearest gene. Use 3D contacts (Hi-C, Capture-C), correlation with expression across samples, or a perturbation (CRISPRi of the element) to find out.




Q4. From 10 aligned sites a column has 7 A, 1 C, 2 G and 0 T. With a pseudocount of 1 per base and a uniform background, what are the log-odds weights of A and T? Why not use zero for T?






Answer





\(p_A = 8/14 = 0.571\), \(w_A = \log_2(0.571/0.25) = +1.19\). \(p_T = 1/14 = 0.071\), \(w_T = \log_2(0.071/0.25) = -1.81\). Without a pseudocount \(p_T = 0\) and \(w_T = -\infty\): any site with T there would be rejected, although 10 sites cannot show that T is impossible.




Q5. What is the information content of a column with frequencies A 0.25, C 0.25, G 0.25, T 0.25? And of A 1.0? What does each look like in a sequence logo?






Answer





\(2 + 4 \times 0.25 \log_2 0.25 = 2 - 2 = 0\) bits: an empty column. A 1.0: \(2 + 1 \times \log_2 1 = 2\) bits: a single A of full height.




Q6. A TF motif is scanned with a threshold of \(p < 10^{-5}\) per position and strand. About how many matches do you expect by chance in 1 Mb? In a 3.1 Gb genome?






Answer





\(2 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-5} = 20\) per Mb; \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-5} = 62\,000\) in the genome. More than the number of peaks of most TF ChIP-seq experiments.




Q7. In GM12878, 78% of CTCF peaks contain a CTCF motif match, but only 4% of CTCF matches on chr21 lie in a CTCF peak. Give three reasons why a motif match may not be bound.






Answer





Any three of: the match is in closed chromatin or wrapped on a nucleosome; the CpG in the motif is methylated (CTCF is methylation-sensitive); the match is weak (low score); a needed partner TF is absent; the TF’s concentration only fills the best sites; many matches are chance hits in sequence the TF never samples. Matches in ATAC peaks were bound 39% of the time, matches outside 2%.




Q8. The plus strand of a region reads …TTGCGCCCCCTGGTGGCAA…. A CTCF scan reports a match on the minus strand. Write the matched site in the orientation of the JASPAR consensus (GCCACCAGGGGGCGC). Which way does it point on the chromosome?






Answer





The reverse complement of GCGCCCCCTGGTGGC is GCCACCAGGGGGCGC, the consensus. On a minus-strand match the motif reads right to left, so it points towards lower coordinates (←). It forms loops with + sites (→) to its left: convergent pairs.




Q9. A pioneer factor binds a site in closed chromatin in progenitor cells. Which assays would show (a) binding before opening, (b) opening, (c) activation of the enhancer?






Answer






ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN of the pioneer TF gives a peak where ATAC-seq has none (yet). (b) ATAC-seq peak appears; nucleosomes are moved (MNase-seq). (c) H3K27ac (p300/CBP) and other TFs arrive; eRNAs; the target gene’s expression rises.





Q10. A paper lists 900 “super-enhancers” in a lymphoma line and claims they form a distinct class of regulatory elements. What is the main criticism?






Answer





The cutoff is drawn on a continuous ranking of stitched H3K27ac (or Mediator) signal; there is no gap that separates a class. When super-enhancers are dissected genetically, their parts often act like ordinary enhancers whose effects add up. The ranking is useful (it highlights identity genes and oncogenes), but “a distinct class” needs functional evidence.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Build a position weight matrix (PWM) from aligned binding sites with pseudocounts, and score sequences with it on both strands, by hand.
Compute the information content of a motif column and read a sequence logo.
Estimate how many chance matches a motif has in a region or a genome, and use that to judge claims about TF binding.
Fetch a matrix from JASPAR in R, scan peak sequences and backgrounds with motifmatchr, and measure enrichment, centrality and the fraction of bound matches.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Build a position weight matrix (PWM) from aligned binding sites with pseudocounts, and score sequences with it on both strands, by hand.
Compute the information content of a motif column and read a sequence logo.
Estimate how many chance matches a motif has in a region or a genome, and use that to judge claims about TF binding.
Fetch a matrix from JASPAR in R, scan peak sequences and backgrounds with motifmatchr, and measure enrichment, centrality and the fraction of bound matches.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Background
PWM. From \(N\) aligned sites, count each base \(b\) at each position \(j\) (\(n_{b,j}\)), add a pseudocount, and divide: \(p_{b,j} = (n_{b,j} + 1) / (N + 4)\) with a pseudocount of 1 per base. The log-odds weight against a background frequency \(q_b\) is \(w_{b,j} = \log_2 (p_{b,j} / q_b)\). The score of a sequence window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Scan both strands: the minus strand is the reverse complement.
Information content of column \(j\) against a uniform background: \(IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j}\) bits, between 0 (no preference) and 2 (one base only). A logo stacks the letters of each column to height \(IC_j\).
Chance matches. An exact \(k\)-mer occurs with probability \(4^{-k}\) per position and strand in random sequence. For a PWM scanned at a \(p\)-value threshold \(p\), a sequence of length \(L\) has about \(2Lp\) matches by chance. Roughly, a motif with \(I\) bits of information is found about once every \(2^I\) bp per strand.
Bound or not. A TF binds only a small fraction of its motif matches: accessibility, nucleosomes, DNA methylation, partner TFs and TF concentration decide which.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Data
GM12878 CTCF peaks (ENCODE, IDR conservative, narrowPeak), GM12878 ATAC-seq peaks, the hg38 genome as a bgzipped, indexed FASTA (hg38.fa.bgz with .fai and .gzi, so that any region can be read without unpacking the whole file), the hg38 chromosome sizes and the ENCODE blacklist. From the course repository:
data/download.sh gene-regulation
mkdir -p ~/epi/generegulation && cd ~/epi/generegulation
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
You need samtools (1.10 or newer), bedtools and, in R, the Bioconductor packages JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, universalmotif, Rsamtools, Biostrings, GenomicRanges and rtracklayer (see Install the software you need). The R part runs in about two minutes on a laptop.
Simplification: we use one matrix per TF and a single \(p\)-value threshold (\(10^{-4}\), uniform background). Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting does this properly, with motif databases, enrichment statistics and footprints.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
By hand
Do these on paper. A calculator for \(\log_2\) helps: \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2\); \(\log_2 3 = 1.585\), \(\log_2 (2/3) = -0.585\), \(\log_2 (1/3) = -1.585\).
B1. Build a PWM. Eight binding sites of a GATA-like factor, aligned:
AGATAA   TGATAA   AGATAG   AGATAA
TGATAG   AGATTA   AGATAA   CGATAA

Write the 4 × 6 count matrix (rows A, C, G, T).
Convert it to frequencies with a pseudocount of 1 per base. Why is a pseudocount needed here?
Compute the log-odds weights against a uniform background (\(q_b = 0.25\)). Write down the weight matrix; you will need it in B2.

B2. Score sequences. Using your weights from B1:

Score AGATAA, TGATAG, AGCTAA and GGGGGG. What are the highest and the lowest possible scores?
A sequence on the plus strand reads TTATCT. What does it score as written? What does it score on the minus strand? Where is the motif, and which way does it point?
With a threshold of 6 bits, which of the five sequences are matches?

B3. Information content.

Compute \(IC\) for column 1 and for column 2 of your PWM (with the pseudocounts).
What would \(IC\) of column 2 be without pseudocounts? Why does the pseudocount matter so much more with 8 sites than with 913 (the number of sites behind the JASPAR CTCF matrix)?
A column is 50% A and 50% G, never C or T. What is its \(IC\)? How tall is each letter in the logo?

B4. How many matches by chance? Take the human genome as \(3.1 \times 10^9\) bp of random sequence with equal base frequencies.

How often do you expect the exact 6-mer AGATAA per Mb (both strands)? In the whole genome?
Repeat for the E-box CACGTG. Why is the answer half of (a)? (Write out its reverse complement.)
A PWM is scanned with a threshold of \(p < 10^{-4}\) per position and strand. How many matches do you expect on chr21 (40 Mb of sequence) and in the genome? GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks: what is the largest possible fraction of genome-wide CTCF matches that can be bound?
The CTCF matrix has 16.1 bits of information. Using the rule of thumb, about how often does a CTCF site of that quality occur by chance?

B5. Strand and orientation. A scan of chr1 with the CTCF matrix reports four matches (1-based start, strand):
site 1   1 000 001   +
site 2   1 180 001   −
site 3   1 400 001   −
site 4   1 650 001   +

The JASPAR consensus is GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. Write the plus-strand sequence of the genome at site 2 if it matched the consensus perfectly.
Draw the four sites as arrows. Which pairs are convergent? Loop extrusion by cohesin predicts loops between which sites?
Site 2 is deleted. Which loop do you now expect?

B6. Read a logo. Look at the CTCF logo on the Information content and sequence logos slide (JASPAR MA0139.2, 913 sites).

Which three positions carry the most information? About how many bits each?
Position 9 has G (566 sites) and A (333 sites). What does a mixed column mean for binding? Is a site with A at position 9 a “mutant” site?
Why are the end columns low?
A logo built from only 20 sites without pseudocounts looks “cleaner”, with taller columns. Is that motif more specific?

B7. Judge the claims.

“The CTCF motif is the main determinant of CTCF binding, so CTCF binds essentially every match to its motif.” Use your answer to B4c and the chr21 numbers from the lecture (8583 matches, 369 inside a CTCF peak) to judge the claim.
A paper reports: “TF X has 600 000 motif matches but only 12 000 ChIP-seq peaks. Therefore 98% of its sites are silenced by DNA methylation.” What else could explain the gap? What experiment would test the methylation claim?
A student finds the PU.1 motif in 22% of GM12878 ATAC peaks and concludes that PU.1 binds 22% of the open chromatin in B cells. What is missing from this reasoning? (In the lecture: 12% of GC-matched background windows also have a match.)

B8. Read the figure. You ChIP two TFs, Y and Z, and plot the position of the best match to each one’s motif relative to the summit, as on the centrality slide. Y gives a sharp peak at 0; Z gives a flat histogram, although Z’s motif is found in 40% of its peaks (15% in background). Give two explanations for Z.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
On the command line

C1 — Sequences around the CTCF summits
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ s = $2 + $10; print $1, s - 100, s + 100, "peak" NR }' > ctcf_win.bed
head -2 ctcf_win.bed

grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > genome.txt
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
bedtools shuffle -i ctcf_win.bed -g genome.txt -chrom -excl blacklist.bed -seed 1 > shuf_win.bed

for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  awk '{ print $1 ":" $2 + 1 "-" $3 }' $f.bed > $f.regions
  samtools faidx -n 1000 -r $f.regions $D/hg38.fa.bgz | grep -v '>' | tr acgtn ACGTN > $f.txt
done
wc -l ctcf_win.txt shuf_win.txt
grep -c N shuf_win.txt

Explain the awk in the first command: which column is the summit, and why is the window s − 100 to s + 100? Why does the second awk add 1 to the start?
The genome file is soft-masked (repeats in lower case). What does tr acgtn ACGTN do, and what would go wrong without it?
How many shuffled windows contain an N, and why can that happen?



C2 — Counting words is not motif scanning
for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  echo $f \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCCTC|GAGGG' $f.txt) \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCA[CG][CT]AG[AG][GT]GG|CC[AC][CT]CT[AG][CG]TGG' $f.txt) \
    $(awk '{ gc += gsub(/[GC]/, ""); n += 200 } END { printf "%.3f", gc / n }' $f.txt)
done

The columns are: windows containing CCCTC (on either strand), windows containing an 11-bp degenerate CTCF core (either strand), and GC content. Fill in a table and compute the fraction for each.
CTCF is named “CCCTC-binding factor”. Why is CCCTC a poor test for CTCF sites? Estimate how often a 5-mer occurs in 200 bp of random sequence (both strands).
Why do the shuffled windows have lower GC content than the peak windows, and why does that matter for (a)?

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
In R
library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite)
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
library(motifmatchr); library(universalmotif)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — The CTCF matrix from JASPAR
jaspar <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf_m <- getMatrixByID(jaspar, "MA0139.2")
ctcf_m
cnt <- Matrix(ctcf_m)            # counts: 4 rows (A, C, G, T) x 15 columns
cnt
colSums(cnt)                     # number of sites in each column

How many sites is the matrix built from, and from what kind of experiment? (Look at the type tag.)
Why are the column sums not all equal?



R2 — Frequencies, log-odds, information content and the logo
p   <- (cnt + 0.25) / colSums(cnt + 0.25)  # pseudocount 0.25 per base (1 per column)
lo  <- log2(p / 0.25)                       # log-odds against a uniform background
ic  <- 2 + colSums(p * log2(p))             # information content per column (bits)
round(lo, 2)
round(ic, 2); sum(ic)
consensus <- paste(rownames(cnt)[apply(cnt, 2, which.max)], collapse = "")
consensus
view_motifs(convert_motifs(ctcf_m, "universalmotif"), use.type = "ICM")

Which columns have the highest information content? Compare with your answers to B6.
What is the total information content, and what does the rule of thumb in B4d give?
What is the largest and the smallest weight in lo? Explain the smallest.



R3 — Sequences around the summits
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
summit <- GRanges(seqnames(ctcf), IRanges(start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak, width = 1))
win <- resize(summit, width = 200, fix = "center")
genome <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))
seqs <- getSeq(genome, win)
seqs
mean(letterFrequency(seqs, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
Check that the summit computed here is the same base as in C1. (start() in R is 1-based; see Genomic intervals.)


R4 — Is the motif enriched in the peaks?
flank <- getSeq(genome, shift(win, 3000))                 # 3 kb to the right
shuf  <- shuffle_sequences(seqs, k = 2, rng.seed = 1)     # same dinucleotides, order destroyed
mean(letterFrequency(flank, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
mean(letterFrequency(shuf,  "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
frac_with_match <- function(s)
  mean(motifMatches(matchMotifs(ctcf_m, s, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even"))[, 1])
c(peaks = frac_with_match(seqs), flank = frac_with_match(flank), shuffled = frac_with_match(shuf))

What fraction of peaks, flanking windows and shuffled peaks contain a match?
The two backgrounds control for different things. What does each keep from the peaks, and what does it lose? Which gives the more conservative enrichment, and why?
Compare with B4c: how many chance matches do you expect in a 200-bp window at \(p < 10^{-4}\)? Does that fit the backgrounds?



R5 — Strong and weak peaks
hit <- motifMatches(matchMotifs(ctcf_m, seqs, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even"))[, 1]
q <- cut(rank(ctcf$signalValue, ties.method = "first"), 4, labels = c("Q1 weakest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 strongest"))
tapply(hit, q, mean)
tapply(ctcf$signalValue, q, median)
What fraction of peaks has a match in each quarter? Give two reasons why a CTCF peak could lack a match.


R6 — Where in the peak is the motif?
Listing every match position is slow for 44 000 sequences, so take a random 5000 peaks and a 500-bp window:
set.seed(1)
pick <- sample(length(summit), 5000)
s500 <- getSeq(genome, resize(summit[pick], 500, fix = "center"))
pos  <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, s500, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even", out = "positions")[[1]]
hits <- data.frame(seq = rep(seq_along(pos), lengths(pos)), start = unlist(start(pos)),
                   strand = unlist(lapply(pos, function(x) mcols(x)$strand)),
                   score = unlist(lapply(pos, function(x) mcols(x)$score)))
best <- hits[order(-hits$score), ]
best <- best[!duplicated(best$seq), ]                # best match per peak
best$centre <- best$start + 7 - 250.5                # motif centre relative to the summit
nrow(best) / 5000
mean(abs(best$centre) <= 50)
table(best$strand)
hist(best$centre, breaks = seq(-250, 250, 10), main = "CTCF motif position in peaks",
     xlab = "distance of the best match from the summit (bp)")

What fraction of the 5000 peaks has a match in ±250 bp, and what fraction of best matches lies within 50 bp of the summit?
Why + 7 and − 250.5? (The motif is 15 bp; the window positions run from 1 to 500.)
Are the matches mostly on one strand? What would you expect, and why does strand still matter for CTCF (B5)?



R7 — Most matches are not bound
chr21 <- getSeq(genome, GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, seqlengths(genome)["chr21"])))
L <- sum(letterFrequency(chr21, "ACGT"))
m21 <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, chr21, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even", out = "positions")[[1]][[1]]
length(m21); 2 * L * 1e-4                                # found vs expected by chance
sites21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(start(m21), end(m21)))
atac <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
bound <- overlapsAny(sites21, ctcf)
open  <- overlapsAny(sites21, atac)
c(n = length(sites21), bound = sum(bound), frac_bound = mean(bound))
tapply(bound, open, mean)
c(peaks_chr21 = sum(seqnames(ctcf) == "chr21"),
  with_match = sum(overlapsAny(ctcf[seqnames(ctcf) == "chr21"], sites21)))

How many matches are on chr21, and how many did you expect (B4c)?
What fraction of matches lies in a CTCF peak? Among matches in ATAC peaks, and outside them?
What fraction of chr21 CTCF peaks contains a match? Write one sentence that states both (b) and (c): is the motif necessary, sufficient, both or neither?



R8 — Check your hand calculations
sites <- DNAStringSet(c("AGATAA", "TGATAA", "AGATAG", "AGATAA", "TGATAG", "AGATTA", "AGATAA", "CGATAA"))
pfm <- consensusMatrix(sites)[c("A", "C", "G", "T"), ]
pfm
lo8 <- log2(((pfm + 1) / (8 + 4)) / 0.25)
round(lo8, 2)
score <- function(x) sum(lo8[cbind(match(strsplit(x, "")[[1]], rownames(lo8)), 1:6)])
sapply(c("AGATAA", "TGATAG", "AGCTAA", "GGGGGG", "TTATCT"), score)
score(as.character(reverseComplement(DNAString("TTATCT"))))
Do the numbers agree with B1 and B2?

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — PWMs and logos (B1–B3, B6, R2)





Work column by column. With 8 sites and a pseudocount of 1 per base, every frequency is \((n + 1)/12\), so only four values occur: 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 … 9/12. For the information content, \(-p \log_2 p\) is 0.5 for \(p = 0.5\), 0.5 for \(p = 0.25\), 0.311 for \(p = 0.75\), 0.431 for \(p = 1/6\), 0.299 for \(p = 1/12\). The original papers: Stormo 2000 (PWMs), Schneider & Stephens 1990 (logos).









Hint 2 — chance matches and strands (B4, B5)





Expected count = (number of positions) × (strands) × (probability per position and strand). A palindromic word (equal to its own reverse complement) is the same match on both strands, so it should be counted once. A match on the − strand reads the motif on the reverse complement: write the consensus, then reverse it and complement each base. Convergent CTCF sites: a + site on the left and a − site on the right, pointing towards each other (see the CTCF loop-extrusion slide and Rao et al. 2014).









Hint 3 — command line (C1, C2)





Column 10 of a narrowPeak file is the summit offset from the start (format). samtools faidx reads regions written as chr:start-end (1-based, inclusive) from a bgzipped, indexed FASTA; -r takes them from a file and -n sets the line length. bedtools shuffle with -chrom -excl is the restricted shuffle of Genomic intervals. In a regular expression [CG] means C or G.









Hint 4 — JASPAR and motifmatchr (R1–R7)





JASPAR2024 is a database package; TFBSTools::getMatrixByID reads one matrix from it, and the matrix page is on the JASPAR website. motifmatchr::matchMotifs scans sequences: out = "matches" (default) gives TRUE/FALSE per sequence, out = "positions" the coordinates, strand and score of every match; bg = "even" uses a uniform background, p.cutoff the threshold. Rsamtools::FaFile and getSeq read sequences of a GRanges from an indexed FASTA. universalmotif has shuffle_sequences() (with k = 2 it keeps dinucleotide counts) and view_motifs(). Biostrings has letterFrequency(), consensusMatrix() and reverseComplement().









Hint 5 — judging claims (B7, B8)





Compare the number of matches with the number of peaks, and ask what else differs between bound and unbound matches: accessibility, nucleosomes, methylation, partners, TF level. For a causal claim about methylation, think of an experiment that changes methylation and measures binding (e.g. a DNMT inhibitor or DNMT knockout, or methylation-sensitive binding in vitro). For enrichment, always compare with a background with the same composition.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Counts (columns 1–6):
A   5  0  8  0  7  6
C   1  0  0  0  0  0
G   0  8  0  0  0  2
T   2  0  0  8  1  0

\(p = (n + 1)/12\): column 1 is A 0.50, C 0.17, G 0.08, T 0.25; columns 2–4 have 0.75 for the consensus base and 0.08 for the others; column 5 is A 0.67, T 0.17, C and G 0.08; column 6 is A 0.58, G 0.25, C and T 0.08. Without a pseudocount every unseen base has frequency 0 and weight \(-\infty\), so a single unseen base would veto a site. Eight sites are far too few to call a base impossible.
Weights \(\log_2(p / 0.25)\):

A   1.00  -1.58   1.58  -1.58   1.42   1.22
C  -0.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58
G  -1.58   1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58   0.00
T   0.00  -1.58  -1.58   1.58  -0.58  -1.58
B2. (a) AGATAA = 1.00 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 1.22 = 8.39 (the maximum: the best base in every column). TGATAG = 0 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 0 = 6.17. AGCTAA = 1.00 + 1.58 − 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 1.22 = 5.22. GGGGGG = −1.58 + 1.58 − 1.58 − 1.58 − 1.58 + 0 = −4.75. Minimum: −1.58 in every column = −9.51. (b) As written, TTATCT scores 0 − 1.58 + 1.58 − 1.58 − 0.58 − 1.58 = −1.58. Its reverse complement is AGATAA, which scores 8.39: the motif is on the minus strand, reading right to left on the genome. (c) AGATAA, TGATAG, and TTATCT on the minus strand pass 6 bits. AGCTAA (5.22) is a near miss: a single mismatch at a 1.58-bit position.
B3. (a) Column 1: \(p = (0.50, 0.17, 0.08, 0.25)\); \(\sum -p\log_2 p = 0.5 + 0.431 + 0.299 + 0.5 = 1.73\), so $IC = 2 - 1.73 = $ 0.27 bits. Column 2: \(p = (0.75, 0.08, 0.08, 0.08)\); \(0.311 + 3 \times 0.299 = 1.21\), $IC = $ 0.79 bits. (b) Without pseudocounts column 2 is 100% G: 2 bits. With 8 sites the pseudocount (4 extra “observations”) is a third of the data; with 913 sites it is 0.4%. CTCF’s column 3 (C in 903 of 913 sites) has 1.9 bits with or without it. (c) \(\sum -p\log_2 p = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1\), $IC = $ 1 bit. The stack is 1 bit tall; A and G are each 0.5 bit.
B4. (a) \(4^{-6} = 1/4096\) per position and strand. Per Mb: \(2 \times 10^6 / 4096 \approx\) 490. Genome: \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 / 4096 \approx\) 1.5 million. (b) CACGTG is its own reverse complement (a palindrome): each occurrence is found on both strands but is one site, so about 245 per Mb and 760 000 per genome. (c) chr21: $2 ^6 ^{-4} = $ 8000 (8018 for the exact 40.1 Mb; 8583 found in R7). Genome: \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-4} \approx\) 620 000. Even if every one of the 44 217 peaks held a different match, at most \(44\,217 / 620\,000 \approx\) 7% of matches could be bound. (d) \(2^{16.1} \approx 70\,000\) bp per strand, so about one per 35 kb counting both strands: roughly 30 per Mb, 90 000 in the genome. Still twice the number of CTCF peaks.
B5. (a) A − strand match means the consensus reads on the reverse complement. The plus strand at site 2 reads the reverse complement of GCCACCAGGGGGCGC, which is GCGCCCCCTGGTGGC. (b) Sites: 1 →, 2 ←, 3 ←, 4 →. Convergent pairs (→ … ←): 1–2 and 1–3. Site 4 points away from all the others to its right (none). Cohesin extruding from between 1 and 2 stalls at 1 and 2: the loop is 1–2. 1–3 can form if cohesin passes site 2 (CTCF is not bound at every site in every cell). (c) Without site 2, cohesin stalls at 1 and 3: a larger loop 1–3. (Deleting or inverting CTCF sites re-wires loops in exactly this way.)
B6. (a) Positions 3 (C), 8 (G) and 11 (G), each about 1.9 bits (R2: 1.90, 1.91, 1.82). Position 7 (A, 1.55 bits) is next. (b) Both G and A are tolerated at position 9; G is preferred, but a site with A is a normal site with a slightly lower score, not a mutant. A logo shows a distribution of preferences, not one “correct” sequence. (c) The edges of the motif contact the protein less, and the alignment of sites is less precise at the edges. (d) No. With 20 sites and no pseudocount, unseen bases get frequency 0 and columns look like 2 bits by sampling alone. The apparent specificity is an artefact of the small sample.
B7. (a) The claim fails. On chr21 only 369 of 8583 matches (4.3%) are in a CTCF peak; genome-wide at most 7% could be (B4c). The motif is close to necessary (79% of peaks have a match, R7) but far from sufficient: accessibility, nucleosomes, methylation and the rest of the chromatin context decide. (b) Most matches are expected by chance (B4); most lie in closed chromatin or on nucleosomes; many are weak; X may need a partner; ChIP detects only sites occupied in many cells at once; and X’s concentration may limit occupancy. To test methylation: compare binding before and after removing DNA methylation (DNMT1/3A/3B knockout or a DNMT inhibitor) and check whether new peaks appear at matches that were methylated; or test methylated vs unmethylated DNA in vitro. (c) A background. 12% of GC-matched random windows also have a PU.1 match, so most of the 22% would be there by chance; the enrichment is 1.8×. A match is also not binding: PU.1 ChIP-seq is needed to say where PU.1 is bound.
B8. Z may bind DNA indirectly, through a partner whose motif is at the summit, while Z’s motif is enriched in the peaks because Z and its partner co-occur in the same regulatory regions. Or Z’s matrix is wrong or describes a related TF whose motif is common in such regions (e.g. a GC-rich motif in GC-rich peaks). An antibody problem (the ChIP pulls down another protein) gives the same picture.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) $2 + $10 is the summit as a BED boundary (start + offset). s − 100 to s + 100 is 200 bases in BED, centred on the summit base (s to s + 1). samtools faidx regions are 1-based and inclusive, so the BED start needs + 1 (Genomic intervals). The first window is chr12 53676133 53676333. (b) It turns the lower-case (repeat-masked) bases into upper case. Without it, grep for CCCTC would miss every site in a repeat, and the GC count with [GC] would skip lower-case bases. (c) 1813 of 44 217 shuffled windows contain an N: the shuffle avoids the blacklist but not the assembly gaps (runs of N). Adding the gaps to the exclusion file would fix it.
C2. (a)

A 5-mer has probability \(4^{-5} \approx 0.001\) per position and strand; 200 bp × 2 strands gives about 0.39 expected occurrences, so about a third of random windows contain one (\(1 - e^{-0.39} \approx 0.32\); observed 27.5%, lower because of the AT-rich background). Enrichment 2×, with a third of the background positive: useless for calling sites. The 11-bp core is much more specific but too strict: it misses many real sites that differ at one position. A PWM with a threshold sits between the two.
Peaks are in GC-rich, gene-dense DNA; the shuffled windows are anywhere in the genome (41% GC). A GC-rich word like CCCTC is more frequent in GC-rich DNA anyway, so part of the difference in (a) is composition. R4 uses backgrounds that control for this.










Solutions — R





R1. (a) 913 sites, from ChIP-seq (type: ChIP-seq), human. (b) Some sites in the alignment were shorter or did not cover the outer columns, so the sums fall from 913 to 908 towards the right end.
R2. (a) Columns 3 (1.90), 8 (1.91) and 11 (1.82); then 7 (1.55) and 2 (1.27). Columns 1 and 6 are weakest (0.34, 0.37). (b) Total 16.1 bits; consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. \(2^{16.1} \approx 70\,000\) bp per strand (B4d). (c) Largest about +1.99 (C at position 3); smallest −9.83 (C at position 8, G at position 3, C at position 11): bases never seen get only the pseudocount: in column 8 (911 sites) \(p = 0.25/912\), and \(\log_2(p/0.25) = \log_2(1/912) \approx -9.8\). motifmatchr builds its own weights with a pseudocount of 0.8 in total, so its scores differ slightly from lo.
R3. 44 217 sequences of 200 bp, GC content 0.514 (the genome average is 0.41). The summit is start + peak in R because start() is already the file start + 1, the same base as C1’s BED s–s + 1.
R4. (a) Peaks 78.5%, flanking windows 5.4%, shuffled peaks 8.8%. (b) Flanks keep the regional context (same chromosome, nearby DNA) but not the composition: their GC is 0.445, lower than the peaks’ 0.514. Shuffling keeps the exact dinucleotide composition of each peak, including GC and CpG, but destroys any real sequence structure such as repeats. The shuffled background has more chance matches (8.8%) because the CTCF motif is GC-rich, so it gives the smaller, more conservative enrichment: about 9-fold against shuffled, 15-fold against flanks. (c) \(2 \times 186 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.037\) expected matches per window (186 positions for a 15-bp motif), so about 4% of uniform random windows; GC-rich windows have more, as both backgrounds show.
R5. Q1 weakest 61.5%, Q2 74.1%, Q3 86.2%, Q4 strongest 92.1% (median signalValue 35, 81, 160, 256). Peaks without a match: CTCF bound indirectly or through a weaker or different variant of its motif (JASPAR has other CTCF matrices, e.g. with an upstream module); false-positive peaks among the weakest; or a motif just outside the 200-bp window.
R6. (a) 79.8% of the 5000 peaks have a match within ±250 bp; 94.3% of best matches are within 50 bp of the summit. (b) A 15-bp match starting at position start has its centre at start + 7; the summit lies between positions 250 and 251 of the 500-bp window (centre 250.5). (c) 2054 on + and 1936 on −: about half each, as expected because CTCF sites occur in both orientations in the genome. The strand still matters biologically: it gives the orientation of each site, which decides which loops can form (B5).
R7. (a) 8583 matches; 8018 expected by chance at a uniform background. (b) 369 (4.3%) in a CTCF peak. Of matches in ATAC peaks, 38.8% are bound; outside, 2.2%. (c) 320 of 405 chr21 CTCF peaks (79%) contain a match. “Four in five CTCF peaks contain a CTCF motif, but only one in twenty-three motif matches is bound: the motif is close to necessary but far from sufficient for binding.” (Necessary only approximately: a fifth of peaks lack a match at this threshold.)
R8. The count matrix, the weights and the scores agree with B1 and B2: 8.39, 6.17, 5.22, −4.75, −1.58, and 8.39 for the reverse complement of TTATCT.

Where this leads

The ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq blocks produce the peaks that we scanned here, from raw reads.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting turns R4 into a proper test over hundreds of matrices (HOMER, MEME-SEA, chromVAR) and looks for TF footprints in ATAC data.

Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Stormo 2000, Bioinformatics. DNA binding sites: representation and discovery. PWMs, log-odds scores and information content, from the person who introduced them.
Schneider & Stephens 1990, Nucleic Acids Res. Sequence logos: a new way to display consensus sequences. The logo.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
About this lecture
You can align reads and make a coverage track (From reads to coverage). Whether that track means anything depends on decisions made before the first read was sequenced, and on a handful of numbers you should check before the first peak is called.

Design: biological replicates, controls (input, IgG, none), antibodies, spike-ins for global changes, batches.
QC metrics shared by ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag: library complexity, duplicates, FRiP, fingerprint, strand cross-correlation, replicate concordance, and for ATAC TSS enrichment and fragment sizes.
What each metric looks like on good and bad data, and the ENCODE thresholds.
Real numbers from the course data: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq with its input, and ATAC-seq in two replicates, on chr21.
How to read a methods section, and the red flags in published data.


This unit sits between the alignment unit and the assay blocks. Everything here is reused in the ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, CUT&Tag and differential-analysis units, so it is taught once. The tone is practical: what can go wrong in an epigenomic experiment, how you would see it in the data, and how you decide whether to trust a dataset, your own or a published one. Students know design matrices and normalisation from RNA-seq; we reuse that, and spend the time on what is specific to enrichment assays: controls, enrichment metrics, and global changes. All real-data figures are made with make-design-figs.R from the same reads the students align in the exercise.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: What makes an epigenomic experiment interpretable?
text:
What makes an epigenomic experiment interpretable?


Each step from cells to peaks can fail silently: the pipeline still produces a BAM, a bigWig and a peak list.
Each failure leaves a fingerprint in the data that a QC metric is designed to catch.
Two failures cannot be repaired afterwards: no replicates and no control. Plan them before the experiment.


Walk along the chain. Samples: if conditions and batches are confounded, no analysis can separate them. Chromatin: sonication shears open chromatin more easily, so even DNA with no antibody shows “peaks” at promoters; amplified regions give more reads everywhere. IP: an antibody that binds weakly or cross-reacts gives a low signal-to-noise ratio. Library: if the IP returned very little DNA, PCR copies a few molecules many times. Sequencing: too few reads and weak sites are missed. Analysis: standard normalisation assumes the total amount of the mark is the same in all samples. The rest of the lecture goes through these in order: design first (the part you cannot fix), then the metrics. Point out that a pipeline never fails on bad data; it produces confident-looking output either way.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Replicates: biological, technical and pseudo


Biological replicates (independent cultures, animals, patients) are what a claim about biology needs. ENCODE requires at least two; for differential analysis use at least three per condition, as in RNA-seq.
Technical replicates only measure the noise of the protocol. Pseudoreplicates (random halves of one library) only measure counting noise: a stand-in when there is a single sample, never evidence of reproducibility.


The same logic as in RNA-seq: the variance you need to estimate for a test is the variance between independent biological units. Two growths of a cell line on different days are the minimum for a cell line; for tissues, different animals or donors. Technical replicates (the same chromatin split into two IPs) are useful when developing a protocol, but adding them does not increase n. ENCODE’s consortium decision (Landt et al. 2012) was two biological replicates per ChIP-seq experiment; more replicates did not add many sites. For differential binding or accessibility, power depends on replicates far more than on depth: three per condition is the usual minimum, more when the effect is subtle or the samples are primary tissue. Pseudoreplicates: ENCODE’s pipeline splits the pooled reads at random into two halves and calls peaks on each half; this tells you whether a peak is supported by enough reads, not whether the experiment would replicate. Students should be suspicious of “n = 1, peaks called on pseudoreplicates” in a paper that makes biological claims.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Why a control? The background is not flat
text:
Why a control? The background is not flat


Reads pile up where nothing is bound: open chromatin shears more easily, amplified regions have more DNA, repeats get no unique reads, GC-rich fragments amplify better.
An input library (sheared chromatin, no antibody) shows exactly these biases. Peak callers compare the ChIP to it locally, not to a flat average.


The schematic has the four common causes. Open promoters: sonication preferentially fragments open, nucleosome-free DNA, so input DNA has small bumps at active promoters, which a naive caller would report as peaks of any factor. Copy number: cancer cell lines (K562, HeLa, HepG2) have many amplifications; a 4-copy region gives twice as many reads in both ChIP and input; without the input every amplified region looks enriched. Mappability: repeats get no uniquely mapped reads in either; these gaps and the high-signal artefact regions are why we also use the blacklist. MACS uses the input to estimate a local background rate lambda in 1 kb, 5 kb and 10 kb windows around each candidate peak, which is how the input actually enters the statistics; that is covered in Peak calling. Match the control to the ChIP: same cells, same crosslinking and sonication, similar read length, sequenced at least as deep.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Input, IgG or no control


Input is the standard for ChIP-seq (ENCODE): cheap, complex, captures shearing, copy number and mappability.
IgG mimics the IP but recovers little DNA, so the library is often small and noisy.
ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag have no input: the background is estimated from the sample itself. Comparing conditions and replicates carries the weight instead.


Landt et al. describe both kinds of control and note that an IgG control must yield a library of complexity comparable to the ChIP, which often fails because a non-specific antibody pulls down very little DNA. In practice ENCODE uses inputs. For ATAC-seq there is no sensible control: naked genomic DNA tagmented by Tn5 would model Tn5’s sequence preference but nobody does it routinely. MACS then uses the genome-wide background of the sample, and a local lambda from the sample itself. CUT&Tag sometimes uses an IgG control, and its background is so low that the main concern is different (covered in CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag). Students should know that “no control” is normal for ATAC and a red flag for ChIP.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input on chr21
text:
Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input on chr21


Left: reads per million in 1 kb bins over 400 kb. The ChIP has sharp peaks at the ENCODE peaks; the input is low, with small bumps at some of the same sites.
Right: 100 kb bins over all of chr21. ChIP and input rise and fall together (correlation 0.87): no reads on the unassembled short arm and the centromere, more reads in gene-dense regions. That is background, and the input measures it.


Real data from the exercise: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, 36 bp single-end reads from 2008) and its input (ENCSR000EYX), aligned to chr21, filtered, deduplicated and blacklist-filtered; about 200 000 ChIP and 108 000 input reads on chr21. Left: CTCF peaks are tall and narrow, and most bins between peaks have a few reads in both tracks. Look for the small input bumps under some CTCF peaks: input DNA is enriched at open chromatin, and many CTCF sites are open. Right: at 100 kb scale the ChIP looks almost like the input: 93 of 468 bins have no input reads (the first ~5 Mb of chr21 is the unassembled acrocentric short arm; the gap at 11-13 Mb is the centromere), and the gene-rich distal end of chr21 has more reads in both. This is the background that the peak caller must not report: it compares the ChIP with the local input level, not with the chromosome average. GM12878 has a near-normal karyotype; in a cancer cell line you would also see copy-number steps in both tracks.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Antibodies decide what you measure


A ChIP is only as specific as its antibody. Check: one main band on an immunoblot (ENCODE: at least 50% of the signal), and a second line of evidence: IP–mass spectrometry, a second antibody or an epitope tag, the expected motif, or loss of signal in a knockout or knockdown.
Histone-mark antibodies can cross-react with neighbouring states (H3K4me2 vs me3) or be blocked by a modification next door. Lots differ: record the lot number.


Landt et al. give the ENCODE antibody standards: a primary characterisation (immunoblot or immunofluorescence; on the blot the main band should hold at least 50% of the signal, ideally at the expected size) and one of several secondary characterisations: knockdown, a second antibody against another epitope or a complex member, an epitope-tagged construct, IP followed by mass spectrometry, or motif enrichment in the peaks. Histone antibodies are tested on peptide arrays or with modified nucleosomes. Egelhofer et al. 2011 tested more than 200 histone-modification antibodies and found that about a quarter failed specificity tests. The knockout control is the strongest: if the signal persists in cells lacking the protein, it was not the protein. When reading a paper, look for catalogue and lot numbers and some evidence of validation.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Normalisation assumes the total does not change
text:
Normalisation assumes the total does not change


Standard normalisation (CPM, RPKM, DESeq2 size factors) makes every library the same total. Fine when most sites do not change.
An EZH2 inhibitor removes most H3K27me3 everywhere. The IP still returns DNA, the library is sequenced to the same depth, and after normalisation the tracks look unchanged.
To see a global change you need an external reference added in a known amount: a spike-in.


This is the same assumption students met with DESeq2 size factors: the median-of-ratios method assumes most genes do not change. In RNA-seq this fails for global transcriptional amplification (e.g. MYC); in epigenomics it fails whenever a drug or mutation changes the total amount of a mark: EZH2 inhibitors or EZH2 mutations (H3K27me3), the oncohistone H3K27M (loss of H3K27me3), BET inhibitors and HDAC inhibitors (acetylation), DOT1L inhibitors (H3K79me2). The IP always returns some DNA, library preparation adds PCR cycles until there is enough, and the sequencer gives each sample its 20 million reads. Information about the absolute amount is lost at every one of these steps. Normalising by read depth then redistributes the remaining signal, so a 4-fold global drop looks like no change, or even a gain at the strongest sites.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Spike-in normalisation (ChIP-Rx)


Add the same amount of foreign chromatin (e.g. Drosophila cells, or synthetic modified nucleosomes) to each sample before the IP. The antibody pulls down the fly mark too.
The fly reads measure how efficient the IP was in each sample. Scale each human signal by \alpha = 1/N_\text{fly} (fly reads, in millions).


Orlando et al. 2014 (ChIP-Rx, “reference exogenous genome”) added a fixed number of Drosophila S2 cells to a fixed number of human cells, did the ChIP with antibodies that recognise the conserved mark in both species, and aligned reads to a combined genome. Their normalisation factor was alpha = 1 / (million reads mapped to the fly genome). They showed that a DOT1L inhibitor reduced H3K79me2 globally, which standard normalisation hid. Variants: synthetic barcoded nucleosomes (SNAP-ChIP/ICeChIP), E. coli carry-over DNA in CUT&RUN, and spike-ins for ATAC-seq. Spike-ins add their own uncertainty: the ratio of cells must be accurate (count cells, check the fly fraction in the input), and the spike-in must be added before any step that loses material. When the total does not change, spike-in normalisation only adds noise.

Go through the arithmetic slowly; a version of this is in the exercise and is a natural exam question. Both libraries were sequenced to 20 M reads. In the control, fly reads are 1 M (5%); in the treated sample 4 M (20%): the fly chromatin is the same amount, so a larger share means less human material was pulled down. CPM: 1900 / 19 = 100 and 1600 / 16 = 100, identical. Spike-in: alpha is 1/1 = 1 and 1/4 = 0.25, giving 1900 and 400, a 4.75-fold drop. Note that the CPM values are identical because the domain is a fixed fraction of the human reads; in real data the strongest domains often even appear to gain. In a full analysis the factor is also corrected for the fly fraction in each input (to account for small differences in how many cells were mixed), and DESeq2 can be given these factors as size factors instead of estimating its own.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Batches and confounding


Day of processing, antibody lot, sequencing run and operator all change the data. If they line up with the condition, the effect is not identifiable: no software can fix it.
Spread conditions across batches, record the batches, and put them in the model, ~ batch + condition, exactly as in DESeq2.


Students know design matrices from RNA-seq; the point here is that in epigenomic experiments batch effects are often larger than in RNA-seq, because the IP step adds variability: antibody lot, crosslinking time, sonication efficiency and IP efficiency all vary between days. In the confounded design, the batch2 column equals the treated column in every row, so the design matrix is rank-deficient and DESeq2 refuses to fit it; worse, if you drop batch from the model, it fits happily and attributes the day-2 effect to the treatment. Balanced design: process one control and one treated sample together each day. Also: randomise the order of samples on the sequencer, and use the same antibody lot for a whole study. A PCA of the samples (as in RNA-seq) shows whether samples cluster by batch.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Sequencing depth and saturation


Peaks called by MACS3 on random subsamples of the chr21 reads. CTCF saturates: about 500 peaks from half of the reads on. ATAC does not: weaker accessible sites keep appearing with depth.
ENCODE: 20 M usable fragments per replicate for TFs and narrow marks, 45 M for broad marks, 25 M non-duplicate, non-mitochondrial fragments for ATAC-seq. Depth cannot rescue a poor library: once every unique molecule has been read, more sequencing only adds duplicates.


How to read the figure: each point is a MACS3 run (q < 0.01) on a subsample, for CTCF with the input as control. The chr21 numbers correspond to roughly 70 times as many reads genome-wide: 200 000 CTCF reads on chr21 is about 15 M usable reads in total. CTCF is a strong factor with a long motif and high-occupancy sites, so most of its sites are found with a few million reads; the curve flattens at about 100 000 chr21 reads (some 7 M genome-wide). ATAC-seq measures a continuum of accessibility, and the number of peaks keeps growing; the same is true for weak TFs and for broad marks, where depth decides how much of each domain is called. Landt et al. 2012 (Fig. 3) showed the same for ENCODE TFs: peak numbers keep rising with depth for many factors, with the new peaks increasingly weak. The practical rules: plan depth from the standards, check saturation on your own data by subsampling, and remember that complexity, not depth, limits a poor library (next slide).

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Library complexity: NRF, PBC1, PBC2


Count reads by their start position and strand. A complex library has almost every read at its own position; a bottlenecked library (little starting DNA, too many PCR cycles) has the same molecules many times.
NRF = distinct positions / reads. PBC1 = positions with exactly one read / distinct positions. PBC2 = positions with one read / positions with two.


Definitions from the ENCODE data standards. They are computed on the filtered reads before duplicate removal. NRF is the fraction of reads that are not redundant. PBC1 asks: of the positions with any read, what fraction have exactly one? In a complex library sequenced to moderate depth almost all positions have one read, PBC1 close to 1. PBC2 is the ratio of singletons to doubletons; for a Poisson sample of a huge library, few positions get two reads and PBC2 is large; when a library is exhausted, positions with two, three, many reads become common and PBC2 drops towards 1. ENCODE ChIP-seq thresholds: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 10 is ideal; NRF < 0.5, PBC1 < 0.5 or PBC2 < 1 is a severe bottleneck. ATAC-seq preferred values: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 3. Note that all three depend on depth: the same library sequenced deeper looks less complex, and at very strong peaks, true independent fragments can share a start position (more so for single-end reads and narrow TF sites).

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP)


FRiP = reads overlapping peaks / all mapped (filtered) reads. A direct measure of how much of the library is signal.
Guides: ENCODE inspects TF ChIP with FRiP below 1%; for ATAC-seq FRiP should be > 0.3 (0.2 acceptable). Broad histone marks and good CUT&Tag reach much higher values.
FRiP depends on the peak caller and the number of peaks: compare samples only with the same peak set or the same caller and settings.


Landt et al. 2012: most of 1052 ENCODE TF datasets had FRiP of 1% or more with MACS default peaks, and ENCODE scrutinises experiments below 1%. That threshold suits factors with thousands to tens of thousands of sites; a factor with a few hundred sites can be a perfect experiment at 0.5%. ATAC-seq standard: FRiP > 0.3, values > 0.2 acceptable. FRiP correlates with the number of peaks, which is partly circular: a weak experiment gives fewer peaks and therefore lower FRiP. Computing FRiP against a fixed reference peak set (here the ENCODE peaks) makes samples comparable. For paired-end data, count fragments or reads, but say which.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Real data: FRiP


CTCF ChIP: 22% of reads in the 405 ENCODE CTCF peaks on chr21, which cover only 0.19% of the chromosome. ATAC: 59% and 50% of reads in ATAC peaks (1.5% of chr21). All far above the guidelines.
The input has 1.6% of its reads in CTCF peaks and 8.3% in ATAC peaks: 5–8 times more than uniform. Input DNA is enriched in open chromatin.


FRiP computed against ENCODE’s IDR-thresholded peaks with samtools view -c -L (exercise C3). The red marks show the fraction of chr21 covered by the peaks: what the FRiP would be if reads were spread uniformly. CTCF is a strong, high-quality ChIP: 22% is high for a TF (many good TF datasets are in the 1-10% range). ENCODE reports FRiPs of 46-60% for these ATAC replicates genome-wide, depending on the peak set, consistent with our chr21 values. The input result is the most instructive number on the slide: an input is supposed to be background, yet 8% of its reads fall into 1.5% of the chromosome where ATAC finds open chromatin. That is the sonication bias of slide “Why a control”: open chromatin shears more easily and is better represented in sequencing libraries. It is exactly why a ChIP peak at an open promoter is only meaningful when compared with the input.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
The fingerprint plot


Divide the genome into bins, count reads, sort the bins from fewest to most reads, and plot the cumulative fraction of reads (deepTools plotFingerprint, after the CHANCE method).
A uniform library (input) follows the diagonal. A good ChIP stays low and then rises steeply: a small fraction of the genome holds a large fraction of the reads.


The fingerprint plot is from Diaz et al. 2012 (CHANCE) and is implemented in deepTools plotFingerprint. It needs no peak calling, which makes it useful as a first check and for comparing ChIP with input directly. Read the plot from the right end: if the top 10% of bins (x from 0.9 to 1) hold 60% of the reads, the curve is at 0.4 at x = 0.9. Things to look for: the input should be close to the diagonal; a curve that rises steeply at the very end only (very few bins) can mean amplification artefacts or a few very high regions (blacklisted regions); a ChIP that looks like its input has failed. Broad marks (H3K27me3, H3K36me3) give a gentler bend than TFs, because the signal is spread over a larger part of the genome. With low coverage, many bins are empty, so the curve starts flat at zero for every sample: use bins large enough to have reads in most of them.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Real data: fingerprint of CTCF ChIP and input
text:
Real data: fingerprint of CTCF ChIP and input





The input is closest to the diagonal; CTCF bends further; ATAC has the sharpest elbow.
Top 1% of 1 kb bins hold 8% of input reads, 30% of CTCF reads and 52% of ATAC reads.
All curves are flat up to 0.3–0.4: those bins have no reads at all (short arm, centromere, gaps). Only the rest of the chromosome is informative.



Computed from read 5’ ends in 1 kb bins over chr21 (make-design-figs.R); in the exercise students make the same plot with deepTools plotFingerprint. The input is not on the diagonal: partly because about 30% of the bins cannot receive reads at all, partly the open-chromatin bias from the FRiP slide. Compare like with like: the useful comparison is ChIP against its own input, made at the same bin size. The CTCF curve departs from the input mainly in the last 5% of bins: CTCF binds at a few hundred sites on chr21, each covering less than 1 kb. The ATAC curve bends earlier and harder: accessible sites are more numerous and the signal-to-noise of this ATAC library is excellent (FRiP 50-60%). deepTools also reports quality metrics derived from the curve, such as the elbow point and the Jensen-Shannon distance to the input (CHANCE, Diaz et al. 2012).

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Strand cross-correlation


Single-end reads come from the 5’ ends of fragments: around a bound site, + strand reads pile up to the left, − strand reads to the right, one fragment length apart.
Shift the − strand coverage by k bp and correlate it with the + strand: the correlation peaks at the fragment length. A second peak at the read length (“phantom”) comes from mappability, not from binding.
NSC = CC(fragment) / min(CC); RSC = (CC(fragment) − min) / (CC(read) − min). ENCODE repeats experiments with NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8.


Kharchenko, Tolstorukov and Park 2008 introduced strand cross-correlation (in their SPP package) as a way to estimate the fragment length and the enrichment from single-end data without a peak caller. The phantom peak at the read length appears in every library, including the input: a position that is mappable on the + strand at x is also mappable on the − strand at x + read length, so the coverage of the two strands correlates at that shift for purely technical reasons. Good TF ChIP: the fragment peak is much higher than the phantom peak, RSC > 1. Input or failed ChIP: the phantom dominates, RSC well below 1. NSC compares the fragment peak with the background (the minimum of the curve), and is just above 1 for a weak experiment. Thresholds from Landt et al.: NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8 lead ENCODE to repeat the experiment. Broad histone marks have flat profiles even when they are good, so these metrics are mostly for TFs and narrow marks. With paired-end data the fragment length is measured directly from the pairs.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Real data: CTCF cross-correlation


CTCF: a clear fragment-length peak at 93 bp (ENCODE: 90–95 bp). The read-length position (36 bp, dotted) lies on its rising flank. RSC 1.65 (ENCODE 1.69–1.86): passes.
Input: low, noisy, no fragment peak (RSC ≈ 1).
Our NSC (47) is far above ENCODE’s (4.9–10): NSC depends on how the background minimum is estimated. Compare it only between datasets computed the same way.


Computed in R in the exercise (R1): count the 5’ ends of + and - strand reads at every base of chr21, and correlate the + strand counts at x with the - strand counts at x + k for k from 0 to 1000. The y axes differ by a factor of 60. The CTCF fragments in this 2008 library are short (about 93 bp), so the phantom peak at the read length is not a separate peak but a shoulder on the fragment peak. RSC uses differences above the minimum and agrees well with ENCODE’s value from phantompeakqualtools on the whole genome. NSC divides by the minimum itself; our minimum is much lower than in ENCODE’s genome-wide computation (per-base vs binned counts, which chromosomes and repeats are included), so NSC comes out much higher. The lesson for reading papers: NSC and RSC from the standard tool (phantompeakqualtools, also in the ENCODE and nf-core pipelines) are comparable with the ENCODE thresholds; numbers from home-made implementations are not necessarily.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Replicate concordance


Count reads in bins (or peaks) in each replicate and correlate (deepTools multiBamSummary, plotCorrelation). ATAC rep1 vs rep2: r = 0.94 (log counts) in 10 kb bins, 0.99 in ENCODE peaks.
Smaller bins are noisier: 0.81 in 1 kb bins. Different assays correlate less: ATAC vs CTCF 0.65.
A high correlation is necessary, not sufficient: it is driven by shared background and the strongest regions.


Real data: the two ATAC replicates (ENCSR095QNB, about 480 000 reads each on chr21 after filtering). Bin-level correlation is the quickest check for a swapped or failed sample; plotCorrelation produces a heatmap of all pairwise correlations, and with many samples a PCA does the same job (as in RNA-seq). Use Spearman or Pearson on log counts: raw-count Pearson is dominated by the few largest bins. Why not sufficient: both replicates share the same mappability, GC and open-chromatin background, which alone produces correlation (ChIP and input correlate 0.87 at 100 kb, slide “Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input”). The question “are the same peaks found, and in the same order?” is what IDR answers (next slide). For differential analysis the relevant quantity is the dispersion between replicates in counts per peak, which DESeq2 estimates.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: IDR: are the same peaks found in both replicates?
text:
IDR: are the same peaks found in both replicates?


The irreproducible discovery rate (Li et al. 2011) compares the ranks of matched peaks in two replicates and keeps the peaks that are consistently strong. ENCODE’s TF and ATAC peak sets (including the ones we use) are IDR-thresholded.
ENCODE passes an experiment if the rescue and self-consistency ratios (true replicates vs pseudoreplicates) are both < 2. Details in Peak calling.


IDR is analogous to FDR, but for reproducibility rather than significance. The key idea: peaks that are real tend to be ranked high in both replicates, while noise peaks have uncorrelated ranks. The method fits a copula mixture model with a reproducible and an irreproducible component, and gives each peak pair a local IDR. The input to IDR must be a relaxed peak list (e.g. 300 000 peaks with a p-value threshold of 0.01), so that the noise component is represented; a stringent threshold before IDR breaks the method. The ratios: the self-consistency ratio compares the number of IDR peaks from the two pseudoreplicates of each replicate; the rescue ratio compares IDR on true replicates with IDR on pooled pseudoreplicates. Ratios above 2 mean the replicates disagree more than random halves of the data do. Students run IDR in Peak calling; here the concept is enough.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: ATAC-seq: fragment sizes and TSS enrichment
text:
ATAC-seq: fragment sizes and TSS enrichment


Fragment sizes: a nucleosome-free peak below 100 bp, then mono- and di-nucleosome humps (~200 and ~400 bp). ENCODE requires the NFR and mono-nucleosome peaks to be present.
TSS enrichment: Tn5 insertions at TSSs relative to 2 kb away. Here 33 (rep1) and 24 (rep2); ENCODE: > 7 ideal (GRCh38, RefSeq TSSs), and reports 28–30 and 22–23 for these replicates.
Also check the mitochondrial fraction (here 14% and 10% genome-wide) and FRiP. Details in ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder.


These two plots are the ATAC-specific QC; they replace the cross-correlation, which makes little sense for paired-end data where the fragment length is measured directly. The fragment-size ladder is the nucleosome signature: Tn5 cuts in linker DNA, so fragments that span one, two or three nucleosomes are enriched; a library with no ladder suggests over-digested or naked DNA. The TSS enrichment counts Tn5 insertion sites (read ends shifted +4/-5) in a window around all protein-coding TSSs on chr21 (602 TSSs), divided by the level 1900-2000 bp away, smoothed over 51 bp; the maximum is the score. It is the most robust single signal-to-noise metric for ATAC-seq: active promoters are open in almost every cell type. ENCODE’s thresholds depend on the TSS annotation (RefSeq vs GENCODE) and on the exact method, so compare like with like; our chr21 values are close to ENCODE’s genome-wide values for the same replicates. Rep2 has a lower TSS enrichment and FRiP than rep1 but higher complexity: no single metric decides.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Reading a MultiQC report


MultiQC collects the logs of fastp, Bowtie2, samtools, Picard, deepTools, MACS and many more into one HTML report, one row per sample. nf-core pipelines produce one at the end of every run.
Read it across samples: the bad sample is the one that differs from its replicates. Then open the plots behind the number (duplication curve, fingerprint, cross-correlation).


Ewels et al. 2016. The general statistics table is a summary; the value is in comparing samples side by side. In the schematic, rep3 has fewer reads, a lower alignment rate, 63% duplicates, NRF 0.37, FRiP of 0.04 and RSC 0.6, and its fingerprint looks halfway to an input: the IP worked poorly and the library was amplified from very little DNA. A defensible decision: exclude it and say so, or redo it. What is not defensible: keeping it in a differential analysis without comment, or dropping it silently. Show students an nf-core/chipseq or nf-core/atacseq MultiQC report in the browser if time allows; the course pipelines produce one.

From the ENCODE data standards pages (ChIP-seq TF, histone, ATAC-seq; current at the time of writing) and Landt et al. 2012. Thresholds are guides for flagging, not laws: a factor with few sites can have a low FRiP and be fine, broad marks have flat cross-correlation curves, and complexity metrics depend on depth. ENCODE itself marks data with coloured audit flags rather than rejecting them outright. The value of the table is as a reference point when you look at your own numbers or at a paper’s supplementary QC table. TSS enrichment thresholds depend on the TSS annotation and the exact method, so compare like with like.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Red flags in published data


No input for a ChIP-seq, or the same input reused for unrelated cell types. n = 1 with claims about differences between conditions.
FRiP of 1–2% for a histone mark, a fingerprint that looks like the input, duplication above 50% with no comment, fewer reads than the standard.
A global change (inhibitor, knockout of a writer) normalised by read depth. Conditions processed on different days. No antibody catalogue or lot number.


A checklist for reading methods sections and supplementary tables, and the core of the “judge the design” exam questions. Each flag is not automatically fatal, but each should be explained. Where to find the information: GEO entries often list the controls and the number of replicates; supplementary tables sometimes give FRiP and duplication. If the raw data are public, you can compute all of these metrics yourself in an hour, which is what the exercise does for an ENCODE dataset. Good practice to point out: ENCODE and the nf-core pipelines report all of these metrics by default, and the ENCODE portal flags experiments that fail them.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Summary

input for ChIP (shearing, copy number, mappability); IgG often too little DNA; ATAC has none

Students should leave able to compute NRF, PBC1, PBC2 and FRiP from counts, read a fingerprint and a cross-correlation plot, explain what an input corrects and why spike-ins are needed for global changes, and critique a study design. Next: the ATAC-seq block, where TSS enrichment and fragment sizes are covered properly, and the ChIP-seq block, where the input enters the peak caller.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia. Where most of the metrics and thresholds in this lecture come from.
Kharchenko, Tolstorukov & Park 2008, Nat Biotechnol. Design and analysis of ChIP-seq experiments for DNA-binding proteins. Strand cross-correlation and the SPP peak caller.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments. The IDR method.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome. ChIP-Rx spike-in normalisation.
Diaz, Park, Lim & Song 2012, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. Normalization, bias correction, and peak calling for ChIP-seq. CHANCE and the fingerprint plot.
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin & Käller 2016, Bioinformatics. MultiQC: summarize analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report.

title: Quiz: epigenetic inheritance
text:
Short questions on inheritance across generations and how to judge the claims. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is the difference between an intergenerational and a transgenerational effect? Give an example of each.






Answer





Intergenerational: the offspring differs because it was itself exposed, as an embryo or as a germ cell (e.g. F1 offspring of a mother who was undernourished in pregnancy, or of a father on a high-fat diet). Transgenerational: an effect in a generation that was never exposed (e.g. F3 after a pregnancy exposure), which requires information to pass through the germline. Examples of the second are robust in plants (epiRILs, paramutation) and worms (small-RNA inheritance).




Q2. A pregnant rat is exposed to a chemical. Which generation is the first that was never exposed, and why? What if the father had been exposed instead?






Answer





F3. The F1 is exposed as an embryo, and the F1’s primordial germ cells, which will form F2, are already present in that embryo. For a paternal exposure the sperm (F1) are exposed, so F2 is the first unexposed generation.




Q3. Name the two waves of DNA methylation reprogramming in mammals. Which of them do imprints survive?






Answer





Wave 1 after fertilisation (preimplantation embryo) and wave 2 in primordial germ cells. Imprinting control regions are protected in wave 1 (ZFP57/TRIM28) and erased in wave 2, then re-established according to the sex of the embryo.




Q4. Give two reasons why stable epialleles are common in plants but rare in mammals.






Hint





Think about when the germline forms, and about how a silent state can be re-made each generation.









Answer





Plants form gametes late, from somatic shoot cells, and do not erase methylation in the gametes (MET1 keeps CG methylation through meiosis); mammals set aside the germline early and erase it. Plants also restore methylation with RNA-directed DNA methylation and amplify small RNAs with RNA-dependent RNA polymerases, which mammals lack.




Q5. What is paramutation? Give the example and one requirement.






Answer





A heritable change in one allele caused by its interaction with the other allele in the same plant. At maize b1, the weak B’ allele converts the strong B-I allele into a new B’, which stays weak and converts others in turn. It needs a tandem-repeat array about 100 kb upstream of b1 and an RNA-directed silencing pathway. The canonical B-I and B’ alleles have seven repeats; seven is not a strict minimum (five-repeat alleles can be fully paramutagenic and three-repeat alleles less effective). See the repeat-array experiments.




Q6. People conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter had 0.488 vs 0.515 methylation at the IGF2 DMR compared with their same-sex siblings. What does this show, and what does it not show?






Answer





It shows that prenatal (periconceptional) exposure is associated with a lasting, small (5% relative, 0.027 absolute) methylation difference in blood decades later, with genetics and family environment partly controlled by the sibling design. It does not show inheritance (the exposed were embryos: an F1 effect), causation of disease, or effects in other tissues.




Q7. An array study finds 50 CpGs with p < 0.05 in both F1 and F3 out of 20 000 tested, and calls them “persistent epimutations”. Is this convincing?






Answer





No. With no true effects, \(20\,000 \times 0.05^2 = 50\) CpGs are expected to be significant in both generations by chance. The overlap must be compared with this expectation, the tests corrected for multiple testing, and the result replicated.




Q8. A mouse study measures 40 pups from 4 exposed and 4 control mothers and treats the pups as independent. What is the problem, and how should it be analysed?






Answer





Pups of one litter share mother, uterus, milk and cage, so they are not independent: the real n is 4 per group. Pup-level tests have an inflated false-positive rate when litters differ (about 33% in the lecture’s simulation). Analyse litter means or use a mixed model with litter as a random effect, and use more litters.




Q9. Sperm RNA from male mice on a high-fat diet, injected into normal zygotes, causes metabolic changes in the offspring. Which alternative explanations does this design rule out, and what does it leave open?






Answer





It rules out the father’s behaviour, seminal fluid, shared environment and maternal effects of the exposed father, and points to RNA as a sufficient carrier. It leaves open whether the effect is physiological (the injected amount differs from one sperm’s payload), whether it reproduces across labs, and whether it lasts beyond F1: it is an intergenerational result.




Q10. List four design features that would make a claim of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals convincing.






Answer





Any four of: test the first unexposed generation (F3 after pregnancy, F2 after paternal exposure); isogenic animals; IVF/embryo transfer and cross-fostering; litters as the unit, many litters; a pre-specified outcome with multiple-testing correction; an identified carrier shown to be sufficient and necessary; independent replication.
