title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
Background
The F0–F3 rule. An exposure of a pregnant F0 female reaches the F1 embryo and the F1’s germ cells (the future F2). The first generation that was never exposed is F3. For an exposure of a father, or of a female before pregnancy, it is F2.
Expected false positives. With \(m\) independent tests at level \(\alpha\) and no true effects, about \(m\alpha\) tests are significant, and the probability of at least one is \(1 - (1-\alpha)^m\). The probability that one null test is significant in each of \(k\) independent experiments is \(\alpha^k\).
Power and “too much success”. If each of \(n\) independent experiments has power \(p\) to detect a true effect, the probability that all \(n\) are significant is \(p^n\).
Unit of replication. In animal studies the exposure is given to F0 parents, so litters (or F0 animals) are the independent units, not the pups.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
Data
No download is needed. The R part simulates study designs with known truth, so you can see what the analysis does when there is no inheritance. The numbers in the By-hand questions come from published papers (cited in the lecture).

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
By hand
B1. Which generation? For each design, say which generation is the first that was never exposed, and whether the reported result is intergenerational or transgenerational.

Pregnant mice are given a high-fat diet; F2 offspring have higher blood glucose.
Male mice are stressed before mating; F1 offspring are more anxious.
Male mice are stressed before mating; F2 offspring are more anxious.
Pregnant rats are exposed to a fungicide; F3 males have lower sperm counts.
Women who were in utero during a famine have children (F2) with higher adiposity.

B2. The Dutch Hunger Winter study. Heijmans et al. (2008) compared 60 people conceived during the 1944–45 famine with their same-sex siblings. Mean IGF2 DMR methylation was 0.488 (exposed) and 0.515 (siblings).

Compute the absolute and the relative difference.
The difference was 0.48 SD of the controls. What is the SD of methylation among the siblings?
What does the sibling design control for? Name two things it does not control for.
Is this evidence of transgenerational inheritance? Explain with the F0–F3 rule.

B3. Överkalix by numbers. A study of 300 grandchildren tests the food supply of each of the 4 grandparents, against 3 causes of death, separately in grandsons, granddaughters and both.

How many tests is that? How many p < 0.05 would you expect if nothing is true?
If the tests were independent, what is the probability of at least one p < 0.05?
A replication in a 40× larger cohort reports, for the one pre-specified finding, HR = 1.55 (95% CI 1.02–2.35). What does the confidence interval tell you? Why is this replication more informative than the original finding, even though its p-value is not small?

B4. Overlap across generations. An array study tests 450 000 CpGs in F1, F2 and F3 (exposed vs control), with no true effects, and calls a CpG “differentially methylated” at p < 0.01.

How many DM CpGs do you expect per generation?
How many in both F1 and F2? In all three?
The paper reports “43 CpGs that remain differentially methylated from F1 to F3”. Is that more than chance? What should the authors have done?

B5. Litters. A study exposes 3 pregnant mice and keeps 3 controls. Each has a litter of 8; all 48 pups are phenotyped, and the exposed pups differ with p = 0.003 (t-test, 24 vs 24).

What is the true number of independent units per group?
Why can the pup-level p-value be misleading? Give a biological reason why litters differ.
Propose a better analysis and a better design.

B6. Too much success. A paper reports 8 independent experiments, each with about 10 animals per group, all significant. Assume each experiment had power 0.6.

What is the probability that all 8 are significant?
With power 0.5? What would you conclude?

B7. Epimutations vs mutations. Arabidopsis has about \(1.35 \times 10^8\) bp and, for this question, assume \(2 \times 10^6\) methylated CG sites per haploid genome. Use \(7 \times 10^{-9}\) mutations per bp per generation and \(10^{-4}\) epimutations per CG site per generation.

How many new mutations and how many new CG epimutations do you expect per haploid genome per generation?
Does a rate of 10⁻⁴ per site per generation imply that a particular epiallele disappears within a few generations? If that were its constant reversion probability, what would the mean waiting time be? Why are epimutations a source of heritable variation?

B8. Read the reprogramming figure. Look at the figure Two waves of reprogramming in mammals in the lecture.

At which two stages is methylation lowest?
Imprints survive one wave and not the other. Which, and why does that make sense for their function?
A methylation mark set by a father’s diet in his sperm: what must happen for it to reach his grandchildren?

B9. Judge three claims. For each, state what was shown, name the most important alternative route (genetics, shared environment, behaviour, direct exposure, chance), and propose one design change.

“Grandchildren of men who smoked before puberty are heavier: smoking is inherited epigenetically” (a cohort study of 166 fathers, many outcomes).
“Offspring of male mice fed a high-fat diet have impaired glucose tolerance; injecting sperm RNA from these males into normal zygotes reproduces it.”
“Mothers who licked their pups more had pups with lower methylation at the glucocorticoid-receptor promoter; this methylation is inherited.”

B10. Plants vs mammals. Give two biological reasons why transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is common in plants and rare in mammals.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
In R
Only base R and ggplot2 (optional) are needed. Every simulation is seeded, so you get the numbers in the solutions.

R1 — Genome-wide tests across three generations
set.seed(1)
n_cpg <- 20000; n <- 8                     # 20 000 CpGs, 8 exposed and 8 control animals
mu <- rbeta(n_cpg, 2, 2)                   # each CpG has its own typical methylation level
g  <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), each = n)        # TRUE = exposed
rowt <- function(M, g) {                   # Welch t-test p-value for every row of M
  a <- M[, g]; b <- M[, !g]
  va <- apply(a, 1, var) / ncol(a); vb <- apply(b, 1, var) / ncol(b)
  t  <- (rowMeans(a) - rowMeans(b)) / sqrt(va + vb)
  df <- (va + vb)^2 / (va^2 / (ncol(a) - 1) + vb^2 / (ncol(b) - 1))
  2 * pt(-abs(t), df)
}
p <- sapply(c("F1", "F2", "F3"), function(gen)
  rowt(matrix(rnorm(n_cpg * 2 * n, mean = mu, sd = 0.05), nrow = n_cpg), g))
colSums(p < 0.05)
table(generations_significant = rowSums(p < 0.05))
colSums(apply(p, 2, p.adjust, method = "BH") < 0.05)
hist(p[, "F1"], breaks = 20, main = "F1, no true effect", xlab = "p-value")

There is no true effect anywhere. How many CpGs reach p < 0.05 in each generation? Compare with the expected number.
How many are significant in two and in all three generations? Compare with \(20000 \times 0.05^2\) and \(20000 \times 0.05^3\).
How many survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction? Describe the p-value histogram: what would it look like if some CpGs had a true effect?
Change the threshold to 0.001. How many CpGs are significant in all three generations now?



R2 — Litters, not pups
set.seed(2)
one_study <- function(n_litters = 4, pups = 6, sd_litter = 1, sd_pup = 1) {
  litter <- rep(1:(2 * n_litters), each = pups)
  group  <- rep(c("control", "exposed"), each = n_litters * pups)
  y <- rnorm(2 * n_litters, 0, sd_litter)[litter] + rnorm(length(litter), 0, sd_pup)  # no exposure effect
  m <- tapply(y, litter, mean); gl <- tapply(group, litter, `[`, 1)
  c(pups    = t.test(y[group == "exposed"], y[group == "control"])$p.value,
    litters = t.test(m[gl == "exposed"], m[gl == "control"])$p.value)
}
p2 <- replicate(2000, one_study())
rowMeans(p2 < 0.05)
sapply(c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1), function(s) mean(replicate(2000, one_study(sd_litter = s))["pups", ] < 0.05))

What is the false-positive rate when each pup is treated as independent, and when litter means are compared?
How does the false-positive rate depend on the SD between litters? Why is it correct when that SD is 0?
Change n_litters = 12, pups = 2. What happens to the pup-level false-positive rate, and why?



R3 — Confounding by genotype
set.seed(3)
n <- 400
region  <- rep(c("north", "south"), each = n / 2)        # the famine hit the north
exposed <- region == "north"
snp  <- rbinom(n, 2, ifelse(region == "north", 0.45, 0.25))   # allele frequency differs by region
meth <- 0.50 + 0.04 * snp + rnorm(n, 0, 0.05)                 # methylation depends on genotype only
summary(lm(meth ~ exposed))$coefficients
summary(lm(meth ~ exposed + snp))$coefficients
tapply(snp, region, mean)

What does the naive model conclude about the grandchildren of the famine region?
What happens when genotype is in the model? Why?
In a real cohort you rarely know the causal SNP. Name two designs or analyses that reduce this kind of confounding.



R4 — Forking paths in a small historical cohort
set.seed(4)
one_cohort <- function(n = 300) {
  food <- matrix(rbinom(n * 4, 1, 0.3), n, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("PGF", "PGM", "MGF", "MGM")))
  sex  <- sample(c("M", "F"), n, replace = TRUE)
  outc <- cbind(allcause = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), cvd = rbinom(n, 1, 0.2), diabetes = rbinom(n, 1, 0.05))
  p <- c()
  for (gp in colnames(food)) for (o in colnames(outc)) for (s in c("M", "F", "both")) {
    keep <- if (s == "both") rep(TRUE, n) else sex == s
    tab <- table(factor(food[keep, gp], 0:1), factor(outc[keep, o], 0:1))
    p[paste(gp, o, s)] <- fisher.test(tab)$p.value
  }
  p
}
res <- replicate(500, one_cohort())
nrow(res)
mean(apply(res, 2, min) < 0.05)
mean(colSums(res < 0.05))
sort(res[, 1])[1:3]

How many tests does one cohort get? In what fraction of null cohorts is at least one p < 0.05?
Compare with your answer to B3(b). Why is the simulated fraction lower than \(1 - 0.95^{36}\)? (Hint: Fisher’s exact test with rare outcomes.)
Look at the three smallest p-values of the first cohort. Write the headline a newspaper might make of the smallest.



R5 — Power and the winner’s curse
set.seed(5)
eff <- c(F1 = 1, F2 = 0.5, F3 = 0.25)     # a real effect that halves every generation (SD units)
sim <- sapply(eff, function(e) replicate(4000, {
  x <- rnorm(10, e); y <- rnorm(10)
  c(p = t.test(x, y)$p.value, d = mean(x) - mean(y)) }), simplify = "array")
power <- apply(sim["p", , ] < 0.05, 2, mean)
power
sapply(names(eff), function(gn) mean(sim["d", sim["p", , gn] < 0.05, gn]))
power.t.test(delta = 0.25, sd = 1, power = 0.8)$n
power["F3"]^3

What is the power to detect the effect in F1, F2 and F3 with 10 animals per group?
Among studies that find a significant F3 effect, what is the average estimated effect? Why is it larger than the true 0.25?
How many animals per group would 80% power in F3 require?
Three independent labs each test F3 with n = 10. What is the probability that all three find p < 0.05, even though the effect is real?

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — generations (B1)





Ask where the germ cells of each generation were when the exposure happened. Primordial germ cells form in the embryo during pregnancy; sperm form in the adult father.









Hint 2 — expected counts (B3, B4)





Expected false positives \(= m \alpha\); in all of \(k\) independent generations \(= m \alpha^k\); at least one \(= 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m\). See the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure for FDR control.









Hint 3 — designs (B5, B9)





Go through the six routes in the lecture figure Many routes, one claim: germline mark, direct exposure, genes, shared environment, parental behaviour, chance. Which ones does the design close?









Hint 4 — R functions (R1–R5)





replicate repeats a simulation; t.test, fisher.test and lm are the tests; p.adjust corrects for multiple testing; power.t.test computes power or sample size. For mixed models with litter as a random effect, see lme4::lmer.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) First unexposed is F3; an F2 effect is intergenerational (F2 was exposed as germ cells in the F1 fetus). (b) First unexposed is F2; F1 effect is intergenerational. (c) F2 was never exposed: transgenerational (if the design excludes other routes). (d) F3 after a pregnancy exposure: transgenerational. (e) The women (F1) were exposed in utero, and their eggs (F2) were already forming then: intergenerational.
B2. (a) \(0.515 - 0.488 = 0.027\) absolute; \(0.027 / 0.515 = 5.2\%\) relative. (b) \(0.027 / 0.48 \approx 0.056\). (c) Controls half the genetic background, the family’s social environment and (roughly) birth period. It does not control for differences between siblings in other early-life conditions, for the half of the genome not shared, or for reverse causation through health; and blood composition may differ. (d) No. The exposed people were embryos at the time: an F1 effect of direct exposure. It shows a lasting effect of the prenatal environment.
B3. (a) \(4 \times 3 \times 3 = 36\) tests; \(36 \times 0.05 = 1.8\) expected false positives. (b) \(1 - 0.95^{36} = 0.84\). (c) The interval excludes 1, barely: the effect could be anywhere from 2% to 135% higher mortality. It is more informative because the hypothesis was specified in advance (one test, not 36), and the sample is 40× larger. The other original findings (diabetes, cardiovascular) did not replicate.
B4. (a) \(450\,000 \times 0.01 = 4500\). (b) Both F1 and F2: \(450\,000 \times 0.01^2 = 45\); all three: \(450\,000 \times 0.01^3 = 0.45\). (c) 43 in all three would be far more than 0.45, so not explained by independent chance alone, but consider why tests might not be independent: the same control animals or batch used across generations, the same array batch, cell-type composition or litter structure shared between generations. The authors should correct for multiple testing (FDR), balance exposed and control animals from each generation across processing batches, use independent controls, and replicate in new animals.
B5. (a) 3 per group: the exposure was given to the mothers. (b) Pups in a litter share a mother, uterus, milk and cage, and litter size differs; litters differ for reasons unrelated to the exposure, and the t-test counts that difference 8 times. (c) Analyse litter means (n = 3 vs 3), or a mixed model with litter as a random effect; better, use many more litters (e.g. 10–15 per group), cross-foster, and randomise exposure to dams.
B6. (a) \(0.6^8 = 0.017\). (b) \(0.5^8 = 0.0039\). Eight successes in a row with such power are unlikely even if the effect is real: suspect unreported experiments, flexible analysis, or overestimated effects (Francis 2014 made exactly this argument, with p = 0.004).
B7. (a) Mutations: \(7 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.35 \times 10^8 \approx 0.9\) per haploid genome per generation. Epimutations: \(10^{-4} \times 2 \times 10^6 = 200\). (b) No: the high genome-wide count reflects millions of sites. With a constant per-site reversion probability of 10⁻⁴, the geometric waiting time has mean 1/10⁻⁴ = 10 000 generations. Actual gain and loss rates differ and depend on genomic context. Epimutations supply many new heritable variants, and some persist long enough for selection to act; their greater reversibility than DNA mutations does not make all epialleles short-lived.
B8. (a) In the blastocyst (preimplantation embryo) and in primordial germ cells as they enter the gonad. (b) Imprints survive wave 1 (they must be kept in every cell of the body of that generation) and are erased in wave 2 (so they can be reset according to the sex of the individual whose gametes are being made). (c) It must survive in the zygote and through preimplantation demethylation (wave 1) into the embryo, then survive or be rebuilt through PGC erasure (wave 2) in the F1 germline, and still have an effect in F2.
B9. (a) An association across generations; candidates: shared environment and culture (diet, wealth, household smoking), genetics, chance (many outcomes, small subgroup). Fix: a pre-specified single outcome in an independent, larger cohort, adjusting for family socioeconomic status and the parents’ own smoking and BMI. (b) Shown: a carrier in sperm RNA sufficient for an F1 phenotype. It is intergenerational; it does not show transmission to F2. Fix: test F2 by mating F1 animals to controls, with several independent litters and replication in another lab. (c) The methylation followed maternal behaviour, and cross-fostering reversed it (Weaver et al. 2004): behavioural transmission, not germline inheritance. Fix: cross-fostering and embryo transfer already show this; the claim “inherited” should be “transmitted by behaviour”.
B10. Plants form gametes late from somatic shoot cells without a PGC-like erasure, and maintain CG methylation through meiosis (MET1) with RNA-directed DNA methylation to restore non-CG methylation; mammals erase methylation in two waves (preimplantation and PGCs) and package sperm DNA with protamines. Plants (and worms) also have RNA-dependent RNA polymerases that amplify silencing small RNAs each generation, which mammals lack.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 1001, 942 and 911 CpGs with p < 0.05 in F1, F2 and F3; expected \(20\,000 \times 0.05 = 1000\). (b) 134 CpGs are significant in exactly two generations (expected \(3 \times 20\,000 \times 0.05^2 \times 0.95 \approx 143\)) and 4 in all three (expected 2.5). (c) None survives BH correction in any generation. The histogram is flat (uniform), as it should be under the null; true effects would add a spike near 0. (d) At p < 0.001: 14, 16 and 14 per generation (expected 20) and none in all three (expected \(20\,000 \times 10^{-9}\)).
R2. (a) Pups: 33% false positives; litter means: 4–5% (0.0415 in our run). (b) 5.2%, 7.7%, 16.6% and 33.1% for a litter SD of 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1. With no litter effect, pups really are independent and the t-test is valid; the larger the between-litter variation, the more the pup-level test mistakes litter differences for an exposure effect. (c) The rate drops to 13%: with more, smaller litters the litter differences average out, and the pseudo-replication is milder. The correct analysis still uses litters.
R3. (a) Grandchildren from the famine region have higher methylation: +0.0152, p = 0.0085: a “transgenerational effect of famine”. (b) Adjusted for genotype, the exposure effect is +0.0027, p = 0.61, and the SNP effect is 0.039 per allele: the difference came entirely from allele frequency (mean number of methylation-raising alleles 0.875 in the north vs 0.555 in the south). (c) Within-family comparisons (siblings, cousins), genome-wide genotyping with adjustment for ancestry (principal components) and known meQTLs; in animals, isogenic strains.
R4. (a) 36 tests; about 63% of null cohorts have at least one p < 0.05 (0.626 in a run of 500; 0.638 with 1000 cohorts in the lecture figure), 1.26 significant tests on average. (b) \(1 - 0.95^{36} = 0.84\) assumes independent tests with exact 5% error. Here the tests share data (the “both” group contains the M and F groups; the same outcome is used for four grandparents), and Fisher’s exact test is conservative when outcomes are rare (diabetes, 5%). (c) The smallest are maternal grandmother × diabetes × granddaughters (p = 0.0097) and paternal grandmother × diabetes × grandsons (p = 0.020). Headline: “Grandmother’s childhood diet predicts granddaughters’ diabetes deaths”: a sex-specific, line-specific finding from pure noise.
R5. (a) Power 0.55, 0.18 and 0.087 for F1, F2 and F3. (b) 0.85: only studies whose estimate happened to be large reach significance (the winner’s curse), so a significant small study overestimates the effect, here more than threefold. (c) power.t.test gives n ≈ 252 per group for 80% power at 0.25 SD. (d) \(0.087^3 \approx 0.0007\) (0.00066): three small labs will almost never all replicate a real but small F3 effect, and if they all do, suspect selective reporting.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic inheritance
text:
Where this leads

DNA methylation biology covers imprinting, PGC reprogramming and plant methylation pathways in more depth.
Epigenomics and genetic variation shows how much methylation is under genetic control (meQTL), the confounder of R3.
Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers uses methylation as a record of exposure and age within one lifetime.
Differential methylation covers the statistics of genome-wide methylation tests (R1) properly.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
About this lecture
A few hundred CpGs predict a person’s age from a blood sample to within about 3–4 years. Such epigenetic clocks are the best-known methylation biomarkers, and a good case study in building, testing and over-interpreting a predictor.

Methylation changes with age: single CpGs, and why one is not enough.
Penalised regression (elastic net): a linear model with a price on complexity, chosen by cross-validation.
Train, test, overfitting, leakage: a preview of Machine learning from scratch.
Published clocks: Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, DunedinPACE; age acceleration; what clocks do and do not measure.
Cell-free DNA: methylation tells which tissue a fragment came from; cancer detection.
Data: Hannum et al. 2013 (656 people, 450k) to build a clock; GSE42861 (Methylation arrays) to test it.


Students know linear models from RNA-seq (design matrices) and arrays from Methylation arrays. This lecture uses the same arrays for a different purpose: not to find CpGs associated with a trait (EWAS), but to predict a number for a new sample. That changes what counts as success: not a p-value but the error on samples the model has never seen. The machine-learning vocabulary (training and test data, overfitting, regularisation, cross-validation) is introduced here in its simplest form and returns in the machine learning block. Every number in the figures comes from data you will use in the exercise: the Hannum blood data set, from which we train our own clock, and the rheumatoid arthritis data set of the previous lecture, which serves as an independent test.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Methylation changes with age


Some CpGs gain methylation with age (ELOVL2: r = 0.86), others lose it (r = −0.73). The trends are steady over eight decades.
But at any one age the spread is large: from ELOVL2 alone you could guess age only to within about ±10 years.


Real data, whole blood of 656 people aged 19 to 101 (Hannum et al. 2013). The CpG in ELOVL2 (cg16867657), a fatty-acid elongase gene, is the most robust age-associated CpG known: it rises from about 0.45 in young adults to 0.85 in the very old, in blood and in many other tissues. Age-related gains are typical of CpG islands that are Polycomb targets in stem cells (bivalent promoters), while losses are typical of CpGs outside islands. Why methylation drifts with age is not fully understood: imperfect maintenance over many cell divisions, changes in the composition of the stem-cell pool, and programmed changes all play a part. Note the residual scatter: at age 60, ELOVL2 ranges from about 0.55 to 0.80. A single CpG is a weak predictor; many CpGs with partly independent noise can average it out.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Many CpGs, each weakly related to age
text:
Many CpGs, each weakly related to age


Of 26 127 CpGs in our subset, only 50 have |r| > 0.5 with age, but 470 have |r| > 0.3: lots of small, partly redundant signals.
Combining them in one linear model is the obvious idea. The problem: 26 127 CpGs, 459 people for training.


The histogram shows the correlation of each CpG with age across the 656 people. Most are near zero (no relation), with long tails on both sides. The subset was chosen by variance across people, without looking at age, plus the CpGs of the Horvath clock and of a tissue atlas (more on the leakage this implies later). On the full array there are about 470 000 CpGs; the pattern is the same. A linear model with all of them has more unknowns than observations: there are infinitely many sets of coefficients that fit the training data perfectly. The rest of the first half of the lecture is about how to choose a sensible one.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Penalised regression: a price on complexity
text:
Penalised regression: a price on complexity


Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients; lasso (L1) sets most of them exactly to zero; the elastic net (α between 0 and 1) does both and keeps groups of correlated CpGs together.
Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge and DunedinPACE are all elastic nets on CpG β values.


The loss function is the familiar residual sum of squares plus a penalty. With λ = 0 it is ordinary least squares, which with more CpGs than people fits the training data exactly and predicts nonsense. As λ grows, large coefficients become expensive; the lasso penalty (sum of absolute values) produces exact zeros, which is why clocks end up with a few hundred CpGs rather than all of them: the model selects variables. The ridge part (sum of squares) stops the lasso from picking one CpG at random out of a group of highly correlated neighbours. Zou and Hastie (2005) introduced the elastic net; glmnet (Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani) is the R package everybody uses. The link to students’ RNA-seq knowledge: DESeq2’s shrinkage of fold changes is also a penalty (a prior) that trades a little bias for much less variance. α = 0.5 is the usual choice in clock papers; λ is chosen by cross-validation.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Choosing λ: cross-validation inside the training set
text:
Choosing λ: cross-validation inside the training set


The test set is touched once, at the end. λ (and every other choice) is tuned by k-fold cross-validation on the training set.
Leakage: selecting CpGs by their age correlation in all samples, then splitting, makes the test error look too good.


This is the core logic of supervised learning, and it returns in Machine learning from scratch. Split the samples once into training and test (here 70/30, at random, 459 and 197 people). Within the training set, split again into 10 folds; for each fold, fit the model on the other 9 for a whole path of λ values and predict the held-out fold; average the errors over folds for each λ; pick the λ with the lowest cross-validated error. Refit on all training data with that λ and predict the test set once. Anything learned from the test samples, even indirectly, leaks: choosing CpGs by their correlation with age in all 656 people, normalising all samples together with a method that uses the outcome, or trying ten models and reporting the best test result. In genomics there are subtler leaks: related individuals in training and test, technical replicates of one sample split across sets, or (for sequence models) overlapping regions. The cure is always the same: decide everything on the training data.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: The elastic net on real data
text:
The elastic net on real data


Left: cross-validated error against λ. The minimum (lambda.min) keeps 313 CpGs; the more conservative lambda.1se keeps 36.
Right: coefficients enter the model one by one as λ decreases; most CpGs never enter.


Real output of cv.glmnet with α = 0.5 on the 459 training samples (20 seconds on a laptop). Read the left panel from right to left: with a strong penalty (large λ) no CpG is in the model and the prediction is just the mean age, with an error variance near the variance of age (about 200 years²). As λ decreases, CpGs enter and the error drops steeply, then flattens: from log λ ≈ 0 to the left, adding CpGs no longer helps. lambda.1se is the largest λ whose error is within one standard error of the minimum: almost as good, much simpler (36 CpGs). Right: the coefficient paths of the 12 largest CpGs; the units are years per unit of β, so a coefficient of 50 means that 0.1 more methylation adds 5 years. Of the 313 CpGs selected, 32 are also in Horvath’s clock: different clocks share only some CpGs, because many CpGs carry similar information and the lasso picks among them somewhat arbitrarily.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Training error lies; test error tells the truth
text:
Training error lies; test error tells the truth


Elastic net: median absolute error 1.2 years on training data, 3.7 years on the 197 held-out people (r = 0.93).
Ordinary least squares on the top-k CpGs: with 440 CpGs the training error falls to 0.5 years while the test error explodes to 18 years.


Left: predictions for the training and test samples. Training predictions hug the diagonal; test predictions scatter more. The gap between the two is overfitting: the model has partly learned the noise of its training samples. Right: the same idea without a penalty. We take the k CpGs most correlated with age in the training data and fit an ordinary linear model. With 5–100 CpGs, training and test error are similar (3.7–4 years). As k approaches the number of training samples (459), the model can fit the training data almost exactly: training error drops to half a year, and the test error rises to 8 years at k = 400 and 18 years at k = 440. A penalised model avoids this by refusing to make coefficients large unless the data strongly support it. This curve, training error going down and test error going down then up, is the most important picture in machine learning.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Horvath’s pan-tissue clock (2013)


Elastic net on ~8 000 samples from 51 tissues and cell types (27k and 450k arrays): 353 CpGs; median error 3.6 years in test data.
Trained on a transformed age, F(age): logarithmic in childhood, linear after 20. Applied to Hannum’s blood: r = 0.92, but in-sample: Hannum’s data were in Horvath’s training set.


Horvath combined 82 public data sets (39 for training, 32 for testing) and restricted himself to the 21 369 CpGs present on both the 27k and 450k arrays. The age transformation: methylation changes fast in childhood and slowly in adults, so a linear model of raw age fits poorly across the whole lifespan; F(age) = log(age + 1) − log(21) below 20 and (age − 20)/21 above stretches childhood. The model predicts F(age) and the inverse transformation turns it back into years. The striking result was that one set of CpGs works in almost every tissue (except sperm, which looks “young”, and some cancers). Right panel: we apply Horvath’s published coefficients (Additional file 3 of the paper) to the Hannum data. It works well, but this is not a fair test: Hannum’s GSE40279 was one of Horvath’s training sets (his Additional file 1). Always check which data a published model has already seen.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Four generations, defined by the target
text:
Four generations, defined by the target


First-generation clocks predict chronological age: the better they get, the less they can say beyond the calendar.
Later clocks predict health: PhenoAge (clinical biomarkers), GrimAge (time to death), DunedinPACE (pace of decline).


A clock that predicted chronological age perfectly would be useless as a biomarker: it would tell you the birth date. The interesting part of a first-generation clock is its error, and the error mixes biology (people who age faster) with noise. Second-generation clocks change the target. PhenoAge (Levine et al. 2018, 513 CpGs) is trained on “phenotypic age”, a mortality-weighted combination of chronological age and nine blood tests (albumin, creatinine, glucose, CRP, lymphocyte percentage, mean cell volume, red cell distribution width, alkaline phosphatase, white cell count). GrimAge (Lu et al. 2019, 1 030 CpGs) first builds methylation surrogates of seven plasma proteins (including GDF15, PAI-1, cystatin C) and of smoking pack-years, then combines them to predict time to death in the Framingham Offspring cohort. DunedinPACE (Belsky et al. 2022, 173 CpGs) is trained on the rate at which 19 biomarkers of organ function declined between ages 26 and 45 in the Dunedin birth cohort (born 1972–73), and is expressed as years of biological ageing per calendar year (mean about 1). GrimAge and DunedinPACE predict mortality and morbidity better than first-generation clocks.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: An external test: another lab, another cohort
text:
An external test: another lab, another cohort


GSE42861 (151 arrays, Methylation arrays), noob-normalised: our clock r = 0.92, median error 3.2 years; Horvath r = 0.87, 4.3 years.
Both predict about 2.4 years too old on average: a shift between data sets (lab, normalisation, population), not biology.


This is the fair test: samples from a different study, lab and country, processed with a different normalisation than either training set. Both clocks keep their correlation with age, but the whole cloud is shifted upwards: our clock by 2.5 years and Horvath’s by 2.3 years on median. Such offsets are typical when a clock meets new data; Horvath himself reported a median error of 3.8 years on this very data set (it was one of his test sets) after his own normalisation (a BMIQ variant). For a single person, an offset of 2–3 years matters; for comparing groups measured in the same batch it cancels out. This is why age acceleration is defined relative to the data at hand (next slide), and why comparing a person’s DNAm age measured in one lab with norms from another is dangerous.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Age acceleration: the residual, not the difference
text:
Age acceleration: the residual, not the difference


Age acceleration = residual of DNAm age regressed on chronological age in your data. Removes offsets (here +2.5 y) and the flattening of the slope (0.90).
RA vs control: no difference (p = 0.94). The raw difference (DNAm age − age) would carry the offset and an age trend.


Fit a line of DNAm age on chronological age in the data set (red line), and use each person’s vertical distance to the line. The red segments show the most accelerated and the most decelerated person. Two artefacts disappear: the global offset between data sets, and the fact that clocks systematically predict too young in old people and too old in young people (a slope below 1, here 0.90: a regression-to-the-mean effect of the penalty and of noise). With the raw difference, any group that is older on average would look “decelerated” just because of the slope. In GSE42861 the age acceleration of our clock does not differ between RA patients and controls (means −0.03 and +0.03 years), and current smokers are 1.1 years more accelerated than never smokers (not significant here). Published analyses often also adjust for estimated blood cell composition (“intrinsic” age acceleration) or deliberately keep it (“extrinsic”), because part of what a blood clock measures is the ageing of the immune cell mix.

With a slope below 1, young people look “old” and old people “young” on the raw difference. The residual compares each person with others of the same age.
Acceleration is relative to the reference data: a different cohort gives a different line.


A worked example of the definition. The fitted line comes from regressing DNAm age on age in the whole data set; here it is 12 + 0.8 × age. Person A’s DNAm age is 6 years above her calendar age, but exactly what the data predict for 30-year-olds: acceleration 0. Person B is 3 years above the line: accelerated. Person C has a negative raw difference, but is only 2 years below the line. The exam asks this kind of calculation. A practical consequence: an age acceleration value is not portable between studies unless the same reference line is used; commercial “biological age” tests that report a single number per person hide this choice.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: What clocks measure, and what they do not
text:
What clocks measure, and what they do not

Associated with: mortality, frailty, smoking, obesity, HIV, Down syndrome (accelerated); centenarians’ offspring and some calorie-restriction studies (slower). Effects are modest: a few years.
Partly: changes in blood cell composition (naive T cells decline with age), mitotic history of stem cells, and maintenance errors.
Not: a measure of “true biological age” in one number, a cause of ageing, or a reliable per-person diagnostic. Different clocks correlate only moderately with each other.
Noise: technical replicates of the same DNA can differ by up to 9 years for some clocks (Higgins-Chen et al. 2022); principal-component clocks fix much of this.


The evidence that clocks capture something biological: age acceleration predicts mortality independently of chronological age and of classical risk factors (best for GrimAge and DunedinPACE), it is higher in conditions of accelerated ageing (HIV, Down syndrome, Werner syndrome in some studies), and it is partly heritable. But: blood clocks are strongly influenced by the composition of white blood cells, which itself changes with age and disease; individual CpGs of the clocks have poor test-retest reliability on arrays, so a single measurement of a person is noisy (Higgins-Chen et al. 2022 found differences up to 9 years between technical replicates and fixed it by training on principal components instead of single CpGs). Clocks are correlational: nothing shows that changing methylation at clock CpGs changes ageing. Keep this in mind for the next slide.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Judge the claim: “our intervention reverses epigenetic age”
text:
Judge the claim: “our intervention reverses epigenetic age”

15 volunteers, one supplement, DNAm age measured before and after 12 months; “2.5 years younger”. What would you ask?
No control group: regression to the mean, seasonal and batch effects between the two array runs.
Measurement noise: replicate differences of several years for single-CpG clocks; was each sample run in duplicate, in the same batch?
Multiple clocks: five clocks reported, one significant.
Composition: did the intervention shift blood cell counts (e.g. fewer neutrophils after an infection cleared)?
Meaning: is a lower clock value a lower risk of disease? That needs outcomes, not a biomarker.


This is the critical-reading skill that the exam tests. Claims of epigenetic age reversal by supplements, diets or drugs are common, and most rest on small uncontrolled studies. Each bullet is a design flaw students should be able to name: no randomised control, the two time points measured in different batches (a batch effect of a few years is easy, see the external test with a 2.4-year offset), technical noise of single-CpG clocks, selective reporting across clocks, and changes in cell composition that move blood clocks without any change inside cells. Even a real, controlled reduction of a clock value is a surrogate endpoint: it shows that methylation changed, not that health improved. DunedinPACE was designed for intervention studies (high test-retest reliability), and a randomised trial (CALERIE, calorie restriction) found a small slowing of DunedinPACE but no clear effect on the other clocks tested (Waziry et al. 2023).

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Beyond age: methylation biomarkers

what it predicts

smoking exposure, pack-years
epidemiology; verifying self-report

tumour classifiers
CNS tumour type (Capper et al. 2018)
clinical diagnosis, from the same EPIC arrays


cfDNA methylation
tissue of origin, cancer signal
liquid biopsy (next slides)




Clocks are one example of a general recipe: a penalised model or classifier on array or sequencing methylation data. The most consequential clinical application so far is the DKFZ classifier of central nervous system tumours (Capper et al. 2018): a random forest trained on 450k data (and now run on EPIC arrays) assigns a tumour to a methylation class across the roughly 100 known CNS tumour types, and changed the diagnosis in up to 12% of prospective cases. It is now part of the WHO classification of brain tumours. The smoking CpG AHRR came up in Methylation arrays as a positive control; a single CpG is a better marker of recent smoking than many questionnaires. All of these inherit the issues of this lecture: training data, external validation, batch, composition. Epigenetics in disease and therapy returns to tumour classification.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Cell-free DNA: fragments of dying cells
text:
Cell-free DNA: fragments of dying cells


Plasma DNA is mostly from blood cells (55% white blood cells, 30% erythroid progenitors), plus endothelium (10%) and liver (1%) in healthy people (Moss et al. 2018).
Tissue damage or a tumour adds DNA with its own methylation pattern.


When cells die by apoptosis, their chromatin is cut between nucleosomes, and the nucleosome-protected fragments of about 167 bp reach the blood, where they are cleared within minutes to hours. A tube of blood contains a few thousand genome equivalents of cell-free DNA (cfDNA), so every locus is present in a few thousand copies, but each copy carries the methylation pattern of the cell it came from. Cell-type-specific methylation is very stable (Loyfer et al. 2023: replicates of the same sorted cell type are more than 99.5% identical), so a fragment from hepatocytes can be recognised among fragments from blood cells. Applications: tissue damage (liver, heart, pancreatic beta cells after islet transplantation), transplant rejection, sepsis, and cancer, where tumour DNA (ctDNA) adds both tumour-specific methylation (CpG island hypermethylation) and the methylation of the tissue of origin. Prenatal testing uses the same idea (placental cfDNA in maternal blood).

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Deconvolution with a reference atlas


The same linear algebra as the Houseman method: non-negative least squares against a 25-cell-type atlas (Moss et al. 2018; 6 105 of its CpGs are on the 450k array).
Blood of the GSE42861 samples comes out as 61% neutrophils, then lymphocytes and monocytes. Simulated liver DNA is recovered: 1% added → 0.94% estimated.


Left: each of the 151 whole-blood samples from Methylation arrays, deconvolved against the Moss atlas (bars sorted by the neutrophil fraction). The result is sensible: neutrophils dominate, then T cells, NK cells, monocytes and B cells; a few percent go to erythroid progenitors and other tissues (breast 1.6%), which is the noise floor of the method on array data. The atlas splits CD4 and CD8 T cells differently from the Reinius reference used in Methylation arrays (CD8 is larger here), a reminder that fractions depend on the reference. Right: simulated cfDNA. We mix a blood profile with a known fraction of the atlas’s hepatocyte profile, add measurement noise (SD 0.03 in β) and deconvolve 20 times per fraction. Down to 1% the estimate is close to the truth (0.94% for 1%); with nothing added it reports about 0.1%: the noise floor that sets the detection limit. Real cfDNA is harder: few genome copies per locus, so sequencing depth limits sensitivity, which is why methods like Loyfer’s count fragments with fully tissue-specific patterns rather than averaging CpGs.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Cancer detection from cfDNA methylation







CCGA validation (Liu et al. 2020), targeted bisulfite sequencing of cfDNA





specificity (non-cancer called non-cancer)
99.3%


sensitivity, all cancer types, stage I / II / III / IV
18% / 43% / 81% / 93%


tissue of origin predicted correctly (when a signal was found)
93%




By hand: screening 100 000 people with 1% prevalence, sensitivity 50%, specificity 99.3% → 500 true and 693 false positives: PPV 42%.
Early tumours shed little DNA (often < 0.1% of cfDNA), which is why stage I sensitivity is low.


The Circulating Cell-free Genome Atlas study (Liu et al. 2020, 6 689 participants) used targeted bisulfite sequencing of more than 100 000 methylation regions and a classifier trained on cancer and non-cancer samples. The results show both the promise and the problem. Specificity is very high, which is necessary for screening healthy people, and the tissue of origin is usually right, because tumours keep much of the methylation of their tissue. But sensitivity depends steeply on stage: the cancers we most want to find early shed the least DNA. The positive predictive value calculation is the essential exam skill: with a rare disease, even 99.3% specificity produces many false positives relative to true positives. Clonal haematopoiesis (expanded blood clones with mutations, common in older people) confounds mutation-based liquid biopsy; methylation tests are affected less, but blood cell composition still matters. Large randomised screening trials (such as NHS-Galleri in England) are testing whether such tests reduce late-stage cancers and deaths, the outcome that matters.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Summary

clocks
Horvath 353 CpGs, 51 tissues; Hannum 71; PhenoAge, GrimAge (health, death); DunedinPACE (pace)

GSE42861: our clock 3.2 y, Horvath 4.3 y, both +2.4 y offset

Students should leave able to: explain what the elastic net penalty does and why clocks have a few hundred CpGs; describe a correct train/test/cross-validation scheme and spot leakage; read a CV curve and a train-vs-test plot; compute age acceleration as a residual by hand; say what first-, second- and third-generation clocks are trained to predict; list reasons a clock difference between two groups may not be biological; explain how cfDNA methylation reveals the tissue of origin; and compute a positive predictive value from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence. The machine learning block (Machine learning from scratch, What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works) generalises these ideas.

title: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Horvath 2013, Genome Biol. DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types. The pan-tissue clock; its supplement lists all data sets and coefficients.
Hannum et al. 2013, Mol Cell. Genome-wide methylation profiles reveal quantitative views of human aging rates. The blood clock and the data set of this unit.
Levine et al. 2018, Aging. An epigenetic biomarker of aging for lifespan and healthspan. PhenoAge: training on health instead of age.
Belsky et al. 2022, eLife. DunedinPACE, a DNA methylation biomarker of the pace of aging. Pace of ageing from a longitudinal cohort.
Higgins-Chen et al. 2022, Nat Aging. A computational solution for bolstering reliability of epigenetic clocks. How noisy clocks are, and a fix.
Moss et al. 2018, Nat Commun. Comprehensive human cell-type methylation atlas reveals origins of circulating cell-free DNA in health and disease. The atlas and cfDNA deconvolution.

title: Quiz: from reads to coverage
text:
Short questions on reads, alignment, filtering and coverage tracks. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A base in a Phred+33 FASTQ file has the quality character + (ASCII 43). What is its Q, and the probability that the base call is wrong? What would the same character mean in a Phred+64 file?






Hint





Q = ASCII − offset, and \(p = 10^{-Q/10}\).









Answer





Phred+33: Q = 43 − 33 = 10, \(p = 10^{-1} = 0.1\), one error in ten. In Phred+64, ASCII 43 would be Q = −21, which is impossible: Phred+64 qualities start at @ (ASCII 64). Seeing characters below ; in a file tells you it is Phred+33.




Q2. Decode the FLAGs 163 and 1040. What kind of read is each, and would samtools view -F 1804 keep it?






Hint





Subtract the largest power of two that fits, and repeat. 1804 = 1024 + 512 + 256 + 8 + 4.









Answer





163 = 128 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 2 of a properly paired fragment, on the forward strand, mate on the reverse strand. Kept. 1040 = 1024 + 16: a single-end read on the reverse strand, marked as a duplicate. Removed by -F 1804, because 1804 contains the 1024 bit.




Q3. A proper pair of 50 bp reads: read 1 has FLAG 99 and POS 20 001, read 2 has FLAG 147 and POS 20 251. How long is the fragment, and what is TLEN in each line?






Answer





Read 2 ends at 20 251 + 50 − 1 = 20 300. Fragment = 20 300 − 20 001 + 1 = 300 bp. TLEN = +300 for read 1 (the leftmost), −300 for read 2.




Q4. A read aligned with MAPQ 1 and the tags AS:i:-6 XS:i:-6. What does this tell you about the read, and should it go into a coverage track?






Answer





The best alignment score (AS) equals the second-best (XS): the read fits at least two places equally well, typically copies of a repeat, and bowtie2 reported one of them at random. MAPQ 1 means the position is very likely wrong. Remove it (MAPQ ≥ 30): otherwise its signal is spread at random over the copies. The repeat then has no signal at all, which means no information, not no binding.




Q5. Why are duplicates usually removed in ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq but usually kept in RNA-seq? When can removing them in ChIP-seq hurt?






Answer





In RNA-seq a highly expressed gene produces so many fragments that many share a start position by chance: removing them would compress the expression of the most expressed genes. In ChIP and ATAC, each position is covered by few independent fragments from a small amount of DNA, so identical start positions are mostly PCR copies, and an amplified fragment would look like a peak. Removing them can hurt at very strong, narrow peaks with single-end reads: there are only a few hundred possible start positions per strand, so independent fragments collide (saturation). In the CTCF data, 49% of reads inside peaks were flagged as duplicates against 4% outside.




Q6. 60% of the aligned reads of an ATAC-seq library are on chrM. You make a CPM track of the nuclear genome without removing the chrM reads. Compared with a track made after removing them, are the nuclear values too high or too low, and by what factor?






Answer





Too low, by a factor of 2.5. CPM divides by all reads in the BAM. Only 40% of the reads are nuclear, so the denominator is 1/0.4 = 2.5 times too large. Two libraries with different chrM fractions would look different even if their nuclear signal were the same.




Q7. A ChIP library has 20 million filtered reads, extended to 200 bp; the effective genome size is 2.7 × 109 bp. A base is covered by 45 fragments. What is its RPGC value? What is the CPM of a bin overlapped by 45 reads?






Hint





Average coverage = reads × fragment length / genome size.









Answer





Average coverage \(= 2 \times 10^7 \times 200 / 2.7 \times 10^9 = 1.48\). RPGC \(= 45 / 1.48 = 30.4\): 30 times the genome average. CPM \(= 45 \times 10^6 / (2 \times 10^7) = 2.25\).




Q8. After depth scaling, a 50 bp bin has 9 ChIP reads and 1 input read; another has 1 ChIP read and 0 input reads. Compute \(\log_2\)((ChIP + 1) / (input + 1)) for both. Why add 1?






Answer





log2(10/2) = 2.32 and log2(2/1) = 1.0. Without the pseudocount the second bin would be 1/0 = ∞, the most “enriched” bin in the genome on the strength of a single read. Adding 1 to both counts makes the ratio of small counts shrink towards 0 (no change), while large counts are hardly affected.




Q9. In a single-end ChIP-seq experiment, the coverage of the reads themselves (not extended) shows two humps about 180 bp apart around each binding site, with a dip in between. Explain the pattern. What should you do before making a coverage track?






Answer





Each read is one end of a fragment that spans the site. Fragments sequenced from the + strand put their reads to the left of the site, those from the − strand to the right, so the reads form two humps about one fragment length apart, and the site itself is between them. The distance (here about 180 bp) estimates the fragment length. Extend every read in its own direction to that length (bamCoverage --extendReads 180): the extended reads overlap on the site and give one peak. (Paired-end data give each fragment directly.)




Q10. To save time, a student aligns whole-genome ChIP-seq reads to a reference that contains only chr21. Most reads align, many with MAPQ 42. Explain what has gone wrong, and why the high MAPQ is no reassurance.






Answer





Reads from the other chromosomes were forced onto chr21 wherever the sequence was most similar (repeats, paralogues, processed pseudogenes), creating false signal. MAPQ only compares the places the aligner can see: if the true origin is not in the reference, a read can look unique on chr21 and get MAPQ 42. Align to the whole genome and select chr21 afterwards. (The course data avoid this by including only reads that ENCODE placed on chr21 or chrM against the whole genome.)

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Background
Phred quality. \(Q = -10 \log_{10} p\), where \(p\) is the probability that the base call is wrong; \(p = 10^{-Q/10}\). In FASTQ, Q is stored as one character: ASCII code − 33 (all current data) or − 64 (Illumina files from about 2008–2011, like the ones here).
SAM FLAG bits: 1 paired, 2 proper pair, 4 unmapped, 8 mate unmapped, 16 reverse strand, 32 mate reverse strand, 64 first in pair, 128 second in pair, 256 secondary, 512 QC fail, 1024 duplicate, 2048 supplementary. POS is the leftmost aligned base, 1-based. For a proper pair, TLEN = (rightmost base of the pair) − (leftmost base) + 1, positive for the leftmost read, negative for its mate.
Normalisation. CPM = count × 106 / (reads in the library). RPGC divides the coverage by the average coverage, reads × fragment length / effective genome size. A fold change over input divides depth-scaled ChIP by depth-scaled input; a pseudocount (usually 1) is added to both so that empty bins give 0 on the log scale instead of ±∞.
The filtering chain used in this course (the ENCODE recipe): MAPQ ≥ 30 and -F 1804 → mark and remove duplicates → keep the chromosomes of interest (no chrM) → remove reads in blacklisted regions.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Data
GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, single-end 36 bp, sequenced 2011) and its input control (ENCSR000EYX, single-end 28 bp, 2009). To keep the exercise small, the FASTQ files contain only the reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM against the whole genome: 390 097 ChIP reads and 476 372 input reads, untrimmed, with their original names and qualities (see data/prepare-reads.sh). The reference is chr21 + chrM of hg38. You also need the ENCODE blacklist, and for comparison ENCODE’s CTCF fold-change bigWig and peaks.
data/download.sh enrichment-alignment     # FASTQ, reference, bowtie2 index, ENCODE files
mkdir -p ~/epi/align && cd ~/epi/align
D=/path/to/course/data                    # where download.sh put the files
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (1.10 or newer), bedtools, deeptools, macs3 and IGV (see Install the software you need). The whole command-line part runs in about 2 minutes with 8 threads on a laptop or a login node; on a cluster, put the commands in a script and submit it with sbatch --cpus-per-task=8.






A shortcut, and what it hides



A real analysis aligns to the whole genome. Aligning to chr21 + chrM only would force reads from other chromosomes onto the most similar chr21 sequence; we avoid that by starting from reads that ENCODE already placed on chr21 or chrM. The consequence: alignment rates look almost perfect, library sizes are about 1% of the real ones, and some multi-mappers look more unique than they are (their other copies are on chromosomes we left out). The steps, commands and decisions are exactly those of a full analysis.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
By hand
