Highest density: chr21 8234456 8234568 (12 reads in 112 bp, 107 per kb) and chr21 6369257 6372342 (215 reads in 3.1 kb, 70 per kb), against an average of 2.9 input reads per kb on chr21: 24–37 times too many, after MAPQ and duplicate filtering. (The 520 bp region at 10.01 Mb in the lecture figure had 451 input reads before filtering, but 448 of them had MAPQ 1: there the MAPQ filter already did the work.)
C6. predicted fragment length is 100 bps (from 359 paired + and − strand peaks; about 1 s).
C7. Each command takes 2–5 s. (a) The effective genome size is the part of the genome where reads can align. chr21 has 46 709 983 bases, of which 6 621 364 are N (unsequenced gaps, mostly the short arm and the centromere); 40 088 619 are A, C, G or T. A stricter value would also subtract unmappable repeats; deepTools lists such values for whole genomes and several read lengths. (b) RPGC / CPM = \(40\,088\,619 / (100 \times 10^6) = 0.40\) (B5c); at the summit of the peak at chr21:43 789 481 the CPM track reads 1063 and the RPGC track 426.
C8. (a) Three ENCODE peaks, at about 43.789, 43.811 and 43.817 Mb, each with a peak in both tracks. (b) + strand reads are piled up to the left of the summit, − strand reads to the right, about 100 bp apart (the lecture figure Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites). (c) The input has only 116 397 reads on all of chr21, about 3 per kb, and 377 reads in this 50 kb window: most 50 bp bins have 0 or 1 input read, so the ratio jumps between bins. ENCODE’s fold change (MACS2) uses a local background from the input averaged over 1 kb and 10 kb, never lower than the genome-wide average, and pools two replicates.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 326 213 ChIP reads on chr21; MAPQ 0–1: 72 811 (22.3%); MAPQ ≥ 30: 75.9% (247 580 reads, the same as samtools view -c -q 30 chip.sorted.bam chr21). Reading the BAM takes about 2 s. (b) Input on chr21: 25.1% MAPQ 0–1, 74.4% ≥ 30: slightly more multi-mappers than the ChIP. The input reads are 28 bp, the ChIP reads 36 bp; a shorter read is unique in fewer places. (The ChIP is also enriched at CTCF sites, which are mostly in unique sequence.)
R2. (a) 77 450 duplicates (25.8%): exactly the number samtools markdup reported. (b) chrM: 54.9% of the ChIP’s chrM reads are duplicates, chr21: 19.7%. chrM is 16.6 kb with 52 069 filtered reads, about 3 per base: nearly every possible (start, strand) is used several times, even without PCR.
R3. (a) The shapes agree, but bamCoverage’s values are a little higher: at the summit (chr21:43 789 481) 194 extended reads cover the base, 194 × 106 / 197 587 = 982 CPM, while the bamCoverage track reads 1063. bamCoverage counts every read that overlaps a 10 bp bin, even by one base, so a bin collects a few more reads than any single base in it. (b) Without extension the peak splits into two humps about 100 bp apart, with a dip at the summit (the + and − strand reads on either side), as in the lecture figure.
R4. (a) Median offsets −50 bp (+ strand) and +48 bp (− strand): a fragment of about 98 bp, in agreement with MACS3’s 100 bp. (Reading the BAMs and the R steps take a few seconds each.) (b) 54 003 of 197 587 reads (27.3%) have their 5’ end within 300 bp of one of the 405 summits on chr21. For a TF ChIP this is a good value (ENCODE’s guidelines treat FRiP below 1% as a warning sign).
R5. (a) 33 287 bins are used (not blacklisted, non-zero in both). Pearson correlation of the log2 values: 0.63 over all bins, 0.91 over the 466 bins that contain an ENCODE peak. The tracks agree on the peaks and much less on the background. (b) ENCODE pooled two replicates, we used one; ENCODE’s MACS2 fold change uses a local background from the input smoothed over 1–10 kb (and a genome-wide floor), we divided 50 bp bins with a pseudocount of 1; ENCODE estimated its own fragment length and cropped the ChIP reads to 28 bp; and ENCODE used the whole genome, so some reads are placed differently.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Where this leads

Experimental design and QC turns the numbers in your C5 table into QC metrics: library complexity from duplicates, FRiP (R4b), fingerprints and strand cross-correlation.
ChIP-seq peak calling starts from chip.final.bam and input.final.bam and replaces the noisy per-bin ratio with MACS3’s local Poisson background.
ATAC-seq processing and peak calling uses the same chain with paired-end reads, adapter trimming that really matters, chrM removal and the Tn5 shift.
The production version of all of this is nf-core/chipseq or nf-core/atacseq.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Langmead & Salzberg 2012, Nat Methods. Fast gapped-read alignment with Bowtie 2.
Li et al. 2009, Bioinformatics. The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools.
Chen et al. 2018, Bioinformatics. fastp: an ultra-fast all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor.
Ramírez et al. 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. deepTools2: a next generation web server for deep-sequencing data analysis.
Amemiya, Kundaje & Boyle 2019, Sci Rep. The ENCODE Blacklist: identification of problematic regions of the genome.
Robinson et al. 2011, Nat Biotechnol. Integrative genomics viewer.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
About this lecture
ATAC-seq processing and peak calling ended with one set of peaks for all samples. Now we ask which of those regulatory elements are more open in one cell type (or condition) than in another. Most of the statistics is the DESeq2 you know from RNA-seq; this lecture spends its time on what is different.

From peaks and BAM files to a count matrix: consensus peaks, what to count.
The running example: B cells vs CD4 T cells from three donors (Corces et al. 2016), and why the design is paired.
Exploration: reads in peaks, PCA, sample correlation.
Normalisation, the central difference from RNA-seq: peaks, background, spike-ins, and what a global change does.
DESeq2 on peaks: dispersion, MA and volcano plots, shrinkage.
Interpretation: marker genes, nearest-gene caveats, agreement with RNA-seq.


Students have done a full DESeq2 analysis of RNA-seq. Say so at the start: the negative binomial model, the design formula, the Wald test and the multiple-testing correction are exactly what they know. The new ideas are where the rows of the matrix come from (peaks found in the data, not genes from an annotation), what normalisation assumes when the total amount of open chromatin can differ between samples, and how to turn a list of differential peaks into biology. The running example is real: the Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis atlas, 590 650 fixed-width peaks, which is exactly the kind of consensus peak set the previous unit ended with. The result of this unit (B-specific and T-specific peaks) is the input to Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The question


Two cell types share most of their open chromatin (promoters of housekeeping genes), but each has its own enhancers.
Differential accessibility (DA): which peaks have more fragments in one group than in the other, more than donors differ among themselves?
Answers can be all-or-none (an enhancer open only in B cells) or quantitative (2.5-fold more open).


Walk through the four peaks: the first is shared (a promoter, open in both), the second is open only in B cells, the third only in T cells, the fourth is open in both but more in B cells. In counts, these become rows of a matrix: one row per peak, one column per sample. The question is the same as in RNA-seq, with peaks instead of genes. Note that the figure shows two donors per cell type: without replicates we could not say whether a difference is larger than the difference between two people. Typical applications: cell types (as here), treatment vs control, a knockout, a time course, disease vs healthy tissue.

title: Differential accessibility
section: What is the same as RNA-seq, and what is not
text:
What is the same as RNA-seq, and what is not


Same: a count matrix, the negative binomial GLM, the design formula, dispersion shrinkage, Wald test, Benjamini–Hochberg, fold-change shrinkage. DESeq2 or edgeR run unchanged.
Different: the rows are found in the data; the normalisation assumption (“most features do not change”) is shakier; the result is a list of regions, which needs annotation before it means anything.


This slide is the map of the lecture. Everything in grey is a recap; everything in red is new. A useful way to say it: DESeq2 does not know whether a row is a gene or a peak. It sees counts. All the epigenomics-specific decisions happen before (which regions, what to count, which normalisation) and after (what the regions are near, what binds there). That is also why published differential accessibility analyses differ so much: the statistics are standard, the choices around them are not.

title: Differential accessibility
section: One set of regions for all samples
text:
One set of regions for all samples


Every sample must be counted in the same regions. Peaks called per sample must be combined into a consensus set.
Union and merge (A) is simple, but nearby elements fuse into wide regions of unequal width.
Fixed-width peaks (B): extend each summit to 500 bp, keep the most significant, drop those that overlap it. Used by Corces et al. 2016 and by ArchR; DiffBind re-centres on summits (± 200 bp).
Keep only peaks found in at least k samples (DiffBind default: 2) or call peaks on pooled data per group, so one noisy sample does not add thousands of peaks.


The consensus step is a design choice with consequences. A merged region of 3 kb that contains a promoter and an enhancer will be counted as one feature: if the enhancer opens and the promoter does not, the change is diluted. Fixed-width peaks keep elements separate and make counts comparable between peaks (every peak is 500 bp, so count differences between peaks are not due to width). The iterative procedure in panel B is what Corces et al. describe: summits from MACS2 extended to 500 bp, ranked by significance, overlapping lower-ranked peaks removed. It is also the default in ArchR. Calling peaks on each group’s pooled reads (rather than per sample) is common too; the important thing is not to call peaks on one group only, which biases the test towards that group. The previous unit (ATAC-seq processing and peak calling) built such a consensus set; here we start from Corces’s.

title: Differential accessibility
section: What to count in a peak
text:
What to count in a peak


ATAC-seq measures Tn5 insertions: each fragment end is a cut site in open chromatin. Fragment 4 spans the peak without a single cut inside it.
Counting fragments that overlap the peak (featureCounts with pairs, bedtools multicov) is the common default; counting insertions (fragment ends, shifted +4/−5) is more precise and what ArchR and chromVAR use.
Either way: one number per peak per sample, integer counts, no normalisation yet.


For RNA-seq students counted reads per gene with featureCounts or salmon. Here it is the same, with peaks as features. Two subtleties. First, a long fragment spanning the peak (fragment 4) says that the DNA at both ends was accessible, not the peak itself; insertion counting does not count it. Second, with read counting (not fragment counting) a fragment with both ends in the peak counts twice, which breaks the Poisson assumptions mildly; count pairs (featureCounts -p –countReadPairs) or insertions. With 500-bp peaks and mostly short fragments the two methods give highly correlated counts; the choice matters more for nucleosome-scale questions. The Corces count matrix counts fragments per peak.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Counting on the command line
# consensus peaks (BED) -> SAF, the simple annotation format of featureCounts
awk 'BEGIN { OFS = "\t"; print "GeneID", "Chr", "Start", "End", "Strand" }
     { print "peak" NR, $1, $2 + 1, $3, "." }' consensus.bed > consensus.saf

# count fragments (read pairs) per peak, all samples at once
featureCounts -F SAF -a consensus.saf -p --countReadPairs -B -C \
  -T 8 -o atac_counts.txt sample1.bam sample2.bam sample3.bam ...

# or, with bedtools: one column per BAM
bedtools multicov -bams sample1.bam sample2.bam -bed consensus.bed > atac_counts.bed

-p --countReadPairs: count fragments, not reads. -B -C: both ends aligned, on the same chromosome.
SAF is 1-based (start + 1), BED is 0-based: the boundary from Genomic intervals again.
The output is the matrix: peaks × samples. Corces et al. provide it, so the exercise starts there.


featureCounts is the same program students used for RNA-seq; with SAF they give it intervals instead of a GTF. By default featureCounts assigns a fragment that overlaps two features to neither (ambiguous); with non-overlapping fixed-width peaks this rarely matters, and –fracOverlap or -O change the behaviour. bedtools multicov is slower but transparent. A third route is csaw::windowCounts or DiffBind::dba.count in R, which read the BAMs directly. On the cluster, run featureCounts in an sbatch job with -T set to the number of cores requested. The matrix has one row per peak, an integer count per sample, and that is all DESeq2 needs.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The dataset: Corces et al. 2016


ATAC-seq of 13 FACS-sorted blood cell types from 7 healthy donors (plus AML samples we ignore): 590 650 peaks (hg19) × 132 libraries, GEO GSE74912.
Our comparison: B cells vs CD4 T cells from the 3 donors with both (1022, 4983, 5483): 8 libraries.
Column names encode donor and cell type: Donor4983-CD4-9A-150120 = donor 4983, CD4 T cells (code 9), library A, run date. Early samples are just 4983-7A (code 7 = monocytes): decode from the GEO sample table, never guess.


Corces et al. sorted cells directly from bone marrow or blood of healthy donors and ran an optimised ATAC protocol (Fast-ATAC) on about 5000 cells each. The GEO series lists every library with its donor and cell type, which is how we decoded the numeric codes: 1 HSC, 2 MPP, 3 LMPP, 4 CMP, 5 GMP, 6 MEP, 7 monocytes, 9 CD4 T, 10 CD8 T, 11 NK, 13 B, 14 CLP, 15 erythroblasts. The design is unbalanced: progenitors come from donors 4983, 6792, 7256 and 2596, mature lymphocytes from 1022, 2596, 4983, 5483. Only three donors gave both B cells and CD4 T cells; donor 2596 has CD4 T cells but no B-cell library, so it cannot be paired and we leave it out (the exercise asks what including it would do). The peaks are on hg19; the course uses GRCh38, next slide.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The peaks are hg19: liftOver
gr19 <- GRanges(atac$Chr, IRanges(atac$Start + 1, atac$End))   # 0-based starts in the file
lo   <- liftOver(gr19, import.chain("hg19ToHg38.over.chain"))  # a GRangesList: 0, 1 or more pieces
table(lengths(lo))



result of liftOver
peaks




no match in GRCh38 (deleted or rearranged)
159


split into ≥ 2 pieces
1 375


one piece, but not 500 bp or a different chromosome
46


one piece, 500 bp: kept
589 070 (99.7%)




Dropping 0.3% of the peaks is fine here. Better still, when you have the reads: re-align to GRCh38 and call peaks there.


This is the liftOver from Genomic intervals, now with real numbers. The file’s Start column is 0-based (End − Start = 500), so add 1 when building a GRanges. liftOver returns a list because one input range can map to zero, one or several pieces. A peak that is split, or whose lifted width is no longer 500 bp, spans a gap or rearrangement between the builds; we drop those rather than guess. We give each peak an ID from its row in the original file (peak000001…) so that hg19 and hg38 versions can always be matched. The counts do not change: liftOver moves the coordinates, not the reads. That is also the limitation: reads that would map differently in GRCh38 (new sequence, fixed errors) are not recovered.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Technical and biological replicates


Biological replicates = independent donors. They carry the variation the test must beat.
Technical replicates (A, B) = two libraries from the same sorted cells. They measure library noise only: sum them (collapseReplicates), do not count them as extra samples.
8 libraries → 6 columns: 3 donors × 2 cell types.


Treating technical replicates as biological replicates is pseudo-replication: the model would think donor 5483 is two people and underestimate the variance between people, giving too many significant peaks. Summing counts is right because a technical replicate is just more sequencing of the same material (the two libraries correlate at r = 0.94 on log CPM in this dataset, against 0.77–0.93 between donors of the same cell type). DESeq2::collapseReplicates sums the columns that share a label. Sorting matters too: each population is FACS-sorted on surface markers (CD19 for B cells, CD4 for T helpers), so the purity of the sort is part of the biological sample.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Why pair by donor?


If donors differ (genotype, age, sex, sample handling), each B-cell sample shares part of that difference with the T-cell sample from the same person.
~ donor + celltype compares every donor with itself: the donor effect is removed, and the celltype coefficient is the within-donor log fold change.
The cost: one coefficient per extra donor. With 6 samples, the residual degrees of freedom drop from 4 to 2.


The toy numbers are on the slide. Unpaired, the difference of 1.0 (log2 scale) is small against a within-group SD of about 2 (donors differ a lot), so nothing is significant. Paired, the three within-donor differences are 1.0, 1.2 and 0.8: a consistent increase. This is the paired t-test idea in a GLM, same as in RNA-seq experiments with patients. In DESeq2 the last term in the design is the one results() tests by default, so put the variable of interest last. Whether pairing pays off depends on how big the donor effect is compared with the cost in degrees of freedom; we will check that on the real data.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Exploration: reads in peaks per library
text:
Exploration: reads in peaks per library


Reads in peaks range from 0.6 to 25 million per library: a 40-fold range, partly sequencing depth and partly signal-to-noise (the fraction of reads in peaks, FRiP).
Erythroblasts are low in every donor (Corces et al. report poor replicate agreement for them, r ≈ 0.5). The B-cell library of donor 1022 has 4.6 M reads in peaks; the B cells of 4983 and 5483 have 17–18 M (5483: two libraries summed).


The count matrix only has reads in peaks, not total reads, so we cannot compute FRiP here; in your own data you have both (Experimental design and QC). Two libraries with the same depth can have very different counts in peaks if one is noisier (more reads in background, mitochondria, dead cells). For differential analysis this matters in two ways: low counts mean less power for that sample, and differences in FRiP feed directly into the normalisation question later. Erythroblasts are a hard sample (Corces et al. note R = 0.55 between technical replicates against 0.94 for other cell types), a reminder to look at QC per sample before a comparison.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Signal-to-noise differs between libraries


Same depth, FRiP 40% vs 10%: a typical peak gets 4 times fewer fragments in library 2.
Normalising by total reads makes every peak “4-fold up” in library 1. Normalising within peaks says nothing changed.
Which one is right depends on why FRiP differs. A worse library? Then within-peak normalisation. Fewer or weaker open sites in the cells? Then the total-read answer may be the biology.


This is the first half of the normalisation story and the most important idea of the lecture. FRiP mixes technology (how many dead cells, how well transposition worked, how deep the library is relative to its complexity) and biology (how much of the genome is open). A cell type with fewer open sites (e.g. quiescent cells, or erythroblasts which compact their chromatin before enucleation) will have lower FRiP for biological reasons. The counts cannot distinguish the two; QC metrics (TSS enrichment, fragment-size distribution, mitochondrial fraction) and knowledge of the system can.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
PCA: cell type dominates


VST of 127 515 peaks with mean count ≥ 10, all 77 healthy libraries, the 10 000 most variable peaks.
Libraries cluster by cell type, not by donor (shape). PC1 runs from stem and progenitor cells (left) to mature cells (right); PC2 separates the erythroid branch (MEP → erythroblasts).


Exactly as in RNA-seq: variance-stabilising transformation (vst, blind = TRUE), then prcomp on the most variable rows. The picture follows the haematopoietic tree: HSC and MPP together, LMPP, CMP and GMP nearby; MEP on the way to erythroblasts (PC2); CLP between the progenitors and the mature lymphocytes; monocytes, B, NK and T cells are all mature and sit at the right of PC1, and separate from each other on later components. Erythroblasts spread out more than the others, matching their poor replicate agreement. Donor (point shape) adds little on top. Corces et al. made the same point more strongly: accessibility classifies cell types better than RNA does. For our test this is good news: the cell-type signal is large compared with donor variation.

title: Differential accessibility
section: The six samples of our comparison
text:
The six samples of our comparison


Pearson correlation of log2 CPM over 75 922 peaks (mean CPM ≥ 2), all 8 libraries.
Technical replicates: r = 0.94. Same cell type, other donor: 0.77–0.88 (B), 0.87–0.93 (CD4). B vs CD4: 0.19–0.37.
The 1022 B-cell library correlates least with its group: fewest reads in peaks (4.6 M).


Point out the block structure: B cells with B cells, T cells with T cells; inside each block, the technical replicates of 5483 are the most similar pair. This justifies summing technical replicates. Also note that 1022 B cells correlate less with the other B cells (0.77–0.84) than 4983 and 5483 do with each other (0.84–0.88): a lower-quality library (4.6 M reads in peaks) is noisier. With only 3 donors per group, one weaker sample matters; DESeq2’s dispersion estimates will absorb it, at a cost in power.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Normalisation: median of ratios, on peaks
text:
Normalisation: median of ratios, on peaks


DESeq2 size factor for sample j: s_j = \text{median}_i \, \dfrac{k_{ij}}{\left(\prod_{v} k_{iv}\right)^{1/m}}, the median over peaks of the count divided by the peak’s geometric mean.
The same as for genes. The assumption is too: the typical (median) peak does not change.
Here, for the 1022 B-cell library: size factor 0.46 from the median ratio, 0.35 from total counts in peaks.


Recap, students know this formula. Each peak votes with its ratio to a pseudo-reference sample; the median is robust to the minority of peaks that change. The histogram is the real distribution of log2 ratios for one sample. The two lines differ because the reads of 1022_Bcell are distributed differently across peaks: relatively fewer reads in the strongest peaks, consistent with a noisier library. Neither is “wrong”; they answer different questions. Total-count normalisation says “the same number of reads in peaks in every sample”; median ratio says “the typical peak is unchanged”. TMM (edgeR) makes the same assumption as the median ratio with a trimmed mean of log ratios, and gives similar factors.

title: Differential accessibility
section: When most peaks do change: a global opening
text:
When most peaks do change: a global opening


A treatment that opens chromatin everywhere (e.g. an HDAC inhibitor) gives more fragments in every peak. Sequenced to the same depth, the extra signal is diluted.
Peak-based size factors make the median peak unchanged: the global opening disappears, and only the relative change (p5) survives, at half its size.
Background bins (reads outside peaks) can recover it, if the background truly is constant.


Go through the numbers. Truth: all peaks double, p5 quadruples, background unchanged. The treated library has 1400 reads’ worth of material, but the sequencer gives 1000 reads, so everything is scaled by 1000/1400. The raw ratio is then 1.43 for most peaks. Median-of-ratios normalisation divides by 1.43: most peaks become 1.0 (no change) and p5 becomes 2.0. Normalising by the background (which went from 720 to 514 reads) divides by 0.71 and recovers 2 and 4. This is the same problem as the EZH2-inhibitor example in Experimental design and QC, now for accessibility. The by-hand exercise has a version of it. Note the symmetry: a global closing would be hidden in the same way.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Four ways to normalise, four assumptions
text:
Four ways to normalise, four assumptions


No method is assumption-free. Pick the one whose assumption you can defend for your experiment, and say it in the methods.
If two reasonable methods disagree, the disagreement is the result: report it (Reske et al. 2020 found the number and direction of DA peaks change with the method).


Library size: the total signal per cell is the same, fine when FRiP is similar across samples. Peak-based (median ratio, TMM): most peaks are unchanged, the default in DESeq2 and edgeR; wrong under global change. Background bins (csaw’s normFactors on 10-kb bins, Lun & Smyth): the reads outside peaks are noise at a constant rate per cell; wrong when signal-to-noise differs for technical reasons (a library with more dead cells has more background, gets a larger size factor from background normalisation, and its peaks are then deflated). Spike-ins: add a fixed amount of foreign chromatin per cell (e.g. Drosophila nuclei) before transposition; for ATAC this is not yet routine. A fifth option is a set of reference peaks assumed constant (e.g. housekeeping promoters). Reske, Wilson & Chandler 2020 re-analysed an ATAC dataset with different normalisations and obtained different numbers of DA peaks and even different biological conclusions.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Real data: the choice changes the answer
text:
Real data: the choice changes the answer


DESeq2 and TMM factors agree within 10%; total counts differ by up to 25% (B cells of 1022 and 4983).
Same model, same data: 19 438 / 17 202 peaks up in B / up in T with DESeq2 factors, 18 342 / 19 074 with TMM, 23 703 / 13 540 with total counts.
Total counts shift all fold changes towards B (median log2 FC 0.52 vs 0.26 with DESeq2 factors): relative to the typical peak, the B-cell libraries have more reads in peaks.


Thresholds: padj < 0.05 and |MLE log2 fold change| > 1 for this comparison. Most of the strong cell-type-specific peaks are found by all three; the difference is in the hundreds to thousands of moderate peaks, and in the balance between “up” and “down”. The median log fold change over all tested peaks is a quick diagnostic: 0.26 with DESeq2 factors, 0.19 with TMM, 0.52 with total counts. (It is not exactly 0 even with peak-based factors, because the median is taken over many all-or-none peaks, and DESeq2 computes its factors only from peaks with no zero count.) Is the extra 0.26 with total counts real (B cells have more accessible chromatin) or technical (the B-cell libraries happen to have better signal-to-noise)? Without spike-ins or another external reference we cannot tell, and for a comparison of two cell types the conservative, conventional choice is peak-based. For a treatment expected to change chromatin globally, that default needs to be questioned.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Tools: DiffBind and csaw


DiffBind: peak-based. Builds the consensus, counts, then calls DESeq2 or edgeR. What we do by hand in this unit.
csaw: window-based. No peak calling; counts in sliding windows, normalises on background bins, tests each window, merges windows into regions and controls the FDR over regions.
Neither is installed in this course: the exercise does the same steps with DESeq2 and edgeR directly.


DiffBind (Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Stark & Brown) was written for ChIP-seq of transcription factors (oestrogen receptor in breast cancer) and is widely used for ATAC too. Its defaults have changed between versions: since version 3 it normalises by full library size by default, and offers DESeq2/TMM/background options (dba.normalize). csaw (Lun & Smyth 2016) avoids the circularity of calling peaks and testing in the same data, handles regions of any width, and makes the FDR refer to regions rather than windows. For narrow, well-defined ATAC peaks the two approaches give similar answers; csaw shines for broad or shifting signals. The statistical core of both is the negative binomial GLM.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
DESeq2 on peaks
dds <- DESeqDataSet(se, design = ~ donor + celltype)       # se: peaks x 8 libraries, rowRanges in hg38
dds <- collapseReplicates(dds, groupby = dds$unit)         # 8 libraries -> 6 samples
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3, ]              # 211 824 of 589 070 peaks
dds <- DESeq(dds)                                          # about 1 minute
res <- results(dds, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", type = "apeglm")   # about 2 minutes

Exactly the RNA-seq workflow. Filter first: most of the 589 070 peaks were called in other cell types and have almost no reads in B or T cells.
celltype levels CD4, Bcell: positive log2 fold change = more open in B cells.


The filter keeps peaks with at least 10 fragments in at least 3 of the 6 samples (3 = the size of the smaller group, so a peak open in only one cell type is kept). Without it DESeq2 runs on 589 070 rows, most of them zeros, which costs time and multiple-testing burden; independent filtering in results() would remove many of them anyway. Factor levels: DESeq2 compares to the first level, so set CD4 first. The name of the coefficient is printed by resultsNames(dds). Run times are on one core of a server; on a laptop expect 2–4 minutes for DESeq() and a bit more for apeglm.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Dispersion: paired or not


The familiar picture: noisy per-peak estimates, a fitted trend, shrunk final values. Typical dispersion ≈ 0.4 (coefficient of variation ≈ 60% between donors), higher than for genes.
Here the donor effect is small: only 47 peaks have a significant donor term (LRT). Pairing costs 2 degrees of freedom: 36 703 peaks at padj < 0.05 paired, 41 671 unpaired.


Dispersion is the squared coefficient of variation between biological replicates, beyond Poisson noise. ATAC peaks are noisier than genes: they are small (500 bp), counts are lower, and library quality varies. The dashed trend is the unpaired fit, lower because the residual degrees of freedom are 4 instead of 2 and the donor term absorbs little. This is a real, honest result: in this dataset of sorted cells from healthy adults, the donor effect is weak, and the paired model finds fewer peaks. Should we switch to the unpaired design because it gives more hits? No: choose the design from the structure of the experiment before looking at the number of hits. The paired design is the right one for a paired experiment; it protects against donor effects when they exist (e.g. patients with different genotypes or treatments), and the cost here is modest (most strong peaks are found by both).

title: Differential accessibility
text:
MA plot and fold-change shrinkage


Left: maximum-likelihood fold changes are huge and noisy for weak peaks (few reads: 0 vs 5 is “infinitely” open).
Right: apeglm shrinks uncertain fold changes towards 0 and leaves well-measured ones alone. Use shrunk values to rank and filter by effect size, and for plots.
Blue/orange: padj < 0.05 and |shrunk LFC| > 1. Where counts are high, the grey cloud of unchanged peaks sits on 0: the normalisation assumption holds for most peaks.


Same as for RNA-seq; students have probably used lfcShrink. Two things to read from an MA plot of peaks. First, the shape: a cell-type comparison gives many large fold changes (cell-type-specific enhancers are often all-or-none), so the plot looks more dramatic than a typical RNA-seq treatment. Second, the centre of the grey cloud: if it sat at +0.5 instead of 0, the normalisation would be suspect (or there is a global change). The p-values come from the unshrunk model; shrinkage changes the effect sizes, not which peaks are significant. Our definition of a differential peak uses both: padj < 0.05 from results(), |log2 fold change| > 1 from the shrunk estimate.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Volcano plot


19 404 peaks more open in B cells and 16 897 more open in CD4 T cells (padj < 0.05, |shrunk log2 FC| > 1), out of 211 824 tested.
17% of tested peaks differ more than 2-fold: B and T cells are distinct lineages, so this is expected. A drug treatment typically moves hundreds, not tens of thousands.


The y axis is −log10 of the adjusted p-value, the x axis the shrunk log2 fold change. The two arms are roughly symmetric, a sign that the normalisation is not biased towards one side. These two lists are the result of the unit and the starting point of Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting, which asks which transcription factor motifs are enriched in B-specific vs T-specific peaks (expect EBF1, PAX5, PU.1/SPIB, OCT2 for B; TCF7/LEF1, RUNX, ETS, GATA3 for T). The exercise saves them as differential_peaks.tsv.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Do the peaks make sense? Marker loci
text:
Do the peaks make sense? Marker loci


Each bar is one peak (mean normalised count over 3 donors): blue = open in B, orange = open in T, grey = not differential.
PAX5 (B-cell identity factor): 31 peaks whose nearest TSS is PAX5 open in B, none in T. BCL11B (T-cell commitment): 58 open in T, 1 in B.
Other markers: CD79A, MS4A1, CD19, BLK, EBF1 (B); CD3E, TCF7, LEF1, GATA3, CD28 (T).


A sanity check every analysis should include: do the known marker genes come out on the right side? They do. Note how many peaks a single regulator gene has: PAX5 and BCL11B sit in large regulatory landscapes with dozens of enhancers, and the large intron of PAX5 is full of B-specific elements. Not every peak near a marker changes: promoters of these genes can be accessible (poised) in both cell types, and some elements near EBF1 open in T cells. A short table of counts per marker is in the exercise (R9).

title: Differential accessibility
section: From peaks to genes: the nearest-TSS caveat
text:
From peaks to genes: the nearest-TSS caveat


Only 8% of B-specific and 14% of T-specific peaks are within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS (20% of all tested peaks): DA peaks are mostly distal.
Assigning each peak to its nearest gene is a first guess, right for perhaps half of enhancers. Better links use contacts or correlation (Linking regulatory elements to genes).


Promoters tend to be accessible in many cell types, enhancers are cell-type specific: that is why differential peaks are depleted at promoters. For the distal majority, the nearest gene is a convenient label, not a mechanism. The exercise annotates each peak with its nearest protein-coding TSS (GenomicRanges::distanceToNearest, as in Genomic intervals). Tools such as ChIPseeker or GREAT make this a one-liner and add rules (GREAT assigns a regulatory domain to each gene). Keep the distance in the table; a peak 400 kb from its “nearest gene” in a gene desert is not evidence about that gene.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Does accessibility agree with expression?


RNA-seq from the same study (GSE74246), B vs CD4 T cells from 4 donors, DESeq2 ~ donor + celltype.
Genes near B-open peaks go up in B (median RNA log2 FC +0.5), near T-open peaks go up in T (−0.6). Promoter peaks agree well (Spearman 0.69), distal peaks less (0.42).


The RNA donors (1022, 2596, 5852, 7653) are only partly the same people as the ATAC donors, so this is a comparison of cell types, not of matched samples. The agreement is clear but far from perfect, for good reasons: a distal peak may not regulate its nearest gene; a gene can have several elements changing in opposite directions; accessibility can be primed before expression (or remain after it); and expression is also regulated after transcription. A promoter peak and its own gene are linked directly, which is why their correlation is higher. About two thirds of DA peaks (67% for B, 71% for T) have a nearest gene that changes in the same direction. This is the starting point of Linking regulatory elements to genes.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The result to reuse
tab <- data.frame(peak_id = names(dds), chr = seqnames(dds), start = start(dds), end = end(dds),
                  baseMean = res$baseMean, log2FoldChange = shr$log2FoldChange, lfcSE = shr$lfcSE,
                  pvalue = res$pvalue, padj = res$padj, nearest_gene = ..., dist_to_tss = ...)
tab$class <- ifelse(tab$padj < 0.05 & tab$log2FoldChange >  1, "B_up",
             ifelse(tab$padj < 0.05 & tab$log2FoldChange < -1, "T_up", "ns"))
write.table(tab, "differential_peaks.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

Definition: differential = padj < 0.05 and |shrunken log2 FC| > 1; B_up = more open in B cells, T_up = more open in CD4 T cells. GRCh38, 1-based coordinates, 500 bp.
Keep all tested peaks (class ns included): motif enrichment needs a background.


This table is the hand-over to Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting. Two decisions are written into it and should be in any methods section: the thresholds (FDR 5%, at least 2-fold), and the background (all 211 824 peaks that passed the count filter, which are accessible in B or T cells; a better background for motifs than random genomic sequence, because it has the same GC and chromatin context). Coordinates are GRanges, 1-based closed; when writing BED from them, subtract 1 from start (Genomic intervals). A variant worth knowing: results(dds, lfcThreshold = 1) tests |LFC| > 1 directly instead of filtering afterwards, which is stricter (here 10 153 and 7 503 peaks).

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Limitations of this analysis

Sorted populations are still mixtures: a 2% contamination of T cells in the B-cell sort puts T-cell peaks into the B-cell counts. “Specific” means “much more”, not “only”. Single-cell ATAC avoids this, at the price of sparse counts.
Peaks lifted from hg19: 0.3% lost; reads were aligned to an older genome.
Fixed 500-bp peaks: good for TF sites and comparable counts, but a broad domain is cut into pieces or partly missed.
Peaks called in all 13 cell types: the set includes elements never open in B or T cells (filtered out), and misses none that are open in only one sample.
Three donors per group: dispersion estimates rely heavily on the trend; one weak library (1022) carries a lot of weight.
Normalisation: peak-based by choice. A real global difference in accessibility between B and T cells would be hidden.


These are the questions to ask of any differential accessibility paper, too. Mixtures: Corces et al. sorted with strict gates, but purity is never 100%, and for rare populations contamination can dominate. Peak set: calling peaks on all cell types together, then testing two of them, is fine (the consensus is not biased towards one of the two groups), which is a design point worth contrasting with calling peaks on one group only. Fixed width: some of the strongest B-cell elements are clusters of several peaks (super-enhancer-like), and counting them as independent peaks inflates the number of DA “elements”. A common follow-up is to merge DA peaks within a few kb before counting regions.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




consensus peaks
one region set for all samples; fixed-width summit peaks keep elements apart


counting
fragments (or Tn5 insertions) per peak; featureCounts / multicov; integer counts


replicates
donors are biological replicates; technical replicates are summed


design
~ donor + celltype for paired samples; decide before looking at the hit count


normalisation
peak-based (median ratio, TMM) assumes most peaks unchanged; background bins, spike-ins otherwise


global change
hidden by peak-based size factors; FRiP differences can fake or hide it


statistics
DESeq2/edgeR exactly as for RNA-seq; filter low-count peaks; shrink fold changes


interpretation
DA peaks are mostly distal; nearest gene is a guess; check markers and RNA


this dataset
211 824 peaks tested; 19 404 B_up, 16 897 T_up (padj < 0.05, |LFC| > 1)




Students should leave able to: compute a median-of-ratios size factor by hand; explain why a global change in accessibility is invisible to peak-based normalisation and what to do about it; write the design formula for a paired experiment and say what each coefficient means; read an MA and a volcano plot of peaks; and say what “nearest gene” can and cannot tell. Next: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting, which asks which transcription factors explain the B- and T-specific peaks.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Corces et al. 2016, Nat Genet. Lineage-specific and single-cell chromatin accessibility charts human hematopoiesis and leukemia evolution. The dataset of this unit.
Love, Huber & Anders 2014, Genome Biol. Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2. The model, unchanged for peaks.
Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Nature. Differential oestrogen receptor binding is associated with clinical outcome in breast cancer. The paper that introduced DiffBind.
Lun & Smyth 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. csaw: a Bioconductor package for differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data using sliding windows. Windows, background normalisation, region-level FDR.
Robinson & Oshlack 2010, Genome Biol. A scaling normalization method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data. TMM, and why the total is not the right normaliser.
Reske, Wilson & Chandler 2020, Epigenetics Chromatin. ATAC-seq normalization method can significantly affect differential accessibility analysis and interpretation. The normalisation choice, on real data.

title: Glossary
text: Short definitions of the terms used in the course, grouped by topic. The unit where a term is taught is given in italics.

title: Glossary
text:
Chromatin and gene regulation
Nucleosome — 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4). What is epigenetics?
Histone mark — a chemical modification of a histone residue, named histone–residue–position–modification (H3K27ac = histone H3, lysine 27, acetylated). What is epigenetics?
Writer / reader / eraser — enzymes that add a mark, proteins that bind it, and enzymes that remove it. What is epigenetics?
Euchromatin / heterochromatin — open, gene-rich chromatin vs compact chromatin; constitutive heterochromatin (H3K9me3, HP1) is compact in all cells, facultative (H3K27me3, Polycomb) only in some. What is epigenetics?
Nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) — a stretch of a few hundred bp without nucleosomes at active promoters and enhancers, where transcription factors bind. What is epigenetics?
CpG island — a ~1 kb CpG-rich, usually unmethylated region, often at a promoter (GC > 50%, CpG observed/expected > 0.6). What is epigenetics?
Cis-regulatory element — DNA that controls a gene on the same chromosome: promoter, enhancer, silencer, insulator. Gene regulation
Core promoter — the ~100 bp around the TSS where the transcription machinery assembles (TATA box, Initiator). Gene regulation
Enhancer — a regulatory element that activates a promoter from a distance, independent of orientation; primed (H3K4me1), active (+H3K27ac) or poised (+H3K27me3). Gene regulation
Super-enhancer — a cluster of enhancers with exceptional H3K27ac or Mediator signal; a useful but debated category. Gene regulation
Insulator — a boundary element that blocks enhancer–promoter communication, in vertebrates mostly bound by CTCF. Gene regulation
Transcription factor (TF) / motif — a protein that binds a specific DNA sequence / the set of sequences it prefers. Gene regulation
Position weight matrix (PWM) — a 4 × k table of log-odds scores per base and position, used to score candidate binding sites. Gene regulation
Information content — how far a motif column is from uniform, in bits (0–2); the height of a sequence logo. Gene regulation
Pioneer factor — a TF that can bind its motif on nucleosomal DNA and open chromatin for others (FOXA, PU.1, EBF1). Gene regulation
Mediator / co-activator — protein complexes that connect TFs to RNA polymerase II or modify chromatin (p300/CBP writes H3K27ac). Gene regulation

title: Glossary
text:
Intervals, reads and files
0-based half-open / 1-based closed — BED counts boundaries between bases from 0 (length = end − start); GTF, SAM, VCF and GRanges number bases from 1 and include both ends. Genomic intervals
BED / narrowPeak / bigWig — interval file / BED6 + signal, −log10 p and q, summit offset / indexed binary signal track. Genomic intervals
Genome build — a version of the reference genome (GRCh37/hg19, GRCh38/hg38); coordinates are only valid within one build. Genomic intervals
liftOver / chain file — conversion of intervals between builds using aligned blocks. Genomic intervals
Phred quality — Q = −10 log10(error probability); Phred+33 and Phred+64 are two ways to write it as characters. From reads to coverage
SAM FLAG / MAPQ — a bit field describing a read’s alignment (paired, reverse strand, duplicate, …) / the aligner’s confidence that the position is right. From reads to coverage
Multi-mapping read — a read that aligns equally well to several places, typically in repeats. From reads to coverage
Duplicate — an alignment flagged as a possible PCR or optical copy, usually from matching fragment ends; independent molecules can also share ends. From reads to coverage
Blacklist (exclusion list) — regions prone to anomalous signal across many sequencing experiments, removed before analysis. From reads to coverage
CPM / RPGC — reads per million / reads per genomic content (1× coverage): two ways to normalise coverage tracks. From reads to coverage

title: Glossary
text:
Experimental design and QC
Biological / technical replicate / pseudoreplicate — independent samples / repeated measurement of one sample / a random half of one sample’s reads. Experimental design and QC
Input / IgG control — sonicated chromatin without immunoprecipitation / IP with a non-specific antibody; both model background. Experimental design and QC
Spike-in normalisation — scaling by reads from added foreign chromatin (e.g. Drosophila) so that global changes are not normalised away. Experimental design and QC
FRiP — the fraction of reads in peaks: a signal-to-noise measure. Experimental design and QC
NRF / PBC1 / PBC2 — library complexity: distinct/total reads; positions with one read / distinct positions; one-read / two-read positions. Experimental design and QC
Fingerprint plot — cumulative read share against ranked genome bins; enriched libraries bend away from the diagonal. Experimental design and QC
Strand cross-correlation (NSC, RSC) — correlation of + and − strand coverage at increasing shifts; the peak gives the fragment length, NSC and RSC its strength. Experimental design and QC

title: Glossary
text:
ATAC-seq
Tn5 / tagmentation — the transposase that cuts DNA and inserts sequencing adapters in one step; it prefers open DNA. ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
+4/−5 shift — the correction that moves read ends to the centre of Tn5’s 9-bp duplicated site. ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
Nucleosome ladder — fragment-length peaks below 100 bp (nucleosome-free) and at ~200, ~400 bp (mono-, di-nucleosomes). ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
TSS enrichment — Tn5 insertions at TSSs relative to the flanks; an ATAC quality score. ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
Local lambda (λ_local) — MACS’s background expectation at a position: the largest of the genome-wide and local estimates. ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, Peak calling
IDR — irreproducible discovery rate: the probability that a peak is not reproducible, from the ranks of peaks in two replicates. ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, Peak calling
Consensus peak set — one set of regions used for all samples, e.g. fixed-width 500-bp summit-centred peaks. ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
Size factor / TMM — per-sample scaling of counts (DESeq2 median of ratios / edgeR trimmed mean of M-values). Differential accessibility
Global change — a change in accessibility or binding over most of the genome; peak-based normalisation hides it. Differential accessibility
Motif enrichment — more peaks with a motif match in a target set than in a background, tested with Fisher’s exact (hypergeometric) test. Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
chromVAR deviation / deviation z-score — a bias-corrected relative accessibility deviation at peaks with a motif / that deviation standardised using GC- and accessibility-matched background peak sets. Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
Footprint — a dip in Tn5 insertions at a bound TF site, flanked by high accessibility. Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Glossary
text:
ChIP-seq and successors
Formaldehyde crosslinking — fixing proteins to nearby DNA before fragmentation. ChIP-seq: the assay
Native ChIP — ChIP without crosslinking, on MNase-digested nucleosomes; used for histone marks. ChIP-seq: the assay
Hyper-ChIPable region — a highly expressed locus that gives signal with almost any antibody. ChIP-seq: the assay
Broad peak / domain — an enriched region of many kb (H3K27me3, H3K36me3), called by joining enriched bins across gaps. Peak calling
Rescue / self-consistency ratio — ENCODE’s IDR checks comparing true replicates with pseudoreplicates; both should be below 2. Peak calling
Peak annotation — assigning each peak a category (promoter, intron, distal) and a nearby gene. Annotation and differential binding
Greylist — regions with abnormal input signal (often copy-number gains) masked in differential analysis. Annotation and differential binding
CUT&RUN / CUT&Tag — antibody-tethered MNase / Tn5 cutting in permeabilised nuclei; low background, few cells. CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
SEACR — a peak caller for CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag that thresholds blocks of contiguous signal by their total signal. CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
Chromatin state — a recurring combination of marks, learned by an HMM over binarised marks (ChromHMM). Combining marks into chromatin states
Hidden Markov model: emission / transition — P(observed marks | state) / P(next state | this state); Viterbi gives the most probable state path. Combining marks into chromatin states

title: Glossary
text:
DNA methylation
5mC / 5hmC — 5-methylcytosine / 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, the first TET oxidation product. DNA methylation biology
DNMT1 / DNMT3A, 3B / TET — maintenance methyltransferase (with UHRF1) / de novo methyltransferases / dioxygenases that start active demethylation. DNA methylation biology
Imprinting control region (ICR) — a region methylated on one parental allele that sets allele-specific expression. DNA methylation biology
Partially methylated domain (PMD) — a large, low and variable methylation domain, common in cultured and cancer cells. DNA methylation biology
CG / CHG / CHH contexts; RdDM — the sequence contexts of plant methylation; RNA-directed DNA methylation silences transposons. DNA methylation biology
Bisulfite conversion — chemistry that turns unmethylated C into U (read as T) and leaves 5mC (and 5hmC) as C. Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
Three-letter alignment — aligning C→T converted reads to C→T and G→A converted genomes (Bismark). Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
M-bias — methylation level by read position; ends affected by end repair are trimmed. Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
Conversion rate — the fraction of unmethylated C converted, estimated from non-CpG C or a lambda spike-in. Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
RRBS / EM-seq / TAPS — MspI-reduced representation bisulfite sequencing / enzymatic conversion / TET-assisted pyridine borane sequencing. Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
β value / M value — methylated / total signal (0–1) / log2 of methylated over unmethylated. Differential methylation, Methylation arrays
Beta-binomial / overdispersion — a binomial whose probability varies between replicates; overdispersion is the extra variance beyond sampling noise. Differential methylation
DML / DMR — differentially methylated locus / region. Differential methylation
Infinium I / II probes — two bead types per CpG measured in one colour channel / one bead type per CpG measured in two colour channels on Illumina methylation arrays. Methylation arrays
Detection p-value / noob / functional normalisation — probe signal vs negative-control background / within-array background and dye correction / between-array normalisation guided by control probes. Methylation arrays
Cross-reactive probe — an array probe that also matches other loci; removed before analysis. Methylation arrays
Cell-type deconvolution (Houseman) — estimating cell fractions of a mixed sample from reference profiles of sorted cells. Methylation arrays
EWAS / genomic inflation λ — a linear model per CpG / median χ² divided by 0.455, which is 1 when the test statistics are well calibrated. Methylation arrays
Epigenetic clock / age acceleration — a penalised-regression predictor of age from CpGs / predicted minus expected age (the residual). Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
cfDNA / ctDNA — cell-free DNA in plasma / its tumour-derived part; methylation reveals the tissue of origin. Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
modBAM (MM/ML tags) / bedMethyl — long-read BAM with per-read modification calls and probabilities / a per-site methylation count table (modkit). Methylation and chromatin from long reads
Haplotagging / allele-specific methylation — assigning reads to a phased haplotype (parental origin requires additional information) / methylation that differs between the two copies. Methylation and chromatin from long reads
XCI escape — genes expressed from both X chromosomes despite X inactivation. Methylation and chromatin from long reads
Fiber-seq / m6A footprint — accessibility marked on single DNA molecules by an adenine methyltransferase. Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Glossary
text:
3D genome
Contact map — a symmetric matrix of Hi-C ligation counts between genomic bins. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
Proximity ligation / ligation junction — joining DNA ends held close by crosslinking / the duplicated restriction overhang at the join (GATCGATC for MboI). Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
Valid pair / dangling end / self-circle — a ligation product of two fragments / an unligated fragment / a fragment ligated to itself. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
Cis/trans ratio — the share of contacts within vs between chromosomes. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
Matrix balancing (ICE) — iterative scaling that gives every bin the same total coverage. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
P(s) / observed/expected — mean contact frequency against genomic distance / a contact divided by that expectation. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
Chromosome territory — the nuclear region occupied by one chromosome. 3D genome organisation
A/B compartment — active or inactive chromatin that preferentially contacts its own type; from the first eigenvector of the O/E correlation matrix. Calling compartments, TADs and loops
TAD / insulation score — a self-interacting domain of ~0.1–1 Mb / the contact sum across a sliding window, whose minima are boundaries. Calling compartments, TADs and loops
Loop extrusion — cohesin reels DNA into a growing loop until it meets CTCF bound in the convergent orientation. 3D genome organisation
APA — aggregate peak analysis: the mean of many loop windows, scored as centre over a corner. Calling compartments, TADs and loops

title: Glossary
text:
Integration and variation
ABC score — activity (√(accessibility × H3K27ac)) × contact of an element, as a share of all elements near the gene. Linking regulatory elements to genes
CRISPRi screen — dCas9-KRAB silencing of candidate elements to measure their effect on a gene’s expression. Linking regulatory elements to genes
Linkage disequilibrium (LD) — correlation of alleles between nearby variants; a GWAS lead SNP tags many candidates. Epigenomics and genetic variation
Fine-mapping / credible set — estimating which variant in a locus is causal / the smallest set holding 95% of that probability. Epigenomics and genetic variation
caQTL / meQTL / eQTL — variants associated with accessibility / methylation / expression. Epigenomics and genetic variation
Allelic imbalance / reference mapping bias — unequal reads from the two alleles in one person / the tendency of reference-allele reads to align more often. Epigenomics and genetic variation

title: Glossary
text:
Machine learning
Supervised learning / feature / label — fitting a model to labelled examples / an input variable / the answer to predict. Machine learning from scratch
Logistic regression / log-odds — a linear model of log(p/(1 − p)). Machine learning from scratch
Gradient descent / learning rate — fitting by small steps downhill on the loss / the step size. Machine learning from scratch
Training / validation / test set — data to fit / to choose settings / to report performance once. Machine learning from scratch
Overfitting / regularisation (lasso, ridge, elastic net) — fitting the training data but not new data / penalising large coefficients to prevent it. Machine learning from scratch
Cross-validation — rotating held-out folds within the training data to estimate performance. Machine learning from scratch
Precision / recall / ROC and PR curves — TP/(TP + FP) / TP/P / performance over all thresholds; ROC AUC is the chance a random positive outranks a random negative. Machine learning from scratch
Class imbalance — very unequal class sizes; accuracy can hide poor minority-class performance, and precision falls as positives become rarer even if TPR, FPR and ROC AUC stay the same. Machine learning from scratch
Leakage — test information reaching training, e.g. overlapping windows or homologous sequences on different chromosomes. What people try to predict
Matched negatives / baseline — negatives with the same GC (or accessibility) as the positives / the simplest sensible model to beat. What people try to predict
One-hot encoding — each base as a column of one 1 and three 0s. How a CNN reads DNA
Convolutional filter — a learned 4 × k weight matrix that scans a sequence like a PWM. How a CNN reads DNA
ReLU / max pooling / dense layer — max(0, x) / keeping the largest activation / a weighted sum of all inputs. How a CNN reads DNA
Epoch / early stopping — one pass over the training data / keeping the model with the best validation loss. How a CNN reads DNA
In-silico mutagenesis — changing every base and recording the change in prediction. What did the model learn? Variant effects
Attribution (gradient × input, DeepLIFT, SHAP) — the importance of each base for one prediction. What did the model learn? Variant effects
Variant effect — prediction(alt) − prediction(ref), on the logit scale. What did the model learn? Variant effects

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
About this lecture
ChIP-seq: the assay, TFs vs histone marks showed how chromatin immunoprecipitation finds where a protein or a mark sits. CUT&RUN (2017) and CUT&Tag (2019) answer the same question with a different trick: bring the enzyme to the antibody inside the nucleus, so only the target’s neighbourhood is cut.

The assays: pA–MNase and pA–Tn5 tethered to an antibody in situ; why the background is so low.
What changes in the data: far fewer cells and reads, fragment sizes, duplicates, an IgG control, E. coli spike-in.
Peak calling on sparse data: SEACR vs MACS3.
Caveats: the open-chromatin bias of Tn5, and when ChIP is still the better choice.
Running example: K562 CUT&Tag for H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 (Kaya-Okur et al. 2020) against ENCODE ChIP-seq of the same marks in the same cell line, chr21.


The running example is real data: the replicate-1 CUT&Tag samples of the Henikoff lab’s CUT&Tag tutorial (GEO GSE145187), paired-end 2 × 25 bp, for H3K27me3, H3K4me3 and an IgG control in K562 cells, restricted to the read pairs that align to chr21 (and the E. coli pairs used as spike-in). For comparison we use ENCODE’s filtered ChIP-seq alignments for the same two marks and the input control in K562 (Bernstein lab, 36-bp single-end), also on chr21. Every number on the slides comes from running the commands of the exercise on these files. Peak calling for ChIP-seq (MACS, the local lambda) is in Peak calling; differential binding and spike-in normalisation under global changes are in Annotation and differential binding. This lecture concentrates on what is different.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: ChIP fragments everything; CUT&RUN/Tag cut only at the target
text:
ChIP fragments everything; CUT&RUN/Tag cut only at the target


ChIP: shear all the chromatin, then enrich. Unmarked DNA that sticks to beads and tubes is sequenced too → a carpet of background.
CUT&RUN / CUT&Tag: the antibody brings an enzyme to the target in intact nuclei; DNA elsewhere is never cut, so it never enters the library.


The left side is the problem the in-situ methods solve. In ChIP-seq, the whole genome is fragmented and solubilised; an immunoprecipitation typically enriches the target by a factor of ten to a few hundred, so most of the library is still background, and you need deep sequencing (ENCODE asks for 20 M usable fragments for narrow marks, 45 M for broad ones) and an input control to see the signal over it. Crosslinking, sonication and the IP need millions of cells. In CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag nothing is fragmented except where the enzyme is tethered. The background is not zero (we will see where it comes from), but it is low enough that 3–8 million reads, from thousands to a few hundred thousand cells, give a usable profile. Caveat to say early: low background is a property of the chemistry, not a guarantee of correctness; the antibody still decides what you measure.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Two protocols, one idea


CUT&RUN (Skene & Henikoff 2017): protein A–MNase, activated by Ca2+ on ice; cut fragments diffuse out of the nucleus and are collected; adapters are ligated afterwards.
CUT&Tag (Kaya-Okur et al. 2019): protein A–Tn5 loaded with sequencing adapters, activated by Mg2+; cutting and adapter insertion are one step, then PCR directly.


Both start with unfixed cells or nuclei bound to concanavalin A–coated magnetic beads and permeabilised with digitonin, so antibodies and the fusion enzyme can enter. Protein A (or the protein A/G fusion used in newer kits) binds the Fc part of the antibody; in CUT&Tag a secondary antibody is usually added to increase the number of protein A binding sites. In CUT&RUN, MNase is inactive until calcium is added; the reaction is done at 0 °C to limit diffusion of the cut fragments, then stopped with EGTA, and the small fragments released into the supernatant are purified and turned into a library. In CUT&Tag the Tn5 is the same hyperactive transposase as in ATAC-seq (ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder), pre-loaded with the Nextera adapters; after binding, the nuclei are washed with 300 mM NaCl to remove unbound Tn5 (it sticks to open chromatin, a point we return to), and magnesium starts tagmentation. The whole CUT&Tag protocol takes a day, ends with PCR, and needs no library preparation kit. Both methods have automated, plate-based and single-cell versions (single-cell CUT&Tag already in Kaya-Okur et al. 2019, and later droplet-based and multi-target variants).

A fair summary: for histone marks on limited material, CUT&Tag is now the default in many labs; for comparison with public data, or for TFs with weak binding, ChIP or CUT&RUN.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: Real data: the same marks, ChIP vs CUT&Tag
text:
Real data: the same marks, ChIP vs CUT&Tag


K562, chr21, CPM-scaled. CUT&Tag: 17 380 H3K4me3 and 45 130 H3K27me3 fragments on chr21; ChIP: 94 538 and 141 487 reads.
Same peaks, but between them CUT&Tag is almost empty; ChIP and input have reads everywhere.


The OLIG2/OLIG1 region and the interferon-receptor genes on chr21 (33.0–33.5 Mb), in 2-kb bins, counts per million. OLIG2 is a classic Polycomb target outside the nervous system: a broad H3K27me3 domain, very clean in CUT&Tag, visible but on a high background in ChIP. The interferon-receptor genes (IFNAR2, IL10RB, IFNAR1, IFNGR2) are expressed in K562 and carry sharp H3K4me3 peaks at their promoters in both assays. Look at the scale of each track: CUT&Tag peaks reach several thousand CPM because almost all fragments are in peaks; the ChIP input has reads in every bin. The IgG track is sparse (2 544 distinct fragments on chr21). Note also the small H3K27me3 ChIP bump at the IFNAR1 promoter (~33.32 Mb), where CUT&Tag has nothing: active promoters often show up weakly in ChIP of any mark because open chromatin shears and is recovered more easily. The CUT&Tag numbers are what remained of whole libraries of 1.6 M (H3K4me3) and 3.0 M (H3K27me3) read pairs; ENCODE’s ChIP libraries had 6.9 M and 9.3 M filtered reads.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Fragment sizes


The enzyme cuts where it can reach DNA: linkers. Histone-mark libraries are a nucleosome ladder; TF CUT&RUN libraries are dominated by short fragments (< 120 bp) protected by the factor.
Tn5 also reaches DNA on the nucleosome surface where it faces outwards, once per helical turn: a 10-bp ripple in CUT&Tag.


Paired-end sequencing gives the fragment length of every molecule, so the fragment-length distribution is the first QC plot. For a histone mark you expect the mono-nucleosome peak at about 150–200 bp (the 147 bp of nucleosomal DNA plus some linker), and di- and tri-nucleosomes. In CUT&Tag the measured length includes no adapter, but the Tn5 duplication of 9 bp makes each fragment 9 bp longer than the DNA between the two cuts. For transcription factors, CUT&RUN fragments of 50–120 bp come from MNase cutting close to the bound factor; selecting short fragments (< 120 bp) sharpens TF peaks, and the footprint of the factor can be seen at base-pair resolution (Skene & Henikoff 2017). The 10-bp periodicity is the same phenomenon as in ATAC-seq: on a nucleosome, the DNA backbone faces outwards once per ~10.4 bp, which is where Tn5 can insert.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Real data: fragment-length distribution


Median fragment length: H3K4me3 252 bp, H3K27me3 229 bp, IgG 330 bp.
H3K27me3: mono-nucleosome peak at ~200 bp, di-nucleosomes at ~390 bp, and a 10.3-bp ripple across the mono-nucleosome peak; only 6% of fragments are < 120 bp.


Left: fragment-length distributions of the three libraries on chr21 (5-bp smoothing). The peaks are a little longer than 147 bp plus a short linker because Tn5 duplicates 9 bp at each insertion and cuts a few bases into the linker. H3K4me3 has more short fragments (12% < 120 bp) than H3K27me3 (6%): at active promoters there is a nucleosome-free region. The IgG (2 544 fragments after removing duplicates) is broad and noisy, with more long fragments: untethered cutting is not anchored to one nucleosome. Right: a zoom on the H3K27me3 mono-nucleosome peak with 3-bp smoothing; the strongest periodic component of the detrended histogram has a period of 10.3 bp, the helical repeat of DNA on the nucleosome surface. For a TF CUT&RUN library you would instead see most fragments below 120 bp. With single-end ChIP-seq (the ENCODE data we compare with) the length of each molecule is unknown.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: Processing: the same building blocks, different settings
text:
Processing: the same building blocks, different settings


Bowtie2 end-to-end, --very-sensitive, fragments 10–700 bp, --no-mixed --no-discordant: only properly aligned pairs.
A second alignment to the E. coli genome counts the spike-in.


This follows the Henikoff-lab CUT&Tag data-processing tutorial (Zheng, Ahmad and Henikoff, protocols.io) and nf-core/cutandrun. For these 25-bp reads we follow the tutorial and omit adapter trimming. Adapter read-through can occur for fragments shorter than 25 bp; the 10-bp minimum does not exclude all such fragments, although end-to-end alignment rejects many adapter-contaminated reads. Inspect the read QC rather than assuming short reads never need trimming. With longer reads (e.g. 2 × 150) you must trim Nextera adapters, just as for ATAC-seq, because many CUT&Tag fragments are shorter than the read. The E. coli alignment uses two more options (–no-overlap –no-dovetail) to avoid counting human reads that happen to align to E. coli. The filters after alignment are those of From reads to coverage for enrichment assays: MAPQ ≥ 30 and proper pairs. Duplicates are the step that differs, next slide.

text:
Align, filter, count
bowtie2 -p 8 --end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-mixed --no-discordant -I 10 -X 700 \
        -x hg38_chr21_chrM -1 R1.fastq.gz -2 R2.fastq.gz 2> h3k27me3.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - | samtools sort -o h3k27me3.raw.bam
samtools view -u -q 30 -f 2 -F 1804 h3k27me3.raw.bam chr21 | ... \
  | samtools markdup -s - h3k27me3.bam            # mark duplicates, keep them

Our FASTQ files contain only the pairs that aligned to chr21 or chrM in the full genome, plus the E. coli pairs; that is why 98–100% of the human pairs align again, and why 26% of the IgG pairs do not (they are E. coli). After MAPQ ≥ 30, proper pairs and chr21: 17 380 H3K4me3, 45 130 H3K27me3 and 16 941 IgG fragments. The original whole libraries contained 1.58 M H3K4me3 and 2.98 M H3K27me3 read pairs before our filtering: typical CUT&Tag sequencing depths. The chr21 fraction of enriched reads depends on the mark, so multiplying chr21 counts by the inverse chromosome-size fraction would not reliably estimate usable whole-genome fragments. The duplication rates of the two marks are low (5–7%) because these libraries were sequenced far from saturation; the IgG is 85% duplicates. The filter chain is the one of From reads to coverage for enrichment assays; markdup without -r only marks duplicates.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Duplicates are expected


Few cells, few molecules: a library from 104–105 cells saturates quickly; extra sequencing re-reads the same fragments.
Tethered Tn5 cuts the same linkers in different cells: identical coordinates do not prove a PCR copy.
Henikoff-lab advice: keep duplicates for abundant histone marks; remove them for IgG, TFs and low-input samples.


In ChIP-seq, two reads at exactly the same position are almost always PCR copies, because sonication cuts randomly and the library contains millions of distinct molecules. In CUT&Tag both assumptions fail. Cutting is not random: Tn5 tethered to a given nucleosome reaches only a few linker positions, so different cells give the same fragment. And the number of distinct molecules is small, because there are few cells and the enzyme makes few cuts. High duplication is therefore expected and is not by itself a sign of a bad library. It still tells you about complexity: if you sequence a library to a duplication rate of 80%, more sequencing is pointless. IgG libraries are the extreme case: very few distinct molecules, so they are dominated by duplicates. The safe practice is to compute the duplication rate, keep duplicates for histone marks, and check that conclusions do not change if they are removed.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Real data: duplication and depth


Marks: 5–7% duplicates (sequenced far from saturation). IgG: 85%: few distinct molecules, so we remove its duplicates.
The IgG also has 9.2% of its pairs on chrM and 3.6% from E. coli: little tethered human DNA, so carry-over and accessible DNA dominate.


A: the fraction of chr21 fragments marked as duplicates (same start and end). B: pairs on chrM as a fraction of the whole library (0.03% H3K27me3, 0.26% H3K4me3, 9.2% IgG): mitochondrial DNA is nucleosome-free and abundant, and untethered pA–Tn5 inserts there just like Tn5 in ATAC-seq. C: E. coli pairs as a fraction of the library. All three panels say the same about the IgG: without a tethered target, the reaction produces few human fragments, so whatever else is in the tube (carry-over DNA, open chromatin, mtDNA) makes up the library, and PCR copies of the few molecules make up most of the reads. For the two marks the duplication rates are low; the argument of the previous slide (identical fragments can be real) matters for deeply sequenced libraries.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: A spike-in for free: E. coli carry-over
text:
A spike-in for free: E. coli carry-over


pA–Tn5 and pA–MNase are made in E. coli; a little bacterial DNA comes with the enzyme and is tagmented too.
Same enzyme batch, same amount per reaction → E. coli reads act as an internal ruler. Scale factor ∝ 1 / (E. coli fragments).


Why a spike-in at all: CPM normalisation assumes that the total amount of signal is the same in every sample. Treat cells with an EZH2 inhibitor and H3K27me3 falls everywhere; every sample is still sequenced to the same depth, so CPM hides most of the loss (here 909 vs 800, −12%, while the truth is −60%). A spike-in that is added in the same amount to every reaction rescales the samples: the fraction of spike-in reads goes up when the target goes down. In the Henikoff tutorial the scale factor is S = C / (number of E. coli fragments), with C an arbitrary constant such as 10 000, and the normalised track is the fragment coverage × S. For CUT&RUN, the original protocol added a defined amount of yeast or Drosophila DNA, and the carry-over E. coli DNA from the pA–MNase preparation was later shown to work as well (Meers et al. 2019). The full treatment of normalisation under global changes, including spike-in normalisation for ChIP-seq, is in Annotation and differential binding.
