The IgG has ~250 times more E. coli than the marks: it makes few human fragments, so the same carry-over is a large share.
The ruler only works if every reaction got the same amount of enzyme from the same batch. Check the spike-in fraction, do not trust it blindly.


E. coli pairs were counted by aligning all read pairs to the E. coli K-12 genome (U00096.3) with the Henikoff-lab settings; our FASTQ files contain all of them, so these are whole-library numbers. According to the Henikoff tutorial, the E. coli fraction ranges from about 0.01% to 10% in typical H3K27me3 CUT&Tag of 65 000 K562 cells; ours are at the low end. The scale factor is S = 10 000 / E. coli pairs. Two points. First, these samples are different antibodies, so their spike-in-scaled signals are not comparable; spike-in scaling is for the same mark across conditions. Second, it assumes every reaction got the same amount of E. coli DNA; with different enzyme batches or amounts, or very different cell numbers, the factors reflect handling. Replicates whose spike-in-scaled totals agree are the best check. Commercial kits now often add a defined spike-in (E. coli DNA of known amount, or barcoded designer nucleosomes) instead of relying on carry-over.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: IgG: what the negative control measures
text:
IgG: what the negative control measures


A non-specific IgG brings pA–Tn5 nowhere in particular: what remains is untethered cutting, mostly in open chromatin (promoters).
It is sparse (2 544 distinct fragments on chr21), so it cannot be used like a ChIP input for a local λ, but it shows where false peaks would be.


Profile of fragment centres around the 290 active protein-coding TSSs on chr21 (TSSs in an ENCODE H3K4me3 peak and without H3K27me3 within 2 kb), in 500-bp bins, as enrichment over a uniform distribution. The deduplicated IgG is 8 times enriched within ± 500 bp of active TSSs (the peak bin about 10 times); the ChIP input is almost flat (1.06 times). The IgG shows where untethered or non-specifically bound pA–Tn5 cuts: accessible DNA, as in ATAC-seq. That is why the IgG is the right control for CUT&Tag: it shows the background that a target’s peaks have to beat. It also shows its limits: with a few thousand fragments it cannot give a smooth local background, the motivation for SEACR on the next slides. A no-antibody control, or ATAC-seq of the same cells, shows the same thing.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Peak calling on sparse data

MACS3 models background with a Poisson λ estimated from a control or from the sample’s neighbourhood (Peak calling). In CUT&Tag most of the genome has zero reads: λ is tiny, so almost any pile-up looks significant, and the control is too sparse to estimate λ well.
SEACR (Meers, Tenenbaum & Henikoff 2019) avoids the background model: it works on blocks of contiguous signal and asks how much signal a block must contain to be more typical of the target than of the IgG.
Both are used: nf-core/cutandrun runs SEACR by default and MACS3 as an option.


This slide is text because the point is conceptual. Recall the MACS logic: at each position compare the pileup k with λ_local = max(λ_BG, λ_1k, λ_5k, λ_10k). With 300 000 fragments on chr21, λ_BG is about 300 000 × 200 / (4 × 10^7) ≈ 1.5 for a 200-bp window, and in large regions the local windows are empty. A dozen fragments is then extremely significant, which is right for strong peaks but also lets through small piles of untethered cutting at open chromatin. MACS3 still works on CUT&Tag data, especially with the IgG as control and a strict cutoff; many published analyses use it. SEACR was designed for exactly this situation and is the method the CUT&RUN/Tag developers recommend; it has two settings (stringent, relaxed) and either an IgG control or a fixed top fraction.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
SEACR: thresholds from signal blocks


A block = a run of non-zero coverage in the bedGraph; its AUC = total signal in it.
Threshold t: where the fraction of blocks above t that are target (not IgG) blocks is highest (stringent), or at the knee below it (relaxed).


Walk through it. Panel A: target and IgG bedGraphs are cut into blocks wherever the coverage drops to zero, and each block gets an AUC (the sum of coverage times bp). Panel B: for every possible AUC threshold t, SEACR counts the target blocks above t and the IgG blocks above t, and computes the fraction that are target blocks. At low t many IgG blocks pass; at high t almost only target blocks do. The stringent threshold is the t with the highest fraction (1 minus that fraction is reported as an empirical FDR); the relaxed threshold is lower, roughly at the knee of the curve. Panel C: blocks above the threshold are merged when they are closer than a tenth of the mean block width, and blocks that overlap an IgG block above the threshold are removed. Without an IgG, SEACR keeps the top fraction of blocks by AUC (e.g. 0.01 = top 1%). With “norm”, SEACR rescales the IgG to the target before comparing; use “non” only if the tracks are already normalised (for example with the spike-in). Because blocks are defined by contiguous non-zero coverage, SEACR works best on sparse data: very deep data turn the whole genome into one block.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Running SEACR and MACS3
# fragments -> bedGraph (zero-coverage regions omitted)
bedtools genomecov -bg -i h3k4me3.frag.bed -g chrom.sizes > h3k4me3.bedgraph
# SEACR: with the IgG as control, or the top 1% of blocks
bash SEACR_1.3.sh h3k4me3.bedgraph igg.bedgraph norm stringent h3k4me3_seacr_igg
bash SEACR_1.3.sh h3k4me3.bedgraph 0.01 non stringent h3k4me3_seacr_top1
# MACS3 on the fragments, IgG as control
macs3 callpeak -t h3k4me3.bam -c igg.bam -f BAMPE -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 -n h3k4me3_macs

SEACR output: one line per region, with total signal (AUC), maximum and the position of the maximum.


The SEACR script is a bash wrapper around an R script (github.com/FredHutch/SEACR); it needs bedtools and R on the PATH. The bedGraph is made from the fragment BED (one line per read pair, from the leftmost to the rightmost base), so the signal is fragment coverage, as for paired-end ChIP. For H3K27me3 we call MACS3 in –broad mode, as for broad ChIP-seq marks (Peak calling). –keep-dup all because we kept the duplicates on purpose. Each call takes seconds on chr21.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Real data: SEACR vs MACS3


H3K4me3: SEACR (IgG) 135 and MACS3 128 peaks, ~87% in ENCODE peaks, FRiP 0.91–0.94. “Top 1%” keeps only 8: 1% of just 980 signal blocks.
H3K27me3: SEACR (IgG) is the most sensitive (77% of ENCODE regions found) but least precise (44% in ENCODE); MACS3 --broad lies in between.


Six calls on the same chr21 data, scored against ENCODE’s ChIP peaks for the same mark (492 H3K4me3 and 1 451 H3K27me3 regions on chr21). For the sharp mark, the two callers agree closely. For the broad mark the result depends strongly on the settings: the deduplicated IgG is so sparse (2 544 fragments) that SEACR’s threshold ends up low and many small blocks pass; the top-1% rule keeps only the 62 strongest domains, which are all in ENCODE’s set but miss most of it. MACS3 in broad mode is in between. The top-1% number depends on how many blocks there are, i.e. on depth and on the size of the genome analysed: on chr21 alone 1% is very few; on a whole genome the same rule gives thousands. Lesson: compare callers in a browser, and report the caller, its settings and the control in the methods.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Signal-to-noise: FRiP and the fingerprint


FRiP in the same ENCODE peaks: H3K4me3 0.88 CUT&Tag vs 0.33 ChIP; H3K27me3 0.23 vs 0.084. Controls: IgG 0.033, input 0.032 (no enrichment: 0.012).
Fingerprint: CUT&Tag puts 90% (H3K4me3) and 30% (H3K27me3) of its reads in the top 1% of 5-kb bins; ChIP 23% and 6%, input 3%.


The fair comparison uses one reference set of peaks for both assays: ENCODE’s ChIP peaks, which if anything favours ChIP. Each read or fragment is counted once, at its centre. A: the fingerprint (the logic of deepTools plotFingerprint): sort 5-kb bins by count and plot the cumulative fraction of reads. A library without enrichment follows the diagonal; the more the curve bends to the bottom right, the more of the reads sit in a few bins. The CUT&Tag curves are flat for most of chr21 because most bins have no fragments at all; the ChIP curves sit close to the input. The IgG also looks concentrated (13% of reads in the top 1% of bins): sparse data look enriched, which is why the fingerprint is read together with the control. B: FRiP. The broad mark has lower FRiP in both assays because ENCODE’s narrow peaks capture only part of the broad domains.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: How many reads do you need?
text:
How many reads do you need?


H3K27me3: CUT&Tag finds 54% of the ENCODE regions with 45 000 fragments; ChIP needs ~110 000 reads for the same (47% at 90 000, 65% at 140 000).
H3K4me3: CUT&Tag finds the strong promoter peaks (91% of the strongest quarter) with a few thousand fragments, then levels off at ~32%: it does not see the weak, mostly distal ENCODE peaks.


Both libraries were subsampled to the same number of reads (fragments) on chr21, five times each; a peak counts as detected if it has more reads than expected (p < 0.001) from the library’s own background density outside all ENCODE peaks. The H3K27me3 panel is the textbook result: at equal depth CUT&Tag detects far more, and ChIP needs about 2.5 times as many reads to catch up. The H3K4me3 panel is the honest complication. ENCODE’s set includes many weak peaks (median 9–14 ChIP reads, mostly away from TSSs); the CUT&Tag library has almost no fragments there even at full depth, so more sequencing would not help much. These may be weak real H3K4me3 sites that this low-input library cannot reach, partly ChIP background, or differences between two K562 cultures in two labs. This is one library of 1.6 M pairs, made for a methods paper. Scaled to the genome (chr21 ≈ 1.5%), 45 000 chr21 fragments correspond to about 3 M fragments, 110 000 ChIP reads to about 7 M.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
The open-chromatin bias of Tn5


Tn5 that is free or loosely bound prefers accessible DNA, so CUT&Tag can show small peaks at active promoters for any target, including repressive marks.
High-salt washes reduce it; IgG, ATAC-seq or ChIP of the same mark reveal it.


Tn5 is the ATAC-seq enzyme: wherever it is not tethered, it inserts into nucleosome-free DNA. Kaya-Okur et al. 2019 introduced the 300 mM NaCl washes to remove unbound pA–Tn5 for exactly this reason; the same group later turned the effect into an assay (CUTAC: low-salt tagmentation with an H3K4me2 antibody maps accessibility, Henikoff et al. 2020). Wang & Zhang (2021, preprint) argued that Tn5-based profiling methods in general carry an open-chromatin bias, most visible for marks and factors with weak signal. Be balanced: for abundant histone marks the bias is small relative to the true signal; for sparse targets, and in single-cell CUT&Tag where every cell has very few fragments, it matters more. The practical consequences: do not interpret small CUT&Tag peaks at active promoters for a repressive mark without checking IgG and a second method, and use the IgG to remove open-chromatin peaks.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
section: Real data: H3K27me3 at active promoters
text:
Real data: H3K27me3 at active promoters


IgG: 8.1× enriched at active promoters (input 1.06×): untethered pA–Tn5 does go to open chromatin.
H3K27me3 CUT&Tag: 0.25× at active promoters (ChIP 0.29×) and 21× at Polycomb-marked promoters (ChIP 2.1×). In this abundant-mark, high-salt dataset the bias is swamped by the true signal.


Enrichment of read centres within ± 500 bp of 290 active TSSs and of 47 TSSs inside ENCODE H3K27me3 peaks on chr21, relative to a uniform distribution (log scale). This is the balanced view: the open-chromatin bias is real and visible in the IgG, but for H3K27me3 with 300 mM salt washes it does not create H3K27me3 signal at active promoters; CUT&Tag is depleted there just like ChIP. The bias becomes a problem when the tethered signal is weak relative to the untethered background: rare marks, weak antibodies, very few cells, single cells, and transcription factors whose sites are themselves in open chromatin (where a TF peak and an accessibility peak cannot be told apart without controls). Check with the IgG, with ATAC-seq of the same cells, and where possible with ChIP or CUT&RUN.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
QC for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag

The left column refers to Experimental design and QC for epigenomic assays and the ChIP-seq units. Most rows change because of the chemistry. A useful extra QC in CUT&Tag is the fraction of reads in known open chromatin (e.g. in ATAC-seq peaks of the same cell type) for a target that should not be there; and, as always, two biological replicates whose signal correlates in genomic bins. ENCODE’s FRiP threshold of 1% was made for ChIP; for CUT&Tag of abundant marks a FRiP far above that is expected, and a FRiP close to the IgG’s is a failed experiment.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Production pipelines

nf-core/cutandrun (Nextflow): trimming, Bowtie2 to the genome and to a spike-in genome, duplicate marking (removed only for the IgG by default), spike-in or CPM scaling, SEACR and/or MACS2 peaks, IgG-based filtering, FRiP and fragment QC, a MultiQC report.
The Henikoff-lab CUT&Tag data processing and analysis tutorial (Zheng, Ahmad & Henikoff, protocols.io): the steps of this lecture, one by one.

nextflow run nf-core/cutandrun -profile singularity --input samplesheet.csv \
    --genome GRCh38 --outdir results --peakcaller seacr,macs2

The pipeline is described in Hodgetts et al., JOSS 2026. Its sample sheet has one line per FASTQ pair with a group, a replicate number and the name of the control group (the IgG). As always with nf-core: run it once on the cluster with a container profile, read the MultiQC report, and know what each step does, which is what the exercise is for. Defaults change between versions; check the documentation of the version you run and report it in the methods.

text:

Tn5 open-chromatin bias
IgG, ATAC-seq, ChIP of the same mark


CUT&Tag for a weakly bound TF
high-salt washes strip it
CUT&RUN or ChIP


over-sequencing
90% duplicates, no new information
look at saturation; pool libraries sensibly




Each row is a mistake seen in published work or in the methods sections of papers. Ask students which of them they could detect from the fragment-length plot, the duplication rate, the IgG track or the E. coli fraction alone.

title: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Summary







topic
key idea




principle
antibody-tethered enzyme cuts in situ; uncut DNA never enters the library


CUT&RUN
pA–MNase + Ca2+, fragments diffuse out; good for TFs


CUT&Tag
pA–Tn5 with adapters + Mg2+, PCR directly; good for histone marks, low input


data
2–8 M reads, high FRiP, fragment ladder, many (often real) duplicates


spike-in
E. coli carry-over DNA: scale factor ∝ 1 / E. coli fragments


control
IgG: sparse, shows untethered (open-chromatin) cutting


peaks
SEACR: AUC threshold from target vs IgG blocks; MACS3 also used


caveats
Tn5 open-chromatin bias; salt washes vs TF binding; small reference data sets




Students should leave able to: explain why the background is low, read a fragment-length plot of a CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag library, decide whether duplicates should be removed, compute a spike-in scale factor and say when it is valid, explain the SEACR threshold, compute FRiP and judge a claim based on small CUT&Tag peaks at active promoters.

title: Quiz: combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Short questions on binarisation, hidden Markov models and chromatin-state annotations. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A bin has these marks present: H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, nothing else. Another has H3K4me1 only. A third has H3K4me3 and H3K27me3. Name the likely element for each.






Answer





Active enhancer (EnhA); weak or primed enhancer (EnhWk); bivalent promoter (TssBiv), typical of developmental genes in stem cells, or of a mixture of cells in which the promoter is active in some and Polycomb-repressed in others.




Q2. A mark has on average 0.5 reads per 200-bp bin on a chromosome. In a bin with normal input coverage, how many reads are needed to call the mark present at \(P(X \ge k) < 10^{-4}\)? Use \(P(X \ge 5 \mid 0.5) = 1.7 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(P(X \ge 6 \mid 0.5) = 1.4 \times 10^{-5}\). What happens in a bin where the input is three times its average?






Hint





With control data, λ is the mark’s mean multiplied by the local input enrichment.









Answer





k* = 6 reads (\(P(X \ge 5) = 1.7 \times 10^{-4}\) is not below \(10^{-4}\), \(P(X \ge 6) = 1.4 \times 10^{-5}\) is). With three times the input, λ = 1.5 and the threshold rises (to 9 reads), so regions with high background (amplifications, artefact-prone repeats) need more reads before a mark is called.




Q3. In a ChromHMM model, state 4 has emission probabilities H3K4me3 0.02, H3K27ac 0.05, H3K4me1 0.10, H3K36me3 0.85, H3K27me3 0.01, H3K9me3 0.03. Compute the probability of a bin with only H3K36me3 present under state 4. What is the state?






Answer





\(0.98 \times 0.95 \times 0.90 \times 0.85 \times 0.99 \times 0.97 = 0.68\). Transcribed gene body (Tx).




Q4. What does the transition matrix of a chromatin-state HMM tell you? Give one biologically expected pattern.






Answer





For each state, the probability that the next 200-bp bin is in each state. Most of the probability is on the diagonal (states extend over many bins). Off the diagonal, expected neighbours: active TSS next to TSS-flanking states and those next to transcribed states (promoter → gene body); enhancer states next to weak enhancer states; Polycomb states next to quiescent ones.




Q5. A toy HMM has two states, A and Q, start probabilities 0.5/0.5, P(mark | A) = 0.8, P(mark | Q) = 0.1, and P(stay) = 0.9. The first two bins are 1, 0. Compute the forward probabilities \(\alpha_2(A)\) and \(\alpha_2(Q)\).






Hint





\(\alpha_1(s) = \pi_s\, P(o_1 \mid s)\); \(\alpha_2(s) = \left[\sum_r \alpha_1(r)\, a_{rs}\right] P(o_2 \mid s)\).









Answer





\(\alpha_1(A) = 0.5 \times 0.8 = 0.4\), \(\alpha_1(Q) = 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.05\). \(\alpha_2(A) = (0.4 \times 0.9 + 0.05 \times 0.1) \times 0.2 = 0.073\); \(\alpha_2(Q) = (0.4 \times 0.1 + 0.05 \times 0.9) \times 0.9 = 0.0765\). The total probability of the observations “1, 0” is 0.1495, and P(bin 2 in Q | bins 1–2) = 0.0765/0.1495 = 0.51.




Q6. Why can’t you choose the number of states by picking the model with the highest likelihood?






Answer





A model with more states can always fit the data at least as well (it contains the smaller one as a special case), so the likelihood keeps increasing with K. Penalised criteria such as BIC still choose very many states on genome-sized data. In practice one chooses the smallest K whose states are interpretable, distinct and reproducible, often by comparing a series of models (ChromHMM’s CompareModels).




Q7. A state covers 2% of the genome and 0.5% of chr21 bins overlap a RefSeq TSS. 18% of TSS bins are in that state. Compute the fold enrichment of the state at TSSs.






Answer





Fold enrichment = (fraction of TSS bins in the state) / (fraction of all bins in the state) = 0.18 / 0.02 = 9. (The 0.5% is not needed: it would be needed for the reverse question, what fraction of the state’s bins are at TSSs: 0.18 × 0.005 / 0.02 = 4.5%.)




Q8. What is the difference between a concatenated and a stacked ChromHMM model? Which would you use to ask “which enhancers are active in B cells but not in T cells”?






Answer





Concatenated: one set of states learned from all cell types together, with a separate segmentation per cell type (state definitions shared). Stacked: the marks of all cell types are the observation of one model, which gives one segmentation of the genome whose states encode patterns across cell types. Both can answer the question: with a concatenated model, find bins in an enhancer state in B cells and another state in T cells; a stacked model may directly have a “B-cell-only enhancer” state.




Q9. A paper reports: “the risk variant lies in an active-enhancer state in GM12878 (Roadmap E116), so it disrupts an enhancer of the nearest gene, IKZF3.” List what has and has not been shown.






Answer





Shown: the chromatin at the variant in a lymphoblastoid cell line looks like an active enhancer (H3K4me1 + H3K27ac). Not shown: that the element is a functional enhancer, that it regulates IKZF3 (the nearest gene is often not the target), that the variant changes its activity (allele-specific signal, reporter assays, CRISPR editing), or that GM12878 is the relevant cell type for the disease. The causal variant may also be another one in linkage disequilibrium.




Q10. Give two reasons why two ChromHMM segmentations of the same cell type, from two labs, can differ.






Answer





Different sequencing depth (deeper data → more bins pass the Poisson threshold), different antibodies or protocols (different efficiency per mark), a different set of marks, different binarisation thresholds or bin sizes, a different number of states or a different local optimum of the EM, and different cell populations (culture conditions, passage, mixtures).

title: Exercise: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Background
Bins and binarisation. The genome is cut into 200-bp bins. For each mark, a bin is called 1 if its read count \(k\) is improbably high under a Poisson background: \(P(X \ge k \mid \lambda) < 10^{-4}\). Without a control, λ is the mark’s mean count per bin; with an input control, ChromHMM multiplies it by the local input enrichment (input reads in the bin ± 5 bins, plus a pseudocount, relative to the input’s mean).
The HMM. Each bin has a hidden state \(s_t\). The model has initial probabilities \(\pi_s\), transition probabilities \(a_{rs} = P(s_{t+1} = s \mid s_t = r)\), and for each state and mark an emission probability \(e_{sm} = P(\text{mark } m \text{ present} \mid s)\). Marks are independent given the state:
\[P(o_t \mid s) = \prod_m e_{sm}^{\,o_{tm}} (1 - e_{sm})^{1 - o_{tm}}\]
Forward (probability of the data): \(\alpha_1(s) = \pi_s P(o_1 \mid s)\); \(\alpha_t(s) = \big[\sum_r \alpha_{t-1}(r)\, a_{rs}\big] P(o_t \mid s)\); \(P(o_{1..T}) = \sum_s \alpha_T(s)\).
Viterbi (best state path): the same with max instead of sum, \(\delta_t(s) = \max_r [\delta_{t-1}(r)\, a_{rs}]\, P(o_t \mid s)\); remember the best \(r\) and trace back from the best final state.
Fold enrichment of state \(s\) for an annotation \(A\) = (fraction of \(A\)’s bins that are in \(s\)) / (fraction of all bins that are in \(s\)).

title: Exercise: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Explore: transitions versus emissions
The demo is a small ChromHMM-style model: three hidden states, TSS (active promoter), Tx (transcribed gene body) and Pc (Polycomb-repressed), along 150 bins of 200 bp. Each state emits four binary marks, independently given the state, with the probabilities in the emission table (presets or sliders). The true self-transition is the probability that the next bin stays in the same state (the rest is split evenly between the other two states); it is used to generate the simulated sequence: first the hidden states, then the marks of each bin (top four rows). The model then forgets the true states and decodes the marks three ways, all with the same emissions: Viterbi (the single most probable path), the posterior P(state | all marks) from the forward–backward algorithm (stacked colours; the most probable state per bin is what ChromHMM reports), and emissions only (each bin gets the state that best explains its own marks). The decoder has its own decoder self-transition; at 1/3 it has no preference for staying, and Viterbi becomes the same as emissions only. Black ticks under a strip mark wrongly decoded bins. New sequence draws new random numbers; any other change re-simulates with the same random numbers.



E1. With the default settings (clear marks, both self-transitions 0.9), how many bins does each method decode correctly, and how many segments does each path have? Look at the emissions-only strip inside the long transcribed region (5–15 kb): which state does it give to bins with no mark at all? Compute P(no marks | state) for the three states from the emission table to explain it, and say why Viterbi does not do the same.
E2. Press 1/3 (emissions only), then move the decoder self-transition to 0.6, 0.9 and 0.99. For each, note the Viterbi accuracy, the number of Viterbi segments and log P(marks | decoder). At which value is log P highest? Try 0.925 too. What does this suggest about how the transition probabilities can be learned?
E3. Choose noisy marks (decoder 0.9). Compare the three methods. Then set the decoder to 1/3 and to 0.99. When do transitions matter most, and what goes wrong when the decoder is too sticky?
E4. Choose clear marks again and set the true self-transition to 0.6 (short elements), keeping the decoder at 0.9. Compare Viterbi with emissions only. Then press = true (decoder 0.6). Which decoder setting fits these data better, by accuracy and by log P?






Solutions





E1. Correct: Viterbi 96%, posterior 98%, emissions only 79%; segments: true 12, Viterbi 10, posterior 12, emissions only 55. Unmarked bins in the gene body are called Pc by emissions only: P(no marks | Pc) = 0.90 × 0.98 × 0.97 × 0.35 = 0.299, P(no marks | Tx) = 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.30 × 0.97 = 0.249, P(no marks | TSS) = 0.15 × 0.25 × 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.034. A bin without H3K36me3 is slightly better explained by Pc, whose only common mark (H3K27me3) is also absent. Viterbi keeps such bins in Tx: switching Tx → Pc → Tx costs two transition factors of (1 − 0.9)/2 = 0.05, against staying (0.9 × 0.9), which is far more than the 0.299/0.249 = 1.2-fold gain in the emission. This is the toy example of the lecture with real-looking marks: one missed mark does not split an element.

At 1/3, Viterbi is identical to emissions only (55 segments). Raising the self-transition smooths the path. Log P is highest near the true value: the maximum is at about 0.925, the fraction of steps that stay in this particular sequence (138 of 149, 12 segments). Choosing the transitions that make the observed marks most probable recovers how long the elements really are: that is what Baum–Welch does when it learns the transition matrix.
E3. With noisy marks (decoder 0.9): Viterbi 85% (8 segments), posterior 89% (12), emissions only 49% (84 segments). Single bins are now unreliable, so the neighbours carry most of the information: transitions matter most when the emissions are weak. At decoder 1/3 all methods drop to 49%. At 0.99 the decoder is too sticky: Viterbi merges real elements into 3 segments and falls to 70% (log P −326.8, worse than −321.6 at 0.9).
E4. With true self-transition 0.6 the sequence has 70 segments. A decoder at 0.9 over-smooths: Viterbi 82% (43 segments), worse than emissions only (87%, 76 segments). With = true (0.6), Viterbi reaches 90% (57 segments), and log P rises from −347.6 to −313.2. The transition matrix must describe the data: if it assumes longer elements than exist, the HMM erases short ones (such as a short enhancer between two other states). ChromHMM learns the transitions from the data for this reason.

text:
In R
You need GenomicRanges, rtracklayer and ggplot2. Work in the same folder:

R1 — Which mark combinations occur?

sum(head(nz, 10)) / sum(nz)

How many of the 64 possible combinations occur at least once? What fraction of bins has no mark?
Among bins with at least one mark, what fraction is covered by the ten most common combinations? Decode the top five (the string is H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3).



R2 — Name the states and compare with Roadmap
seg <- import("model_8/GM12878_8_segments.bed", format = "bed")
rm  <- import(file.path(D, "roadmap_E116_18state_hg38.bed.gz"), format = "bed")
rm  <- rm[seqnames(rm) == "chr21"]
bins <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(seq(1, by = 200, length.out = nrow(b)), width = 200))   # ChromHMM's bins, in file order
bins$ours <- seg$name[findOverlaps(bins, seg, select = "first")]
mid <- resize(bins, 1, fix = "center")
bins$rm <- rm$name[findOverlaps(mid, rm, select = "first")]
ct <- table(ours = bins$ours, roadmap = bins$rm)
round(100 * prop.table(ct, 1), 1)          # for each of our states: % of its bins in each Roadmap state
round(100 * prop.table(table(bins$ours)), 2)

For each of your states, which Roadmap state does it overlap most, and with what percentage? Write down a mapping (e.g. E1 → TssA).
Which of your states are “pure” (most bins in one Roadmap state) and which are mixtures? Why can an 8-state model not reproduce 18 states?
What fraction of chr21 is in your quiescent state(s), and in Roadmap’s 18_Quies?



R3 — Enrichment at TSSs, done by hand
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(resize(tx, 1, fix = "start"))
at_tss <- overlapsAny(bins, tss)
body <- overlapsAny(bins, reduce(tx)) & !at_tss
st <- paste0("E", rownames(em))                 # state names as in the segmentation
fe <- function(sel) (table(factor(bins$ours[sel], levels = st)) / sum(sel)) /
                    (table(factor(bins$ours, levels = st)) / length(bins))
round(cbind(TSS = fe(at_tss), gene_body = fe(body)), 2)

Which states are most enriched in TSS bins and in gene-body bins? Compare with ChromHMM’s own overlap.txt (C3), which uses RefSeq instead of GENCODE.
Why is the enrichment of the quiescent state at TSSs below 1, and what is the maximum possible fold enrichment of a state?



R4 — Viterbi with the learned model
viterbi <- function(O, em, tr, init) {          # O: bins x marks (0/1); em: states x marks
  E <- as.matrix(em[, colnames(O)]); A <- log(as.matrix(tr)); K <- nrow(E); n <- nrow(O)
  le <- O %*% t(log(E)) + (1 - O) %*% t(log(1 - E))       # log P(o_t | s), n x K
  d <- matrix(0, n, K); bp <- matrix(0L, n, K)
  d[1, ] <- log(init) + le[1, ]
  for (t in 2:n) {
    cand <- d[t - 1, ] + A                                 # K x K: from r (rows) to s (cols)
    bp[t, ] <- apply(cand, 2, which.max)
    d[t, ] <- cand[cbind(bp[t, ], 1:K)] + le[t, ]
  }
  path <- integer(n); path[n] <- which.max(d[n, ])
  for (t in n:2) path[t - 1] <- bp[t, path[t]]
  path
}
O <- as.matrix(b[, colnames(em)])
init <- rep(1 / nrow(em), nrow(em))
v <- viterbi(O, em, tr, init)
ours <- as.integer(sub("E", "", bins$ours))
mean(v == ours)                                           # agreement with ChromHMM's posterior decoding
# without transitions: assign each bin its most likely state from the emissions alone
le <- O %*% t(log(as.matrix(em))) + (1 - O) %*% t(log(1 - as.matrix(em)))
nt <- apply(le, 1, which.max)
mean(nt == ours); c(segments_viterbi = sum(diff(v) != 0) + 1, segments_no_transitions = sum(diff(nt) != 0) + 1)

How often does your Viterbi path agree with ChromHMM’s assignment (which uses the posterior of each bin)? Why are they not identical?
How many segments does the Viterbi path have, and how many does the emission-only assignment have? What do the transitions contribute?

title: Exercise: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Poisson thresholds (B1, C1)





\(\lambda\) = reads / bins; with a control, λ is scaled by the local input enrichment. The ChromHMM manual describes BinarizeBam/BinarizeBed: options -b (bin size), -p (Poisson threshold, default 10-4), -n (read shift, default 100 bp), -u and -w (pseudocount and window of the control). The cell-mark file table has four columns: cell type, mark, read file, control file.









Hint 2 — HMM algorithms (B3, B4, R4)





Write the forward and Viterbi recursions as a table with one column per bin and one row per state. Work with probabilities on paper; in code, use logarithms (products of many small numbers underflow). Rabiner’s tutorial on HMMs (Proc IEEE 1989) is the classic reference; Ernst & Kellis 2012 and the ChromHMM manual describe the model ChromHMM uses (multivariate Bernoulli emissions).









Hint 3 — LearnModel and its outputs (C2, C3)





LearnModel [options] inputdir outputdir numstates assembly; -l restricts output to the chromosomes in a file, -p sets the number of processors, -noautoopen stops it from opening a browser. Outputs are described in the ChromHMM manual: emissions_K.txt, transitions_K.txt, *_segments.bed (chromosome, start, end, state), *_overlap.txt (fold enrichments), *_neighborhood.txt. Ernst & Kellis 2017 (Nat Protoc) discusses choosing the number of states.









Hint 4 — Roadmap states (C4, R2)





The 18-state model’s states, emissions and colours are described on the Roadmap chromatin-state page and in the Roadmap 2015 paper (Fig. 4). bedtools intersect -wo reports the number of overlapping bases as the last column. In R, findOverlaps(..., select = "first") and tile().

title: Exercise: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) 46 709 983 / 200 ≈ 233 550 bins; λ = 600 000 / 233 550 = 2.57. (b) \(k^* = 11\): \(P(X \ge 11) = 7.8 \times 10^{-5} < 10^{-4}\), while \(P(X \ge 10) = 3.4 \times 10^{-4}\) is still above. (c) λ = 5.14; the threshold rises (to 16 reads). A region with more input reads (an amplification, a repeat with mappability problems, an open region that shears easily) gives more ChIP reads without enrichment; a higher threshold avoids calling the mark there. (d) λ halves, the threshold falls a little, but the counts at true sites halve too, so fewer bins pass: the mark is called present in fewer bins (low sensitivity), most for broad, weakly enriched marks (H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3). The model then learns low emission probabilities for that mark, and states defined by it become weak or merge with “quiescent”. Unequal depth between marks or between cell types changes the states.
B2. (a) 1 active TSS (TssA); 2 active enhancer (EnhA); 3 transcribed (Tx); 4 bivalent TSS / Polycomb-associated promoter (TssBiv); 5 quiescent. (b) State 1: 0.08 × 0.85 × 0.30 × 0.97 × 0.98 × 0.99 = 0.0192. State 2: 0.95 × 0.70 × 0.92 × 0.96 × 0.99 × 0.99 = 0.576. State 2 is ~30 times more likely. (c) State 4: it is the only one with a high H3K27me3 emission. Against state 1 the H3K27me3 term is 0.85 vs 0.02, a factor of ~40; the H3K4me1 term (0.55 vs 0.30) and the missing H3K27ac (0.95 vs 0.15) also favour state 4.
B3. (a) \(\alpha_1\): A = 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, Q = 0.5 × 0.1 = 0.05. \(\alpha_2\) (observation 0): A = (0.4 × 0.9 + 0.05 × 0.1) × 0.2 = 0.073; Q = (0.4 × 0.1 + 0.05 × 0.9) × 0.9 = 0.0765. \(\alpha_3\) (observation 1): A = (0.073 × 0.9 + 0.0765 × 0.1) × 0.8 = 0.0587; Q = (0.073 × 0.1 + 0.0765 × 0.9) × 0.1 = 0.0076. (b) \(P(1,0,1) = 0.0587 + 0.0076 = 0.0663\). (c) For the last bin the backward term is 1, so \(P(s_3 = A \mid o) = 0.0587 / 0.0663 = 0.885\).
B4. (a) \(\delta_1\): A 0.4, Q 0.05. \(\delta_2\): A = max(0.4 × 0.9, 0.05 × 0.1) × 0.2 = 0.072 (from A); Q = max(0.4 × 0.1, 0.05 × 0.9) × 0.9 = 0.0405 (from Q). \(\delta_3\): A = max(0.072 × 0.9, 0.0405 × 0.1) × 0.8 = 0.0518 (from A); Q = max(0.072 × 0.1, 0.0405 × 0.9) × 0.1 = 0.0036 (from Q). (b) Best end A (0.0518), back-pointers A ← A ← A: path A A A with probability 0.0518. Brute force: AAA = 0.5 × 0.8 × 0.9 × 0.2 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.0518; next best QQQ = 0.0036 and AQQ = QQA = 0.0032; the eight paths sum to 0.0663 (B3). The 0 in the middle is explained as a missed mark, not as a switch. (c) With P(stay) = 0.6: AAA = 0.5 × 0.8 × 0.6 × 0.2 × 0.6 × 0.8 = 0.0230; AQA = 0.5 × 0.8 × 0.4 × 0.9 × 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.0461. The path becomes A Q A. P(stay) sets how strongly the model smooths along the genome: the higher it is, the longer the segments and the more isolated bins are absorbed.
B5. (a) Fraction of CpG-island bins in the state: 120 / 640 = 0.1875; fraction of all bins in the state: 1 120 / 233 549 = 0.0048; fold enrichment = 39. (b) 120 / 1 120 = 11% of the state’s bins are CpG-island bins. CpG islands are a tiny part of the genome (0.27% of bins here): a state can be 39 times enriched at them and still have most of its bins elsewhere (here in the flanks of promoters and at promoters without islands).
B6. (a) The run length is geometric with mean 1 / (1 − 0.999) = 1000 bins = 200 kb. (b) The flanks of promoters lead into active TSSs and into transcribed regions: the model has learned the typical order promoter flank → TSS → transcribed gene body; transitions record which elements are neighbours along the genome.
B7. Models with more states contain the smaller ones as special cases, so the likelihood always increases; it cannot choose K. Instead: look for the smallest model whose states are biologically distinct and interpretable (enrichments), check that states are reproducible (e.g. between replicates or chromosomes), and compare models with ChromHMM’s CompareModels (how well each state of a big model is represented in smaller ones). The Roadmap consortium chose 15 states for 5 marks and 18 for 6 marks this way.
B8. (a) Shown: in GM12878, the chromatin at the variant looks like an active enhancer (H3K4me1 + H3K27ac). Not shown: that it acts as an enhancer, that its target is the nearest gene, that the variant changes it, that GM12878 is the relevant cell type, or that this variant (and not one in LD) is causal. (b) Not shown: that the differences are biological. Different labs, antibodies, depths (10 M vs Roadmap’s subsampled depth), processing and possibly marks change binarisation and states. A fair comparison needs the same marks processed the same way at the same depth, ideally in one concatenated model, with replicates.









Solutions — command line





Numbers from our run (ChromHMM 1.28, Java 19, bedtools 2.30.0). The command-line part takes about 1.5 minutes (binarisation 12 s; learning 6 s, 15 s and 47 s for 4, 8 and 12 states).
C1. (a) Cell type, mark, read file (in the directory given as $D), control file. ChromHMM needs the chromosome lengths to know how many bins each chromosome has; with only chr21 in the file, only chr21 is binarised. (b) Bins called 1: H3K4me3 2.97%, H3K27ac 1.77%, H3K4me1 3.61%, H3K36me3 2.22%, H3K27me3 0.88%, H3K9me3 0.96%; 91.9% of the 233 549 bins have no mark at all. Reads on chr21 (replicates 1 + 2): H3K4me3 791 771, H3K27ac 141 058, H3K4me1 401 955, H3K36me3 158 528, H3K27me3 154 148, H3K9me3 285 065, input 134 625. The sharp marks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac) give strong local enrichment, so a few percent of bins pass easily. The broad marks cover more of the genome biologically (H3K36me3 over every expressed gene body, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 over large domains), but their enrichment per 200-bp bin is weak, so with ~150 000 reads only 1–2% of bins pass the Poisson threshold. This is the depth-dependence of B1(d): with replicate 1 alone, H3K36me3 was called in 0.74% of bins and H3K27me3 in 0.73%, which is why we merged two replicates.
C2. (a) From emissions_8.txt (columns in ChromHMM’s own order): E1 H3K36me3 0.34 → transcribed (Tx); E2 H3K4me1 0.71 → weak enhancer (EnhWk); E3 H3K4me1 0.96, H3K27ac 0.92, H3K4me3 0.82 → TSS-flanking/active-enhancer-like (TssFlnkU); E4 H3K4me3 0.94, H3K27ac 0.91, little H3K4me1 → active TSS (TssA); E5 H3K4me3 0.92, H3K4me1 0.71, no H3K27ac → flanking TSS (TssFlnk); E6 nothing → quiescent; E7 H3K9me3 0.37, H3K4me3 0.13 → ZNF genes and repeats / heterochromatin; E8 only H3K27me3 0.04 → weak Polycomb (ReprPCWk) or quiescent. (b) 71 iterations, final log-likelihood −63 805 (ChromHMM’s scale). It rises from −70 792 (4 states) to −63 805 (8) to −61 374 (12): always up, by less and less. (c) 4 states: active promoter/enhancer, weak H3K4me1(+H3K4me3), transcribed, quiescent; no Polycomb or heterochromatin state at all. 8 states: separates TSS from flanks, and adds H3K9me3 and weak H3K27me3 states. 12 states: two quiescent states, an H3K4me1 + H3K36me3 state (an enhancer inside a transcribed gene, Roadmap’s EnhG), several TSS-flank states, and a state with H3K9me3 together with H3K27ac/H3K4me1. More states first separate biologically meaningful classes, then start to split them into variants that are hard to interpret.
C3. (a) Fold enrichments (RefSeq annotation in ChromHMM’s COORDS): E4 is 55-fold enriched at CpG islands and 57-fold at TSSs (24-fold within 2 kb); E5 10-fold at CpG islands and 7-fold at TSSs; E3 3.6-fold at TSSs, 5.5-fold within 2 kb; E1 5.3-fold at exons and 3.0-fold over genes, but depleted at TSSs (0.34). E6 is depleted everywhere (~0.5). This supports the names: E4 active TSS, E3/E5 flanks, E1 gene bodies. (b) E4 peaks exactly at the TSS (57-fold at 0, 17 at −1 kb, 35 at +1 kb); E3 and E5 are highest about 1–2 kb on either side (E3 6.6 at −1 kb and 5.8 at +1 kb; E5 ~10 at ±1–2 kb); E1 increases downstream (0.34 at 0 → 0.72 at +2 kb) as the transcribed body begins.
C4. (a) The lifted-over Roadmap segmentation covers 35.1 Mb of chr21 (the rest is unassembled sequence or did not lift over). Of that: 18_Quies 65.9%, 13_Het 8.3%, 6_TxWk 7.5%, 17_ReprPCWk 6.4%, 5_Tx 3.7%, 12_ZNF/Rpts 2.3%, 11_EnhWk 1.9%, all promoter and enhancer states together a few percent. Quiescent dominates, as in our model. (b) E1 overlaps 5_Tx (1.22 Mb) and 6_TxWk (1.11 Mb): transcribed, as named. E3 overlaps 3_TssFlnkU (264 kb) and 9_EnhA1 (162 kb), then 8_EnhG2 and 1_TssA: an “upstream flank / active enhancer” state. E7 (R2) overlaps 12_ZNF/Rpts and 13_Het.









Solutions — R





The R part runs in about two minutes (most of it the Viterbi loop).
R1. (a) 46 of the 64 combinations occur; 91.9% of bins have no mark. (b) The ten most common combinations cover 91% of the marked bins. Top five, as % of all bins: 000100 (H3K36me3 only, 1.77%: gene bodies), 001000 (H3K4me1 only, 1.33%: weak/primed enhancers and promoter flanks), 111000 (H3K4me3 + H3K27ac + H3K4me1, 0.89%: active promoters and their flanks), 000010 (H3K27me3 only, 0.79%: Polycomb), 000001 (H3K9me3 only, 0.65%: heterochromatin). The rest are mostly variants of the promoter/enhancer combinations; impossible-looking combinations (e.g. H3K9me3 with H3K4me3) are rare.
R2. (a) E1 → 5_Tx (50%) / 6_TxWk (45%); E2 → 11_EnhWk (51%); E3 → 3_TssFlnkU (44%) / 9_EnhA1 (27%); E4 → 1_TssA (86%); E5 → 4_TssFlnkD (30%), 11_EnhWk (19%), 2_TssFlnk (19%); E6 → 18_Quies (88%); E7 → 12_ZNF/Rpts (61%) / 13_Het (27%); E8 → 18_Quies (55%) / 17_ReprPCWk (21%) / 6_TxWk (11%). (b) Pure: E4, E6, and E1 (if Tx and TxWk are counted together). Mixtures: E3 (flanking promoter and active enhancer), E5 (three flank/enhancer states), E8 (quiet with weak Polycomb). Eight states cannot carry the distinctions of eighteen; also our H3K27me3 is called in only 0.9% of bins, so our model has no strong Polycomb or bivalent state, while Roadmap learned those from many epigenomes where they are common (GM12878 itself has only 0.24% 16_ReprPC and 0.04% 14_TssBiv on chr21). (c) E6 covers 67.1% of chr21 (E8, nearly unmarked, another 21.8%); Roadmap’s 18_Quies 65.9% of the part it covers. Both say: two-thirds of the chromosome carries none of the six marks.
R3. (a) TSS bins: E4 80-fold, E5 9.6, E3 3.1, E2 2.8; gene-body bins: E1 3.7, the promoter/enhancer states 2.2–2.5 (genes are where regulatory elements are), E6 0.57. Same picture as ChromHMM’s RefSeq-based table, with slightly different numbers because GENCODE has more transcripts. (b) Quiescent bins are where no mark is, and TSSs of protein-coding genes are rarely completely unmarked; the enrichment is below 1 because the state is under-represented there. The maximum fold enrichment is 1 / (fraction of the genome in the state), reached if every annotated bin is in the state: for E4 (0.40% of chr21) that is 250.
R4. (a) 98.2% of bins get the same state. ChromHMM assigns each bin the state with the highest posterior probability (forward–backward), which is optimal bin by bin; Viterbi gives the single most probable path, optimal for the whole sequence. They differ at segment boundaries and in short ambiguous stretches. (Our Viterbi also uses uniform initial probabilities, which only affects the first bin.) (b) The Viterbi path has 3 603 segments (ChromHMM’s own segmentation has 4 064 lines); assigning each bin its best state from the emissions alone gives 18 327 segments and agrees with ChromHMM for only 73% of bins. The transitions smooth: they absorb single bins where a mark was missed or called by chance, and keep elements in one piece.

title: Exercise: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Where this leads

Epigenomics and genetic variation tests whether trait-associated variants are enriched in chromatin states of particular cell types, with proper background models.
Linking regulatory elements to genes asks which gene an enhancer state regulates.
What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works includes imputing missing marks, which is how the Roadmap 25-state model was made.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
About this lecture
Every cell in your body carries (almost) the same genome, yet a neuron and a B cell use very different genes. This lecture is about the layer of information on top of the DNA sequence that helps decide which genes a cell uses, and remembers that decision.

What “epigenetic” means, and why the word is used in two different ways.
Chromatin: how 2 m of DNA is packed into a nucleus, and why packing controls access.
Histone modifications: the marks you will map with ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag.
DNA methylation: the mark you will map with bisulfite and long-read sequencing.
How a state can be remembered through cell division.
A map of the assays in this course, and what each one measures.


This is the first unit of the course and sets up the vocabulary for everything else. Students know transcription and transcription factors from their bachelor’s; most have heard “histone” and “DNA methylation” but few can say what H3K27me3 means or why it should be heritable. The aim today is a working mental model, not a catalogue: by the end they should be able to look at a genome-browser view of a few histone marks and say “this is an active promoter, this is a repressed gene”. Every later unit builds on this.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
One genome, many cell types


A B cell, a neuron and a liver cell share the same DNA sequence, but express different sets of genes.
The identity is stable: a liver cell divides into liver cells, not neurons, long after the signal that made it a liver cell is gone.
So something besides the sequence is (1) different between cell types and (2) copied when a cell divides.


Start from the puzzle that created the field. Cell identity is both different and stable. Transcription factors explain “different”: a liver cell has liver TFs. But TF levels fluctuate and the initial signals during development are transient, so something must also remember. The two candidates we study in this course are chromatin (histones and their modifications) and DNA methylation. Exceptions to “same genome” exist (B and T cells rearrange their receptor genes, somatic mutations), but they do not explain cell identity.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
What does “epigenetic” mean?





Waddington (1940s–50s): the “epigenetic landscape”. A cell rolls downhill into one of several valleys (fates); the genes shape the landscape.
Narrow definition (Riggs et al. 1996): mitotically and/or meiotically heritable changes in gene function that cannot be explained by changes in DNA sequence.
Broad definition (Bird 2007): the structural adaptation of chromosomal regions so as to register, signal or perpetuate altered activity states.



In practice “epigenomics” means measuring chromatin and DNA methylation genome-wide, whether or not the state is heritable.


Two meanings coexist and cause confusion in papers. The narrow, classical one demands heritability: a state that is copied through cell division (mitotic) or even to offspring (meiotic) without a change in sequence. The broad one, which most genomics papers use, calls any chromatin feature “epigenetic”, including states that are rebuilt every time by transcription factors. When a paper says “epigenetic regulation”, ask which one they mean: is there evidence the state is self-perpetuating, or is it just a chromatin mark that correlates with expression? We come back to this in the unit on epigenetic inheritance. Waddington’s landscape is a metaphor, not a mechanism, but it captures the two properties from the previous slide: valleys are different (identity) and walls are high (stability).

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Two meters of DNA in a nucleus
text:
Two meters of DNA in a nucleus


A human diploid genome is 6.4 \times 10^9 bp, about 2 m of DNA, packed into a nucleus about 10 µm across.
Packing is hierarchical: DNA → nucleosomes (“beads on a string”, 11 nm) → loops and domains → chromosome territories.
Packing is not just storage: the more compact a region, the harder it is for proteins to reach the DNA.


Numbers to make it concrete: 0.34 nm per base pair, times 6.4 billion is about 2.2 m. If the nucleus were a football (22 cm), the DNA would be a thread about 40 km long. Each level of the figure is the subject of one part of the course: nucleosomes and their marks (ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq), loops, TADs and compartments (Hi-C). The 30 nm fibre found in textbooks is largely absent in living cells; we skip it. The key message is the last bullet: compaction is a regulatory layer, because a transcription factor or polymerase needs access to its sequence.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
The nucleosome





147 bp of DNA wrapped about 1.7 turns around a histone octamer: two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
Nucleosomes are separated by linker DNA (about 20–80 bp). The linker histone H1 sits where DNA enters and leaves.
Each histone has a flexible tail that sticks out of the particle. The tails carry most of the modifications.



The nucleosome core particle was solved at atomic resolution in 1997 (Luger et al.), one of the key papers. The drawing is simplified to two layers of four histones; in the real structure H3–H4 form a tetramer in the middle, flanked by two H2A–H2B dimers. DNA contacts the octamer every 10 bp or so, where the minor groove faces the histones; this is why some sequences wrap more easily than others. The tails are unstructured and accessible to enzymes, which is why they are the main target of the modifications on the next slides. H1 is not part of the core; it stabilises the more compact forms.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Nucleosomes come in a regular repeat
text:
Nucleosomes come in a regular repeat


Digest chromatin with an enzyme that cuts only linker DNA (micrococcal nuclease, MNase) and you get a ladder: about 150, 350, 550 bp …: one, two, three nucleosomes.
The step of the ladder is the nucleosome repeat length, about 190–200 bp in human cells (147 bp core + linker).
You will see the same ladder in the fragment lengths of every ATAC-seq library.


This is the 1970s experiment that showed chromatin is a repeating unit (Kornberg 1974 proposed the model). The enzyme can only reach linker DNA, so cuts fall between nucleosomes. Fragment sizes are therefore multiples of the repeat length, plus the core. The same logic underlies ATAC-seq: the Tn5 transposase also prefers linker and nucleosome-free DNA, so the fragment-length histogram of an ATAC library has a big nucleosome-free peak under 100 bp, then a mono-nucleosome peak near 200 bp, then di-nucleosomes near 400 bp. Students will compute this in the ATAC units. MNase-seq maps nucleosome positions genome-wide this way.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Nucleosomes block access; regulatory DNA is open
text:
Nucleosomes block access; regulatory DNA is open


Most of the genome is wrapped in nucleosomes. Active promoters and enhancers have a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of a few hundred bp.
Transcription factors bind in the NDR; well-positioned nucleosomes flank it (the +1 nucleosome sits just downstream of the transcription start site, TSS).
“Open” (accessible) chromatin is what ATAC-seq and DNase-seq measure: about 1–3% of the genome in a given cell type.


The NDR is the defining feature of active regulatory DNA. Most transcription factors cannot bind a motif wrapped on a nucleosome; a few “pioneer” factors can (gene-regulation unit), and they open the region for the rest. Chromatin remodelers then slide or evict nucleosomes. The +1 nucleosome is strongly positioned downstream of the TSS; the -1 nucleosome upstream. This figure is the picture students should have in mind when they look at an ATAC-seq peak: a peak is an NDR. The 1–3% number varies with cell type and peak caller, so treat it as an order of magnitude.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Histone tails carry chemical modifications


Enzymes add small groups to amino acids in the tails: acetylation (ac) and methylation (me1, me2, me3) of lysines (K), phosphorylation of serines, and more.
Over 100 different modifications are known. A handful of them are well understood and mapped routinely; those are the ones in this course.
Modifications act in two ways: they change how tightly the histone holds DNA, and they recruit proteins that recognise them.


Point at H3 and H4 tails, which carry the best-studied marks. Lysine acetylation removes the positive charge of the lysine side chain; DNA is negative, so the tail binds DNA less tightly and the chromatin loosens. Methylation does not change the charge: its effect comes almost entirely from proteins that bind methylated lysines. Ubiquitylation of H2A (H2AK119ub, by Polycomb PRC1) and H2B are on the C-terminal tails and are much larger additions. The “histone code” hypothesis (Strahl & Allis 2000) proposed that combinations of marks are read like a code; the modern view is less strict, but combinations do define chromatin states (chromatin-states unit).

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Reading the name of a histone mark
text:
Reading the name of a histone mark


H3K27me3 = histone H3, lysine (K) at position 27, tri-methylated.
H3K27ac is the same lysine, acetylated. One lysine can carry either mark but not both: the two are mutually exclusive, and they mean opposite things.
Positions count from the N-terminus of the mature histone.


A small slide but students need to be able to decode the names fluently, and it is a typical exam question. K is the one-letter code for lysine, S serine, R arginine, T threonine. me1/me2/me3 are mono-, di- and tri-methylation; a lysine can carry up to three methyl groups. H3K27 is a nice example because the same residue is either acetylated (active enhancers and promoters) or tri-methylated (Polycomb repression). Histone variants get their own names: H3.3, H2A.Z, CENP-A (later slide).

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Writers, readers and erasers


Writers add a mark: histone acetyltransferases (HATs, e.g. p300/CBP), lysine methyltransferases (e.g. EZH2, SETD2).
Erasers remove it: histone deacetylases (HDACs), lysine demethylases (e.g. KDM6/UTX).
Readers bind it and bring in other machinery: bromodomains read acetyl-lysine, chromodomains and PHD fingers read methyl-lysine.
Marks are dynamic: they are turned over by writers and erasers, some within minutes.


The writer/reader/eraser framing is the single most useful way to think about any chromatin mark. For each mark you meet in the course, ask: who writes it, who reads it, who erases it. Examples: p300/CBP write H3K27ac at enhancers; BRD4 reads it with its bromodomains and recruits the transcription machinery; HDACs erase it. EZH2 (in the PRC2 complex) writes H3K27me3; KDM6A/UTX and KDM6B/JMJD3 erase it. Many of these enzymes are drug targets (HDAC inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitors, BET inhibitors that block BRD4): see the cancer-epigenetics unit.

This table is the most important reference of the course; students should know it by heart. Read it with the figure: a gene model with promoter, an upstream enhancer, the gene body, and where each mark sits. Two pairs are worth stressing. H3K4me1 without H3K27ac marks a primed enhancer, with H3K27ac an active one (Creyghton et al. 2010; Rada-Iglesias et al. 2011). H3K4me3 is at the promoter (narrow, a few kb), H3K36me3 over the gene body (broad, as long as the gene), because SETD2 travels with elongating RNA polymerase II. The two repressive marks are different systems: H3K27me3 (Polycomb) silences developmental genes that may be needed in another cell type; H3K9me3 silences repeats and transposons, mostly permanently.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Real data: an active gene in B cells
text:
Real data: an active gene in B cells


ENCODE ChIP-seq in GM12878, a B-lymphoblastoid cell line (the course’s main dataset). Each track: enrichment over input (fold change).
H3K4me3 and H3K27ac peak at the promoter; H3K36me3 covers the gene body; H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are absent.


First look at real data, in a genome-browser layout like IGV. Explain how to read a track: x is position along the chromosome, y is how many more reads than in the input control, so a value of 1 means “no enrichment”. The gene model at the bottom shows exons as boxes and the arrow gives the direction of transcription. Point out that the H3K36me3 signal increases towards the 3’ end, as expected for a mark deposited during elongation. The H3K4me1 signal flanks the H3K4me3 peak. The figure is made by make-chromatin-figs.R from ENCODE files listed in data/manifest.tsv; students make the same plots in the exercise.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Real data: two kinds of silence
text:
Real data: two kinds of silence


Left: the HOXD cluster. Developmental genes, silent in B cells, covered by a broad H3K27me3 domain (Polycomb).
Right: a zinc-finger (ZNF) gene cluster on chr19, marked by H3K9me3 (with H3K36me3 over the gene bodies that are still transcribed).
Repressive marks form broad domains (tens to hundreds of kb), not sharp peaks: this matters for peak calling later.


The HOX genes pattern the body axis during development; in a B cell they are off, but they are kept in a repressed state that could in principle be reversed (facultative heterochromatin). H3K27me3 covers the whole cluster, more than 100 kb. The ZNF cluster is the classical place for H3K9me3 in euchromatin; the ZNF genes themselves are transcribed but their 3’ ends carry H3K9me3 together with H3K36me3, an unusual combination. Broad domains matter technically: a peak caller made for sharp TF peaks (MACS default) will cut a broad domain into many fragments, which is why the ChIP units teach broad-domain calling.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Euchromatin and heterochromatin


Euchromatin: open, gene-rich, early-replicating, where most active genes are.
Constitutive heterochromatin: compact, H3K9me3, read by HP1; repeats, pericentromeres, telomeres. The same in all cell types.
Facultative heterochromatin: H3K27me3 (Polycomb); developmental genes silenced in this cell type but active in another.


The terms date from the 1920s (Heitz), when heterochromatin was the part of the chromosome that stayed condensed and darkly stained through interphase. In modern terms it is defined by the marks. HP1 (heterochromatin protein 1) binds H3K9me3 through its chromodomain, dimerises and bridges nucleosomes, compacting the region. In the Hi-C units, heterochromatin is the B compartment, euchromatin the A compartment. In imaging, heterochromatin sits at the nuclear periphery (lamina-associated domains) and around the nucleolus.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Read–write feedback: how a mark can spread and persist
text:
Read–write feedback: how a mark can spread and persist


Some writers carry a reader for their own product. PRC2 (writer of H3K27me3) is activated when its EED subunit binds H3K27me3; SUV39H1 (writer of H3K9me3) has a chromodomain that binds H3K9me3.
A mark therefore recruits more of itself to neighbouring nucleosomes: domains spread until something stops them.
The same loop can restore a mark after it is diluted, which is the key to memory.


This is the mechanism behind both broad domains (previous slides) and inheritance (next slide). Positive feedback makes a state bistable: a region tends to be either fully marked or not marked, and it stays that way. For Polycomb, PRC2 binding to H3K27me3 through EED allosterically stimulates the methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Margueron et al. 2009). Spreading is limited by boundaries such as active transcription, CTCF sites and the turnover by erasers. Mathematical models of this bistability (Dodd et al. 2007) are a good further read for students with a modelling interest.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Through DNA replication: diluted, then restored
text:
Through DNA replication: diluted, then restored


At replication, old histones (with their marks) are split randomly between the two daughter strands; new, unmarked histones fill the gaps.
Each daughter gets about half the marked nucleosomes. Read–write feedback then re-marks the new neighbours.
Whether histone marks are truly self-sustaining through many divisions is still debated; for H3K27me3 the evidence is strongest.


This is why histone-based memory is harder than DNA methylation: the information is halved at every replication and must be restored from a 50% template. In flies and in mammalian cells, removing the Polycomb recruitment sequence leads to loss of H3K27me3 over a few divisions, which suggests the domain needs both DNA-sequence recruitment and the read-write loop (Laprell et al. 2017; Coleman & Struhl 2017). The plant FLC example later is one of the clearest cases of mitotic memory of a Polycomb state. Be honest with students: this is an active research field, not settled textbook material.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: DNA methylation: a mark on the DNA itself
text:
DNA methylation: a mark on the DNA itself


In mammals, a methyl group is added to carbon 5 of cytosine, almost only in CpG dinucleotides: 5-methylcytosine (5mC).
CpG is palindromic: both strands carry a CpG, and both are usually methylated together.
About 70–80% of CpGs in a human somatic cell are methylated. The exceptions are mostly in CpG islands at promoters.
Plants also methylate CHG and CHH (H = A, C or T).


The methyl group sits in the major groove and does not change base pairing: 5mC still pairs with G, which is why it survives replication as information but is invisible to normal sequencing. Bisulfite sequencing (methylation units) converts unmethylated C to U but leaves 5mC, turning the mark into a sequence difference. Long-read technologies (nanopore, PacBio) detect 5mC directly from the signal. 5mC can be oxidised by TET enzymes to 5hmC, 5fC and 5caC, which are intermediates in active demethylation; bisulfite cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC. In plants the non-CG contexts are maintained by different enzymes (CMT3, DRM2 via RNA-directed DNA methylation), covered in methylation-biology.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Copying DNA methylation through replication


After replication the new strand is unmethylated: each CpG is hemimethylated.
UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated CpGs and recruits DNMT1, which methylates the new strand: the pattern is copied.
DNMT3A/3B methylate de novo (new sites, e.g. during development); TET enzymes start active removal.
Because the template is copied site by site, DNA methylation is the clearest example of a mitotically heritable epigenetic mark.


This is the textbook mechanism for epigenetic memory, proposed in 1975 (Holliday & Pugh; Riggs), and it fits the narrow definition perfectly: the information is in the pattern, and a dedicated enzyme copies it to the daughter strand. Copying is not perfect (about 1 error in 20–1000 CpGs per division depending on context), which is one origin of the drift that epigenetic clocks measure. Passive demethylation happens if DNMT1 is absent or blocked during replication; this is how the primordial germ cells and the early embryo erase most methylation. The de novo enzymes DNMT3A and DNMT3B (Okano et al. 1999) set the patterns in the first place.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
CpG islands


The human genome has only about a quarter of the CpGs expected from its base composition. Methylated C mutates easily to T (spontaneous deamination), so CpGs are slowly lost.
CpG islands (CGIs) are about 1 kb stretches that keep a high CpG density because they are unmethylated. About 60–70% of human gene promoters have one.
CGI promoters are usually unmethylated even when the gene is off; methylation of a CGI promoter means stable silencing (inactive X, imprinted genes, some genes in cancer).


Deamination of C gives U, which repair recognises as foreign; deamination of 5mC gives T, a normal base, so the resulting T:G mismatch is often repaired the wrong way. Over evolutionary time, methylated CpGs become TpG or CpA, which depletes CpG genome-wide (observed/expected ratio about 0.2–0.25). Islands escape because they are protected from methylation, mostly by being bound by transcription machinery and proteins such as CFP1 and KDM2B that recognise unmethylated CpG. The classical definition (Gardiner-Garden & Frommer 1987): at least 200 bp, GC content above 50%, observed/expected CpG above 0.6. In tumours, hypermethylation of CGI promoters silences tumour suppressors (cancer-epigenetics unit).

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Remodelers and histone variants


Chromatin remodelers use ATP to slide, evict or exchange nucleosomes (e.g. SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, INO80 families). They create and maintain NDRs.
Histone variants replace canonical histones at specific places: H2A.Z flanks promoters and enhancers, H3.3 is deposited in active genes independently of replication, CENP-A defines centromeres.


Remodelers are the motors of chromatin: modifications recruit them, and they physically move nucleosomes. SWI/SNF (BAF) subunits are mutated in about 20% of human cancers, which shows how important access is. Variants differ by a few amino acids from the canonical histones but are deposited by dedicated chaperones at specific places. CENP-A is a beautiful example of an epigenetically defined locus: centromeres are defined by CENP-A nucleosomes, not by a specific sequence, and neocentromeres can form on ordinary DNA. H3.3 is also the histone that carries the K27M oncohistone mutation in paediatric gliomas.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Beyond one dimension: the 3D genome


Chromosomes occupy territories; active and inactive chromatin separate into A and B compartments.
Within them, loops and topologically associating domains (TADs) bring enhancers close to the promoters they regulate, often over 10–1000 kb.
Measured with Hi-C (3D genome units).


A teaser only. The point here: a 1D track (previous slides) does not tell us which promoter an enhancer talks to. Loops are made by cohesin extruding DNA until it hits CTCF bound in a convergent orientation; that is why CTCF is in the course dataset. Compartments correlate strongly with the marks: A is H3K27ac/H3K36me3-rich, B is H3K9me3/H3K27me3-rich and lamina-associated. Students will compute compartments themselves from a Hi-C matrix.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Epigenetic memory in action


X inactivation: in female mammals one X is silenced early in development (Xist RNA, H3K27me3, CGI methylation) and stays silent in all descendants.
Genomic imprinting: some genes are expressed only from the maternal or only the paternal copy, set by DNA methylation in the germ line.
Vernalisation in plants: Arabidopsis remembers winter. Cold silences the flowering repressor FLC by Polycomb (H3K27me3), and the silence is kept through cell divisions after it warms up, so the plant flowers in spring.


Three examples that fit the narrow definition: a state set by a transient signal and remembered through mitosis. X inactivation shows memory at the scale of a whole chromosome; calico cats are the visible result of random X inactivation. Imprinting shows memory from the parents’ germ lines: the paternal and maternal copies differ only in methylation at imprinting control regions. The figure uses H19: its imprinting control region is methylated on the paternal allele (set in the male germ line), so H19 is expressed only from the maternal copy. Vernalisation is the plant example (Umeå has a strong plant-science community); it is one of the best-studied cases of quantitative Polycomb memory: the longer the cold, the more cells switch FLC off (an all-or-none switch per cell). The epigenetic-inheritance unit asks which claims of memory across generations hold up.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Cause or consequence?


Marks correlate with activity, but correlation does not show that the mark causes it. H3K36me3 is deposited because the gene is transcribed.
Causal tests: replace a histone with a mutant that cannot be modified (e.g. lysine → arginine), tether a writer to a gene (epigenome editing: dCas9 fused to a writer or eraser), or remove the writer.
Treat “epigenetic regulation of gene X” with care: is the mark a driver, a lock that keeps a decision, or a footprint of transcription?


This is the critical-thinking slide and should come back throughout the course. Some marks are clearly downstream of transcription (H3K36me3, H3K79me2). Others act as locks: in flies, replacing all H3 copies with H3K27R derepresses Polycomb target genes, showing the lysine itself is needed for repression. Epigenome editing (dCas9-p300, dCas9-KRAB, dCas9-DNMT3A) can test whether placing a mark changes expression and whether the change is remembered after the tool is gone. Most genome-wide studies, including the ones we analyse, are correlational.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: What the assays in this course measure
text:
What the assays in this course measure

This is the map of the course. Every assay turns a chromatin property into DNA fragments that are sequenced, and every one has its own way of being wrong: Tn5 sequence bias in ATAC, antibody specificity and input in ChIP, incomplete bisulfite conversion, ligation artefacts and distance decay in Hi-C. The analysis always ends in the same kinds of objects: intervals (peaks, domains), signal tracks, and counts in regions. That is why the next units are on genomic intervals and on going from reads to coverage.

Next units: gene regulation (transcription factors, enhancers), then the technical foundation (intervals, reads to coverage).

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Luger et al. 1997, Nature. Crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle at 2.8 Å resolution. The atomic picture of the nucleosome.
Kornberg 1974, Science. Chromatin structure: a repeating unit of histones and DNA. The nucleosome model, from the ladder of digestion fragments.
Strahl & Allis 2000, Nature. The language of covalent histone modifications. The “histone code” hypothesis.
Barski et al. 2007, Cell. High-resolution profiling of histone methylations in the human genome. One of the first genome-wide maps of histone marks by ChIP-seq.
Bird 2007, Nature. Perceptions of epigenetics. A short essay on what the word should mean.
Allis & Jenuwein 2016, Nat Rev Genet. The molecular hallmarks of epigenetic control. A broad review of the whole field.

title: Quiz: Peak calling
text:
Short questions on calling ChIP-seq peaks and on replicate reproducibility. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. An input has 20 M reads; d = 200 bp; effective genome size 2.7 × 10⁹. Around a candidate summit the input has 3 reads in 200 bp, 15 reads in 1 kb and 80 reads in 10 kb. Compute λBG, λd, λ1k, λ10k and λlocal.






Hint





λw = reads in the window × d / w. λlocal is the maximum.









Answer





λBG = 20 × 10⁶ × 200 / (2.7 × 10⁹) = 1.48; λd = 3 × 200/200 = 3; λ1k = 15 × 200/1000 = 3; λ10k = 80 × 200/10 000 = 1.6. λlocal = 3.




Q2. A ChIP has 40 M reads and its input 10 M. Which library does MACS scale by default, and by what factor? A summit has a raw ChIP pileup of 48: what k enters the Poisson test?






Answer





The larger library, the ChIP, is scaled down to the input: factor 10/40 = 0.25, so k = 12.




Q3. Why does MACS take the maximum of the λ estimates rather than their mean?






Answer





To be conservative: if any scale shows a high background (an input pile-up, an open or amplified region), the candidate must exceed it. A mean would let local artefacts through as peaks.




Q4. With λlocal = 2, a summit has k = 12 and P(X ≥ 12) = 1.4 × 10⁻⁶. What fold enrichment does MACS report? Would the same summit be more or less significant if the input were 10 times deeper (same λ in expectation)?






Answer





(12 + 1)/(2 + 1) = 4.3. Same expected λ, so the same p-value in expectation; but λ would be estimated far more precisely, with fewer summits whose λ is set by a single stray input read.




Q5. MACS without an input uses λBG and the 10-kb window of the ChIP. Why not the 1-kb window? What kinds of false peaks appear without an input?






Answer





A 1-kb window of the ChIP contains the peak itself and would raise λ to the peak’s level. False peaks: open promoters (sonication bias), amplified regions (copy number), hyper-ChIPable highly expressed genes, collapsed repeats not in the blacklist.




Q6. Why does a narrow peak caller find very few peaks in H3K36me3 data, even when the domains are obvious in a 1-kb-bin coverage track? What does SICER/epic2 do instead?






Answer





Each base in a broad domain is only slightly enriched (the reads are spread over tens of kb), so few bases pass a strict per-base test. SICER/epic2 count reads in 200-bp bins, keep bins above a lenient threshold, join them across small gaps into islands and test each island as a whole: many slightly enriched bins add up to strong evidence.




Q7. Why is IDR run on peaks called with -p 0.01 and not on the final peak set?






Answer





IDR estimates where rank agreement breaks down by fitting a reproducible and an irreproducible (noise) component. It needs noise peaks in its input; a thresholded set has almost none and the model cannot be fitted properly.




Q8. An experiment has Nt = 12 000, Np = 14 000, N1 = 15 000, N2 = 5 000. Compute the rescue and self-consistency ratios. Does it pass ENCODE’s criteria, and what is the problem?






Answer





Rescue 14 000/12 000 = 1.17 (passes); self-consistency 15 000/5 000 = 3.0 (fails, > 2). Replicate 2 supports far fewer peaks than replicate 1: shallower, less complex or less enriched. Resequence or replace replicate 2.




Q9. A study reports “18 000 peaks in the control and 11 000 in the treated cells, so the factor loses 7 000 binding sites”. What is wrong with this inference?






Answer





Peak numbers depend on depth, signal-to-noise, thresholds and the input; a site can weaken without disappearing, or fall just below a threshold by chance. Without replicates and a statistical test on read counts in a common set of regions (differential binding), and without considering a global change (spike-ins), the numbers say little.




Q10. In the course data, MACS’s λlocal at most CTCF summits was set by the 100-bp window of the input, not by λBG. Why, and is that a problem?






Answer





The input is shallow (about 3 reads per kb): λBG = 0.29, so a single input read within 50 bp of a summit gives λd = 1, already higher. The background estimate is then driven by single reads, which is noisy and makes MACS conservative near any stray input read. A deeper input would make λd a real estimate.

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
Background
MACS with an input. Single-end reads are extended to the fragment length \(d\) and piled up. The larger library is scaled down to the size of the smaller one. At each base the pileup \(k\) is compared with \[\lambda_\text{local} = \max(\lambda_\text{BG},\ \lambda_d,\ \lambda_\text{1k},\ \lambda_\text{10k}),\] where \(\lambda_\text{BG} = N_\text{input} \times d / G\) (\(G\) the effective genome size) and \(\lambda_w\) = (input reads in a window of width \(w\) centred on the base) \(\times\, d / w\). The p-value is \(P(X \ge k)\) for \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_\text{local})\); MACS converts p-scores of all bases to q-values (Benjamini–Hochberg), joins bases below the cutoff into peaks and reports the summit, the fold enrichment \((k + 1)/(\lambda + 1)\), \(-\log_{10} p\) and \(-\log_{10} q\). Without an input, MACS uses \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window of the ChIP itself.
Broad marks. SICER/epic2 divide the genome into bins (200 bp), keep bins above a lenient threshold, join them across small gaps into islands and test each island against the input. macs3 --broad links strong regions through weaker ones (--broad-cutoff).
IDR. Two replicates are called leniently; matched peaks are ranked in each; a mixture model separates a reproducible component (correlated ranks) from an irreproducible one (independent ranks). The IDR of the top \(n\) peaks is the expected fraction of irreproducible peaks among them. ENCODE compares \(N_t\) (IDR peaks from true replicates) with \(N_p\) (from pooled pseudoreplicates) and \(N_1\), \(N_2\) (each replicate’s self-pseudoreplicates): rescue ratio \(\max(N_t, N_p)/\min(N_t, N_p)\) and self-consistency ratio \(\max(N_1, N_2)/\min(N_1, N_2)\) should both be below 2.

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
By hand
B1. Depth scaling and λ. A ChIP has 30 M reads and its input 15 M; \(d = 200\) bp; effective genome size \(2.7 \times 10^9\). At a candidate summit the raw ChIP pileup is 36 fragments. In the input, windows centred on the summit contain: 2 reads in 200 bp, 16 reads in 1 kb and 45 reads in 10 kb.

What happens to \(\lambda_d\) when a single input read happens to fall in the 200-bp window? Why does that argue for sequencing the input at least as deep as the ChIP?
B3. With and without an input. In the course data, MACS3 finds 521 CTCF peaks with the input and 816 without. Of the 299 peaks found only without the input, 36% have a CTCF motif within 50 bp of the summit and 9% are in ENCODE’s peak set; of the 521 called with the input, 72% and 72%.

B4. Which caller?
