title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
On the command line

C1 — Process the second replicates
The chain function of ChIP-seq: the assay; define it again if you are in a new shell:
chain() {   # usage: chain <name> <reads.fastq.gz> <33 or 64>
  local s=$1
  if [ "$3" = 64 ]; then zcat $2 | perl -pe 'tr/@-~/!-_/ if $. % 4 == 0' | gzip > $s.fastq.gz
  else cp $2 $s.fastq.gz; fi
  fastp -w $T -i $s.fastq.gz -o $s.trim.fastq.gz -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -U $s.trim.fastq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools sort -@ 4 -o $s.sorted.bam -
  samtools index $s.sorted.bam
  samtools view -b -q 30 -F 1804 -o $s.q30.bam $s.sorted.bam
  samtools markdup -s $s.q30.bam $s.markdup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.markdup.bam
  samtools view -b -F 1024 -o $s.dedup.bam $s.markdup.bam chr21
  bedtools intersect -v -abam $s.dedup.bam -b blacklist.bed > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
}
chain ctcf_rep2     $D/gm12878_ctcf_chip_rep2.fastq.gz      64
chain h3k36me3_rep2 $D/gm12878_h3k36me3_chip_rep2.fastq.gz  33
for s in ctcf ctcf_rep2 h3k36me3 h3k36me3_rep2; do
  echo $s $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam) $(grep "^READ:" $s.markdup.txt | cut -d' ' -f2) \
    $(grep "DUPLICATE SINGLE:" $s.markdup.txt | cut -d' ' -f3)
done
How many filtered reads does each replicate have, and what fraction of the MAPQ-filtered reads were duplicates? Which replicate is the weaker library?


C2 — Fragment length per replicate
for s in ctcf ctcf_rep2 h3k36me3 h3k36me3_rep2; do
  echo $s $(macs3 predictd -i $s.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 2>&1 | grep "predicted fragment" | grep -o "[0-9]* bps")
done
Do the two CTCF replicates agree? The two H3K36me3 replicates?


C3 — Call CTCF peaks with the input, and keep the background tracks
mkdir -p macs
macs3 callpeak -t ctcf.final.bam -c ctcf_input.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 -q 0.01 --bdg \
  -n ctcf --outdir macs 2> macs/ctcf.log
grep -E "^# (d|total tags|Range|Larger)" macs/ctcf_peaks.xls
grep "Pileup will" macs/ctcf.log
wc -l macs/ctcf_peaks.narrowPeak
sort -k8,8gr macs/ctcf_peaks.narrowPeak | head -3
ls macs

Which library was scaled, and by what factor? (Compute it from the two totals.)
What do columns 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the strongest peak mean?
What do the files ctcf_treat_pileup.bdg and ctcf_control_lambda.bdg contain? (You use them in R1.)



C4 — Without an input, and at other thresholds
macs3 callpeak -t ctcf.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 -q 0.01 -n ctcf_noinput --outdir macs 2> macs/ctcf_noinput.log
grep "Range" macs/ctcf_noinput_peaks.xls
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz | awk '$1 == "chr21"' | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > encode_ctcf.bed
for p in ctcf ctcf_noinput; do
  f=macs/${p}_peaks.narrowPeak
  echo $p $(wc -l < $f) $(bedtools intersect -u -a $f -b encode_ctcf.bed | wc -l) $(bedtools intersect -u -a encode_ctcf.bed -b $f | wc -l)
done
for q in 0.1 1e-5 1e-10 1e-20; do
  macs3 callpeak -t ctcf.final.bam -c ctcf_input.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 -q $q -n ctcf_q$q --outdir macs 2> /dev/null
  f=macs/ctcf_q${q}_peaks.narrowPeak
  echo q=$q $(wc -l < $f) $(bedtools intersect -u -a $f -b encode_ctcf.bed | wc -l)
done

How many peaks with and without the input? What fraction of each set is in ENCODE’s set, and what fraction of ENCODE’s 405 peaks does each recover?
How does the number of peaks change with the q-value cutoff? Is there a natural cutoff?



C5 — A broad mark: three ways
K="-t h3k36me3.final.bam h3k36me3_rep2.final.bam -c h3k36me3_input.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 --nomodel --extsize 200"
macs3 callpeak $K -q 0.01 -n k36_narrow --outdir macs 2> macs/k36_narrow.log
macs3 callpeak $K --broad --broad-cutoff 0.1 -q 0.01 -n k36_broad --outdir macs 2> macs/k36_broad.log
grep -w -e chr21 $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > chr21.sizes
epic2 -t h3k36me3.final.bam h3k36me3_rep2.final.bam -c h3k36me3_input.final.bam \
  --chromsizes chr21.sizes --effective-genome-fraction 0.858 --fragment-size 200 \
  --bin-size 200 --gaps-allowed 3 --false-discovery-rate-cutoff 0.05 > k36_epic2.bed 2> k36_epic2.log
for f in macs/k36_narrow_peaks.narrowPeak macs/k36_broad_peaks.broadPeak k36_epic2.bed; do
  grep -v "^#" $f | awk -v f=$f '{ n++; w += $3 - $2; if ($3 - $2 > m) m = $3 - $2 } END { printf "%s %d regions, %.0f kb, mean %.0f bp, max %d bp\n", f, n, w / 1000, w / n, m }'
done

Why --nomodel --extsize 200? Why give both replicates as -t? What is --effective-genome-fraction 0.858?
Compare the three results: number of regions, total length, widths. Load them in IGV with the H3K36me3 bigWigs of ChIP-seq: the assay at chr21:33,220,000-33,600,000.



C6 — IDR on two CTCF replicates
samtools merge -f ctcf_pool.final.bam ctcf.final.bam ctcf_rep2.final.bam
for s in ctcf ctcf_rep2 ctcf_pool; do
  macs3 callpeak -t $s.final.bam -c ctcf_input.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 -p 0.01 \
    -n ${s}_p01 --outdir macs 2> macs/${s}_p01.log
  sort -k8,8gr macs/${s}_p01_peaks.narrowPeak > ${s}_p01.narrowPeak
done
wc -l ctcf_p01.narrowPeak ctcf_rep2_p01.narrowPeak ctcf_pool_p01.narrowPeak
idr --samples ctcf_p01.narrowPeak ctcf_rep2_p01.narrowPeak --peak-list ctcf_pool_p01.narrowPeak \
  --input-file-type narrowPeak --rank p.value --soft-idr-threshold 0.05 --use-best-multisummit-IDR \
  --output-file ctcf_idr.txt --plot --log-output-file ctcf_idr.log
grep -E "Final parameter|passing" ctcf_idr.log
awk '$12 >= -log(0.05) / log(10)' ctcf_idr.txt | cut -f1-10 | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > ctcf_idr05.narrowPeak
wc -l < ctcf_idr05.narrowPeak
echo $(bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf_idr05.narrowPeak -b encode_ctcf.bed | wc -l) $(bedtools intersect -u -a encode_ctcf.bed -b ctcf_idr05.narrowPeak | wc -l)

Why -p 0.01 and not -q 0.01? Why sort by column 8?
How many peaks pass IDR < 0.05? What are the four fitted parameters (the order is μ, σ, ρ, π)? Open ctcf_idr.txt.png.
How do your IDR peaks compare with ENCODE’s?



C7 — Pseudoreplicates and ENCODE’s ratios
idr_pair() {   # usage: idr_pair <a.bam> <b.bam> <pooled peaks> <name>; prints the number of peaks with IDR < 0.05
  for x in $1 $2; do
    macs3 callpeak -t $x -c ctcf_input.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 -p 0.01 -n tmp --outdir macs 2> /dev/null
    sort -k8,8gr macs/tmp_peaks.narrowPeak > $x.p01.narrowPeak
  done
  idr --samples $1.p01.narrowPeak $2.p01.narrowPeak --peak-list $3 --input-file-type narrowPeak \
    --rank p.value --soft-idr-threshold 0.05 --use-best-multisummit-IDR --output-file $4.txt 2> /dev/null
  echo $4 $(awk '$12 >= -log(0.05) / log(10)' $4.txt | wc -l)
}
for s in ctcf ctcf_rep2 ctcf_pool; do
  samtools view -b -s 7.5 -U $s.pr2.bam -o $s.pr1.bam $s.final.bam
done
idr_pair ctcf.pr1.bam      ctcf.pr2.bam      ctcf_p01.narrowPeak      N1
idr_pair ctcf_rep2.pr1.bam ctcf_rep2.pr2.bam ctcf_rep2_p01.narrowPeak N2
idr_pair ctcf_pool.pr1.bam ctcf_pool.pr2.bam ctcf_pool_p01.narrowPeak Np

What does samtools view -s 7.5 -U ... do? Count the reads in ctcf_pool.pr1.bam and ctcf_pool.pr2.bam.
Compute the rescue and self-consistency ratios with \(N_t\) from C6. Does the experiment pass ENCODE’s criteria? Which replicate limits it?

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
Explore: a Poisson peak caller
The demo runs the MACS test of the Background on simulated data: 20 kb of a 2.7-Gb genome with four true binding sites A–D (▲, strengths 100%, 30%, 55% and 15%), fragments \(d = 200\) bp. The top track shows the ChIP pileup \(k\) (brown), the input pileup (grey) and \(\lambda_\text{local}\) (blue); the strip below it shows which estimate sets \(\lambda_\text{local}\) at each base. The bottom track shows \(-\log_{10} p\) or \(-\log_{10} q\), the cutoff (red) and the called peaks (green at a true site, crimson elsewhere). The sliders set the depth of the ChIP, the depth of the input (as % of the ChIP), the signal at the strongest site (fragments per 10 M reads), the local background (× the genome average, in ChIP and input alike), a 2-kb bump of extra background in both ChIP and input (open chromatin or a copy-number gain), and the cutoff. The tick boxes switch the input and the local windows off; without an input the demo does what MACS does: \(\max(\lambda_\text{BG}, \lambda_\text{10k})\) from the ChIP itself. Drag the cursor to read the by-hand numbers at one base; the table gives them at the four sites. The q-values are Benjamini–Hochberg over the 2000 scored positions of this window (MACS uses all bases of the genome, which is stricter).



E1. The calculation of B1, live. At the start, drag the cursor to site A. Read \(k\) and the four λ values. Which one sets \(\lambda_\text{local}\), and how many input reads does it correspond to? Check the fold enrichment. Now look at site D in the table: what sets its λ, and how far above \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) is it? Untick local λ windows: what happens to the p-value at D?
E2. A bump in the background. Click open-chromatin bump (×8 in ChIP and input, input used). Are there false peaks? Put the cursor at 10.5 kb, in the bump: what are \(k\) and \(\lambda_\text{local}\), and which window sets it? Then click … without input: how many false peaks now, and what is λ at 10.5 kb? Why does the 10-kb window of the ChIP not catch the bump? Finally tick use input control again but untick local λ windows. What does this say about why MACS takes the maximum of several λ estimates?
E3. Depth and power. Click start and move ChIP reads through 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 M (the input follows). Which sites are called at each depth? How do \(k\) and λ at site A change with depth, and what happens to the fold enrichment and to the p-value?
E4. A shallow input. Click shallow input (the input has 10% of the ChIP’s reads). What happened to the ChIP pileup and to \(\lambda_\text{BG}\)? How many sites are called now? Look at site C: what sets its λ? Compare with B2.






Solutions





E1. At site A, \(k = 65\) fragments; \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 20 \times 10^6 \times 200 / 2.7 \times 10^9 = 1.48\), \(\lambda_d = 2.00\), \(\lambda_\text{1k} = 1.60\), \(\lambda_\text{10k} = 1.76\). The 200-bp window sets \(\lambda_\text{local} = 2.00\): \(\lambda_d\) = (input reads in 200 bp) × 200/200, so two input reads. \(-\log_{10} p = 72.2\); fold enrichment \((65 + 1)/(2 + 1) = 22.0\). Site D: \(k = 14\), and four input reads happen to fall within 100 bp of it, so \(\lambda_d = 4.00\), 2.7 times \(\lambda_\text{BG}\); \(-\log_{10} p = 4.1\), \(-\log_{10} q = 2.7\), just called. Against \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) alone (local windows off), \(\lambda = 1.48\) and \(-\log_{10} p = 9.1\): a handful of input reads moves the p-value by five orders of magnitude, which is why a shallow input makes λ noisy (B2).
E2. With the input: still 4 peaks, all at true sites, no false ones. At 10.5 kb, \(k = 13\) but \(\lambda_\text{1k} = 13.0\) (13 input reads in 1 kb, × 200/1000), so \(\lambda_\text{local} = 13.0\) and \(-\log_{10} p = 0.3\): nothing. Without the input: 6 peaks, 2 of them false, inside the bump (\(-\log_{10} q\) up to 4.9); at 10.5 kb \(\lambda_\text{local} = 4.56\) (the ChIP’s 10-kb window) and \(-\log_{10} p = 3.0\). A 10-kb window averages the 2-kb bump with 8 kb of ordinary background, so it sees roughly \((8 + 2 \times 8)/10 = 2.4\) times the background, not 8 times; a 1-kb window of the ChIP would include the peak itself, which is why MACS cannot use one without an input. With the input but no local windows (\(\lambda_\text{BG}\) only), the whole bump becomes one false peak of about 2 kb (\(-\log_{10} q = 13\)). Each λ estimate catches bias at one scale: \(\lambda_d\) a narrow pile-up of input reads, \(\lambda_\text{1k}\) an open-chromatin bump, \(\lambda_\text{10k}\) a broad region such as a copy-number gain, and \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) is the floor where the input is too sparse to say anything. The maximum is the conservative choice: a base must beat the worst of them. (Note that the bump also costs sites B and C some significance: their 10-kb windows include it.)
E3. 5 M and 10 M: A, B and C are called, D is not (\(k = 3\) and 6). 20, 40 and 80 M: all four, with D at \(-\log_{10} q\) = 2.7, 8.4 and 16.4. At site A, \(k\) = 12, 31, 65, 129, 255 and \(\lambda_\text{local}\) = 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.2, 5.9: both grow with the depth. The enrichment over the genome average, \(k/\lambda_\text{BG}\), stays near 40 (32, 42, 44, 44, 43); the reported fold enrichment \((k+1)/(\lambda+1)\) rises from 6.5 to 37, because at low depth the pseudocount of 1 and λ values set by single input reads weigh heavily. The p-value improves enormously (\(-\log_{10} p\) from 9 to 310). Relative Poisson noise falls as \(1/\sqrt{\lambda}\): more reads do not make a site more enriched, they make the same enrichment more certain. Weak sites need depth; the number of peaks depends on depth, so do not compare peak numbers between samples of different depth.
E4. The ChIP is scaled down to the input: its pileup is multiplied by 0.10 and rounded up, so \(k\) at A is \(\lceil 65 \times 0.1 \rceil = 7\), and \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 2 \times 10^6 \times 200 / 2.7 \times 10^9 = 0.15\). Only site A is called (\(-\log_{10} q = 6.8\)). At site C (\(k = 4\)), a single input read falls in the 200-bp window: \(\lambda_d = 1.00\), almost 7 times \(\lambda_\text{BG}\), and \(-\log_{10} p = 1.7\). With a shallow input, λ is decided by single reads, and scaling the ChIP down throws away most of its information: sequence the input at least as deeply as the ChIP (B2).

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
In R
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(GenomicAlignments); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/chip")
np <- function(f) import(f, format = "narrowPeak")

R1 — The local λ, recomputed
pk <- np("macs/ctcf_peaks.narrowPeak")
summit <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(start(pk) + pk$peak, width = 1))
trt <- import("macs/ctcf_treat_pileup.bdg", format = "bedGraph")
lam <- import("macs/ctcf_control_lambda.bdg", format = "bedGraph")
summit$k <- trt$score[findOverlaps(summit, trt, select = "first")]
summit$lambda <- lam$score[findOverlaps(summit, lam, select = "first")]
inp <- resize(granges(readGAlignments("ctcf_input.final.bam")), 1, fix = "start")   # input 5' ends
d <- 100; G <- 40088619
lam_w <- function(w) countOverlaps(resize(summit, w, fix = "center"), inp, ignore.strand = TRUE) * d / w
L <- cbind(BG = length(inp) * d / G, d = lam_w(d), k1 = lam_w(1000), k10 = lam_w(10000))
head(cbind(L, max = apply(L, 1, max), macs = summit$lambda))
cor(apply(L, 1, max), summit$lambda)
table(colnames(L)[apply(L, 1, which.max)])
p <- -ppois(ceiling(summit$k) - 1, summit$lambda, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
summary(p - pk$pValue)
i <- which.max(summit$lambda); c(start(summit)[i], k = summit$k[i], L[i, ], macs_p = pk$pValue[i])

Does your \(\lambda_\text{local}\) agree with MACS’s? Which window sets it at most summits, and why (how many input reads per kb are there)?
Why ceiling(summit$k)? (Hint: what has been done to the ChIP pileup?) How close are your p-values to MACS’s column 8?
Look at the summit with the highest λ: what are \(k\) and the four λ values? Why is the input high there?



R2 — Does the motif support the weak peaks?
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(motifmatchr) })
con <- RSQLite::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf <- getMatrixByID(con, "MA0139.2")
fa <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38_chr21_chrM.fa"))
has_motif <- function(p) {
  around <- GRanges(seqnames(p), IRanges(start(p) + p$peak - 50, width = 101))
  as.vector(motifMatches(matchMotifs(ctcf, getSeq(fa, around), p.cutoff = 1e-4)))
}
lax <- np("macs/ctcf_q0.1_peaks.narrowPeak")
lax <- lax[order(-lax$pValue)]
m <- has_motif(lax)
round(tapply(m, ceiling(seq_along(m) / 100), mean), 2)
set.seed(1)
rnd <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(sample(15e6:46e6, 2000), width = 1)); rnd$peak <- 0L
mean(has_motif(rnd))
What fraction of peaks has the motif in each block of 100 peaks (strongest first)? In random DNA?


R3 — What did the input remove?
noi <- np("macs/ctcf_noinput_peaks.narrowPeak")
extra <- noi[!overlapsAny(noi, pk)]
enc <- np(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz")); enc <- enc[seqnames(enc) == "chr21"]
inp_ratio <- function(p) median(countOverlaps(resize(GRanges("chr21", IRanges(start(p) + p$peak, width = 1)), 1001, fix = "center"),
                                            inp, ignore.strand = TRUE) / (length(inp) * 1001 / G))
sapply(list(with_input = pk, without = noi, only_without = extra), function(p)
  c(n = length(p), motif = mean(has_motif(p)), in_encode = mean(overlapsAny(p, enc)), input_ratio = inp_ratio(p)))
Compare the three sets. Are the extra peaks in places where the input is unusually high?


R4 — Broad domains and transcribed genes
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), which = chr21)
genes <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding" & width(gtf) > 5000]
k4 <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_h3k4me3_fc.bigWig"), which = chr21, as = "RleList")
genes$k4 <- mean(k4[promoters(resize(genes, 1, fix = "start"), 1000, 1001)])
active <- reduce(genes[genes$k4 > 5], ignore.strand = TRUE); silent <- reduce(genes[genes$k4 < 1], ignore.strand = TRUE)
ep <- read.delim("k36_epic2.bed")
calls <- list(narrow = granges(np("macs/k36_narrow_peaks.narrowPeak")),
              broad = import("macs/k36_broad_peaks.broadPeak", format = "BED", extraCols = c(s = "numeric", p = "numeric", q = "numeric")),
              epic2 = GRanges(ep$X.Chromosome, IRanges(ep$Start + 1, ep$End)))
frac <- function(a, b) sum(width(intersect(reduce(a), b, ignore.strand = TRUE))) / sum(width(b))
sapply(calls, function(g) c(n = length(g), kb = sum(width(reduce(g))) / 1e3, median_width = median(width(g)),
                            active = frac(g, active), silent = frac(g, silent)))
What fraction of active and of silent gene-body bases does each caller cover? Which result would you use, and how would you report the parameters?


R5 — The IDR output
idr <- read.delim("ctcf_idr.txt", header = FALSE)
nrow(idr); sum(idr$V12 >= -log10(0.05))
plot(rank(-idr$V15), rank(-idr$V19), col = ifelse(idr$V12 >= -log10(0.05), "darkgreen", "red"), pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     xlab = "rank in replicate 1", ylab = "rank in replicate 2")
cor(idr$V15, idr$V19, method = "spearman")
pass <- GRanges(idr$V1, IRanges(idr$V2 + 1, idr$V3))[idr$V12 >= -log10(0.05)]
c(ours_in_encode = sum(overlapsAny(pass, enc)), encode_found = sum(overlapsAny(enc, pass)), encode = length(enc))
summary(width(pass))

How many matched peaks are there, and how many pass? Where in the rank plot do the failing peaks lie?
What fraction of ENCODE’s chr21 peaks do you recover? Why fewer than ENCODE?

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — λ and Poisson (B1, B2, R1)





Scale the larger library down: factor = smaller total / larger total. \(\lambda_w = n_w \times d / w\). \(\lambda_\text{local}\) is the maximum. Read \(P(X \ge k)\) from the table. MACS’s fold enrichment is \((k + 1)/(\lambda + 1)\). Everything is described in the MACS3 callpeak documentation (--slocal, --llocal, --scale-to, --bdg) and in Zhang et al. 2008. ppois(k - 1, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) is \(P(X \ge k)\).









Hint 2 — controls and thresholds (B3, B5, C4, R2, R3)





Without a control MACS3 uses only λBG and --llocal from the ChIP (see the log line Range for calculating regional lambda). Motif scanning: motifmatchr matchMotifs, the CTCF matrix MA0139.2 in JASPAR2024. bedtools intersect -u reports each feature of -a once if it overlaps -b.









Hint 3 — broad marks (B4, B8, C5, R4)





epic2 (SICER algorithm, Zang et al. 2009): --bin-size, --gaps-allowed, --effective-genome-fraction (effective genome size / chromosome length: 40 088 619 / 46 709 983). MACS3 --broad and --broad-cutoff in the callpeak documentation. The broadPeak format is BED6+3 (UCSC). H3K9me3 domains lie largely in repeats: think about MAPQ filtering.









Hint 4 — IDR (B6, B7, C6, C7, R5)





The IDR README documents the output columns: 11 local IDR and 12 global IDR (both −log10), 15 and 19 the scores of the two replicates. Li et al. 2011 describe the model; Landt et al. 2012 and the ENCODE TF ChIP-seq pipeline the pseudoreplicate scheme. samtools view -s SEED.FRACTION subsamples reads; -U FILE writes the reads that were not selected.

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
Solutions
Numbers from running the commands as written (MACS3 3.1.0, IDR 2.0.3, epic2 0.0.54, samtools 1.21, bedtools 2.30, R 4.6, Bioconductor 3.23).






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) The ChIP is larger; it is scaled by \(15/30 = 0.5\): \(k = 18\). (b) \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 15 \times 10^6 \times 200 / (2.7 \times 10^9) = 1.11\); \(\lambda_d = 2 \times 200/200 = 2\); \(\lambda_\text{1k} = 16 \times 200/1000 = 3.2\); \(\lambda_\text{10k} = 45 \times 200/10\,000 = 0.9\). \(\lambda_\text{local} = 3.2\). (c) \(P(X \ge 18 \mid 3.2) = 9.5 \times 10^{-9}\). Against \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 1.11\), direct calculation gives about \(3.6 \times 10^{-16}\) (slightly larger than the value in the λ = 1 column): over seven orders of magnitude more significant, because the input shows a local excess within 1 kb. (d) \((18 + 1)/(3.2 + 1) = 4.5\).
B2. At the same summit as B1, the expected local counts fall tenfold: 0.2 in 200 bp, 1.6 in 1 kb and 4.5 in 10 kb. The genome-wide background is \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 1.5 \times 10^6 \times 200 / (2.7 \times 10^9) = 0.11\) per 200 bp. Most 200-bp windows hold 0 reads, but whenever one input read falls there, \(\lambda_d = 1 \times 200/200 = 1\), nine times \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) (0.11): the background estimate jumps up and down with single reads, and peaks near a stray input read lose significance while others do not. With too few reads the local windows estimate nothing; the input should be at least as deep as the ChIP (ENCODE requires matching depth).
B3. (a) \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window of the ChIP. A 1-kb (or \(d\)) window of the ChIP would be dominated by the peak itself and swallow it. (b) The extra peaks are a mixture: 36% have the motif (random DNA 4%), so many are real weaker CTCF sites that the conservative input-based λ (often a single input read in 100 bp) rejected; but 64% have no motif and only 9% are in ENCODE’s set, so many are noise. With the input, precision is much higher (72% motif). (c) Cancer cell lines with copy-number gains (amplified regions look enriched), weak antibodies (peaks at open promoters and hyper-ChIPable regions dominate), and broad marks (no local correction at all).
B4. (a) Narrow: point sources. (b) Narrow, or both: promoter peaks of 1–3 kb (narrow peaks plus --call-summits work well; broad gives wider regions). (c) Broad: Polycomb domains of tens of kb. (d) Broad: gene bodies. (e) Broad for the gene bodies, narrow for the promoter-proximal pausing peak; often both. (f) Broad; and most of the signal is in repeats where reads have low MAPQ, so filtering to unique reads leaves holes; such analyses keep multi-mappers or use repeat-family-level counting.
B5. (a) If every real site had the motif and noise peaks had it at the random rate (4%), the real fraction would be (motif fraction − 0.04)/(1 − 0.04). With an average motif fraction of 70% over the 573 peaks that gives \(573 \times (0.70 - 0.04)/0.96 \approx 390\) real sites. It is a lower bound: CTCF also binds some sites without a strong motif match, and some real summits are more than 50 bp from the motif. (b) Weak real sites and noise overlap in strength: the p-value distribution is continuous, there is no gap. ENCODE uses replicate consistency (IDR) to decide how far down the list to go.
B6. (a) IDR estimates the irreproducible component from the data: it needs noise peaks in the input to see where ranks stop agreeing. A pre-thresholded list contains almost only reproducible peaks; the model then cannot separate the components. (b) Ranks are comparable between replicates with different depths, signal-to-noise and score scales; the copula model only needs the order. (c) Ranks agree only as far as the weaker replicate supports peaks: the IDR curve rises earlier, \(N_t\) is limited by replicate 2. The self-pseudoreplicates of the shallow replicate give fewer peaks (\(N_2 < N_1\)), raising the self-consistency ratio.
B7. X: rescue 34/30 = 1.13, self-consistency 28/25 = 1.12: passes. Y: rescue 31/8 = 3.9 (fails), self-consistency 1.3: each replicate is fine on its own, but the two disagree much more than random halves of the pooled data: biological or technical differences between the replicates (different conditions, a failed or mislabelled replicate, a different antibody lot). Z: rescue 17/15 = 1.13, self-consistency 32/9 = 3.6 (fails): one replicate is much weaker (shallow or low enrichment) than the other.
B8. Narrow calling of a broad mark (the reported “peaks” are fragments of domains, biased to CpG islands where H3K27me3 is densest); comparing peak counts is not a differential analysis (peak numbers depend on depth, signal-to-noise and thresholds; a site can be weaker without crossing a threshold); no replicates or statistics are mentioned; a global change (a knockout of a Polycomb component may reduce H3K27me3 everywhere) needs spike-in normalisation; and “lost at 800 sites” equates absence of a peak with absence of the mark. (Any three.)









Solutions — command line





C1. CTCF replicate 1: 197 587 filtered reads, 77 450 duplicates of 299 649 MAPQ-filtered reads (26%). Replicate 2: 120 076 reads, 238 193 duplicates of 391 106 (61%): a much less complex library, the weaker replicate. H3K36me3: 70 741 (786 duplicates of 72 024, 1%) and 98 982 reads (1 356 duplicates, 1%). The two chains take about a minute.
C2. CTCF: 100 and 109 bp: they agree. H3K36me3: 246 and 258 bp, similar by chance, but each comes with a long list of “alternative” lengths (C3 of ChIP-seq: the assay): there is no clear fragment-length signal in a broad mark, so set it yourself.
C3. (a) The ChIP (197 587 tags) is scaled to the input (116 397): factor 0.589 (“Pileup will be based on sequencing depth in control”). d = 100, regional λ windows 1 kb and 10 kb. 521 peaks. (b) Strongest peak (chr21:45 152 346–45 152 622): column 7 fold enrichment 56.8 at the summit, column 8 −log10 p = 184.8, column 9 −log10 q = 177.1, column 10 summit offset 150 bp from the peak start. (c) The ChIP pileup (scaled to the input’s depth) and the local λ along chr21, as bedGraph. Calling takes about 2 seconds.
C4. (a) With input 521 peaks, 377 (72%) in ENCODE’s set, recovering 377 of 405 (93%). Without input 816 peaks, 402 (49%) in ENCODE’s set, recovering 403 of 405. The log says Range for calculating regional lambda is: 10000 bps only. (b) q < 0.1: 573 peaks (387 in ENCODE); 0.01: 521 (377); 10⁻⁵: 413 (343); 10⁻¹⁰: 319 (293); 10⁻²⁰: 246 (239). The number falls smoothly; the stricter the cutoff, the larger the fraction in ENCODE’s set (68% → 97%). No natural cutoff.
C5. (a) The fragment length of a broad mark cannot be estimated (C2), so we set it; the two replicates are pooled to get more reads, against the same input; 40 088 619 / 46 709 983 = 0.858 is the mappable (non-N) fraction of chr21, which epic2 uses to compute its background. (b) MACS3 narrow: 11 regions, 3 kb, mean 255 bp. MACS3 --broad: 123 regions, 48 kb, mean 392 bp, max 1 493 bp. epic2: 671 domains, 3 769 kb, mean 5.6 kb, max 83 799 bp. In IGV, only epic2 follows the gene bodies visible in the coverage. Each call takes a few seconds.
C6. (a) IDR needs noise in its input (B6a); the files are sorted by −log10 p so that the strongest peaks come first (the order IDR’s --rank p.value uses and the order ENCODE truncates). 763, 570 and 691 lenient peaks. (b) 291 of 472 matched peaks pass IDR < 0.05; parameters μ = 1.95, σ = 0.56, ρ = 0.79, π = 0.60 (60% of the matched peaks are estimated to be reproducible). (c) 281 of the 291 are in ENCODE’s conservative set; 283 of ENCODE’s 405 chr21 peaks are recovered. IDR takes a few seconds.
C7. (a) -s 7.5: keep each read with probability 0.5, decided by a hash of the read name with seed 7, so the split is reproducible; -U writes the reads that were not kept to a second file. 158 696 and 158 967 reads. (b) \(N_1 = 409\), \(N_2 = 223\), \(N_p = 333\), \(N_t = 291\). Rescue ratio 333/291 = 1.14; self-consistency 409/223 = 1.83. Both below 2: passes, but replicate 2 (the low-complexity library) limits the experiment and brings self-consistency close to the limit. The whole block takes about 30 seconds.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Yes: correlation 0.998 with MACS’s λ at the 521 summits (the small differences come from how MACS centres the control windows). λd sets the background at 337 summits, λ1k at 92, λ10k at 49, λBG at 43. The input has 116 397 reads over 40 Mb, about 3 per kb: any single input read within 50 bp of a summit gives λd = 1, more than three times λBG = 0.29. (b) The ChIP pileup has been multiplied by 0.589, so it is not an integer; MACS rounds it up before the Poisson test. With ceiling, the p-values agree with column 8 to within 0.0005 (−log10 units). (c) chr21:33 605 968: k = 107.2 (182 fragments × 0.589), λBG 0.29, λd 13, λ1k 2.2, λ10k 0.43; −log10 p = 59.4. Thirteen input reads in 100 bp: an open CTCF site in an active gene-dense region, which the input of this experiment over-represents (ChIP-seq: the assay). The R part takes about a minute.
R2. Blocks of 100 peaks, strongest first: 0.91, 0.86, 0.71, 0.59, 0.55, 0.55 (the last block has 73 peaks). Random 101-bp windows: 0.036. Motif support falls with rank but stays far above random.
R3. With input: 521 peaks, 72% motif, 72% in ENCODE, median input ratio 2.4 (input reads within 500 bp of the summit / expected). Without input: 816, 60%, 49%, 2.4. Found only without input: 299, 36%, 9%, 2.1. The extra peaks are not in places with an unusually high input: they are weaker sites and noise that the input-based local λ rejected (a single input read near a summit is enough). The input acts here more as a stricter, locally varying threshold than as a correction for big artefacts; in a cancer cell line with amplifications the second role would dominate.
R4. Narrow: 11 regions, 2.8 kb, median 212 bp, covering 0.04% of active gene-body bases and 0% of silent ones. Broad: 123, 48 kb, median 332 bp, 0.85% and 0.01%. epic2: 671, 3 769 kb, median 1 799 bp, 57.9% of active and 6.7% of silent gene-body bases. epic2 is the useful result for this sparse broad mark; report the bin size (200 bp), gaps (3 bins), fragment size (200 bp), FDR (0.05), effective genome fraction, and that both replicates were pooled.
R5. (a) 472 matched peaks, 291 pass. The failing ones are at the weak end in both replicates and scattered (ranks unrelated), and some are strong in one replicate only. Spearman correlation of the two replicates’ scores 0.84. (b) 283 of 405 (70%). ENCODE used the full genome-wide reads of both replicates (deeper, so weaker sites are supported), and its replicate 2 limits ours: our IDR peaks are a strict subset of the strongest ones. Their median width is 266 bp.

title: Exercise: Peak calling
text:
Where this leads

Annotation and differential binding takes peaks further: where they are relative to genes, profiles around them, and differences between cell types with replicates.
CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag has almost no background, and callers such as SEACR that exploit it.
Chromatin states combines several marks into states, a different answer to “where are the domains?”.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
About this lecture


The wet lab: crosslinking, fragmentation (sonication or MNase), immunoprecipitation, library. What each step does, and what it gets wrong.
The signal: a population average; sharp peaks for transcription factors, broad domains for many histone marks; the input control.
Strands and resolution: why reads come in two shifted piles, and how far a binding site can be pinned down.
Real data: GM12878 CTCF and H3K36me3 ChIP-seq with their inputs (chr21), and ENCODE tracks of seven marks.


This is the assay unit of the ChIP-seq block. Students already know how to turn reads into a filtered BAM and a coverage track (From reads to coverage) and the QC metrics shared by all enrichment assays (Experimental design and QC); we use both without repeating them. Here the question is what the experiment physically measures, because every artefact in the data comes from a step in the figure. The input control is the same chromatin taken through every step except the immunoprecipitation: keep that definition in mind, it explains what the input can and cannot correct. The next units are Peak calling, then Annotation and differential binding. CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag replace steps 2 and 3 and have their own unit.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Two kinds of target


A transcription factor contacts a short motif: every enriched fragment overlaps the same site, so the reads pile up in a narrow peak.
A histone mark sits on nucleosomes, often on hundreds of them in a row: the enriched fragments tile a broad domain.
Same protocol, same reads; the shape of the signal decides how we call peaks and how deep we sequence.


The antibody defines the experiment. Against a protein (CTCF, a TF, Pol II, a chromatin remodeller) we see where the protein was when the cells were fixed. Against a histone modification (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K27me3) we see which nucleosomes carry the mark. The geometry follows: a TF occupies 10–30 bp, and any fragment that carries it must overlap that point, so the peak is about two fragment lengths wide at the base. A mark like H3K36me3 covers a transcribed gene body of tens of kilobases; every nucleosome there can be pulled down, so reads are spread thinly over the whole domain. The ENCODE standards reflect this: 20 million usable fragments per replicate for TFs and narrow marks, 45 million for broad marks, because a broad domain spreads its reads over a larger area. H3K4me3 and H3K27ac are in between: a few nucleosomes around a promoter or enhancer.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
From ChIP to ChIP-seq


The chemistry is from the 1980s; only the readout changed: one locus by PCR → arrays (ChIP-chip, 2000) → sequencing (ChIP-seq, 2007).
Sequencing gave the whole genome at once, with no probe design, better resolution and repeat-aware mapping.


Gilmour and Lis (1984) used UV light to crosslink RNA polymerase to DNA in E. coli; Solomon, Larsen and Varshavsky (1988) introduced formaldehyde and showed that histone H4 stays on a highly transcribed Drosophila gene. In the same year, Hebbes, Thorne and Crane-Robinson immunoprecipitated native, unfixed nucleosomes with antibodies against acetylated histones: the ancestor of native ChIP. For two decades a ChIP was read out locus by locus with PCR. ChIP-chip hybridised the DNA to microarrays (Ren et al. 2000 for yeast Gal4 and Ste12; Iyer et al. 2001), limited by probe density and cross-hybridisation in repeats. In 2007 four papers sequenced ChIP DNA on the then-new short-read instruments: Johnson et al. (NRSF), Robertson et al. (STAT1), Barski et al. (histone methylations in human T cells) and Mikkelsen et al. (chromatin states in mouse ES cells). MACS and SPP, the first widely used peak callers, followed in 2008. ChIP-exo (2011) and ChIP-nexus (2015) trimmed fragments to the protein; CUT&RUN (2017) and CUT&Tag (2019) dropped the immunoprecipitation altogether.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Step 1: crosslinking with formaldehyde


Formaldehyde is small and enters cells within seconds. It reacts with primary amines, mostly lysine side chains on proteins and the exocyclic amino groups of A, C and G, and joins two amines that are within about 2 ångström by a methylene bridge. So it fixes direct protein–DNA contacts and protein–protein contacts, which means a protein that never touches DNA can still be fixed to it through a partner. The reaction is stopped with glycine and reversed by heating to 65 °C for several hours. Fixation is a trade-off: too short and transient binders are lost during the long washes; too long and the epitope is chemically modified, the chromatin becomes hard to shear, and big crosslinked complexes give background everywhere. One percent formaldehyde for about ten minutes at room temperature is the usual compromise. For co-factors and chromatin remodellers people add a longer protein–protein crosslinker such as DSG first. Every increase in capture also captures more non-specific, indirect contacts: crosslinking is one of the reasons ChIP peaks are not proof of direct binding.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Step 2: fragmenting the chromatin


Sonication uses ultrasound to break DNA by cavitation. It needs no enzyme and works on crosslinked chromatin, which is why it is the standard for TF ChIP. It is hard to standardise: the result depends on the instrument, the volume, the number of cycles and how much the chromatin was fixed, so fragment sizes are broad, typically 100–600 bp. And it is not random: open, nucleosome-depleted chromatin breaks more easily, so promoters are over-represented among the fragments even without any antibody (next slide). Micrococcal nuclease (MNase) is an endo-exonuclease that cuts where no protein protects the DNA: in the linkers between nucleosomes. Partial digestion gives a ladder of mono-, di- and tri-nucleosomes; extensive digestion gives mostly mono-nucleosomes, about 147 bp plus some linker. MNase is the method of choice for native ChIP of histone marks because it gives nucleosome resolution. It prefers AT-rich DNA, and it can over-digest fragile nucleosomes, so MNase-based data have their own biases.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Real data: the input is not flat
text:
Real data: the input is not flat


Input coverage around the TSSs of chr21 protein-coding genes, active (H3K4me3 high) vs silent, relative to the chr21 average.
Input of the CTCF ChIP: 14× the average at active TSSs, 1.3× at silent ones. Input of the H3K36me3 ChIP: about 1.1× at both.
Inputs differ between protocols. The control must come from the same chromatin preparation as the ChIP.


Real data from the exercise (make-chipintro-figs.R): 72 active TSSs (ENCODE H3K4me3 fold change above 5 within 1 kb) and 107 silent ones (below 1), reads extended to 100 bp. The CTCF input (ENCODE ENCSR000EYX, Yale, 2009, 28 bp reads) is strongly enriched at active promoters: 14 times the chromosome average at the TSS itself (median over TSSs 12 times), 2.5 times 2 kb away. That is sonication bias, plus perhaps easier release of open chromatin from the nuclei. The input that came with the H3K36me3 experiment (ENCSR000AKJ, Broad, 2010) shows almost none of it. Two consequences. A peak at an active promoter is not evidence of binding unless it beats the input there; MACS uses the input’s local level, which is how this bias enters peak calling (Peak calling). And an input is only a good control for a ChIP made from the same chromatin with the same fragmentation: borrowing another lab’s input, or an input from a different cell type, corrects the wrong biases. Note how much depth matters, too: about 3 input reads per kb on chr21 here.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Steps 3–4: immunoprecipitation, and very little DNA
text:
Steps 3–4: immunoprecipitation, and very little DNA


Walk through the amounts; they explain most library problems. Ten million human cells contain about 66 µg of DNA (6.6 pg per diploid cell). The antibody, bound to protein A or G on magnetic beads, recovers a few nanograms, of the order of a ten-thousandth of the chromatin. Of those few nanograms, most is still background: chromatin that stuck to the beads, the tube or the antibody. In the CTCF ChIP of this course about 22% of the reads fall in ENCODE’s CTCF peaks (FRiP, Experimental design and QC), an excellent value; many good TF ChIPs are at a few percent. With a few nanograms, library preparation needs 10–15 PCR cycles, and the fewer molecules went in, the more PCR duplicates come out: the CTCF replicate 2 library in Peak calling has 61% duplicates. In the lab, enrichment is checked by ChIP-qPCR before sequencing: percent of input at a known bound site (often 1–20%) against a negative region (often below 0.1%). For the formula, the input Ct is first adjusted for the fraction of chromatin that was set aside as input (subtract log2 of the dilution factor).

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Antibodies: four ways to fail


Experimental design and QC covered how antibodies are validated (immunoblot, a second antibody or epitope tag, knockout). Here the focus is what each failure looks like in the data, because that is what you see when you read a paper. Cross-reactivity: histone-methylation antibodies often bind neighbouring methylation states (K4me2 and K4me3) or similar sequence contexts (H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 share an ARKS motif); a TF antibody can bind a paralog with a different motif. Masking: an adjacent modification (phosphorylation of H3S10 during mitosis next to K9me3), a partner protein or the crosslink itself can hide the epitope, so the “loss” of a peak may be a change next door. Weak or sticky antibodies give a ChIP that looks like its input: low FRiP, a fingerprint near the diagonal, peaks mostly at open promoters (the input bias of the previous slide), and high duplication because little DNA was recovered. Lot-to-lot variation: polyclonal sera are produced in animals and differ between bleeds; recombinant monoclonal antibodies are more reproducible. Egelhofer et al. 2011 found that about a quarter of the histone-modification antibodies they tested failed specificity tests.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: A ChIP signal is a population average
text:
A ChIP signal is a population average


A ChIP-seq library is made from millions of cells, and each fragment comes from one cell. A peak’s height adds up how many cells had the protein there at the moment of fixation, how long it stays (a TF that binds for seconds is captured less often than one that stays for minutes), and technical efficiencies at that site: crosslinkability, epitope access, shearing, copy number and mappability. So comparing heights between different sites of the same sample says little about occupancy. Comparing the same site between samples processed the same way is meaningful: that is differential binding (Annotation and differential binding). Heterogeneity is invisible: site C could be bound in every cell of a minority cell type or in half of all cells. Single-cell methods (single-cell CUT&Tag) and sorting answer that question; bulk ChIP cannot. Co-binding of two factors at a site in a bulk ChIP likewise does not mean they bind together in one cell; sequential ChIP (re-ChIP) is needed for that.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Native ChIP: no crosslinking


Histones stay on DNA without fixation because a nucleosome is stable in the salt conditions of a ChIP, so histone marks can be mapped on native chromatin digested with MNase. Advantages: no epitope masking by formaldehyde, often a cleaner IP, nucleosome resolution, and no crosslinking artefacts. Barski et al. 2007, one of the first ChIP-seq papers, used native MNase ChIP for histone methylations. Disadvantages: most TFs dissociate or slide during digestion and washes, so native ChIP is not used for them; MNase cuts AT-rich linkers preferentially and can destroy fragile, often highly active, nucleosomes. Both methods use an input made the same way as the ChIP; for native ChIP of a mark, a ChIP of total H3 is a useful second control because it shows nucleosome occupancy (a mark per nucleosome rather than per base of DNA). CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag are also usually done on native, unfixed nuclei.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Real data: seven antibodies, one locus
text:
Real data: seven antibodies, one locus


ENCODE fold change over input for GM12878 at chr21:33.0–33.62 Mb, in 500-bp bins (make-chipintro-figs.R). Gene colours: green = active (H3K4me3 fold change above 5 at the TSS), red = silent (below 1), grey = in between. Walk down the tracks. CTCF: needles. H3K4me3: a peak at each active promoter (IFNAR1, IFNGR2, TMEM50B, GART/SON, DONSON; weaker at IFNAR2 and IL10RB). H3K27ac: promoters plus a few distal sites, the candidate enhancers. H3K4me1: wider areas around promoters and enhancers. H3K36me3: carpets over the bodies of transcribed genes, starting a little after the TSS. H3K27me3: a broad domain over the silent OLIG1/OLIG2 genes, developmental regulators of glia that a B-cell line has no use for (Polycomb repression). H3K9me3 is low here, but shows small peaks at active promoters: H3K9me3 belongs in heterochromatin, so these are most likely the open-chromatin and “hyper-ChIPable” artefacts discussed later, a reminder that every track has background structure. The y scales differ per track.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Where the marks sit on a gene
text:
Where the marks sit on a gene


A summary diagram of the shapes students will meet for the rest of the course (chromatin-intro introduced the marks themselves). Promoter marks, H3K4me3 and H3K27ac, sit on the nucleosomes flanking the nucleosome-free region at the TSS, so their profile has a dip exactly at the TSS. H3K4me1 marks enhancers and the flanks of promoters, and is depleted where H3K4me3 is high. H3K36me3 is deposited by SETD2, which travels with elongating RNA polymerase II, so it covers transcribed gene bodies and rises towards the 3’ end. H3K27me3 (Polycomb) forms broad domains over silent developmental genes; at “bivalent” promoters in stem cells it coexists with a weak H3K4me3. CTCF marks insulators and loop anchors (3D genome units). H3K9me3 covers constitutive heterochromatin: repeats, pericentromeres, ZNF gene clusters. Chromatin states combines all of these into states with an HMM.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Real data: profiles around genes


Left: at 72 active TSSs, H3K4me3 and H3K27ac dip at the TSS (the nucleosome-free region) and peak on the flanking nucleosomes; H3K4me1 is depleted.
Right: H3K36me3 covers the bodies of active genes (mean fold change 2.2) and not of silent ones (0.45).


Averages of ENCODE fold-change tracks at base resolution, genes on the minus strand flipped (make-chipintro-figs.R). Left: H3K27ac reaches 21.6 at +230 bp and 17.7 at −300 bp, with 8.1 at the TSS itself; H3K4me3 has 4.1 at the TSS and about 10–12 on the flanks. The dip is the nucleosome-free region, typically 150–200 bp, occupied by the transcription machinery and TFs rather than nucleosomes: a histone ChIP cannot be enriched where there are no histones. H3K4me1 is lowest (0.5) at the TSS and highest about 1 kb away. H3K36me3 is nearly absent at the TSS and rises into the gene. Right: 69 active and 49 silent protein-coding genes longer than 5 kb, gene bodies scaled to 20 bins. H3K36me3 rises after the TSS and stays high to the end of the gene, then falls. This is the shape of a mark written co-transcriptionally. These are the kind of plots made with deepTools computeMatrix and plotHeatmap in Annotation and differential binding.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Real data: how far does the signal extend?
text:
Real data: how far does the signal extend?


Correlation of the signal between two 100-bp bins at a given distance, along chr21. CTCF loses it within a few hundred bp; H3K4me3 within a few kb; H3K36me3 and H3K27me3 keep it over tens of kb.


This is a peak-free way to measure “sharp” and “broad”. For each mark: ENCODE fold change in 100-bp bins over the long arm of chr21, log-transformed, and the Pearson correlation between bins d apart. At 200 bp CTCF is down to 0.14 while the histone marks are around 0.4–0.5; at 1 kb CTCF is at 0.06, H3K4me3 0.35, H3K36me3 0.41; at 10 kb H3K4me3 0.12 but H3K36me3 still 0.33 and H3K27me3 0.23. The first steep drop for every mark is noise (two bins share fragments only up to a fragment length apart). The tail is biology: the size of the regions over which the mark is laid down. The broad tail is why peak callers for histone marks join neighbouring windows into domains (Peak calling).

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Why reads come in two shifted piles
text:
Why reads come in two shifted piles


A single-end read is the 5’ end of a fragment. Fragments that carry a bound TF extend to either side of it; those sequenced from their left end give + strand reads to the left of the site, those sequenced from their right end give − strand reads to the right. The two piles are about one fragment length d apart (From reads to coverage showed this for CTCF and used it to extend reads). Shifting the + strand pile by k and correlating it with the − strand gives the strand cross-correlation, which peaks at k = d, plus a “phantom” peak at the read length from mappability (Experimental design and QC introduced NSC and RSC). For a broad domain, both strands cover the same 20 kb; shifting by a few hundred bp hardly changes the overlap, so the curve is flat. That is why fragment-length estimation, NSC and RSC are made for TFs and narrow marks and are unreliable for broad marks; with paired-end reads the fragment length is simply measured.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Real data: a TF and a broad mark
text:
Real data: a TF and a broad mark


CTCF: a clear fragment peak, cross-correlation 0.15 at 93 bp; its input is flat (≤ 0.002).
H3K36me3: no peak at any shift, values around 0.0013, 100 times lower; the ChIP is above its input only because both strands share the same domains.
Fragment-length estimates and NSC/RSC are tools for TFs and narrow marks.


Computed in R exactly as in the exercise (make-chipintro-figs.R): 5’ ends of the filtered reads per strand on the long arm of chr21, Pearson correlation of + strand counts at x with − strand counts at x + k; a 25-bp running mean is drawn because the H3K36me3 curve is noisy at single-base resolution. Note the y-axes: the two panels differ by a factor of 100. CTCF peaks at 93 bp (macs3 predictd says 100 bp; ENCODE 90–95 bp); the read-length position (36 bp) sits on the rising flank at 0.09, so there is no separate phantom peak here. H3K36me3 has 70 741 reads spread over tens of megabases of gene bodies: the + and − strand reads correlate weakly at every shift because they fall in the same domains, and the maximum at 294 bp is noise. A peak caller asked to build its model on this mark finds few paired strand peaks; for broad marks one sets the fragment length (e.g. from the sonication profile, or 147 bp for MNase) or uses paired-end reads.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Real data: H3K36me3 over transcribed genes
text:
Real data: H3K36me3 over transcribed genes


Our own reads (exercise), CPM in 1-kb bins. H3K36me3 covers the transcribed genes from a little after the TSS to the end; the input is flat.
In active gene bodies: 75.6 H3K36me3 reads per kb per million vs 31.4 in the input; in silent genes 23.4 vs 27.4.


Reads from the H3K36me3 ChIP (ENCSR000AKE replicate 1, Broad, 51 bp) and its input aligned and filtered with the chain from From reads to coverage: 70 741 and 73 652 reads on chr21 after filtering, extended to 200 bp. The CTCF track is shown for contrast (note its different y scale). Gene colours: green active, red silent, grey in between (H3K4me3 at the TSS). The H3K36me3 enrichment is modest, about 2.4-fold over input in active gene bodies, and spread over 10–50 kb: in 1-kb bins it is clear, at a single base it would be invisible. The chr21 average is 24.9 reads per kb per million: silent genes sit at the background level, and the input itself is a little higher in active, gene-dense regions (31.4), which is why the ChIP is compared with the input rather than with the chromosome average. This dataset is sparse (only 0.42% of the 22 million reads in the library are on chr21, about half the share in the input), which is why calling broad domains in it is a challenge in Peak calling.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
section: Resolution: where exactly is the protein?
text:
Resolution: where exactly is the protein?


In ChIP-seq the protein is somewhere inside each enriched fragment, and the fragment ends are where sonication happened to break the DNA. With enough fragments, the centre of the + and − strand piles (the summit) locates the site within tens of base pairs, and a motif search around the summit narrows it to the motif. ChIP-exo (Rhee and Pugh 2011) adds a lambda exonuclease step on the beads: it digests each strand 5’→3’ until it is blocked by the crosslinked protein, so the read starts line up at the protein’s border, and the distance between + and − strand borders is the footprint. ChIP-nexus (He et al. 2015) is a simpler library protocol with the same idea. Higher resolution separates closely spaced sites, shows the footprint of a complex, and reveals indirect binding (a factor with the footprint of another). CUT&RUN gets similar resolution because the tethered MNase cuts right next to the antibody-bound protein.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Peaks that are not binding


Four ways to get a convincing peak that does not mean “this protein binds this DNA”. Hyper-ChIPable regions: Teytelman et al. 2013 found that in yeast highly expressed genes give ChIP signal with antibodies against unrelated proteins, even GFP in cells without GFP; Jain et al. 2015 found “phantom peaks” at active promoters in Drosophila. Mock IPs (IgG, or an epitope-tag ChIP in cells without the tag) reveal them; be suspicious of a factor whose peaks are all at the most active promoters. Indirect binding: crosslinking captures a protein through its partner; such peaks lack the factor’s motif and are often weaker; ENCODE found that many TF peak sets are dominated by motifs of other factors. Copy number: an amplified region has more reads in every library; the input corrects it only if it comes from the same cells (K562 has many amplifications; Annotation and differential binding uses it). Repeats: collapsed repeats attract reads (blacklist); multi-copy regions lose unique reads (MAPQ filter), so absence of signal there means “unknown”.

A planning table to pull the lecture together; each row links to a step on the earlier slides. Histone ChIPs need fewer cells because every nucleosome in a domain can be captured, while a TF is present at a few thousand sites. Epitope tagging (FLAG, HA, or a tag knocked into the endogenous gene) is a common way around a poor antibody, with the tag-only ChIP as a control. title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Beyond ChIP-seq








method
what changes
why use it




ChIP-exo, ChIP-nexus

Mint-ChIP and other barcoded ChIP

CUT&RUN

low background, few cells, no sonication


CUT&Tag
antibody-tethered Tn5 inserts adapters at the target
very few cells, single-cell versions


spike-in ChIP (ChIP-Rx)

quantitative comparisons under global changes




ChIP-seq is still the reference method (ENCODE’s thousands of datasets are ChIP-seq), but for many histone marks CUT&Tag has replaced it in new studies because it needs far fewer cells and gives much lower background. The CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag unit covers those. Spike-ins come back in Annotation and differential binding, where normalisation under a global change matters. Mint-ChIP (Mint = multiplexed, indexed T7) and similar barcoding methods pool many samples into one IP, which removes IP-to-IP variation between samples.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




crosslinking
formaldehyde joins amines within ~2 Å; captures direct and indirect contacts; reversed at 65 °C


fragmentation
sonication: random-ish, biased to open chromatin; MNase: linker cuts, nucleosome resolution (native ChIP)


IP and library
a few ng of DNA from µg of chromatin, mostly background; PCR duplicates when yields are low


antibodies
cross-reactivity, masking, weak/sticky, lot variation: each with a signature in the data


input
same chromatin, no IP; shows shearing, copy number and mappability; must match the ChIP


signal shape
TF: sharp peak around the site; histone marks: nucleosome-scale to 100-kb domains


strands
+ reads left, − reads right of a site, d apart; flat cross-correlation for broad marks


interpretation
a population average; height ≠ occupancy; peaks can be indirect or artefacts




Students should be able to draw the protocol and say what each step can get wrong, compute DNA amounts and a percent-input, predict the shape of a track for a TF and for a mark, explain why the input is needed and why it must match, and read a strand cross-correlation plot. Next: Peak calling turns these reads into peaks, with the input entering through the local λ.

title: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Solomon, Larsen & Varshavsky 1988, Cell. Mapping protein-DNA interactions in vivo with formaldehyde: evidence that histone H4 is retained on a highly transcribed gene. The formaldehyde ChIP.
Johnson, Mortazavi, Myers & Wold 2007, Science. Genome-wide mapping of in vivo protein-DNA interactions. One of the first ChIP-seq papers (NRSF).
Barski et al. 2007, Cell. High-resolution profiling of histone methylations in the human genome. Native ChIP-seq of 20 histone methylations; the shapes on our profile slide.
Park 2009, Nat Rev Genet. ChIP-seq: advantages and challenges of a maturing technology. A clear review of the assay and its analysis.
Rhee & Pugh 2011, Cell. Comprehensive genome-wide protein-DNA interactions detected at single-nucleotide resolution. ChIP-exo.
Teytelman et al. 2013, PNAS. Highly expressed loci are vulnerable to misleading ChIP localization of multiple unrelated proteins. Hyper-ChIPable regions.

title: Quiz: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Short questions on annotating peaks, reading heatmaps and testing differential binding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A gene on the − strand spans 50 000–80 000 (TSS at 80 000). A peak is centred at 80 600. With a promoter window of TSS ± 1 kb, what is its category, and is it upstream or downstream of the TSS?






Answer





Promoter (600 bp from the TSS). For a − strand gene, larger coordinates are upstream: the peak is 600 bp upstream (distance −600).




Q2. 35% of a TF’s peaks are “promoters” with a ±3 kb window and 18% with ±1 kb. Which number would you report, and what else must you report with it?






Answer





Either, but with the window. Also the annotation used (which genes and transcripts) and the priority rule. The category depends on all three, so numbers from different papers are comparable only with the same settings.




Q3. Why is “the nearest gene” a weak assignment of a distal peak to a target gene? Name one better kind of evidence.






Answer





Enhancers act over tens to hundreds of kb and often skip the nearest gene. Better: 3D contacts (Hi-C, HiChIP), correlation of the element’s activity with gene expression across samples, or perturbation (CRISPRi/deletion changes the gene’s expression).




Q4. An average profile of H3K27ac around 5 000 peaks shows a clear peak. What can the heatmap show that the profile cannot?






Answer





Whether all regions have a similar signal or a few strong regions dominate the average; subgroups with different shapes; regions with no signal at all; whether the pattern is the same in all samples. Each row is one region.




Q5. Why must a consensus region set for differential binding include peaks from all conditions?






Answer





Regions that only have signal in one condition would otherwise be missing, so gains (or losses) in that condition could never be found: the test is biased towards the condition whose peaks were used.




Q6. Two ChIP libraries have equal depth. Sample B has FRiP 0.3, sample A 0.15, and all peaks are 2× higher in B. Give one biological and one technical explanation. Which normalisation does each call for?






Answer





Biological: B has twice as much of the mark at its sites (a global increase) → library-size normalisation, or better spike-ins, keeps the difference. Technical: B’s IP was more efficient → normalising on peaks (DESeq2’s median-of-ratios) removes the artefact. The data alone cannot tell them apart.




Q7. Spike-in reads: control 30 000 and 30 000, treated 90 000 and 90 000. A region has 450 reads in each sample. Compute spike-in size factors and normalised counts. What happened to the region?






Answer





Geometric mean = √(30 000 × 90 000) = 51 962. Size factors 0.577, 0.577, 1.732, 1.732. Normalised counts 780 and 260: the region lost two thirds of its signal (log2FC −1.58), although the raw counts are identical.




Q8. In whole-genome inputs, chr22 holds 1.46% of the reads in cell line X and 1.14% in cell line Y. What does that imply for a differential binding analysis of chr22 regions between X and Y?






Answer





X has about 1.28× more chr22 DNA relative to its genome (a copy-number gain): every chr22 region gets about +0.36 log2 units in X before any biology. Correct with input-based copy-number factors, greylists, or by comparing within equal copy number; otherwise many “gains” in X are copy number.




Q9. After an EZH2 inhibitor, a paper finds H3K27me3 “redistributed”: lost from some domains and gained at others, using reads-per-million normalisation and no spike-in. Why might the “gains” be artefacts?






Answer





EZH2 inhibition lowers H3K27me3 globally. Normalising to equal totals scales the remaining signal up, so domains that lost less than average (or kept their mark) appear gained. A spike-in (or a western blot showing the global loss) is needed before calling gains.




Q10. Which parts of a differential binding analysis with DESeq2 are exactly as in RNA-seq, and which are different?






Answer





Same: the count matrix (features × samples), negative binomial model, dispersion estimation, design formula with batch, Wald/LRT tests, FDR, MA and volcano plots, the need for ≥ 3 biological replicates. Different: the features are derived from the data (consensus peaks or windows), fragments are counted, normalisation must consider signal-to-noise, copy number and global changes (spike-ins), and the input/background must be considered.

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Background
Annotation. Each peak gets one category by priority (ChIPseeker default: promoter > 5’ UTR > 3’ UTR > exon > intron > downstream > distal intergenic), with “promoter” = TSS ± a window (here 1 kb), and its nearest TSS with a signed distance (negative = upstream, positive = downstream, relative to the gene’s strand).
Differential binding. Regions from all conditions (union of peak sets, or peaks found in at least n samples) → reads (fragments) counted per region and sample → normalisation → negative binomial test (DESeq2/edgeR) with a design formula, exactly as for genes in RNA-seq.
Size factors. DESeq2 divides each sample’s counts by a size factor \(s_j\). Median-of-ratios (default): \(s_j\) = median over regions of (count / geometric mean of the region’s counts). Library size: \(s_j \propto N_j\). Background: median-of-ratios on large bins without peaks. Spike-in: \(s_j \propto N_{\text{spike},j}\). Each assumes something is constant between samples: all reads, most peaks, the background, or the spike-in.

You need bedtools, deeptools, samtools and the R packages DESeq2, ChIPseeker, txdbmaker, GenomicAlignments, rtracklayer (see Install the software you need; BiocManager::install(c("ChIPseeker", "txdbmaker"))). The command line takes about a minute, the R part about two.






Simplifications



Two cell lines are an extreme contrast with thousands of real differences, and two replicates per group is the minimum, not the recommendation (three or more). The two experiments also differ in read length and date: technical variables confounded with cell type. Everything is on chr21.

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
By hand
B1. Annotate peaks. Gene G1 is on the + strand with its TSS at 10 000, exons 10 000–10 300, 15 000–15 200 and 29 500–30 000. Gene G2 is on the − strand from 40 000 to 52 000 (its TSS is at 52 000). Using a promoter window of TSS ± 1 kb, “downstream” = up to 300 bp after the gene end, and ChIPseeker’s priority, give the category, the nearest TSS and the signed distance to it for peaks centred at: a 9 400; b 10 800; c 15 100; d 22 000; e 30 200; f 51 500; g 35 000.
B2. Nearest gene. Peak g of B1 is a strong H3K27ac peak. A paper lists G2 as its target gene. What would you need to believe that? Name two kinds of data that would support or refute it.
B3. Consensus regions. Condition A has peaks at chr1:100–600, 2 000–2 400 and 9 000–9 300; condition B at 450–900, 5 000–5 500 and 9 100–9 500.
