  -S h3k27ac_gm12878_rep1.cpm.bw h3k27ac_gm12878_rep2.cpm.bw h3k27ac_k562_rep1.cpm.bw h3k27ac_k562_rep2.cpm.bw \
  --samplesLabel GM12878_1 GM12878_2 K562_1 K562_2 -a 3000 -b 3000 --binSize 50 -p $T -o h3k27ac.mat.gz 2> /dev/null
plotHeatmap -m h3k27ac.mat.gz -o h3k27ac_heatmap.png --colorMap Oranges --zMax 150 \
  --heatmapHeight 12 --refPointLabel centre

Explain the awk that makes genes_chr21.bed. Why must column 6 hold the strand?
Open tss_heatmap.png. About what fraction of chr21 protein-coding genes look active? Where is H3K36me3 relative to the TSS?
Open h3k27ac_heatmap.png and answer B9.

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
In R
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(GenomicAlignments); library(rtracklayer); library(DESeq2) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/chipdiff")

R1 — Annotate three peak sets
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(ChIPseeker); library(txdbmaker) })
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), which = chr21)
seqlevels(gtf, pruning.mode = "coarse") <- "chr21"
txdb <- makeTxDbFromGRanges(gtf[gtf$type %in% c("gene", "transcript", "exon", "CDS", "UTR")])
np <- function(f) { p <- import(f, format = "narrowPeak"); p[seqnames(p) == "chr21"] }
sets <- list(CTCF = np(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz")),
             H3K27ac_GM12878 = np(file.path(D, "gm12878_h3k27ac_peaks.bed.gz")),
             H3K27ac_K562 = np(file.path(D, "k562_h3k27ac_peaks.bed.gz")))
ann <- lapply(sets, annotatePeak, TxDb = txdb, tssRegion = c(-1000, 1000), verbose = FALSE)
st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ann), function(n) data.frame(set = n, getAnnoStat(ann[[n]]))))
round(xtabs(Frequency ~ Feature + set, st), 1)
sapply(ann, function(a) { d <- abs(as.data.frame(a)$distanceToTSS); c(within1kb = mean(d <= 1000), over10kb = mean(d > 10000), median = median(d)) })
plotAnnoBar(ann)

What fraction of each peak set is at promoters, in introns, distal intergenic? How do CTCF and H3K27ac differ, and why?
Run annotatePeak once more for CTCF with ChIPseeker’s default tssRegion = c(-3000, 3000). How does the promoter fraction change?



R2 — Count and test
bl <- import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz"))
cons <- import("consensus.bed")
smp <- c(GM_1 = "h3k27ac_gm12878_rep1", GM_2 = "h3k27ac_gm12878_rep2", K562_1 = "h3k27ac_k562_rep1", K562_2 = "h3k27ac_k562_rep2",
         GM_input = "input_gm12878", K562_input = "input_k562")
centre <- function(s) {                              # fragment centres: shift each read 100 bp along its strand
  r <- granges(readGAlignments(file.path(D, paste0(s, ".chr21.bam"))))
  r <- r[!overlapsAny(r, bl)]
  resize(resize(r, 200, fix = "start"), 1, fix = "center")
}
mid <- lapply(smp, centre)
cnt <- sapply(mid, function(m) countOverlaps(cons, m, ignore.strand = TRUE))
rownames(cnt) <- paste0("chr21:", start(cons), "-", end(cons))
colSums(cnt); sapply(mid, length); round(colSums(cnt) / sapply(mid, length), 3)
cd <- data.frame(cell = factor(c("GM12878", "GM12878", "K562", "K562")), row.names = names(smp)[1:4])
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cnt[, 1:4], cd, ~ cell)
dds <- DESeq(dds, quiet = TRUE)
sizeFactors(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("cell", "K562", "GM12878"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-8, 8))

Why count fragment centres rather than reads? What is FRiP for each library?
How many regions are significantly higher in K562, and how many in GM12878? Which steps are identical to an RNA-seq analysis?



R3 — Three normalisations
lib <- sapply(mid[1:4], length)
bins <- tileGenome(c(chr21 = 46709983), tilewidth = 10000, cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE)
bins <- bins[start(bins) > 13e6 & !overlapsAny(bins, cons, maxgap = 5000) & !overlapsAny(bins, bl)]
bg <- sapply(mid[1:4], function(m) countOverlaps(bins, m, ignore.strand = TRUE))
sf <- cbind(peaks_RLE = sizeFactors(dds), library = lib / exp(mean(log(lib))), background = estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(bg))
round(sf, 3)
test <- function(s) { d <- dds; sizeFactors(d) <- s; results(DESeq(d, quiet = TRUE), contrast = c("cell", "K562", "GM12878")) }
rs <- lapply(as.data.frame(sf), test)
sapply(rs, function(r) c(up = sum(r$padj < 0.05 & r$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
                         down = sum(r$padj < 0.05 & r$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
                         median_lfc = median(r$log2FoldChange)))

Compare the three sets of size factors. Which assumption does each make?
How do the numbers of up and down regions and the median log2 fold change change? Explain the direction of the shift with FRiP (B7) and copy number (B6).



R4 — Copy number from the inputs
ix <- read.delim(file.path(D, "h3k27ac_idxstats.tsv"))
ix <- ix[ix$chrom %in% paste0("chr", c(1:22, "X")), ]
share <- with(ix, tapply(mapped, list(chrom, sample), sum))
share <- sweep(share, 2, colSums(share), "/")
cn <- share[, "input_k562"] / share[, "input_gm12878"]
round(sort(cn), 2)
barplot(sort(cn), las = 2, ylab = "K562 / GM12878 input share")
Which chromosomes are over- and under-represented in K562 relative to GM12878? What does that mean for a differential analysis restricted to chr21?


R5 — A global change, simulated
set.seed(42)
n <- 2000; mu <- rlnorm(n, log(100), 1)
change <- rep(0.5, n); change[1:100] <- 1                 # treatment halves the mark at 95% of the peaks
truth <- cbind(ctrl = mu, ctrl = mu, ctrl = mu, trt = mu * change, trt = mu * change, trt = mu * change)
depth <- 1e6 / colSums(truth)                             # every library is sequenced to the same depth
counts <- matrix(rnbinom(length(truth), mu = sweep(truth, 2, depth, "*") * 0.2, size = 20), n)
spike <- c(5000, 5000, 5000, 10000, 10000, 10000) * c(1, 1.05, 0.95, 1, 0.97, 1.03)   # fly reads: same fly chromatin, half the human
colnames(counts) <- paste0(c("c", "c", "c", "t", "t", "t"), 1:6)
cd2 <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), each = 3), c("ctrl", "trt")), row.names = colnames(counts))
d2 <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, cd2, ~ group)
r_rle <- results(DESeq(d2, quiet = TRUE))
sizeFactors(d2) <- spike / exp(mean(log(spike)))
r_spk <- results(DESeq(d2, quiet = TRUE))
sapply(list(RLE = r_rle, spike_in = r_spk), function(r) c(down = sum(r$padj < 0.05 & r$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
  up = sum(r$padj < 0.05 & r$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE), median_lfc = median(r$log2FoldChange),
  unchanged_peaks_lfc = median(r$log2FoldChange[1:100])))

Read the simulation: what is the truth, and why are the treated spike-in counts twice the control ones?
What does each normalisation conclude? Which peaks does standard normalisation call “up”, and why?



R6 — The strongest differences, and their nearest genes
pc <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding"]
pc_tss <- resize(pc, 1, fix = "start")
nn <- distanceToNearest(cons, pc_tss, ignore.strand = TRUE)
r <- rs$peaks_RLE
top <- data.frame(region = rownames(cnt), lfc = round(r$log2FoldChange, 1), padj = signif(r$padj, 2),
                  nearest_gene = pc_tss$gene_name[subjectHits(nn)], kb_to_tss = round(mcols(nn)$distance / 1000, 1))
head(top[order(r$log2FoldChange), ], 8)        # higher in GM12878
head(top[order(-r$log2FoldChange), ], 8)       # higher in K562
Which regions differ most in each direction, and how far are they from the nearest protein-coding TSS? Some top regions are at chr21:5–10 Mb, near the centromere: why would you check those in a browser before believing them?

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — annotation (B1, B2, R1)





Check the categories in priority order; a peak in an intron within 1 kb of a TSS is “promoter”. For a − strand gene, upstream means larger coordinates. ChIPseeker: annotatePeak (tssRegion, genomicAnnotationPriority), plotAnnoBar; a TxDb from a GTF with txdbmaker::makeTxDbFromGRanges.









Hint 2 — consensus and counting (B3, C2, R2)





bedtools merge needs sorted input; DiffBind’s dba.peakset(minOverlap = 2) builds a consensus of peaks in at least two samples. countOverlaps counts per region; resize(resize(r, 200, fix = "start"), 1, fix = "center") turns each read into the centre of its 200-bp fragment.









Hint 3 — normalisation (B4–B7, R3, R5)





Median of ratios: divide each count by the geometric mean of its row, take each sample’s median (DESeq2 vignette; estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix). You can set your own with sizeFactors(dds) <- s. Background bins and efficiency bias: Lun & Smyth 2016 and the csaw book. Spike-ins: Orlando et al. 2014.









Hint 4 — deepTools (C3, C4, B9)





computeMatrix (reference-point / scale-regions; one group per BED file), plotHeatmap (--sortUsingSamples, --zMax, --kmeans), bamCoverage. In a GTF the 9th column holds key "value"; pairs; BED needs 0-based starts.

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Solutions
Numbers from running the commands as written (bedtools 2.30, deepTools 3.5.1, samtools 1.21, R 4.6, DESeq2 and ChIPseeker from Bioconductor 3.23).






Solutions — by hand





B1. a 9 400: within 1 kb of G1’s TSS → promoter, −600 (upstream). b 10 800: in the first intron but within 1 kb → promoter (priority), +800. c 15 100: exon (exon 2 of G1), +5 100. d 22 000: intron, +12 000 from G1. e 30 200: 200 bp after G1’s end → downstream; nearest TSS G1 at +20 200 (G2’s TSS is 21 800 away). f 51 500: within 1 kb of G2’s TSS → promoter; G2 is on the − strand, so 51 500 is 500 bp downstream: +500. g 35 000: distal intergenic; nearest TSS is G2’s (17 000 away; G1’s is 25 000), and since G2 runs leftwards from 52 000, 35 000 lies beyond its 3’ end: +17 000.
B2. That an element 17 kb beyond the 3’ end of G2 regulates G2 rather than G1 or another gene further away. Support would come from 3D contacts (Hi-C, HiChIP, Capture-C) between g and G2’s promoter, from correlation between g’s acetylation and G2’s expression across many samples, and above all from perturbation (CRISPR interference or deletion of g changes G2’s expression). Nearest-gene assignment alone is a hypothesis.
B3. (a) 100–900 (A and B overlap), 2 000–2 400 (A only), 5 000–5 500 (B only), 9 000–9 500 (both): four regions, two condition-specific. (b) Regions where only B has signal are not in the set, so a gain in B cannot be counted; the region set itself is biased towards A.
B4. (a) Library size is equal, so log2(B/A) = log2 1.5 = 0.58 for every peak: all up. (b) Geometric means per peak: √(100·150) = 122.5, 244.9, 367.4, 489.9; ratios A: 0.816 (all four), B: 1.225. Size factors 0.816 and 1.225; after normalisation all four peaks are equal: log2FC = 0. (c) Background bins hold almost all reads (99.9%), so equalising them is nearly the same as equalising the totals. (d) Biology: B has 1.5 times more H3K27ac at all its peaks (e.g. after an HDAC inhibitor) → library size or background normalisation is right (or, better, spike-in). Technical: B’s IP was more efficient (higher FRiP) → peak-based normalisation is right. The counts alone cannot tell them apart; a spike-in or an orthogonal measurement can.
B5. (a) Geometric mean of the fly reads 70 354; size factors 0.57, 0.63, 1.71, 1.65; normalised counts 1 055, 1 055, 352, 352. (b) 352/1 055 = 0.33: domain X lost two thirds of its H3K27me3 (log2FC −1.58). Default normalisation (if most domains lose the same fraction) would centre them on zero: “no change”, with any domain that lost less looking “gained”. (c) The same fly chromatin went into every IP, but treated cells had a third of the human H3K27me3, so the IP pulled down much less human DNA and the fly reads made up a larger share of the same sequencing depth.
B6. (a) 1.45/1.17 = 1.24: about 24% more chr21 DNA per genome in K562 than on average (e.g. 4 copies in a near-triploid genome), relative to GM12878. (b) log2(1.24) = +0.31 in K562, purely from copy number. Correct by including the input-derived copy-number ratio as an offset or normalisation factor for chr21 regions, by subtracting scaled input, or by comparing only regions of equal copy number.
B7. If peaks are equal per cell, K562 reads in peaks are a smaller fraction of its library (0.40 vs 0.55): log2(0.40/0.55) = −0.46. The observed −0.33 is in between, consistent with a lower K562 FRiP partly offset by its extra chr21 copies (+0.31, B6) and by real differences.
B8. n = 1 per condition (no estimate of variability; no test is valid); no spike-in although HDAC inhibitors raise acetylation globally (reads per million would hide a global increase and could even turn it into apparent decreases at many sites); reads-per-million normalisation assumes the total is unchanged; “increased/decreased” by an unspecified cutoff rather than a statistical test; probably no input (copy number unaffected here, but background). Better: ≥ 3 biological replicates per condition, a spike-in (or synthetic nucleosome standards) added before the IP, an input per sample, DESeq2 with spike-in size factors on a consensus region set, and a western blot of total H3K27ac.
B9. (a) Regions with H3K27ac in both cell lines are mostly promoters of widely expressed genes, the strongest acetylated sites in any cell type. (b) Yes: every consensus region is tested in all samples; the grouping only shows where each peak set came from. Low K562 signal there may be a real but weaker region or background; the test decides. (c) Groups defined by peak sets are reproducible and interpretable; k-means starts from random centres and gave different cluster sizes on repeated runs of plotHeatmap.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) GM12878 H3K27ac 77 287 and 63 771 reads, 51 bp; K562 138 349 and 64 594 reads, 36 bp; inputs 67 706 (GM12878, 51 bp) and 238 922 (K562, 36 bp). (b) chr21 share: GM12878 H3K27ac 1.11% and 1.11%, K562 H3K27ac 1.30% and 1.31%, GM12878 input 1.17%, K562 input 1.45%. chr22: GM12878 input 1.14%, K562 input 1.46%. K562 has relatively more chr21 and chr22 DNA (R4).
C2. 567 GM12878 and 483 K562 peaks on chr21; 841 consensus regions: 378 GM12878 only, 170 both, 293 K562 only. Median width 687 bp, maximum 15 802 bp (merged neighbouring peaks).
C3. The cluster at 25.4–25.5 Mb is strong in both GM12878 replicates and absent in K562. The nearest protein-coding gene is MRPL39, more than 100 kb away (a lncRNA, LINC00158, lies within the cluster). Each bamCoverage run takes a few seconds.
C4. (a) The first awk keeps chr21 gene lines of protein-coding genes; the second extracts the gene name from column 9 and prints BED6: chromosome, start − 1 (BED is 0-based), end, name, score, strand. computeMatrix uses the strand to put the TSS at the start of − strand genes and to flip their profiles. 220 genes. (b) About a third of the genes (the top of the heatmap) have H3K4me3 and H3K27ac at the TSS and H3K36me3 downstream; H3K36me3 starts after the TSS and continues into the gene body. (c) See B9. The two computeMatrix runs take about 20 s each.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Promoter (±1 kb): CTCF 18.3%, H3K27ac GM12878 33.3%, K562 40.0%. Introns (1st + other): 42.5%, 39.9%, 36.6%. Distal intergenic: 32.6%, 17.1%, 17.2%. Median distance to the nearest TSS 8.6 kb, 3.6 kb and 2.2 kb; 47%, 32% and 27% are more than 10 kb away. H3K27ac marks active promoters and enhancers; CTCF binds insulators and loop anchors, mostly away from promoters. (b) With the default ±3 kb (annotatePeak(sets$CTCF, TxDb = txdb)), ChIPseeker splits promoters into ≤ 1 kb (18.3%), 1–2 kb (7.2%) and 2–3 kb (6.4%): 31.9% of CTCF peaks are now “promoter”, taken from introns (33.3% instead of 42.5%) and distal intergenic (29.9% instead of 32.6%). The category depends on the window. Building the TxDb and annotating take about 30 s.
R2. (a) A single-end read starts at one end of its fragment; the fragment centre (100 bp into the read’s direction for 200-bp fragments) is where the chromatin was, so it is counted in the right region even near region edges. FRiP: 0.555 and 0.549 (GM12878), 0.395 and 0.442 (K562), inputs 0.042 and 0.049. (b) 264 regions higher in K562 and 245 higher in GM12878 (padj < 0.05) of 841. Identical to RNA-seq: the DESeqDataSet, design ~ cell, size factors, dispersion estimation, the Wald test, Benjamini–Hochberg and the MA plot.

Peaks: most regions unchanged; library: total reads correspond to the same material; background: non-peak DNA is the same. (b) Up/down: 264/245 (peaks), 229/280 (library), 182/319 (background); median log2FC −0.01, −0.33, −0.76. The K562 libraries have a lower FRiP, so relative to all reads, or to background reads, their peaks look lower; with background bins the effect is stronger because the K562 background is also inflated by extra chr21 copies. The strong differences (|log2FC| > 3) are significant under all three.
R4. Over-represented in K562: chr7 1.32, chr1 and chr22 1.27, chr21 1.23, chr6 1.19; under-represented: chrX 0.68, chr14 0.69, chr13 0.76, chr9 0.81. On chr21 every region starts with about +0.3 log2 units in K562 counts before any biology; a normalisation computed within chr21 (peaks or background bins of chr21) absorbs part of it, a genome-wide one would not.
R5. (a) 2 000 peaks; in the treated samples 95% of peaks have half the signal and 5% (the first 100) are unchanged; all libraries are sequenced to the same depth, so the treated libraries contain relatively more reads per remaining peak. The same fly chromatin is pulled down in every sample, but treated IPs contain half as much human DNA, so fly reads double. (b) Standard normalisation: 1 region down, 43 up; median log2FC −0.03, and the 100 truly unchanged peaks get log2FC +0.91: they look gained because everything else was scaled up. Spike-in size factors: 1 562 down, 0 up, median log2FC −1.04, unchanged peaks −0.10: the truth.
R6. Higher in GM12878: a cluster of regions at chr21:25.41–25.50 Mb (log2FC −6.6 to −7.5), 111–178 kb from MRPL39, the nearest protein-coding TSS; and the APP promoter (−6.8). Higher in K562: the KCNJ6 promoter at 38.12 Mb (+9.6) and a region 31 kb from it (+9.2), and regions in gene deserts near NCAM2, TCP10L and TMPRSS15. Regions at 5–10 Mb (near TPTE) lie in the pericentromeric part of chr21, full of segmental duplications that are partly copied on other chromosomes: mapping artefacts and copy-number differences between the cell lines can produce huge apparent differences there. Look at them in a browser, check the input and the mappability before believing them.

title: Exercise: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Where this leads

Differential accessibility runs the same analysis on ATAC-seq counts, with more replicates.
Linking regulatory elements to genes replaces “nearest gene” with contacts and correlation.
Chromatin states combines several marks into a single annotation of each region.
CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag produce cleaner data for the same questions; the downstream analysis is the same.

title: Quiz: ATAC-seq
text:
Short questions on Tn5, fragment lengths and ATAC-seq QC. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What does ATAC-seq measure, and why does a peak of ATAC signal usually mark regulatory DNA?






Hint





Where can a large enzyme reach the DNA in a nucleus?









Answer





It measures where the Tn5 transposase could insert its adapters into the DNA of intact nuclei: accessibility. DNA wrapped on nucleosomes or packed in compact chromatin is protected. Active promoters, enhancers and insulators have a nucleosome-depleted region where transcription factors bind, so Tn5 inserts there often and the reads pile up into a peak.




Q2. “Tagmentation” combines two steps of ordinary library preparation. Which two, and what is the main practical advantage?






Answer





Fragmentation of the DNA and adapter ligation: Tn5 cuts the DNA and joins an adapter to each new end in one reaction. No sonication, end repair or ligation, so the protocol is fast (hours) and needs little material (hundreds to tens of thousands of cells), and it is done on native chromatin in the nucleus.




Q3. A read pair has read 1 on the + strand at POS 2 000 001 and read 2 on the − strand at POS 2 000 151; both reads are 100 bp. How long is the fragment, and at which positions did Tn5 insert (ignore the +4 / −5 shift)?






Hint





The 5’ end of a − strand read is its rightmost base.









Answer





Insertions at 2 000 001 (5’ end of read 1) and 2 000 250 (5’ end of read 2: 2 000 151 + 100 − 1). Fragment length 2 000 250 − 2 000 001 + 1 = 250 bp, TLEN = +250 for read 1 and −250 for read 2. A mono-nucleosome fragment.




Q4. Why do ATAC-seq fragment lengths show peaks below 100 bp, near 200 bp and near 400 bp?






Answer





Tn5 inserts into nucleosome-free DNA and linkers, not into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome. Two insertions in the same open region give a short (< 100 bp) fragment; two insertions in linkers on either side of one nucleosome give ~147 bp plus linker ≈ 200 bp; around two nucleosomes ≈ 400 bp. The steps are the nucleosome repeat length (~190 bp).




Q5. Tn5 is loaded with two adapter types, A and B, in equal amounts. What fraction of fragments can be amplified and sequenced? Why?






Answer





50%. Each end gets A or B at random, so fragments are A–B, B–A, A–A or B–B with probability ¼ each. PCR needs one primer site of each kind, and the sequencer reads from A and from B, so only A–B and B–A fragments (\(2 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12\)) are amplified exponentially and sequenced.




Q6. A library has 30 M mapped reads, 9 M of them on chrM. What is the chrM fraction, why is it so high, and what protocol change would reduce it?






Answer





9 / 30 = 30%. Mitochondrial DNA has no nucleosomes (all of it is accessible) and is present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell, so it attracts many Tn5 insertions once the lysis lets Tn5 into the mitochondria. Omni-ATAC (different detergents plus a wash step that removes much of the cytoplasm) typically brings it down to a few percent. Remove chrM reads before peak calling either way.




Q7. Insertions around 5000 TSSs are summed per bp over ±2 kb. The outer 100 bp at each end contain 600 and 400 insertions; the highest 10-bp bin near the TSS contains 1 200. Compute the TSS enrichment. Is the library acceptable by ENCODE’s GRCh38 thresholds?






Hint





Background = (600 + 400) / 200 insertions per bp.









Answer





Background = 1000 / 200 = 5 per bp. Central bin = 1200 / 10 = 120 per bp. TSS enrichment = 120 / 5 = 24: well above 7, “ideal” (ENCODE: < 5 concerning, 5–7 acceptable, > 7 ideal, for RefSeq TSSs on GRCh38).




Q8. Library P has a strong nucleosome ladder (peaks at ~200, ~400, ~600 bp, taller than the peak below 100 bp) and a TSS enrichment of 2. Library Q has almost only fragments shorter than 120 bp, no 200-bp peak, and a TSS enrichment of 6. What probably went wrong with each?






Answer





P: many dead or dying cells. Apoptotic DNA is cut between nucleosomes and gives a ladder by itself; the DNA of damaged nuclei is tagmented everywhere, so there is little enrichment at TSSs. The fragment plot alone would look fine; the TSS profile reveals the problem. Q: over-tagmentation: too much Tn5 for the number of nuclei (or too few nuclei counted), so fragments are short and the nucleosome information is lost; signal-to-noise is only borderline.




Q9. In the TSS-enrichment profile of a good library, short (< 100 bp) fragments peak right at the TSS, while mono-nucleosome (180–250 bp) fragment centres peak about 150 bp downstream and dip at the TSS. Explain.






Answer





Active promoters have a nucleosome-depleted region just upstream of and at the TSS: short fragments come from two insertions inside it. Mono-nucleosome fragments contain one nucleosome, so their centres mark nucleosome positions: the well-positioned +1 nucleosome just downstream of the TSS (and the −1 upstream), and a dip where there is no nucleosome.




Q10. A paper compares bulk ATAC-seq of whole blood from patients and healthy donors and concludes that “the disease rewires the epigenome of immune cells”. Which alternative explanation must be ruled out first?






Answer





A change in cell-type composition. Blood is a mixture (neutrophils, T cells, B cells, monocytes …), each with its own accessible sites. If patients have more of one cell type, its specific sites gain signal in bulk without any change of chromatin within a cell type. Sorted populations, deconvolution, or single-cell ATAC-seq address this. (Batch effects from processing patients and controls on different days are the second thing to check.)

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Compute a fragment length and the two Tn5 insertion sites from the positions of a read pair, by hand and from a BAM file.
Explain why ATAC-seq fragment lengths come in nucleosome steps with a 10.5-bp ripple, and read a fragment-length plot of a good and a bad library.
Compute the chrM fraction of a library, and see why a subset of the genome gives a misleading number.
Compute a TSS enrichment score with the ENCODE definition, from counts by hand and from real insertions in R.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Background
Tagmentation. Tn5 transposase loaded with two kinds of adapters (A and B) cuts accessible DNA and joins an adapter to each new end. Only fragments with an A at one end and a B at the other are amplified and sequenced.
Fragments and insertions. In a properly paired read pair, the leftmost read is on the + strand and the other on the − strand. The fragment runs from the 5’ end of the + read (its POS) to the 5’ end of the − read (its POS + aligned length − 1). Its length is reported in SAM column 9, TLEN, positive for the leftmost mate and negative for the other. Each fragment end is one Tn5 insertion (to within a few bp; the exact +4 / −5 shift is in ATAC-seq processing and peak calling).
Fragment-length classes (conventions vary a little between papers): nucleosome-free < 100 bp; mono-nucleosome ≈ 180–250 bp; di-nucleosome ≈ 315–473 bp.
TSS enrichment (ENCODE): sum the insertions at each position from −2000 to +2000 bp around all TSSs (flipping − strand genes), divide by the mean per-bp count in the outer 100 bp at each end, and report the value at the centre. ENCODE’s pipeline reports the maximum of this profile averaged in 10-bp bins. On GRCh38 with RefSeq TSSs: < 5 concerning, 5–7 acceptable, > 7 ideal.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Data
ENCODE GM12878 ATAC-seq, replicate 1 (ENCSR095QNB), paired-end 2 × 101 bp. To keep the exercise small, the files contain only the read pairs that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, as the original, untrimmed reads (adapters and all). We align them to a reference that contains only chr21 and chrM. This is a shortcut: genome-wide numbers (in particular the chrM fraction) are distorted, and we correct for that in C3.
data/download.sh atacseq-intro          # reads (~0.6 GB), chr21+chrM reference and bowtie2 index, GTF, bigWigs
mkdir -p ~/epi/atac && cd ~/epi/atac
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
T=8                                     # threads
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (≥ 1.10), deepTools and R with GenomicRanges, rtracklayer and ggplot2 (see Install the software you need). Trimming takes under a minute and the alignment 5–15 minutes with 8 threads; everything else runs in seconds to a minute. On the cluster, put C1–C2 in an sbatch script with --cpus-per-task=8.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. From read positions to a fragment. A properly paired read pair (both reads 100 bp after trimming, no clipping; positions are 1-based SAM POS):

Where are the two 5’ ends (the Tn5 insertion sites)? (b) How long is the fragment, and what are the TLEN values of the two reads? (c) Which class of fragment is it, and what does it most likely contain? (d) Another pair: read 1 on the − strand at POS 9 800 001, read 2 on the + strand at POS 9 800 001, both 62 bp after trimming. How long is this fragment, and why are the reads only 62 bp long?

B2. Why steps of ~200 bp? The nucleosome core is 147 bp and the nucleosome repeat length in GM12878 is about 190 bp.

Explain in two sentences why Tn5 fragments cluster below 100 bp, near 200 bp and near 400 bp, but are rare at 120 bp.
Predict the approximate position of the tri-nucleosome peak.
Why does the mono-nucleosome peak sit at about 180–200 bp rather than at 147 bp?
Why is there hardly anything below 35 bp?

B3. chrM fraction. samtools idxstats on a full (whole-genome) standard ATAC-seq library gives 40 M mapped reads, of which 12 M are on chrM.

What is the chrM fraction? How many nuclear reads are left?
ENCODE asks for 25 M non-duplicate, non-mitochondrial reads (single-end; for paired-end, 25 M fragments). Ignoring duplicates, how many reads must you sequence to get 25 M nuclear reads with this chrM fraction, and with an Omni-ATAC library that has 3% chrM?
In this exercise our files hold only chr21 and chrM reads. Suppose idxstats gives 1.5 M reads on chr21 and 0.4 M on chrM. A student reports a chrM fraction of 21%. What is wrong? chr21 holds about 1.5% of the nuclear genome: estimate the chrM fraction of the full library.

B4. TSS enrichment from counts. Insertions from 2000 TSSs are summed per bp in a ±2 kb window. The outer 100 bp on the left contain 1 050 insertions in total, the outer 100 bp on the right 950. The 10-bp bin with the most insertions (just upstream of the TSS) holds 2 450.

What is the background (insertions per bp)? (b) What is the TSS enrichment (using the 10-bp bin)? (c) Is the library acceptable by ENCODE’s GRCh38 thresholds? (d) A second library has the same background per bp (after scaling to depth) but only 400 insertions in that bin. Its enrichment? What might have happened? (e) Why do we normalise by the flanks rather than by the total number of reads?

B5. Two adapters.

Tn5 is loaded with equal amounts of adapters A and B. What fraction of fragments carries A at one end and B at the other?
By mistake the Tn5 was loaded with 80% A and 20% B. What fraction is usable now?
In a single nucleus, an accessible site exists on two alleles. If each allele gives exactly one fragment covering the site, what is the probability that at least one of the two fragments can be sequenced? What does this mean for single-cell ATAC-seq?

B6. Read the plots. Three libraries (schematic):

Library X: a tall peak at 50 bp, a smaller peak at 200 bp, a small bump at 400 bp, 10-bp ripples below 150 bp. TSS enrichment 18.
Library Y: almost all fragments shorter than 120 bp, smooth decay, no peak at 200 bp. TSS enrichment 6.
Library Z: peaks at 200, 400 and 600 bp that are taller than the peak at 50 bp. TSS enrichment 2.5.

For each, say whether you would use it, and what most likely happened in the lab. Which single plot would have misled you for library Z?
B7. Judge the design. A study compares ATAC-seq of tumour tissue (6 patients) and adjacent normal tissue (6 patients). All tumours were processed in one week and all normal samples three months later. The paper reports 8 000 regions that “gain accessibility in cancer, reflecting epigenetic reprogramming”.
Name two reasons why these regions might differ without any change of chromatin within a given cell type, and one change to the design or analysis that would help.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
On the command line

C1 — Trim the adapters
fastp -i $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R2.fastq.gz \
      -o rep1_R1.trim.fastq.gz -O rep1_R2.trim.fastq.gz \
      --adapter_sequence CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT --adapter_sequence_r2 CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT \
      --length_required 20 -w $T -j rep1.fastp.json -h rep1.fastp.html 2> rep1.fastp.log
grep -A3 "Filtering result" rep1.fastp.log
grep -i "adapter" rep1.fastp.log

How many read pairs are there? How many reads had adapter sequence trimmed? Open rep1.fastp.html and look at the insert-size plot that fastp estimates from the overlap of the two reads: does it look familiar?
CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT is the reverse complement of the Tn5 mosaic end. Why does a read contain it when the fragment is shorter than 100 bp? Draw it.



C2 — Align, mark duplicates, filter
bowtie2 --very-sensitive -X 2000 -p $T -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM \
        -1 rep1_R1.trim.fastq.gz -2 rep1_R2.trim.fastq.gz 2> rep1.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m - - \
  | samtools sort -@ 4 -o rep1.all.bam -
samtools index rep1.all.bam
samtools markdup -r -f rep1.markdup.txt -@ $T rep1.all.bam rep1.dedup.bam
samtools index rep1.dedup.bam
samtools view -b -f 2 -F 1804 -q 30 rep1.dedup.bam chr21 > rep1.chr21.bam
samtools index rep1.chr21.bam
cat rep1.bowtie2.log
head -12 rep1.markdup.txt

What is the overall alignment rate? What fraction of pairs aligned concordantly exactly once?
What does -X 2000 do, and what would happen to the di- and tri-nucleosome fragments with bowtie2’s default (500)?
What fraction of reads were duplicates? (The generic reasons and the -F 1804 filter are explained in From reads to coverage.)



C3 — The chrM fraction
samtools idxstats rep1.all.bam | tee rep1.idxstats.txt
for c in chr21 chrM; do echo $c $(samtools view -c -F 1804 -q 30 rep1.dedup.bam $c); done
idxstats prints chromosome, length, mapped reads, unmapped reads.

What fraction of the mapped reads is on chrM in our files?
As in B3c, estimate the chrM fraction of the full library, assuming chr21 carries a share of the nuclear reads equal to its share of the genome (46.7 Mb of 3.1 Gb). ENCODE’s QC of the full library (all chromosomes) reports 13.9%. How close are you?
Compare the chrM share before and after removing duplicates and low-MAPQ reads (second command). Why could duplicates be more common on chrM?



C4 — Fragment lengths
samtools view -f 66 rep1.chr21.bam \
  | awk '{ print ($9 < 0) ? -$9 : $9 }' | sort -n | uniq -c \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $2, $1 }' > rep1.fraglen.txt
awk '{ n += $2 } $1 < 100 { s += $2 } END { print n, s / n }' rep1.fraglen.txt
sort -k2,2nr rep1.fraglen.txt | head -3

Why -f 66? (Decode the flag with samtools flags 66.) What would go wrong if you took column 9 of every read?
How many fragments are there, and what fraction is shorter than 100 bp? What is the most common length?



C5 — Fragments and insertion sites as BED
samtools view -f 66 rep1.chr21.bam \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ L = ($9 < 0) ? -$9 : $9; s = ($9 < 0) ? $8 : $4; print $3, s - 1, s - 1 + L, L }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > rep1.fragments.bed
awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, $2, $2 + 1; print $1, $3 - 1, $3 }' rep1.fragments.bed \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > rep1.insertions.bed
head -3 rep1.fragments.bed; wc -l rep1.fragments.bed rep1.insertions.bed

Explain the awk program: why $8 when TLEN is negative, and why s − 1?
Check the first line by hand: is the fragment length (column 4) equal to end − start?
The insertion file has one base per fragment end, without the +4 / −5 shift. Why is that good enough for a TSS profile over ±2 kb, but not for footprinting?



C6 — A coverage track for IGV
bamCoverage -b rep1.chr21.bam -o rep1.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads --binSize 10 -p $T
Load rep1.cpm.bw, $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz, $D/gm12878_h3k4me3_fc.bigWig and $D/gm12878_h3k27ac_fc.bigWig in IGV (genome hg38) and go to chr21:44,870,000-44,950,000 (ITGB2, the β2 integrin of white blood cells). Where are the ATAC peaks relative to the H3K4me3 and H3K27ac signal? Find an ATAC peak with neither mark.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
section: Explore: where the nucleosome ladder comes from
text:
Explore: where the nucleosome ladder comes from
The demo simulates tagmentation of chromatin. The top panel shows one fibre: nucleosomes (147 bp cores) separated by linkers, with a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) in the middle. Tn5 inserts (red triangles) at random into accessible DNA (linkers, the NDR and empty nucleosome slots) and, ten times more rarely, inside a nucleosome. The DNA is cut at every insertion, each new end gets adapter A or B at random, and only A–B fragments (green) are amplified and sequenced; fragments shorter than 35 bp are lost in the clean-up. The histogram collects the sequenced fragment lengths from 2000 such fibres. Sliders: linker length (the nucleosome repeat length is 147 bp + linker), NDR width, nucleosome occupancy (the chance that a slot holds a nucleosome) and Tn5 amount per nucleus; 10.5 bp helical preference lets Tn5 prefer one face of the DNA helix; log scale shows the long tail. Do B2, B5 and B6 first.



E1. The ladder. At the default settings (linker 45 bp, NDR 300 bp, occupancy 90%, Tn5 ×1), read the peaks of the ladder. What is the step between the mono- and di-nucleosome peaks, and how does it compare with the nucleosome repeat length? Set the linker to 20 bp and then to 70 bp: where do the mono and di peaks go? Use the top panel to explain what a 190 bp fragment contains.
E2. Two adapters. Read the share of fragments lost because both ends got the same adapter. Does it change when you move any slider? Compare with your answer to B5(a), and find an A–A or B–B fragment in the top panel.
E3. Too much and too little Tn5. Click too much (×8) and then too little (×¼). For each, read the nucleosome-free and mono-nucleosome shares, the share of A–B fragments lost as too short, and describe the histogram (try the log scale). Which library of B6 does too much Tn5 resemble? Can any setting of this demo produce library Z, and why not? Why does a peak near 150 bp remain with too much Tn5?
E4. Open chromatin and the helix. Back at ×1, set the NDR width to 0 and then to 800 bp, and the occupancy to 60%. Which share changes, and why? Finally untick log scale and tick 10.5 bp helical preference: what new pattern appears on the histogram? Count the spikes between 40 and 100 bp.






Solutions





E1. Peaks near 53, 187, 379 and 561 bp. The mono→di step is 192 bp, the nucleosome repeat length (147 + 45 = 192 bp); the tri peak is about another 190 bp further. Linker 20 bp: mono and di peaks near 171 and 333 bp (repeat length 167); linker 70 bp: near 193 and 405 bp (repeat length 217). A ~190 bp fragment runs from an insertion in one linker to an insertion in the next linker, with one uncut nucleosome in between: the core (147 bp) plus parts of the two linkers. The mono peak sits a little below the repeat length because a fragment runs between consecutive cuts: on each side it ends at the cut closest to the nucleosome, so it holds only part of each linker (B2c).
E2. About 50% of all fragments (between 49.8% and 50.5% at every setting) are A–A or B–B: each end gets A or B with probability ½, independently, so A–B or B–A has probability \(2 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac12\) (B5a). The loss does not depend on the chromatin or on the amount of Tn5. In the top panel the grey dashed fragments with two blue or two orange ends are lost.
E3. Too much Tn5 (×8): 49 insertions per kb instead of 6; 68% of the sequenced fragments are nucleosome-free and only 1.2% are mono-nucleosomal, the di peak is gone, and 83% of the A–B fragments are lost as shorter than 35 bp: the linkers and the NDR are cut into tiny pieces. This is library Y of B6. The peak near 150 bp is the nucleosome core itself: Tn5 cuts the linkers on both sides but rarely inside a nucleosome, so a “core-sized” fragment survives while the mono peak at ~190 bp disappears. Too little Tn5 (×¼): 1.5 insertions per kb; only 13.6% nucleosome-free, 12.9% mono and 19.1% di, a long tail of multi-nucleosome fragments (18% of the A–B fragments are longer than 1000 bp and not shown), and few fragments lost as too short (9.6%). Long fragments dominate and the nucleosome-free peak is weak: the “too little Tn5” curve of the lecture. Library Z cannot be made here: Z is a library of dead cells, whose ladder looks fine; what is wrong is the missing TSS enrichment, which a fragment-length histogram cannot show.
E4. The nucleosome-free share changes: NDR 0 bp gives 25.5%, NDR 800 bp gives 35.9% (default 29.5%), and occupancy 60% gives 43.9% with fewer mono and di fragments. More free DNA means more pairs of insertions close together without a nucleosome in between. With the helical preference the histogram gets a ripple: sharp spikes about 10.5 bp apart (near 41, 52, 63, 73, 84 and 94 bp: about six between 40 and 100 bp), on the nucleosome-free peak and continuing onto the mono peak, as on the lecture slide The 10.5-bp ripple: Tn5 can only reach the backbone on one face of the helix, once per 10.5 bp turn, so distances between two insertions prefer multiples of 10.5 bp. (In the demo this is a simplification: one face of the whole fibre is “exposed”; in a nucleus it is the DNA lying on the nucleosome surface.)

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
In R
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(ggplot2)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/atac")

R1 — The fragment-length distribution
fl <- read.table("rep1.fraglen.txt", col.names = c("len", "n"))
sum(fl$n)
ggplot(fl[fl$len <= 1000, ], aes(len, n)) + geom_line()
ggplot(fl[fl$len <= 1000, ], aes(len, n)) + geom_line() + scale_y_log10()
peak_in <- function(lo, hi) { x <- fl[fl$len >= lo & fl$len <= hi, ]; x$len[which.max(x$n)] }
c(nfr = peak_in(30, 120), mono = peak_in(150, 280), di = peak_in(300, 480))
c(nfr = sum(fl$n[fl$len < 100]), mono = sum(fl$n[fl$len >= 180 & fl$len <= 250])) / sum(fl$n)

Describe the plot. Where are the nucleosome-free, mono- and di-nucleosome peaks?
What can you see on the log scale that you cannot see on the linear one?
The raw counts are noisy at the di-nucleosome peak. Smooth them with a running mean over 11 bp, stats::filter(fl$n, rep(1/11, 11)), and find the peak again. Note: fl must have one row per length with no gaps for this to be correct; check with all(diff(fl$len) == 1) over the range you use.



R2 — The 10.5-bp periodicity
x <- merge(data.frame(len = 1:1000), fl, all.x = TRUE); x$n[is.na(x$n)] <- 0
x$trend <- as.numeric(stats::filter(x$n, rep(1/31, 31)))
p <- x[x$len >= 40 & x$len <= 150, ]
p$ratio <- p$n / p$trend
plot(p$len, p$ratio, type = "l"); abline(h = 1, col = "grey")
mx <- p$len[which(diff(sign(diff(p$ratio))) == -2) + 1]
mx; diff(mx); mean(diff(mx))

What do you see after dividing by the trend? At which lengths are the maxima, and what is their mean spacing?
Some maxima are spurious wiggles 1–3 bp apart. Look at diff(mx): how would you make the estimate more robust? (One option: keep only maxima that are the highest point within ±4 bp; another: spec.pgram() on p$ratio - 1 and take 1 / freq at the highest peak.)



R3 — TSS enrichment
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(granges(resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start")))
length(tss)

ins <- import("rep1.insertions.bed")                        # one base per insertion
win <- resize(tss, 4001, fix = "center")                     # ±2 kb
h   <- findOverlaps(ins, win, ignore.strand = TRUE)
d   <- start(ins)[queryHits(h)] - start(tss)[subjectHits(h)]
d   <- ifelse(as.character(strand(tss))[subjectHits(h)] == "-", -d, d)   # orient by strand
prof <- tabulate(d + 2001, 4001)                             # insertions at -2000 ... +2000

bg   <- mean(prof[c(1:100, 3902:4001)])                      # outer 100 bp at each end
norm <- prof / bg
bin10 <- tapply(norm, (seq_along(norm) - 1) %/% 10, mean)
c(background = bg, centre = mean(norm[2001 + (-5:5)]), tss_enrichment = max(bin10))
plot(-2000:2000, stats::filter(norm, rep(1/11, 11)), type = "l",
     xlab = "distance to TSS (bp)", ylab = "insertions / flank mean")
abline(h = c(1, 7), col = c("grey", "red"), lty = 2)

How many TSSs are used? What is the background (insertions per bp), and what is the TSS enrichment? How does it compare with ENCODE’s thresholds and with ENCODE’s own value for this library (29.6, genome-wide, RefSeq TSSs)?
Remove the line that orients by strand and recompute. What happens to the shape of the profile, and why?
The maximum is not exactly at 0. Where is it, and what lies on either side of it (think of the NDR and the +1 nucleosome)?
Why do we use unique() on the TSSs? What would happen to the score if a highly expressed gene with 12 transcripts starting at the same base were counted 12 times?



R4 — Nucleosome-free versus mono-nucleosome fragments
fr  <- import("rep1.fragments.bed")
mid <- (start(fr) + end(fr)) %/% 2
w   <- width(fr)
prof_mid <- function(pos, flank = 1000) {
  pts <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(pos, width = 1))
  h <- findOverlaps(pts, resize(tss, 2 * flank + 1, fix = "center"), ignore.strand = TRUE)
  d <- pos[queryHits(h)] - start(tss)[subjectHits(h)]
  d <- ifelse(as.character(strand(tss))[subjectHits(h)] == "-", -d, d)
  p <- tabulate(d + flank + 1, 2 * flank + 1)
  p / mean(p[c(1:100, (2 * flank - 98):(2 * flank + 1))])
}
nfr  <- prof_mid(mid[w < 100])
mono <- prof_mid(mid[w >= 180 & w <= 250])
sm <- function(v) stats::filter(v, rep(1/21, 21))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(-1000:1000, sm(nfr),  type = "l", col = "darkgreen", main = "< 100 bp",   xlab = "distance to TSS", ylab = "relative")
plot(-1000:1000, sm(mono), type = "l", col = "steelblue", main = "180-250 bp", xlab = "distance to TSS", ylab = "relative")
which.max(sm(mono)[1001:2001]) - 1          # +1 nucleosome: distance of the downstream maximum

Describe the two profiles. Where is the +1 nucleosome, and where is the −1?
Why use the fragment centre here rather than the insertion sites?
If you had only single-end reads, could you make these plots? Why not?
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — read positions and TLEN (B1, C4, C5)





SAM POS is the leftmost aligned base, 1-based, for reads on either strand. A − strand read’s 5’ end is its rightmost base: POS + aligned length − 1. TLEN is the distance from the leftmost to the rightmost aligned base of the pair, + for the leftmost mate. See the SAM specification (section 1.4) and samtools flags to decode flags.









Hint 2 — fragment classes and the ladder (B2, B6, R1, R2)





A fragment needs two insertions; Tn5 cannot insert into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome. Count how much DNA lies between two linkers separated by one, two or three nucleosomes. The 10.5-bp ripple is the helical repeat of DNA: Buenrostro et al. 2013, Fig. 2. For running means see stats::filter; for the periodogram spec.pgram.









Hint 3 — chrM (B3, C3)





If chr21 carries a fraction \(f\) of the nuclear reads, the full library had about \(n_{21} / f\) nuclear reads, and chrM fraction ≈ \(n_M / (n_M + n_{21}/f)\). samtools idxstats counts reads per reference sequence from the index; samtools view -c counts reads that pass filters.









Hint 4 — TSS enrichment (B4, R3)





Background = (sum of the two flank counts) / 200 bp. Enrichment = (count in the central bin / bin width) / background. ENCODE’s definition and thresholds are on the ATAC-seq standards page and the terms page. In R: resize, findOverlaps, tabulate.









Hint 5 — adapters and tools (B5, C1, C2)





Each end independently gets A or B. fastp detects adapters from the overlap of paired reads and from the sequence you give. bowtie2 manual: -X is the maximum fragment length for a valid paired-end alignment. samtools fixmate -m adds the mate tags that samtools markdup needs. bamCoverage with --extendReads fills in the whole fragment of a proper pair.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Read 1 is on the + strand, so its 5’ end is its POS: 33 500 101. Read 2 is on the − strand, so its 5’ end is its rightmost base: 33 500 247 + 100 − 1 = 33 500 346. (b) Fragment = 33 500 346 − 33 500 101 + 1 = 246 bp; TLEN = +246 for read 1 and −246 for read 2. (c) Mono-nucleosome size (180–250 bp): most likely two insertions in the linkers on either side of one nucleosome. (d) Both reads cover the same 62 bases: the fragment is 62 bp, nucleosome-free. The reads were 101 bp when sequenced, but after 62 bases they ran into the adapter of the other end, which fastp trimmed off.
B2. (a) Tn5 inserts only into DNA that is not wrapped on a nucleosome. Two insertions in the same open stretch (NDR or long linker) give a short fragment; any fragment that contains a nucleosome must be at least ~147 bp plus some linker, so lengths between ~100 and ~150 bp need an unusual geometry and are rarer. Fragments spanning one or two nucleosomes are ~one or two repeats long. (b) About 3 × 190 ≈ 570 bp (in our data a weak shoulder at 550–600 bp, visible only on the log scale). (c) The fragment contains the 147-bp core plus parts of the linkers on both sides, where Tn5 cut: 147 + two partial linkers ≈ 180–210 bp. (d) Very short fragments are lost in the cleanup (columns and beads do not keep them), cannot be amplified efficiently, and give reads too short to align uniquely (we also drop reads < 20 bp after trimming). Two Tn5 dimers also cannot insert right next to each other.
B3. (a) 12 / 40 = 30%; 28 M nuclear reads. (b) 25 / 0.70 = 35.7 M reads; with 3% chrM 25 / 0.97 = 25.8 M: Omni-ATAC saves about 10 M reads per sample. (c) 0.4 / 1.9 = 21% is the share of chrM among chr21 + chrM reads, not among all reads. The full library had about 1.5 M / 0.015 = 100 M nuclear reads, so chrM ≈ 0.4 / (0.4 + 100) ≈ 0.4%.
B4. (a) (1050 + 950) / 200 = 10 insertions per bp. (b) 2450 / 10 bp = 245 per bp; 245 / 10 = 24.5. (c) Yes, well above 7 (“ideal”). (d) 400 / 10 = 40 per bp; 40 / 10 = 4: “concerning”. Most insertions are background: dead or damaged cells, over-digestion, or a failed reaction (B6). (e) Total reads include chrM, peaks of every kind and background, and depend on depth; the flanks measure the background of this library at comparable positions, so the score is a pure signal-to-noise ratio that does not depend on sequencing depth.
B5. (a) \(2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 =\) 50%. (b) \(2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 =\) 32%. (c) Each fragment is usable with probability ½, so \(P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.5^2 =\) 75%. A quarter of accessible sites are missed in a single nucleus by chemistry alone, before any losses in cleanup, PCR or sequencing: single-cell ATAC data are inherently sparse (mostly 0 or 1 fragment per site per cell).
B6. X: a good library: nucleosome-free peak, ladder, 10-bp ripple, high TSS enrichment. Use it. Y: over-tagmentation (too much Tn5 for the number of nuclei, or fewer nuclei than counted): the DNA is cut so often that nucleosomal fragments are rare; signal-to-noise is borderline (6). Usable for peaks with care; repeat with more nuclei if possible. Z: dead or dying cells. Apoptotic DNA is already cut into a nucleosome ladder, and DNA from damaged nuclei is tagmented everywhere, so the ladder is strong but there is almost no enrichment at TSSs (2.5, “concerning”). Do not use. The fragment-length plot alone would have made Z look like a fine library: always check the TSS profile too.
B7. (1) Cell composition: tumours contain different cells (tumour cells, immune infiltrate, stroma) than normal tissue; sites specific to a more abundant cell type gain signal in bulk without any chromatin change in any one cell. (2) Batch: all tumours were processed together and all normals months later, so processing day (Tn5 lot, cell viability, nuclei counting, sequencing run) is completely confounded with the condition. Also: tumour copy-number gains increase signal over amplified regions. Helps: process tumour and normal samples together in randomised batches; sort cell populations or use single-cell ATAC or deconvolution; check QC (TSS enrichment, fragment sizes) per group; account for copy number. “Epigenetic reprogramming” is a claim about mechanism that the data do not show.









Solutions — command line





Run times on a shared server with 8 threads: C1 24 s, C2 11.5 min (bowtie2 --very-sensitive is slow; on a quiet laptop with 8 cores expect 5–15 min), duplicate marking 24 s, C3–C6 a few seconds each.
C1. (a) 6 088 187 read pairs; 5 992 127 pairs (11 984 254 reads) pass the filters. Adapter was trimmed from 4 667 844 reads (38%): more than a third of the fragments are shorter than the 101-bp reads. fastp’s insert-size estimate peaks at 42 bp: the nucleosome-free peak again. (fastp reports a duplication rate of 56%, inflated by the many identical chrM fragments.) (b) Sequencing starts at one end of the fragment and continues for 101 cycles. If the fragment is only 60 bp, the last 41 cycles read the mosaic end and adapter on the other side. Untrimmed, those bases do not match the genome and the read fails end-to-end alignment.
C2. (a) 99.65% overall; 94.5% of pairs concordantly exactly once, 4.4% more than once (multi-mappers; MAPQ < 30 removes most of them). Very high because these reads were selected as ones ENCODE had aligned to chr21 or chrM. (b) -X 2000 sets the largest fragment that counts as a valid (“concordant”, properly paired) alignment. With the default of 500 bp, the tri-nucleosome fragments and part of the di-nucleosome fragments would not be flagged as proper pairs (flag 2), and -f 2 would remove them: the ladder would be cut off at 500 bp. (c) markdup flags 8 865 403 of 11 942 569 reads, 74%, almost all on chrM (C3c).
C3. (a) idxstats: chr21 1 111 555, chrM 10 831 014 mapped reads: 90.7% on chrM. (b) \(10.83 / (10.83 + 1.112 / 0.0151) = 10.83 / 84.6 =\) 12.8%, close to ENCODE’s 13.9% for the whole library. The assumption is rough (chr21 has an unmappable p-arm, and open chromatin is not uniform over chromosomes), but good enough. (c) After removing duplicates and MAPQ < 30: chr21 504 621, chrM 2 143 835 reads (81% chrM). On chr21, 20% of the reads were duplicates (632 859 → 504 621); on chrM, 80% (10.75 M → 2.14 M). chrM is only 16.6 kb and covered thousands of times, so two independent fragments with exactly the same two ends are common: many “duplicates” there are not PCR copies but saturation. (The same is true for very strong peaks in deep libraries.)
C4. (a) -f 66 = 2 + 64: properly paired and first in pair. Each fragment is counted once, and TLEN is taken with its absolute value because the first read can be either the left or the right mate. Taking column 9 from every read would count each fragment twice, and half the values would be negative. (b) 252 213 fragments; 28.7% shorter than 100 bp; the most common length is 45 bp (1 908 fragments).
C5. (a) For each first-in-pair read: L = |TLEN|; the fragment starts at the leftmost mate’s POS, which is the read’s own POS if TLEN > 0 and the mate’s position (PNEXT, column 8) if TLEN < 0. SAM positions are 1-based, BED starts are 0-based, hence s − 1; the BED end is start + length. (b) The first line is chr21  5032522  5032580  58: 5 032 580 − 5 032 522 = 58. (c) Over ±2 kb, a 4–5 bp offset is invisible (we even average over 10-bp bins). Footprints are dips of a few bp at a TF motif; there the exact position of each insertion matters, and the shift must be applied (ATAC-seq processing and peak calling).
C6. (3 s.) At ITGB2, ATAC peaks sit at the two promoters (44.921 and 44.929 Mb, both with H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) and at several sites in the gene body and upstream with H3K27ac but little H3K4me3 (candidate enhancers). The histone signal is broader than the ATAC peak and often highest on its flanks: the marks are on the nucleosomes next to the open DNA. The ATAC peak at 44.893 Mb has neither mark: load $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz and you find a CTCF peak right on it (chr21:44 892 886–44 893 046), an insulator or loop anchor rather than a promoter or enhancer.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) A tall nucleosome-free peak at 45 bp with ripples, a broad mono-nucleosome peak near 200 bp and a weak di-nucleosome bump near 390 bp; 28.7% of fragments are < 100 bp and 16.1% are 180–250 bp. The raw which.max gives 45, 177 and 389 bp: the mono peak is flat-topped and noisy, so the raw maximum lands on one of the 10-bp spikes. (b) On the log scale the long tail is visible: the di-nucleosome bump, a weak shoulder at 550–600 bp (tri), and a smooth decay out to 1 kb. On the linear scale everything above 400 bp is squashed to the axis. (c) With an 11-bp running mean the peaks are at 45, 210 and 391 bp. fl has no gaps up to 700 bp (TRUE), so the running mean is over 11 consecutive lengths.
R2. (a) Below 150 bp the counts oscillate around the trend with maxima about every 10 bp (45, 54, 66, 75, 86, 95, 105, 115, 126 …), and the ripple continues into the mono-nucleosome peak (151, 167, 177, 187, 198 bp in the lecture figure). The naive maxima (mx) are 25 positions with a mean spacing of 4.3 bp: many are 2–4-bp noise wiggles. (b) Keeping only maxima that are the highest within ±4 bp leaves 45, 54, 66, 75, 86, 95, 105, 115, 126, 132, 138: spacing 10.1 bp between 45 and 126 (two spurious maxima at 132/138 drag the mean over all to 9.3). spec.pgram() puts the highest peak at a period of 10.0 bp (10.3 with pad = 9, a finer frequency grid). Expected: the helical repeat, ~10.5 bp. With 250 000 fragments from one chromosome, ±0.5 bp is as precise as it gets.
R3. (a) 602 TSSs; background 20.7 insertions per bp; centre (±5 bp) 33.1; TSS enrichment 34.0 (maximum of the 10-bp bins). Far above 7 (“ideal”), and close to ENCODE’s 29.6 for the full library (different TSS set, annotation and method; our chr21 subset is also small). (b) Without orientation the score is 32.8 and the profile becomes symmetric around 0: the upstream NDR peak of + strand genes and the downstream side of − strand genes are averaged, and the asymmetry (open upstream, +1 nucleosome downstream) disappears. (c) The highest 10-bp bin is at −140 bp (the 11-bp running mean peaks at −92 bp): the maximum is in the nucleosome-depleted region just upstream of the TSS, where TFs bind; downstream the signal drops where the +1 nucleosome sits. (d) A TSS shared by 12 transcripts would be counted 12 times: its insertions would weigh 12 times in the aggregate. Highly expressed genes tend to have many annotated transcripts and open promoters, so duplicates would inflate the score.
R4. (a) Nucleosome-free fragment centres peak at about −107 bp (15.8 × the flanks) and fall sharply downstream of the TSS. Mono-nucleosome fragment centres dip at the TSS (7.4 ×) and peak at +124 bp (the +1 nucleosome) and at −91 bp upstream (14.1 ×). The upstream peak is not a clean −1 nucleosome: in a highly accessible promoter, two insertions on either side of the whole NDR also make a ~200-bp fragment. (b) A nucleosome sits in the middle of a mono-nucleosome fragment, between the two insertions: the centre estimates the dyad. Insertions mark where the DNA was open, i.e. the linkers either side. (c) No: single-end reads give one insertion per fragment and no fragment length, so you can neither split fragments by size nor find their centres.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Where this leads

ATAC-seq processing and peak calling shifts the insertions by +4 / −5, calls peaks with MACS3 and builds consensus peaks across replicates.
Differential accessibility counts fragments in peaks across samples and uses DESeq2, as in RNA-seq.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting uses the insertion sites at base resolution, and has to deal with the Tn5 sequence bias.
Single-cell ATAC-seq uses the same fragments, one barcode per nucleus: the fragment-length and TSS-enrichment QC are computed per cell.
