title: Quiz: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Short questions on processing ATAC-seq reads, calling peaks and combining replicates. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A read pair from an ATAC-seq library aligns as read 1 on the + strand at BED [52 000, 52 100) and read 2 on the − strand at BED [52 310, 52 410). Give the fragment length and the two Tn5 insertion sites (BED, after the +4/−5 shift).






Hint





The + read’s 5’ end is its start; the − read’s 5’ end is its end.









Answer





Fragment [52 000, 52 410), 410 bp. Insertions at \(52\,000 + 4 = 52\,004\) and \(52\,410 - 5 = 52\,405\) (BED 52004 52005 and 52405 52406), 401 bp apart.




Q2. Why is the shift +4 on one strand and −5 on the other, when Tn5 cuts symmetrically?






Answer





Tn5 cuts the two strands 9 bp apart and both fragments keep a copy of those 9 bp. The insertion is the centre of the 9 bp: 4 bases in from either end. From a + read’s BED start (the first of the 9 bases) that is +4. A − read’s 5’ end is the last of the 9 bases, but BED stores the end as the boundary after it, so the centre is end − 5. In 1-based coordinates both are 4 bases (+4 and −4).




Q3. Bowtie2 is run with its default maximum fragment length (500 bp) and only properly paired reads are kept. Which part of the ATAC-seq fragment-size distribution is lost, and does it matter for peak calling?






Answer





Fragments longer than 500 bp, that is the di- and tri-nucleosome fragments, become “not concordant” and are removed. For peak calling on nucleosome-free regions it matters little (the short fragments carry most of the signal), but you lose part of the library and the nucleosome ladder, which is a QC readout and the input to nucleosome-positioning analyses. Use -X 2000.




Q4. In 10 kb around a candidate peak MACS3 counts 800 insertions. The window used for counting is 150 bp. The genome-wide expectation is \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 5\). There is no control. What is \(\lambda_\text{local}\)? The peak has \(k = 30\); is it more or less significant than it would be against \(\lambda_\text{BG}\)?






Hint





Scale the 10-kb count to 150 bp. Without a control MACS3 uses \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window.









Answer





\(\lambda_\text{10k} = 800 \times 150 / 10\,000 = 12\), so \(\lambda_\text{local} = \max(5, 12) = 12\). The peak is less significant than against \(\lambda_\text{BG}\): \(P(X \ge 30 \mid 12)\) is much larger than \(P(X \ge 30 \mid 5)\). The local background is high (an open region, an amplified segment); the peak must stand out from its neighbourhood, not from the genome average.




Q5. Two ways to call ATAC-seq peaks with MACS3 are -f BAMPE and a BED of insertion sites with --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150. In one sentence each, what is piled up?






Answer





BAMPE: whole fragments, from the start of one read to the end of its mate. Insertion mode: a 150-bp window centred on each Tn5 cut site (two per fragment), ignoring the DNA between the cuts.




Q6. After deduplicating with samtools markdup -r, a student calls peaks on insertion sites with MACS3’s default --keep-dup 1. What goes wrong?






Answer





--keep-dup 1 keeps one tag per position and strand. Insertion sites from different fragments often hit the same base at strong sites (Tn5 has sequence preferences), and they are all independent events, so the strongest peaks are flattened. Duplicates were already removed at the fragment level, where they can be recognised (same start and same end); use --keep-dup all.




Q7. Sample A has 20 million insertions after filtering, 7.2 million of them in peaks. Sample B, from the same cell type and with the same peak caller settings, has a FRiP of 0.11. Compute FRiP for A. What could explain B?






Answer





FRiP(A) = 7.2 / 20 = 0.36, above ENCODE’s 0.3. A FRiP of 0.11 means most of B’s insertions fall in closed chromatin: dead or damaged cells (naked DNA is accessible everywhere), over-transposition, or poor nuclei preparation. Check the fragment-size distribution and TSS enrichment for B before using it.




Q8. Replicate 1 has 50 000 peaks, replicate 2 has 30 000. 27 000 of replicate 2’s peaks overlap a replicate-1 peak. A colleague says “90% of peaks are reproducible”. Why is that a weak statement, and what is a better analysis?






Answer





The number depends on the thresholds and is asymmetric: 90% of replicate 2’s peaks overlap replicate 1, but at most 54% of replicate 1’s 50 000 peaks can overlap replicate 2. A lenient replicate 1 catches almost anything. Better: call both leniently, rank the peaks, and ask how far down the ranking the two replicates agree (IDR, or a rank-consistency curve); report the number of peaks that pass a reproducibility threshold.




Q9. Three samples have peaks with summits at positions 10 000 (score 22), 10 300 (score 35) and 10 650 (score 18). Build the fixed-width (500 bp) consensus with iterative overlap removal. How many peaks remain, and where are they?






Hint





Windows are summit ± 250. Start with the highest score; drop what overlaps it; continue with the next highest that is left.









Answer





Windows: [9750, 10250), [10050, 10550), [10400, 10900). Keep 10 300 (35); it overlaps both others, so both are dropped. One peak remains: [10050, 10550). (A plain bedtools merge would give one 1150-bp region [9750, 10900).)




Q10. A paper calls ATAC-seq peaks on the full BAM, without removing mitochondrial reads, and reports the 20 “most accessible regions” in the genome. What do you expect to find in that list?






Answer





The mitochondrial genome. mtDNA has no nucleosomes and many copies per cell, so its pileup is far above any nuclear region; the top peaks will all be on chrM (and possibly in blacklisted repeats). Remove chrM reads and blacklisted regions before peak calling, and look at the top of a peak list in a browser.

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
About this lecture
In What is epigenetics? we saw that active promoters and enhancers are nucleosome-depleted: the DNA there is open. ATAC-seq maps that open DNA genome-wide, from a few thousand cells, in an afternoon. It is the most used chromatin assay today, and its data carry more than peaks: the lengths of the fragments tell you where the nucleosomes are.

Why measure accessibility, and how it was done before ATAC-seq (DNase-seq, FAIRE, MNase-seq).
The Tn5 transposase: cutting and adding adapters in one step, and what that does to the library.
The fragment-length distribution and the nucleosome ladder, down to the 10-bp helical period.
ATAC-specific QC: mitochondrial reads, TSS enrichment, and what a bad library looks like.
Protocol variants and experimental design.


This is the first unit of the ATAC-seq block. Students already know nucleosomes, NDRs and the MNase ladder from What is epigenetics?, and the generic steps of alignment, duplicates and blacklists from From reads to coverage and Experimental design and QC. Here the focus is what is special about ATAC-seq: the enzyme, the fragments it makes, and the QC that follows from that. The following unit, ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, does the Tn5 shift in detail, peak calling and consensus peaks. All real-data figures in this lecture come from ENCODE GM12878 ATAC-seq replicate 1 (ENCSR095QNB), reads from chr21 and chrM, processed with exactly the commands of the exercise.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Open chromatin marks regulatory DNA


Promoters and enhancers that are in use have a nucleosome-depleted region where transcription factors bind. Elsewhere the DNA is wrapped in nucleosomes.
An enzyme added to nuclei cuts, or tags, mostly where it can reach the DNA. Count where it acted, and the pile-ups are the accessible regions.
Accessibility is mark-free: no antibody, no prior choice of protein. One assay finds promoters, enhancers and insulators (CTCF sites) at once.


The logic of every accessibility assay: use a large enzyme as a probe for access. Nucleosomes protect the DNA wrapped on them; linkers are partly accessible; NDRs are very accessible. A peak of accessibility does not tell you which factor is bound or whether the element is active or poised; that is what histone marks and TF ChIP add. But it is the best single map of “where the regulatory DNA of this cell type is”. About 1–3% of the genome is accessible in a given cell type; across all cell types studied by ENCODE, millions of distinct accessible sites have been found (Thurman et al. 2012). The weak cuts in linkers in the figure come back later: they make the nucleosome ladder.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Before ATAC-seq: four ways to find open DNA
text:
Before ATAC-seq: four ways to find open DNA


DNase I hypersensitive sites (1970s–80s, Southern blots): active genes are more sensitive to DNase I. DNase-seq (Boyle et al. 2008; Hesselberth et al. 2009) maps them genome-wide.
FAIRE: crosslink, shear, and keep the DNA that is not bound to proteins. MNase-seq does the opposite: digest everything unprotected and sequence the nucleosome cores.
ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al. 2013) gives the DNase-seq answer, plus nucleosome positions, from far fewer cells.


DNase I hypersensitivity is the classic marker of regulatory DNA: Weintraub and Groudine showed in 1976 that active globin genes are more DNase-sensitive, and individual hypersensitive sites at enhancers and the beta-globin LCR were mapped by Southern blot in the 1980s. DNase-seq turned that into a genome-wide map and was the main ENCODE accessibility assay; Thurman et al. 2012 is the landmark paper. It needs millions of cells and careful titration of the enzyme. FAIRE (Giresi et al. 2007) is simple but has low signal-to-noise. MNase-seq gives a negative image: nucleosomes, with the NDR as a gap. ATAC-seq won because it is fast, works on 500–50 000 cells, and its fragments contain both kinds of information. DNase-seq is still used, and single-hit DNase protocols give very clean footprints.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
ATAC-seq in one picture


Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin: lyse cells gently, add the Tn5 transposase loaded with sequencing adapters to the nuclei, purify the DNA and amplify by PCR.
Tn5 inserts its adapters into accessible DNA in the nucleus, so the library is made where the chromatin is intact.
No size selection is needed, and the whole protocol takes about three hours.


The original protocol (Buenrostro et al. 2013) used 50 000 cells, a lysis buffer with NP-40, 30 minutes of transposition at 37 °C, a column cleanup and PCR with barcoded primers. The number of PCR cycles is chosen by qPCR on a small aliquot to avoid over-amplification. Because transposition and library construction are the same step, there is no fragmentation, end repair or ligation: this is why it needs so little material. The price is that the library structure is set by the enzyme, which is what the next slides are about.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Tn5: cut and paste in one step
text:
Tn5: cut and paste in one step


Tn5 is a bacterial transposase. A hyperactive mutant is loaded with two kinds of short DNA adapters, each ending in the 19-bp mosaic end it recognises.
A Tn5 dimer cuts both strands of the target DNA and joins an adapter to each new end: tagmentation (tagging + fragmentation).
The two cuts are 9 bp apart. Filling the gaps copies those 9 bp onto both fragments. Read ends must therefore be shifted (+4 / −5 bp) to mark the centre of the insertion; ATAC-seq processing and peak calling does this.


Adey et al. 2010 developed in vitro tagmentation with hyperactive Tn5 for making sequencing libraries (Nextera); Buenrostro’s insight was to do it on native chromatin. The transposase stays bound to the DNA after insertion and is removed during purification (SDS or the column). The 9-bp staggered cut leaves a 9-nt single-stranded gap on each fragment; the first step of the PCR (5 minutes at 72 °C) fills it. So the 9 bp next to every insertion appear on both neighbouring fragments. For peaks of hundreds of bp the shift does not matter; for footprinting and for the precise position of insertions it does. Here we only need to remember that each read’s 5’ end is (within a few bp) a Tn5 insertion.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Two adapters: only half the fragments can be sequenced
text:
Two adapters: only half the fragments can be sequenced


Tn5 is loaded with adapter A and adapter B at random. A fragment gets one adapter at each end: A–B, B–A, A–A or B–B, each with probability ¼.
The PCR uses one primer for A and one for B, and the sequencer reads from A (read 1) and B (read 2). Only A–B and B–A fragments are amplified and sequenced: 2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 50\%.
Fragments longer than about 1 kb are also lost: they amplify and cluster poorly. Reads come mostly from fragments shorter than ~600 bp.


This is a property of the Nextera chemistry. A–A and B–B fragments can only be copied linearly (one primer) and in addition fold back into hairpins (suppression PCR), so they are effectively absent. For bulk ATAC-seq this costs half the material but does not bias which regions are seen. It matters for single-cell ATAC-seq: each cell has two copies of each site, and losing half of the fragments is one reason scATAC data are so sparse. Long fragments are lost because two insertions far apart are needed, and long molecules amplify and form clusters less efficiently on the flow cell. This size limit is why ATAC is mostly blind to the inside of closed chromatin: fragments from there are too long.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: A read pair is a fragment, and a fragment is two insertions
text:
A read pair is a fragment, and a fragment is two insertions


Paired-end sequencing reads both ends of each fragment. The 5’ end of each read sits at a Tn5 insertion site.
The aligner reports the fragment length (template length, TLEN, column 9 of SAM): positive for the leftmost mate, negative for the other.
This is why ATAC-seq is sequenced paired-end: it gives two insertion sites and the length between them, and the length carries information.


Students met TLEN in From reads to coverage. Here it gets a meaning: it is the distance between two Tn5 insertions, and the distribution of these distances is the next slide. With 2×100 bp reads and fragments shorter than 100 bp, both reads run through the whole fragment into the adapter on the other side, which is why adapters must be trimmed before alignment (the read would otherwise not align end-to-end). In the exercise we trim with fastp. Single-end ATAC-seq exists but loses the fragment lengths and half the insertion sites.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Why fragment lengths come in steps
text:
Why fragment lengths come in steps


Two insertions in the same open region (or the same linker) give a short, nucleosome-free fragment, under ~100 bp.
Two insertions in linkers on either side of one nucleosome give a fragment of about 180–250 bp; around two nucleosomes ~350–450 bp, and so on.
So the fragment-length histogram is a nucleosome ladder, the same one as in the MNase experiment of What is epigenetics?


The key idea of the lecture. Tn5 cannot insert into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome (with a few exceptions at the edges), so any fragment that contains a nucleosome is at least 147 bp plus whatever linker on either side. The mono-nucleosome fragments are mostly from just outside open regions and from accessible linkers in otherwise ordinary chromatin. This is how one ATAC-seq library contains both maps: short fragments mark the open sites, nucleosome-sized fragments mark the positioned nucleosomes around them (NucleoATAC and similar tools exploit this). The repeat in human cells is about 190 bp.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Real data: the nucleosome ladder


GM12878, ENCODE ATAC-seq replicate 1, 252 213 fragments on chr21 after filtering.
A large nucleosome-free peak (mode 45 bp), then mono- (210 bp) and di-nucleosome (391 bp) peaks. On a log scale (inset) a weak tri-nucleosome shoulder near 550–600 bp is visible too.


This is the plot to make for every ATAC-seq library, first. 28.7% of the fragments are shorter than 100 bp, 16.1% are 180–250 bp. The step between the mono and di peaks, about 180 bp, is close to the nucleosome repeat length (~190 bp). The peaks are broad because linker lengths vary and Tn5 does not always cut in the middle of a linker. The spikes on the mono peak (e.g. 167, 177, 187 bp) are the same 10-bp periodicity as on the next slide, continuing into nucleosomal fragments; with only 250 000 fragments on one chromosome the curve is also noisy. The sharp drop below about 35 bp is not biology: the shortest fragments are lost in the cleanup, and reads that short fail the length filter after trimming. Notice the small ripples on the nucleosome-free peak: next slide. ENCODE requires that the nucleosome-free and mono-nucleosome peaks are both present.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
The 10.5-bp ripple: DNA’s helical turn











DNA on a nucleosome (and DNA lying on any surface) exposes its backbone once per helical turn, about 10.5 bp. Tn5 cuts where it can reach, so fragment lengths prefer steps of ~10.5 bp.
Bottom: fragment counts divided by a smooth trend. The peaks are 10.2 bp apart on average.


Buenrostro et al. 2013 showed this periodicity in the first ATAC-seq paper; it is a sign that the fragments really come from chromatinised DNA. The detrending is done in the figure script: divide the counts by a running mean over 31 bp so that only the short-range wiggle remains. The ripple is clearest between 40 and 200 bp. A library made from naked DNA (or a very over-tagmented one) loses both the ladder and the ripple. Not every pipeline checks the periodicity, but it is a nice sanity check that costs nothing.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Tn5 is not a perfectly random cutter
text:
Tn5 is not a perfectly random cutter


Base composition of the genome around 200 000 insertion sites (5’ ends of + strand reads, chr21). Random cutting would give flat lines at the genome average.
Tn5 has a weak, symmetric sequence preference centred on the 9-bp duplicated stretch, and prefers GC-rich DNA.
The bias is small per site but matters for footprinting and for comparing regions of different sequence. Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting corrects for it.


Every enzyme-based assay has a sequence bias: DNase I and MNase too (MNase strongly prefers AT-rich DNA). For Tn5 the preference is a palindromic, roughly symmetric pattern, because the enzyme acts as a dimer. In the figure, position 0 is the first base of the + strand read, so the 9-bp duplicated stretch runs from 0 to +8 and its centre is at +4; the pattern is mirror-symmetric around that centre, which is the reason for the +4 / −5 shift. For peak calling the bias averages out. For TF footprints, where you look for a dip of a few bp in the insertion profile, the enzyme’s preference alone can create or hide a “footprint”. Tools such as TOBIAS model and remove it.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Mitochondrial DNA soaks up Tn5


mtDNA is a 16.6-kb circle without nucleosomes, present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell. All of it is accessible.
In the original protocol, often 20–50% of reads come from chrM. They cost sequencing but carry no information about nuclear chromatin.
Remove chrM reads before peak calling and before computing other QC metrics; report the chrM fraction as a QC number.


The arithmetic in the figure is an order-of-magnitude argument: about 130 Mb of open nuclear DNA against tens of Mb of naked mtDNA, so a large share of insertions can land in chrM if Tn5 gets into the mitochondria. The lysis detergent permeabilises the mitochondrial membranes as well. The fraction varies enormously by cell type: cells with many mitochondria (heart, muscle, liver) are worst. Omni-ATAC (Corces et al. 2017) changes the lysis and washes away much of the cytoplasm, which typically brings chrM down to a few percent. Note also that nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs) in the nuclear genome attract chrM-like reads; that is one reason blacklists exist.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Real data: the chrM fraction


In our chr21 + chrM read set, 90.7% of the aligned reads are on chrM. That number is not the library’s chrM fraction: chr21 is only 1.5% of the genome.
Scale chr21 up to the whole genome: chrM ≈ 12.8% of all reads. ENCODE’s own QC of the full library reports 13.9%.


An honest-simplification moment (principle 10). We only have reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, so the chrM share in our files is grossly inflated. The estimate: if chr21 holds about f = 1.5% of the nuclear reads (its share of the genome length, roughly), the whole library had chr21_reads / f nuclear reads, and chrM fraction = chrM / (chrM + chr21 / f). The estimate (12.8%) is close to ENCODE’s value computed from all reads (13.9%; 11.7 M of 83.7 M mapped reads), so the shortcut works. In the exercise students compute this with samtools idxstats. For a standard-protocol library from a cell line, 14% is good; Omni-ATAC libraries are often below 5%.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
The TSS enrichment score


Active promoters are the most reliably open sites in every cell type, so a good library has many insertions at TSSs relative to the DNA a few kb away.
ENCODE definition: aggregate insertions in ±2 kb around all TSSs, divide by the mean of the outer 100 bp at each end, and take the value at the centre (ENCODE’s pipeline: the maximum of the profile in 10-bp bins).
A signal-to-noise measure that needs no peak calling and works on any library, even a shallow one.


TSS enrichment has largely replaced FRiP as the headline QC number for ATAC-seq, because FRiP depends on the peak caller and the depth while TSS enrichment does not. The flanks at ±1.9–2 kb are mostly closed chromatin, so they measure background: insertions anywhere, from naked DNA of dead cells and from random tagmentation. Thresholds depend on the TSS annotation: ENCODE uses RefSeq TSSs, with < 5 concerning, 5–7 acceptable and > 7 ideal on GRCh38 (6 and 10 on hg19). Strand matters: each TSS window is flipped for − strand genes so downstream is always to the right. The ENCODE pipeline actually computes read coverage (not 5’ ends) in 400 bins of 10 bp, and reports the maximum of the mean profile; the exact numbers therefore differ a little between tools.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Real data: TSS enrichment


602 protein-coding TSSs on chr21 (GENCODE), insertions from 252 213 fragments. TSS enrichment = 34.0.
Far above ENCODE’s “ideal” threshold of 7. ENCODE’s genome-wide value for this library: 29.6.
The profile is asymmetric: the maximum is upstream of the TSS (around −140 to −90 bp), in the NDR; the sharp drop just downstream is the +1 nucleosome.


Our number uses protein-coding TSSs of chr21 only, GENCODE rather than RefSeq, and insertion sites rather than read coverage, so it is not identical to ENCODE’s; it should be in the same range. Many TSSs on chr21 are of genes not expressed in B cells, and they contribute flat profiles: the score is an average over active and inactive promoters. That is why the score also depends on the cell type and annotation, and why thresholds are rough. A score of 3 would mean the library is mostly background; a score of 30 means a very clean library.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Short and long fragments see different things
text:
Short and long fragments see different things


Split the fragments by length: nucleosome-free (< 100 bp) and mono-nucleosome (180–250 bp). Plot fragment centres around TSSs.
Nucleosome-free fragments pile up just upstream of the TSS (the NDR). Mono-nucleosome fragments dip at the TSS and peak on both sides: the +1 nucleosome at +124 bp, and upstream a peak at −91 bp.


This is the nucleosome map hidden in an ATAC-seq library, made with nothing more than a length filter. The +1 nucleosome (fragment centres peak at +124 bp here) is the best-positioned nucleosome of an active promoter. The upstream peak (−91 bp) is less clean: in a very accessible promoter, two insertions on either side of the whole NDR also give a 180–250 bp fragment, so not every ‘mono-nucleosome-sized’ fragment contains a nucleosome. The nucleosome-free fragments peak at about −100 bp, in the NDR just upstream of the TSS. Peak callers for ATAC usually use all fragments or just the nucleosome-free ones; the choice is part of the next unit. Each curve is divided by its own flank mean, so shapes are compared, not absolute numbers; with 600 TSSs on one chromosome the curves are noisy. Tools such as NucleoATAC do this properly genome-wide.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Real data: ATAC-seq next to histone marks
text:
Real data: ATAC-seq next to histone marks


GM12878 at ITGB2 (chr21), the β2 integrin (CD18) of white blood cells, strongly expressed in B-lymphoblastoid cells. Our ATAC coverage, ENCODE ATAC peaks, and ENCODE H3K4me3 and H3K27ac (fold change over input).
ATAC peaks sit at promoters (with H3K4me3) and enhancers (H3K27ac without H3K4me3). The ATAC peak is narrow, in the NDR; the histone marks are on the flanking nucleosomes.


ITGB2 is on the − strand, so it is transcribed right to left. Most of its GENCODE transcripts start at 44.921 Mb (strong H3K4me3, an ATAC peak in the middle of it); others start at an upstream promoter at 44.929 Mb, inside a broad H3K27ac region with several ATAC peaks (promoter plus candidate enhancers). The ATAC peaks in the gene body with H3K27ac but little H3K4me3 (44.91 Mb) are candidate intronic enhancers. On the left is the promoter of PTTG1IP, the strongest ATAC peak in the window. The ATAC track is coverage from our own chr21 alignment (fragments, counts per million), the histone tracks are ENCODE fold-change bigWigs from chromatin-intro. Point out that ATAC and H3K27ac do not have the same shape: the histone mark is on nucleosomes, so it is often highest on either side of the ATAC peak, with a dip where the nucleosomes are missing. Also point out the small ATAC peak at 44.893 Mb without either histone mark: it sits on a CTCF peak (ENCODE GM12878 CTCF), so accessibility finds insulators too.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: What a bad library looks like
text:
What a bad library looks like


Too much Tn5 per nucleus (too few cells): almost all fragments short, the ladder disappears, background rises. Too little (too many cells): long fragments dominate, the nucleosome-free peak is weak.
Dead or damaged cells: naked or degraded DNA is tagmented everywhere. The ladder may even look strong, but the TSS profile is flat.
Always look at both plots: the fragment lengths say how the reaction went, the TSS profile says whether the result has signal.


These are schematic curves, not real data, drawn to show the typical patterns (the Grandi et al. 2022 protocol paper has real examples). The Tn5-to-nuclei ratio is the main knob of the reaction, which is why cell counts matter. Dead cells are the most common problem with primary samples: apoptotic DNA is cleaved between nucleosomes and gives a strong ladder by itself, and necrotic DNA is accessible everywhere. Both reduce the TSS score. Remedies: dead-cell removal, DNase treatment of the culture before harvesting (Omni-ATAC), sorting live cells. A third failure: too much PCR, which shows up as a high duplicate rate (From reads to coverage).
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

The right-hand column comes from the ENCODE quality-metric records of this experiment (replicate 1), except where it says otherwise; our own chr21 numbers agree in range. Note that this library would fail the strict complexity standards (NRF 0.80 < 0.9) while being excellent on TSS enrichment: real data rarely pass every box, and ENCODE flags such issues rather than discarding the data. The generic metrics (duplicates, complexity, FRiP, replicates, IDR) are taught in Experimental design and QC; what is ATAC-specific is the first three rows. Do not memorise the thresholds; know what each metric measures and in which direction “bad” lies.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Protocol variants








protocol
change
why




standard (Buenrostro 2013)
NP-40 lysis, 50 000 cells
the original


Fast-ATAC (Corces 2016)
digitonin, lysis and tagmentation together
blood cells; fewer chrM reads


Omni-ATAC (Corces 2017)
NP-40 + Tween-20 + digitonin, wash, PBS in the reaction
less chrM, better signal-to-noise; works on frozen tissue


single-cell ATAC
tagment nuclei in bulk, then barcode each nucleus (droplets or combinatorial indexing)
cell types in a mixture; a later unit


multiome
scATAC + scRNA from the same nucleus
links accessibility to expression




The chemistry is the same Tn5 everywhere, so the fragment ladder, TSS enrichment and chrM logic apply to all of them.


Omni-ATAC is now the default for most labs: the detergent mix permeabilises the nuclear membrane while the wash removes much of the mitochondria, and the PBS and detergents in the transposition mix improve signal-to-noise. Corces et al. 2017 showed it works on cryosections of frozen tissue. Fast-ATAC was designed for haematopoietic cells. Single-cell ATAC is mentioned only as a pointer: it has its own analysis problems (sparsity, cell calling, doublets) and its own unit. CUT&Tag also uses Tn5, but tethered to an antibody: that is in the ChIP-seq block.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Designing an ATAC-seq experiment

Cells and nuclei: count them. The Tn5-to-nuclei ratio sets the fragment sizes; 50 000 cells is the classic amount, Omni-ATAC works from fewer. Start from viable cells (> 80–90% alive) or clean nuclei.
Fresh, cryopreserved or frozen: viably frozen cells (DMSO) work well; snap-frozen tissue needs nuclei isolation (Omni-ATAC). Fixed cells are not suitable for standard ATAC.
Replicates: at least two biological replicates per condition, processed together. Accessibility differs with cell type composition: in tissue, a “difference” can just be a different mix of cells.
Sequencing: paired-end; ≥ 25 M usable fragments per sample for peaks, more for footprinting.


Practical points students will meet when they read or plan a study. Processing replicates together matters because the tagmentation step varies from day to day; a batch of samples done on one day and controls on another confounds condition with batch (the design and QC unit). Formaldehyde fixation blocks Tn5 access, though fixed-cell protocols exist. Tissue heterogeneity is the biggest interpretation problem in bulk ATAC-seq of tissues and the reason single-cell ATAC exists. The 25 M number is the ENCODE standard for peak calling; footprinting needs 100 M or more.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: Aligning ATAC-seq reads: the short version
text:
Aligning ATAC-seq reads: the short version
# 1. trim the Nextera adapter that reads run into when the fragment is short
fastp -i R1.fastq.gz -I R2.fastq.gz -o trim_R1.fastq.gz -O trim_R2.fastq.gz \
      --adapter_sequence CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT --adapter_sequence_r2 CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT

# 2. align pairs; allow fragments up to 2 kb (default is 500)
bowtie2 --very-sensitive -X 2000 -x hg38_chr21_chrM -1 trim_R1.fastq.gz -2 trim_R2.fastq.gz \
  | samtools fixmate -m - - | samtools sort -o all.bam
samtools markdup -r all.bam dedup.bam

# 3. QC on all reads, then keep good pairs off chrM
samtools idxstats all.bam                                       # chrM fraction
samtools view -b -f 2 -F 1804 -q 30 dedup.bam chr21 > rep1.bam  # proper pairs, MAPQ>=30

The same steps as in From reads to coverage, with two ATAC details: trim adapters and -X 2000 so that nucleosomal fragments are not thrown out as discordant.


The exercise runs exactly this (with paths and threads). Adapter trimming matters more than in ChIP-seq because ATAC fragments are often shorter than the reads. CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT is the reverse complement of the Tn5 mosaic end; fastp can also find it from the overlap of the two reads. The -X 2000 is the maximum fragment length for a concordant pair; with the default 500 bp, tri-nucleosome fragments would be flagged as not properly paired and removed. -F 1804 removes unmapped, mate-unmapped, secondary, QC-failed and duplicate reads. Production pipelines (ENCODE ATAC pipeline, nf-core/atacseq) do the same, plus the Tn5 shift, which is in the next unit.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
section: What ATAC-seq does not tell you
text:
What ATAC-seq does not tell you

Which protein is bound: an ATAC peak is an NDR. Motifs, footprints or ChIP are needed to name the factor (Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting).
Whether the element is active: poised enhancers and bivalent promoters are accessible too. Combine with H3K27ac or expression.
What a change means: in bulk tissue, more accessibility can mean more cells of one type. And accessibility is a snapshot, mostly maintained by TFs, not an inherited “epigenetic” state.
Long-range closed chromatin: heterochromatin gives few, long fragments; ATAC is not the assay for H3K9me3 or Polycomb domains.


A critical-reading slide. Claims like “the epigenetic landscape is remodelled” in an ATAC-seq paper usually mean “the accessible sites differ between conditions”, which can be explained by TF levels, cell composition, or cell cycle. Accessibility at most sites is lost within hours when the TF that maintains it is removed: it is a readout of TF activity, which is the basis of chromVAR and similar methods in the motifs unit. None of this makes ATAC less useful; it tells you what question it answers.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




accessibility
NDRs at active promoters, enhancers, insulators; ~1–3% of the genome


history
DNase hypersensitivity → DNase-seq; FAIRE; MNase-seq (nucleosomes)


Tn5
cuts and adds adapters in one step (tagmentation); 9-bp duplication → +4 / −5 shift


two adapters
only A–B fragments are sequenced: 50% of fragments usable


fragment length
= distance between two insertions = TLEN; nucleosome ladder (< 100, ~200, ~400 bp) and 10.5-bp ripple


bias
weak, symmetric sequence preference; matters for footprinting


chrM
naked, many copies: often 10–50% of reads; Omni-ATAC reduces it


TSS enrichment
insertions at TSSs / mean of outer 100 bp at ±2 kb; > 7 ideal (ENCODE, GRCh38)


bad libraries
over-/under-tagmentation (fragment sizes), dead cells (flat TSS profile)




Students should leave able to explain why fragment lengths come in nucleosome steps, compute a fragment length and a chrM fraction from read positions and counts, compute a TSS enrichment from counts, and judge a library from its fragment-length and TSS plots. Next: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, where the reads become shifted insertion sites and peaks.

title: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Boyle et al. 2008, Cell. High-resolution mapping and characterization of open chromatin across the genome. DNase-seq: the first genome-wide map of DNase hypersensitive sites.
Thurman et al. 2012, Nature. The accessible chromatin landscape of the human genome. ENCODE’s DNase map of 125 cell types: what accessible DNA is and how it differs between cells.
Adey et al. 2010, Genome Biol. Rapid, low-input, low-bias construction of shotgun fragment libraries by high-density in vitro transposition. Tn5 tagmentation for sequencing libraries (the chemistry behind Nextera).
Buenrostro et al. 2013, Nat Methods. Transposition of native chromatin for fast and sensitive epigenomic profiling of open chromatin, DNA-binding proteins and nucleosome position. ATAC-seq: the fragment ladder, the 10.5-bp period and footprints, all in the first paper.
Corces et al. 2017, Nat Methods. An improved ATAC-seq protocol reduces background and enables interrogation of frozen tissues. Omni-ATAC.
Grandi et al. 2022, Nat Protoc. Chromatin accessibility profiling by ATAC-seq. A modern protocol with QC examples of good and bad libraries.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
About this lecture
Cancer is the disease where the epigenome has been studied most, and where epigenetics reaches the clinic: as drug targets and as diagnostic tests. The running example is real: TCGA colon cancer and lower-grade glioma methylation arrays.

The cancer methylome: global loss, focal gain at CpG islands.
Silencing tumour suppressors: MLH1 and microsatellite instability; the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP).
Mutated epigenetic regulators: IDH, DNMT3A/TET2, EZH2, oncohistones, SWI/SNF.
Epigenetic drugs and how they work.
Methylation as a diagnostic: tumour classification and cell-free DNA.


Students know DNA methylation chemistry, CpG islands and the main histone marks from What is epigenetics? and DNA methylation biology; the 450k/EPIC array and beta values are covered in Methylation arrays. This lecture applies them to disease. Cancer is the main example because it is where the evidence is deepest, but the same ideas (methylation as a stable cell-identity record, regulators as drug targets) apply to haematological and developmental disorders. The exercise analyses the same TCGA data shown in the figures: about 37 600 CpGs, 297 colon tumours and 38 normal colon samples, and 513 gliomas.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: The cancer methylome in one picture
text:
The cancer methylome in one picture


Global hypomethylation: CpGs that are normally methylated (repeats, gene-poor regions, gene bodies) lose methylation (Feinberg & Vogelstein 1983).
Focal hypermethylation: some CpG-island promoters, normally unmethylated, become methylated and their genes are silenced.
Both happen in the same tumour, and both are detectable in early lesions.


These two changes were the first epigenetic alterations found in cancer. Feinberg and Vogelstein measured less methylation at specific genes in colon cancers than in matched normal mucosa in 1983. CpG-island hypermethylation of tumour suppressors (RB1, VHL, CDKN2A, MLH1, BRCA1) was established in the 1990s, largely by the Baylin, Jones, Herman and Issa groups. The figure is a cartoon; the next slide shows the real data. Keep in mind the “cause or consequence” question from What is epigenetics?: a change found in tumours may drive growth, or may be a by-product of the many divisions and the altered state of a cancer cell.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: Real data: global loss, focal gain
text:
Real data: global loss, focal gain


TCGA colon adenocarcinoma, Illumina 450k: open-sea CpGs median beta 0.69 in normal colon vs 0.64 in tumours; CpG-island CpGs 0.21 vs 0.25.
In 38 patients with both samples, the tumour has lower open-sea methylation in 37 and higher island methylation in 36.
Tumours are much more variable than normal tissue.


Each dot in the left panel is one sample; normal colon samples form a tight cluster, tumours spread in both directions. The paired comparison (right) removes differences between people: almost every tumour has lost open-sea methylation and gained island methylation relative to the patient’s own normal colon. The global change looks small (0.05) because the 450k array mostly measures CpGs in and near genes; whole-genome bisulfite sequencing shows that the loss is concentrated in large domains (next slide), where it can be 0.2–0.3. Purity also matters: a tumour sample with 60% cancer cells shows only 60% of the cancer cells’ change. Students compute this in the exercise.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Where methylation is lost


Loss is concentrated in partially methylated domains (PMDs): large, late-replicating, lamina-associated, gene-poor regions (Berman et al. 2012).
Many focal CGI gains lie inside these domains.
Proposed consequences: less tightly silenced repeats and transposons, chromosomal instability; effects on gene expression are modest.


PMDs were first seen in cultured fibroblasts and then in cancers. They coincide with late replication, the nuclear lamina and the B compartment of Hi-C (3D genome organisation), and they tend to lose methylation in dividing cells, perhaps because maintenance methylation has less time to finish in late-replicating DNA. The loss is therefore partly a record of how many times a cell has divided, which links it to epigenetic clocks. Be cautious about causal claims: hypomethylation of repeats and pericentromeric satellites is associated with chromosomal instability (mouse models with low DNMT1 develop tumours), but for most human tumours we cannot say which consequences matter.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Which CpG islands gain methylation?


Many CGIs hypermethylated in cancer are Polycomb (H3K27me3) targets in stem cells: developmental genes that were already off (Widschwendter et al. 2007).
In the tumour the silent-but-plastic Polycomb state is replaced by DNA methylation: a more stable lock.
The same switch happens slowly in ageing normal tissue.


This was a key insight from three papers in 2007 (Widschwendter, Ohm, Schlesinger): the genes that are methylated in tumours are not a random set, nor mainly tumour suppressors, but Polycomb targets in embryonic stem cells. These genes are usually silent already in the cell of origin, so their methylation changes little in expression; what it changes is the ability to switch them on again during differentiation. That is one model for how epigenetic changes lock a cell in a stem-like state. It also explains why the same CGIs gain methylation with age in normal tissue, and why they are useful biomarkers: they are reliably unmethylated in normal cells and methylated in tumours, regardless of whether they drive anything.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Real data: single CpG islands


SFRP2, GATA4, SEPTIN9: methylated (beta > 0.3) in 91%, 81%, 74% of colon tumours, low in every normal sample.
MGMT in 37%, MLH1 in 13%, CDKN2A only in 3% on this array; GAPDH (a housekeeping gene) never.
Methylated SEPTIN9 in plasma DNA is the basis of an approved blood test for colorectal cancer.


Each panel is the mean beta over the promoter CGI probes of one gene (19 to 38 probes; CDKN2A has only 5 on the subset in the exercise). SFRP2 and GATA4 are typical Polycomb-target CGIs: methylated in almost every tumour, so excellent markers, but their methylation does not separate tumours into groups. MLH1 is different: methylated in a minority, and then strongly (beta 0.4–0.7): that is a functional, selected event, next slide. The CDKN2A number is low because the array probes average over the p16 and p14ARF promoters and because purity dilutes the signal; reported frequencies of p16 methylation in colon cancer by methylation-specific PCR are higher. The SEPTIN9 test (Epi proColon) detects methylated SEPTIN9 DNA in plasma; it is less sensitive than colonoscopy, a point we return to with cell-free DNA.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: Silencing a tumour suppressor: the epigenetic hit
text:
Silencing a tumour suppressor: the epigenetic hit


Knudson’s two hits can be genetic or epigenetic: a mutation plus promoter methylation, a deletion plus methylation, or methylation of both copies.
Classic examples: MLH1 (sporadic MSI colon cancer), CDKN2A, BRCA1 (some breast and ovarian cancers), VHL (some renal cancers).
MGMT methylation in glioblastoma is a predictive biomarker: the tumour cannot repair the damage made by temozolomide (Hegi et al. 2005).


Promoter CGI methylation is a heritable, clonal silencing event, so it can act like a mutation in tumour evolution. The evidence that it is functional rather than incidental comes from cases where it replaces a genetic hit: in tumours with a BRCA1 promoter methylation, BRCA1 is usually not mutated, and the tumours behave like BRCA1-mutant tumours (for example in their response to PARP inhibitors, an active clinical question). MGMT is a DNA repair enzyme that removes the O6-methylguanine lesion made by alkylating drugs. Hegi et al. 2005 showed that glioblastoma patients with a methylated MGMT promoter benefit from temozolomide, and MGMT methylation testing is now routine in neuro-oncology.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: Real data: MLH1 methylation causes microsatellite instability
text:
Real data: MLH1 methylation causes microsatellite instability


37 of 297 colon tumours have a methylated MLH1 promoter; 36 of them are MSI-high, and their MLH1 RNA is about 8-fold lower (log2 6.2 vs 9.1).
25 MSI-high tumours have an unmethylated MLH1: mostly inherited (Lynch syndrome) or somatic mutations in mismatch-repair genes.
Clinically, MLH1 methylation testing helps separate sporadic MSI cancers from Lynch syndrome.


MLH1 is a mismatch-repair gene. When both copies are silenced, replication errors in repetitive DNA are not corrected and microsatellites change length: microsatellite instability (MSI), with a very high mutation burden. Herman et al. 1998 showed that sporadic MSI colon cancers have methylated MLH1, and that demethylation with 5-aza-deoxycytidine restores expression. Here MSI status comes from the MANTIS score (above 0.4 = MSI-high), computed from the exome sequences. The point to stress: a methylation change completely explains a genetic phenotype. Clinically, an MSI-high or MLH1-negative tumour triggers testing for Lynch syndrome, which is inherited; tumour MLH1 methylation (often with BRAF V600E) usually supports a sporadic origin, but does not exclude inherited or constitutional predisposition. Early onset, multiple primary tumours or a strong family history can still warrant germline and constitutional MLH1 epimutation evaluation; see GeneReviews: Lynch syndrome. MSI-high tumours also respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
The CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP)


Select 1000 CGI CpGs that are unmethylated in normal colon and variable in tumours, cluster the 297 tumours: a group of 69 (23%) methylates many of them at once: CIMP-high.
First proposed by Toyota et al. (1999); confirmed with a marker panel by Weisenberger et al. (2006).


Walk through the heatmap: rows are CpGs, columns are tumours, dark is methylated. CIMP-high tumours (left, red bar) have many of these islands methylated; CIMP-low an intermediate set; non-CIMP few. The bars below already show the associations of the next slide. The selection step matters: we use only CpGs unmethylated in normal colon, so the clusters reflect gains in the tumour rather than differences in normal tissue or in contaminating cells. The number of groups is a choice (we cut the tree at three; TCGA described four groups). The existence of CIMP was debated for years because early studies used few markers; Weisenberger et al. 2006 screened 195 markers in 295 tumours and showed that CIMP-positive tumours form a distinct subset.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
What goes with CIMP-high


CIMP-high tumours: 43% BRAF V600E (vs 1–4% in the others), 49% MSI-high, 92% right-sided, and almost all MLH1-methylated tumours.
CIMP is a subtype with its own origin (serrated precursor lesions), not a random accumulation.


Numbers from make-cancer-figs.R: of 68 CIMP-high tumours with mutation data, 29 have BRAF V600E; of 35 BRAF V600E tumours overall, 29 are CIMP-high. Weisenberger et al. reported an odds ratio of 203 for BRAF mutation in CIMP-positive tumours. 30 of the 37 MLH1-methylated tumours are CIMP-high: MLH1 is one of the islands that gets methylated in this phenotype, and when it does, the tumour becomes MSI. Right-sided (proximal) location reflects a different precursor, the sessile serrated lesion. Whether BRAF mutation causes the hypermethylation, or a hypermethylating cell state favours BRAF-mutant clones, is still debated; experiments suggest BRAF V600E can promote CIMP-like methylation through transcriptional repressors, but this is not settled.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Driver or passenger?


Driver: silences an expressed tumour suppressor (MLH1, CDKN2A, BRCA1): selected because it gives a growth advantage.
Passenger: methylates a gene that was already silent (most Polycomb targets): no advantage, but a stable record of the tumour’s history.
For diagnostics both are useful; for biology and therapy, only drivers matter.


A useful way to classify any methylation change in cancer. Tests for driver status: is the gene expressed in the normal cell of origin, is it silenced in the tumour, does restoring it slow growth, does methylation substitute for a mutation (mutually exclusive), and is it clonal? Most of the hundreds of hypermethylated CGIs in a CIMP tumour fail these tests: they are passengers carried along with a cell state. That does not make them useless: their sheer number and stability make them the best markers for detecting and classifying tumours, the topic of the last part of the lecture.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Mutated epigenetic regulators


Tumour sequencing found frequent mutations in writers, erasers, readers and remodellers, and even in histones.
Most are loss of function; some create a new function (mutant IDH, oncohistones).


Before about 2010, epigenetic changes in cancer were thought of as secondary to genetic ones. Large sequencing projects changed that: chromatin regulators are among the most frequently mutated genes in human cancer. The grid groups the examples of this lecture by what the protein does. Note the tissue specificity: EZH2 gain-of-function in germinal-centre lymphoma, loss in myeloid disease; SETD2 and PBRM1 in clear-cell renal carcinoma; SMARCB1 in rhabdoid tumours. The following slides take the clearest cases one by one. This is a selection, not a complete list.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: IDH mutations: an oncometabolite blocks demethylation
text:
IDH mutations: an oncometabolite blocks demethylation


Mutant IDH1 (R132) or IDH2 (R140, R172) converts alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) into D-2-hydroxyglutarate (Dang et al. 2009).
2-HG competitively inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases: TET enzymes and JmjC histone demethylases (Xu et al. 2011).
Result: CGI hypermethylation, more H3K9/H3K27 methylation, blocked differentiation (Figueroa et al. 2010; Lu et al. 2012).


This is the clearest link between metabolism and the epigenome. IDH1/2 mutations are heterozygous point mutations at one arginine in the active site, found in most lower-grade gliomas, about 20% of AML, cholangiocarcinoma and chondrosarcoma. The mutant enzyme gains a new activity and makes millimolar amounts of 2-HG. TET2 loss and IDH mutation are mutually exclusive in AML and give similar methylation profiles (Figueroa 2010), which is genetic evidence that they act in the same pathway. Turcan et al. 2012 showed that introducing mutant IDH1 into astrocytes is sufficient to create the glioma hypermethylator phenotype. Hypermethylation at CTCF sites can also disrupt insulators and let enhancers activate oncogenes such as PDGFRA (Flavahan et al. 2016).

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: Real data: G-CIMP in IDH-mutant glioma
text:
Real data: G-CIMP in IDH-mutant glioma


513 TCGA lower-grade gliomas: 419 IDH-mutant, 94 IDH-wild-type.
Of CGI CpGs unmethylated in IDH-wt tumours, a median 8.1% are methylated (beta > 0.3) in IDH-mutant tumours vs 1.5% in IDH-wt; 751 island CpGs are > 0.2 higher, only 21 lower.
The glioma CpG island methylator phenotype (G-CIMP, Noushmehr et al. 2010) is a readout of the IDH mutation.


The heatmap shows the 400 island CpGs that differ most between the groups; the IDH-mutant block is uniformly methylated, so in practice the methylation profile alone predicts IDH status very accurately. This is an example of a driver that acts through the epigenome: the hypermethylation is the mechanism of the mutation, not a passenger. Clinically, IDH status defines the WHO glioma classes (IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, IDH-wild-type glioblastoma), and methylation arrays are now used to make that call (classifier slide). In the exercise students compute these numbers.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
DNMT3A and TET2: clonal haematopoiesis


DNMT3A and TET2 loss-of-function mutations let a blood stem cell clone expand.
Such clones are found in about 10% of people aged 70–79 (Jaiswal et al. 2014): clonal haematopoiesis.
DNMT3A is mutated in 22% of AML (Ley et al. 2010); the clone is a first step, more mutations are needed.


DNMT3A is the de novo methyltransferase; TET2 starts active demethylation. Losing either changes the methylation of haematopoietic stem cells and favours self-renewal over differentiation, so the clone grows slowly over decades. Jaiswal et al. 2014 sequenced blood exomes of 17 182 people: clonal mutations were rare below 40 and found in 9.5% at 70–79; carriers had an 11-fold higher risk of blood cancer, though the absolute risk stays low, and a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, probably through inflammatory macrophages. Ley et al. 2010 found DNMT3A mutations in 62 of 281 AML patients, most at R882. This is a good example of an epigenetic regulator acting early: mutations in DNMT3A are often the first in the leukaemic lineage.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
EZH2: oncogene or tumour suppressor


Gain: EZH2 Y641 mutations in germinal-centre lymphoma; with wild-type EZH2, they raise H3K27me3 (Morin 2010; Sneeringer 2010).
Loss: PRC2 components deleted or inactivated in some MDS, T-ALL and MPNST.
Same enzyme, opposite roles: an EZH2 inhibitor helps only where the tumour depends on PRC2.


The Y641 story is a lesson in reading biochemistry. Morin et al. found the mutation and reported that it reduced activity on an unmethylated peptide, which looked like loss of function. Sneeringer et al. showed that the mutant is poor at the first methylation but better than wild type at converting me2 to me3, so the heterozygous cell makes more H3K27me3 overall. That locks germinal-centre B cells in a proliferative state by repressing differentiation genes. In myeloid malignancies and T-ALL, PRC2 behaves as a tumour suppressor instead. Tazemetostat, an EZH2 inhibitor, received accelerated FDA approvals for follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma in 2020, but those approvals were withdrawn in June 2026 after an increased rate of second primary malignancies in the confirmatory trial (FDA withdrawal notice).

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Oncohistones


H3K27M in diffuse midline glioma of children: 78% of DIPGs (Wu et al. 2012; Schwartzentruber et al. 2012).
The mutant histone is a small fraction of all H3 but binds EZH2 and inhibits PRC2: H3K27me3 falls genome-wide (Lewis et al. 2013).
H3K36M in 95% of chondroblastomas; H3G34W in giant cell tumour of bone (Behjati et al. 2013).


Histone genes were not expected to be cancer genes: there are many copies, so one mutant allele makes only a few percent of the H3 in a cell. The K27M mutant is dominant because methionine at position 27 sits in the EZH2 active site and blocks the enzyme, so PRC2 cannot methylate the wild-type histones either. Lewis et al. 2013 also showed that K-to-M mutations at K9 and K36 inhibit the matching methyltransferases. The H3.3 genes are H3F3A and H3F3B (new names H3-3A and H3-3B); H3.1 K27M is in HIST1H3B. These tumours are now diagnosed by the mutation and by their methylation profile, and the loss of H3K27me3 is visible by immunohistochemistry.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
SWI/SNF: remodellers as tumour suppressors


SWI/SNF (BAF) subunits are mutated in about 20% of human cancers (Kadoch et al. 2013).
Rhabdoid tumours: biallelic SMARCB1 loss is essentially the only recurrent event (Lee et al. 2012).
Loss leaves PRC2 unopposed, creating a dependency on EZH2 (Knutson et al. 2013).


SWI/SNF complexes slide and evict nucleosomes at enhancers, so loss of a subunit changes which enhancers are accessible. In rhabdoid tumours exome sequencing found almost no other recurrent mutations, which shows that disrupting a chromatin regulator can be enough to drive a cancer. SWI/SNF and Polycomb oppose each other at many genes; without SMARCB1, PRC2 keeps differentiation genes silent, and the tumour cells depend on EZH2. Knutson et al. 2013 showed regression of rhabdoid xenografts with an EZH2 inhibitor; tazemetostat was approved for epithelioid sarcoma, a tumour that also lacks SMARCB1 (INI1), before its FDA approvals were withdrawn in June 2026 (see the EZH2 slide). A synthetic dependency of this kind is the logic behind many epigenetic drugs.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Epigenetic drugs: the targets


Approved drugs hit DNMT1, HDACs, mutant IDH1/2 and menin–KMT2A; BET bromodomain inhibitors remain in trials.
EZH2: tazemetostat is a historical example; its FDA approvals were withdrawn in June 2026 because of second primary malignancy risk.
Most work best in blood cancers or in tumours defined by a specific mutation.


Go through the table from top to bottom and connect each row to the writer/reader/eraser vocabulary of What is epigenetics?. Azacitidine and decitabine are the oldest, used in myelodysplastic syndromes and AML. HDAC inhibitors are approved for T-cell lymphomas. Tazemetostat (approved 2020, FDA approvals withdrawn June 2026) targets EZH2. IDH inhibitors are the best example of precision epigenetic therapy: ivosidenib and enasidenib for IDH-mutant AML, and vorasidenib (2024) for IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma. Revumenib (2024) blocks the menin–KMT2A interaction in KMT2A-rearranged leukaemia. BET inhibitors such as JQ1 displace BRD4 from acetylated chromatin and showed strong effects in models, but toxicity and modest efficacy have so far kept them out of routine use. Approval status here is for the US FDA, checked November 2026; the June 2026 FDA notice documents the tazemetostat withdrawal.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Hypomethylating drugs


Azacitidine and decitabine are cytidine analogues built into DNA during replication; they trap and deplete DNMT1.
Methylation is then diluted with each division; silenced genes and endogenous retroviruses come back on.
dsRNA from retroviruses triggers an interferon response: viral mimicry (Chiappinelli et al. 2015; Roulois et al. 2015).


The drugs need dividing cells, act slowly and are given in repeated cycles; responses in MDS typically take several cycles. Fenaux et al. 2009 showed a survival benefit of azacitidine over conventional care in higher-risk MDS. Azacitidine is a ribonucleoside and is mostly built into RNA; decitabine is a deoxyribonucleoside and goes only into DNA. How the drugs work in patients is still debated: re-expression of tumour suppressors, differentiation, and the immune response through viral mimicry may all contribute. The viral-mimicry idea motivates combining them with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Methylation-based tumour classification


Capper et al. (2018): a random forest trained on 2 801 reference samples in 91 classes (82 tumour, 9 normal), from 450k/EPIC arrays.
Prospectively, 88% of 1 104 cases matched a class; the diagnosis was revised in 12%.
Works because methylation records the cell of origin and is stable in fixed tissue.


Brain tumours are hard to classify by histology and inter-observer variability is high. The classifier gives raw scores (votes of 10 000 trees) that are calibrated by multinomial logistic regression into probabilities; a score of at least 0.9 assigns a class, otherwise the case is “no match” and goes back to the pathologist. The same array gives a copy-number profile (1p/19q codeletion, amplifications). The tool is freely available and methylation classes are part of the 2021 WHO classification of CNS tumours. Two lessons from machine learning (Machine learning from scratch): the classifier cannot recognise a class it was not trained on, and scores must be calibrated before they are used as confidence.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
section: Real data: a classifier in our tumours
text:
Real data: a classifier in our tumours


Elastic net on 35 710 CpGs, trained on 201 colon tumours, tested on 84 held-out patients: predicts MSI-high from methylation alone, using 41 CpGs.
All 63 MSS tumours correct; 14 of 21 MSI-high found: 12 of 14 with MLH1 methylation, only 2 of 7 without.
The model learned the MLH1/CIMP route to MSI; it misses most MSI-high tumours without MLH1 methylation in this test set.


This is the exercise’s R4 in miniature. The split is by patient so no person contributes to both training and test. The elastic net (glmnet) is penalised logistic regression, like the epigenetic clocks in Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers. Ask students to predict which tumours are missed before showing the colours: the model relies strongly on MLH1/CIMP-associated patterns and misses five of the seven MSI-high tumours without MLH1 methylation in this test set. This result does not establish that such tumours have no methylation changes, or that all methylation-based classifiers would miss them; identifying Lynch syndrome requires further genetic evaluation. A classifier is only as good as the biology it can measure, and a good test-set accuracy (77 of 84, 92% here) can hide a systematically missed subgroup.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
Cancer detection from cell-free DNA


Plasma contains short DNA fragments, mostly from blood cells; a small fraction comes from a tumour.
Tumour fragments carry tumour-specific methylation; the pattern also reveals the tissue of origin.
Liu et al. (2020): 99.3% specificity; sensitivity 18% in stage I, 93% in stage IV across all cancer types.


Methylation is better suited than mutations for this task because many regions change together, the changes are shared between patients, and the pattern says which tissue the DNA came from. The CCGA study (Liu et al. 2020) sequenced bisulfite-converted plasma DNA at more than 100 000 targeted regions in 6 689 participants. Note the stage dependence: early tumours shed little DNA, which is exactly where screening would help most. Whether such tests reduce cancer deaths in screening is being tested in large trials. The general use of methylation as a biomarker, and its pitfalls, are the subject of Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers.

title: Epigenetics in disease and therapy
text:
The arithmetic of screening


Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with 50% sensitivity and 99.3% specificity, PPV is 42% at 1% prevalence; at 95% specificity only 9%.
In a screening population most positives can be false, so specificity matters more than it seems.


PPV = sens × prev / (sens × prev + (1 − spec) × (1 − prev)). At 1% prevalence: 0.5 × 0.01 / (0.005 + 0.007 × 0.99) = 0.42. With 95% specificity: 0.005 / (0.005 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 0.09. This is an exam-type calculation. It explains why cfDNA tests are tuned for very high specificity even at the cost of sensitivity, and why they are first used in high-risk groups. Each false positive leads to imaging and sometimes biopsy.

Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

title: Annotation and differential binding
text:
About this lecture


Describe: annotate peaks relative to genes (ChIPseeker); profiles and heatmaps (deepTools).
Compare: consensus regions → counts → normalisation → DESeq2, the RNA-seq workflow on peaks.
Normalisation is where ChIP differs from RNA-seq: signal-to-noise, copy number and global changes (spike-ins).
Real data: H3K27ac in GM12878 (B-lymphoblastoid) and K562 (erythroleukaemia), two ENCODE replicates each, chr21.


Peak calling gave us peak sets per sample. This unit asks two questions. For one condition: where are the peaks, and what does the signal look like around genes or around the peaks? Between conditions: which regions differ, with replicates and a statistical test. The second part is RNA-seq again (students know DESeq2), so the time goes to what differs. The comparison dataset is H3K27ac (active promoters and enhancers) in two very different cell lines from the same lab (Broad), two biological replicates each, with ENCODE’s filtered alignments restricted to chr21. Two cell lines are an extreme contrast, chosen because the data are public and comparable; a real study would compare conditions of one cell type, ideally with three or more replicates. Annotation also uses the CTCF peaks from earlier units.

title: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Annotating peaks


ChIPseeker (Yu, Wang and He 2015) is the common Bioconductor tool: annotatePeak takes peaks and a TxDb (a transcript database, here built from the GENCODE GTF with txdbmaker) and returns, for each peak, a genomic category and the nearest TSS. HOMER annotatePeaks.pl does the same on the command line, and in Genomic intervals students did the core of it with distanceToNearest. Three choices change the answer and must be reported: the promoter window (±1 kb here; ±3 kb is ChIPseeker’s default, which makes almost a third of the genome “promoter-proximal” in gene-dense regions); the annotation (all transcripts of all genes including lncRNAs, or protein-coding only); and the priority used when a peak overlaps several features. The categories are descriptive; they are not evidence of function.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Real data: where are the peaks?
text:
Real data: where are the peaks?


H3K27ac: 33% (GM12878) and 40% (K562) of peaks at promoters; CTCF: 18%, and 33% distal intergenic.
Median distance to the nearest TSS: H3K27ac 3.6 kb and 2.2 kb, CTCF 8.6 kb; 47% of CTCF peaks are more than 10 kb from any TSS.


ChIPseeker on the ENCODE peak sets on chr21 (405 CTCF, 567 GM12878 H3K27ac and 483 K562 H3K27ac peaks), promoter = TSS ± 1 kb, all GENCODE basic genes including lncRNAs (exercise R1). H3K27ac marks active promoters and enhancers, so a third or more of its peaks are promoters and most of the rest are in introns and intergenic DNA (candidate enhancers). CTCF is mostly away from promoters: insulators, loop anchors. The right panel is the cumulative distribution of distances; the steps at zero are the peaks that overlap a TSS. On a genome-wide scale the fractions differ (chr21 is gene-poor, which raises the distal fractions), so compare the marks, not the numbers with other papers.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: The nearest gene is not the target
text:
The nearest gene is not the target


Every annotation tool reports a nearest gene, and many papers then do gene-set enrichment on the nearest genes of their peaks. For promoter peaks that is reasonable; for distal peaks it is a guess. Enhancers act over tens to hundreds of kilobases within topologically associating domains, often skipping the nearest gene; CRISPR interference screens (e.g. Fulco et al. 2019, Gasperini et al. 2019) found that a large share of functional enhancer–gene pairs do not involve the nearest gene. On chr21, the strongest GM12878-specific H3K27ac region (later slide) is more than 100 kb from the nearest protein-coding TSS. Tools such as GREAT assign each region to genes within a regulatory domain rather than only the nearest one. Better links come from 3D contacts (Hi-C, HiChIP), correlation of enhancer activity with gene expression across samples, and perturbation: Linking regulatory elements to genes.

title: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Profiles and heatmaps


deepTools (Ramírez et al. 2016) computeMatrix builds a matrix of signal (from bigWig files) in bins around a set of regions; plotProfile draws the column means and plotHeatmap draws the matrix itself with the profile on top. Two modes: reference-point (around TSSs or peak centres) and scale-regions (whole gene bodies stretched to a common length, as in the H3K36me3 metagene of ChIP-seq: the assay). Regions on the minus strand are flipped so that “downstream” is always to the right. The heatmap is what makes the plot honest: an average profile with a peak could come from all regions having a moderate peak or from a few regions with a huge one. Regions can be sorted, grouped by BED file (one group per file) or clustered (–kmeans; note that k-means clustering depends on a random start, so groups defined by biology are more reproducible). In R, EnrichedHeatmap and ChIPseeker’s tagHeatmap do the same.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Real data: four marks around chr21 TSSs
text:
Real data: four marks around chr21 TSSs





220 protein-coding genes, ±5 kb around the TSS, ENCODE GM12878 fold-change tracks, sorted by H3K4me3.
The top third of genes: H3K4me3 and H3K27ac at the TSS and H3K36me3 downstream: active.
The rest: little of any active mark; some have H3K27me3.
One look tells you how many genes are active and that the marks agree.



Exercise C4. All four columns are sorted by the same order (H3K4me3). The dip at the TSS in H3K4me3 and H3K27ac is the nucleosome-free region (ChIP-seq: the assay). H3K36me3 is only downstream of the TSS of active genes, as expected for a mark of transcription elongation. H3K27me3 shows a few strong rows among the silent genes (Polycomb targets such as OLIG1/OLIG2) and is weak overall in this cell line. The colour scale (zMax) is set per mark; always check the scale before comparing intensities between columns.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Real data: H3K27ac in two cell types
text:
Real data: H3K27ac in two cell types





841 consensus H3K27ac regions on chr21, grouped by which cell line’s peak set contains them: 378 GM12878 only, 170 both, 293 K562 only.
CPM tracks of our four libraries, ±3 kb around the region centres.
Replicates agree; cell-type-specific regions are nearly empty in the other cell line.



Exercise C2–C4: consensus = union of ENCODE’s replicated H3K27ac peaks of the two cell lines, merged and blacklist-filtered; bamCoverage CPM tracks from ENCODE’s filtered BAMs (chr21), reads extended to 200 bp. Grouping by peak-set membership is a quick, descriptive view of differential binding; it is not a test: a region called in one cell line only can still have substantial signal in the other (peak calling has thresholds, and the K562 profiles in the “GM12878 only” group are low but not zero). The shared regions are mostly promoters of housekeeping genes. The proper comparison counts reads in all regions in all samples and tests the difference with replicates: next.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Differential binding is RNA-seq on peaks
text:
Differential binding is RNA-seq on peaks


Once there is a count matrix, the statistics are those of RNA-seq: DESeq2 or edgeR, negative binomial with dispersion shared across features, design formula with batch and condition, FDR. DiffBind (Ross-Innes et al. 2012; Stark and Brown) wraps exactly this: it builds the consensus (by default peaks found in at least two samples), counts reads, normalises and calls DESeq2 or edgeR. csaw (Lun and Smyth 2016) avoids peak calling altogether: it counts reads in sliding windows, tests every window and merges significant windows into regions, controlling the FDR over regions. What differs from RNA-seq: the features are made from the data, so the consensus must be built from all conditions (peaks of one condition only would bias the test towards that condition); one counts fragments (here the centre of each extended read); and above all normalisation.

The GM12878 libraries put more of their reads into peaks: a signal-to-noise difference between the two experiments, not necessarily biology.
Read length differs too (51 vs 36 bp): a technical variable confounded with cell type, as are the dates of the experiments.


Exercise R2. Counts are fragment centres (reads shifted 100 bp along their strand) falling in the consensus regions. FRiP differs by about 0.1–0.15 between the cell lines. Is that because K562 truly has less H3K27ac in peaks relative to the rest of its genome, or because one IP worked better? From these data alone you cannot tell; that is exactly the question each normalisation answers differently (next slides). The confounding is real for any comparison of public data from different experiments: cell line, date, read length and sequencing run all change together. With only two replicates per group the dispersion estimates are weak; three or more is the recommendation, as for RNA-seq.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Normalisation: what is assumed to be constant?
text:
Normalisation: what is assumed to be constant?


This slide is the core of the unit. Every normalisation makes something equal between samples, and that something must truly be the same. Library size: total reads; fine if the IPs are equally efficient, wrong if one sample has a higher FRiP (its peaks all look up). Reads in peaks (DESeq2’s median-of-ratios on the count matrix, edgeR’s TMM): assumes most peaks do not change, the same assumption as for genes; wrong when most peaks change in one direction. Background bins (csaw’s approach for “composition bias”): large windows away from peaks are assumed to be pure background, the same in all samples; wrong when the IP efficiency differs (then the better sample’s peaks look up and its background looks down) or when copy number differs. Spike-in: a fixed amount of foreign chromatin per sample; the only option when the total amount of the mark changes, as with an EZH2 or DOT1L inhibitor (Experimental design and QC). DiffBind 3 changed its default from reads-in-peaks to full library size precisely because the choice matters; its documentation discusses the alternatives.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Real data: three normalisations, three answers
text:
Real data: three normalisations, three answers


Same counts, same test (DESeq2, padj < 0.05), different size factors: 264 / 245, 229 / 280, 182 / 319 regions up / down in K562.
The size factors differ most for K562 rep 1: 1.43 (peaks), 1.70 (library), 1.94 (background).


Exercise R3. MA plots: log2 fold change K562/GM12878 against mean count; black = significant; red dashed line = median log2 fold change. With the default (median-of-ratios on peaks), the cloud is centred on zero by construction. With library size, the median shifts to −0.33: the K562 libraries have fewer reads in peaks (lower FRiP), so most peaks look lower in K562. With background bins, −0.76: the K562 libraries have relatively more reads in the background, because of lower FRiP and because K562’s chr21 has extra copies (next slide). The diagonal stripes are regions with zero reads in one cell line. Which answer is right? It depends on what you believe is constant. For two cell lines with thousands of cell-type-specific enhancers there is no ground truth; most analysts would accept the peak-based default here and say so, and check that conclusions about individual strong regions (|log2FC| > 3) do not depend on the choice: they do not.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Copy number differs between cell lines
text:
Copy number differs between cell lines


Share of all reads per chromosome, K562 / GM12878. The inputs show K562’s karyotype: chr22 and chr21 1.2–1.3×, chr9 0.81, chrX 0.68.
Any region on an amplified chromosome gets more reads in every library: a “gain” in K562 unless the counts are corrected.


From ENCODE’s idxstats of the whole filtered BAMs (data/h3k27ac_idxstats.tsv; exercise R4). GM12878 is a near-diploid lymphoblastoid line; K562 is a near-triploid chronic myeloid leukaemia line with many gains and losses (the BCR-ABL1 amplification on 22q, loss of 9p including CDKN2A). The input share is a direct, coarse copy-number readout (the H3K27ac ChIPs, circles, follow it partly but mix in biology). chr21 has about 1.23 times the expected share in K562: every chr21 region has a head start in K562 counts, which partly offsets the lower FRiP. Remedies: DiffBind subtracts scaled control reads or masks “greylist” regions with abnormal input signal; one can include the input-derived copy number as an offset, or compare cell types only within regions of equal copy number. Copy number matters most for cancer samples compared with normal tissue.

text:
Global changes need spike-ins
A fixed amount of Drosophila chromatin is added to each sample before the IP. DESeq2 accepts any size factors, so use the fly reads:
