Read counts look unchanged; spike-in normalised, region A has lost half its signal.
In R: sizeFactors(dds) <- s before DESeq(dds).


Experimental design and QC introduced spike-ins (ChIP-Rx, Orlando et al. 2014) with a CPM-style scaling factor α = 1/N_fly. Here the same idea enters the differential analysis: the size factor of each sample is proportional to its spike-in reads (the geometric mean of 50 000, 60 000, 100 000 and 110 000 is 75 793). Why does the treated sample have more fly reads? Both got the same fly chromatin, but the treated cells had half as much of the human mark, so the IP pulled down less human DNA and the fly made up a larger share of the library. A refinement used in practice: correct the spike-in factor by the fly/human ratio in each sample’s input, which absorbs errors in how many cells were mixed. Spike-ins add noise, and they are only valid if the antibody sees the fly mark like the human one and the spike was added before any step that loses material.

title: Annotation and differential binding
section: Simulated: a global loss, with and without spike-ins
text:
Simulated: a global loss, with and without spike-ins


2 000 peaks, 3 + 3 samples, every library sequenced to the same depth. Truth: 95% of peaks lose half their mark, 5% are unchanged.
Standard normalisation: the halved peaks look unchanged (mean log2FC −0.05) and the 5% unchanged peaks look up (+0.93). Spike-in: −1.06 and −0.10, the truth.


A simulation, because no small public dataset with a known global change and spike-ins fits our chr21 setup (exercise R5 runs it). Negative binomial counts with a fixed dispersion; the spike-in reads double in the treated samples, with 5% noise. DESeq2’s median-of-ratios assumes most peaks are unchanged, so it re-centres the 95% halved peaks on zero; the few truly unchanged peaks then appear to gain (43 significant “gains” with standard normalisation, 0 with spike-ins; 1 vs 1 562 significant losses). This is how papers on EZH2 inhibitors or H3K27M tumours can wrongly report “redistribution” of H3K27me3 to new sites. Whenever a treatment targets a writer or eraser of the mark you profile, plan spike-ins (or an orthogonal measurement: western blot, mass spectrometry) before the experiment.

title: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Real data: a differential locus


chr21:25.3–26.25 Mb: a cluster of strong H3K27ac regions in GM12878, absent in K562; 27 of 35 consensus regions here are significantly higher in GM12878.
The cluster lies > 100 kb from the nearest protein-coding TSS (MRPL39): which gene it regulates is a separate question.


Fragment-centre counts in 2-kb bins, CPM; bars below are the consensus regions coloured by the DESeq2 result (default normalisation). The GM12878 cluster at 25.4–25.5 Mb is the region with the largest fold changes on chr21 (log2FC −6 to −7.5). Clusters of strong H3K27ac over tens of kilobases are often called super-enhancers; this one sits in a gene desert near a lncRNA (LINC00158) and far from protein-coding genes. The peak at the GABPA/ATP5PF promoters is shared and not significant: housekeeping promoters are the stable reference that peak-based normalisation relies on. At the other extreme, the strongest K562-specific regions include the KCNJ6 promoter and the DSCR4 region (chr21:38.1 Mb). Interpretation (which genes, which TFs) needs expression data, motifs and contacts: Linking regulatory elements to genes, Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting.

For most ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq comparisons, DiffBind or a few lines of DESeq2 on a peak count matrix are enough (Differential accessibility did the same with ATAC). csaw is attractive when peak calling is unreliable (broad or diffuse marks, shifted peaks), because it tests windows directly. For broad marks, counting in genes (H3K36me3) or promoters ± a few kb (H3K27me3 at CpG islands) is often more robust than domain calls. Whatever the tool, report the consensus rule, the counting unit, the normalisation and the design formula.

Each row has a counterpart in the literature. Our own example has two of them: two replicates only, and technical variables (lab date, read length, IP efficiency) confounded with cell type. That is acceptable for a teaching comparison of two very different cell lines with thousands of real differences; it would not be for subtle effects of a treatment.

text:
Summary

a label; distal elements often regulate other genes

Students should be able to annotate a peak by hand given a gene model, explain why nearest-gene assignment is weak, read a deepTools heatmap, set up a differential binding analysis, compute spike-in size factors and normalised counts by hand, predict how each normalisation behaves under different FRiPs, copy numbers and global changes, and spot the pitfalls in a methods section. Next units: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag, then Chromatin states.

title: Annotation and differential binding
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Yu, Wang & He 2015, Bioinformatics. ChIPseeker: an R/Bioconductor package for ChIP peak annotation, comparison and visualization. Peak annotation.
Ramírez et al. 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. deepTools2: a next generation web server for deep-sequencing data analysis. computeMatrix and plotHeatmap.
Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Nature. Differential oestrogen receptor binding is associated with clinical outcome in breast cancer. The study behind DiffBind: differential binding in patient samples.
Lun & Smyth 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. csaw: a Bioconductor package for differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data using sliding windows. Windows, composition and efficiency biases.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome. Spike-in normalisation.
Chen et al. 2016, Mol Cell Biol. The overlooked fact: fundamental need for spike-in control for virtually all genome-wide analyses. Why normalising to totals hides global changes.

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Background
The protocol. Formaldehyde crosslinks proteins to DNA (and to each other) within ~2 Å; chromatin is fragmented by sonication (crosslinked ChIP) or micrococcal nuclease (native ChIP of histones); an antibody on protein A/G beads pulls down the target; crosslinks are reversed at 65 °C, the DNA is purified (typically 1–10 ng), made into a library and sequenced. The input is the same chromatin taken through every step except the immunoprecipitation.
Amounts. A diploid human cell has about 6.6 pg of DNA. One base pair of double-stranded DNA weighs about 650 g/mol (Avogadro’s number \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) /mol).
ChIP-qPCR, percent of input. If a fraction \(f\) of the chromatin was kept as input, first adjust its Ct: \(Ct_\text{input,adj} = Ct_\text{input} - \log_2(1/f)\). Then \(\%\text{input} = 100 \times 2^{\,Ct_\text{input,adj} - Ct_\text{ChIP}}\). Fold enrichment between two regions is \(2^{\Delta Ct}\).
Signal shapes. A transcription factor gives sharp peaks about two fragment lengths wide, with + strand reads to the left of the site and − strand reads to the right (separated by the fragment length \(d\)). Histone marks give nucleosome-scale peaks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac: 1–5 kb, with a dip at the nucleosome-free TSS) or broad domains (H3K36me3 over transcribed gene bodies; H3K27me3, H3K9me3 over silent regions, tens to hundreds of kb).

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
By hand
B1. How much DNA, and how much of it is signal? A CTCF ChIP starts from \(5 \times 10^6\) cells. 1% of the sheared chromatin is kept as input. The IP returns 4 ng of DNA with fragments of about 200 bp.

How much DNA is in the chromatin? How much in the input aliquot?
What fraction of the chromatin DNA did the IP recover?
Suppose 20% of the IP DNA comes from the 40 000 CTCF sites of the genome. How many 200-bp fragments is that? Each site exists in two copies per cell: what fraction of all site copies in the sample ended up in the IP?
The library is sequenced to 20 M reads with FRiP 0.2. On average, how many reads per CTCF site? Compare with (c): what does sequencing do to the library?

B2. ChIP-qPCR. 1% of the chromatin was kept as input. Ct values: input 25.0 (primer pair at site X); ChIP at site X 27.4; ChIP at a negative control region 32.6 (assume the input Ct is the same for both primer pairs).

Compute the percent of input at site X and at the negative region.
What is the fold enrichment of site X over the negative region?
A colleague reports “0.19% of input” as weak. Is it? What would you compare it with?

B3. Strands and resolution.

Around 300 summits of a TF, + strand read 5’ ends peak at −58 bp and − strand 5’ ends at +62 bp. Estimate the fragment length. Why is there no read 5’ end exactly at the summit?
In a ChIP-exo experiment for the same factor, + strand read starts pile up at −12 bp and − strand starts at +14 bp. What do these positions mean, and how large is the protected region?
Why do the same two calculations fail for H3K36me3?

B4. Which antibody? Four ChIP-seq tracks of the same cells, over a 400-kb region with two active genes, one silent developmental gene cluster and an intergenic stretch:

Track A: about 15 needle-like peaks, 300–500 bp wide, in genes and between them.
Track B: 2–4 kb peaks at the TSSs of the two active genes, each with a small dip at the TSS itself.
Track C: low, 30–60 kb “carpets” over the bodies of the two active genes, starting about 1 kb after the TSS and highest towards the 3’ end.
Track D: a 150-kb low plateau over the silent gene cluster, nothing over the active genes.


Match each track to one of: H3K27me3, CTCF, H3K36me3, H3K4me3. Give one reason for each.
For which tracks would macs3 predictd find a clear fragment length? Which would need about 45 M reads per replicate by ENCODE’s standards?
Why does track B dip at the TSS?

B5. Read the figures (lecture: Real data: the input is not flat and Real data: profiles around genes).

The input of the CTCF ChIP reaches 14 times the chr21 average at active TSSs, the input of the H3K36me3 ChIP about 1.1 times. Give two reasons why two inputs from the same cell line can differ this much.
A CTCF peak at an active promoter is twice as high as the input there. A CTCF peak in a gene desert is twice as high as the input there too. Which one contains more reads? Are both equally convincing?
Around active TSSs, H3K4me1 is lowest at the TSS and highest about 1 kb away, while H3K4me3 is high on both flanks. What does that tell you about where each mark sits?

B6. Judge the design.

A lab makes a ChIP of a TF in GM12878 and, to save money, uses an input sequenced from K562 cells that was available from ENCODE. What can go wrong?
Another lab sequences the ChIP to 30 M reads and the input to 2 M reads. What happens to a peak caller’s estimate of the local background?
A paper maps a transient co-activator that has no DNA-binding domain with 1% formaldehyde for 5 minutes and finds almost no peaks. Suggest two changes to the protocol.

B7. Hyper-ChIPable? A new antibody against transcription factor Z gives 3 000 peaks. 85% of them lie at the promoters of the 10% most highly expressed genes, and none has the known motif of Z. A ChIP with a non-specific IgG in the same cells gives weaker peaks at many of the same promoters.

What is the most likely explanation?
Name two experiments that would test whether Z binds these promoters.

B8. Crosslinked or native? For each, choose X-ChIP (formaldehyde + sonication) or N-ChIP (no fixation + MNase) and give a reason: (a) H3K27me3 in 50 000 sorted cells; (b) a TF that binds for a few seconds; (c) the positions of H3K4me3 nucleosomes around TSSs, at nucleosome resolution; (d) the co-activator of B6c.
B9. Peak heights. In one CTCF ChIP, site A has 400 reads and site B 100 reads, with similar inputs. A student concludes that CTCF occupies site A in four times as many cells as site B. List three other explanations. What comparison would be meaningful?

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the reads
for f in gm12878_ctcf_chip gm12878_ctcf_input gm12878_h3k36me3_chip gm12878_h3k36me3_input; do
  echo $f $(zcat $D/$f.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 { n++; if (length($0) > l) l = length($0) } END { print n, l }') \
    $(zcat $D/$f.fastq.gz | head -400000 | awk 'NR % 4 == 0' | fold -w1 | LC_ALL=C sort -u | tr -d '\n')
done
For each file: how many reads, how long, and which quality characters occur? Which files are Phred+64 and which Phred+33 (lowest and highest character)?


C2 — The alignment chain as a function
The chain of From reads to coverage, wrapped in a shell function so that it can be run on any single-end sample:
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
chain() {   # usage: chain <name> <reads.fastq.gz> <33 or 64>
  local s=$1
  if [ "$3" = 64 ]; then zcat $2 | perl -pe 'tr/@-~/!-_/ if $. % 4 == 0' | gzip > $s.fastq.gz
  else cp $2 $s.fastq.gz; fi
  fastp -w $T -i $s.fastq.gz -o $s.trim.fastq.gz -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -U $s.trim.fastq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools sort -@ 4 -o $s.sorted.bam -
  samtools index $s.sorted.bam
  samtools view -b -q 30 -F 1804 -o $s.q30.bam $s.sorted.bam
  samtools markdup -s $s.q30.bam $s.markdup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.markdup.bam
  samtools view -b -F 1024 -o $s.dedup.bam $s.markdup.bam chr21
  bedtools intersect -v -abam $s.dedup.bam -b blacklist.bed > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
}
chain ctcf           $D/gm12878_ctcf_chip.fastq.gz      64
chain ctcf_input     $D/gm12878_ctcf_input.fastq.gz     64
chain h3k36me3       $D/gm12878_h3k36me3_chip.fastq.gz  33
chain h3k36me3_input $D/gm12878_h3k36me3_input.fastq.gz 33
for s in ctcf ctcf_input h3k36me3 h3k36me3_input; do
  echo $s $(samtools view -c -F 4 $s.sorted.bam) $(samtools view -c -F 4 $s.sorted.bam chrM) \
    $(grep "DUPLICATE SINGLE:" $s.markdup.txt | cut -d' ' -f3) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done

For each sample: aligned reads, reads on chrM, duplicates, final reads on chr21. Which library has the most duplicates, and where are they?
The two inputs have very different chrM fractions. Does that matter for a chr21 analysis? (Think about what samtools view ... chr21 does.)



C3 — Can the fragment length be estimated?
for s in ctcf h3k36me3; do
  macs3 predictd -i $s.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 2>&1 | grep -E "paired peaks|predicted fragment|alternative"
done
Compare the two. How many “alternative” fragment lengths does MACS3 suggest for H3K36me3, and what does that tell you?


C4 — Fingerprints of a sharp and a broad mark
plotFingerprint -b ctcf.final.bam ctcf_input.final.bam h3k36me3.final.bam h3k36me3_input.final.bam \
  --labels CTCF CTCF_input H3K36me3 H3K36me3_input --binSize 1000 --region chr21 \
  --plotFile fingerprint.png --outRawCounts fingerprint.tsv -p $T
Open fingerprint.png. Which curve is closest to the diagonal? How does the H3K36me3 curve differ in shape from the CTCF curve? (Experimental design and QC explains how to read the plot.)


C5 — Tracks for the browser
bamCoverage -b ctcf.final.bam -o ctcf.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p $T
for s in h3k36me3 h3k36me3_input; do
  bamCoverage -b $s.final.bam -o $s.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 200 --binSize 50 -p $T
done
Load the three bigWigs in IGV (genome hg38), together with $D/gm12878_h3k36me3_fc.bigWig, and go to chr21:33,220,000-33,600,000. Where is H3K36me3 enriched relative to the genes (IFNAR1, IFNGR2, TMEM50B, GART, SON, DONSON)? Zoom in to a single 50-bp bin inside a gene body: how many reads support it?

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
In R
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(GenomicAlignments); library(rtracklayer) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/chip")

R1 — Strand cross-correlation, sharp vs broad
rd <- function(s) granges(readGAlignments(paste0(s, ".final.bam")))
reads <- lapply(c(ctcf = "ctcf", ctcf_input = "ctcf_input", h3k36me3 = "h3k36me3", h3k36me3_input = "h3k36me3_input"), rd)
sapply(reads, length)
crosscor <- function(gr, maxk = 500, from = 13e6, to = 46709983) {
  five <- resize(gr, 1, fix = "start")                       # 5' end of each read
  five <- five[start(five) >= from & start(five) <= to - maxk]
  n <- to - from + 1 - maxk
  p <- tabulate(start(five)[as.vector(strand(five) == "+")] - from + 1, n + maxk)
  m <- tabulate(start(five)[as.vector(strand(five) == "-")] - from + 1, n + maxk)
  ip <- which(p[1:n] > 0)
  mp <- mean(p[1:n]); sp <- sd(p[1:n]); mm <- mean(m); sm <- sd(m)
  sapply(0:maxk, function(k) (sum(p[ip] * m[ip + k]) / n - mp * mm) / (sp * sm))
}
cc <- sapply(reads, crosscor)
apply(cc, 2, function(x) c(max = max(x[-(1:41)]), at = which.max(x[-(1:41)]) + 40))   # ignore k < 41
cc[c(1, 37, 52, 101, 201, 301) , ]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(0:500, cc[, 1:2], type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "shift (bp)", ylab = "cross-correlation", main = "CTCF")
matplot(0:500, cc[, 3:4], type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "shift (bp)", ylab = "cross-correlation", main = "H3K36me3")

Explain what crosscor computes. Why does it start at 13 Mb?
Where is the maximum for each sample, and how large is it? Which maxima are meaningful?
The rows of cc printed are shifts 0, 36, 51, 100, 200 and 300 bp. Is there a phantom peak at the read length for CTCF?



R2 — Is the input flat?
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), which = chr21)
genes <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding"]
k4 <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_h3k4me3_fc.bigWig"), which = chr21, as = "RleList")
tss <- resize(genes, 1, fix = "start")
tss$k4 <- mean(k4[promoters(tss, 1000, 1001)])
table(cut(tss$k4, c(0, 1, 5, Inf), include.lowest = TRUE))
around <- function(gr, tss, w = 500) {
  n <- countOverlaps(promoters(tss, w, w + 1), resize(gr, 1, fix = "start"), ignore.strand = TRUE)   # 5' ends within +-500 bp
  mean(n) / (length(gr) * (2 * w + 1) / 40088619)                             # observed / expected
}
sapply(reads[c("ctcf_input", "h3k36me3_input")], function(gr)
  c(active = around(gr, tss[tss$k4 > 5]), silent = around(gr, tss[tss$k4 < 1])))

How many protein-coding TSSs on chr21 are active (H3K4me3 fold change > 5) and silent (< 1)?
How many times more input reads than expected fall within 500 bp of active and of silent TSSs, for each input? Why is ignore.strand = TRUE needed here?



R3 — H3K36me3 in gene bodies
gb <- genes[width(genes) > 5000]
gb$k4 <- mean(k4[promoters(resize(gb, 1, fix = "start"), 1000, 1001)])
rpkm <- function(gr, g) sum(countOverlaps(g, resize(gr, 1, fix = "start"), ignore.strand = TRUE)) / sum(width(g)) * 1e3 / length(gr) * 1e6
grp <- list(active = gb[gb$k4 > 5], silent = gb[gb$k4 < 1])
sapply(grp, length)
sapply(grp, function(g) c(H3K36me3 = rpkm(reads$h3k36me3, g), input = rpkm(reads$h3k36me3_input, g)))
1e3 / 40088619 * 1e6
first <- function(g) resize(g, 2000, fix = "start"); last <- function(g) resize(g, 2000, fix = "end")
c(first2kb = rpkm(reads$h3k36me3, first(grp$active)), last2kb = rpkm(reads$h3k36me3, last(grp$active)))

What does rpkm() compute? What is the value for a uniform library (the line 1e3 / 40088619 * 1e6)?
Compare H3K36me3 and input in active and in silent gene bodies. What is the enrichment over input in active genes?
Compare the first and the last 2 kb of active genes. Which enzyme and process explain the difference?



R4 — How far does the signal extend?
bins <- tileGenome(c(chr21 = 46709983), tilewidth = 1000, cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE)
bins <- bins[start(bins) > 13e6]
cnt <- sapply(reads, function(gr) countOverlaps(bins, resize(gr, 1, fix = "start")))
ac <- function(x, lag) cor(x[1:(length(x) - lag)], x[(1 + lag):length(x)])
lags <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)
round(sapply(c("ctcf", "h3k36me3", "h3k36me3_input"), function(s) sapply(lags, function(l) ac(log1p(cnt[, s]), l))), 3)

What is the correlation between the counts of 1-kb bins 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 kb apart, for each sample?
Why does CTCF still show some correlation at 50 kb, and the input too? (Hint: what else varies along a chromosome?) What extra correlation does H3K36me3 have?

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — amounts and qPCR (B1, B2)





Mass of one fragment = length × 650 g/mol / \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) /mol. Number of site copies = sites × 2 × cells. For qPCR, an input of 1% is 100-fold diluted relative to the whole chromatin: subtract \(\log_2 100 = 6.64\) cycles. Each cycle doubles: \(\Delta Ct = 1\) is a factor 2. See e.g. the percent-input method.









Hint 2 — strands and shapes (B3, B4, C3, R1)





A single-end read is the 5’ end of a fragment; + strand reads start at the left end of their fragment, − strand reads at the right end. In ChIP-exo the exonuclease stops at the crosslinked protein (Rhee & Pugh 2011). The strand cross-correlation is described in Kharchenko et al. 2008 and in Experimental design and QC; MACS3’s model in the predictd documentation. Where marks sit on genes: Barski et al. 2007.









Hint 3 — controls and artefacts (B5–B7)





Sonication breaks open chromatin more easily; amplified DNA gives more reads everywhere; inputs from different preparations have different biases. Landt et al. 2012 describe ENCODE’s control requirements; Teytelman et al. 2013 and Jain et al. 2015 describe hyper-ChIPable regions and phantom peaks. For the local background of a peak caller, see the MACS λ in Zhang et al. 2008.









Hint 4 — commands (C1–C5)





perl -pe 'tr/@-~/!-_/ if $. % 4 == 0' converts Phred+64 to Phred+33 on every fourth line (From reads to coverage). Shell functions: local keeps a variable inside the function; $1, $2, $3 are its arguments (bash manual). plotFingerprint samples 500 000 bins by default; bamCoverage --extendReads sets the fragment length for single-end reads.









Hint 5 — R (R1–R4)





resize(x, 1, fix = "start") is strand-aware: it gives each read’s 5’ end. countOverlaps only counts features on the same strand unless ignore.strand = TRUE (genes and reads both have a strand). tabulate counts how often each integer occurs; promoters(x, up, down) makes a window around each TSS; mean() of an RleList over a GRanges gives the mean signal per range (rtracklayer import).

title: Exercise: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Solutions
All numbers come from running the commands as written (fastp 0.23.4, bowtie2 2.4.4, samtools 1.21, bedtools 2.30, MACS3 3.1.0, deepTools 3.5.1, R 4.6 with Bioconductor 3.23).






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) \(5 \times 10^6 \times 6.6\) pg \(= 33\) µg; the input aliquot 0.33 µg. (b) \(4 \text{ ng} / 33\,000 \text{ ng} = 0.012\%\). (c) One 200-bp fragment weighs \(200 \times 650 / (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 2.2 \times 10^{-19}\) g; 0.8 ng is \(3.7 \times 10^9\) fragments. Site copies: \(40\,000 \times 2 \times 5 \times 10^6 = 4 \times 10^{11}\). So about 0.9% of all site copies were captured: crosslinking, fragmentation, antibody binding and washes each lose most of the material. (d) \(20 \text{ M} \times 0.2 / 40\,000 = 100\) reads per site on average, out of about 93 000 fragments per site in the IP: sequencing samples a tiny fraction of the library (and PCR has made copies of each molecule), which is why duplicates appear only when the number of distinct molecules is small.
B2. (a) \(Ct_\text{input,adj} = 25.0 - 6.64 = 18.36\). Site X: \(100 \times 2^{18.36 - 27.4} = 100 \times 2^{-9.04} = 0.19\%\). Negative region: \(100 \times 2^{18.36 - 32.6} = 0.0052\%\). (b) \(2^{32.6 - 27.4} = 2^{5.2} = 37\)-fold. (c) Not weak: percent input depends on the antibody and the factor, and what matters is the comparison with negative regions (37-fold here) and with a mock IP (IgG). Most of the chromatin at site X is not crosslinked to the factor, or is lost; 0.1–1% is typical for a TF.
B3. (a) \(58 + 62 = 120\) bp. The protein covers the summit: a fragment can only end outside the crosslinked protein, so 5’ ends cannot fall on the site itself, and sonication rarely breaks right next to it. (b) The exonuclease trims each fragment’s 5’ end up to the crosslinked protein: −12 and +14 are the left and right borders of the protected region, about 26 bp, the footprint of the protein (or complex) on the DNA. (c) H3K36me3 has no single site: + and − strand reads both cover the whole domain, so their distributions overlap and the shift between them is not visible; strand peaks cannot be paired (C3, R1).
B4. (a) A = CTCF (sharp, ~2 fragment lengths wide, intergenic as well as genic); B = H3K4me3 (promoter, nucleosome-scale, dip at the nucleosome-free TSS); C = H3K36me3 (gene bodies of transcribed genes, rising to the 3’ end); D = H3K27me3 (broad Polycomb domain over a silent developmental cluster). (b) A clear fragment length: A, and probably B (narrow peaks with strand separation); not C or D. ENCODE’s 45 M reads per replicate apply to broad marks: C and D. (c) The nucleosome-free region at an active TSS has no histones, so a histone mark cannot be there; the signal comes from the −1 and +1 nucleosomes.
B5. (a) Different sonication (more or stronger sonication shears open chromatin preferentially), different fixation, different cell batches and handling (nuclei preparation, chromatin release), different library protocols and read lengths (28 vs 51 bp), and depth. (b) The promoter peak has many more reads (the input there is about 10 times higher than in a gene desert), but both have the same enrichment over their local background. Equal fold enrichment does not imply equal statistical evidence: under a Poisson background model, the larger promoter counts generally give a smaller p-value at the same ChIP/input ratio. The promoter is also more vulnerable to sonication and nonspecific-binding biases, so matching inputs and antibody-specificity controls remain essential. (c) H3K4me3 sits on the nucleosomes immediately flanking the TSS (−1 and +1 and a few downstream); H3K4me1 sits further out, on nucleosomes 1–2 kb away, and is depleted where H3K4me3 is high (the same lysine cannot be both mono- and trimethylated).
B6. (a) K562 has a different karyotype (many amplifications and losses) and different open chromatin: amplified regions of GM12878 are not corrected, K562-specific open regions make GM12878 peaks there look weaker, and GM12878-specific open promoters are uncorrected. The input must come from the same chromatin. (b) With 2 M input reads the 1-kb and even the 10-kb windows contain few reads, so local estimates are noisy; MACS scales the larger library down to the smaller one and the background is often set by the genome-wide λ, which ignores local biases. Sequence the input at least as deep as the ChIP. (c) Crosslink longer (e.g. 10–15 min) and add a protein–protein crosslinker such as DSG before formaldehyde; or use an epitope tag with a validated antibody; check by ChIP-qPCR at expected sites before sequencing.
B7. (a) Hyper-ChIPable regions: highly expressed promoters and genes give ChIP signal with almost any antibody (open chromatin, high protein density, sticky). The lack of the motif and the IgG signal both point that way. (b) ChIP in cells where Z is knocked out or degraded (the peaks should disappear); a second antibody against a different epitope, or an epitope-tagged Z with a tag-only control; check whether the motif of Z is enriched in the remaining peaks after removing those shared with IgG; CUT&RUN with the same antibody (much lower background).
B8. (a) N-ChIP: histone marks survive without fixation and MNase gives clean, low-input libraries (or CUT&Tag). (b) X-ChIP: without crosslinking a short-lived TF is lost during digestion and washes. (c) N-ChIP: MNase gives mono-nucleosomes, so each read is one nucleosome. (d) X-ChIP with longer fixation and a double crosslinker: it does not bind DNA itself.
B9. Differences in crosslinking efficiency or epitope accessibility between the sites, residence time (a longer-bound site is captured more often), local shearing (open chromatin), copy number (site A amplified), mappability (part of site B in a repeat), and, at very strong sites, duplicates removed. Meaningful: the same site compared between samples processed the same way (differential binding).









Solutions — command line





C1. CTCF ChIP 390 097 reads of 36 bp, characters B…f; CTCF input 476 372 reads, up to 28 bp, C…]: both Phred+64 (no character below ;, and f would be Q69 as +33). H3K36me3 98 689 reads of 51 bp, $…A; its input 131 839 reads of 51 bp, $…?: Phred+33, from an early Illumina instrument whose qualities top out at Q27–32 (< = Q27).
C2. The four chains take about 2.5 minutes in all.

The CTCF input has the most duplicates (283 747), almost all on chrM (From reads to coverage, C5b); the CTCF ChIP has 77 450, many at strong CTCF sites. The H3K36me3 ChIP has almost none (786): its reads are spread over large domains, so two fragments rarely share a start. (b) No: chrM reads are removed when the BAM is cut to chr21, before normalisation; the chrM fraction only reflects how much mitochondrial DNA went into each input (it would matter for CPM if chrM were kept).

C3. CTCF: 359 paired peaks, predicted fragment length 100 bp, one alternative (100). H3K36me3: 305 paired peaks, predicted 246 bp, with 17 alternative lengths between 24 and 595 bp. MACS3 found “peaks” on both strands, but the shift between them is not stable: there is no well-defined fragment-length signal in a broad mark. For broad marks, set the fragment length yourself (from the sonication profile, or use paired-end data).
C4. The two inputs are closest to the diagonal; the H3K36me3 input is the flattest. CTCF bends sharply at the very end: its top 1% of bins hold 30% of the reads (input 8%). H3K36me3 bends gradually over a large part of the range: top 1% of bins only 10% of its reads, but top 10% of bins 49% (CTCF 53%, its input 32%). 44% of the H3K36me3 bins have no read at all (a sparse library). That gradual bend is the fingerprint of a broad mark.
C5. H3K36me3 is enriched over the bodies of IFNAR1, IFNGR2, TMEM50B, GART, SON and DONSON, from a little after the TSS to the 3’ end, and not between genes. In a single 50-bp bin there are only a few reads (the library has 70 741 reads on all of chr21): broad marks are visible only when you look at many kilobases at once.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) It counts the 5’ ends of + and − strand reads at every base from 13 Mb to the end of chr21 and computes, for each shift k, the Pearson correlation between + strand counts at x and − strand counts at x + k, using only the positions with a + strand read for the sum of products (the others contribute zero). The first 13 Mb are the unassembled short arm and the centromere, with no reads. Reading the BAMs and computing all four curves takes about a minute. (b) CTCF: maximum 0.152 at 93 bp, the fragment length. CTCF input: 0.0021 at 95 bp, 70 times lower: a trace of the strongest sites (open CTCF sites are over-represented in the input), but essentially flat. H3K36me3: 0.0022 at 294 bp and its input 0.0007 at 331 bp: both noise; there is no fragment-length peak. H3K36me3 is above its input at every shift because both strands fall in the same domains. (c) At the read length (row 2, k = 36) CTCF has 0.092, on the rising flank towards the fragment peak (0.15 at 100); with a fragment length close to the read length, the phantom peak is hidden in the shoulder.
R2. (a) 72 active, 107 silent, 41 in between (220 in all). (b) CTCF input: 8.4× the expected count within 500 bp of active TSSs, 0.96× at silent TSSs. H3K36me3 input: 1.06× and 0.83×. The first input is strongly biased towards open promoters, the second hardly. TSSs and genes have a strand, and so do reads; without ignore.strand = TRUE, only reads on the same strand as the gene are counted, half of them.
R3. (a) Reads (5’ ends) per kb of gene body per million reads in the library. A uniform library gives 24.9 on chr21. (b) 69 active and 49 silent genes longer than 5 kb. Active: H3K36me3 75.6, input 31.4 (2.4-fold enrichment). Silent: 23.4 and 27.4: no enrichment. The input is itself above average in active genes, so comparing the ChIP with the chromosome average would overstate the enrichment. (c) First 2 kb 30.5, last 2 kb 88.6: H3K36me3 is deposited by SETD2, which travels with the elongating RNA polymerase II, so the mark accumulates towards the 3’ end.

title: Quiz: ChIP-seq: the assay
text:
Short questions on the ChIP-seq protocol and on what its signal means. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Put the steps of a crosslinked ChIP-seq in order, and say for each which artefact it can introduce: immunoprecipitation, library PCR, sonication, formaldehyde fixation, reversal of crosslinks.






Answer





Fixation (too short: transient binders lost; too long: masked epitopes, poor shearing, indirect contacts) → sonication (breaks open chromatin more easily: promoters over-represented) → immunoprecipitation (cross-reactivity, sticky background, lot variation) → reversal of crosslinks and DNA purification (very little DNA) → library PCR (duplicates when few molecules went in).




Q2. What is an input control, and which three biases does it capture?






Answer





A sample of the same crosslinked, fragmented chromatin, taken through every step except the immunoprecipitation and sequenced. It shows the background the ChIP would have without enrichment: fragmentation bias towards open chromatin, copy number (amplified regions give more reads), and mappability/repeat artefacts (collapsed repeats, unmappable gaps). It must come from the same chromatin preparation as the ChIP.




Q3. A ChIP is made from \(2 \times 10^6\) human cells and returns 2 ng of DNA. What fraction of the chromatin DNA is that (6.6 pg per cell)?






Answer





Chromatin DNA: \(2 \times 10^6 \times 6.6\) pg \(= 13.2\) µg. \(2 / 13\,200 = 0.015\%\).




Q4. In ChIP-qPCR, 1% of the chromatin was kept as input. The input Ct is 24.0; the ChIP Ct at a bound site is 26.0. What is the percent of input?






Hint





Adjust the input Ct by \(\log_2 100 = 6.64\).









Answer





\(Ct_\text{input,adj} = 24.0 - 6.64 = 17.36\); \(100 \times 2^{17.36 - 26.0} = 100 \times 2^{-8.64} = 0.25\%\).




Q5. Sketch the expected ChIP-seq track over an actively transcribed 40-kb gene for (a) H3K4me3, (b) H3K36me3, (c) a TF bound at the promoter and at one intronic enhancer.






Answer






A 1–3 kb peak around the TSS, with a dip at the TSS itself (nucleosome-free region) and most signal on the first nucleosomes downstream. (b) A low, wide enrichment over the gene body, starting about 1 kb after the TSS and increasing towards the 3’ end, ending near the end of the gene. (c) Two narrow peaks a few hundred bp wide, one at the promoter and one at the enhancer.





Q6. Single-end reads around CTCF sites: + strand 5’ ends peak 48 bp left of the summits, − strand 5’ ends 50 bp right. What is the fragment length? Why does the same calculation fail for H3K27me3?






Answer





About 98 bp. H3K27me3 forms broad domains: + and − strand reads both cover the whole domain, so there are no separated strand peaks and the cross-correlation is flat.




Q7. Why can native ChIP (no crosslinking, MNase) map histone marks but not most transcription factors?






Answer





Nucleosomes are stable on DNA during MNase digestion and the washes, so histones and their marks are retained without fixation. Most TFs bind for seconds to minutes and are not covalently held, so they dissociate or slide during digestion and washes, and their sites are lost or blurred.




Q8. CTCF site A has twice as many reads as site B in the same ChIP. Give two reasons, other than occupancy, that could explain it.






Answer





Any two of: better crosslinking or epitope access at A; longer residence time; open chromatin at A shears more easily (more fragments); A is amplified (copy number); part of B lies in a less mappable region; duplicate removal compressing B or A differently. Compare the same site between samples instead.




Q9. An antibody against a TF gives peaks mainly at the promoters of the most highly expressed genes, without its motif. An IgG ChIP shows weaker peaks at the same places. What is going on, and what control would settle it?






Answer





“Hyper-ChIPable” regions: highly expressed genes and active promoters give signal with almost any antibody. ChIP in cells lacking the TF (knockout/degron) or with a tagged TF and a tag-only control: real binding disappears in the knockout, the artefact does not.




Q10. What does ChIP-exo add to ChIP-seq, and how?






Answer





Near base-pair resolution: a 5’→3’ exonuclease trims each crosslinked fragment up to the protein, so read starts mark the borders of the protein–DNA contact (a footprint) instead of random sonication breaks.

title: Peak calling
text:
About this lecture


MACS step by step for ChIP-seq with an input: fragment length, pileup, the local λ, Poisson p-values, q-values, peaks and summits.
What the input does, and what happens without one. Thresholds: how many peaks are real?
Broad domains: why narrow callers fail on H3K36me3, and how SICER/epic2 and --broad help.
Replicates: the IDR model in detail, pseudoreplicates and ENCODE’s peak sets.


ATAC-seq processing and peak calling introduced MACS3 and the local λ for data without a control, and the idea of IDR. Here we do ChIP-seq with an input, where the control enters the statistics, and we go into the IDR model properly. Running examples: the CTCF ChIP-seq used since From reads to coverage, now with its second replicate, and the H3K36me3 ChIP-seq from ChIP-seq: the assay, now with two replicates. Everything is on chr21 and every number on the slides comes from commands in the exercise. The figure is the plan of the lecture: the five steps of MACS, then broad marks, no control and replicates in the box at the bottom.

MACS finds strong regions, pairs a + strand pile with a − strand pile downstream, and takes their typical distance as d. Each read is then extended to d.
For broad marks the estimate is unstable: set d yourself (--nomodel --extsize 200) or use paired-end reads (-f BAMPE).


The model step of MACS (Zhang et al. 2008): it scans the genome for regions with high tag counts (by default 5 to 50 times enriched, the “model fold” in the log), keeps up to 1000 of them, finds the + and − strand tag peaks in each, and builds a histogram of the distance between them; d is its mode (MACS3 also reports the cross-correlation and “alternative” lengths). Numbers from macs3 predictd in the exercise. For CTCF the answer is stable and agrees with the strand cross-correlation from ChIP-seq: the assay (93 bp) and with ENCODE (90–95 bp). For H3K36me3 MACS still finds 305 paired peaks, but the distances are all over the place: there is no fragment-length peak in a broad mark. If the model fails completely, MACS stops with “too few paired peaks” and you have to give –nomodel –extsize. For paired-end data the fragments are measured, and none of this is needed. ENCODE’s TF pipeline takes d from the strand cross-correlation (phantompeakqualtools) and passes it to MACS2.

title: Peak calling
section: Steps 2–3: pileup and the local λ
text:
Steps 2–3: pileup and the local λ


The pileup k at a base is the number of extended ChIP fragments covering it. The expected number under background, λ, is estimated from the input in four ways: the genome-wide average λBG, and the input reads in windows of d (100 bp here), 1 kb (–slocal) and 10 kb (–llocal) around the base, each scaled to the width of one fragment. The original paper (Zhang et al. 2008) used 1, 5 and 10 kb; MACS2 and MACS3 use d, 1 kb and 10 kb. The maximum is taken. Depth: the libraries are first made comparable, by default by scaling the larger one down to the smaller one; here the ChIP has 197 587 reads and the input 116 397, so the ChIP pileup is multiplied by 0.589. This is the summit with the highest λ in our data: 13 input reads fall within 100 bp of it, a little pile of input at a strong CTCF site (input DNA is enriched at open CTCF sites, ChIP-seq: the assay). The test still gives p = 10^-59, because 182 ChIP fragments overlap that base. The exercise has you compute these numbers yourself from the input BAM, and they match MACS to the third decimal.

title: Peak calling
section: Real data: λ at 521 CTCF summits
text:
Real data: λ at 521 CTCF summits


Left: the summit of the slide before. The ChIP pileup (brown) and the local λ (blue), which rises under the peak because the input has reads there.
Right: with a shallow input (3 reads per kb), the 100-bp window sets λ at 337 of 521 summits; λBG (0.29) at only 43.


From MACS3’s own bedGraph output (–bdg: _treat_pileup.bdg and _control_lambda.bdg) and from recounting the input reads around each summit in R (exercise R1); the two agree (correlation 0.998). Away from peaks λ jumps between 0.29 (λBG), values set by the 1-kb window, and integers set by single input reads in the 100-bp window: with 116 000 input reads on 40 Mb, one input read in 100 bp is already 3.4 times λBG. That makes the background estimate noisy, and it is the reason the input should be sequenced at least as deeply as the ChIP. The λ also shows why a peak at a site where the input piles up gets a weaker p-value than the same peak in a clean region: this is the open-chromatin and copy-number correction in action.

The same 25 fragments: overwhelming against the genome average, convincing against the local input, and nothing special inside a region where the input is 10.


This is the calculation the exam asks for: choose λlocal as the maximum, then read the p-value from a table or compute it. Students do not need to compute a Poisson tail by hand beyond a few terms; they need to know which λ to use and how p changes with λ. The table values are exact upper tails (ppois in R). MACS reports −log10 p at the summit in column 8 of the narrowPeak file and the fold enrichment in column 7; for fold enrichment MACS uses (pileup + 1)/(λ + 1): at the real summit of the previous slides (107.2 + 1)/(13 + 1) = 7.73, exactly column 7. The last column of the table (λ = 10) is what happens in an amplified region or at a hyper-ChIPable promoter where the input is high: the same pileup is no longer significant. With real data, MACS also accounts for the depth scaling, so k is a fractional number; MACS rounds it up before the test.

title: Peak calling
text:
From p-values to peaks

MACS scores every base by −log10 p, and converts the scores to q-values (Benjamini–Hochberg on the p-scores of all bases, weighted by how many bases have each score).
Peak = a run of bases with q below the cutoff (default 0.05; ENCODE and this course 0.01), joined across gaps up to a read length, at least d long. Summit = the base with the highest pileup.

The q-value is computed over positions, not over peaks, so “q < 0.01” does not mean that 1% of the peaks are false; it is a convenient ranking scale. The Poisson model also ignores extra-Poisson variation (overdispersion), so p-values of MACS are too small in absolute terms; peaks are best treated as a ranked list. That is why the number of peaks depends smoothly on the cutoff and why ENCODE chooses the final set with replicates (IDR) rather than with the q-value. Numbers from the exercise: our replicate 1 against its input; the ENCODE set is the conservative IDR set from two replicates of the full data (405 peaks on chr21).

title: Peak calling
section: Real data: how many peaks are real?
text:
Real data: how many peaks are real?


Right: the fraction of peaks with a CTCF motif within 50 bp of the summit, by rank. Top 50 peaks: 90%; ranks 500–573: 43–60%; random DNA: 4%.
There is no clean break: weak peaks are a mixture of weak real sites and noise.


Peaks from the most lenient call (q < 0.1, 573 peaks) ranked by p-value, in bins of 50; motif matches with the JASPAR 2024 CTCF matrix (MA0139.2, motifmatchr, p < 10^-4) in 101 bp around each summit. The motif is an independent check, not used by the peak caller. Even the weakest bins are 10–15 times above random DNA, so most weak peaks are still real CTCF sites, but a growing fraction is noise or indirect. The red line marks q < 0.01, our standard cutoff (521 peaks, 72% with the motif). Left: fewer peaks at stricter cutoffs, and almost all strict peaks are also in ENCODE’s set. Motif enrichment is a good validation for a TF with a strong motif; for histone marks there is no such check, and replicates are the only internal validation.

title: Peak calling
section: What the input does: CTCF without a control
text:
What the input does: CTCF without a control


Without input: 816 peaks instead of 521. The 299 extra peaks: 36% with a CTCF motif, 9% in ENCODE’s set.
No input means λ from the ChIP itself (λBG and its 10-kb window): no correction for open chromatin, copy number or input pile-ups.


Exercise C4 and R3. Without a control, MACS3 uses the ChIP’s own genome-wide λ and its 10-kb window (a 1-kb window of the ChIP would contain the peak). It finds more peaks: 403 of ENCODE’s 405 (vs 377 with the input), but also 299 that the input-based call rejects, and only 36% of those carry a motif. Some extras are real weak CTCF sites that the conservative λd (a single input read in 100 bp) suppressed; many are not. For CTCF in a near-diploid cell line the damage is modest, because CTCF peaks are strong; for a weaker factor or a cancer cell line with amplifications, missing input produces many false peaks at open promoters and amplified regions. ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag routinely run without input (Experimental design and QC): for ATAC, there is no sensible control; for CUT&Tag, the background is very low.

title: Peak calling
section: Broad marks need a different caller
text:
Broad marks need a different caller


A narrow-peak caller asks, base by base, “is this position much higher than background?” In a broad domain the answer is usually no: H3K36me3 spreads its reads over tens of kilobases, so each base is only slightly enriched. Broad callers pool evidence across windows. SICER (Zang et al. 2009) divides the genome into 200-bp windows, marks windows above a lenient threshold, joins them into “islands” if separated by at most a few windows (the gap), scores each island as a whole and compares it with the control; epic2 (Stovner and Sætrom 2019) is a fast reimplementation. MACS3 –broad does a two-level call: strong regions at the usual cutoff are linked by weaker regions above –broad-cutoff. Other approaches: hidden Markov models (e.g. hiddenDomains, or chromatin-state models in Chromatin states), and simply counting reads in fixed large windows or in gene bodies. ENCODE’s histone pipeline calls MACS2 narrow peaks at a lenient threshold and keeps those that are replicated or pseudoreplicated, which works for the narrower marks better than for broad ones.

title: Peak calling
section: Real data: H3K36me3 with three callers
text:
Real data: H3K36me3 with three callers


Same reads (2 replicates, 170 000 reads on chr21), same input. MACS3 narrow: 11 peaks on all of chr21 (2.8 kb). MACS3 –broad: 123 regions (48 kb). epic2: 671 domains, 3.8 Mb, up to 84 kb long.


Exercise C5. The domains are obvious by eye in 1-kb bins, but no single base passes a strict test: this library is sparse (about 2 reads per kb on average) and the enrichment over input is about 2.4-fold. The narrow call finds 11 peaks on the whole chromosome; –broad finds slightly more, as fragments of domains; epic2 joins 200-bp windows across gaps of up to 600 bp and finds the domains over IFNAR1, IFNGR2/TMEM50B and GART/SON/DONSON. All runs used –nomodel –extsize 200 (MACS) or –fragment-size 200 (epic2), because the fragment length cannot be estimated for this mark. With deeper data (ENCODE recommends 45 M reads for broad marks), MACS –broad does much better; with sparse data, pooling windows is what makes calling possible.

title: Peak calling
section: Real data: do the domains cover the right genes?
text:
Real data: do the domains cover the right genes?





epic2 domains cover 58% of the bases of active gene bodies, but only 6.7% of silent ones.
59% of all epic2 domain bases lie in active gene bodies (genes > 5 kb).
A biological check without a gold standard: H3K36me3 should follow transcription.



Active and silent genes as in ChIP-seq: the assay (H3K4me3 fold change at the TSS above 5 or below 1; 69 and 49 protein-coding genes longer than 5 kb). MACS narrow and –broad cover less than 1% of active gene bodies. The 6.7% of silent gene bodies covered by epic2 is a mixture of false positives, genes that are transcribed without a strong H3K4me3 peak, and domains extending from neighbouring active genes. For broad marks there is no motif to check, so biology (transcribed genes for H3K36me3, Polycomb targets for H3K27me3) and replicates are the validation. Note the trade-off: bigger gaps and lower window thresholds give longer domains, which merge neighbouring genes; the parameters should be chosen with the biology in mind and reported.

title: Peak calling
text:
Reproducibility: the IDR model


ATAC-seq processing and peak calling introduced IDR with a simple rank-consistency curve; here is the model itself (Li, Brown, Huang and Bickel 2011). Input: the two replicates’ lenient peak lists, matched by overlap, each peak with a score (MACS p-value). Only the ranks are used, so differences in depth or signal-to-noise between replicates do not matter. The ranks are mapped to a latent scale (a copula), where the model is a mixture of two components: reproducible peaks, whose latent scores are correlated between replicates (ρ) and shifted upwards (μ, σ), with proportion π; and irreproducible peaks, independent between replicates. The parameters are fitted by EM. Each peak gets a local idr, the posterior probability that it belongs to the irreproducible component; the IDR of a set of peaks is the average local idr of the peaks in it, taken from the most reproducible down, so it is an expected fraction of irreproducible peaks, analogous to a q-value. The input must contain noise: run it on lenient calls (p < 0.01, up to 300 000 peaks genome-wide in ENCODE), never on peaks already thresholded at q < 0.01.

title: Peak calling
section: Real data: IDR on two CTCF replicates
text:
Real data: IDR on two CTCF replicates


763 and 570 lenient peaks; 472 matched; 291 pass IDR < 0.05. Fitted: μ = 1.95, σ = 0.56, ρ = 0.79, π = 0.60.
281 of our 291 IDR peaks are in ENCODE’s conservative set (405 on chr21, from deeper data).


Exercise C6 and R4: idr 2.0 with –rank p.value, the pooled peaks as the peak list (as in ENCODE) and –use-best-multisummit-IDR. Left: ranks of the matched peaks in the two replicates; green = IDR < 0.05. The strong peaks agree; from rank ~300 down, the ranks become unrelated. Replicate 2 is the weaker library (120 076 reads after filtering, with 61% of its reads flagged as duplicates), so it limits how far down the list we can go. Right: the IDR curve stays near zero for the first ~250 peaks and then rises steeply; the cutoff at 0.05 falls at 291. ENCODE’s conservative set has more peaks because it was called on the whole genome with the full reads. 283 of ENCODE’s 405 chr21 peaks are recovered; most of the rest are weaker peaks that our shallow replicate 2 cannot support.

title: Peak calling
text:
ENCODE’s reproducibility workflow


Pseudoreplicates are random halves of the reads: they differ only by sampling, so IDR between them tells you how many peaks the data could support if the replicates were perfect copies. Np (pooled pseudoreplicates) close to Nt (true replicates) means the true replicates are as consistent as random halves: rescue ratio 1.14 here. N1 and N2 (self-pseudoreplicates of each replicate) measure each replicate’s own strength; their ratio of 1.83 shows that replicate 2 supports far fewer peaks than replicate 1, close to ENCODE’s limit of 2. ENCODE flags an experiment if either ratio exceeds 2. The released sets: “conservative” = the Nt peaks from true replicates; “optimal” = the larger of the Nt and Np sets (here the Np set). Experimental design and QC introduced the ratios; here they are computed on real data. With only one replicate, pseudoreplicates can still give a reproducibility-filtered set, but they say nothing about biological variation.

production




Benchmark papers (e.g. Thomas et al. 2016; Wilbanks and Facciotti 2010) find that callers agree on the strong peaks and differ on the weak ones, and that the choice of thresholds and controls matters more than the choice of tool. nf-core/chipseq runs MACS2 with narrow or broad mode per antibody and a consensus across replicates; the ENCODE TF pipeline runs SPP or MACS2 with IDR and the histone pipeline MACS2 with replicated/pseudoreplicated peaks. SEACR is in CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag.

title: Peak calling
text:
Summary







step
key fact




fragment length
MACS pairs + and − strand peaks; d ≈ 100 bp for our CTCF; unstable for broad marks: set it


pileup
extended fragments over each base; the larger library is scaled to the smaller


local λ
\max(\lambda_\text{BG}, \lambda_d, \lambda_\text{1k}, \lambda_\text{10k}) from the input, each scaled to d


test
p = P(X \ge k), Poisson(λlocal); q-values by BH over bases; peaks = runs below the cutoff


thresholds
no natural cutoff; motif fraction falls with rank; use replicates to decide


input
removes open-chromatin, copy-number and pile-up artefacts; without it: more, less specific peaks


broad marks
pool windows (SICER/epic2, --broad); validate with biology


IDR
ranks only; mixture of reproducible and independent components; lenient input; IDR < 0.05


ENCODE sets
Nt, Np, N1, N2; rescue and self-consistency ratios < 2




Students should be able to choose λlocal and compute a Poisson tail from a table, explain depth scaling, say what the input does and what happens without it, explain why narrow callers fail on broad marks and what a broad caller does instead, describe the IDR model in words and compute the ENCODE ratios. Next: Annotation and differential binding, where peaks are annotated and compared between cell types.

title: Peak calling
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Zhang et al. 2008, Genome Biol. Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS). The fragment model and the local λ.
Zang et al. 2009, Bioinformatics. A clustering approach for identification of enriched domains from histone modification ChIP-Seq data. SICER: windows joined into islands.
Stovner & Sætrom 2019, Bioinformatics. epic2 efficiently finds diffuse domains in ChIP-seq data. The broad caller used here.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments. IDR.
Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia. IDR, pseudoreplicates and the ratios in practice.
Thomas, Thomas, Holloway & Pollard 2016, Brief Bioinform. Features that define the best ChIP-seq peak calling algorithms. A benchmark of callers.

Fold change over input. ENCODE signal tracks give, at each position, how many times more ChIP reads there are than in the input control (normalised to depth). 1 means no enrichment; values below 1 mean fewer reads than input.
CpG observed/expected for a sequence of length \(L\):
\[\text{CpG o/e} = \frac{\text{number of CpG}}{(\text{number of C}) \times (\text{number of G}) / L}\]
The denominator is the number of CpGs expected if C and G were placed independently. A CpG island (Gardiner-Garden & Frommer) is at least 200 bp with GC content above 50% and CpG o/e above 0.6.

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
By hand
B1. Counting nucleosomes.

The nucleosome repeat length is 190 bp, of which 147 bp are wrapped around the octamer. How long is the linker?
How many nucleosomes are there in a diploid human cell (\(6.4 \times 10^9\) bp)? How many histone H3 molecules?
A promoter has a nucleosome-depleted region of 200 bp. How many nucleosomes would fit there at the normal repeat?

B2. The ladder. Chromatin is digested lightly with MNase. With a repeat of 190 bp and a core of 147 bp, which fragment sizes do you expect for mono-, di- and tri-nucleosomes if the enzyme trims the linker completely? And if it cuts in the middle of each linker? Sketch the gel.
B3. Names. Write out in words: (a) H4K16ac, (b) H3K9me2, (c) H3S10ph, (d) H2AK119ub1. (e) Can one H3 tail carry both H3K27ac and H3K27me3? Can one nucleosome carry H3K4me3 and H3K27me3?
B4. Predict the marks. For each element, say which of the six marks you expect to be high (H) or low (L):

The promoter of a highly expressed housekeeping gene.
The body of the same gene.
A primed enhancer that is not (yet) active.
An active enhancer.
The promoter of a HOX gene in a blood cell.
A zinc-finger gene cluster on chr19.

B5. Read the tracks. Look at the figures Real data: an active gene in B cells and Real data: two kinds of silence in the lecture.

CD74 is on the − strand. Where is its TSS on the plot, and which marks peak there?
In which direction does the H3K36me3 signal over CD74 increase, and why?
The HOXD cluster: name one mark that is high and one that is low over the whole cluster. Is this region open or closed chromatin?
ZNF100 carries H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 over the same body. Why is this unusual?

B6. Dilution through replication.

A domain of 40 nucleosomes is fully marked with H3K27me3. Replication splits old histones randomly between the daughters, and the cell has no way to re-mark. What fraction of the nucleosomes in the domain is marked after 1, 2 and 5 divisions?
DNA methylation is copied by DNMT1 with a maintenance fidelity of about 99.9% per CpG per division (a site is lost with probability 0.001). What fraction of the methylated CpGs is still methylated after 50 divisions? Compare with (a).

B7. CpG o/e by hand. Compute GC content and CpG o/e for these two 20 bp sequences, and decide which is more CpG-island-like:
S1: ACGCGTTCGACGCGGCCGTA
S2: ATGCATTGCAAGTCCATGCA
B8. Cause or consequence? A paper shows that genes with high H3K36me3 are highly expressed and concludes that “H3K36me3 activates transcription”. Give an alternative explanation, and propose one experiment that could tell the two apart.

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
section: Explore: read–write feedback and memory through replication
text:
Explore: read–write feedback and memory through replication
The demo simulates 150 cells, each with a Polycomb domain of 60 nucleosomes that are marked (H3K27me3) or unmarked, in the spirit of Dodd et al. 2007 (Cell, doi:10.1016/j.cell.2007.02.053). A marked nucleosome loses its mark at the turnover rate. An unmarked nucleosome is marked at a rate set by the read–write feedback and by how many of its neighbours within the recruitment range are marked (the rate grows with the square of the marked fraction, because PRC2 is activated by H3K27me3; a linear loop does not give a stable switch). At every replication each marked nucleosome goes to the followed daughter with probability ½ and is otherwise replaced by a new, unmarked histone (B6). A nucleation pulse (think of the cold that silences FLC in vernalisation) marks the six central nucleosomes for the chosen time. Panel (a) shows four cells as kymographs (time to the right, nucleosomes as rows, ▼ = replication), (b) the fraction marked over time, (c) how many cells end up silenced. A simplification: nothing opposes marking outside the domain (in cells, transcription and active marks do).



E1. Start with strong feedback, start silenced. What happens to a cell’s domain at each replication, and how long does it take to recover? What fraction of the domain stays marked, and how many cells are still silenced at the end? Then click weak feedback, start silenced. Compare with B6(a).
E2. Click weak feedback, no division. How many cells keep the mark now? Go back to strong feedback, start silenced and lower the feedback step by step (1.2, 1.1, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8). Where is memory lost? At feedback 1.0, set replication to every 12 h. What does this say about histone-based memory in fast-dividing cells?
E3. Click 2 days of cold: all cells start unmarked and the nucleation region is marked during the pulse. Look at the four kymographs and the histogram in (c). Is a cell partly silenced, or silenced or not? Set the pulse to 12, 24, 48, 96 and 168 h and note the % silenced each time. How does this explain vernalisation, where the longer the winter, the more FLC is silenced?
E4. With 1 week of cold, set the feedback to 0.6. What is left after the cold? Then return to 2 days of cold and set the recruitment range to “all” (any nucleosome can recruit any other). Why do fewer cells switch?






Solutions





E1. At each replication about half of the marks are lost at once (a light vertical stripe in the kymograph, a drop to about 40–45% in the single-cell curves), and the read–write loop re-marks the gaps within a few hours. The domain stays about 84% marked (turnover keeps it below 100%), and all 150 cells are still silenced at 480 h. With weak feedback (0.6 per hour) the loop cannot restore the mark between divisions: the mean is 21% at 96 h and 0 at the end, 0% silenced. Without any re-marking, B6(a) gives \((1/2)^n\), 3% after 5 divisions; weak feedback only slows the loss.
E2. Without division, the same weak feedback keeps 74% of the cells silenced (60% of the domain marked on average, a broad spread between cells). Replication is the hard part: the mark must be rebuilt from a 50% template every cycle. With division every 22 h, the % of cells silenced at the end is 100% at feedback 1.2 and 1.1, 95% at 1.0, 83% at 0.9, 32% at 0.8 and 0% at 0.6. At feedback 1.0 and replication every 12 h only 38% stay silenced. The faster the cells divide, the stronger the feedback must be; this is one reason why histone-based memory is debated, while DNA methylation, copied site by site by DNMT1, is the textbook memory mark.
E3. Each cell is either silenced (70–90% marked) or not (0%): in (c), 44 cells sit at 0 and 106 at 70% or more, none in between (71% silenced). Silenced: 30% after 12 h, 48% after 24 h, 71% after 48 h, 94% after 96 h, 99% after 168 h. A cell switches when the nucleation region happens to collect enough marks for the feedback to take over; a longer pulse gives more chances. So the fraction of cells switched grows with the length of the cold, while each cell is all-or-none, which is how Angel et al. 2011 (doi:10.1038/nature10241) explained quantitative vernalisation: a Polycomb-based switch that flips independently in each cell.
E4. With feedback 0.6 even a week of cold leaves nothing: 6% of the domain is marked at the end of the cold and 0% of cells are silenced at 480 h. Nucleation without the read–write loop leaves no memory. With recruitment from the whole domain, the few marks in the nucleation region are diluted among 59 unmarked nucleosomes, so the local density stays low and (with the squared rate) the loop does not start: only 7% of cells switch, against 71% with ±4. Local spreading from a nucleation site, then maintenance, is the picture for FLC and for Polycomb response elements in flies.

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
In R
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Biostrings)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
bw <- function(m) file.path(D, sprintf("gm12878_%s_fc.bigWig", tolower(m)))
marks <- c("H3K4me3", "H3K4me1", "H3K27ac", "H3K36me3", "H3K27me3", "H3K9me3")
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
genes <- gtf[gtf$type == "gene" & gtf$gene_type == "protein_coding"]
names(genes) <- genes$gene_name

R1 — Your own browser view
plot_tracks <- function(region) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(length(marks), 1), mar = c(1, 6, 0.5, 1), las = 1)
  for (m in marks) {
    s <- import(bw(m), which = region, as = "RleList")[[as.character(seqnames(region))]]
    v <- as.numeric(s[start(region):end(region)])
    plot(start(region):end(region), v, type = "h", col = "grey30", xaxt = "n",
         xlab = "", ylab = m, ylim = c(0, max(5, max(v))))
  }
  par(op)
}
plot_tracks(genes["CD79A"] + 10000)     # the gene plus 10 kb on each side

Plot CD79A (a B-cell receptor gene). Which state is it in?
Plot ALB (albumin, made in the liver) and HOXD10. Describe each in one sentence.
Pick any gene you like and predict its state before you plot it.



R2 — A table of states
mean_signal <- function(m, regions) {
  s <- import(bw(m), which = regions, as = "RleList")
  sapply(seq_along(regions), function(i) {
    r <- regions[i]; mean(s[[as.character(seqnames(r))]][start(r):end(r)])
  })
}
pick <- c("CD74", "CD79A", "PAX5", "MS4A1", "GAPDH", "ACTB",
          "ALB", "NEUROD1", "HOXD10", "HOXD13", "ZNF43", "ZNF208")
g    <- genes[pick]
prom <- promoters(g, upstream = 1000, downstream = 1000)
tab <- data.frame(row.names = pick,
  K4me3_prom  = mean_signal("H3K4me3",  prom),
  K27ac_prom  = mean_signal("H3K27ac",  prom),
  K36me3_body = mean_signal("H3K36me3", g),
  K27me3_body = mean_signal("H3K27me3", g),
  K9me3_body  = mean_signal("H3K9me3",  g))
round(tab, 1)

Classify each gene as active, Polycomb-silenced, H3K9me3-marked or silent without a strong repressive mark. Which B-cell genes are active?
ACTB (β-actin) is one of the most highly expressed genes in every cell, yet its promoter looks silent in the table. Find out why: look at its transcripts and their start sites, and compute H3K4me3 at each.

actb <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$gene_name == "ACTB"]
at   <- unique(resize(actb, width = 1, fix = "start"))
data.frame(tss = start(at), H3K4me3 = round(mean_signal("H3K4me3", promoters(at, 1000, 1000)), 1))
granges(genes["ACTB"])

ALB and NEUROD1 are silent in B cells, but have little H3K27me3 compared with HOXD10. What does that say about how genes are kept off?



R3 — An average profile around TSSs
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start"))
win <- promoters(tss, upstream = 5000, downstream = 5001)     # 10 001 bp, TSS in the middle
profile <- function(m) {
  s <- import(bw(m), which = reduce(win), as = "RleList")$chr21
  mat <- t(sapply(seq_along(win), function(i) {
    v <- as.numeric(s[start(win)[i]:end(win)[i]])
    if (as.character(strand(win)[i]) == "-") rev(v) else v     # orient all genes left to right
  }))
  colMeans(mat)
}
pr  <- sapply(c("H3K4me3", "H3K27ac", "H3K4me1", "H3K36me3", "H3K27me3"), profile)
pos <- -5000:5000
matplot(pos, pr, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, xlab = "distance to TSS (bp)", ylab = "mean fold change")
legend("topright", colnames(pr), col = 1:5, lty = 1, lwd = 2)
pos[which.max(pr[, "H3K4me3"])]

Why does the code reverse the signal for − strand transcripts?
Where is the maximum of H3K4me3: upstream or downstream of the TSS, and by how much? Which nucleosome sits there?
Look at the signal exactly at the TSS (pr[pos == 0, ]) compared with ±500 bp. What do you see, and why?
Describe H3K4me1 and H3K36me3 around the TSS. Do they match the figure The marks you will meet in this course?



R4 — CpG islands and H3K4me3
chr21 <- readDNAStringSet(file.path(D, "hg38_chr21.fa.gz"))[[1]]
cpg_oe <- function(x) {
  f <- as.numeric(letterFrequency(x, c("A", "C", "G", "T")))    # A, C, G, T counts
  as.numeric(countPattern("CG", x)) * sum(f) / (f[2] * f[3])
}
cpg_oe(chr21)

pw   <- promoters(tss, upstream = 500, downstream = 500)
seqs <- DNAStringSet(Views(chr21, start = start(pw), end = end(pw)))
oe   <- sapply(seqs, cpg_oe)
gc   <- letterFrequency(seqs, "GC", as.prob = TRUE)[, 1]
cgi  <- oe > 0.6 & gc > 0.5
k4   <- mean_signal("H3K4me3", pw)
table(cgi)
tapply(k4, cgi, median)
boxplot(k4 + 0.1 ~ cgi, log = "y", names = c("low CpG", "CpG-island-like"), ylab = "H3K4me3 fold change + 0.1")

What is the CpG o/e of the whole of chr21? Why is it so far below 1?
What fraction of chr21 protein-coding promoters is CpG-island-like?
Compare H3K4me3 at CpG-island-like and low-CpG promoters. Suggest a mechanism (hint: proteins with a CXXC domain bind unmethylated CpG).

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — nucleosome arithmetic (B1, B2)





Linker = repeat − core. Each nucleosome has two copies of each core histone. If the linker is trimmed away, an \(n\)-nucleosome fragment is \(n\) cores plus \(n-1\) linkers; if the cut is in the middle of each linker, it is \(n\) repeat lengths.









Hint 2 — names and marks (B3, B4)





The pattern is histone – residue (one-letter code) – position – modification. K = lysine, S = serine; me = methyl, ac = acetyl, ph = phosphate, ub = ubiquitin. One residue holds one kind of modification at a time; a nucleosome has two copies of H3.









Hint 3 — dilution (B6)





Without re-marking, each division halves the marked fraction: \(0.5^n\). For DNA methylation each site survives one division with probability \(0.999\), so \(0.999^{50}\) after 50.









Hint 4 — CpG o/e (B7, R4)





Count C, G and the dinucleotide CG (read along one strand; overlapping counts like CGCG contain 2 CpGs). Expected CpG = C × G / L. letterFrequency and countPattern do the counting in R.









Hint 5 — reading bigWigs (R1–R3)





import with which = reads only the regions you ask for; as = "RleList" returns one run-length vector per chromosome, which you index by position. promoters and resize respect strand. For ACTB (R2b), compare the gene’s coordinates with the starts of its transcripts.

Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) \(190 - 147 = 43\) bp. (b) \(6.4 \times 10^9 / 190 \approx 3.4 \times 10^7\) nucleosomes, each with 2 H3: about \(6.7 \times 10^7\) H3 molecules (plus the replication-independent variant H3.3). (c) About one (\(200 / 190\)): an NDR is the gap left by one or two missing nucleosomes.
B2. Linker trimmed away: \(147\), \(2 \times 147 + 43 = 337\), \(3 \times 147 + 2 \times 43 = 527\) bp. Cut in the middle of each linker: \(190\), \(380\), \(570\) bp. Real digests lie in between, so bands are fuzzy: about 150, 350, 550 bp. The ladder steps by the repeat length in both cases.
B3. (a) Histone H4, lysine 16, acetylated. (b) Histone H3, lysine 9, di-methylated. (c) Histone H3, serine 10, phosphorylated (a mitotic mark). (d) Histone H2A, lysine 119, mono-ubiquitylated (written by Polycomb PRC1). (e) Not on the same tail: lysine 27 carries either an acetyl or methyl groups. But a nucleosome has two H3 tails, and H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 can sit on the same nucleosome: these bivalent promoters are common in embryonic stem cells, at developmental genes that are silent but ready.

(b) It increases towards the 3’ end, i.e. towards the left for this − strand gene: SETD2 travels with RNA polymerase II, and more of the gene has been transcribed towards the 3’ end. (c) H3K27me3 is high over the whole cluster; H3K27ac and H3K36me3 are low. Closed, Polycomb-repressed chromatin. (d) H3K36me3 means active transcription, H3K9me3 means heterochromatin: usually exclusive. ZNF genes are the exception: KRAB zinc-finger genes carry both over their 3’ exons, which contain repeat-like zinc-finger motifs.
B6. (a) \(0.5\), \(0.25\), \(0.5^5 \approx 0.03\). Without re-marking, a histone domain is gone within a few divisions. (b) \(0.999^{50} \approx 0.95\). DNA methylation is copied site by site and survives many divisions; histone memory needs read–write feedback to restore the half that is lost at every division.

The ACTB gene in GENCODE runs from 5 526 409 to 5 563 902 on the − strand, so its “start” (the TSS used by promoters(gene)) is 5 563 902. That belongs to one long, rare transcript. The main ACTB transcripts start at about 5 530 601, where H3K4me3 is about 6. Lesson: promoters() on a gene uses the outermost transcript start, which is often not the main promoter. Use transcript start sites (as in Genomic intervals).
Silence does not always need a repressive mark. ALB is simply never switched on in B cells: no activators bind its liver enhancers, so it has no active marks, but no Polycomb either. Polycomb (H3K27me3) is concentrated on developmental regulators such as HOX genes, which must be kept firmly off, often CpG-island genes.
