The TSS sits in the nucleosome-depleted region: no nucleosome, no histone mark. (d) H3K4me1 has a minimum near the TSS and is higher on the flanks (1.8 at −1 kb, 1.5 at +2 kb): it flanks promoters, as in the figure. H3K36me3 is lowest just downstream of the TSS and rises into the gene body (1.4 at +5 kb), but stays low upstream.
R4. (a) 0.275: chr21 has about a quarter of the CpGs expected from its C and G content. Methylated CpGs mutate to TpG/CpA by deamination, so CpGs are lost over evolutionary time. (b) 365 of 602 TSSs (61%) are CpG-island-like. (c) Median H3K4me3 fold change 6.1 at CpG-island-like promoters, 0.6 at the others; 63% vs 11% have H3K4me3 above 5. CXXC-domain proteins (CFP1, part of the SET1 complex that writes H3K4me3; also KDM2A/B) bind unmethylated CpG and bring H3K4 methylation to CpG islands. This is one reason why CpG islands are marked as promoters even when the gene is expressed at a low level.

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
Where this leads

Gene regulation explains how transcription factors open the nucleosome-depleted regions you saw in R3.
Genomic intervals and From reads to coverage explain how the bigWigs and peaks used here are made.
The ChIP-seq block maps these marks yourself, including broad domains like the HOXD H3K27me3 domain.
DNA methylation biology returns to CpG islands, maintenance methylation (B6) and imprinting.

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Luger et al. 1997, Nature. Crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle at 2.8 Å resolution.
Kornberg 1974, Science. Chromatin structure: a repeating unit of histones and DNA.
Strahl & Allis 2000, Nature. The language of covalent histone modifications.
Barski et al. 2007, Cell. High-resolution profiling of histone methylations in the human genome.
Bird 2007, Nature. Perceptions of epigenetics.
Allis & Jenuwein 2016, Nat Rev Genet. The molecular hallmarks of epigenetic control.

title: Quiz: what is epigenetics?
text:
Short questions on chromatin, histone marks and DNA methylation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Give the narrow (classical) definition of an epigenetic change. Is a histone mark that is put back by transcription factors every time the cell divides “epigenetic” in this sense?






Answer





A mitotically and/or meiotically heritable change in gene function that cannot be explained by a change in DNA sequence (Riggs et al. 1996). A mark that is simply rebuilt by transcription factors after each division is not self-perpetuating, so it is not epigenetic in the narrow sense; the information is carried by the transcription factors. In the broad sense used by “epigenomics” it would still be called epigenetic.




Q2. What is H3K27ac? Where in the genome do you find it, and what does it tell you?






Answer





Histone H3, lysine 27, acetylated. It sits at active promoters and enhancers and marks them as active (as opposed to primed or poised). It is written by p300/CBP and read by bromodomain proteins such as BRD4.




Q3. An MNase digest of chromatin gives bands at about 150, 350 and 550 bp. What are they, and what is the nucleosome repeat length?






Answer





Mono-, di- and tri-nucleosomes: MNase cuts only the linker DNA between nucleosomes. The steps between bands give the repeat length, about 200 bp here (147 bp core + linker).




Q4. A gene has a sharp H3K4me3 peak at its TSS and H3K36me3 over its body. A second gene is covered by a 100 kb domain of H3K27me3. Describe the state of each.






Answer





The first is actively transcribed: H3K4me3 marks its active promoter and H3K36me3 is laid down by SETD2 travelling with the elongating polymerase. The second is silenced by Polycomb (facultative heterochromatin), typical for developmental regulators such as HOX genes in a cell type where they are not needed.




Q5. What is the difference between constitutive and facultative heterochromatin? Give the mark of each.






Answer





Constitutive heterochromatin is compact in every cell type (repeats, pericentromeres, telomeres) and carries H3K9me3, read by HP1. Facultative heterochromatin is silent in some cell types but active in others (developmental genes, the inactive X) and carries H3K27me3, written by Polycomb PRC2.




Q6. Explain how a pattern of CpG methylation is copied when the DNA is replicated.






Hint





What does a CpG look like just after the replication fork has passed?









Answer





CpG is palindromic, so both strands are methylated. After replication each daughter duplex has a methylated old strand and an unmethylated new strand: the CpG is hemimethylated. UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated CpGs and recruits DNMT1, which methylates the new strand. The pattern is copied site by site.




Q7. Why does a histone mark need a “read–write” mechanism to survive many cell divisions, while DNA methylation does not need one in the same way?






Answer





At replication the old, marked histones are split randomly between the two daughters and new unmarked histones fill the gaps, so each daughter inherits only about half of the marks; without re-marking the mark halves at every division (\(0.5^n\)). A writer that is activated by its own mark (PRC2 binding H3K27me3) restores the mark on the new neighbours. DNA methylation is copied from a template at each site by DNMT1, so it is kept directly.




Q8. The human genome has a CpG observed/expected ratio of about 0.25. Why so low, and why are CpG islands an exception?






Answer





Methylated cytosine deaminates spontaneously to thymine, and the resulting T:G mismatch is often repaired the wrong way, so methylated CpGs turn into TpG/CpA over evolutionary time. CpG islands are kept unmethylated (mostly at promoters), so they are not lost and keep a high CpG density (o/e above 0.6).




Q9. In GM12878 B cells the ALB (albumin) gene has no active marks and almost no H3K27me3. HOXD10 has no active marks and a lot of H3K27me3. Both are silent. What is the difference?






Answer





ALB is silent because the activators it needs (liver transcription factors) are absent: nothing opens or marks it. HOXD10 is actively kept silent by Polycomb, a system that represses developmental regulators that must stay firmly off in this cell type. Silence does not always need a repressive mark.




Q10. Genes with high H3K36me3 are highly expressed. Does H3K36me3 activate transcription? How could you test it?






Answer





Not necessarily: H3K36me3 is deposited by SETD2, which travels with the elongating polymerase, so expression causes the mark (reverse causation). Tests: block transcription and see whether the mark disappears; remove the writer (SETD2 knockout) or mutate the residue (H3K36M or K36R) and see whether expression changes.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
About this lecture
Each histone-mark track answers one question (“is there H3K4me1 here?”). The genome’s regulatory elements are defined by combinations of marks. This lecture turns six tracks into one annotation: a chromatin state for every 200 bp.

The combinatorial idea: which combinations mean promoter, enhancer, transcribed, repressed.
Binarisation: a Poisson test per 200-bp bin turns read counts into present/absent.
ChromHMM, a hidden Markov model: emission and transition matrices, learning, decoding, choosing the number of states, naming states by their enrichments.
Reference epigenomes: Roadmap/ENCODE 15- and 18-state models; Segway briefly; what states are used for.
Running example: GM12878, six ENCODE marks + input, chr21, our own ChromHMM model compared with the published Roadmap one.


The marks were introduced in What is epigenetics? Chromatin, nucleosomes, histone marks, DNA methylation, and the elements (promoters, enhancers, insulators) in Promoters, enhancers, insulators, transcription factors. Here we ask how to read six tracks together, systematically, for the whole genome. Students have not met hidden Markov models before; we build one from scratch with a toy example, and the exam questions are of that size (a forward or Viterbi step by hand, an emission product, reading an emission matrix). The running example uses ENCODE’s filtered alignments of the six GM12878 marks of the Roadmap 18-state model (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3, Bernstein lab), replicate 1, plus the input, restricted to chr21. Every number comes from the exercise commands.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: One mark is ambiguous; combinations are not
text:
One mark is ambiguous; combinations are not


H3K4me1 alone: a primed or weak enhancer. + H3K27ac: an active enhancer. H3K4me3 + H3K27ac: an active promoter. H3K4me3 + H3K27me3: a bivalent promoter.
Six marks, present/absent: 26 = 64 combinations, but a handful dominate the genome.


This is the observation behind chromatin states (Ernst & Kellis 2010; Ernst et al. 2011). Each row is a type of element defined by marks; the names on the right are the mnemonics of the Roadmap 18-state model, which we meet again at the end. Two points to stress. First, the same mark appears in several rows: H3K4me1 is at enhancers and at the flanks of promoters; H3K27ac at both active promoters and active enhancers; H3K36me3 in transcribed gene bodies and, together with H3K9me3, over zinc-finger gene clusters. Only the combination is specific. Second, absence is information too: most of the genome carries none of these marks (“quiescent”), and a model must have a state for it. The pale circles mean the mark is often but not always present in bins of that state.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Real data: six marks, one locus
text:
Real data: six marks, one locus


GM12878, ENCODE fold change over input. Below: our binarised marks (200-bp bins) and the states learned in this lecture.
Interferon-receptor genes (chr21:33.25–33.55 Mb): promoters (red), flanks and enhancers (orange, yellow), transcribed bodies (green); our 8 states and Roadmap’s 18 agree on the main pattern.


The same locus as the CUT&Tag tracks in CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag, now in GM12878. Top: ENCODE fold change over input for the six marks (the bigWigs of What is epigenetics?). Middle: the binarised calls in 200-bp bins (exercise C1). Bottom: our 8-state segmentation and the Roadmap 18-state segmentation of the same cell line (E116), with Roadmap’s colours (red promoters, orange flanks, yellow enhancers, green transcription, grey Polycomb, white/pale quiescent). Walk along it: IFNAR2, IL10RB, IFNAR1 and IFNGR2 are expressed; each has a red TSS state, orange/yellow flanks, and a green body where H3K36me3 is called. Note that H3K36me3 is called in scattered bins along gene bodies, not continuously: the broad marks are sparse after binarisation, and the HMM’s transitions fill in the gaps. Point out the gaps between genes, where both models say quiescent.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Why a model, not rules?

Rules (“H3K4me3 and H3K27ac → promoter”) need thresholds for every mark and break on noise: one missing bin splits an element in two.
Real elements are wider than a bin and come in typical neighbourhoods (promoter → flanking → transcribed).
A probabilistic model learns, from the data, (1) which mark combinations occur and (2) which ones follow each other along the genome.


Without a model you could cluster bins by their mark vector (k-means on binary vectors) and get much of the way: the emission part of ChromHMM is in effect a clustering of bins. What the HMM adds is the spatial part: a bin’s state also depends on its neighbours, so a single bin where a mark was missed by chance does not change the annotation. It also gives probabilities rather than hard calls. ChromHMM is unsupervised: no element types are given; they are named afterwards by looking at the learned parameters and at enrichments. This is the same logic as clustering cells in single-cell RNA-seq and naming the clusters by marker genes, which some students will know.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Step 1: bins and a Poisson threshold
text:
Step 1: bins and a Poisson threshold


The genome is cut into 200-bp bins; each read is placed by its 5′ end shifted 100 bp towards the fragment centre.
A mark is present (1) in a bin if the count is improbably high under a Poisson background: P(X \ge k \mid \lambda) < 10^{-4}.


This is ChromHMM’s BinarizeBam (or BinarizeBed). The expected count λ is the mark’s genome-wide mean count per bin, multiplied by the local enrichment of the control (input) around the bin: the input count in the bin ± 5 bins, plus a pseudocount, relative to the input’s mean. So regions with more input (amplifications, repeats with mappability artefacts) need more reads. Bin 7 on the slide is the example: 9 reads would pass against λ = 1, but not against λ = 2. The threshold 10^-4 is the default; it is the same Poisson logic as the MACS peak caller in Peak calling, applied to fixed bins instead of a sliding window. The 100-bp shift approximates moving from the 5′ end of a single-end read to the middle of the fragment, the same idea as read extension in From reads to coverage for enrichment assays. Binarising throws away information about how strong the signal is; ChromHMM accepts that loss for robustness against differences in depth and antibody efficiency between marks. Models on continuous signal exist (Segway, later).

# cell  mark  reads  control

The cell-mark file table has four columns: cell type, mark, reads, control. Two ENCODE replicates per mark were merged (and the two input replicates); the input has 134 625 reads on chr21. Binarisation takes about 12 seconds. 91.9% of the 233 549 bins have no mark at all. The sharp marks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1) are called in a few percent of bins; the broad marks only in about 1–2%, although biologically they cover more: their enrichment per 200-bp bin is weak and needs depth. With replicate 1 alone, H3K36me3 was called in 0.74% of bins and H3K27me3 in 0.73%, and the learned “transcribed” state had an emission of only 0.09: depth matters, which is why the Roadmap consortium subsampled all marks to comparable depth before learning its models.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Real data: which combinations occur?


46 of 64 combinations occur; 91.9% of bins have no mark; the ten most common combinations cover 91% of the marked bins.
Top five: H3K36me3 alone (gene bodies), H3K4me1 alone (weak enhancers), H3K4me3 + H3K27ac + H3K4me1 (active promoters), H3K27me3 alone, H3K9me3 alone.


Percentages are of bins with at least one mark; the dots below each bar show the combination (exercise R1). This is the empirical basis of chromatin states: out of 64 possible combinations, a few recur, and they are the ones biology predicts. Rare combinations (H3K9me3 with H3K4me3, H3K27me3 with H3K27ac) are mostly noise, or real but rare elements. A model with 8–18 states is a compact description of these frequent patterns plus their neighbourhoods. Note that the marked bins are only 8% of chr21.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
A hidden Markov model


Hidden: each bin has one state we do not observe. Observed: the six binary marks.
Emission: the state determines the probability of each mark. Transition: the state of the next bin depends only on the state of this bin (Markov).


Define the three ingredients of an HMM. The initial probabilities π_s: the chance that the first bin is in state s. The transition matrix A, with entry a_rs = P(state of bin t+1 = s | state of bin t = r); each row sums to 1. The emission probabilities: in ChromHMM, for each state s and mark m, a single number e_sm = P(mark m present | state s). Given these, the probability of any sequence of states together with the observations is a product: π for the first bin, then for each bin one transition and one emission. The word “hidden” just means we never see the states; we infer them. The same model family is used for gene finding, CpG island detection, copy-number segmentation and, in ATAC-seq, HMMRATAC.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Emissions: a product over marks


P(\text{bin} \mid s) = \prod_m e_{sm}^{\,o_m}(1 - e_{sm})^{1 - o_m}: marks are independent given the state.
The observation (H3K4me3 + H3K27ac) is ~47× more likely under TssA than under EnhA.


o_m is 1 if mark m is present in the bin and 0 if absent; the formula takes e if present and 1 − e if absent. The emission probabilities on the slide are made up but close to the real ones (compare with the learned matrix in a few slides). The independence assumption is a simplification: given that a bin is a promoter, H3K4me3 and H3K27ac are not truly independent, but treating them so keeps the model small (one number per state and mark) and works well in practice. Note how strongly the absence of H3K4me1 pushes against EnhA: 1 − 0.9 = 0.1. A bin is not assigned the state with the highest emission alone; the transitions also count, which is the next slide.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Transitions smooth along the genome: the Viterbi path
text:
Transitions smooth along the genome: the Viterbi path


Each δ = probability of the best path ending in that state; keep the best predecessor (grey arrows), trace back from the end.
The single 0 in bin 3 is absorbed: switching to Q and back costs 0.1 × 0.1, more than one missed mark.


Work through the first columns on the slide. Bin 1 (observed 1): δ(A) = 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, δ(Q) = 0.5 × 0.1 = 0.05. Bin 2 (1): δ(A) = max(0.4 × 0.9, 0.05 × 0.1) × 0.8 = 0.288; δ(Q) = max(0.4 × 0.1, 0.05 × 0.9) × 0.1 = 0.0045. Bin 3 (0): δ(A) = 0.288 × 0.9 × 0.2 = 0.0518; δ(Q) = max(0.288 × 0.1, 0.0045 × 0.9) × 0.9 = 0.0259. And so on. At the end Q wins (0.00272 > 0.00121), and the back-pointers give A A A A Q Q. Notice bin 5: δ(A) > δ(Q) there, but the best complete path goes through Q, because the decision is made for the whole sequence. This is the Viterbi algorithm. The forward algorithm is the same calculation with a sum instead of the max, and gives the probability of the observations; combined with a backward pass it gives, for each bin, the posterior probability of each state. ChromHMM by default assigns each bin the state with the highest posterior; the two usually agree. Students do a forward and a Viterbi calculation by hand in the exercise.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Learning the parameters


Nobody tells the model what a promoter is: emissions and transitions are fitted to maximise the likelihood of the binarised data (Baum–Welch, an EM algorithm).
EM finds a local optimum; ChromHMM’s default “information” initialisation makes runs reproducible.


E-step: with the current parameters, compute for every bin the posterior probability of each state (forward–backward). M-step: re-estimate each emission e_sm as the posterior-weighted fraction of bins with mark m present, and each transition from the posterior-weighted counts of consecutive state pairs. Repeat until the log-likelihood changes less than a threshold or a maximum number of iterations is reached (ChromHMM: 200). This is the same structure as fitting a Gaussian mixture or k-means: guess, assign softly, update, repeat. Like them it can end in different local optima depending on the start; ChromHMM’s default initialisation chooses initial emissions from the data in a deterministic way. On chr21 with six marks (234 000 bins) learning an 8-state model takes about 15 seconds on 4 threads; the Roadmap models were learned jointly across many epigenomes, i.e. on hundreds of millions of bins.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Running ChromHMM
java -mx4G -jar ChromHMM.jar LearnModel -b 200 -l chr21.sizes binary model_8 8 hg38

Output: emissions_8.png/.txt, transitions_8.png/.txt, GM12878_8_segments.bed (one line per segment), browser files, and enrichment tables for TSSs, genes, CpG islands.
OverlapEnrichment and NeighborhoodEnrichment compute the same enrichments for any annotation you give it.


LearnModel learns the model, decodes the training data and makes the standard plots. The last argument (hg38) tells it which built-in annotation files to use for the enrichment heatmaps (RefSeq TSS, TES, genes, exons, CpG islands from the COORDS folder of the ChromHMM download). -l restricts the output to the chromosomes in the file. With the default options, the result is deterministic. MakeSegmentation applies an existing model to new binarised data (for example another cell type), CompareModels compares the emissions of two models, Reorder renames and reorders states. The command takes a few seconds per iteration on chr21.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Real data: the emission matrix


Ours: active TSS (E4), TSS flanks (E3, E5), weak enhancer (E2), transcribed (E1), H3K9me3 (E7), weak H3K27me3 (E8) and quiescent (E6).
Roadmap’s 18 states, learned on many epigenomes, also separate genic enhancers, bivalent and strong Polycomb states; the shared states have similar emissions.


Rows are states, columns marks, values P(mark present | state). Names are given by rules on the emissions (in make-chromstates-figs.R) and checked against the enrichments of the next slides. E4 (0.94 H3K4me3, 0.91 H3K27ac, 0.07 H3K4me1) matches Roadmap’s 1_TssA almost exactly. E3 has all three active marks, like 3_TssFlnkU. E5 has H3K4me3 and H3K4me1 without H3K27ac, like 4_TssFlnkD. E1’s H3K36me3 emission (0.34) is lower than Roadmap’s 5_Tx (0.66): our H3K36me3 is less deep. E7 (H3K9me3 0.37 plus some H3K4me3) is the ZNF/repeats state. Our model has no strong Polycomb state: H3K27me3 is called in under 1% of bins, and in GM12878 strong Polycomb domains are rare on chr21 (Roadmap gives 0.24% 16_ReprPC). Learned from one chromosome of one cell line, the model sees few examples of rare states; Roadmap learned one joint model across many epigenomes and applied it to all 98 with H3K27ac.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Real data: the transition matrix


Most probability on the diagonal: expected run lengths 229 kb (quiescent), 10.6 kb (transcribed), 1.3 kb (TSS states), 0.7 kb (weak enhancer).
Off the diagonal: TSS → TSS flank → weak enhancer; weak enhancer ↔︎ weak Polycomb; quiescent bins almost never jump straight to an active state.


The expected length of a run of state s is 1 / (1 − a_ss) bins: 0.999 gives 1000 bins, here about 229 kb for E6. Off-diagonal entries are the typical neighbours: E4 (TssA) goes next mostly to E3 (0.09) and E5; E5 (TssFlnk) to E2 (0.14), the weak enhancer; E2 to E8 (0.15). E1 (Tx) is entered mainly from the flanking states. The transition matrix is learned together with the emissions; it encodes typical element sizes and orders, which is what lets the HMM smooth noisy binarised data. Read row by row: each row sums to 1.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Naming states by enrichment


Fold enrichment of a state for an annotation A: \dfrac{\text{bins in state and in } A \,/\, \text{bins in } A}{\text{bins in state} \,/\, \text{all bins}}.
E4 (TssA): 80× at TSS bins, 51× at CpG islands, 39× at ATAC peaks; E1: 6.7× at exons, 3.7× over gene bodies; E6 (quiescent): depleted everywhere (0.2–0.6).


Fold enrichments computed in R over 200-bp bins (exercise R3 and make-chromstates-figs.R): for each annotation, the fraction of its bins in each state divided by the fraction of all bins in the state. Annotations: CpG islands from ChromHMM’s COORDS folder, GENCODE protein-coding TSSs, exons and gene bodies, and two GM12878 peak sets from earlier units (ATAC-seq and CTCF ChIP-seq), which were not used to learn the model. That E4 is 39-fold enriched at ATAC peaks and E2/E3 at ATAC and CTCF peaks is independent support. ChromHMM computes the same table itself (OverlapEnrichment, exercise C3). The maximum possible fold enrichment of a state is 1 / its genome fraction (E4: 0.40% → 250).

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Real data: states around the TSS
text:
Real data: states around the TSS


E4 (TssA) peaks at the TSS (105×); E3 and E5 rise on both flanks (~11–23× at 1–2 kb); E1 (transcribed) increases downstream into the gene body.
The spatial order promoter flank → TSS → flank → transcribed body is learned, not given.


Strand-aware: positive positions are downstream in the direction of transcription. For each offset from 602 protein-coding TSS positions on chr21 (GENCODE), the fold enrichment of each state (log scale). E4 reaches ~105-fold within 200 bp of the TSS. E5 (H3K4me3 + H3K4me1, no H3K27ac) is highest about 2 kb downstream: the H3K4me1-marked flank of active promoters, Roadmap’s TssFlnkD (“downstream”). E3 is highest upstream (~11× at −1.2 kb), like TssFlnkU. E1 (H3K36me3) is depleted at the TSS and rises downstream, as transcription elongation marks the body towards the 3’ end. ChromHMM’s NeighborhoodEnrichment gives the same with RefSeq (exercise C3).

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
How many states?


More states always fit better: the likelihood cannot choose K. BIC tends to choose far too many on genome-sized data.
In practice: learn several K, keep the smallest that resolves the distinctions you care about, and check that states are interpretable and reproducible.


A: ChromHMM’s final log-likelihood for 4–18 states on our data; every extra state improves the fit (−70 792 for 4 to −59 925 for 18). B and C: the 4- and 12-state emission matrices. With 4 states there is one “active” promoter/enhancer state, a weak H3K4me1 state, transcribed and quiescent; Polycomb and heterochromatin are absorbed into quiescent. With 12 states: two quiescent states, an enhancer-in-gene-body state (H3K4me1 + H3K36me3, like Roadmap’s EnhG), several TSS-flank states and an H3K9me3 + H3K27ac state that is hard to interpret. The Roadmap consortium chose 15 states for 5 marks by learning models of up to ~20 states and keeping the smallest that captured the states seen in the larger models (CompareModels), across many epigenomes; Ernst & Kellis 2017 recommend the same. Training time grows with K: 6 s for 4 states, 15 s for 8, 47 s for 12 on chr21. Larger models also need more iterations (here 43, 71, 130).

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Our states vs the published Roadmap model
text:
Our states vs the published Roadmap model


E4 → 86% Roadmap TssA; E6 → 88% Quies; E1 → 95% Tx/TxWk; E7 → 61% ZNF/Rpts + 27% Het. Mixtures: E3 (TssFlnkU + EnhA), E5 (flanks + EnhWk), E8 (Quies + ReprPCWk).
In six coarse classes (promoter, enhancer, transcribed, Polycomb, heterochromatin, quiescent) the two maps agree on 68% of bins, but on only 36% of the bins that are not quiescent in both.


Each row: where the bins of one of our states fall in the Roadmap E116 segmentation (only the 35 Mb of chr21 that Roadmap covers after liftover). Strong agreement for the clear states. The coarse-class agreement shows how much of the apparent agreement comes from the quiescent majority; among marked bins the two maps often disagree on the class, mostly between neighbouring classes (promoter flank vs enhancer, weak transcription vs quiescent). Reasons: different data (ENCODE alignments of 2011 data reprocessed for GRCh38 vs Roadmap’s uniformly processed hg19 data), our model learned on one chromosome of one cell type vs Roadmap’s joint model across many epigenomes, 8 vs 18 states, and liftover. This is the honest message: segmentations are models, and two reasonable models of the same cell type agree on the main structure and differ in the details.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
section: Most of the genome is quiet
text:
Most of the genome is quiet


Our quiescent state covers 67% of chr21 (plus 22% nearly unmarked, E8); Roadmap’s 18_Quies 66% of what it covers.
Promoter and enhancer states together: ~5% (ours) and ~6% (Roadmap). Transcribed: 5% (ours) vs 11% (Roadmap Tx + TxWk).


Percentages of 200-bp bins on chr21. The regulatory part of the genome is small: active promoters 0.4%, flanks and enhancers a few percent. Roadmap assigns more of chr21 to transcription (Tx 3.7% + TxWk 7.5%) and to heterochromatin (Het 8.3%) than we do, because it calls H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 more sensitively (deeper, pooled across epigenomes, and its weak states TxWk and Het capture low levels of the marks). Our E8 (21.8%, only 4% H3K27me3) corresponds partly to Roadmap’s ReprPCWk, partly to Quies. These numbers are typical: in Roadmap epigenomes, quiescent states cover ~60–70% of the genome.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Reference epigenomes: Roadmap and ENCODE

Roadmap Epigenomics (2015): 111 reference epigenomes (+ 16 from ENCODE = 127) with a common ChromHMM model: 15 states from 5 core marks (H3K4me3, H3K4me1, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3), 18 states with H3K27ac (98 epigenomes), 25 states on imputed data (12 marks).
ENCODE (2012, and later): ChromHMM and Segway segmentations of the tier-1 cell lines, including GM12878 and K562; the SCREEN registry of candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) is the newer, element-based annotation.
Full-stack ChromHMM (Vu & Ernst 2022): one stacked model of > 1000 datasets, 100 states, a single annotation of the genome that is the same for all cell types.


These are the annotations most papers use: you download the segmentation of your cell type (here E116 = GM12878) rather than learn your own, as long as your cell type is among them. Points to remember: Roadmap’s segmentations are on hg19, with liftOver versions for hg38 (the ones we use); state names are the mnemonics (TssA, TssFlnk, Tx, EnhG, EnhA, EnhWk, ZNF/Rpts, Het, TssBiv, EnhBiv, ReprPC, Quies, …). For a new cell type with only some marks, the imputed 25-state model and tools that learn with missing data are options. ENCODE’s own cCRE registry (SCREEN) classifies elements from DNase, H3K4me3, H3K27ac and CTCF instead of genome-wide states. Text-only slide on purpose: the important thing is to know these resources exist and what was used to make them.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Concatenated and stacked models


Concatenated (Roadmap): one set of states, a separate map per cell type → compare cell types bin by bin (“enhancer in B cells, Polycomb in liver”).
Stacked: one map; states encode cross-cell-type patterns.


To compare cell types with a concatenated model, the same marks must be available in all of them, ideally from comparable data (the Roadmap processing pipeline uniformly subsampled reads to the same depth for this reason). Stacked models need no such alignment of states but get very many states quickly; the full-stack model of Vu & Ernst has 100 states. Learning a separate model per cell type and then matching the states by hand is possible but makes comparisons subjective.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
What states are used for


Variants: GWAS hits for a trait are enriched in enhancer states of the relevant cell types (Roadmap 2015; Epigenomics and genetic variation).
Cell types: which elements change state between cell types or with disease.


Panel A is schematic, in the spirit of Figure 9 of the Roadmap 2015 paper: variants associated with immune diseases fall preferentially in enhancer states of immune cells, cholesterol-related variants in liver enhancers, and so on. This is how many GWAS papers propose the cell type in which a non-coding variant acts; the statistics (enrichment with matched backgrounds, LD) are in Epigenomics and genetic variation. Panel B: annotate one variant by looking up its state in several reference epigenomes. Caveat: a state annotation says what the chromatin looks like, not that the element regulates any particular gene, and not that the variant changes it. That needs Linking regulatory elements to genes and experimental tests.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Other segmentation methods









method
input
model
resolution




ChromHMM
binarised marks
multivariate Bernoulli HMM
200 bp


Segway
continuous signal (e.g. −log10 p)
dynamic Bayesian network, Gaussian emissions
1 bp


IDEAS, EpiCSeg, Spectacle
signal or counts
joint across cell types / count models / spectral learning
100–200 bp




They agree on the main classes (promoter, enhancer, transcribed, Polycomb, heterochromatin, quiet); they differ in detail and in how many states they find.


Segway (Hoffman et al. 2012) models the continuous signal directly with a dynamic Bayesian network, and was used for ENCODE’s 2012 segmentations alongside ChromHMM; working at base resolution it can find small elements but is much slower. ENCODE combined the two into a consensus annotation for the tier-1 cell lines. IDEAS shares information across cell types; EpiCSeg uses a negative multinomial count model; Spectacle learns HMM parameters by spectral methods. Students do not need to know these beyond the existence of alternatives; the conceptual model is the ChromHMM one.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Caveats

States are labels for mark combinations, not proof of function: “EnhA” means “looks like an active enhancer”.
They depend on the marks profiled, the antibodies, the depth and the binarisation threshold: the same cell type profiled twice can give different maps.
Cell populations are mixtures: a “bivalent” bin may be a mix of active and repressed cells.
200-bp resolution, one state per bin, marks independent given the state: simplifications that work, not biology.


These are the questions to ask of any paper that uses chromatin states. A typical overreach: “variant X lies in an enhancer state, therefore it disrupts an enhancer of gene Y”. Another: comparing segmentations of two cell types profiled in different labs at different depths and interpreting the differences as biology. For bivalent states in particular: true bivalency (both marks on the same nucleosome or nearby on the same DNA molecule) has been shown in embryonic stem cells by sequential ChIP, but in a mixed population, H3K4me3 + H3K27me3 in one bin may come from different cells. A state map is a hypothesis generator.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Summary







topic
key idea




combinatorial code
elements are defined by combinations of marks, not single marks


binarisation
200-bp bins; 1 if P(X \ge k \mid \lambda) < 10^{-4}, λ from the mark mean × local input


HMM
hidden state per bin; emissions (product of Bernoullis); transitions (Markov)


algorithms
forward (sum), Viterbi (max), Baum–Welch (EM, local optimum)


interpretation
emission matrix + enrichment at TSS, genes, CpG islands → state names


number of states
no statistical answer; interpretability and reproducibility


references
Roadmap 15/18/25-state models; ENCODE; full-stack 100-state annotation


uses
variant annotation, comparing cell types; caveat: annotation ≠ function




Students should leave able to: binarise a bin with a Poisson threshold, compute an emission probability, do a forward and a Viterbi step on a toy HMM, name states from an emission matrix and enrichments, explain why the number of states is a choice, and say what a chromatin-state annotation can and cannot support.

title: Combining marks into chromatin states
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Ernst et al. 2011, Nature. Mapping and analysis of chromatin state dynamics in nine human cell types. Chromatin states across ENCODE cell lines, and their use for GWAS variants.
Ernst & Kellis 2012, Nat Methods. ChromHMM: automating chromatin-state discovery and characterization. The software.
Hoffman et al. 2012, Nat Methods. Unsupervised pattern discovery in human chromatin structure through genomic segmentation. Segway.
Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium 2015, Nature. Integrative analysis of 111 reference human epigenomes. The reference 15/18/25-state annotations.
Ernst & Kellis 2017, Nat Protoc. Chromatin-state discovery and genome annotation with ChromHMM. Practical guide: binarisation, number of states, interpretation.
Vu & Ernst 2022, Genome Biol. Universal annotation of the human genome through integration of over a thousand epigenomic datasets. The full-stack model.

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Background
The assays. In CUT&RUN, protein A–MNase bound to an antibody cuts DNA next to the target in permeabilised nuclei (activated by Ca2+); the fragments diffuse out and are made into a library. In CUT&Tag, protein A–Tn5 loaded with sequencing adapters is bound instead and, activated by Mg2+, cuts and inserts the adapters in one step; the library is made by PCR. DNA far from the antibody is not cut, so the background is low.
Fragments. Paired-end reads give one fragment per pair, from the leftmost to the rightmost base. A histone-mark library is a nucleosome ladder (≈ 150–200 bp, ≈ 350 bp, …); TF CUT&RUN libraries are dominated by fragments < 120 bp.
Spike-in. pA–Tn5 and pA–MNase are made in E. coli and carry a little bacterial DNA, which is tagmented too. If every reaction received the same amount of enzyme, the number of E. coli fragments is a ruler: scale factor \(S = C / n_\text{E. coli}\) (here \(C = 10\,000\)), and normalised signal = fragment coverage × \(S\).
SEACR (Meers, Tenenbaum & Henikoff 2019) splits a bedGraph into blocks of contiguous non-zero signal and gives each block its total signal (area under the curve, AUC). With an IgG control, the threshold \(t\) is the AUC at which the fraction of blocks above \(t\) that come from the target (rather than the IgG) is highest (“stringent”); target blocks above \(t\) are merged and those overlapping IgG blocks above \(t\) are removed. Without a control, SEACR keeps the top fraction of blocks by AUC (e.g. 0.01).
FRiP: the fraction of reads (fragments) that fall in peaks.

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Data
K562 CUT&Tag from Kaya-Okur et al. 2020 (GEO GSE145187), the replicate-1 samples of the Henikoff-lab CUT&Tag tutorial: H3K27me3 (SRR12246717), H3K4me3 (SRR11074254) and IgG (SRR11923224), paired-end 2 × 25 bp. We kept only the read pairs that align to chr21 or chrM, or to E. coli (the spike-in); the reads are the original records. For comparison: ENCODE ChIP-seq of the same marks in K562 (Bernstein lab, single-end 36 bp; filtered alignments of replicate 1, cut to chr21) and ENCODE’s peaks for them.



file

CUT&Tag reads (59 k, 25 k and 294 k pairs)

E. coli K-12 MG1655 genome (spike-in reference)

ENCODE ChIP-seq and input, chr21 (ENCFF392ZKG, ENCFF564SVK, ENCFF226FKB)

from earlier units



data/download.sh cutrun-cuttag      # peaks, GTF; the reads and BAMs come from data/prepare-cuttag.sh
mkdir -p ~/epi/cuttag && cd ~/epi/cuttag
D=/path/to/course/data
T=8
git clone https://github.com/FredHutch/SEACR.git      # SEACR is a bash + R script
SEACR=$PWD/SEACR/SEACR_1.3.sh
You need bowtie2, samtools (1.16 or later), bedtools, macs3, R, and SEACR. The whole command-line part runs in about a minute on 8 threads, because the files are small.
Honest simplifications: we use one replicate per mark and only chr21; the reads were selected because they aligned to chr21 (or E. coli) in the full genome, so mis-alignments from other chromosomes cannot happen here; the ChIP comparison uses ENCODE’s alignments rather than our own processing. Experimental design and QC for epigenomic assays explains why two biological replicates are the minimum for real work.

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Why fewer reads? A ChIP-seq library for H3K27me3 has 20 million reads with a FRiP of 0.08. A CUT&Tag library for the same mark has 3 million fragments with a FRiP of 0.6.

How many reads (fragments) fall in peaks in each library?
Where are the other reads in each library, and what does that say about why ChIP needs an input control?
Give two reasons from the chemistry why the CUT&Tag background is so low.

B2. Fragment lengths. Sketch the fragment-length distribution you expect for (i) CUT&RUN of a transcription factor, (ii) CUT&Tag of H3K27me3, (iii) a CUT&Tag IgG control. Mark the approximate positions of the peaks. Why can’t you draw this plot for the ENCODE ChIP-seq data used in this exercise?
B3. Duplicates. After filtering, a CUT&Tag H3K4me3 library has 1 200 000 fragments, of which 84 000 are duplicates (same start and end); the IgG from the same experiment has 180 000 fragments, of which 150 000 are duplicates.

Compute both duplication rates.
For which library would you remove duplicates, and why? What would happen to the H3K4me3 signal at the strongest promoters if you removed them there?
The H3K4me3 library is sequenced ten times deeper and the duplication rate rises to 60%. Is the library worse? What did the extra sequencing buy?

B4. Spike-in. Three CUT&Tag reactions for H3K27me3 used the same pA–Tn5 batch and 50 000 cells each:



sample
human fragments
E. coli fragments




control 1
4 000 000
800


control 2
2 500 000
500


EZH2 inhibitor
3 000 000
2 000




Compute the scale factor \(S = 10\,000 / n_\text{E. coli}\) and the spike-in-normalised total signal (human fragments × \(S\)) for each sample.
By how much does the inhibitor reduce H3K27me3? What would CPM normalisation have shown?
The inhibitor sample was later found to have been processed with a new batch of pA–Tn5. What does that do to your conclusion?

B5. A SEACR threshold by hand. The AUCs of the signal blocks of a small CUT&RUN target track and its IgG are:
target: 120, 95, 60, 44, 30, 22, 15, 9, 6, 4, 3, 2 — IgG: 14, 8, 5, 4, 3, 2, 2, 1

For thresholds \(t\) = 2, 5, 8 and 10, count the target blocks and the IgG blocks with AUC > \(t\), and compute the fraction of target blocks among them.
SEACR’s stringent threshold is the \(t\) with the highest fraction, among thresholds where some IgG block still passes. Which \(t\) is it, how many target blocks pass, and what is the empirical FDR (1 − fraction)?
The IgG block with AUC 14 overlaps one of the target blocks. What happens to that block?

B6. Why not MACS? A CUT&Tag sample has 300 000 fragments on a 40-Mb chromosome. Compute \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) for a 200-bp window (fragments × window / chromosome length). How surprising are 8 fragments in a window, \(P(X \ge 8 \mid \lambda)\)? (Use \(P(X \ge 8 \mid 1.5) \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-4}\).) Why does this make MACS3 call small piles of untethered cutting as peaks, and how does SEACR avoid it?
B7. Judge the claim. A paper uses CUT&Tag of H3K27me3 on 1000 sorted cells and reports that “H3K27me3 is present at 40% of active promoters, revealing a new layer of Polycomb regulation”. No IgG was sequenced; the peaks were called with MACS3 without a control. List what is missing and what you would check first.
B8. Choose the assay. Which of ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag would you choose, and why: (a) H3K4me3 in 5000 sorted haematopoietic stem cells; (b) a transcription factor with a fast off-rate in a cell line; (c) H3K27ac in 40 frozen tumour biopsies, to be compared with published ENCODE/Roadmap data; (d) H3K27me3 in single cells.

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
On the command line

C1 — Align to the genome and to E. coli
bowtie2-build --threads $T $D/ecoli_U00096.3.fa ecoli > /dev/null
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3 igg; do
  bowtie2 -p $T --end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-mixed --no-discordant --phred33 -I 10 -X 700 \
    -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -1 $D/k562_cuttag_${s}_R1.fastq.gz -2 $D/k562_cuttag_${s}_R2.fastq.gz \
    2> $s.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - | samtools sort -@ 4 -o $s.raw.bam
  samtools index $s.raw.bam
  bowtie2 -p $T --end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-overlap --no-dovetail --no-mixed --no-discordant \
    --phred33 -I 10 -X 700 -x ecoli -1 $D/k562_cuttag_${s}_R1.fastq.gz -2 $D/k562_cuttag_${s}_R2.fastq.gz \
    2> $s.ecoli.log > /dev/null
done
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3 igg; do echo $s; cat $s.bowtie2.log; samtools idxstats $s.raw.bam | head -2; done

What do -I 10 -X 700, --no-mixed and --no-discordant do? Why are reads not adapter-trimmed?
What fraction of each sample’s pairs aligned to chr21 + chrM? The IgG has many pairs that did not align: where are they from? (Check igg.ecoli.log.)
How many reads of each sample are on chrM? Compare with the size of the whole library (H3K27me3 2 984 630, H3K4me3 1 581 710, IgG 2 127 635 read pairs). Why is the IgG so different?



C2 — Filter and mark duplicates
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3 igg; do
  samtools view -u -q 30 -f 2 -F 1804 $s.raw.bam chr21 \
    | samtools collate -u -O - | samtools fixmate -m -u - - | samtools view -u -f 2 - \
    | samtools sort -u - | samtools markdup -s - $s.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.bam
  echo $s $(samtools view -c -f 64 $s.bam) fragments $(samtools view -c -f 64 -f 1024 $s.bam) duplicates
done

The filters are those of From reads to coverage for enrichment assays: what does each do? Note that markdup runs without -r: duplicates are marked, not removed.
Give the number of fragments and the duplication rate of each library. Do they fit the expectation that CUT&Tag libraries have many duplicates?



C3 — Fragments, bedGraphs and fragment lengths
grep -w chr21 $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > chrom.sizes
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3 igg; do
  F=0; [ $s = igg ] && F=1024        # duplicates removed from the IgG only
  samtools view -u -F $F $s.bam | samtools sort -n -u - | bedtools bamtobed -bedpe -i - 2> /dev/null \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '$1 == $4 { s = ($2 < $5 ? $2 : $5); e = ($3 > $6 ? $3 : $6); print $1, s, e }' \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > $s.frag.bed
  bedtools genomecov -bg -i $s.frag.bed -g chrom.sizes > $s.bedgraph
  echo $s $(wc -l < $s.frag.bed) fragments, median length \
    $(awk '{ print $3 - $2 }' $s.frag.bed | sort -n | awk '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print a[int(NR / 2)] }')
done

Explain the awk line: which columns of the BEDPE output are used, and why is that the fragment?
What are the median fragment lengths? Why is the IgG different?



C4 — Peaks with SEACR and MACS3
mkdir -p peaks
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3; do
  bash $SEACR $s.bedgraph igg.bedgraph norm stringent peaks/${s}_seacr_igg > /dev/null
  bash $SEACR $s.bedgraph 0.01 non stringent peaks/${s}_seacr_top1 > /dev/null
done
macs3 callpeak -t h3k4me3.bam -c igg.bam -f BAMPE -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 -n h3k4me3_macs --outdir peaks 2> peaks/h3k4me3_macs.log
macs3 callpeak -t h3k27me3.bam -c igg.bam -f BAMPE -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all --broad --broad-cutoff 0.1 -n h3k27me3_macs --outdir peaks 2> peaks/h3k27me3_macs.log
wc -l peaks/*stringent.bed peaks/*Peak
head -3 peaks/h3k4me3_seacr_igg.stringent.bed

What are the six columns of a SEACR output line?
How many peaks does each call give? Why does “top 1%” give so few?
Why --keep-dup all, and why --broad for H3K27me3?



C5 — FRiP and comparison with ENCODE ChIP-seq
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27me3; do
  zcat $D/k562_${m}_chip_peaks.bed.gz | awk '$1 == "chr21"' | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge > enc_$m.bed
  echo $m ENCODE peaks: $(wc -l < enc_$m.bed)
  n=$(wc -l < $m.frag.bed); k=$(bedtools intersect -u -a $m.frag.bed -b enc_$m.bed | wc -l)
  echo "  CUT&Tag FRiP in ENCODE peaks: $k / $n"
  n=$(samtools view -c $D/k562_${m}_chip_chr21.bam)
  k=$(bedtools intersect -u -abam $D/k562_${m}_chip_chr21.bam -b enc_$m.bed | samtools view -c -)
  echo "  ChIP    FRiP in ENCODE peaks: $k / $n"
  for p in peaks/${m}_seacr_igg.stringent.bed peaks/${m}_seacr_top1.stringent.bed peaks/${m}_macs_peaks.[nb]*Peak; do
    echo "  $p: $(wc -l < $p) peaks, $(bedtools intersect -u -a $p -b enc_$m.bed | wc -l) in ENCODE," \
         "$(bedtools intersect -u -a enc_$m.bed -b $p | wc -l) ENCODE peaks found," \
         "FRiP $(bedtools intersect -u -a $m.frag.bed -b $p | wc -l) / $(wc -l < $m.frag.bed)"
  done
done

Compute FRiP in the same (ENCODE) peaks for CUT&Tag and ChIP of each mark. How many reads did each library have on chr21?
For each peak call: what fraction of the peaks are in ENCODE’s set, and what fraction of ENCODE’s peaks are found? Which caller would you pick for each mark?
Why is “FRiP in our own peaks” not a fair way to compare two assays?



C6 — The E. coli spike-in
for s in h3k27me3 h3k4me3 igg; do
  e=$(grep -E "concordantly (exactly 1 time|>1 times)" $s.ecoli.log | awk '{ n += $1 } END { print n }')
  echo $s E. coli pairs: $e scale factor: $(echo "10000 / $e" | bc -l)
done
# a spike-in-scaled bedGraph, e.g. for H3K27me3:
e=$(grep -E "concordantly (exactly 1 time|>1 times)" h3k27me3.ecoli.log | awk '{ n += $1 } END { print n }')
bedtools genomecov -bg -i h3k27me3.frag.bed -g chrom.sizes -scale $(echo "10000 / $e" | bc -l) > h3k27me3.spikein.bedgraph

What percentage of each whole library (sizes in C1c) is E. coli? Why does the IgG have so much more?
Our files contain all E. coli pairs of the libraries but only the chr21 human pairs. Does that matter for the scale factors?
Would you use these factors to compare H3K27me3 with H3K4me3? Between two H3K27me3 samples, what would you check first?

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
In R
You need GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, GenomicAlignments and ggplot2. Work in the same folder:
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(GenomicAlignments); library(ggplot2)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/cuttag")
L21 <- 46709983
fr <- lapply(c(h3k4me3 = "h3k4me3", h3k27me3 = "h3k27me3", igg = "igg"), function(s) import(paste0(s, ".frag.bed")))
rd <- function(f) granges(readGAlignments(file.path(D, paste0(f, "_chr21.bam"))))
chip <- list(h3k4me3 = rd("k562_h3k4me3_chip"), h3k27me3 = rd("k562_h3k27me3_chip"), input = rd("k562_input"))
mid <- function(g) resize(g, 1, fix = "center")      # count each fragment / read once, at its centre
enc <- lapply(c(h3k4me3 = "h3k4me3", h3k27me3 = "h3k27me3"), function(m) {
  x <- import(file.path(D, sprintf("k562_%s_chip_peaks.bed.gz", m)), format = "narrowPeak")
  reduce(x[seqnames(x) == "chr21"])
})
sapply(fr, length); sapply(chip, length)

R1 — Fragment lengths
fl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fr), function(s) data.frame(sample = s, len = width(fr[[s]]))))
ggplot(fl[fl$len < 700, ], aes(len, colour = sample)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(x = "fragment length (bp)", y = "fragments")
sapply(split(fl$len, fl$sample), function(v) c(median = median(v), lt120 = mean(v < 120), mono = mean(v >= 120 & v < 300)))
h <- tabulate(width(fr$h3k27me3), 1000)
plot(140:300, h[140:300], type = "l", xlab = "fragment length (bp)", ylab = "fragments")   # zoom

Where are the nucleosome peaks? What fraction of fragments is shorter than 120 bp?
In the zoom on H3K27me3, how far apart are the small ripples? Where do they come from?



R2 — Signal-to-noise: FRiP and the fingerprint
S6 <- list(ct_k4 = fr$h3k4me3, chip_k4 = chip$h3k4me3, ct_k27 = fr$h3k27me3,
           chip_k27 = chip$h3k27me3, igg = fr$igg, input = chip$input)
peaks_for <- c(ct_k4 = "h3k4me3", chip_k4 = "h3k4me3", ct_k27 = "h3k27me3", chip_k27 = "h3k27me3",
               igg = "h3k4me3", input = "h3k4me3")
frip <- sapply(names(S6), function(n) mean(overlapsAny(mid(S6[[n]]), enc[[peaks_for[n]]])))
round(frip, 3)
bins <- tile(GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, L21)), width = 5000)[[1]]
fp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(S6), function(n) {
  cnt <- sort(countOverlaps(bins, mid(S6[[n]])))
  data.frame(sample = n, x = seq_along(cnt) / length(cnt), y = cumsum(cnt) / sum(cnt))
}))
ggplot(fp, aes(x, y, colour = sample)) + geom_line() + geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "fraction of 5-kb bins", y = "cumulative fraction of reads")
sapply(S6, function(g) { cnt <- sort(countOverlaps(bins, mid(g)), decreasing = TRUE)
  sum(cnt[1:ceiling(0.01 * length(cnt))]) / sum(cnt) })

Give FRiP in the ENCODE peaks for the four mark libraries and the two controls. The ENCODE peaks cover 1.2% of chr21: what FRiP would a library with no enrichment at all have?
What fraction of reads is in the top 1% of 5-kb bins for each library? How do the fingerprint curves of CUT&Tag and ChIP differ?



R3 — How many reads do you need?
detect <- function(g, p, n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed); g <- mid(g[sample(length(g), n)])            # subsample n reads
  k <- countOverlaps(p, g)                                     # reads in each ENCODE peak
  bg <- sum(!overlapsAny(g, p)) / (L21 - sum(width(p)))        # background reads per bp
  mean(ppois(k - 1, bg * width(p), lower.tail = FALSE) < 1e-3) # fraction of peaks detected
}
for (m in c("h3k4me3", "h3k27me3")) for (n in c(2000, 5000, 10000, 17000, 45000)) {
  ct <- if (n <= length(fr[[m]])) mean(sapply(1:5, function(s) detect(fr[[m]], enc[[m]], n, s))) else NA
  ch <- mean(sapply(1:5, function(s) detect(chip[[m]], enc[[m]], n, s)))
  cat(m, n, "CUT&Tag", round(ct, 2), "ChIP", round(ch, 2), "\n")
}
q <- import(file.path(D, "k562_h3k4me3_chip_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak"); q <- q[seqnames(q) == "chr21"]
q$ct <- countOverlaps(q, mid(fr$h3k4me3))
q$quartile <- cut(rank(-q$signalValue, ties.method = "first"), 4, labels = c("strongest", "2nd", "3rd", "weakest"))
tapply(q$ct >= 3, q$quartile, mean)

Explain detect(): what is the background model, and what makes a peak “detected”?
For H3K27me3, how many ChIP reads are needed to detect as many ENCODE peaks as CUT&Tag does with 45 000 fragments? (Extend the ChIP series to 90 000 and 140 000 reads.)
For H3K4me3, CUT&Tag levels off at about a third of the ENCODE peaks. Which ENCODE peaks does it find, and which not? Give two possible explanations.



R4 — The IgG and the open-chromatin background
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(resize(tx, 1, fix = "start"))
act <- tss[overlapsAny(tss, enc$h3k4me3, maxgap = 500) & !overlapsAny(tss, enc$h3k27me3, maxgap = 2000)]
rep <- tss[overlapsAny(tss, enc$h3k27me3, maxgap = 500)]
c(length(tss), length(act), length(rep))
enr <- function(g, t) { r <- reduce(resize(t, 1000, fix = "center"))
  mean(overlapsAny(mid(g), r)) / (sum(width(r)) / L21) }
round(sapply(S6, function(g) c(active = enr(g, act), repressed = enr(g, rep))), 2)

What does enr() compute? What value would a uniformly distributed library give?
How enriched is the IgG at active promoters, compared with the ChIP input? What does that tell you about where untethered pA–Tn5 cuts?
Is H3K27me3 CUT&Tag enriched at active promoters in these data? Compare with ChIP. Does this rule out an open-chromatin bias in CUT&Tag in general?

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — FRiP, reads in peaks, depth (B1, C5, R2)





Reads in peaks = FRiP × reads. A library with no enrichment has a FRiP equal to the fraction of the genome covered by the peaks. Count each fragment once with bedtools intersect -u. FRiP for ChIP is described in the ENCODE ChIP-seq standards and in Experimental design and QC for epigenomic assays.









Hint 2 — fragment lengths and duplicates (B2, B3, C2, C3, R1)





Nucleosomal DNA is 147 bp plus linker; Tn5 adds a 9-bp duplication. samtools markdup marks pairs with the same two ends; -s prints statistics, -r would remove them. See the duplicate section of the CUT&Tag tutorial (Zheng, Ahmad & Henikoff) and Kaya-Okur et al. 2019. bedtools bamtobed -bedpe writes one line per pair: chromosome, start, end of mate 1, then of mate 2.









Hint 3 — spike-in (B4, C6)





\(S = C / n_\text{E. coli}\); normalised signal = fragments × \(S\). CPM normalisation divides by each library’s total and so assumes the total amount of the mark is the same in all samples. Meers et al. 2019 (eLife) introduced E. coli carry-over DNA as a spike-in for CUT&RUN; the CUT&Tag tutorial (section on spike-in calibration) applies it to CUT&Tag. Normalisation under global changes is treated fully in Annotation and differential binding.









Hint 4 — SEACR and MACS3 (B5, B6, C4)





The SEACR README describes the arguments (target bedGraph, control bedGraph or a fraction, norm/non, stringent/relaxed, prefix) and the output columns. The threshold rule is in Meers, Tenenbaum & Henikoff 2019. For MACS3, see the callpeak documentation (-f BAMPE, --broad, --keep-dup) and Peak calling. \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) = reads × window / genome size.









Hint 5 — R (R2–R4)





tile() cuts a range into bins; countOverlaps() / overlapsAny() count reads per bin or peak; resize(x, 1, fix = "center") turns each read into its centre, so a read is counted once. ppois(k - 1, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) is \(P(X \ge k)\). The fingerprint plot is the one of deepTools plotFingerprint.

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) ChIP: 0.08 × 20 M = 1.6 M reads in peaks; CUT&Tag: 0.6 × 3 M = 1.8 M. Similar numbers of useful reads from seven times fewer reads. (b) In ChIP, 18.4 M reads (92%) are spread over the genome: DNA that was sheared everywhere and carried along nonspecifically; its local density follows copy number, mappability and sonication bias, which is why ChIP needs an input to estimate the local background. In CUT&Tag, 1.2 M reads are outside peaks: untethered cutting (open chromatin), weak sites, E. coli. (c) Only DNA next to the tethered enzyme is cut, so the rest of the genome never becomes library molecules; unbound enzyme is washed away before activation (for CUT&Tag with 300 mM NaCl); no immunoprecipitation of solubilised chromatin, so nothing sticks to beads.
B2. (i) TF CUT&RUN: a main peak at ~50–120 bp (the factor’s footprint plus flanks), plus a smaller mono-nucleosome peak at ~150–200 bp. (ii) H3K27me3 CUT&Tag: a ladder with peaks near 150–200 bp, ~350 bp and ~550 bp, with a ~10-bp ripple. (iii) IgG: few, mostly random fragments of all sizes, with nucleosomal and long fragments (untethered Tn5 cuts linkers in open chromatin). The ENCODE ChIP-seq data are single-end, so the fragment length of each molecule is unknown (only an average can be estimated from strand cross-correlation, Peak calling).
B3. (a) H3K4me3: 84 000 / 1 200 000 = 7%; IgG: 150 000 / 180 000 = 83%. (b) Remove them in the IgG: it has very few distinct molecules, so the duplicates are PCR copies that would turn a handful of random fragments into apparent peaks. Keep them for H3K4me3: identical fragments there are partly independent cuts at the same linkers in different cells; removing them would cap the signal at the strongest promoters (each position can contribute only one fragment) and compress the dynamic range. (c) The library is not worse; it has been sequenced close to saturation. The extra sequencing mostly re-read molecules already seen; it added few new fragments. Preseq-style saturation curves tell you when to stop.
B4. (a) \(S\) = 12.5, 20 and 5; normalised totals: 4.0 M × 12.5 = 50 M, 2.5 M × 20 = 50 M, 3.0 M × 5 = 15 M. (b) The two controls agree (50 M each, which supports the spike-in); the inhibitor has 15/50 = 30% of the control level, a 70% loss. CPM would set all three totals to 106 and hide the global loss; only local redistribution would remain visible. (c) The scale factor now depends on how much E. coli DNA the new batch carries; the 70% may be partly or entirely a batch effect. Repeat with one batch, or use an added spike-in of known amount (e.g. Drosophila chromatin or barcoded nucleosomes).
B5. (a) t = 2: target 11, IgG 5 → 11/16 = 0.69; t = 5: 9 and 2 → 0.82; t = 8: 8 and 1 → 0.89; t = 10: 7 and 1 → 0.875. (b) t = 8: 8 target blocks pass (120, 95, 60, 44, 30, 22, 15, 9); empirical FDR = 1 − 0.89 = 0.11. (Above t = 14 no IgG block passes and the fraction is trivially 1; SEACR excludes that case.) (c) It is removed: target blocks that overlap an IgG block above the threshold are discarded as likely artefacts.
B6. \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 300\,000 \times 200 / (4 \times 10^7) = 1.5\). \(P(X \ge 8) \approx 2 \times 10^{-4}\): 8 fragments look significant, although a dozen fragments from untethered cutting at an open promoter are expected in CUT&Tag. The local λ windows of MACS are mostly empty in sparse data, and the IgG is too sparse to give a reliable local λ. SEACR does not test positions against a Poisson background; it compares whole blocks of target and IgG signal by their total, so a small pile has to beat the IgG’s blocks, not an almost-zero λ.
B7. Missing: an IgG (or no-antibody) control, a comparison with ATAC-seq or with H3K27me3 ChIP/CUT&RUN in the same cells, replicates, the salt conditions of the washes, and a peak caller that takes the control into account. With 1000 cells, a few fragments per promoter are expected from untethered pA–Tn5 in open chromatin. Check first whether the same promoters have IgG signal and ATAC-seq peaks, and whether the “H3K27me3” signal there scales with accessibility rather than with known Polycomb targets.
B8. (a) CUT&Tag (or CUT&RUN): few cells, an abundant, well-validated mark. (b) CUT&RUN (gentle washes, short footprint fragments) or ChIP with crosslinking; CUT&Tag’s high-salt washes would strip a weakly bound factor. (c) ChIP-seq, or CUT&RUN/Tag with a validation set: frozen tissue is harder for in-situ methods, and comparability with ENCODE/Roadmap ChIP data is part of the question. (d) Single-cell CUT&Tag (or a droplet-based variant); be aware of the open-chromatin bias, which matters most with the few fragments per cell.









Solutions — command line





Numbers from our run (Bowtie2 2.4.4, samtools 1.21, bedtools 2.30.0, MACS3 3.1.0, SEACR 1.3; 8 threads). The whole command-line part takes about 35 s.
C1. (a) -I 10 -X 700: a pair is concordant only if the fragment is 10–700 bp; --no-mixed drops pairs where only one mate aligns, --no-discordant drops pairs that align but not as a proper pair. The reads are 25 bp, so a read only runs into the adapter if the fragment is shorter than 25 bp, which hardly happens; with 2 × 150-bp reads you must trim, as for ATAC-seq. (b) H3K27me3: 58 803 pairs, 99.6% aligned (75.7% concordantly once, 24.0% more than once); H3K4me3: 25 102 pairs, 98.6%; IgG: 293 653 pairs, only 74.3%. The 75 504 IgG pairs that did not align are the E. coli carry-over: igg.ecoli.log reports 75 492 pairs aligned concordantly to E. coli. (c) chrM: 1 994 reads (997 pairs) for H3K27me3, 8 328 (4 164 pairs) for H3K4me3, 391 904 (195 952 pairs) for the IgG, i.e. 0.03%, 0.26% and 9.2% of the whole libraries. Mitochondrial DNA has no nucleosomes and many copies; without a tethered target, the IgG reaction shows mostly untethered Tn5 activity, which, like ATAC-seq, goes to accessible DNA.
C2. (a) -q 30 unique alignments; -f 2 proper pairs; -F 1804 removes unmapped, mate-unmapped, secondary, QC-fail and already-marked duplicates; region chr21 drops chrM; collate/fixmate/view -f 2 remove pairs that lost a mate in the first filter. (b) H3K27me3: 45 130 fragments, 2 356 duplicates (5.2%); H3K4me3: 17 380 fragments, 1 225 (7.0%); IgG: 16 941 fragments, 14 397 (85%). The marks have few duplicates: these libraries were sequenced far from saturation (about 3 and 1.6 million pairs), so the “duplicates are expected” argument matters less here than for deeply sequenced libraries. The IgG, with very few distinct molecules, is almost all duplicates.
C3. (a) bamtobed -bedpe writes chromosome, start and end of one mate (columns 1–3) and of the other (4–6). The fragment runs from the smaller of the two starts to the larger of the two ends, exactly as in ATAC-seq processing and peak calling (but without the Tn5 shift: here we want the fragment, not the insertion sites). $1 == $4 keeps pairs on one chromosome. (b) Median length 229 bp (H3K27me3), 252 bp (H3K4me3), 330 bp (IgG, 2 544 fragments after removing duplicates). Marked nucleosomes are cut out in their linkers, mostly as mono-nucleosomes; untethered cutting in the IgG is spread over longer, more random fragments.
C4. (a) Chromosome, start, end, total signal in the region (AUC), maximum signal, and the region where the maximum is reached. (b) SEACR with IgG: 1 115 (H3K27me3) and 135 (H3K4me3) regions; SEACR top 1%: 62 and 8; MACS3: 444 broad and 128 narrow peaks. “Top 1%” is 1% of the blocks, and these sparse bedGraphs have few blocks (980 for H3K4me3, 7 305 for H3K27me3), so it keeps only the 8 and 62 strongest; the 0.01 default was chosen for genome-wide data. (c) Duplicates were deliberately kept (marked) in the BAMs of the marks; MACS3’s default would keep one fragment per position. H3K27me3 forms broad domains, which narrow-peak calling splits into many fragments; --broad links weaker neighbouring regions into domains (Peak calling). MACS3 reports a mean fragment size of 294 bp for H3K4me3 (from the pairs).
C5. (a) ENCODE chr21: 492 H3K4me3 and 1 451 H3K27me3 regions. H3K4me3: CUT&Tag 15 790 / 17 380 = 0.91, ChIP 31 021 / 94 538 = 0.33. H3K27me3: CUT&Tag 15 294 / 45 130 = 0.34, ChIP 12 545 / 141 487 = 0.089. CUT&Tag reaches 3–4 times the FRiP with 3–5 times fewer reads. (b) H3K4me3: SEACR-IgG 135 peaks, 118 (87%) in ENCODE, 157 of 492 ENCODE peaks (32%) found, FRiP 0.94; top 1%: 8, 100%, 13 (3%), 0.26; MACS3: 128, 112 (88%), 144 (29%), 0.93. H3K27me3: SEACR-IgG 1 115, 495 (44%), 1 111 of 1 451 (77%), FRiP 0.80; top 1%: 62, 100%, 359 (25%), 0.33; MACS3 broad: 444, 269 (61%), 735 (51%), 0.59. For H3K4me3 SEACR with IgG and MACS3 agree; for H3K27me3 SEACR-IgG is the most sensitive but less precise (the deduplicated IgG is so sparse that the threshold is low), MACS3 is in between. There is no single right answer; check in a browser. (c) Each assay would be scored against peaks called from its own data, so a lenient caller or wide peaks inflate FRiP. To compare assays, count both in the same reference regions.
C6. (a) E. coli pairs: 231 (H3K27me3), 355 (H3K4me3), 75 492 (IgG): 0.008%, 0.022% and 3.55% of the libraries; scale factors 43.3, 28.2 and 0.13. The amount of E. coli DNA per reaction is roughly constant, but the IgG produces very few human fragments, so E. coli makes up a large fraction of its library. (b) No: the factor uses only the E. coli count, and all E. coli pairs of each library are in our files. (Applied to chr21 coverage it gives the same relative scaling as genome-wide.) (c) No: different antibodies have different efficiencies, so spike-in-scaled signals of two marks are not comparable. Between two samples of the same mark, check that they were made with the same enzyme batch and amount and similar cell numbers, and that replicates agree in their spike-in-normalised totals (as in B4).









Solutions — R





The R part runs in about a minute.
R1. (a) Median lengths 229 (H3K27me3), 252 (H3K4me3) and 330 bp (IgG). The mono-nucleosome peak is at ~200 bp and the di-nucleosome peak at ~390 bp for H3K27me3 (both include the 9-bp Tn5 duplication and some linker); 6% (H3K27me3), 12% (H3K4me3) and 10% (IgG) of fragments are shorter than 120 bp. (b) About 10 bp apart (the figure script estimates 10.3 bp for H3K27me3): Tn5 inserts where the DNA backbone faces outwards on the nucleosome surface, once per helical turn, so fragment ends inside a nucleosome are spaced by ~10 bp.
R2. (a) FRiP, counting each read at its centre: CUT&Tag H3K4me3 0.88, ChIP H3K4me3 0.33; CUT&Tag H3K27me3 0.23, ChIP 0.084; IgG 0.033 and input 0.032 in the H3K4me3 peaks. With no enrichment, FRiP ≈ the fraction of chr21 covered by the peaks, 0.012. (The C5 numbers are a little higher because there a fragment counts if any base overlaps a peak.) Note that both controls are 2.7 times above the uniform expectation in H3K4me3 peaks: open promoters are over-represented in both (R4). (b) Top 1% of 5-kb bins: CUT&Tag H3K4me3 0.90, ChIP 0.23; CUT&Tag H3K27me3 0.30, ChIP 0.058; IgG 0.13; input 0.031. The CUT&Tag curves stay at zero for most of the bins and rise steeply at the end (most bins are empty, a few hold most reads); the ChIP curves are close to the input’s, bending only gently.
R3. (a) Background = reads outside all ENCODE peaks per bp, assumed uniform; a peak is detected if its read count is improbable under a Poisson with that rate times its width (p < 0.001). Simple, and the same rule for both assays. (b) CUT&Tag detects 54% of the H3K27me3 peaks with 45 000 fragments; ChIP detects 23% at 45 000 reads, 47% at 90 000 and 65% at 140 000 (figure script, 5 subsamples each), so it needs about 110 000 reads, roughly 2.5 times more. (c) It finds 91% of the strongest quarter of ENCODE’s H3K4me3 peaks (78% of which are at protein-coding TSSs) and almost none (2–3%) of the two weakest quarters, which have a median of 9–14 ChIP reads and are mostly distal. Either those weak ChIP peaks are weak real H3K4me3 sites (e.g. at enhancers) that this shallow CUT&Tag library cannot reach, or part of them are ChIP background; the K562 lines of the two labs may also differ. More CUT&Tag sequencing would help only if the library has enough distinct molecules.
R4. (a) The fraction of read centres falling within ± 500 bp of the TSSs, divided by the fraction of chr21 those windows cover: 1 means no enrichment. 602 protein-coding TSS positions; 290 active (in an H3K4me3 peak, no H3K27me3 within 2 kb); 47 in H3K27me3 peaks. (b) IgG: 8.1-fold enriched at active promoters; input: 1.06. The untethered pA–Tn5 in the IgG reaction cuts where DNA is accessible, like ATAC-seq; this is the open-chromatin background of CUT&Tag. (c) No: H3K27me3 CUT&Tag is depleted at active promoters (0.25, ChIP 0.29) and 20.5-fold enriched at H3K27me3 promoters (ChIP 2.1). In this abundant-mark, high-salt dataset the open-chromatin background is swamped by the true signal. That does not rule out the bias for weak targets, low cell numbers or single cells, where the few tethered fragments compete with the same untethered background (Wang & Zhang 2021).

title: Exercise: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Where this leads

Annotation and differential binding treats spike-in normalisation for global changes, and differential analysis of peaks, for ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN/Tag alike.
Combining marks into chromatin states combines several histone marks into one annotation; CUT&Tag data of several marks can be used the same way.
Single-cell and multi-target versions (single-cell CUT&Tag, multi-CUT&Tag, nano-CT) apply the same chemistry with cell barcodes; the open-chromatin bias and the sparsity discussed here matter even more there.

title: Quiz: CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
text:
Short questions on in-situ chromatin profiling. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In one sentence each: what is cut, by what, and where, in ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag?






Answer





ChIP-seq: all chromatin is fragmented (sonication or MNase) everywhere, then the target is enriched by immunoprecipitation. CUT&RUN: protein A–MNase bound to the antibody cuts DNA next to the target in intact nuclei; the fragments diffuse out. CUT&Tag: protein A–Tn5 bound to the antibody cuts next to the target and inserts sequencing adapters in the same step.




Q2. Why is the background of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag so much lower than that of ChIP-seq?






Answer





DNA that is not near the antibody is never cut, so it never becomes a library fragment; in ChIP-seq every piece of the genome is a fragment, and the unspecific part of the immunoprecipitation (DNA sticking to beads, tubes, antibody) is sequenced along with the target. Unbound enzyme is also washed away before it is activated.




Q3. A CUT&RUN library for a transcription factor has most fragments between 50 and 120 bp; the H3K27me3 library from the same lab peaks at 160 bp with a second peak at 330 bp. Explain both.






Answer





MNase cuts on both sides of the bound factor, close to it, so the protected fragment is short (the factor’s footprint plus a little flanking DNA). For a histone mark the enzyme cuts in the linkers around a marked nucleosome, giving mono-nucleosomal fragments (~150–200 bp) and, where a linker was not cut, di-nucleosomes (~330 bp).




Q4. In ChIP-seq, duplicates are removed routinely. Why does the Henikoff lab recommend keeping them in CUT&Tag of abundant histone marks, but removing them from the IgG?






Answer





In CUT&Tag, Tn5 tethered to the same nucleosome cuts the same linker positions in different cells, so fragments with identical coordinates can be independent molecules; removing them compresses the signal at the strongest sites. The IgG library has very few distinct molecules, so its duplicates are mostly PCR copies of the same rare fragments and would exaggerate a few random positions.




Q5. Two CUT&Tag reactions for H3K27me3 used the same pA–Tn5 batch and the same number of cells. Control: 2500 E. coli fragments; EZH2 inhibitor: 6250 E. coli fragments; both libraries have 4 million human fragments. Compute the spike-in scale factors (S = 10 000 / E. coli fragments) and the ratio of normalised H3K27me3 signal, inhibitor / control.






Answer





S = 4 for the control and 1.6 for the inhibitor. The normalised signal is fragments × S: 16 M vs 6.4 M, a ratio of 0.4, i.e. a 60% global loss of H3K27me3, which CPM normalisation would have hidden (both have 4 M fragments).




Q6. Under which condition is the E. coli carry-over DNA a valid spike-in? Name one situation in which it would mislead.






Answer





When every reaction received the same amount of E. coli DNA, i.e. the same amount of enzyme from the same batch, with comparable numbers of cells. It misleads if samples were processed with different enzyme batches or amounts, or with very different cell numbers, or if some E. coli DNA is lost differently between reactions; the scale factors then reflect handling, not biology.




Q7. Why is MACS3’s Poisson model awkward for CUT&Tag data, and what does SEACR do instead?






Answer





Most of the genome has no reads, so the background λ (genome-wide or from the sparse IgG) is very small and small piles of reads look highly significant; the control is too sparse to estimate a local λ. SEACR does not model background per position: it cuts the bedGraph into blocks of contiguous non-zero signal, computes each block’s total signal (AUC), and picks the AUC threshold at which the blocks above it are most likely to come from the target rather than the IgG (or keeps the top fraction of blocks if there is no IgG).




Q8. A CUT&Tag library for H3K27me3 has 300 000 fragments; 210 000 fall in peaks. A ChIP-seq library for the same mark has 9 million reads, 1.6 million in the same peaks. Compute both FRiPs. Which experiment needed more sequencing for the same number of reads in peaks?






Answer





CUT&Tag FRiP = 210 000 / 300 000 = 0.70; ChIP FRiP = 1.6 / 9 = 0.18. To get 210 000 reads in peaks, ChIP would need 210 000 / 0.18 ≈ 1.2 million reads, four times as many; the rest of the ChIP reads are background.




Q9. A study profiles H3K9me3 by CUT&Tag in 500 cells and reports “new H3K9me3 peaks at hundreds of active promoters”. What would you check before believing it?






Answer





Whether the promoter peaks are also in the IgG and in ATAC-seq of the same cells (Tn5’s open-chromatin bias: untethered or loosely bound pA–Tn5 inserts into accessible DNA, worst with low input and weak targets); whether high-salt washes were used; whether H3K9me3 ChIP or CUT&RUN of the same cells shows them; replicate agreement; the peak caller and its control.




Q10. Give one reason to choose CUT&RUN over CUT&Tag, and one reason to choose ChIP-seq over both.






Answer





CUT&RUN: transcription factors and other weakly bound proteins, because CUT&Tag’s high-salt washes (needed to remove free Tn5) can strip them from DNA; also less open-chromatin bias. ChIP-seq: comparison with the huge body of public ChIP-seq data (ENCODE, Roadmap) processed the same way, fixed or frozen tissue, or targets where in-situ methods have not been validated.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Compute median-of-ratios size factors by hand, and predict what a global change in accessibility or a difference in signal-to-noise does to them.
Write and explain the design matrix of a paired experiment (~ donor + celltype), and say when pairing helps.
Read an MA plot and a volcano plot of peaks, and interpret a log2 fold change and an adjusted \(p\)-value.
Turn a public peak × sample count matrix into a differential accessibility analysis in R: decode the samples, lift the peaks to GRCh38, build a SummarizedExperiment, explore, run DESeq2 with collapsed technical replicates, shrink fold changes, and compare normalisations and designs.
Annotate differential peaks with their nearest gene, check them against known markers and against RNA-seq, and save the result for Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Background
The count matrix. One row per peak (a consensus set shared by all samples), one column per library, integer counts of fragments in the peak. From here on the analysis is the RNA-seq one: DESeq2 or edgeR.
Size factors (DESeq2, median of ratios). For peak \(i\) and sample \(j\) with count \(k_{ij}\) and \(m\) samples:
\[ s_j = \operatorname{median}_i \frac{k_{ij}}{\left( \prod_{v=1}^{m} k_{iv} \right)^{1/m}} \]
Peaks with a zero in any sample are left out of the median. Normalised count = \(k_{ij} / s_j\). The assumption: the typical peak does not change. TMM (edgeR) makes the same assumption; normalising by total reads assumes the total signal per cell is the same; background-bin normalisation (csaw) assumes that reads outside peaks are constant.
Design. ~ donor + celltype fits one baseline per donor and one cell-type effect shared by all donors: the cell-type coefficient is the within-donor log2 fold change. ~ celltype ignores who is who.
FRiP (fraction of reads in peaks) = reads in peaks / all reads. Expected count in a peak ≈ depth × FRiP × (that peak’s share of the reads in peaks).
Our definition of a differential peak, used again in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting: adjusted \(p\) < 0.05 and |shrunken log2 fold change| > 1. Positive = more open in B cells (B_up), negative = more open in CD4 T cells (T_up).

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Data
ATAC-seq and RNA-seq count matrices from Corces et al. 2016 (GEO GSE74912 and GSE74246), the UCSC hg19 → hg38 liftOver chain, and the GENCODE v46 annotation. From the course repository:
data/download.sh differential-accessibility      # about 70 MB (plus the GTF, 40 MB)
mkdir -p ~/epi/diffacc && cd ~/epi/diffacc
D=/path/to/course/data                           # where download.sh put the files

corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz: columns Chr Start End (hg19, 0-based starts, 590 650 peaks of 500 bp) followed by 132 libraries (77 from healthy donors, the rest from AML patients and bulk CD34+ cells).
corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz: gene symbols × 81 RNA-seq libraries.

What the column names mean. From the GEO sample table of GSE74912 (each library is listed with its donor and cell type): Donor4983-CD4-9A-150120 is donor 4983, CD4 T cells, cell-type code 9, library A, sequenced on 2015-01-20. The early libraries have only donor and code: 4983-7A is donor 4983, code 7 (monocytes), library A. The codes are 1 HSC, 2 MPP, 3 LMPP, 4 CMP, 5 GMP, 6 MEP, 7 monocyte, 9 CD4 T cell, 10 CD8 T cell, 11 NK cell, 13 B cell, 14 CLP, 15 erythroblast. Libraries A, B (C) of the same donor and cell type are technical replicates (Corces et al. 2016, Supplementary Table 1).
Shortcuts, said plainly. We start from the authors’ count matrix, not from BAM files (counting is shown in the lecture and in ATAC-seq processing and peak calling), and the peaks were called on hg19 and are lifted to GRCh38 rather than re-called.
The R part runs in about 12 minutes in total and needs about 4 GB of memory. On the cluster, run the R part in an interactive job or wrap it in an sbatch script (Rscript diffacc.R).
