Compute the geometric mean of each row. (Hint: \(100 \cdot 200 \cdot 50 = 10^6\).)
Divide each count by its row’s geometric mean, and take the median per column. These are the size factors.
Compute the normalised counts of p4. Which peak changes, and in which sample?
Compute size factors from total counts instead (column sums, divided by their geometric mean; a calculator helps). Why is S2’s factor larger than with the median of ratios, and what does that do to p1–p3 in S2?

What is the FRiP of each library?
Normalise with the median of ratios computed on the four peaks (two samples: the ratio drug/control of the size factors is the median of the per-peak ratios). What fold change do you report for each peak?
Normalise instead by the background reads. What fold change do you report now?
Normalise by total reads. What do you get?
Give one biological and one technical explanation for the data. What extra information would let you decide between them?

B3. Paired or unpaired. Three donors give B cells and CD4 T cells (6 samples, ordered D1-T, D1-B, D2-T, D2-B, D3-T, D3-B, with CD4 T as the reference level).

Write the design matrix for ~ celltype (columns: intercept, celltypeBcell).
Write the design matrix for ~ donor + celltype (columns: intercept, donorD2, donorD3, celltypeBcell).
How many residual degrees of freedom does each model have? What does the intercept mean in (b)?
In the toy figure of the lecture, the paired test wins clearly. In the real data, 47 peaks have a significant donor effect and the paired model finds fewer differential peaks (36 703 vs 41 671 at padj < 0.05). Explain both observations. Which model would you report, and why?

B4. Technical replicates. Donor 5483 has two B-cell libraries, A and B, with 120 and 80 fragments in a peak.

What count goes into the collapsed sample?
A colleague instead keeps A and B as two samples in ~ celltype. How many “B-cell replicates” does the model think there are? Will the \(p\)-values be too small or too large? Why?

B5. How many reads per peak? A library has 40 million fragments and FRiP 0.25; the consensus set has 100 000 peaks.

What is the mean number of fragments per peak?
Another library has 10 million fragments and FRiP 0.4. Mean per peak? Which library gives more information per peak?
A peak gets 5 fragments in a sample. Ignoring biological variation (Poisson), what is the relative standard deviation of that count? Would you trust a 4-fold difference between 5 and 20 fragments in two single samples?

B6. Read the MA plot. Look at the MA plots in the lecture (MLE on the left, apeglm-shrunk on the right).


Why do the MLE fold changes fan out to ±8 at the left of the plot?
Why does shrinkage change the left of the plot much more than the right?
Where is the centre of the grey cloud? What would you suspect if it were at +0.7?
Are there coloured points with small mean counts on the right panel? Why are there few?

Which peaks are differential by our definition, and in which direction?
How many times more open is peak a in CD4 T cells than in B cells?
Peak c is significant but not differential by our definition. Is it “not changed”? What would you write about it?
Why is peak b’s MLE fold change so large, and why is it not significant?

B8. Judge the claim. A paper reports: “Peaks more open in B cells are near genes such as PAX5 and CD79A, so these peaks drive B-cell gene expression. Moreover, 30% of B-specific peaks are near genes that are not more expressed in B cells, showing that accessibility and expression are uncoupled.”
Give two reasons why the first sentence overstates what was shown, and two reasons why a B-specific peak can sit next to a gene that is not differentially expressed.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the count matrix
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | head -30
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | grep -c .
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | grep -E -- '-(Bcell|CD4)-'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -3 | cut -f1-6
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | awk '{ w[$3 - $2]++ } END { for (k in w) print k, w[k] }'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | head -25

How many columns, and how many libraries? Which B-cell and CD4 T-cell libraries are there, and from which donors? Which donors have both?
Are the coordinates 0-based or 1-based? (Use the widths.)
Which chromosomes are present? Which are absent, and what would that mean for comparing male and female donors?



C2 — Reads in peaks for one library, and the peaks as BED
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | awk -F'\t' '
  NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Donor1022-Bcell-13-150120") c = i; next }
  { s += $c; if ($c == 0) z++ }
  END { print "column", c, "reads in peaks", s, "peaks with 0 reads", z }'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -f1-3 > corces_hg19.bed
head -2 corces_hg19.bed

How many reads in peaks does the B-cell library of donor 1022 have, and in how many peaks does it have no read at all?
Why do so many peaks have zero reads in a B-cell library? (Where were the peaks called?)

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
section: Explore: normalisation under a global change
text:
Explore: normalisation under a global change
The demo simulates 3 control and 3 treated libraries (about 2 million reads each) over 2000 peaks, 2000 background bins and a spike-in added in a fixed amount per cell. Because the simulation knows how much material each cell had, it can show the true size factor of every library (red lines in panel b). Scenario sets the biology: a fraction of the peaks changes by a common log2 fold change (a global loss, as for H3K27me3 after an EZH2 inhibitor, or a global gain, as for a drug that opens chromatin everywhere), and 100 peaks are always truly up 4-fold. Extra background in treated adds unenriched DNA to the treated libraries (dead cells, a poorer transposition or IP): their FRiP drops without any change in the cells. Normalise by picks the size factors: total reads, median of ratios on the peaks (DESeq2), TMM on the peaks (edgeR), median of ratios on the background bins (csaw-like), or spike-in reads. Panel (a) is the MA plot, coloured by the simulated truth; solid points are called at BH 5% (a moderated t-test on log counts, simpler than DESeq2), and red rings are false calls. Panel (b) counts the calls.



E1. Start with no global change. Click through the five normalisations. How close are the size factors to the true ones (red lines), and how many true and false calls does each give?
E2. Click global loss (EZH2 inhibitor): 90% of the peaks drop to 25% (log2 FC −2). With the median of ratios, where does the cloud of truly changed peaks sit in the MA plot, how many peaks are called down, and how many false calls up are there? Where are the 190 unchanged peaks? Compare the size factors of T1–T3 with the true ones. Then switch to TMM, total reads, background bins and spike-in.
E3. Click noisier treated libraries only: no peak changes except the 100 truly up ones, but the treated libraries carry twice as much background. Read the FRiP of each library. Which normalisations now give hundreds of false calls, and in which direction? Why is the error larger with background bins than with total reads?
E4. Click loss + noisier libraries. Which normalisation still gives the right answer? Which assumption does each of the others break? This unit is ATAC-seq, but Annotation and differential binding makes the same argument for ChIP-seq: what would a peak-based normalisation report for an H3K27me3 ChIP after EZH2 inhibition, and what does the experiment need?






Solutions





E1. With no global change all five agree with the truth to within a few percent (the spike-in factors scatter most, because of the 5% pipetting error simulated for each sample) and all find the 100 truly up peaks, with at most one false call. When nothing global happens and FRiP is similar, the choice of normalisation hardly matters.
E2. Median of ratios assumes that the typical peak is unchanged. Here the typical peak did change, so the method makes it unchanged: the 1710 truly lost peaks sit around log2 FC 0 (median log2 FC of all peaks −0.07), only 6 are called down, and the 190 unchanged peaks are pushed up to about +2, giving 191 false calls up (the 100 truly up peaks now sit at +4). The treated size factors (0.74, 0.44, 0.61) are about half the true ones (1.43, 0.85, 1.18). TMM makes the same assumption and gives the same answer (191 false up). Spike-in and background bins recover the truth: 1708 of 1810 changed peaks called down, 100 true up, one false call. Total reads lands in between (1706 down, 16 false up, median log2 FC −1.78 instead of −2): the loss also lowers FRiP from 29% to 16–19%, so the total is only partly driven by the peaks.
E3. FRiP is 29% in the control libraries and 17–20% in the treated ones. Median of ratios, TMM and spike-in are right (no false calls). Total reads gives 1675 false calls down and background bins 1823. With more background, a treated library spends fewer reads in peaks, so per total read its peaks look lower. Background bins are worse because their assumption (background is the same in every library) is exactly what was broken: the treated size factor follows the inflated background, and every peak is pushed down by the full factor 2.
E4. Only the spike-in is right (1707 down, 100 up, 2 false up): it counts reads per cell, whatever happens to the peaks or the background. Median of ratios and TMM assume most peaks are unchanged (189 false up, 5 down); total reads and background bins assume the background per cell is the same (132 and 185 false down). For ChIP-seq this is the case of the Annotation and differential binding lecture: after an EZH2 inhibitor, peak-based normalisation hides the loss of H3K27me3 and makes the few unchanged sites look gained; an IP that worked less well behaves like the extra background here. Plan spike-in chromatin (ChIP-Rx) before the experiment, or measure the total amount of the mark (western blot, mass spectrometry). For ATAC-seq, spike-ins are not yet routine, so think about whether a global change is plausible and report how the result depends on the normalisation (R7).

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
In R
You need DESeq2, edgeR, apeglm, GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, data.table, ggplot2 and ggrepel (see Install the software you need).
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer)
  library(SummarizedExperiment); library(DESeq2); library(edgeR); library(ggplot2); library(ggrepel)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Load and decode the samples
atac <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz"))        # about 5 s
dim(atac)
cn <- names(atac)[-(1:3)]
healthy <- grep("^(Donor)?[0-9]+-", cn, value = TRUE)
re <- "^(?:Donor)?([0-9]+)-(?:[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*-)?([0-9]+)([A-C]?)(?:-[0-9]+)?$"
m  <- regmatches(healthy, regexec(re, healthy, perl = TRUE))
code2type <- c(`1` = "HSC", `2` = "MPP", `3` = "LMPP", `4` = "CMP", `5` = "GMP", `6` = "MEP",
               `7` = "Mono", `9` = "CD4", `10` = "CD8", `11` = "NK", `13` = "Bcell",
               `14` = "CLP", `15` = "Ery")
samples <- data.frame(sample = healthy, donor = sapply(m, `[`, 2),
                      celltype = unname(code2type[sapply(m, `[`, 3)]), rep = sapply(m, `[`, 4))
table(samples$celltype, samples$donor)

Explain the regular expression piece by piece. Which part captures the donor, the cell-type code and the replicate letter? Why must the optional cell-type word start with a letter? (Try what happens to Donor7256-1A-110614 if it may start with a digit.)
How many healthy libraries, donors and cell types are there? Which donors have both B cells and CD4 T cells?
Which columns did grep leave out, and what are they?



R2 — Lift the peaks to GRCh38
gr19 <- GRanges(atac$Chr, IRanges(atac$Start + 1, atac$End))
chainf <- tempfile(fileext = ".chain")
writeLines(readLines(gzfile(file.path(D, "hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz"))), chainf)
lo <- liftOver(gr19, import.chain(chainf))
table(pmin(lengths(lo), 2))                                     # 0, 1, 2 or more pieces
keep <- which(lengths(lo) == 1)
gr38 <- unlist(lo[keep])
ok <- width(gr38) == 500 & as.character(seqnames(gr38)) == as.character(seqnames(gr19)[keep])
sum(!ok)
keep <- keep[ok]; gr38 <- gr38[ok]
names(gr38) <- sprintf("peak%06d", keep)
length(gr38)

How many peaks fail, how many split into several pieces, and how many single pieces change width or chromosome? What fraction is kept?
Why atac$Start + 1?
Why name the peaks by their row number in the original file?



R3 — A SummarizedExperiment of the eight libraries
sel <- samples[samples$celltype %in% c("Bcell", "CD4") & samples$donor %in% c("1022", "4983", "5483"), ]
cnt <- as.matrix(atac[keep, sel$sample, with = FALSE])
rownames(cnt) <- names(gr38)
cd <- DataFrame(donor = factor(sel$donor), celltype = factor(sel$celltype, levels = c("CD4", "Bcell")),
                rep = sel$rep, row.names = sel$sample)
cd$unit <- paste(cd$donor, cd$celltype, sep = "_")
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = cnt), rowRanges = gr38, colData = cd)
se
colSums(assay(se)) / 1e6
lcpm <- cpm(assay(se), log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)[rowMeans(cpm(assay(se))) >= 2, ]
round(cor(lcpm), 2)

How many reads in peaks does each library have? Which is the smallest?
What is the correlation between the technical replicates of donor 5483 (B cells; CD4 T cells)? Between the B-cell libraries of different donors? Between B and T cells?



R4 — PCA: all cell types, then our six samples
cnt_all <- as.matrix(atac[keep, samples$sample, with = FALSE])
use <- rowMeans(cnt_all) >= 10
dall <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cnt_all[use, ], data.frame(samples[, 2:3], row.names = samples$sample), ~ 1)
vall <- vst(dall, blind = TRUE)                                  # a few seconds
plotPCA(vall, intgroup = "celltype", ntop = 10000)

dds <- DESeqDataSet(se, design = ~ donor + celltype)
dds <- collapseReplicates(dds, groupby = dds$unit)
colData(dds)
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = c("celltype", "donor"))

In the PCA of all 77 libraries, which cell types group together? Is there a donor effect you can see?
After collapseReplicates, how many columns are there, and what are the counts of 5483_Bcell (compare with the two libraries in se)?
In the PCA of the six samples, what separates on PC1? On PC2?



R5 — DESeq2 with the paired design
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3, ]
nrow(dds)
system.time(dds <- DESeq(dds))
resultsNames(dds)
plotDispEsts(dds)
res <- results(dds, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)

How many peaks pass the filter? Why “≥ 10 reads in ≥ 3 samples” and not “in all 6”?
How long does DESeq() take? What is the typical dispersion (median(dispersions(dds)))? What coefficient of variation between donors is that?
How many peaks have padj < 0.05, in each direction?



R6 — Fold-change shrinkage, MA and volcano plots
system.time(shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", type = "apeglm"))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-8, 8), main = "MLE")
plotMA(shr, ylim = c(-8, 8), main = "apeglm")
cls <- ifelse(!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & shr$log2FoldChange >  1, "B_up",
       ifelse(!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & shr$log2FoldChange < -1, "T_up", "ns"))
table(cls)
vol <- data.frame(lfc = shr$log2FoldChange, p = -log10(res$padj), cls = cls)
ggplot(vol[!is.na(vol$p), ], aes(lfc, p, colour = cls)) + geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(B_up = "#2a6f97", T_up = "#e67e22", ns = "grey70"))

How many B_up and T_up peaks are there?
Compare res$log2FoldChange and shr$log2FoldChange for the peaks with baseMean < 20. What does shrinkage do to them?
How many peaks would pass |MLE log2FC| > 1 instead? Why is the difference small here?



R7 — Three normalisations
tot <- colSums(counts(dds))
y <- normLibSizes(DGEList(counts(dds)))
eff <- y$samples$lib.size * y$samples$norm.factors
sf <- rbind(DESeq2 = sizeFactors(dds), TMM = eff / exp(mean(log(eff))), total = tot / exp(mean(log(tot))))
round(sf, 2)
dt <- dds
sizeFactors(dt) <- sf["total", ]
dt <- DESeq(dt, quiet = TRUE)
rt <- results(dt, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
c(B_up = sum(rt$padj < 0.05 & rt$log2FoldChange > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
  T_up = sum(rt$padj < 0.05 & rt$log2FoldChange < -1, na.rm = TRUE))
c(DESeq2 = median(res$log2FoldChange, na.rm = TRUE), total = median(rt$log2FoldChange, na.rm = TRUE))

Compare the three rows of size factors. Which libraries differ most between the median-of-ratios and the total-count factors?
How many peaks are differential (here with the MLE fold change) with total-count normalisation? Compare with sum(res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > 1, na.rm = TRUE) and the same for < -1.
What is the median log2 fold change under each normalisation? What would have to be true for the total-count result to be the right one?



R8 — Paired vs unpaired
du <- dds
design(du) <- ~ celltype
du <- DESeq(du, quiet = TRUE)
ru <- results(du, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
c(paired = sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), unpaired = sum(ru$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  both = sum(res$padj < 0.05 & ru$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
c(paired = median(dispersions(dds)), unpaired = median(dispersions(du)))
dl <- DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ celltype, quiet = TRUE)
sum(results(dl)$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

Which design finds more peaks? How much do the two lists overlap?
How many peaks have a significant donor effect (LRT)? Relate this to B3d.



R9 — Nearest gene and marker genes
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), feature.type = "transcript")
tss <- unique(resize(gtf[gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding"], width = 1, fix = "start"))
mcols(tss) <- mcols(tss)["gene_name"]
dn <- distanceToNearest(rowRanges(dds), tss, ignore.strand = TRUE)
ann <- data.frame(peak = rownames(dds), gene = tss$gene_name[subjectHits(dn)], dist = mcols(dn)$distance,
                  lfc = shr$log2FoldChange, padj = res$padj, cls = cls)
tapply(ann$dist <= 1000, ann$cls, mean)
mk <- c("PAX5", "CD79A", "MS4A1", "CD19", "EBF1", "BLK", "CD3E", "BCL11B", "TCF7", "LEF1", "GATA3", "CD28")
t(sapply(mk, function(g) table(factor(ann$cls[ann$gene == g], levels = c("B_up", "T_up", "ns")))))
head(ann[order(ann$padj), ], 10)

What fraction of B_up, T_up and non-differential peaks lie within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS? Why are differential peaks depleted at promoters?
Do the B-cell markers have B_up peaks and the T-cell markers T_up peaks? Which marker has peaks in both directions?
Look at the 10 most significant peaks. How far are they from their nearest TSS? Would you name these genes in a paper as “targets”?



R10 — Does it agree with RNA-seq?
rna <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz"))
rc <- as.matrix(rna[, -1]); rownames(rc) <- rna[[1]]
rcol <- grep("-(Bcell|CD4Tcell)$", colnames(rc), value = TRUE)
rcd <- data.frame(donor = factor(sub("-.*", "", rcol)),
                  celltype = factor(ifelse(grepl("Bcell", rcol), "Bcell", "CD4"), levels = c("CD4", "Bcell")),
                  row.names = rcol)
ddr <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(rc[, rcol], rcd, ~ donor + celltype)
ddr <- DESeq(ddr[rowSums(counts(ddr) >= 10) >= 2, ], quiet = TRUE)
rr <- results(ddr, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4")
ann$rna <- rr$log2FoldChange[match(ann$gene, rownames(rr))]
tapply(ann$rna, ann$cls, median, na.rm = TRUE)
prom <- ann$cls != "ns" & ann$dist <= 1000 & !is.na(ann$rna)
dist <- ann$cls != "ns" & ann$dist >  1000 & !is.na(ann$rna)
c(promoter = cor(ann$lfc[prom], ann$rna[prom], method = "spearman"),
  distal   = cor(ann$lfc[dist], ann$rna[dist], method = "spearman"))
ggplot(ann[prom, ], aes(lfc, rna, colour = cls)) + geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  geom_text_repel(data = ann[prom & ann$gene %in% mk, ], aes(label = gene), colour = "black")

Which donors are in the RNA-seq comparison? Are they the same as in the ATAC comparison?
What is the median RNA log2 fold change of the genes nearest to B_up, T_up and non-differential peaks?
Why is the correlation higher for promoter peaks than for distal peaks?



R11 — Save the result
tab <- data.frame(peak_id = rownames(dds), chr = as.character(seqnames(dds)), start = start(dds), end = end(dds),
                  baseMean = res$baseMean, log2FoldChange = shr$log2FoldChange, lfcSE = shr$lfcSE,
                  log2FoldChange_mle = res$log2FoldChange, pvalue = res$pvalue, padj = res$padj,
                  nearest_gene = ann$gene, dist_to_tss = ann$dist, class = cls)
write.table(tab, "differential_peaks.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
table(tab$class)
The file has one row per tested peak (GRCh38, 1-based closed coordinates as in GRanges, 500 bp). Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting starts from it.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — size factors (B1, B2, R7)





Geometric mean of three numbers = cube root of their product. With two samples, the median of the per-peak ratios S2/S1 is the ratio of the two size factors. Normalised count = count / size factor. The DESeq2 vignette explains size factors; TMM is in normLibSizes (formerly calcNormFactors) and Robinson & Oshlack 2010; background bins in the csaw book.









Hint 2 — design matrices (B3, R5, R8)





model.matrix(~ donor + celltype, data) prints the matrix in R. Residual degrees of freedom = samples − columns. The intercept in ~ donor + celltype is the reference donor in the reference cell type. DESeq2 vignette: multi-factor designs; the likelihood ratio test compares a full and a reduced design.









Hint 3 — replicates (B4, R3, R4)





collapseReplicates sums the counts of columns with the same groupby value. A SummarizedExperiment holds the matrix, the row ranges and the sample table together (vignette); DESeqDataSet(se, design) turns it into a DESeq2 object.









Hint 4 — Poisson and depth (B5)





For a Poisson count with mean \(\lambda\) the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), so the relative SD is \(1/\sqrt{\lambda}\). Real replicates add biological variation on top (the dispersion).









Hint 5 — MA plots, shrinkage and results (B6, B7, R6)





plotMA, lfcShrink with type = "apeglm" (Zhu et al. 2019). A log2 fold change of \(-2.3\) is a ratio of \(2^{-2.3}\). Shrinkage changes fold changes, not \(p\)-values.









Hint 6 — liftOver and annotation (R2, R9)





rtracklayer::liftOver returns a GRangesList; lengths() gives the number of pieces per peak. import.chain needs an uncompressed chain file. distanceToNearest gives the nearest TSS, as in Genomic intervals. The UCSC liftOver documentation explains the chain files.









Hint 7 — reading the data (C1, C2, R1)





The GEO sample list of GSE74912 gives donor and cell type for every library. data.table::fread reads gzipped files directly. In the regular expression, (?:...) is a group that is not captured, ? makes it optional; see ?regex in R.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) p1: \((10^6)^{1/3} = 100\); p2: \((64\,000)^{1/3} = 40\); p3: \((2.7 \times 10^7)^{1/3} = 300\); p4: \((64\,000)^{1/3} = 40\). (b) Ratios S1: 1, 1, 1, 0.5 → median (of four: the mean of the middle two) 1. S2: 2, 2, 2, 8 → 2. S3: 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.25 → 0.5. (c) p4 normalised: 20, 160, 20. p4 is 8-fold more open in S2; p1–p3 are identical in all samples after normalisation. (d) Column sums 460, 1200, 230; geometric mean \((460 \cdot 1200 \cdot 230)^{1/3} \approx 503\); factors 0.92, 2.39, 0.46. S2’s total includes the extra reads in p4, so its factor is too large: p1–p3 in S2 become \(200/2.39 = 84\) instead of 100, a false 16% decrease, and p4’s increase shrinks from 8-fold to about 6.1-fold (21.9 in S1, 134 in S2). One strongly changing peak drags the total; the median ignores it.
B2. (a) Control FRiP \(500/1000 = 0.5\); drug \(800/1000 = 0.8\). (b) Per-peak ratios drug/control are all 1.6, so the size-factor ratio is 1.6, and every normalised fold change is 1: no differential peak. (c) Background ratio \(200/500 = 0.4\); normalised fold change \(1.6/0.4 =\) 4 for every peak: a global 4-fold opening. (d) Totals are equal (1000), so the fold change is the raw 1.6. (e) Biological: the drug opens chromatin everywhere (e.g. an HDAC inhibitor), so the true answer is close to (c). Technical: the control library has more background (more dead or damaged cells, worse transposition), so its peaks look weaker; then (b) is right and the “opening” is an artefact. To decide: QC per library (TSS enrichment, fragment-size distribution, mitochondrial fraction, FRiP across replicates), a spike-in (a fixed number of foreign nuclei per sample), or an orthogonal measurement (e.g. imaging of chromatin compaction, or a set of loci known not to change).
B3. (a)

\(6 - 2 = 4\) and \(6 - 4 = 2\). In (b) the intercept is the (log) level of donor D1’s CD4 T cells; donorD2 is how much D2 differs from D1 in both cell types; celltypeBcell is the B vs T log2 fold change within a donor.
Pairing removes donor-to-donor variation that both cell types share, but costs one parameter per extra donor. In this dataset (sorted cells from healthy adults) donors differ little, so the gain is small and the loss of 2 of 4 residual degrees of freedom dominates: fewer hits. Report the paired model: it is the design of the experiment, chosen before seeing results; choosing the model that gives more hits is a form of \(p\)-hacking. With patients or donors that differ more (genotype, age, treatment), pairing usually gains a lot.

B4. (a) \(120 + 80 = 200\). (b) Four B-cell “replicates” instead of three (the model thinks 5483 is two people). The variance between technical replicates is smaller than between people, so the dispersion is underestimated and the \(p\)-values are too small (pseudo-replication). Also, donor 5483 gets double weight.
B5. (a) \(40 \times 10^6 \times 0.25 / 10^5 = 100\). (b) \(10 \times 10^6 \times 0.4 / 10^5 = 40\). The first: depth beats FRiP here (100 vs 40 reads per peak), although the second library is cleaner. (c) \(1/\sqrt{5} \approx 0.45\): 45%. Between 5 and 20 the Poisson noise alone is large (and biological variation adds to it); a 4-fold difference between two single samples at this depth is weak evidence. This is what dispersion estimation and shrinkage handle.
B6. (a) Few reads: a peak with 0 vs 3 fragments has an MLE fold change that is huge and poorly determined. (b) apeglm shrinks in proportion to the uncertainty: weak peaks have large standard errors and are pulled to 0; strong peaks are well measured and keep their fold change. (c) At 0. A centre at +0.7 means the typical peak looks 1.6-fold more open in B cells: either a global difference (B cells more open overall) that peak-based normalisation should have removed (so check the normalisation), or a normalisation computed on a different set of peaks than the one plotted. (d) Few: a peak needs enough reads to reach |shrunk LFC| > 1 and padj < 0.05; weak peaks are shrunk below 1 or not significant.
B7. (a) a: T_up (padj tiny, shrunk −2.3); d: B_up (padj 0.02, shrunk 2.6). b and c are not. (b) \(2^{2.3} \approx 4.9\) times more open in CD4 T cells. (c) No: it is significantly more open in B cells, by about \(2^{0.7} \approx 1.6\)-fold. It fails only our effect-size threshold. Write “modestly more accessible (1.6-fold, padj 0.001)” if it matters; the threshold is a convention for making lists, not a test of “no change”. (d) baseMean 4: a few reads, so the MLE is noisy and huge; the standard error is also huge, so the Wald test is not significant and apeglm shrinks it to 0.4.
B8. First sentence: “near” a gene is not “regulating” it (the nearest gene is a guess, often wrong for distal elements); and correlation of accessibility and expression is not causation (“drive” needs perturbation, e.g. CRISPR deletion or inhibition of the element). A B-specific peak next to a non-DE gene: the peak regulates a different, more distant gene; the gene is expressed in both cell types from other elements; the element is primed (open before expression starts, or a repressor binds); or the gene is not expressed in either because another factor is missing. 30% non-concordance is therefore expected, not evidence of “uncoupling”.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 135 columns: Chr Start End and 132 libraries. B cells: Donor1022-Bcell-13-150120, Donor4983-Bcell-13A-150120, Donor5483-Bcell-13A-150305, Donor5483-Bcell-13B-150305. Donors 1022, 4983 and 5483 have both; 2596 has CD4 T cells only. (b) Every peak has End − Start = 500 (590 650 peaks), so the file uses BED-style 0-based starts, from summit − 250 to summit + 250. (c) chr1–22 and chrX (chr1 has the most peaks, 51 405; chr21 the fewest, 6887). No chrY and no chrM: the authors removed them (chrM reads are a known ATAC artefact). Without chrY, male and female donors differ only on chrX, where one X is inactive in females; a donor’s sex can still create chrX differences, which the paired design absorbs.
C2. (a) Column 27; 4 650 539 reads in peaks; 46 335 peaks with no read at all. (b) The peaks were called on all 13 cell types (and AML samples) together, so many are elements open only in other cell types (e.g. erythroid or myeloid enhancers).

Run times are from one server core; a laptop is 1.5–3 times slower.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Where this leads

Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting reads differential_peaks.tsv, extracts the sequences of B_up and T_up peaks (GRCh38) and asks which transcription factor motifs are enriched, using the ns peaks as background.
Linking regulatory elements to genes replaces “nearest TSS” (R9) with contacts and activity, and returns to the RNA concordance (R10).
Experimental design and QC covers spike-ins and FRiP, the tools for deciding between the normalisations in B2 and R7.
Single-cell ATAC (ArchR, Signac) uses the same consensus peaks and counts, summed over cells of a type (“pseudobulk”) for differential tests.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Corces et al. 2016, Nat Genet. Lineage-specific and single-cell chromatin accessibility charts human hematopoiesis and leukemia evolution.
Love, Huber & Anders 2014, Genome Biol. Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2.
Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Nature. Differential oestrogen receptor binding is associated with clinical outcome in breast cancer.
Lun & Smyth 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. csaw: a Bioconductor package for differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data using sliding windows.
Robinson & Oshlack 2010, Genome Biol. A scaling normalization method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

title: Quiz: differential accessibility
text:
Short questions on count matrices, normalisation, design and interpretation of differential accessibility. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In RNA-seq the features to count come from a GTF file. Where do the features come from in a differential accessibility analysis, and why must all samples be counted in the same set?






Hint





Think about what happens to a peak that was called in sample 1 but not in sample 2.









Answer





From the data: peaks called in the samples and combined into one consensus set (merged, or fixed-width around summits). Every sample must be counted in the same regions, otherwise rows do not correspond: a peak missing from one sample’s own peak list still has reads there (maybe fewer), and those reads are exactly what the test needs. A peak “absent” from a sample’s peak calls is a low count, not a missing value.




Q2. Three samples have counts 30, 60 and 120 in peak A, and 10, 20 and 40 in peak B. Compute the geometric mean of each peak and the ratios of each count to it. If these were the only two peaks, what would the size factors be?






Hint





\(30 \cdot 60 \cdot 120 = 216\,000 = 60^3\).









Answer





Peak A: geometric mean 60, ratios 0.5, 1, 2. Peak B: \((8000)^{1/3} = 20\), ratios 0.5, 1, 2. The medians are 0.5, 1 and 2: these are the size factors. After normalisation both peaks are identical across samples (60 and 20).




Q3. A treatment opens chromatin at almost every peak by about 2-fold, and the libraries are sequenced to the same depth. You run DESeq2 with default size factors. What do you expect to see in the MA plot, and why?






Answer





A cloud centred at log2 fold change 0 and few differential peaks. The median-of-ratios size factors assume that the typical peak does not change, so they absorb the global 2-fold opening (the treated sample gets a larger size factor). Only peaks that change more or less than the typical peak appear as differential, and with a shrunken effect. To see the global change you need a reference that does not change with the treatment: background bins (if the background is constant), a spike-in, or known invariant regions.




Q4. Library 1 has 30 million fragments and FRiP 0.30; library 2 has 30 million fragments and FRiP 0.15. Both come from the same cell type. What is the expected ratio of counts in a typical peak? Would you normalise by total fragments or within peaks, and why?






Answer





\(30 \times 0.30 = 9\) M vs \(30 \times 0.15 = 4.5\) M fragments in peaks: a typical peak has 2 times more fragments in library 1. Same cell type, so the difference in FRiP is most likely technical (signal-to-noise of the library), and normalising within peaks (median of ratios, TMM, or reads in peaks) is right. Total-fragment normalisation would make every peak look 2-fold more open in library 1.




Q5. Three donors each give a treated and an untreated sample. Write the DESeq2 design formula. What is the meaning of the coefficient you test, and how many residual degrees of freedom are there?






Answer





~ donor + treatment (the variable of interest last). The treatment coefficient is the log2 fold change treated vs untreated within a donor, averaged over donors. Six samples, four coefficients (intercept, two donor terms, treatment): \(6 - 4 = 2\) residual degrees of freedom.




Q6. Donor 5483 has two B-cell ATAC libraries made from the same sorted cells (A and B). What should you do with them before DESeq2, and what goes wrong if you treat them as two biological replicates?






Answer





They are technical replicates: sum their counts into one sample (collapseReplicates). Treated as two donors, they make the variance between donors look smaller than it is (two libraries of one person agree better than two people do), so dispersions are underestimated and \(p\)-values too small: pseudo-replication. The donor also gets twice the weight.




Q7. A peak has baseMean 3, MLE log2 fold change 5.8 and padj 0.4; after apeglm shrinkage its log2 fold change is 0.3. Another has baseMean 900, log2 fold change −1.6 (shrunk −1.6), padj \(10^{-12}\). Interpret both.






Answer





The first has very few reads: the 5.8 is a noisy estimate (e.g. 0 vs 4 fragments), not significant, and shrinkage pulls it towards 0 because its standard error is large. No evidence of a difference. The second is well measured: \(2^{1.6} \approx 3\) times less accessible in the numerator group (more open in the reference group), highly significant; shrinkage does not change it. With the threshold padj < 0.05 and |LFC| > 1 it is differential.




Q8. In the B vs CD4 T-cell comparison, 8% of B-specific peaks but 20% of all tested peaks lie within 1 kb of a TSS. Explain the difference. What does it imply for linking differential peaks to genes?






Answer





Promoters tend to be accessible in many cell types (housekeeping and poised promoters), so they are less often differential; cell-type-specific regulation is mostly in distal enhancers. Most differential peaks therefore have no gene of their own: “nearest gene” is a guess, often tens or hundreds of kb away, and the true target may be a more distant gene contacted in 3D. Use the nearest gene as a label, not as a conclusion.




Q9. You use the Corces peaks, which were called on hg19, with a GRCh38 gene annotation. What must you do first, and what can go wrong?






Answer





Lift the peaks to GRCh38 with liftOver (chain file hg19ToHg38). Some peaks fail to map (deleted or rearranged regions: 159 of 590 650 here), some split into pieces (1375) or change width; drop those. Without lifting, bedtools or GenomicRanges would happily overlap hg19 peaks with hg38 genes and give wrong nearest genes, with no error message (Genomic intervals).




Q10. A study compares ATAC-seq of tumour and normal tissue from different patients, with tumours sequenced in 2019 and normal tissue in 2022. It reports 40 000 differential peaks with DESeq2 default normalisation. Name two problems with the design and one with the normalisation.






Answer





Design: (1) condition is confounded with batch (year of sequencing), so batch effects cannot be separated from tumour vs normal; (2) samples are unpaired (different patients) and tissues are mixtures of cell types: differences in cell-type composition (immune infiltration, stroma) appear as differential peaks. Normalisation: tumours often have different global accessibility and different signal-to-noise (FRiP) from normal tissue; peak-based size factors assume most peaks do not change, which may not hold, and a global difference would be hidden or distorted. Check FRiP and the MA plot, and compare with another normalisation.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
About this lecture

ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag measure different things, but they all hand you the same raw material: DNA fragments from enriched regions, read by a sequencer. This lecture is the shared processing that turns those reads into a signal track you can trust.

Reads: FASTQ, base qualities, adapters, trimming.
Alignment: bowtie2, SAM/BAM, FLAGs, MAPQ and multi-mapping reads.
Filtering: duplicates, the blacklist, chrM, the order of the steps.
Coverage: read extension, CPM and RPGC, fold change over input, with deepTools.
Real data throughout: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq and its input, chr21.


Students have done RNA-seq, so FASTQ and BAM are not new; what is new is everything that comes after alignment when there is no gene annotation to count on. The running example is the ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq experiment ENCSR000DZN (replicate 1) and its input control, restricted to chr21 so that every command runs in seconds; students run exactly this chain in the exercise. The same chain, with a few assay-specific additions (Tn5 shift, fragment sizes, chrM), is reused in the ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag units. Peak calling is not here: it has its own units. At the end we compare our home-made track with the one ENCODE made from the same data.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Three assays, one kind of data
text:
Three assays, one kind of data


ChIP: crosslink, shear, pull down with an antibody. ATAC: Tn5 cuts open DNA. CUT&Tag: an antibody tethers Tn5 to the target.
Each gives fragments, more of them at the target than elsewhere. We sequence one end (single-end) or both ends (paired-end) of each fragment.
Processing: find where each fragment came from, keep the trustworthy ones, count how many cover each position, compare with the background.


This is the key abstraction of the unit: the biology differs, the data have the same shape. In RNA-seq, reads come from transcripts, and the question is how many per gene. Here, reads come from fragments of genomic DNA, and the question is where in the genome they pile up more than expected. The “background” fragments are important: in ChIP they come from non-specific pull-down and open chromatin; in ATAC from Tn5 cutting anywhere accessible. Everything in this lecture is about separating enrichment from background and artefacts. The details of each assay come in the ATAC, ChIP and CUT&Tag units.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
FASTQ and base quality


Four lines per read: name, sequence, +, quality. Each quality character encodes Q = −10 log10(perror).
Q20 = 1 error in 100, Q30 = 1 in 1000. To decode: ASCII code − offset (33 today, 64 in old Illumina files like this one).


Work through the example on the slide: the character e has ASCII code 101; this 2011 file uses the old Phred+64 encoding, so Q = 37 and the error probability is 10 to the minus 3.7, about 2 in 10 000. The L near the end is Q12, about 6% error. Always check the encoding of old public data: if you read a +64 file as +33, every base looks like Q60–70, which is impossible, and a tool may silently accept it. In the exercise students convert the file to +33 with a one-line Perl tr before trimming. fastp has a –phred64 option, but with fastp 0.23.4 we got different filter counts from run to run with it, so we convert explicitly: one more reason to look at the data rather than trust flags. Modern Illumina instruments also bin qualities into a few values (e.g. 2, 12, 23, 37), so do not expect a smooth spectrum.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Real data: quality along the read
text:
Real data: quality along the read


CTCF ChIP (36 bp, 2011): median Q38, mean Q37 at the start, Q35 at the last base. Input (28 bp, 2009): mean Q27 falling to Q24; at the last base 16% of bases are below Q20.
Quality falls along the read: the sequencing chemistry loses phase cycle by cycle. A few bad bases are tolerated by the aligner; bad tails are trimmed.


These plots come from the first 100 000 reads of each FASTQ file (make-enrichalign-figs.R), the same thing fastp and FastQC show in their reports. The input library is older (2009, Illumina GA) and clearly worse: shorter and lower quality. That matters later: 28 bp reads are less often unique in the genome. A caveat that applies to all course data: these reads were selected because ENCODE could align them to chr21 or chrM, so reads too bad to align are already missing. Real raw data look a bit worse than this.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Adapters and read-through


If the fragment is shorter than the read, the sequencer reads on into the adapter. The adapter part matches nothing in the genome.
Common in ATAC and CUT&Tag (fragments under 100 bp), rare in sonicated ChIP with short reads: fastp found no adapter in our 36 bp CTCF reads.
fastp detects adapters (from the data, or from the overlap of paired reads) and trims them, removes low-quality and too-short reads (tail trimming on request: --cut_right), and writes an HTML report.

fastp -w 8 -i chip.fastq.gz -o chip.trim.fastq.gz -h chip.fastp.html -j chip.fastp.json

In paired-end data the read-through is easy to detect without knowing the adapter: when the fragment is shorter than the read length, read 1 and read 2 overlap completely and each runs into the other’s adapter. fastp uses that overlap. For the CTCF ChIP, fastp found no adapter, and filtered 9514 of 390 097 reads (2.4%) as low quality (by default: more than 40% of bases below Q15) and 13 for too many Ns. For the input, only 348 reads were removed. Trimming matters more with end-to-end alignment (next slides): an untrimmed adapter tail forces mismatches. In the ATAC-seq unit, with 2×100 bp reads of fragments often under 100 bp, the effect is large. Other trimmers: Trim Galore (cutadapt), Trimmomatic; nf-core uses Trim Galore.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Aligning DNA is simpler than aligning RNA
text:
Aligning DNA is simpler than aligning RNA


No splicing: a read from genomic DNA aligns contiguously, with at most a few mismatches and small indels. bowtie2 or BWA-MEM, not STAR.
No annotation: every position of the genome is a possible target. The regions come from the data (peaks), not from a GTF.


Students used STAR or HISAT2, which search for split alignments across introns, or salmon, which skips alignment to the genome altogether. Neither is right here: spliced alignment would invent “introns” in DNA reads, and pseudo-alignment needs a list of transcripts. bowtie2 is the standard for short ChIP, ATAC and CUT&Tag reads; BWA-MEM is common for longer reads and is the default in nf-core/chipseq. You could use STAR with splicing switched off, but there is no reason to. What carries over from RNA-seq: the BAM format, sorting and indexing, MAPQ, samtools.

title: From reads to coverage
section: How bowtie2 finds a position: seed and extend
text:
How bowtie2 finds a position: seed and extend


Step 1: the genome is indexed once (bowtie2-build, an FM index based on the Burrows–Wheeler transform; 27 s for chr21+chrM with 8 threads, an hour or more for the whole human genome). Short substrings of the read, the seeds, are looked up exactly in the index; this is fast because the index makes exact-match lookups cheap. Step 2: each candidate locus is aligned in full with dynamic programming, scoring mismatches (penalty up to 6, less at low-quality bases) and gaps. Step 3: the best alignment is reported, and the gap between best and second best becomes MAPQ. End-to-end mode (the default) is strict: every base must align, so trim first. Local mode soft-clips ends that do not match (S in the CIGAR); it is forgiving, which is why it is popular for CUT&Tag, but it can also hide adapter problems. You do not need the algorithm for the exam; you need to know why a read in a repeat gets a low MAPQ and what soft-clipping is.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
bowtie2 on the command line
# once per genome: build the index (chr21 + chrM in this course; 27 s with 8 threads)
bowtie2-build --threads 8 hg38_chr21_chrM.fa hg38_chr21_chrM

# align, and sort by position on the way out (3 s for 380 000 reads)
bowtie2 -p 8 -x hg38_chr21_chrM -U chip.trim.fastq.gz 2> chip.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools sort -@ 4 -o chip.sorted.bam -
samtools index chip.sorted.bam          # .bai: jump to any region
samtools flagstat chip.sorted.bam       # how many mapped, paired, duplicates ...
samtools idxstats chip.sorted.bam       # reads per chromosome
380570 reads; of these: 2014 (0.53%) aligned 0 times
                        291310 (76.55%) aligned exactly 1 time
                        87246 (22.93%) aligned >1 times

Paired-end: -1 R1.fastq.gz -2 R2.fastq.gz instead of -U. The pipe avoids writing a large unsorted SAM file. “Aligned >1 times” means bowtie2 found more than one valid alignment and reported one of them: these become the low-MAPQ reads. 23% of the ChIP reads on chr21+chrM are multi-mapping; that is not a failure of the experiment, it is what 36 bp reads in a genome full of repeats look like. Only 0.5% did not align at all, much lower than in real data, because the course reads were preselected (slide on the shortcut). The 2014 unaligned reads are mostly reads that ENCODE aligned after cropping them to 28 bp, and whose last bases do not match. For whole-genome indexes, download a prebuilt one (iGenomes, the bowtie2 website) instead of building it.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
The SAM record


A real read from the ChIP BAM. Columns students must be able to read on paper: FLAG, RNAME, POS (1-based leftmost base), MAPQ and CIGAR; and for paired-end data, the mate columns and TLEN. The tags are aligner-specific: AS is this alignment’s score, XS the score of the second-best alignment (only present when there is one), NM the edit distance, MD where the mismatches are. The second tag line is an Alu read (its sequence starts with the classic Alu motif): AS = XS = −5, a tie, so MAPQ 1. A reverse-strand read is stored as the reverse complement of what the sequencer read, and POS is still the leftmost base: the read’s own 5’ end, where the fragment starts, is at POS + length − 1. That matters for extending reads and for Tn5 shifts in ATAC.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Decoding the FLAG by hand


Exam material. FLAG is a sum of powers of two, so each value decodes uniquely: subtract the largest bit that fits, repeat. 99 = 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 1, mate on the reverse strand, proper pair, paired. Its mate is 147 = 128 + 16 + 2 + 1. 83 and 163 are the same pair the other way round. Single-end reads: 0 or 16 when mapped, 4 when unmapped. With samtools: -f keeps reads with all the given bits set, -F drops reads with any of them set. -F 1804 (4 + 8 + 256 + 512 + 1024) is the ENCODE filter: drop unmapped reads, reads whose mate is unmapped, secondary alignments, QC failures and duplicates. samtools flags 1804 decodes it for you; so does the Picard “explain flags” web page.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
MAPQ and reads in repeats


About half of the human genome is repeat-derived (transposons, segmental duplications, satellites). A short read there fits several places equally well.
bowtie2 reports one of them at random, with MAPQ 0 or 1. Keep only MAPQ ≥ 30 (or ≥ 10–20 in some pipelines) for coverage tracks.


MAPQ is phred-scaled like base quality: in principle MAPQ 30 means 1 in 1000 that the position is wrong. Each aligner computes it differently: bowtie2 tops out at 42, BWA at 60, STAR uses 255 for unique. Removing multi-mappers has a cost: repeats become blind spots, with no signal at all. That is no information, not evidence of no binding. Some marks, especially H3K9me3 in heterochromatin, live mostly in repeats; there, people keep multi-mappers or distribute them with an EM algorithm. Mappability tracks (e.g. from GenMap or Umap) give, for each position and read length, whether a read starting there is unique. Longer and paired reads raise mappability.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Real data: MAPQ on chr21


Two peaks: MAPQ 0–1 (22% of ChIP reads, 25% of input reads) and MAPQ 42. Little in between.
Filtering at MAPQ ≥ 30 keeps 76% (ChIP, 36 bp) and 74% (input, 28 bp) of the reads on chr21. Shorter reads are unique less often.


The distribution is strongly bimodal: a read is either unique or not. The intermediate values are reads whose second-best alignment is somewhat worse, e.g. two copies of a repeat that differ by a few bases. The threshold therefore matters less than one might fear: 10, 20 or 30 remove almost the same reads. The input has slightly more multi-mappers on chr21 than the ChIP, partly because its reads are 8 bases shorter and partly because the ChIP reads are enriched at CTCF sites, which are mostly in unique sequence. Overall the input looks more “unique” (91% MAPQ ≥ 30 of all reads) only because two thirds of its reads are on chrM, which is unique in this reference. Keep that in mind when comparing summary numbers between libraries.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Paired-end reads and the fragment


A proper pair: the two reads face each other on opposite strands, at a plausible distance. TLEN = rightmost end − leftmost start + 1 = the fragment length.
Single-end data know only one end: the fragment length must be estimated and the reads extended.


Work through the numbers: read 1 starts at 1001, read 2 (36 bp) ends at 1200, so TLEN = 1200 − 1001 + 1 = 200, positive on the leftmost read and negative on its mate. Paired-end sequencing is now standard for ATAC and CUT&Tag because the fragment length itself is information: the ATAC nucleosome ladder, the CUT&Tag sub-nucleosomal fragments. It also helps mapping: a read in a repeat can be placed by its uniquely mapped mate. Our CTCF data are single-end, as most ChIP-seq before about 2015 was, so we estimate the fragment length later in the lecture. Filtering paired data: -f 2 keeps proper pairs; remove reads whose mate failed filtering, otherwise you get orphan reads (samtools fixmate -m and -F 1804 take care of most of this).

title: From reads to coverage
text:
PCR and optical duplicates


Library preparation includes PCR, so each original molecule can be sequenced many times. Duplicates are defined by position: same start and strand for single-end reads, same both ends for paired-end reads. Optical duplicates are a different artefact: one cluster read as two on the flow cell, recognised by being physically close. samtools markdup (or Picard MarkDuplicates) sets bit 1024 and keeps the copy with the best base qualities; with -r it removes them instead. The paired-end recipe needs name-collated input and samtools fixmate -m first: collate → fixmate -m → sort → markdup. For single-end reads, sort → markdup is enough. Why not in RNA-seq? A highly expressed gene saturates the possible start positions, so many identical starts are real; removing them would compress expression. In ChIP and ATAC, a position is covered by few independent fragments, so identical starts are mostly PCR copies, which would create fake peaks. The duplicate rate also measures library complexity: a high rate means few unique molecules (little input DNA, too many PCR cycles), discussed in Experimental design and QC.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Real data: the blacklist and chrM
text:
Real data: the blacklist and chrM


Blacklist (ENCODE exclusion list): regions with extreme signal in every experiment, input included: satellite repeats, rDNA, centromeres. 910 regions in GRCh38, 24 on chr21. Remove reads there.
chrM: many copies per cell, no nucleosomes. 14% of ChIP reads but 66% of input reads here; in ATAC often 20–80%. Remove before normalising.


Left: input reads pile up in a 520 bp blacklisted region at chr21:10.01 Mb: 451 reads where about 2 are expected from the input’s depth, and 72 ChIP reads. Here 448 of the 451 have MAPQ 1, so the MAPQ filter already removes them; elsewhere it does not: after MAPQ and duplicate filtering, the 3 kb blacklisted region at chr21:6.37 Mb still has 24 times the average input density. The blacklist catches what the other filters miss. Such regions are usually unassembled or collapsed repeats: in the reference there is one copy, in the cell there are many, so reads from all copies land on it, with high MAPQ. They produce “peaks” in every experiment and would dominate any genome-wide ranking. Amemiya, Kundaje and Boyle derived the list from large collections of input (and DNase) data, so it is assay-independent. Right: the share of aligned reads on chrM. Mitochondrial DNA is present in hundreds of copies per cell; in ATAC, Tn5 attacks it eagerly because it is not packed into nucleosomes. For a nuclear chromatin assay, chrM reads are not informative: drop them before computing CPM, otherwise a library with more chrM looks shallower. Also note NUMTs: nuclear copies of mitochondrial sequence pull mitochondrial reads into the nuclear genome, one more reason for the MAPQ filter and the blacklist.

title: From reads to coverage
section: The filtering chain, step by step
text:
The filtering chain, step by step

samtools view -b -q 30 -F 1804 -o chip.q30.bam chip.sorted.bam        # unique, mapped, primary
samtools markdup -s chip.q30.bam chip.markdup.bam                     # flag duplicates (1024)
samtools view -b -F 1024 -o chip.dedup.bam chip.markdup.bam chr21     # drop them, and chrM
bedtools intersect -v -abam chip.dedup.bam -b blacklist.bed > chip.final.bam

The real read counts from the exercise. ChIP: 390 097 raw → 197 587 final reads (51%). Input: 476 372 → 116 397 (24%), because most of its reads are chrM duplicates. Order matters. MAPQ and flag filters first, so that duplicates are judged among reads we trust. Duplicates before taking chr21: it makes no difference here, but marking on the whole BAM is the norm. Blacklist last (or any time), because it removes positions, not reads with problems. For paired-end data add -f 2 to the first step, and mark duplicates on pairs (fixmate -m first). A note on duplicates at strong peaks: in the ChIP, 49% of the reads inside the 405 chr21 CTCF peaks were flagged as duplicates, against 4% outside peaks. With single-end 36 bp reads, a 200 bp peak has only a few hundred possible start positions per strand, so at very strong peaks some “duplicates” are real independent fragments. Dedup compresses the strongest peaks; it is still the standard, because PCR copies are the bigger danger.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Single-end reads need extending


A fragment covers the binding site, but a 36 bp read covers only its first 36 bases. Fragments from the + strand are read from their left end, so their reads sit to the left of the site; fragments from the − strand are read from the right end. The result is two humps, about one fragment length apart, with the site itself in the gap. Extending each read in its own direction to the fragment length rebuilds the fragment and gives one peak on the site. For paired-end data there is nothing to estimate: deepTools uses the real fragment between the mates. The fragment length is estimated from the strand shift: MACS3 predictd pairs + and − strand peaks; the strand cross-correlation used in ENCODE QC computes the correlation of the two strands at every shift. For ATAC, the cut sites are the signal, so ATAC tracks are often built from the Tn5 insertion points (read 5’ ends, shifted), discussed in the ATAC units.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites
text:
Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites


Left: 5’ ends of + strand reads peak about 50 bp left of the CTCF summits, − strand reads about 50 bp right. Median distance between them: ≈ 100 bp = the typical fragment.
macs3 predictd estimates the same: 100 bp. Right: reads extended to 100 bp give one peak, centred on the summits.


These are the 405 ENCODE CTCF peak summits on chr21, with the filtered ChIP reads summed around them (make-enrichalign-figs.R). The medians of the 5’ end positions are −50 bp for + strand reads and +48 bp for − strand reads. The sharp inner edges at about ±18 bp are a footprint: CTCF itself protects about 20–40 bp of DNA, and fragment ends cannot fall inside the protein. 100 bp is shorter than the 150–300 bp a sonicated library usually shows on a gel; for TF ChIP the strand-shift estimate is often shorter than the gel size, because it measures the fragments that actually carry the bound protein. We therefore use –extendReads 100 in the exercise. ENCODE ran its own estimate on the full data set.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Coverage and normalisation: CPM and RPGC
text:
Coverage and normalisation: CPM and RPGC


Raw counts scale with sequencing depth. CPM divides by the number of reads (in millions): the same as CPM in RNA-seq.
RPGC (1× normalisation) scales so the genome average is 1: a value of 38.7 means 38.7 times the average coverage.
Both assume the total amount of signal is comparable between samples. A global change (a drug that removes a mark everywhere) breaks them: spike-ins, in Experimental design and QC.


In deepTools: bamCoverage –normalizeUsing CPM, BPM (like TPM: per bin, then scaled to a million), RPKM, or RPGC with –effectiveGenomeSize. CPM per bin depends on the bin size, because it is a count of reads overlapping a bin; RPGC is a per-base coverage and does not. Effective genome size: the mappable part of the genome, about 2.7–2.9 Gb for human depending on read length (deepTools documents values); in the exercise we use the non-N length of chr21, 40.1 Mb, because our BAM contains chr21 only. Exam-style calculation: 15 million reads of 200 bp fragments over 2.9 Gb gives an average depth of 1.03; a base covered by 40 fragments has RPGC 38.7. These are the RNA-seq ideas students know, with the same weakness: normalising to the total assumes most of the genome does not change. The differential-accessibility unit returns to this.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Fold change over the input


The input (same chromatin, no antibody) shows local background: copy number, open chromatin, mappability, GC bias. Dividing by it removes what ChIP and input share.
bamCompare scales both to the same depth, then reports ratio or log2 ratio per bin, with a pseudocount to avoid dividing by zero.


Background is not flat. Amplified regions, open chromatin (sheared more easily) and repeats all give more reads in the input as well as in the ChIP. Dividing by the input corrects for these. Pseudocount: with 0 input reads, the ratio is infinite; adding 1 to both counts gives log2(5/1) = 2.3 for a bin with 4 ChIP reads, and 0 for an empty bin. The pseudocount shrinks ratios of small counts towards 0, which is what you want for noisy bins. Bin size: a 10 bp bin with 0 or 1 input read gives a meaningless ratio, so ratios use larger bins (50 bp here) or smoothed input. Peak callers like MACS3 do the smarter version: a local background estimated from the input over 1 kb and 10 kb windows. That is in the peak-calling unit.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Coverage tracks with deepTools
# ChIP and input, each normalised to counts per million, reads extended to 100 bp
bamCoverage -b chip.final.bam  -o chip.cpm.bw  --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8
bamCoverage -b input.final.bam -o input.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8

# the same ChIP track as "times the average coverage" (RPGC; chr21 only, so chr21's size)
bamCoverage -b chip.final.bam -o chip.rpgc.bw --normalizeUsing RPGC \
  --effectiveGenomeSize 40088619 --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8

# ChIP over input: depth-scaled, log2 ratio in 50 bp bins, pseudocount 1
bamCompare -b1 chip.final.bam -b2 input.final.bam -o chip_vs_input.log2.bw \
  --operation log2 --scaleFactorsMethod readCount --pseudocount 1 \
  --extendReads 100 --binSize 50 -p 8

Each command takes 2–5 seconds on the chr21 BAMs; on a full human ChIP-seq BAM of 30 million reads, a few minutes. –extendReads without a number uses the mate for paired-end data. –ignoreForNormalization chrX chrM is common when the BAM still contains them. bamCompare –operation ratio gives the plain ratio, comparable with ENCODE’s fold-change track; subtract gives a difference. The output is bigWig, the indexed format from Genomic intervals, so it opens instantly in IGV. Alternatives: MACS3 writes fold-enrichment bedGraphs as part of peak calling (that is what ENCODE’s track is), and nf-core uses bedtools genomecov scaled to one million reads.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Real data: our tracks at a locus
text:
Real data: our tracks at a locus


Three CTCF sites at chr21:43.78–43.82 Mb. Our ChIP CPM track and ENCODE’s fold change agree on where the peaks are.
Our log2 ratio is noisy away from peaks: the input has only 116 000 reads on chr21, about 3 per kb. ENCODE’s track smooths the input over kilobases (MACS2 local λ).


Open these files in IGV (desktop or igv.js) in the exercise: load the bigWigs, the ENCODE peaks and the BAM itself, and zoom in on a peak to see the + and − strand reads on either side of the summit. Points to make: the input is not flat (a bump at 43.806 Mb, and some input reads at the 43.81 Mb CTCF site itself, which is common at strong open sites); the third site at 43.817 Mb is weaker in CPM but has a high ratio, because the input there is low. A ratio track is only as good as its denominator: with a shallow input, smooth it or use larger bins. ENCODE’s fold change is MACS2’s: ChIP pileup divided by a local background from the input over 1 kb and 10 kb windows (and never below the genome-wide average), and it pools two replicates.

title: From reads to coverage
section: Real data: our track against ENCODE’s
text:
Real data: our track against ENCODE’s


Mean signal in 33 287 one-kb bins on chr21 (blacklist and empty bins removed). Bins with an ENCODE peak agree well (r = 0.91); background bins much less (overall r = 0.63).
Same data, different tools and choices: the peaks are robust, the background depends on how you treat the input.


This is how you check a pipeline: compare with a trusted result on the same data. The differences have known causes: we used replicate 1 only, a fragment length of 100 bp, a 50 bp bin ratio with pseudocount 1; ENCODE pooled two replicates, cropped the ChIP reads to 28 bp (the input’s length; see the @PG line of their BAM), and used MACS2’s smoothed local background, which is why its background values sit well below 1 while ours sit around 1. Correlations computed on the log scale (Pearson); Spearman 0.60 over all bins. In the exercise students compute these numbers themselves in R.

title: From reads to coverage
section: The shortcut used in this course
text:
The shortcut used in this course


Honesty slide (design principle 10). Aligning to chr21 + chrM only is fast, but it changes the problem: a read from anywhere else in the genome has nowhere to go but chr21 or chrM, so it lands at the most similar sequence, often with a high MAPQ, because MAPQ only reflects the copies the aligner can see. We avoided most of this by giving students only the reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM against the full genome. The price: alignment rates look perfect (99.5% and 100%), multi-mappers whose other copies are on other chromosomes may get a MAPQ that is too high, and library sizes are 1–2% of the real ones (390 000 of 29.5 million ChIP reads). A real analysis aligns to the whole genome (GRCh38 analysis set, without alt contigs), on a cluster: well under an hour per sample with 8 threads for 30 million short reads. The nf-core pipelines on the next slide do exactly that.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
What the production pipelines do


nf-core/chipseq and nf-core/atacseq run the same chain at scale, with containers and a samplesheet, on a laptop, a server or a SLURM cluster. Differences from our hand-made chain: BWA as the default aligner (bowtie2 available), Picard for duplicates, a stricter filter set (also more than 4 mismatches, soft-clipped reads in ATAC, insert size over 2 kb), bigWigs scaled to a million mapped reads with bedtools, and QC that we cover in Experimental design and QC (fingerprint, strand cross-correlation, library complexity). ENCODE has its own pipeline (ENCODE TF/histone ChIP-seq pipeline) with the same logic: MAPQ 30, -F 1804, duplicates removed, blacklist filtered. Knowing the steps is what lets you read the MultiQC report and choose parameters; running the pipeline without knowing them is how mistakes go unnoticed.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Summary







step
key fact




FASTQ quality
Q = −10 log10 p; Q20 = 1% error, Q30 = 0.1%; check the offset (+33 or +64)


trimming
adapters appear when the fragment is shorter than the read; fastp


alignment
contiguous, no splicing: bowtie2 / BWA; seed and extend; end-to-end vs local


SAM
FLAG = sum of bits (99/147, 83/163, 16, 4, 1024); POS 1-based leftmost; TLEN = fragment


MAPQ
0–1 = several equal places (repeats); keep ≥ 30; repeats become blind spots


duplicates
same start (and end): PCR copies; remove for ChIP/ATAC, not RNA-seq


blacklist, chrM
remove artefact regions and mitochondrial reads before normalising


coverage
extend single-end reads to the fragment (~100 bp here); CPM, RPGC; ratio to input




Students should leave able to decode a FLAG and a quality character on paper, compute TLEN, CPM, RPGC and a fold change with a pseudocount, explain each filtering step and its order, and say what a coverage track does and does not show. Next: Experimental design and QC (replicates, controls, FRiP, fingerprints), then the ATAC and ChIP blocks, which start from the clean BAM files made here.

title: From reads to coverage
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Langmead & Salzberg 2012, Nat Methods. Fast gapped-read alignment with Bowtie 2. The aligner of this unit.
Li et al. 2009, Bioinformatics. The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools. SAM/BAM, FLAGs and MAPQ, defined.
Chen et al. 2018, Bioinformatics. fastp: an ultra-fast all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor. Adapter detection from the data and from read overlap.
Ramírez et al. 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. deepTools2: a next generation web server for deep-sequencing data analysis. bamCoverage, bamCompare and the normalisations.
Amemiya, Kundaje & Boyle 2019, Sci Rep. The ENCODE Blacklist: identification of problematic regions of the genome. How the blacklist was made, and what happens without it.
Robinson et al. 2011, Nat Biotechnol. Integrative genomics viewer. IGV.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Predict an age by hand from clock coefficients, including Horvath’s age transformation.
Fit your own epigenetic clock with the elastic net (glmnet) on public blood methylation data, choosing λ by cross-validation.
Evaluate it honestly: training vs held-out error, an external data set, and the effect of leakage.
Apply Horvath’s published clock and compute age acceleration as a residual.
Deconvolve a methylation profile against a reference atlas, as used for cell-free DNA, and compute a positive predictive value for a screening test.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Predict an age by hand from clock coefficients, including Horvath’s age transformation.
Fit your own epigenetic clock with the elastic net (glmnet) on public blood methylation data, choosing λ by cross-validation.
Evaluate it honestly: training vs held-out error, an external data set, and the effect of leakage.
Apply Horvath’s published clock and compute age acceleration as a residual.
Deconvolve a methylation profile against a reference atlas, as used for cell-free DNA, and compute a positive predictive value for a screening test.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Background
The elastic net. For people \(i\) with age \(y_i\) and CpG β values \(x_{ij}\), glmnet finds the intercept \(a\) and coefficients \(b_j\) that minimise
\[ \frac{1}{2n}\sum_i \Big(y_i - a - \sum_j b_j x_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda \Big[ \alpha \sum_j |b_j| + \frac{1-\alpha}{2} \sum_j b_j^2 \Big]. \]
α = 1 is the lasso (many coefficients exactly 0), α = 0 ridge regression (all shrunk, none 0). Clocks use α = 0.5. λ is chosen by k-fold cross-validation on the training data; the test data are used once, at the end.
Prediction is then a weighted sum: predicted age \(= a + \sum_j b_j \beta_j\).
Horvath’s transformation. Horvath’s clock predicts \(F(\text{age})\) with \(F(a) = \log(a + 1) - \log(21)\) for \(a \le 20\) and \(F(a) = (a - 20)/21\) for \(a > 20\). The inverse: if the linear predictor \(z < 0\), age \(= 21 e^{z} - 1\); otherwise age \(= 21 z + 20\).
Age acceleration is the residual of DNAm age regressed on chronological age in the data at hand: \(\text{AA}_i = \text{DNAmAge}_i - (c_0 + c_1 \cdot \text{age}_i)\).
Deconvolution. A sample’s β values are modelled as a non-negative mixture of reference profiles: \(y \approx R w\), \(w \ge 0\), solved by non-negative least squares (nnls), as in the Houseman method of Methylation arrays.
Screening. Positive predictive value (PPV) = true positives / all positives = \(\dfrac{\text{sens} \cdot p}{\text{sens} \cdot p + (1 - \text{spec})(1 - p)}\) for prevalence \(p\).

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Data
From data/prepare-meth2.sh clocks and data/prepare-meth2.sh arrays:
mkdir -p ~/epi/clocks && cd ~/epi/clocks
D=/path/to/course/data                     # where the course data are



file
what




hannum_gse40279_beta_subset.tsv.gz
Hannum et al. 2013 (GEO GSE40279): β values of 656 whole-blood samples (450k), 26 127 CpGs: the 20 000 most variable CpGs (chosen without looking at age), plus the CpGs of the Horvath clock and of the Moss atlas, plus ELOVL2 cg16867657 and FHL2 cg06639320. Columns: cpg, then one column per GEO sample


hannum_gse40279_samples.tsv
sample table: GEO accession, age, sex, ethnicity, recruitment site, plate


horvath2013_coefficients.csv
Horvath 2013, Additional file 3: intercept and 353 CpG coefficients (column CoefficientTraining)


moss2018_reference_atlas.csv
Moss et al. 2018: β of marker CpGs in 25 cell types and tissues (meth_atlas)


gse42861_idat/, gse42861_samples.tsv
the 151 rheumatoid arthritis / control arrays of Methylation arrays: our external test set



Shortcuts, said plainly. The Hannum β values are the authors’ processed values (not re-normalised from IDATs). We use a CpG subset to keep memory small; a real clock would start from all ~470 000 CpGs. The subset contains the Horvath CpGs, which Horvath selected partly using these very samples: a mild form of leakage for any clock trained on the subset, which is one reason to test on GSE42861 as well.
You need R packages data.table, glmnet, nnls, ggplot2, and (for R6–R7) minfi with IlluminaHumanMethylation450kmanifest. The R part takes about 10 minutes, mostly reading IDATs in R6, and needs about 8 GB of memory.
