title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
section: Explore: fit a clock, overfit it, leak into it
text:
Explore: fit a clock, overfit it, leak into it
The demo fits an elastic net, as in R2, to simulated data: people aged 20–80, P candidate CpGs measured with noise, of which a chosen number change linearly with age (each by 0.008–0.03 in β per decade) and the rest are pure noise. The model is fitted on N training people, along a grid of λ values (coordinate descent on standardised CpGs, as glmnet does), and evaluated on 200 test people it never saw. (a) Predicted against true age at the chosen λ: test people filled, training people as faint circles, with the median absolute errors and the number of CpGs the model uses. (b) Training and test error for every λ, the number of CpGs used at each λ (along the top), and the error of simply guessing the median training age. α moves from ridge (0) to lasso (1). The buttons can first keep only the 50 CpGs most correlated with age, chosen either in the training people or in all people (the leaky procedure of B4(a) and R5).



E1. (links to B5, R3) With the defaults (N = 100, P = 1 000, 20 age CpGs, α = 0.5, λ = 1), read the training and test error and the number of CpGs used. Move λ to the weakest penalty (0.010) and to the strongest (100). What happens to the training error, the test error and the number of CpGs? Why does the strongest penalty give the same error as guessing the median? At which λ is the test error lowest, and why should you not choose λ this way in a real analysis?
E2. (links to R4) At λ = 0.010, compare P = 20 with P = 2 000 candidate CpGs (still 20 age CpGs). Then, with P = 2 000, set N = 400 and N = 20, and read the best test error in (b) for each. What do P ≫ N and the training error have to do with each other?
E3. (links to B3) Back to N = 100, P = 1 000. Set α = 1 (lasso) and find the λ with the lowest test error: how many CpGs does the model use, and how many are age CpGs? Then set α = 0 (ridge): how many CpGs are used at any λ, and what is the best test error now?
E4. (links to B4, R5) Set α = 0.5, λ = 1, and 0 age CpGs: nothing in the data is related to age. Compare the test error and test r for no selection, in training people and in all people (leaky), and the best test error in (b) for each. Which procedure claims to predict age, and why? Finally set 20 age CpGs again and compare the leaky and the honest selection.






Solutions (E1–E4)





E1. At λ = 1: test error 6.0 years, training error 2.7 years, test r = 0.92, 145 CpGs used (18 of the 20 age CpGs and 127 noise CpGs). At λ = 0.010: training error 0.0, test error 5.8, 262 CpGs: with 1 000 CpGs and 100 people the model can fit the training ages exactly, so the training error says nothing about new people. At λ = 100: 0 CpGs, training 14.7 and test 15.1 years: every coefficient is zero, the model predicts the mean training age for everyone, which is as good as guessing the median (15.1). The test error is lowest, 5.7 years at λ = 0.32. Choosing λ by the test error uses the test people to tune the model, so 5.7 is too optimistic: λ must be chosen by cross-validation within the training set (R2), and the test set used once at the end.
E2. At λ = 0.010, P = 20: training 4.4, test 4.5 years: with 20 CpGs and 100 people the model cannot memorise, and training error is honest. P = 2 000: training 0.0, test 6.1: with far more CpGs than people, some combination of noise CpGs always fits the training ages exactly. N = 400 (P = 2 000): best test error 4.1 (at λ = 1, with all 20 age CpGs found); N = 20: best test error 12.2, hardly better than the 14.7-year guess (only 11 of the 20 age CpGs are found). When P ≫ N a zero training error is guaranteed and meaningless; only held-out error and more training samples help. Unpenalised regression on many CpGs (R4) is the extreme case.
E3. α = 1 (lasso): the best test error is 4.7 years at λ = 1.5, with 26 CpGs, of which 14 are age CpGs: the lasso keeps few CpGs and drops most of the noise. α = 0 (ridge): all 1 000 CpGs have non-zero coefficients at every λ, and the best test error is only 9.0 years: ridge shrinks but never removes the 980 noise CpGs, whose small coefficients add up to noise in the prediction. The elastic net (α = 0.5) sits in between (5.7 years, about 200 CpGs). With correlated CpGs (not simulated here) the ridge part of the elastic net would also keep groups of neighbours together (B3).
E4. With 0 age CpGs at λ = 1: no selection gives test error 16.1 years, r = 0.05; selection in the training people 16.1, r = 0.06: both are as bad as the 15.1-year guess, which is correct, because there is nothing to find. The leaky selection gives test error 11.5 years and r = 0.53 (best 10.1 in (b)): it seems to predict age from pure noise. The 50 CpGs were chosen because they happen to correlate with age in the test people too, so the test set is no longer independent of the model. With 20 age CpGs the leak still flatters the model: 4.2 years (leaky) against 5.6 (honest). Every step that looks at the outcome, including feature selection and choosing λ, must be done inside the training data.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
In R
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(glmnet); library(nnls); library(ggplot2) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
b <- fread(file.path(D, "hannum_gse40279_beta_subset.tsv.gz"))
s <- fread(file.path(D, "hannum_gse40279_samples.tsv"))
X <- t(as.matrix(b[, -1])); colnames(X) <- b$cpg          # samples x CpGs
stopifnot(identical(rownames(X), s$gsm))
age <- s$age
dim(X)

R1 — Single CpGs
r <- cor(X, age)[, 1]
r[c("cg16867657", "cg06639320")]                       # ELOVL2, FHL2
head(sort(r), 3); head(sort(r, decreasing = TRUE), 3)
sum(abs(r) > 0.5); sum(abs(r) > 0.3)
fit1 <- lm(age ~ X[, "cg16867657"])
summary(fit1)$r.squared; median(abs(residuals(fit1)))
ggplot(data.frame(age, elovl2 = X[, "cg16867657"]), aes(age, elovl2)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm")

How well does ELOVL2 alone predict age (R², median absolute error)?
How many CpGs have |r| > 0.5?



R2 — Train/test split and an elastic net
set.seed(42)
test  <- sample(nrow(X), round(0.3 * nrow(X)))
train <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), test)
cv <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], age[train], alpha = 0.5, nfolds = 10)
plot(cv)
cv$lambda.min; cv$lambda.1se
cf <- coef(cv, s = "lambda.min")[, 1]
sum(cf[-1] != 0); sum(coef(cv, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0)
head(sort(abs(cf[-1]), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

How many CpGs does the model use at lambda.min and at lambda.1se?
Is ELOVL2 among the selected CpGs? What is its coefficient, in years per unit β?



R3 — Training and test error
mae <- function(p, a) median(abs(p - a))
p_train <- predict(cv, X[train, ], s = "lambda.min")[, 1]
p_test  <- predict(cv, X[test, ], s = "lambda.min")[, 1]
c(train = mae(p_train, age[train]), test = mae(p_test, age[test]))
c(train = cor(p_train, age[train]), test = cor(p_test, age[test]))
p1se <- predict(cv, X[test, ], s = "lambda.1se")[, 1]; mae(p1se, age[test])
ggplot(data.frame(age = age[test], pred = p_test), aes(age, pred)) + geom_point() + geom_abline(linetype = 2)

Report training and test errors. Why do they differ?
How much worse is the 36-CpG model (lambda.1se) on the test set?



R4 — Overfitting without a penalty
rt <- cor(X[train, ], age[train])[, 1]
ols <- function(k, sel = rt) {
  g <- names(sort(abs(sel), decreasing = TRUE))[1:k]
  f <- lm.fit(cbind(1, X[train, g]), age[train]); bb <- f$coefficients; bb[is.na(bb)] <- 0
  c(k = k, train = mae(cbind(1, X[train, g]) %*% bb, age[train]), test = mae(cbind(1, X[test, g]) %*% bb, age[test]))
}
t(sapply(c(10, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 440), ols))

At which k is the test error lowest? What happens as k approaches the number of training samples (459)?



R5 — Leakage
Pure noise: 5 000 random “CpGs” with no relation to age. Select the 100 most age-correlated ones either using all samples (leaky) or using the training samples only (honest), then fit an elastic net on the training set and predict the test set.
set.seed(1)
noise <- matrix(runif(nrow(X) * 5000), nrow(X))
pick <- function(r, k = 100) order(abs(r), decreasing = TRUE)[1:k]
leaky  <- pick(cor(noise, age)[, 1])                        # uses the test samples' ages!
honest <- pick(cor(noise[train, ], age[train])[, 1])
fit_noise <- function(g) {
  set.seed(2); f <- cv.glmnet(noise[train, g], age[train], alpha = 0.5)
  p <- predict(f, noise[test, g], s = "lambda.min")[, 1]
  c(test_mae = mae(p, age[test]), test_r = cor(p, age[test]))
}
rbind(leaky = fit_noise(leaky), honest = fit_noise(honest))
mae(rep(median(age[train]), length(test)), age[test])      # baseline: always predict the median age

What test error and correlation does the leaky procedure report? Compare with the baseline of predicting the median age.
What does the honest procedure give, and why?
Our data file contains Horvath’s 353 CpGs, which Horvath selected using (among others) these Hannum samples. Is that the same kind of leakage? How serious is it for our clock, and how do we check?



R6 — Horvath’s clock and an external test set
hc <- fread(file.path(D, "horvath2013_coefficients.csv"), skip = 2)[, .(cpg = CpGmarker, w = CoefficientTraining)]
h0 <- hc[cpg == "(Intercept)", w]; hc <- hc[cpg != "(Intercept)"]
anti <- function(z) ifelse(z < 0, 21 * exp(z) - 1, 21 * z + 20)
horvath <- function(B) anti(h0 + B[, hc$cpg, drop = FALSE] %*% hc$w)[, 1]
h_hannum <- horvath(X)
c(r = cor(h_hannum, age), mae = mae(h_hannum, age), offset = median(h_hannum - age))

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(minfi))
g <- fread(file.path(D, "gse42861_samples.tsv"))
g$Basename <- file.path(D, "gse42861_idat", g$basename)
rg <- read.metharray.exp(targets = as.data.frame(g))      # about 4 minutes
bg <- getBeta(preprocessNoob(rg)); rm(rg); invisible(gc())
Xg <- t(bg[colnames(X), ])
p_ext <- predict(cv, Xg, s = "lambda.min")[, 1]
h_ext <- horvath(t(bg[hc$cpg, ]))
rbind(ours = c(r = cor(p_ext, g$age), mae = mae(p_ext, g$age), offset = median(p_ext - g$age)),
      horvath = c(r = cor(h_ext, g$age), mae = mae(h_ext, g$age), offset = median(h_ext - g$age)))

Why is the Horvath result on the Hannum data not a fair test? (Look at Additional file 1 of Horvath 2013.)
How do the two clocks do on GSE42861? What is the median offset, and what could cause it?



R7 — Age acceleration
fit <- lm(p_ext ~ g$age)
coef(fit)
g$acc <- residuals(fit)
g$diff <- p_ext - g$age
t.test(acc ~ status, data = g)$p.value
aggregate(cbind(acc, diff) ~ status, data = g, FUN = mean)
aggregate(acc ~ smoking, data = g, FUN = mean)
cor(g$diff, g$age); cor(g$acc, g$age)

What is the slope of DNAm age on age? (b) Do RA patients have accelerated epigenetic ages? (c) Why is the raw difference correlated with age, and the residual not?



R8 — Deconvolution with a methylation atlas
atl <- fread(file.path(D, "moss2018_reference_atlas.csv"))
atl <- atl[!duplicated(CpGs)]                               # markers chosen for two cell types appear twice
R <- as.matrix(atl[, -1]); rownames(R) <- atl$CpGs
common <- intersect(rownames(R), rownames(bg)); R <- R[common, ]
length(common); ncol(R)
deconv <- function(y) { f <- nnls(R, y)$x; names(f) <- colnames(R); f / sum(f) }
W <- t(apply(bg[common, ], 2, deconv))
round(sort(colMeans(W), decreasing = TRUE)[1:8], 3)
set.seed(7)
sim <- sapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1), function(f) {
  y <- (1 - f) * bg[common, 1] + f * R[, "Hepatocytes"] + rnorm(length(common), 0, 0.03)
  deconv(pmin(pmax(y, 0), 1))["Hepatocytes"] })
round(sim, 3)

What does whole blood consist of according to the atlas? Compare with the Houseman estimates of Methylation arrays (granulocytes ~64%).
How well is added hepatocyte DNA recovered? What would limit this in real plasma cfDNA?

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the elastic net and glmnet (B3, R2, R3)





glmnet vignette: cv.glmnet, lambda.min, lambda.1se, coef, predict. Zou & Hastie 2005, Regularization and variable selection via the elastic net. coef(cv) returns a sparse matrix; the first row is the intercept.









Hint 2 — overfitting and leakage (B4, B5, R4, R5)





A model with as many parameters as samples can fit the training data exactly. Leakage = any information from the test samples used before the test (selection, normalisation, model choice). Related individuals (twins) or replicates of one sample in both sets also leak. Machine learning from scratch treats this in depth.









Hint 3 — Horvath’s clock (B2, R6)





Horvath 2013, DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types: Additional file 2 (the transformation, section “Age transformation”), Additional file 1 (which data sets were training and test), Additional file 3 (coefficients). \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.









Hint 4 — age acceleration (B6, R7)





Residuals from lm(DNAmAge ~ age); residuals. A slope below 1 means the clock overestimates the young and underestimates the old.









Hint 5 — reading IDATs (R6)





minfi user’s guide: read.metharray.exp, preprocessNoob, getBeta. The Basename column is the path without _Grn.idat.gz.









Hint 6 — deconvolution and screening (B7, B8, R8)





nnls::nnls solves \(\min \|Ax - b\|\) with \(x \ge 0\). Moss et al. 2018, the atlas paper. For B8 draw a 2×2 table: cancer yes/no × test positive/negative.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) P: 18 + 60·0.70 + 40·0.50 − 30·0.40 = 18 + 42 + 20 − 12 = 68. Q: 18 + 33 + 16 − 18 = 49. (b) +0.02 × (60 + 40 − 30) = +1.4 years for everyone. A batch effect shifts all predictions of that batch; comparing people across batches mixes biology with batch. Real clocks have hundreds of coefficients of both signs, but the sum of their coefficients is rarely zero, so global shifts in β move DNAm age.
B2. (a) F(5) = log 6 − log 21 = 1.792 − 3.045 = −1.25; F(60) = 40/21 = 1.90. (b) z = −1.2: 21·e^{−1.2} − 1 = 21·0.301 − 1 = 5.3 years; z = 2.0: 21·2 + 20 = 62 years. (c) Methylation changes much faster in childhood than in adulthood; on the log scale for children the relation with CpGs is closer to linear, so one linear model fits the whole lifespan.
B3. Model 1: ridge (no zeros). Model 2: lasso (most sparse). Model 3: elastic net (sparse, but keeps more correlated CpGs). The lasso penalty is indifferent between spreading a coefficient over five identical CpGs and putting it all on one, and the geometry of the L1 penalty makes the solution land on one; the L2 part of the elastic net prefers spreading the weight, so correlated CpGs enter together.
B4. Leaky: (a) selection uses the test samples’ ages; (d) the test set is used for model choice, so the reported error is the minimum of five noisy estimates; (e) twins share genotype and family environment, so a twin in the test set is partly “seen” through the co-twin in training: split by pair. (b) is a mild leak in principle (normalisation uses test arrays, though not their ages); most clock papers accept it, but the safest is to normalise each array on its own (noob) or to freeze the normalisation on the training set. (c) is correct.
B5. (a) To the right λ is large: few or no CpGs, the model is too simple (underfitting), error near the variance of age. To the left the penalty is weak: many CpGs, but cross-validation shows no further gain; the curve is flat because the extra CpGs have tiny coefficients. Choose lambda.min for the lowest CV error or lambda.1se (largest λ within one standard error) for a simpler model with similar error. (b) More parameters always fit the training data at least as well; beyond ~100 CpGs the extra parameters fit noise in the training samples, which does not generalise, so the test error rises (overfitting); near k = n the fit is exact and useless.
B6. (a) Fitted: R 10 + 21.25 = 31.25; S 61; T 78. Raw differences: R +8, S −1, T −5. Residuals: R +1.75, S −2, T −3. (b) With a slope below 1 the clock overestimates the young and underestimates the old, so DNAm age − age falls with age (here from +8 to −5) even for people who are not accelerated. The comparison confounds acceleration with age; use residuals (or include age in the model).
B7. (a) CpG 1: 0.9w + 0.1(1 − w) = 0.66 → 0.8w = 0.56 → w = 0.7. Check CpG 2: 0.2·0.7 + 0.8·0.3 = 0.14 + 0.24 = 0.38 ✓. (b) Liver at 5% changes CpG 1 by 0.05·(0.1 − 0.66) ≈ −0.03 and looks like a small shift towards lymphocytes; with two CpGs and three unknowns the system is not identifiable. Add CpGs where liver differs from all blood cells (e.g. unmethylated only in hepatocytes and methylated in all blood cells); many such markers make a small fraction detectable.
B8. (a) Cancers: 800; true positives 0.40·800 = 320; false positives 0.007·99 200 = 694; PPV = 320/1014 = 32%. Two out of three positives are false. (b) 5 000 cancers: TP 2 000; FP 0.007·95 000 = 665; PPV = 2000/2665 = 75%. (c) A positive test must be followed by imaging and biopsy; knowing where to look shortens and cheapens the work-up and reduces harm from searching the whole body.
B9. Problems: no control group (regression to the mean, seasonal effects); before and after samples probably in different array batches (offsets of years are common); technical noise of single-CpG clocks (replicates differ by years); multiple testing across five clocks (one p = 0.04 is expected by chance); small n; possible change in blood cell composition; a lower PhenoAge is a surrogate, not a health outcome. Better: randomised placebo-controlled, all samples (both time points, both arms) on the same arrays in random order, technical replicates, a pre-registered primary clock with high reliability (DunedinPACE or a PC clock), cell composition estimated and modelled, and clinical outcomes.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 26 127 CpGs (rows after the header) × 656 samples; age 19–101, median 65. (b) 426 “Caucasian - European” and 230 “Hispanic - Mexican”. Methylation at some CpGs differs between populations (partly through meQTLs), so a clock trained on one population can be offset in another. (c) Intercept 0.6955 (CoefficientTraining; the shrunk version is 0.8869); 353 CpGs.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) ELOVL2 r = 0.86 (FHL2 0.75); alone it explains R² = 0.74 of the variance in age, with a median absolute error of 4.4 years. Most negative: cg10501210, r = −0.73. (b) 50 CpGs with |r| > 0.5, 470 with |r| > 0.3.
R2. (a) lambda.min = 0.472 with 313 CpGs; lambda.1se keeps 36. (b) Yes: ELOVL2 cg16867657 has the second-largest coefficient, about 45 years per unit β (0.1 more methylation adds 4.5 years); the largest is cg09541794 (72). lambda.1se = 2.52.
R3. (a) Training: median absolute error 1.23 years, r = 0.99; test: 3.71 years, r = 0.93. The model has partly fitted the noise of its training samples; only the test error estimates performance on new people. (b) The 36-CpG model has a test error of 4.4 years: 0.7 years worse, with a tenth of the CpGs.
R4. (a) The test error is lowest around k = 10–100 (3.7–3.9 years). At k = 400 the training error is 0.97 and the test error 8.3; at k = 440 the training error is 0.52 and the test error 17.9 years.
R5. (a) Leaky selection of 100 noise “CpGs”: test median error 8.1 years and r = 0.62, apparently much better than the baseline of predicting the median age (11 years), although the features contain no information about age. The selection used the test samples’ ages, so the chosen features happen to correlate with age in the test set. (b) Honest selection: test error 13.5 years and r = −0.11, worse than the baseline: the model fits noise in the training set, as it should. (c) Yes, in a milder form: Horvath used GSE40279 to choose his 353 CpGs, so they are slightly favoured on these samples. The effect is small for real age CpGs (age signal is strong and replicates), but it is why the external test on GSE42861 is the more trustworthy number (3.2 vs 3.7 years: no sign of optimism here).
R6. (a) GSE40279 (Hannum) was one of Horvath’s 39 training data sets (Additional file 1, row 3). Horvath on Hannum: r = 0.92, median error 3.9 years, median offset −2.3 years. (b) GSE42861: our clock r = 0.92, median error 3.2 years, offset +2.5; Horvath r = 0.87, error 4.3 years, offset +2.3. Different lab, normalisation (noob vs the authors’ processing; Horvath used a BMIQ variant), population (Swedish vs American), age range (22–69 vs 19–101). Horvath reported a median error of 3.8 years on this data set (it was one of his test sets) with his own normalisation.
R7. (a) Slope 0.90 (intercept about 7.9). (b) No: mean acceleration −0.03 (controls) and +0.03 (RA), p = 0.94. Current smokers +1.2 years vs never smokers 0.0 (not significant in this small sample). (c) Because the slope is below 1, DNAm age − age decreases with age; the residual is by construction uncorrelated with age.
R8. (a) 6 105 unique atlas CpGs on the 450k array, 25 cell types. Mean: neutrophils 0.61, CD8 T 0.12, CD4 T 0.07, erythrocyte progenitors 0.04, NK 0.04, monocytes 0.04, B cells 0.03, breast 0.02. Similar to the Houseman estimates (granulocytes ~0.64), but the split between CD4 and CD8 differs: estimates depend on the reference. A few percent go to tissues that cannot be in blood: the noise floor. (b) Estimates 0.000, 0.009, 0.050 and 0.098 for 0, 1, 5 and 10% added: recovered within a fraction of a percentage point. Real cfDNA: a few thousand genome copies per locus, so each CpG is measured with few reads (sampling noise far larger than SD 0.03); low tumour or tissue fractions; and the tissue may be missing from the atlas.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Where this leads

Machine learning from scratch generalises training/test splits, cross-validation and overfitting, and adds classification (ROC and PR curves).
What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works returns to age and tumour-type prediction from methylation, and to genomics-specific leakage.
Epigenetics in disease and therapy covers methylation-based tumour classification.
Methylation and chromatin from long reads: nanopore sequencing of cfDNA reads methylation and fragment patterns together.

title: Exercise: Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Horvath 2013, Genome Biol. DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types.
Hannum et al. 2013, Mol Cell. Genome-wide methylation profiles reveal quantitative views of human aging rates.
Levine et al. 2018, Aging. An epigenetic biomarker of aging for lifespan and healthspan.
Belsky et al. 2022, eLife. DunedinPACE, a DNA methylation biomarker of the pace of aging.
Higgins-Chen et al. 2022, Nat Aging. A computational solution for bolstering reliability of epigenetic clocks.
Moss et al. 2018, Nat Commun. Comprehensive human cell-type methylation atlas reveals origins of circulating cell-free DNA in health and disease.

title: Quiz: epigenetic clocks and biomarkers
text:
Short questions on penalised regression, clock evaluation, age acceleration and cell-free DNA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why can ordinary least squares not be used to fit a clock on 450 000 CpGs from 500 people, and what does the elastic net penalty change?






Hint





Count unknowns and equations.









Answer





With more coefficients than samples there are infinitely many exact fits to the training data; the solution is not unique and predicts new samples badly (overfitting). The elastic net adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients (L1 + L2): the L1 part sets most coefficients to exactly zero (selecting a few hundred CpGs), the L2 part keeps correlated CpGs together and stabilises the fit. The strength λ is chosen by cross-validation.




Q2. A clock has intercept 25 and two CpGs with coefficients 50 and −20. A person has β = 0.6 and 0.5. What is the predicted age? If an array batch adds 0.03 to every β, how does the prediction change?






Answer





25 + 50·0.6 − 20·0.5 = 25 + 30 − 10 = 45. A shift of 0.03 adds 0.03 × (50 − 20) = 0.9 years.




Q3. A clock’s median absolute error is 1.2 years on its training data and 3.7 years on held-out samples. Which number would you report, and why are they different?






Answer





The held-out (test) error, 3.7 years: it estimates performance on new people. The training error is optimistic because the model partly fitted the noise of the training samples (overfitting).




Q4. A paper selects the 500 CpGs most correlated with age in its 400 samples, then reports a 5-fold cross-validated error of an elastic net using those CpGs. What is wrong, and how should it be done?






Answer





The CpG selection used all samples, including those later used for testing in each fold: leakage. The error is too optimistic (with pure noise features this procedure can still produce apparently good predictions). The selection must be repeated inside each training fold (or done on data that is never used for testing), and the final test set should be untouched until the end.




Q5. Horvath’s clock applied to the Hannum data gives r = 0.92. Why is this not evidence that Horvath’s clock generalises?






Answer





The Hannum data (GSE40279) were part of Horvath’s training data. Performance on training data is in-sample and optimistic. Generalisation must be tested on data the model has never seen (e.g. GSE42861, one of his test sets).




Q6. In a cohort, DNAm age = 8 + 0.9 × age. A 40-year-old has DNAm age 47. Compute the raw difference and the age acceleration.






Answer





Raw difference: 47 − 40 = +7. Fitted: 8 + 36 = 44; acceleration = 47 − 44 = +3 years.




Q7. What is the difference between what Horvath’s clock, GrimAge and DunedinPACE were trained to predict?






Answer





Horvath: chronological age (transformed), across many tissues. GrimAge: time to death, via methylation surrogates of seven plasma proteins and smoking pack-years (plus age and sex). DunedinPACE: the rate of decline in 19 biomarkers of organ function over 20 years in one birth cohort (years of ageing per calendar year). The target determines what the score means; the later two predict morbidity and mortality better.




Q8. Give three non-biological reasons why two groups could differ in mean DNAm age acceleration.






Answer





Any three: the groups were measured in different array batches or with different normalisation; they differ in blood cell composition (e.g. inflammation, infection, steroids); they differ in age and the raw difference (not the residual) was used; technical noise with small groups and many clocks tested (multiple testing); different populations (genetic effects on clock CpGs); sample handling (storage, DNA quality).




Q9. Two CpGs: neutrophils β = 0.8 and 0.2; liver β = 0.1 and 0.9. A cfDNA sample (only these two sources) has β = 0.73 at CpG 1. What fraction comes from liver? Check with CpG 2 if it reads 0.27.






Answer





0.8(1 − f) + 0.1f = 0.73 → 0.8 − 0.7f = 0.73 → f = 0.1. CpG 2: 0.2·0.9 + 0.9·0.1 = 0.18 + 0.09 = 0.27 ✓.




Q10. A cancer screening test has 50% sensitivity and 99% specificity; 1% of the screened people have cancer. Of 10 000 people tested, how many positives are true, and what is the positive predictive value?






Answer





100 have cancer: 50 true positives. 9 900 do not: 1% = 99 false positives. PPV = 50/149 = 34%. Most positives are false, even with 99% specificity, because the disease is rare.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
About this lecture
What is epigenetics? defined an epigenetic state as one that is heritable without a change in DNA sequence, and showed how marks survive cell division. This lecture asks the harder question: can a state, or an experience, be passed on to children and grandchildren?

Three meanings of “inheritance”, and the F0–F3 rule.
Why mammals are a hard case: two waves of reprogramming.
The robust cases: plants, C. elegans, a few mouse loci.
The contested cases: famine, diet and stress in humans and mice.
How false “inheritance” arises: confounding, multiple testing, litters, small samples.
What evidence would convince.


This is a judgement unit. There is no new assay; the aim is that students can read a paper or a news story claiming “trauma is inherited through epigenetics” and say what was shown, what was not, and what would be needed. Be fair in both directions: some forms of non-genetic inheritance are rock-solid (plants, worms), and the absence of strong evidence in humans does not prove absence. The exercise has students simulate how false transgenerational signals arise, and read real study designs. The DNA methylation facts used here (maintenance by DNMT1, imprinting) come from What is epigenetics? and DNA methylation biology.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Three kinds of “inheritance”


Mitotic memory: a cell remembers a state through division (X inactivation, Polycomb silencing). Well established.
Intergenerational: the offspring differs because it was exposed (as an embryo, or as a germ cell).
Transgenerational: an effect in a generation that was never exposed. This is the strong claim.


Most confusion in the literature comes from mixing these up. Mitotic memory is the subject of the rest of the course and is not in doubt. Intergenerational effects are very common and not surprising: a mother’s diet in pregnancy changes the fetus, a father’s diet may change his sperm. They do not require any mark to be inherited; they can be a direct effect of the exposure on the next generation’s tissues or germ cells. Transgenerational inheritance requires that information is carried through at least one generation that was never exposed, which in mammals means it must survive the germline. Ask of every paper: which of the three is being claimed, and which was shown?

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Which generation was never exposed?


A pregnant F0 female exposes the F1 embryo and the F1’s germ cells, which will become F2. F3 is the first unexposed generation.
A father (or a female before pregnancy) exposes his germ cells, so F1 is exposed. F2 is the first unexposed generation.
An effect in F1 (or in F2 after a pregnancy exposure) is intergenerational: it can be a direct effect.


This F0–F3 rule is a standard exam question. Primordial germ cells are specified in the mouse embryo at about E7, during the pregnancy, so anything that reaches the fetus also reaches the cells that will make the grandchildren. For paternal exposure, the sperm that make F1 were themselves exposed; F1 germ cells form later, inside F1, so F2 is unexposed. For plants that self-fertilise, the same logic applies with seed and pollen. Many papers that call themselves “transgenerational” report only F1 or F2 after a pregnancy exposure. That does not make them wrong, but the stronger word is not justified.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Two waves of reprogramming in mammals
text:
Two waves of reprogramming in mammals


Wave 1, after fertilisation: most DNA methylation is lost by the blastocyst, then re-established in the epiblast.
Wave 2, in primordial germ cells: methylation is erased almost completely, including imprints, then reset according to the sex of the embryo.
Any mark that is to reach a grandchild must get through both waves, or be rebuilt.


Seisenberger et al. 2012 mapped this in mouse PGCs by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing: global loss during PGC expansion and migration, partly passive (no maintenance), and the last regions (imprints, CpG islands on the X, germline genes) demethylated on entry into the gonads, with TET enzymes helping. Human PGCs show the same erasure (Tang et al. 2015). Histone marks are also extensively remodelled in the germline and the paternal genome is packaged with protamines in sperm, replacing most histones. This is why mammalian transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is a priori unlikely: the system actively wipes the slate. It is a barrier, not a wall: see the next slide.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
What gets through?


Imprinting control regions keep their methylation through wave 1 (protected by ZFP57 and TRIM28), and are reset in wave 2: imprints last one generation by design.
Some IAP retrotransposons partly resist both waves (Lane et al. 2003).
Otherwise a state must be rebuilt each generation, from DNA sequence, from small RNAs, or by a self-reinforcing loop.


Imprinting shows that mammals can carry a methylation mark from the gamete into every cell of the adult, but only for one generation: in the next germline it is erased and rewritten by sex. That is parent-of-origin memory, not inheritance of an experience. IAPs (intracisternal A particles) are young, active endogenous retroviruses; some copies keep methylation in PGCs, presumably because the cost of reactivating them is high. These escapees are the candidate carriers for non-genetic inheritance in mice, and the robust mouse examples later in the lecture are IAPs. Also mention: a sequence that recruits a silencing complex (for example a KRAB zinc-finger binding site) can rebuild the same state every generation. That is real “inheritance” of a state, but the information is in the DNA.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Plants: a germline that forms late
text:
Plants: a germline that forms late


Mammals set germ cells aside early and erase them. Plants make gametes late, from the shoot: a change in a somatic cell lineage can reach the seed.
CG methylation is maintained by MET1 through meiosis; non-CG methylation is restored by RNA-directed DNA methylation.
Demethylation in the plant germline happens mainly in companion cells, not in the gametes.


This is the main reason the plant literature is so different from the mammalian one. There is no PGC-like erasure, so a methylation state (an epiallele) can persist for many generations. In the pollen, the vegetative nucleus loses methylation at transposons and makes small RNAs that are thought to reinforce silencing in the sperm cells; in the female gametophyte the central cell is demethylated by DEMETER (which also produces imprinting in the endosperm). Umeå has a strong plant-epigenetics community, so this is a good place to point students to local research. The methylation contexts (CG, CHG, CHH) and RdDM are covered in DNA methylation biology.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
A natural epimutation: peloric toadflax


Linnaeus described a Linaria vulgaris with radially symmetric flowers (“peloria”) in the 18th century.
Cubas, Vincent & Coen (1999): the gene Lcyc has the same sequence but is heavily methylated and silent; the state is heritable and co-segregates with the flower shape.
Occasional reversion on single branches goes with loss of methylation: an epiallele, not a mutation.


A beautiful case because it was found in nature and has a visible phenotype. Cycloidea controls dorsoventral asymmetry of the flower in snapdragon; its homologue in toadflax is silenced by methylation in the peloric form. The reversion during somatic development is the key evidence that the change is epigenetic: a DNA mutation would not revert at that frequency, and the revertant branches have regained expression and lost methylation. Note what was not shown: what caused the original epimutation. There is no environmental trigger here; it arose spontaneously, like most epialleles.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Arabidopsis epiRILs: heritable traits without DNA differences
text:
Arabidopsis epiRILs: heritable traits without DNA differences


Cross wild type with a methylation mutant (ddm1 or met1) of the same accession, restore the wild-type gene, and self for ~8 generations: lines differ in methylation, hardly in sequence.
Flowering time and height vary and are heritable (~30%) (Johannes et al. 2009).
Specific DMRs act as epigenetic QTL explaining 60–90% of the heritability of flowering time and root length (Cortijo et al. 2014).


This is the cleanest experimental test of whether methylation differences alone can cause heritable trait variation. The genetic background is nearly constant, so variation between lines must come from the epialleles (or from the few transposon insertions that occur in ddm1 backgrounds, which the authors had to check). Two honest caveats: these epialleles were induced by a mutant, so they are larger and more numerous than natural ones; and some hypomethylated regions regain methylation over generations, guided by small RNAs. Still, the result settles the principle in plants: methylation variation can be stably inherited and can shape quantitative traits.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
How often do epialleles arise?


Mutation-accumulation lines (one seed per generation, ~30 generations) measure spontaneous change.
DNA base substitutions: about 7 × 10⁻⁹ per site per generation (Ossowski et al. 2010).
CG methylation gains and losses: about 10⁻⁴ per CpG per generation (van der Graaf et al. 2015): epialleles arise often, and also revert often.


Becker et al. 2011 and Schmitz et al. 2011 sequenced methylomes of Arabidopsis lines propagated by single-seed descent, and van der Graaf et al. 2015 estimated forward and backward epimutation rates from them. The comparison has two sides. Epimutations are about five orders of magnitude more frequent than mutations, so methylation can create heritable variation quickly. Reversion is also much more frequent than DNA back-mutation, but this does not imply loss within a few generations. The genome-wide loss rate estimated by van der Graaf et al. is about 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ per methylated CG per generation: under a constant-rate model the mean waiting time for loss is about 1 600 generations. Rates vary greatly across genomic contexts; some epialleles persist long enough to respond to selection. Most of these spontaneous changes are at single CpGs in gene bodies and have no known phenotype. Students compute expected numbers per genome in the exercise.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Paramutation: one allele converts the other
text:
Paramutation: one allele converts the other


At maize b1, the weakly expressed B’ allele converts the strongly expressed B-I allele into a new B’ when they meet in one plant, at close to 100%.
The converted allele is stably weak in later generations and converts others in turn: a clear breach of Mendel’s rules.
Requires an upstream tandem-repeat array and an RNA-directed silencing pathway. B-I and B’ carry seven repeats about 100 kb upstream (Stam et al. 2002); reduced arrays can still participate.


Paramutation was described by Brink in 1956 at the maize r1 locus and studied in detail at b1 by Vicki Chandler’s group. The two alleles have the same DNA sequence in the region required; they differ in chromatin and methylation of the repeats. Mutations in genes of the RNA-directed DNA methylation pathway (for example mediator of paramutation 1, an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) abolish paramutation, so small RNAs from the repeats are thought to carry the silent state to the other allele. Paramutation-like phenomena have been reported in mice, but are rare and less well understood. For the exam: paramutation is allele interaction, heritable, with a known DNA requirement and a known pathway, the ideal of a well-understood case.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: C. elegans: small RNAs carry memory
text:
C. elegans: small RNAs carry memory


A trigger (dsRNA, a piRNA, starvation) produces small RNAs; an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase amplifies them in each generation.
The nuclear Argonaute HRDE-1 brings H3K9 methylation to the target; small RNAs in the egg restart the loop in the offspring.
Usually lasts 3–5 generations, actively limited; piRNA-triggered silencing can last 20+ (Ashe et al. 2012). Starvation-induced small RNAs persist for at least three generations (Rechavi et al. 2014).


Worms are the best animal example because the mechanism is known and testable with mutants. The amplification step solves the dilution problem: unlike a chemical mark, a small-RNA population can be re-made from itself every generation. Houri-Ze’evi et al. 2016 showed that the duration is regulated, so the default is to forget after a few generations; mutants can extend it. Two lessons for mammals: (1) a carrier needs an amplification or self-reinforcement step to survive many generations; (2) mammals lack the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that worms and plants use, which is one reason to expect shorter-lived effects. Also note worms have a short life cycle and are often isogenic, which removes several confounders.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Mouse metastable epialleles: the robust mammalian cases
text:
Mouse metastable epialleles: the robust mammalian cases








locus
what it is
what is inherited




Avy (agouti viable yellow)
an IAP upstream of agouti; its methylation varies between genetically identical mice and sets coat colour
offspring resemble the mother’s state: incomplete erasure through the female germline (Morgan et al. 1999)


AxinFu (axin fused)
an IAP in Axin; methylation predicts a kinked tail
inherited through both mothers and fathers (Rakyan et al. 2003)


genome-wide screen
variably methylated IAPs in C57BL/6J (Kazachenka et al. 2018)
most are reset after fertilisation and re-established as variable: the variability is inherited, not the parent’s state




Real, but locus-specific, depend on a retrotransposon, and often reflect the strain background.


Morgan et al. 1999 showed that the distribution of coat colours among isogenic Avy offspring depends on the dam’s phenotype, and showed that this maternal effect is not caused by the maternal environment: it follows the allele through the female germline. AxinFu adds paternal transmission, which argues against cytoplasmic or metabolic explanations because sperm contribute little cytoplasm. Kazachenka et al. 2018 then searched the whole genome for similar loci. They found several, but the methylation state of the parent did not predict that of the offspring for the loci they tested: the states are rebuilt from scratch, variably, each generation. So “epigenetic variation that is heritable as a property of the locus” exists; “inheritance of a parental state” is rarer. Diet experiments on Avy mothers have been reported to shift offspring coat colours; this is a pregnancy exposure, so by the F0–F3 rule an F1 effect is intergenerational, and claims of persistence to F2/F3 have given mixed results.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Dutch Hunger Winter: a sibling design
text:
Dutch Hunger Winter: a sibling design


People conceived during the 1944–45 famine had, 60 years later, 5.2% lower methylation at the imprinted IGF2 DMR in blood (0.488 vs 0.515) than their same-sex siblings (Heijmans et al. 2008).
A careful design, but it shows a lasting effect of prenatal exposure (F1), not inheritance.


The study is often cited as evidence for “epigenetic inheritance in humans”. Read it carefully: 60 individuals exposed periconceptionally, each compared with an unexposed same-sex sibling, which controls half the genes and the family environment. The difference is 0.027 in beta, 0.48 SD of the controls, at five CpGs measured by mass spectrometry. Exposure late in gestation showed no such difference. It is an important result about developmental programming, and a nice demonstration that early-embryo methylation can be affected by the environment. It says nothing about transmission to unexposed generations, and nothing about whether the IGF2 change matters for health. Later work (Painter et al. 2008) reported differences in the grandchildren of exposed women; by the F0–F3 rule those grandchildren were exposed as germ cells.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Överkalix: grandparents’ food and grandchildren’s mortality
text:
Överkalix: grandparents’ food and grandchildren’s mortality


Three birth cohorts from Överkalix parish (Norrbotten, northern Sweden): food availability in a grandparent’s pre-pubertal “slow growth period”, judged from harvest records, was associated with grandchildren’s mortality, sex-specifically (Kaati 2002; Pembrey 2006).
A 40× larger Swedish replication (Uppsala multigenerational cohort; Vågerö et al. 2018) supported one finding (paternal grandfather → grandsons, HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.02–2.35) and not the diabetes and cardiovascular findings.


This is a Swedish study and students will meet it in Swedish media. Be fair: it is an ingenious use of historical records, and the partial replication in a much larger cohort is notable. But the original data are small (303 probands, 1818 relatives), the families are interwoven, the exposure is defined by birth year (so cohort effects are confounded with harvests), many grandparent × grandchild-sex × outcome combinations were examined, and there is no biological measurement at all: no mark, no mechanism. The replication’s confidence interval almost touches 1 and the original diabetes signal did not replicate. Conclusion: an intriguing association, not evidence for a germline epigenetic mechanism. The exercise asks students to compute the expected number of false positives for this kind of design.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Fathers, sperm and small RNAs


Paternal diet or early stress in mice changes small RNAs in sperm (tRNA fragments, miRNAs).
Injecting RNA from such sperm into normal fertilised eggs reproduced metabolic or behavioural changes in the offspring (Gapp et al. 2014; Chen et al. 2016; Sharma et al. 2016).
The strongest mammalian evidence for a carrier, but so far mostly for F1: intergenerational.


The injection design is the right kind of experiment: it removes the father’s behaviour, seminal fluid and the maternal environment, and points to a molecule. Sperm RNA payload is changed during epididymal maturation (Sharma 2016), which offers a route from the father’s physiology to the sperm. Open questions: how a small amount of RNA in one sperm has a lasting effect on development, how reproducible the effects are across labs and strains, and whether any of it persists beyond F1. Teach this as a promising, active field where the evidence is genuinely stronger than for most human claims.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Contested claims, and why







claim
issue raised




Endocrine disruptor (vinclozolin) given to pregnant rats lowers male fertility to F4 (Anway et al. 2005)
high doses by injection; reports from other groups, with other exposure routes and strains, have been inconsistent


Odour fear conditioning of F0 mice changes F1 and F2 sensitivity to that odour (Dias & Ressler 2014)
the uniformly significant results across many small experiments are improbable (Francis 2014 estimated p = 0.004); mechanism unclear


Human famine, trauma or smoking affects grandchildren
confounded by genetics, culture and in-utero exposure; no measured carrier




Both mouse studies used good design elements (IVF, cross-fostering in Dias & Ressler); the debate is about reproducibility and statistics.


Present these neutrally. The Anway paper was a landmark that started a field; the Skinner lab has continued to report transgenerational effects, while results from other groups using other exposure routes or strains have been inconsistent (see the reviews in the key papers). The Dias & Ressler paper used IVF and cross-fostering, which closes several routes, and that is to its credit. Francis’s critique is statistical: with the effect sizes and sample sizes reported, the probability that all experiments come out significant is about 0.004, which suggests selective reporting or analysis flexibility. Students can reproduce this kind of argument in the exercise (the power calculation and the “too much success” probability). Make the point that a famous paper is not the same as a replicated finding.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Many routes, one claim


A trait that follows an exposure across generations can travel by six routes. Only one is inheritance of an epigenetic mark.
Genes, shared environment and culture, parental behaviour (e.g. maternal care in rats, Weaver et al. 2004) and direct exposure are all real routes.
And chance, made likely by many tests and small, clustered samples.


This is the slide to remember for the exam. For each study, go through the routes and ask which the design closes. Genetics: relatives share alleles; exposures are not random with respect to ancestry; famine survivors and parents are selected. Shared environment: families pass on diet, wealth, smoking, place of residence. Behaviour: the Weaver et al. maternal-care work in rats showed that a methylation difference in the offspring hippocampus followed the mother’s licking and grooming and was reversed by cross-fostering: a non-germline, behavioural route that still involves methylation. Direct exposure: the F0–F3 rule. Chance: the next slides.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Chance, part 1: forking paths


Simulated Överkalix-like cohorts with no true effect: 300 grandchildren, 4 grandparents × 3 causes of death × 3 sex groups = 36 tests.
64% of null cohorts produce at least one p < 0.05.
Without a pre-specified hypothesis, a “sex-specific, line-specific” finding is expected by chance.


Numbers from make-inheritance-figs.R: 1000 simulated cohorts, each with 36 Fisher tests, 63.8% had at least one p below 0.05, with 1.27 hits on average. The exact numbers depend on the test (Fisher’s exact test is conservative), but the point does not: with 36 tests, finding something is the norm. This does not mean the Överkalix finding is false; it means the original analysis cannot distinguish a real effect from chance, which is why a pre-specified replication (as in Vågerö et al. 2018) matters so much. In the exercise, students run this simulation and change the number of tests.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Chance, part 2: genome-wide tests across generations
text:
Chance, part 2: genome-wide tests across generations


20 000 CpGs, 8 exposed vs 8 control animals per generation, no true effect: about 950 CpGs with p < 0.05 in every generation.
4 CpGs reach p < 0.05 in F1, F2 and F3 (2.5 expected), and none survives FDR correction.
“Methylation changes that persist to F3” can be pure noise.


A common figure in papers is a Venn diagram of DMRs in F1, F2 and F3 with a small overlap called “persistent”. With 20 000 independent tests at 0.05, about 1000 hits per generation are expected, about 50 in any two generations (20 000 × 0.05²) and about 2.5 in all three (20 000 × 0.05³). We got 4. The overlap is no evidence unless it is larger than expected under independence, and unless the hits survive correction. Arrays and WGBS test hundreds of thousands to millions of CpGs, so the problem is larger in real data. Students reproduce this in the exercise.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Chance, part 3: litters are not independent
text:
Chance, part 3: litters are not independent


Pups from one litter share a mother, a uterus and a cage. Treating them as independent inflates the false-positive rate.
4 litters per group, 6 pups each, litter SD = pup SD: 33% false positives when pups are counted; 4–5% when litter means are used.


In transgenerational designs, the exposure is applied to F0 parents, so the independent unit is the litter (or the F0 animal), not the pup. If between-litter variation is large, a handful of litters can differ by chance and every pup in them carries that difference. The simulation shows the false-positive rate climbing from 5% with no litter effect to 33% when the litter SD equals the within-litter SD, and 38% when it is 1.5 times larger. The fix is to analyse litter means, or use a mixed model with litter as a random effect, and to use many litters. Check the methods section: n = 24 animals from 4 litters is n = 4 for the exposure.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Confounding by genes


A simulated cohort: methylation depends only on a genotype (an meQTL); the famine region has a higher frequency of the methylation-raising allele.
Naive comparison: +0.015, p = 0.008. Adjusted for genotype: +0.003, p = 0.61.
In humans, ancestry and local allele frequencies differ between regions, families and exposure groups.


Methylation at many CpGs is strongly determined by nearby genetic variants (methylation QTLs), covered in Epigenomics and genetic variation. If exposure groups differ in ancestry, a methylation difference between their grandchildren can be entirely genetic. Sibling designs (as in the Dutch famine study) control for half of it; within-family designs and genotype adjustment help; in mice, isogenic strains remove it. This also applies to F0 selection: famine and war select who survives and has children.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: Chance, part 4: small studies of small effects
text:
Chance, part 4: small studies of small effects


A real effect that halves each generation (1, 0.5, 0.25 SD), n = 10 per group: power 55%, 18%, 9%.
Studies that reach significance in F3 report on average 0.85 SD, more than three times the true 0.25.
Small, significant, transgenerational effects are expected to be exaggerated, and to shrink on replication.


This is the “winner’s curse”: when power is low, only the studies that happened to overestimate the effect reach significance, so the published effect is inflated. It also explains Francis’s argument: if each experiment has 50% power, eight significant experiments in a row has probability 0.5⁸ ≈ 0.004. A realistic expectation for a real transgenerational effect is that it is small and decays; detecting it needs many independent litters, a pre-specified outcome and replication. Students compute power and the “too much success” probability by hand in the exercise.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
What would convince?


Each design element closes one route; a convincing study combines several, and names a carrier that can be tested.
Plants and worms meet most of these criteria; most mammalian claims meet a few.


Go through the table with the routes from the earlier slide. IVF with embryo transfer and cross-fostering close the maternal and behavioural routes. Testing the first unexposed generation closes direct exposure. Isogenic animals close genetics. Litter-level analysis, pre-registration and multiple-testing correction close chance. Finally, a carrier: show that a specific molecule (an RNA fraction, a methylated locus) is sufficient, for example by injection or by editing the locus, and necessary, by removing it. And replication in an independent lab. In humans most of these are impossible, which is why human transgenerational claims will likely remain associations; that is a statement about the evidence, not about the biology.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
The evidence in one picture


Strong: plants, C. elegans. Solid but rare: specific mouse IAP loci.
Intergenerational, debated: paternal diet and stress via sperm RNA in mice.
Weak for germline transmission: humans; effects of in-utero exposure are real but are not inheritance.


This summary is my reading of the current evidence and of reviews such as Heard & Martienssen 2014 and Horsthemke 2018; students should be able to justify each row with an example and the main caveat. The ranking is about inheritance through the germline of an acquired or variable state, not about whether early-life exposures matter for health (they clearly do). Be ready for the question “so is it all nonsense?”: no. Non-genetic inheritance is established biology in several kingdoms; in mammals it appears to be restricted and short-lived, and the most publicised human claims are the least supported.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
section: A checklist for reading a claim
text:
A checklist for reading a claim







question
why




Which generation shows the effect? Was it exposed?
F0–F3 rule: intergenerational vs transgenerational


What is the unit of replication?
litters, families, F0 animals


How many outcomes, CpGs, subgroups were tested?
forking paths and multiple testing


Are genetics and shared environment controlled?
isogenic strains, siblings, genotype adjustment


Are maternal and behavioural routes closed?
IVF, embryo transfer, cross-fostering


Is there a carrier, and is it sufficient and necessary?
mechanism


Has it been replicated independently?
small studies exaggerate




This table is the practical outcome of the unit. Students apply it in the By-hand part of the exercise to three study descriptions. In the exam, expect a short description of a study and the question “what is shown, and what is missing?”. A good answer names the generation, the unit of replication, one or two confounders and a design that would fix them.

title: Epigenetic inheritance: what is really shown?
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




three meanings
mitotic memory; intergenerational (offspring exposed); transgenerational (never exposed)


F0–F3 rule
pregnancy exposure: F3 is first unexposed; paternal exposure: F2


mammalian barrier
two waves of reprogramming; imprints and some IAPs escape


plants
late germline, MET1 + RdDM: epialleles (Linaria), epiRILs, paramutation


C. elegans
small RNAs amplified each generation; usually 3–5 generations


mouse
IAP metastable epialleles; sperm RNA effects mostly F1


humans
prenatal effects (Dutch famine) real; transgenerational claims (Överkalix) confounded


false signals
forking paths, genome-wide tests, litter effects, genetic confounding, winner’s curse




Students should leave with a vocabulary (intergenerational vs transgenerational), a rule (F0–F3), a reason (reprogramming), a set of robust examples and their mechanisms, and a checklist for claims. Next: Epigenetics in disease and therapy, where the epigenome changes within one body, and Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers, where methylation tracks age.

Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Background
Library complexity. Count the filtered reads (MAPQ ≥ 30, primary; duplicates not yet removed) by position: for single-end reads the 5’ end and strand, for paired-end reads the fragment’s start and end. With \(N\) reads, \(M_\text{distinct}\) distinct positions, \(M_1\) positions with exactly one read and \(M_2\) with exactly two:
\[\text{NRF} = \frac{M_\text{distinct}}{N}, \qquad \text{PBC1} = \frac{M_1}{M_\text{distinct}}, \qquad \text{PBC2} = \frac{M_1}{M_2}\]
ENCODE ChIP-seq: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 10 is ideal; 0.8–0.9 (NRF “compliant”, PBC1 “mild”), PBC2 3–10 (“mild”); NRF or PBC1 below 0.5 or PBC2 below 1 is severe. ATAC-seq preferred values: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 3.
FRiP = reads overlapping peaks / all filtered reads. ENCODE scrutinises TF ChIP-seq with FRiP below 1% (Landt et al. 2012); ATAC-seq should have FRiP > 0.3 (> 0.2 acceptable).
Fingerprint. Count reads in bins, sort the bins, plot the cumulative fraction of reads against the fraction of bins. Input ≈ diagonal; an enriched sample bends towards the lower right.
Strand cross-correlation \(CC(k)\): the correlation between + strand read 5’ ends at \(x\) and − strand read 5’ ends at \(x + k\). It peaks at the fragment length, with a “phantom” peak at the read length.
\[\text{NSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment})}{\min CC}, \qquad \text{RSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment}) - \min CC}{CC(\text{read length}) - \min CC}\]
ENCODE repeats experiments with NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8.
Spike-in (ChIP-Rx). A fixed amount of fly chromatin is added to each sample before the IP. With \(N_\text{fly}\) the reads (in millions) on the fly genome, multiply the human signal by \(\alpha = 1/N_\text{fly}\).

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Data
The CTCF ChIP-seq of GM12878 (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, single-end 36 bp, 2008-era Illumina reads with phred+64 qualities) and its input control (ENCSR000EYX, single-end 27–28 bp), and ATAC-seq of GM12878 in two biological replicates (ENCSR095QNB, paired-end 2 × 101 bp). For each library you get the original, untrimmed reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, plus a Bowtie2 index of chr21 + chrM, the ENCODE peaks (CTCF and ATAC, IDR-thresholded), the blacklist and the GENCODE annotation.
data/download.sh epigenomics-design      # about 1.5 GB
mkdir -p ~/epi/design && cd ~/epi/design
D=/path/to/course/data                   # where download.sh put the files
T=8                                      # threads
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (1.12 or newer), bedtools, deepTools and R with GenomicAlignments (see Install the software you need). The ChIP part runs in a minute; aligning the ATAC-seq reads takes about 10 minutes with 8 threads, so run it as a batch job on the cluster (wrap the alignment block in an sbatch script) and do the by-hand part meanwhile.






A shortcut to be aware of



The reads were selected because ENCODE aligned them to chr21 or chrM. Two consequences: the alignment rate is close to 100% (the reads that would not align were never selected), and the chrM fraction is hugely inflated (all mitochondrial reads were kept, but only 1/60 of the nuclear ones). We therefore compute every metric on chr21 only, where the reads are a faithful sample of the full library. The ENCODE values for the whole genome are given in the solutions for comparison.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Library complexity. Two ChIP-seq libraries were each sequenced to 10 million uniquely mapped reads (before duplicate removal).




library 1

8.2 M

Compute NRF, PBC1 and PBC2 for both, and classify each with the ENCODE ChIP-seq table.
What fraction of library 2’s reads would samtools markdup -r remove? How many usable reads are left?
Library 2 is sequenced again, to 40 M reads. Will NRF go up, stay the same or go down? Will the number of usable reads go up four-fold? Why?
Why must these metrics be computed before duplicate removal?

B2. FRiP. A CTCF ChIP-seq has 18 M filtered reads, of which 540 000 overlap the 45 000 called peaks. The peaks are on average 300 bp wide; the mappable genome is 2.7 Gb.

Compute FRiP. Does it pass the ENCODE guideline?
What FRiP would you expect if the reads were spread uniformly over the mappable genome? How many times more reads are in the peaks than expected?
The input of the same experiment has a FRiP of 0.8% in the same peaks. Why is that higher than your answer in (b)?
An ATAC-seq library has FRiP 0.15. What does ENCODE say? Name two things that could have gone wrong in the experiment.

B3. Read a fingerprint plot. The figure shows four samples, A–D, each with 1-kb bins over the genome.






Which curve is most likely an input? Which is a TF ChIP-seq with strong, sharp peaks? Which is a broad histone mark such as H3K27me3?
For curve B, read off the fraction of reads in the top 10% of bins.
Curve D follows the input until the last 1% of bins, which hold almost 30% of the reads. Is this a good ChIP? What could produce such a curve? (Think about the blacklist and about PCR.)

B4. Strand cross-correlation. Two single-end (36 bp) ChIP-seq experiments give these cross-correlation values:

Compute NSC and RSC for both. Which passes the ENCODE thresholds?
What is the fragment length of experiment X? Why does the curve have a peak at 36 bp at all?
Experiment Y is an H3K36me3 ChIP-seq. Is a low RSC enough to reject it? Which other metric would you look at?

B5. Spike-in normalisation. H3K27me3 ChIP-Rx in control cells and after 7 days of an EZH2 inhibitor. Each sample got the same amount of Drosophila chromatin.
