Normalise the HOXA counts per million human reads. What do you conclude?
Normalise with the spike-in factor \(\alpha = 1/N_\text{fly}\). What do you conclude now? By how much did H3K27me3 change at HOXA?
Why did the fly share of the library go up in the treated sample?
The treated sample accidentally received twice as many human cells as the control (same amount of fly chromatin). How would that bias the result, and which measurement would reveal the mistake?

B6. Judge the design. For each study, list the problems and propose a better design within a similar budget.

“We performed H3K27ac ChIP-seq on a tumour and on adjacent normal tissue from one patient. Peaks were called with MACS2 (no control). We identify 5214 tumour-specific enhancers.”
“ATAC-seq was performed on livers of three Tet2-knockout and three wild-type mice. Knockout livers were collected and processed in week 1 and sequenced on flow cell 1; wild-type livers in week 2 on flow cell 2. Differential accessibility was tested with DESeq2 (~ genotype).”
“CUT&RUN for H3K27me3 in three replicates of DMSO- and EZH2-inhibitor-treated cells. Tracks were normalised to counts per million. H3K27me3 is unchanged at most domains, so we conclude that the inhibitor does not reduce H3K27me3 at Polycomb targets.”

B7. How many reads? You plan a TF ChIP-seq and want 20 M usable fragments per replicate (ENCODE). A pilot run gave: 92% of reads aligned, 80% of the aligned reads have MAPQ ≥ 30, and 15% of those are duplicates.

What fraction of sequenced reads is usable? How many reads must you sequence per replicate?
The duplicate rate was measured at pilot depth (2 M reads). Will it be the same at full depth? What does that mean for your estimate?
The pilot FRiP is 5% and you expect about 20 000 binding sites. On average, how many reads fall into one peak at 20 M usable reads? And at FRiP 0.5%?

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
On the command line

C1 — Produce the filtered BAM files
This is the alignment chain from From reads to coverage: trim with fastp, align with Bowtie2, keep primary alignments with MAPQ ≥ 30 (and proper pairs for paired-end), mark and remove duplicates, keep chr21 and drop blacklisted regions. We keep the intermediate files: filt.bam (filtered, duplicates still in) is what complexity is computed on, final.bam is what everything else uses.
# single-end CTCF ChIP and input (old reads: phred+64 qualities)
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  fastp --phred64 -w $T -i $D/gm12878_$s.fastq.gz -o $s.trim.fq.gz \
        -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -U $s.trim.fq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools view -u -q 30 -F 0x904 - \
    | samtools sort -@ $T -o $s.filt.bam -
  samtools index $s.filt.bam
  samtools markdup -r -s $s.filt.bam $s.dedup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.dedup.bam
  samtools view -b $s.dedup.bam chr21 \
    | bedtools intersect -v -abam - -b $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
done

# paired-end ATAC-seq, two replicates
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  s=atac_$r
  fastp -w $T -i $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R2.fastq.gz \
        -o $s.R1.fq.gz -O $s.R2.fq.gz -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -X 2000 -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM \
          -1 $s.R1.fq.gz -2 $s.R2.fq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools view -u -q 30 -f 2 -F 0x904 - \
    | samtools sort -n -u -@ $T - \
    | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
    | samtools view -u -f 2 - \
    | samtools sort -@ $T -o $s.filt.bam -
  samtools index $s.filt.bam
  samtools markdup -r -s $s.filt.bam $s.dedup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.dedup.bam
  samtools view -b $s.dedup.bam chr21 \
    | bedtools intersect -v -abam - -b $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
done
Then count what is left at each stage:
grep overall *.bowtie2.log
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input atac_rep1 atac_rep2; do
  echo $s $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam chrM) \
       $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam chr21) $(samtools view -c $s.dedup.bam chr21) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done

Make a table: filtered reads, of which chrM, of which chr21; chr21 reads after duplicate removal; final reads. Why are the ATAC numbers dominated by chrM, and why must you not quote this chrM fraction as the library’s (see the warning above)?
What fraction of the chr21 reads were duplicates in each library? Which library is the least complex?
Why does the ATAC loop filter on -f 2 twice, before and after samtools fixmate?



C2 — Library complexity with awk
Single-end: one line per read with chromosome, 5’ end and strand; count identical lines.
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  samtools view -b $s.filt.bam chr21 | bedtools bamtobed -i - \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, ($6 == "+" ? $2 : $3), $6 }' \
    | sort | uniq -c \
    | awk -v s=$s '{ n += $1; m++; if ($1 == 1) m1++; if ($1 == 2) m2++ }
        END { printf "%s reads %d distinct %d M1 %d M2 %d NRF %.3f PBC1 %.3f PBC2 %.2f\n",
              s, n, m, m1, m2, m/n, m1/m, m1/m2 }'
done
Paired-end: one line per fragment (both mates), from a name-sorted BAM.
for s in atac_rep1 atac_rep2; do
  samtools view -b $s.filt.bam chr21 | samtools sort -n - | bedtools bamtobed -bedpe -i - \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ st = ($2 < $5 ? $2 : $5); en = ($3 > $6 ? $3 : $6); print $1, st, en }' \
    | sort | uniq -c \
    | awk -v s=$s '{ n += $1; m++; if ($1 == 1) m1++; if ($1 == 2) m2++ }
        END { printf "%s fragments %d distinct %d M1 %d M2 %d NRF %.3f PBC1 %.3f PBC2 %.2f\n",
              s, n, m, m1, m2, m/n, m1/m, m1/m2 }'
done

Explain the first awk: why is the position of a − strand read its end ($3) and not its start?
Classify the four libraries with the ENCODE tables (ChIP-seq table for ChIP and input, ATAC table for ATAC).
Compare with the genome-wide values that ENCODE reports for the same libraries (in the solutions). Is chr21 a fair sample?



C3 — FRiP
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz > ctcf_peaks.bed
zcat $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz > atac_peaks.bed
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  echo $s CTCF-peaks $(samtools view -c -L ctcf_peaks.bed $s.final.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done
for s in atac_rep1 atac_rep2 ctcf_input; do
  echo $s ATAC-peaks $(samtools view -c -L atac_peaks.bed $s.final.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done
# bases of chr21 inside peaks (overlapping peaks merged)
for p in ctcf atac; do
  awk '$1 == "chr21"' ${p}_peaks.bed | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge | awk -v p=$p '{ s += $3 - $2 } END { print p, NR, s }'
done

Compute the FRiP of each sample. Do the ChIP and the ATAC-seq pass the guidelines?
The assembled part of chr21 is about 40.1 Mb. What FRiP would uniformly spread reads have in each peak set? How many times higher is the input’s FRiP than that? What does this tell you about the input (lecture: the background is not flat)?
We used ENCODE’s peaks, called on the full data of both replicates. Why does that make the FRiPs of the two ATAC replicates comparable? What would change if each replicate’s FRiP were computed with its own peaks?



C4 — Fingerprint
plotFingerprint -b ctcf_chip.final.bam ctcf_input.final.bam atac_rep1.final.bam \
  --labels CTCF input ATAC --region chr21 --binSize 1000 --numberOfSamples 50000 -p $T \
  --JSDsample ctcf_input.final.bam --outQualityMetrics fingerprint_metrics.txt \
  --outRawCounts fingerprint_counts.tab -o fingerprint.png
cut -f1-3,6-8 fingerprint_metrics.txt | column -t -s $'\t'

Open fingerprint.png. Which curve is the input, and how far is it from the diagonal? Which sample is most enriched?
All three curves stay at zero up to about 0.3 on the x axis. Why? (What is on the first 5–10 Mb of chr21?)
The metrics file gives the “elbow point” and the “synthetic” values: what a perfectly uniform sample of the same depth would give. Compare the input with its synthetic value.



C5 — Replicate concordance
for b in 10000 1000; do
  multiBamSummary bins -b atac_rep1.final.bam atac_rep2.final.bam ctcf_chip.final.bam ctcf_input.final.bam \
    --labels ATAC1 ATAC2 CTCF input --region chr21 --binSize $b -p $T \
    -o bins$b.npz --outRawCounts bins$b.tab
  plotCorrelation -in bins$b.npz --corMethod spearman --whatToPlot heatmap --plotNumbers \
    --skipZeros -o cor$b.png --outFileCorMatrix cor$b.txt
done
plotCorrelation -in bins10000.npz --corMethod pearson --log1p --whatToPlot scatterplot \
  --skipZeros -o scatter10k.png
cat cor10000.txt cor1000.txt

What is the Spearman correlation between the ATAC replicates in 10 kb and in 1 kb bins? Why is it lower in smaller bins?
Is CTCF closer to its input or to ATAC? Why is a high correlation between ChIP and input not a good sign?
A correlation of 0.9 between replicates sounds excellent. Why is it not enough to show that the peaks are reproducible? (Lecture: IDR.)

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Explore: fingerprint and library complexity
The demo simulates a ChIP-seq library of 200 000 reads in 20 000 bins of 1 kb (8% of the bins cannot receive reads) and draws its fingerprint, with an input of the same depth (dashed) and the diagonal of a perfectly uniform sample. Enriched reads (the share of reads that come from enriched bins) moves the sample from input-like (0%) to a strong ChIP; enriched bins (% of the genome) sets how many bins share that signal (a TF binds in few places, a broad mark covers many). Complexity is the number of distinct molecules in the library per read sequenced: below about ×3 the same molecules are read again and again. The right panel counts reads per position (5’ end + strand) before duplicate removal and gives NRF, PBC1 and PBC2 with ENCODE’s classes, and the FRiP, with the enriched bins playing the role of peaks.



E1. Three shapes. Click input-like, TF ChIP and broad mark in turn. For each, note the share of reads in the top 10% and top 1% of bins and the FRiP. Where does each curve leave the input? Which of the curves A–D of B3 does each resemble?
E2. A failed ChIP. Click failed ChIP (3% of reads from 0.5% of the bins). How different is its fingerprint from the input? What is its FRiP, and would it pass the 1% guideline? What would a peak caller make of this sample?
E3. Complexity. Click TF ChIP, then lower the complexity step by step from ×10 to ×0.5 (bottlenecked TF). Note NRF, PBC1, PBC2 and the duplicates, and watch the bar chart. Then go to ×100: why is NRF still not close to 1? (Which positions are shared?)
E4. Duplicates and the fingerprint. Click input-like and set the complexity to ×0.5. Compare the curve with the input and read the top 10%. Then tick remove duplicates first. What does a bottlenecked library do to a fingerprint, and what does deduplication do to the FRiP of the TF ChIP?






Solutions





E1. Input-like: top 10% of bins hold 21% of the reads, the top 1% 3%; FRiP 0.5% (the “peaks” are 0.5% of the bins). TF ChIP: 45% and 32%, FRiP 30% (the input has 0.6% in the same bins); the curve runs below the input and then rises almost vertically in the last 0.5% of bins: a sharp elbow at the very end, like curve B. Broad mark: 48% and only 11%, FRiP 61% (input 22%, because the domains cover 20% of the genome); the curve bends away from the diagonal gradually over the whole range, like curve C. All curves stay at 0 for the first 8% of bins: the unmappable bins (C4b). Even the input is below the diagonal, because counts vary by chance (about 10 reads per bin) and by the mild background bias.
E2. The failed ChIP follows the input almost exactly (top 10% 23% vs 21%, top 1% 5% vs 3%). Its FRiP is 3.5%, which passes the 1% guideline, but only because we count in the true sites; a peak caller would find few of them, and the FRiP in its own peaks would be low and dominated by noise. The fingerprint alone does not tell a weak ChIP from an input; compare with the input at the same depth and look at the other metrics.
E3. ×10: NRF 0.87, PBC1 0.88, PBC2 8.6, 13% duplicates (compliant, mild). ×3: 0.75, 0.75, 4.0, 25%. ×1: 0.53, 0.51, 1.9, 47%. ×0.5: NRF 0.36 (concerning), PBC1 0.32 (severe), PBC2 1.3 (moderate), 64% duplicates; the bar chart shifts from “almost all positions have 1 read” to many positions with 2, 3 and 5+ reads. At ×100 NRF is 0.92 and PBC2 17.7, not 1 and ∞: 30% of the reads come from only 100 bins, so independent fragments in strong peaks often start at the same base. Those are not PCR copies, but duplicate marking cannot tell them apart; this is why TF ChIP-seq with very strong peaks can have a lower NRF than its input.
E4. A bottlenecked input (×0.5, NRF 0.37) bends further from the diagonal than the complex input: its top 10% of bins hold 26% of the reads instead of 21%, because some molecules were amplified and read many times (jackpots), which looks like enrichment. After duplicate removal it is closer to the input again (24%). For the TF ChIP, removing duplicates lowers the FRiP from 30.4% to 25.6%: duplicate removal caps the count at each position, and the strongest peaks lose the most. Judge a fingerprint together with the complexity metrics, and compare ChIP and input processed the same way.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Explore: strand cross-correlation
The demo simulates single-end ChIP-seq (200 000 reads on a 1-Mb genome with 300 binding sites). Short repeats make some read start positions unmappable; a longer read reaches unique sequence more often. The left panel sums the 5’ ends of + strand reads (blue) and − strand reads (red) around all binding sites, or around the left edges of the repeats; the shift slider moves the − strand to the left by \(k\) bp. The right panel is the cross-correlation \(CC(k)\) of the + strand at \(x\) and the − strand at \(x + k\), computed as in R1, for \(k\) = 0–600, with the fragment-length peak (green), the read-length peak (orange), the minimum, and NSC and RSC. As in phantompeakqualtools, the fragment peak is searched outside shifts 10 to \(L + 10\). The other sliders set the share of reads that come from binding sites (reads from sites), the fragment length and the read length \(L\).



E1. Why the strands are offset. At the start (\(k = 0\)), where are the + strand and − strand reads relative to the binding site, and why? Move the shift until the two peaks lie on top of each other. What \(k\) is that, what is \(CC(k)\) there, and how does it compare with the fragment length the demo estimates?
E2. The phantom peak. Set \(k = 36\) (the read length) and click repeat edges. What lines up, and why? Now click input: which peak is left? Read NSC and RSC, and the estimated fragment length.
E3. How much signal is enough? Click good TF ChIP, then lower reads from sites to 10, 8, 6, 4 and 0%. Note NSC and RSC. Where does RSC cross ENCODE’s 0.8? What about NSC and its 1.05?
E4. Read length and fragment length. Click 100-bp reads: where is the phantom peak now, and what happens to RSC? Why? Then click short fragments (95 bp). Compare with the course’s CTCF data in R1.






Solutions





E1. + strand reads pile up about 100 bp to the left of the site, − strand reads about 100 bp to the right: a + strand read starts at the left end of a fragment that covers the site, a − strand read at its right end, and fragments are about 200 bp long. The two peaks coincide at \(k \approx 200\), where \(CC(200) = 0.123\); the demo’s fragment estimate is 202 bp with \(CC = 0.125\). This is how the fragment length is estimated from single-end data (MACS’s model and predictd use the same idea).
E2. Around repeat edges the + strand reads drop just after the edge (a read that starts in the repeat cannot be mapped), and the − strand reads drop \(L = 36\) bp further right (a − strand read’s 5’ end is at the end of its \(L\)-mer). Shifting the − strand by 36 bp lines up the two gaps; the same happens at every repeat, so the strands correlate at \(k = L\) in any library, whatever the IP did. In the input only this phantom peak is left (\(CC(36) = 0.107\), minimum 0.070): NSC 1.12, RSC 0.23, and the “fragment length” of 58 bp is just the highest point of a flat, noisy curve outside the excluded shifts.
E3.

NSC stays above 1.05 even for the input: NSC divides by the minimum of the curve, so its value depends on how the background correlation is estimated (here the simulated genome has strong regional coverage differences); RSC, a ratio of differences above the minimum, is the more robust of the two (R1c).
E4. With 95-bp fragments the fragment peak is at 93 bp, close to the read length: the phantom peak at 36 bp sits on its rising flank, as in the course’s 2008 CTCF library (fragment 93 bp, R1a); NSC 3.22, RSC 2.63.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
In R
You need GenomicAlignments and ggplot2. Work in the same folder:
library(GenomicAlignments); library(ggplot2)
setwd("~/epi/design")

R1 — Strand cross-correlation of CTCF
The function counts the 5’ ends of + and − strand reads at each base of chr21 and computes the Pearson correlation between the + strand counts at \(x\) and the − strand counts at \(x + k\). Only positions with a + strand read contribute to the sum of products, which makes it fast.
strand_cc <- function(bam, shifts = 0:1000, len = 46709983) {
  r <- readGAlignments(bam)
  plus <- as.character(strand(r)) == "+"
  fwd <- tabulate(start(r)[plus], len)          # 5' ends of + strand reads
  rev <- tabulate(end(r)[!plus], len)           # 5' ends of - strand reads
  p <- which(fwd > 0)
  m <- mean(fwd) * mean(rev); s <- sd(fwd) * sd(rev)
  sapply(shifts, function(k) {                  # correlation of fwd(x) and rev(x + k)
    q <- p + k; ok <- q <= len
    (sum(fwd[p[ok]] * rev[q[ok]]) / len - m) / s
  })
}
k <- 0:1000
cc_chip  <- strand_cc("ctcf_chip.final.bam")
cc_input <- strand_cc("ctcf_input.final.bam")
frag <- k[k > 50][which.max(cc_chip[k > 50])]
c(fragment = frag, cc_frag = max(cc_chip[k > 50]), cc_read = cc_chip[k == 36], min = min(cc_chip))
d <- rbind(data.frame(k, cc = cc_chip, sample = "CTCF"), data.frame(k, cc = cc_input, sample = "input"))
ggplot(d[d$k <= 500, ], aes(k, cc)) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~sample, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(36, frag), linetype = 2) + labs(x = "strand shift (bp)", y = "cross-correlation")

What is the fragment length? Compute NSC and RSC for the CTCF ChIP (read length 36). Does it pass?
Describe the input curve. Is there a fragment-length peak?
ENCODE reports, for the same replicate genome-wide, RSC 1.69 and NSC 4.9 (phantompeakqualtools). Which of your two numbers agrees, and which does not? (Hint: what decides the minimum of the curve?)



R2 — Replicate concordance in R
b10 <- read.delim("bins10000.tab", check.names = FALSE)
names(b10) <- c("chr", "start", "end", "ATAC1", "ATAC2", "CTCF", "input")
b10 <- b10[rowSums(b10[, c("ATAC1", "ATAC2")]) > 0, ]
c(pearson_raw = cor(b10$ATAC1, b10$ATAC2),
  pearson_log = cor(log1p(b10$ATAC1), log1p(b10$ATAC2)),
  spearman    = cor(b10$ATAC1, b10$ATAC2, method = "spearman"))
ggplot(b10, aes(ATAC1 + 1, ATAC2 + 1)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + coord_equal()
b10$M <- log2((b10$ATAC2 + 1) / sum(b10$ATAC2)) - log2((b10$ATAC1 + 1) / sum(b10$ATAC1))
b10$A <- (log2(b10$ATAC1 + 1) + log2(b10$ATAC2 + 1)) / 2
ggplot(b10, aes(A, M)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "red")

Why is the Pearson correlation of raw counts different from that of log counts? Which would you report?
The MA plot (as for RNA-seq): where is the spread largest, and why?



R3 — Why depth normalisation hides a global change
Simulate 500 H3K27me3 domains and 5000 background bins. The inhibitor removes 75% of H3K27me3 everywhere; the background (unspecific DNA) is unchanged. Both libraries are sequenced to the same depth, and each sample has the same amount of fly spike-in chromatin.
set.seed(1)
true_ctrl <- c(rgamma(500, shape = 4, rate = 0.02), rep(20, 5000))  # domains, then background
true_trt  <- c(0.25 * true_ctrl[1:500], rep(20, 5000))
spike     <- 2000                                                    # fly signal, same in both
depth     <- 2e6
lib <- function(true) {                                              # sequencing = sampling to fixed depth
  p <- c(true, spike) / sum(true, spike)
  as.vector(rmultinom(1, depth, p))
}
ctrl <- lib(true_ctrl); trt <- lib(true_trt)
fly  <- c(ctrl = tail(ctrl, 1), trt = tail(trt, 1))
ctrl <- head(ctrl, -1); trt <- head(trt, -1)
dom <- 1:500
cpm <- function(x) x / sum(x) * 1e6
c(cpm_ratio   = median(cpm(trt)[dom] / cpm(ctrl)[dom]),
  spike_ratio = median((trt[dom] / fly["trt"]) / (ctrl[dom] / fly["ctrl"])))

What are the two median ratios (treated / control at the domains)? Which one recovers the true 0.25?
Why is the CPM ratio not 1, as in the toy example of the lecture, but somewhat below? (Hint: what fraction of the library is background in each sample?)
Set true_trt <- true_ctrl (no change) and rerun. Do both methods give about 1?

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — complexity (B1, C2)





NRF is a fraction of reads, PBC1 a fraction of positions, PBC2 a ratio of counts of positions. Duplicates removed = \(N - M_\text{distinct}\). A library contains a fixed number of distinct molecules: sequencing deeper samples the same molecules again. The ENCODE definitions are on the ENCODE data standards terms page. bedtools bamtobed writes one BED line per read (-bedpe: per pair; needs a name-sorted BAM, samtools sort -n). samtools markdup needs samtools fixmate -m for paired-end data.









Hint 2 — FRiP (B2, C3)





Expected FRiP for uniform reads = fraction of the (mappable) genome covered by peaks. samtools view -c -L file.bed counts the reads that overlap any region of the BED file; bedtools merge collapses overlapping peaks. FRiP is described in Landt et al. 2012.









Hint 3 — fingerprint and cross-correlation (B3, B4, C4, R1)





Read the fingerprint from the right: the top 10% of bins are \(x\) from 0.9 to 1, and they hold \(1 - y(0.9)\) of the reads. See the plotFingerprint manual, including the description of its quality metrics. For NSC and RSC, plug the three numbers into the formulas in Background. The phantom peak and its explanation are in Landt et al. 2012 (Fig. 4) and Kharchenko et al. 2008. readGAlignments reads a BAM file; tabulate counts integers.









Hint 4 — spike-ins and design (B5, B6, R3)





CPM: divide by the human reads in millions. Spike-in: multiply by \(1/N_\text{fly}\) (millions). The method is Orlando et al. 2014. For the design questions go through: biological replicates per condition, control, antibody, batches vs condition, normalisation under a global change. rmultinom draws a fixed total of reads from the given proportions, like a sequencer.









Hint 5 — deepTools and depth (B7, C5, R2)





Usable fraction = product of the fractions kept at each step. multiBamSummary bins counts reads in bins; plotCorrelation plots and writes the correlation matrix. Spearman correlation uses ranks; Pearson on raw counts is dominated by the largest bins.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Library 1: NRF \(8.2/10 = 0.82\), PBC1 \(7.0/8.2 = 0.85\), PBC2 \(7.0/0.9 = 7.8\): NRF compliant (0.8–0.9), mild bottlenecking by PBC1 and PBC2: acceptable. Library 2: NRF \(0.30\), PBC1 \(1.2/3.0 = 0.40\), PBC2 \(1.2/0.6 = 2.0\): NRF concerning, PBC1 severe, PBC2 moderate: a strongly bottlenecked library. (b) \(1 - 0.30 = 70\%\) of the reads are duplicates; 3.0 M usable reads remain. (c) NRF goes down: the library holds a limited number of distinct molecules (judging from PBC2, not many more than the 3 M already seen), so most new reads are copies of molecules already sequenced. The usable reads grow far less than four-fold. More sequencing cannot rescue a library that was amplified from too little DNA; make a new one. (d) After duplicate removal every position has exactly one read, so NRF = PBC1 = 1 by definition; the information is in how many copies there were.
B2. (a) \(540\,000 / 18\,000\,000 = 3\%\): above 1%, passes. (b) Peaks cover \(45\,000 \times 300 = 13.5\) Mb, \(13.5 / 2700 = 0.5\%\) of the mappable genome; expected FRiP 0.5%, so the ChIP has 6 times more reads in peaks than uniform. (c) The input has \(0.8/0.5 = 1.6\) times the uniform expectation. It is not uniform: CTCF sites are often in open chromatin, which shears more easily, and they are in mappable, GC-rich DNA. (In the course data the input’s FRiP in CTCF peaks is about 8 times the uniform expectation, C3.) (d) Below 0.2: not acceptable. Possible causes: too few cells or too much Tn5 for the cell number (over-tagmentation, more background), dead or dying cells (fragmented chromatin), poor nuclei isolation, many mitochondrial reads (these are removed but signal the problem), or a library dominated by background after too many PCR cycles.
B3. (a) A is the input (close to the diagonal). B is the sharp TF: flat for 90% of the bins, then a steep rise. C, a smooth curve bending away from the diagonal over the whole range, is the broad mark. (b) At \(x = 0.9\), \(y \approx 0.23\), so the top 10% of bins hold about 77% of the reads. (c) No: 99% of the genome looks like an input. A few bins with huge counts produce the jump: artefact regions such as satellite repeats, rDNA or the mitochondrial genome (blacklisted regions), or a few PCR jackpots. Check what those bins are; remove the blacklist and duplicates and replot.
B4. (a) X: NSC \(0.32 / 0.15 = 2.13\), RSC \((0.32 - 0.15)/(0.21 - 0.15) = 2.83\): passes both. Y: NSC \(0.26/0.25 = 1.04\), RSC \((0.26 - 0.25)/(0.30 - 0.25) = 0.2\): fails both (NSC < 1.05, RSC < 0.8). (b) About 180 bp: the shift where + and − strand reads correlate best. The read-length (phantom) peak comes from mappability: a position that can be mapped on the + strand can also be mapped on the − strand one read length further, so the two strands correlate at that shift in any library, even an input. (c) No. Broad marks spread over whole gene bodies have flat cross-correlation curves even when the ChIP works. Look at the fingerprint (and FRiP in broad domains), the browser, and the replicate agreement.
B5. (a) Human reads: 23.75 M and 21.25 M. HOXA: \(600/23.75 = 25.3\) and \(450/21.25 = 21.2\) reads per million human reads, a 16% drop: “a mild decrease”. (b) \(\alpha = 1/1.25 = 0.8\) and \(1/3.75 = 0.267\); scaled counts \(600 \times 0.8 = 480\) and \(450 \times 0.267 = 120\): a 4-fold drop (75% loss). (c) The same amount of fly H3K27me3 went into each IP, but the treated cells had much less human H3K27me3 to pull down, so the fly chromatin made up a larger share of the immunoprecipitated DNA (and of the reads). (d) Twice as much human chromatin per fly chromatin makes the fly share smaller, \(\alpha\) larger, and the treated sample looks too high: the loss is underestimated. The input (sequenced without IP) shows the actual human:fly ratio in each sample; ChIP-Rx-type normalisations correct by it.
B6. (a) n = 1 per condition (no biological replicates: no estimate of variability, any difference could be between two people); no input (copy-number changes in the tumour create “tumour-specific peaks”); tumour vs normal adjacent tissue also differ in cell-type composition. Better: tumours and matched normals from at least 3 (better 5+) patients, an input for each sample, the patient as a blocking factor (~ patient + tissue), and peaks called against the input. (b) Genotype is completely confounded with week and flow cell: the design matrix cannot separate them, and ~ genotype attributes every batch effect to the knockout. Better: process and sequence knockout and wild-type livers together (e.g. one KO and one WT per day, all on one flow cell or spread evenly), and include the batch in the model. (c) CPM normalisation assumes the total amount of H3K27me3 is unchanged, which is exactly what an EZH2 inhibitor violates: after normalisation the remaining signal is scaled up and domains look unchanged. Use a spike-in (e.g. Drosophila chromatin or the E. coli DNA carried over in CUT&RUN), or check global levels by western blot / mass spectrometry. The conclusion as written is not supported.
B7. (a) \(0.92 \times 0.80 \times 0.85 = 0.626\); \(20 / 0.626 \approx 32\) M reads per replicate. (b) No: the duplicate rate rises with depth because the library has a limited number of distinct molecules. Expect more than 15% duplicates at 32 M, so sequence more, or (better) check the complexity first (e.g. with a library-complexity extrapolation such as preseq). (c) \(20 \text{ M} \times 0.05 = 1\) M reads in peaks, about 50 reads per peak; at FRiP 0.5%, about 5 reads per peak: too few to call most peaks reliably.









Solutions — command line





Runtimes on a shared (busy) 40-core server with T=8: the alignment block 11 min (ChIP and input 20 s, the rest ATAC, mostly Bowtie2); counting 13 s; complexity 2 s (SE) and 21 s (PE); FRiP 2 s; plotFingerprint 30 s; the two multiBamSummary runs 8 s. In R: R1 12 s, R2 and R3 under a second. Your numbers may differ by a few hundred reads, about 0.1% (Bowtie2 breaks ties between equally good alignments at random).

The ATAC subset is ~94% chrM because the selection kept every mitochondrial read but only the nuclear reads from chr21 (1.5% of the genome). ENCODE’s genome-wide numbers are 13.9% (rep1) and 10.3% (rep2) mitochondrial reads: still substantial, typical of ATAC-seq without a mitochondria-depleting protocol (Omni-ATAC). ENCODE, genome-wide (all reads of the replicate): CTCF rep1 NRF 0.75, PBC1 0.84, PBC2 9.9 (29.5 M reads); ATAC rep1 NRF 0.79–0.80, PBC1 0.80, PBC2 5.1–5.2; rep2 NRF 0.88–0.89, PBC1 0.89, PBC2 9.2–9.6. The ATAC values agree almost exactly; the ChIP values are close (ENCODE also counts reads in repeats and pericentromeres on other chromosomes, which add duplicates). chr21 is a fair sample of the library.

C3. (a) CTCF ChIP: 44 914 / 200 297 = 22.4%, far above 1%. Input: 1690 / 107 975 = 1.6%. ATAC rep1: 283 347 / 482 022 = 58.8%; rep2: 247 495 / 495 353 = 50.0%, both well above 0.3. (ENCODE genome-wide: 54–60% for rep1 and 46–52% for rep2 with their peak sets.) (b) 405 CTCF peaks on chr21 cover 74 287 bp, 0.19% of 40.1 Mb; the 1784 ATAC peaks on chr21 merge into 821 regions covering 620 kb, 1.5% (ENCODE’s IDR peaks list a region once per summit, so many overlap). The input has 1.6% of its reads in CTCF peaks (8 times the uniform expectation) and 8.3% in ATAC peaks (5 times): input DNA is enriched in open chromatin, which is why the ChIP must be compared with the input, not with a flat background. (c) Same peaks for both replicates means the same denominator of “where signal can be”: the FRiP then compares only the signal-to-noise of the libraries. With each replicate’s own peaks, the deeper or better replicate also gets more peaks, which raises its FRiP further; FRiP and peak number are not independent.
C4. (a) The input is the curve closest to the diagonal, but still clearly below it; ATAC is the most enriched (top 1% of 1-kb bins hold about 52% of the ATAC reads, 30% of CTCF reads, 8% of input reads). (b) About 28–40% of the 1-kb bins have no reads in any sample: the short arm of chr21 (0–~5 Mb, unassembled), the centromere (~11–13 Mb) and other gaps and repeats, where nothing can map. With the blacklist and these gaps the “genome” is smaller than the chromosome. (c) Elbow points: CTCF 0.74, input 0.62, ATAC 0.90; the synthetic (perfectly uniform) values are all about 0.51. Even the input is far from its synthetic value: it is not uniform, partly because of the unmappable bins, partly the open-chromatin bias seen in C3. The Jensen–Shannon distance to the input is 0.26 for CTCF and 0.49 for ATAC.
C5. (a) Spearman ATAC1–ATAC2: 0.90 in 10 kb bins, 0.59 in 1 kb bins (bins with reads in at least one sample). Small bins have few reads each, so Poisson counting noise is a larger part of the variation. (b) In 10 kb bins CTCF correlates about equally with its input (0.64) and with ATAC (0.65), and the input correlates even better with ATAC (0.75–0.76) than with CTCF. At this scale all libraries share the same background: mappability, GC content and open chromatin (C3). A ChIP that correlates highly with its input has little specific signal; here CTCF’s signal is in a few hundred narrow peaks, which hardly move a 10 kb-bin correlation. (c) Correlation over bins is dominated by the many background bins and by large-scale coverage variation that both replicates share; it says little about whether the same peaks, in the same order, are found. IDR answers that question.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Fragment length 93 bp (ENCODE: 90–95). \(CC(93) = 0.147\), \(CC(36) = 0.091\), minimum (at ~1 kb) \(0.0032\): NSC \(= 0.147 / 0.0032 \approx 47\), RSC \(= (0.147 - 0.0032)/(0.091 - 0.0032) = 1.65\). Passes both thresholds easily. Note that the phantom peak at 36 bp is hidden on the rising flank of the fragment peak: CTCF fragments here are short. Runtime: about 12 s for both BAM files. (b) The input curve is low and noisy (0.001–0.0025), slowly decreasing with the shift, without a clear fragment-length peak: no enrichment. (c) RSC agrees (1.65 vs 1.69); NSC does not (47 vs 4.9). RSC is a ratio of two differences above the minimum and is robust. NSC divides by the minimum of the curve, the background correlation, which depends on how the background is estimated: per base or in bins, which chromosomes and regions are included (pericentromeric repeats, artefacts), the range of shifts. Compare NSC only between datasets computed the same way.
R2. Pearson of raw counts 0.97, of log counts 0.94, Spearman 0.89 (the 3580 10-kb bins with ATAC reads). (a) Raw counts are dominated by the few bins with very high counts (strong peaks), which inflates the Pearson correlation; log counts or ranks weigh all bins more equally. Report Spearman or Pearson on log counts, and say which. In ENCODE ATAC peaks (the counts used for differential accessibility), the log correlation is 0.99. (b) The spread is largest at low A (few reads): Poisson noise is relatively largest when counts are small, the same funnel shape as an MA plot in RNA-seq.
R3. (a) The CPM ratio is 0.40, the spike-in ratio 0.25: only the spike-in recovers the true 4-fold loss. (b) The domains hold about 100 000 units of signal in the control (500 × a mean of 200) and 25 000 after treatment; the background is 100 000 units in both. So the background is half of the control library but 80% of the treated one, and normalising both to the same total scales the treated sample up by \(200\,000 / 125\,000 = 1.6\): \(0.25 \times 1.6 = 0.40\). The domains seem to lose 60% instead of 75%. Real ChIP data behave in the same way: how much the global change is hidden depends on the share of background in the library. (c) Both give 1.00.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Where this leads

ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder explains the fragment-size distribution and TSS enrichment of these two replicates.
Peak calling calls the CTCF peaks with MACS3 against the input you aligned here, and runs IDR on replicates.
Differential accessibility and Annotation and differential binding use the replicate structure, batches and (for global changes) spike-in factors.
In practice, nf-core/chipseq and nf-core/atacseq compute all of these metrics and collect them in a MultiQC report.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia.
Kharchenko, Tolstorukov & Park 2008, Nat Biotechnol. Design and analysis of ChIP-seq experiments for DNA-binding proteins.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome.
Diaz, Park, Lim & Song 2012, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. Normalization, bias correction, and peak calling for ChIP-seq.
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin & Käller 2016, Bioinformatics. MultiQC: summarize analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report.

title: Quiz: experimental design and QC
text:
Short questions on replicates, controls, normalisation and QC metrics. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A ChIP-seq library has 20 M uniquely mapped reads (before duplicate removal) at 15 M distinct positions; 12 M positions have exactly one read and 2 M have exactly two. Compute NRF, PBC1 and PBC2. Is the library acceptable by the ENCODE standards?






Hint





NRF = distinct / reads; PBC1 = one-read positions / distinct; PBC2 = one-read / two-read positions. ENCODE ideal: > 0.9, > 0.9, > 10.









Answer





NRF \(= 15/20 = 0.75\), PBC1 \(= 12/15 = 0.80\), PBC2 \(= 12/2 = 6\). NRF is “acceptable” (0.5–0.8), PBC1 and PBC2 indicate mild bottlenecking (0.8–0.9 and 3–10). Usable, but sequencing deeper will mostly add duplicates.




Q2. A TF ChIP-seq has 25 M filtered reads, 200 000 of which fall in peaks. What is the FRiP? What would you check before deciding that the experiment failed?






Answer





FRiP \(= 0.2 / 25 = 0.8\%\), below ENCODE’s 1% guideline. Before rejecting it: how many peaks are there (a factor with few genuine sites can have a low FRiP and still be good), the fingerprint against the input, the cross-correlation (RSC), the replicate agreement, and whether the expected motif is enriched at the peak summits.




Q3. Name three sources of reads that are present in a ChIP-seq library but have nothing to do with the antibody’s target. Which of them does an input control correct for, and which does it not?






Answer





Open chromatin shears more easily (more fragments at promoters); copy-number gains (more DNA, more reads); mappability and repeats (no reads, or pile-ups in collapsed repeats); GC and PCR bias. The input, made from the same sheared chromatin without an antibody, shows all of these. It does not model DNA that binds non-specifically to the antibody or the beads: an IgG control does, but it often yields too little DNA for a good library.




Q4. In a fingerprint plot, sample S1 lies almost on the diagonal, and sample S2 stays near 0 until \(x = 0.8\) and then rises to 1. At \(x = 0.9\), S2 is at 0.35. What are S1 and S2 likely to be? What fraction of S2’s reads are in the top 10% of bins?






Answer





S1 is an input (or a failed ChIP): reads spread evenly over the bins. S2 is an enriched ChIP. The top 10% of bins (from 0.9 to 1) hold \(1 - 0.35 = 65\%\) of S2’s reads.




Q5. A single-end 50 bp ChIP-seq has strand cross-correlation 0.12 at 50 bp, 0.10 at its fragment-length peak (220 bp), and a minimum of 0.08. Compute NSC and RSC. What do the two peaks of the curve mean, and is this a good experiment?






Hint





NSC = CC(fragment) / min; RSC = (CC(fragment) − min) / (CC(read) − min).









Answer





NSC \(= 0.10/0.08 = 1.25\); RSC \(= 0.02/0.04 = 0.5\). The peak at 220 bp is the fragment length (enrichment around binding sites); the peak at 50 bp is the “phantom” read-length peak caused by mappability, present in every library. Here the phantom peak is higher than the fragment peak (RSC < 0.8): weak enrichment. ENCODE would repeat a TF ChIP like this; for a broad histone mark a flat curve is less worrying.




Q6. H3K79me2 ChIP-Rx with Drosophila spike-in. Control: 30 M reads, 1.5 M on the fly genome; DOT1L inhibitor: 30 M reads, 6 M on the fly genome. A gene body has 3000 reads in the control and 2400 after treatment. Compare the change with CPM normalisation and with spike-in normalisation.






Answer





CPM per human reads: \(3000/28.5 = 105\) and \(2400/24 = 100\): a 5% drop, “no real change”. Spike-in: \(\alpha = 1/1.5 = 0.67\) and \(1/6 = 0.167\); \(3000 \times 0.67 = 2000\) and \(2400 \times 0.167 = 400\): a 5-fold loss. The inhibitor removed most H3K79me2 everywhere; depth normalisation redistributes what is left and hides it.




Q7. Wild-type samples were sequenced in January and knockout samples in March, three of each. Why can DESeq2 not estimate the knockout effect with ~ batch + genotype? What would happen with ~ genotype?






Answer





Batch and genotype are perfectly confounded: the batch column of the design matrix equals the genotype column, so the two effects cannot be separated (the matrix is not of full rank and DESeq2 refuses to fit it). With ~ genotype the model fits, but every difference between January and March (reagents, antibody lot, sequencing run) is reported as an effect of the knockout. Only a new design helps: process both genotypes in each batch.




Q8. A paper reports peaks “reproducible in two pseudoreplicates” from a single ChIP-seq sample per condition and concludes that 3000 binding sites differ between conditions. What do pseudoreplicates show, and what do they not show?






Answer





Pseudoreplicates are random halves of the reads of one library. Agreement between them shows that a peak is supported by enough reads (counting noise is small). They share the same cells, chromatin, IP and library, so they say nothing about biological or experimental variability. With n = 1 per condition there is no estimate of that variability, and no valid test of differences between conditions.




Q9. ATAC-seq experiments usually have no input control, and nobody computes strand cross-correlation for them. Why is this acceptable, and which QC metrics take their place?






Answer





There is no natural control: Tn5 cutting of open chromatin is the signal, and the background is estimated from the sample itself (genome-wide and local rates in MACS). Paired-end reads measure every fragment length directly, so cross-correlation is not needed. ATAC-specific QC: TSS enrichment (signal to noise; ENCODE > 7 ideal for GRCh38), the fragment-size distribution (nucleosome-free peak and mono-nucleosome peak), the mitochondrial fraction, FRiP (> 0.3), library complexity, and agreement between biological replicates.




Q10. A collaborator wants to rescue a ChIP-seq library with 70% duplicates by sequencing it four times deeper. Will that work?






Answer





No. 70% duplicates means the library contains few distinct molecules (low complexity, typically from too little immunoprecipitated DNA and many PCR cycles). Deeper sequencing mostly reads the same molecules again: the duplicate rate rises further and the number of usable reads grows very little. Make a new library from more starting material (or pool IPs), with fewer PCR cycles.

title: Gene regulation
text:
About this lecture
Chromatin marks tell you where the regulatory DNA is. This lecture is about what that DNA is and who reads it: short sequence elements (promoters, enhancers, silencers, insulators) and the sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) that bind them.

The cis-regulatory code: core promoters, enhancers, silencers, insulators.
Transcription factors: DNA-binding domains, and motifs written as position weight matrices.
Why a TF binds only a small fraction of its motif matches: accessibility, pioneer factors, cooperation.
Combinatorial control: the B-cell TFs behind the GM12878 data.
How all of this shows up in ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, Hi-C and motif analysis.


Students know transcription and “a TF binds a promoter” from their bachelor’s, and from What is epigenetics? they know the six histone marks and that open chromatin is nucleosome-depleted. This unit supplies the sequence side: what the regulatory elements are, how a TF recognises DNA, and how to write that down as a matrix one can scan a genome with. The running example is GM12878, the B-lymphoblastoid cell line used throughout the course: we look at its CTCF peaks, its ATAC peaks and an enhancer cluster at PAX5, the master regulator of B-cell identity. Every later assay unit measures one of the things introduced here.

title: Gene regulation
text:
The cis-regulatory code


A gene’s expression is set by short DNA elements in cis (on the same molecule): the core promoter, enhancers that activate, silencers that repress, and insulators that delimit their reach.
Each element is a cluster of TF binding sites, typically 6–20 bp each, in a stretch of a few hundred bp.
The proteins that read them (TFs, co-factors) act in trans: they are encoded elsewhere and diffuse to their sites.


The cis/trans distinction comes from genetics: a cis-acting mutation affects only the allele on the same chromosome, a trans-acting one (in a TF gene) affects both alleles. Most variants associated with disease in genome-wide association studies are non-coding and fall in enhancers, so this code matters for human genetics too. Scale: a promoter’s core is about 80 bp; an enhancer a few hundred bp; the regulatory domain of a gene can be up to a megabase, usually bounded by CTCF sites (insulators). ENCODE lists close to a million candidate cis-regulatory elements in the human genome, against about 20 000 protein-coding genes: most genes have several enhancers.

title: Gene regulation
text:
The first enhancer (1981)


A 72-bp repeat from the SV40 virus raised transcription of a β-globin gene on the same plasmid about 200-fold.
It worked in either orientation, upstream or downstream, and kilobases away from the start site (1.4 kb upstream, 3.3 kb downstream).
This defines an enhancer: a DNA element that activates transcription from a distance, independent of orientation.


Banerji, Rusconi and Schaffner transfected HeLa cells with a rabbit β-globin gene and measured correctly initiated transcripts by S1 mapping. On its own the plasmid gave barely detectable transcripts; with SV40 DNA in cis, 200 times more, and the activity mapped to the 72-bp repeat. The bars in the figure are schematic: the paper reports the 200-fold enhancement and that the element acted “in either orientation at many positions”. The key word is cis: SV40 DNA on a separate plasmid did nothing. The same year a polyoma virus element gave the same result, and within two years the first cellular enhancer was found in the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, in B cells, which fits our running example. Reporter assays like this one are still the standard functional test; today they are run in parallel on thousands of fragments (massively parallel reporter assays, STARR-seq).

title: Gene regulation
text:
The core promoter


The core promoter (about −40 to +40 around the transcription start site, TSS) is where RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors assemble the pre-initiation complex.
Known elements: TATA box (about −30, bound by TBP), Initiator (Inr, at the TSS), DPE, BRE. Each promoter has only some of them; a minority have a TATA box.
The core promoter decides where transcription starts and in which direction. How often it starts is set mostly by TFs at proximal sites and enhancers.


The general transcription factors (TFIID, which contains the TATA-binding protein TBP and about 13 TAF subunits, plus TFIIA, B, E, F and H) are present in every cell; they are not what makes a gene cell-type specific. The core elements are short and degenerate, so you cannot find promoters by searching for TATA boxes: only a minority of human promoters (often quoted as 10–20%) have one, mostly highly regulated tissue-specific genes. Letters in the consensus sequences are IUPAC codes (W = A or T, R = A or G, Y = C or T, S = C or G). In practice, promoters are mapped from the data: 5’ ends of transcripts (CAGE), H3K4me3, and the GENCODE annotation you used in Genomic intervals. Review: Haberle and Stark 2018.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Two kinds of promoters


CpG observed/expected around all 19 989 protein-coding TSSs: two populations. About half are CpG-island promoters (52% by a strict cutoff), the rest are CpG-poor.
CpG-island promoters: housekeeping and developmental genes, broad TSS, rarely a TATA box, kept unmethylated. 78% carry H3K4me3 in GM12878.
Non-CpG promoters: often tissue-specific, sharper TSS, more TATA boxes. Only 31% are marked in a B-cell line.


CpG observed/expected is the number of CG dinucleotides divided by (number of C × number of G / length): about 0.2–0.25 in bulk human DNA because methylated CpGs mutate to TpG over evolution; near 1 in CpG islands, which escaped methylation in the germline. The cutoff (o/e > 0.6 and GC > 55%, over ±500 bp) is a strict version of the classic Gardiner-Garden and Frommer definition; looser definitions give 55–70% CGI promoters. The H3K4me3 colouring shows why the two classes matter for epigenomics: CpG-island promoters are marked in most cell types (CFP1 binds unmethylated CpG and recruits the H3K4 methyltransferase), while non-CpG promoters are marked only where the gene is used. Silencing differs too: CpG-island promoters of developmental genes are silenced by Polycomb (H3K27me3), and stably by DNA methylation in, for example, X inactivation and cancer. Made with make-generegulation-figs.R.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Promoters are bidirectional


A promoter’s nucleosome-depleted region usually contains two core promoters facing away from each other.
The sense transcript becomes the mRNA. The antisense transcript (PROMPT or upstream antisense RNA) is short, terminated early and degraded by the RNA exosome.
When both directions are productive you get a head-to-head gene pair sharing one promoter region.


Divergent transcription was found by sequencing nascent RNA (GRO-seq) and RNA in cells lacking the nuclear exosome (Preker et al. 2008). The asymmetry comes from sequence downstream of each TSS: the sense direction has 5’ splice sites (U1 snRNP binding suppresses early termination), the antisense direction has early polyadenylation signals. Relevance for the course: an ATAC-seq peak at a promoter is a single NDR, but it hosts two initiation sites, and H3K4me3 and H3K27ac are found on both sides of it (the bimodal shape in the next units). Enhancers show the same bidirectional initiation, which leads to the eRNAs a few slides on.

title: Gene regulation
section: Enhancers can act from far away
text:
Enhancers can act from far away


The ZRS controls SHH in the developing limb from about 1 Mb away, inside an intron of LMBR1, across a gene desert.
Single-base changes in the ZRS cause extra digits (preaxial polydactyly); deleting it in mice abolishes Shh expression in the limb: limbs without digits, an otherwise normal animal.
Lesson: the nearest gene is often not the target. Enhancers are tissue-specific modules; one gene can have many, each for one tissue or stage.


The ZRS (zone of polarising activity regulatory sequence) is the textbook long-range enhancer (Lettice et al. 2003; Sagai et al. 2005). It shows three features at once: distance (about 1 Mb in human), position inside another gene whose expression it does not control, and modularity: SHH has other enhancers for the brain, the gut and the notochord, and only the limb one is lost in these mutants, so the phenotype is restricted to the limbs. This is why “nearest gene” assignment of peaks, which students did in Genomic intervals, is only a first guess. Linking enhancers to genes properly uses 3D contacts (Hi-C, the 3D genome units), correlation across samples, and perturbation (CRISPRi), the topic of the integration unit. Coordinates in the figure are hg38 from GENCODE; the ZRS position is approximate.

title: Gene regulation
section: How an enhancer reaches its promoter
text:
How an enhancer reaches its promoter


The DNA between enhancer and promoter loops out, so that proteins bound at both meet in 3D.
TFs on the enhancer bind co-activators such as Mediator, which contacts RNA polymerase II at the promoter. Cohesin extrudes and holds loops.
Active enhancers are themselves transcribed: short, bidirectional enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), a sign of activity used to map enhancers.


The looping model is supported by chromosome conformation capture (3C, Hi-C, Micro-C) and microscopy, and by experiments where forcing a loop (tethering a protein that self-associates) activates a gene. It is not the whole story: imaging often shows enhancer and promoter several hundred nm apart even when the gene is on, and some models propose transcriptional “hubs” or condensates in which many TFs and co-activators are concentrated. Mediator is a complex of about 30 subunits; it binds activation domains of TFs and Pol II. eRNAs were found by Kim et al. 2010; FANTOM5 (Andersson et al. 2014) used bidirectional CAGE signal to define about 43 000 active enhancers across human cell types. Whether eRNAs have a function or are a by-product is debated; as a marker they are very useful. Loops and cohesin come back in the 3D genome units.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Enhancer states and their marks


Primed: H3K4me1, a pioneer TF may be bound, little accessibility. Active: open core with TFs, H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, eRNAs. Poised (in stem cells): H3K4me1 with H3K27me3.
The core is a nucleosome-depleted region of a few hundred bp; the marks sit on the flanking nucleosomes.
This is why “H3K27ac peak, distal to a TSS, no H3K4me3” is the standard working definition of an active enhancer.


This connects the marks table of What is epigenetics? to enhancer biology. Creyghton et al. 2010 and Rada-Iglesias et al. 2011 showed that H3K27ac separates active from primed or poised enhancers carrying H3K4me1. The poised state (H3K4me1 + H3K27me3) is mostly described in embryonic stem cells, at developmental enhancers that become active upon differentiation. The marks are correlates of activity, not proof of function (the cause-or-consequence slide in What is epigenetics?): only a fraction of H3K27ac-marked elements activate a reporter, and some functional enhancers carry little H3K27ac. The definition H3K27ac minus H3K4me3, away from TSSs, is the one students used to build an enhancer set in Genomic intervals. In the table, “weak” ATAC means accessible in some cells or partly: primed enhancers often give small peaks.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: an enhancer cluster at PAX5
text:
Real data: an enhancer cluster at PAX5


PAX5 is the master regulator of B-cell identity. In GM12878, 500 kb around PAX5 contain 91 ATAC peaks and 71 H3K27ac peaks, most of them far from any TSS, many inside the neighbouring gene ZCCHC7.
H3K4me1 is broad over the whole cluster; H3K27ac and ATAC mark the active cores; H3K4me3 marks the PAX5 promoter (and, weakly, some strong enhancers).


ENCODE fold-change tracks (500-bp bins, maximum per bin) and ATAC IDR peaks from GM12878, plotted by make-generegulation-figs.R. PAX5 is on the minus strand, so its promoter is at the right end of the gene, near 37.03 Mb; the gene extends to the left beyond the window. Many of the active elements lie inside ZCCHC7; which gene each one regulates cannot be read from these tracks (the problem of the ZRS slide again), it needs contact or perturbation data. CTCF peaks are few and sharp: they mark boundaries and loop anchors, not enhancers. Point out the scales: H3K27ac reaches 100-fold enrichment, H3K4me1 only 20-fold, because H3K4me1 is spread over many nucleosomes. Weak H3K4me3 at very active enhancers is normal; it is a reason not to define promoters by H3K4me3 alone.

title: Gene regulation
section: “Super-enhancers”: a useful ranking, a contested category
text:
“Super-enhancers”: a useful ranking, a contested category


Stitch distal H3K27ac peaks within 12.5 kb, rank by total signal, and cut where the curve turns up: 929 regions (6%) hold 45% of the signal in GM12878. They sit near B-cell genes (ETV6, PLCG2, BCL2, PAX5 …).
Whyte et al. 2013 called such regions super-enhancers and proposed they drive cell identity genes.
Critique: the cutoff is arbitrary on a continuous distribution, and dissected super-enhancers often behave as several ordinary enhancers adding up. Use the ranking, be careful with the category.


The method (ROSE) stitches enhancer peaks within 12.5 kb, excludes peaks near TSSs, ranks stitched regions by signal (originally Mediator or H3K27ac ChIP), and draws the cutoff where a line of slope 1 touches the normalised curve. Our version uses H3K27ac peaks and fold-change bigWig signal, so numbers differ from published lists. The biology behind it is real: genes with large, highly active enhancer clusters tend to be cell identity genes and oncogenes, and those clusters are sensitive to BET inhibitors (BRD4) and to loss of Mediator. The critique (Pott and Lieb 2015; Hay et al. 2016 on the α-globin locus) is that there is no evidence for a distinct class with emergent properties: the distribution has no gap, and deleting individual constituents mostly gives additive effects. Read “super-enhancer” as “the top of a ranking of enhancer clusters”.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Silencers and insulators


Silencers bind repressors that recruit co-repressors (HDACs, histone methyltransferases). Example: REST binds the RE1 element and silences neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells.
Insulators delimit where regulation acts: enhancer-blocking (an enhancer cannot activate a promoter on the other side) and barrier (heterochromatin cannot spread past).
In vertebrates most insulator activity depends on CTCF.


Silencers are much less catalogued than enhancers, partly because a loss of function is harder to measure than a gain; recent screens suggest some elements act as enhancers in one cell type and silencers in another. The classic vertebrate insulator is the chicken β-globin HS4 element: its enhancer-blocking activity needs a CTCF site (Bell, West and Felsenfeld 1999), its barrier activity other proteins. A beautiful human example combines CTCF and DNA methylation: at the H19/IGF2 imprinting control region CTCF binds only the unmethylated maternal allele and blocks the shared enhancers from reaching IGF2; on the methylated paternal allele CTCF cannot bind and IGF2 is expressed. We return to methylation-sensitive binding a few slides on.

title: Gene regulation
text:
CTCF and loop extrusion


Cohesin loads on DNA and extrudes a growing loop until it meets CTCF bound in the right orientation.
Loops form between convergent CTCF sites (motifs pointing towards each other): about 90% of loops with a CTCF motif at both anchors in high-resolution Hi-C. Flip one site and the loop is lost.
The result: insulated domains (TADs) in which enhancers find their promoters more easily than across the boundary.


CTCF has 11 zinc fingers and binds a long (about 20 bp) asymmetric motif, so each site has an orientation; the N-terminus of CTCF faces the loop and stops cohesin coming from that side. Rao et al. 2014 found that loop anchors are mostly convergent pairs of CTCF motifs; inverting a single CTCF site with CRISPR re-wires the loop (de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015). Removing CTCF or cohesin acutely (degron experiments) erases most TADs and loops but changes the expression of surprisingly few genes in the short term, a reminder that boundaries are one layer among several. This slide sets up the 3D genome units and the motif-strand question in the exercise. GM12878 has about 44 000 CTCF peaks in the file we use.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Transcription factors


A TF has a DNA-binding domain (DBD) that reads a short motif, and effector domains that recruit co-activators or co-repressors.
Humans have about 1600 TFs, classified by DBD family; half are C2H2 zinc fingers. Members of one family bind similar motifs.
About a quarter still have no known motif.


Numbers from Lambert et al. 2018, a manually curated census (1639 TFs; the counts in the figure are from its database). Each DBD family has a typical motif shape: bHLH factors bind the E-box CANNTG as dimers, bZIP factors palindromes, homeodomains TAAT cores, ETS factors GGAA cores (PU.1 is an ETS factor), forkheads TGTTTAC. Many paralogues share nearly identical motifs, so a motif match rarely tells you which family member binds: an ETS motif in a peak could be PU.1, ETS1, ELF1 or FLI1. Activation domains are mostly intrinsically disordered, acidic or rich in glutamine or proline. The KRAB zinc fingers (344 in the database) mostly silence transposable elements by recruiting KAP1/TRIM28 and SETDB1, which writes H3K9me3; this is the H3K9me3 at ZNF clusters seen in What is epigenetics?.

title: Gene regulation
text:
A motif as a matrix


Align known binding sites, count each base at each position, add a pseudocount, divide to get frequencies p_{b,j}.
The log-odds weight of base b at position j against a background q_b: \;w_{b,j} = \log_2 \dfrac{p_{b,j}}{q_b}. Positive: preferred; negative: disfavoured.
The pseudocount keeps unseen bases from getting -\infty: with only 8 sites, “never seen” does not mean “impossible”.


This is the position weight matrix (PWM), the standard representation of a TF motif (Stormo 2000; Wasserman and Sandelin 2004). The example is an ETS-type site with the GGAA core that PU.1 binds. Walk through one column: column 1 has 6 G, 1 A, 1 C, 0 T. With a pseudocount of 1 per base and 8 sites the frequencies are 7/12, 2/12, 2/12 and 1/12; against a uniform background of 0.25, G scores log2(0.583/0.25) = +1.2 and T scores log2(0.083/0.25) = −1.6. Pseudocount choices vary (JASPAR tools use 0.8 in total, others 1 per base or a fraction proportional to the background); the more sites, the less it matters. A real background is not uniform: the human genome is 41% GC, so q(G) = q(C) ≈ 0.2 and q(A) = q(T) ≈ 0.3. The exercise builds a matrix like this by hand.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Scanning a sequence


The score of a window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Slide the window along the sequence, on both strands (the reverse complement).
A score above a threshold is a match (a predicted site). Tools set the threshold from a p-value: the chance that a random window scores as high.
Summing log-odds assumes the positions contribute independently. Usually a good approximation; dinucleotide models and neural networks relax it.


The second match in the figure only appears on the minus strand: the top strand reads ACTTCC, whose reverse complement is GGAAGT. A scanner reports it with strand “−”, and the motif then points to the left on the genome; this matters for CTCF orientation. The best possible score is the sum of the column maxima (8.4 here); the worst is the sum of the minima. Tools such as FIMO (MEME suite), HOMER, motifmatchr and Biostrings::matchPWM compute an exact p-value per score from the matrix and the background. With p < 1e-4 per window and strand, about 200 windows per Mb pass the threshold by chance, which is the topic of the next slides. The independence assumption fails for some TFs (e.g. flexible spacing in dimers); this is part of why convolutional neural networks, which learn motifs from data, outperform PWMs (machine-learning units).

title: Gene regulation
text:
Information content and sequence logos


Information content of a column (uniform background): \;IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j} bits. 2 bits: one base only; 0 bits: all four equally likely.
A sequence logo draws each column as a stack of height IC_j, each letter scaled by its frequency.
CTCF (JASPAR MA0139.2, from 913 ChIP-seq sites): 15 positions, 16.1 bits in total; the core CCA·…AGGGGGC carries most of it.


Information content is the reduction in uncertainty compared with a random base (2 bits for DNA). Column 3 of CTCF (C in 903 of 913 sites) has 1.9 bits; column 1 only 0.34. The total information content gives a rule of thumb for how often a motif occurs by chance: roughly once every 2^IC bp per strand, so 2^16 ≈ 70 000 bp for a high-scoring CTCF match. JASPAR is the open database of curated TF matrices (2024 release: Rauluseviciute et al.); CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and the HOMER and MEME collections are alternatives. Logo made with universalmotif in make-generegulation-figs.R. Note that this matrix was derived from ChIP-seq peaks, so it describes in vivo binding sites, including bias from the experiment; other matrices come from in vitro assays (SELEX, protein-binding microarrays).

title: Gene regulation
text:
How many matches by chance?


At a p-value threshold p, a sequence of length L has about \;2 L p\; matches by chance (two strands).
chr21 (40 Mb of sequence): 8583 CTCF matches at p < 10^{-4}, close to the 8018 expected by chance. Genome-wide, about 600 000 are expected.
GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks. Even a long, informative motif has far more matches than bound sites.


Log scale on the y axis. This is the point of the slide: motif matches are cheap. A 6-bp exact word occurs once every 4^6 = 4096 bp per strand, about 500 times per Mb on both strands; a typical TF motif with 10–12 bits of information occurs thousands of times per Mb at usual thresholds. The observed counts are close to the expectation because the expectation is computed from the matrix itself with a uniform background, and chr21 is not uniform (41% GC); at stricter thresholds the observed count exceeds the expected one, partly because real CTCF sites are enriched (there are a few hundred bound sites on chr21) and partly because of base composition and repeats. Numbers computed in make-generegulation-figs.R with motifmatchr (exercise R7).

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif
text:
Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif


Of 200 bp around each CTCF summit, 78% contain a match (p < 10^{-4}), against 8% of GC-matched genomic windows and 9% of the same sequences shuffled.
The stronger the peak, the more likely the motif: 62% of the weakest quarter, 92% of the strongest.
Weak peaks without a motif: indirect binding, weaker motif variants, or noise.


Three backgrounds: random genomic windows (4%), windows matched to the GC content of the peaks (8%, because the CTCF motif is GC-rich and so occurs more often in GC-rich DNA), and the peak sequences shuffled so that each keeps its dinucleotide composition (9%). The GC-matched background is the fair one; a random-genome background would overstate the enrichment by a factor of two. This is exactly the issue of the null from the shuffle test in Genomic intervals: here the null must match sequence composition. HOMER uses GC-matched genomic background, MEME/SEA shuffled sequences. The strong dependence on peak strength is typical of ChIP-seq of a direct DNA binder and is a quality check: if the strongest peaks of your TF ChIP do not contain its motif, worry about the antibody.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: the motif sits at the summit
text:
Real data: the motif sits at the summit


Position of the best CTCF match in 500 bp around each summit: a sharp peak at 0. 94% of best matches are within 50 bp of the summit (median distance 6 bp).
In GC-matched background windows the best matches are spread evenly.
Centrality is strong evidence that the motif is what the TF binds; tools such as CentriMo use it as a test.


The summit is the position with the most ChIP fragments, which pile up symmetrically around the protein’s binding position, so a directly bound motif should be at the summit within the precision of the experiment (tens of bp). A motif that is enriched in peaks but spread evenly over them suggests a partner factor or a sequence bias of the region, not the immunoprecipitated TF itself. The same plot centred on ATAC-seq summits is noisier, because an ATAC peak can contain several TFs. Only peaks with a match contribute (81% of peaks within ±250 bp; 17% of the 500-bp background windows have one). The exercise reproduces this histogram on 5000 peaks.

title: Gene regulation
section: Most motif matches are not bound
text:
Most motif matches are not bound


Of the 8583 CTCF matches on chr21, only 369 (4.3%) lie in a GM12878 CTCF peak, although CTCF is one of the most motif-driven TFs.
Matches in accessible DNA (ATAC peaks) are bound 39% of the time, matches elsewhere 2%. The best-scoring quarter of matches is bound 12% of the time, the rest under 2%.
Conversely, 79% of chr21 CTCF peaks have a match: the motif is nearly necessary, far from sufficient.


This is the central quantitative message of the lecture. Accessibility and binding are not independent (CTCF binding itself creates an ATAC peak), so the 39% is not a causal estimate; but the asymmetry is the general pattern. For most TFs the fraction of bound matches is far lower than for CTCF, often well under 1%. The reasons are on the next slide. A consequence for analysis: predicting binding from sequence alone fails; combining sequence with accessibility (as chromVAR and many ML models do) works much better. Numbers from make-generegulation-figs.R; the exercise recomputes them (R7).

title: Gene regulation
section: Why a motif is bound or not
text:
Why a motif is bound or not


Nucleosomes: most TFs cannot bind a motif wrapped on a histone octamer. DNA methylation: some TFs, CTCF among them, do not bind a motif with a methylated CpG.
Cooperativity: TFs that bind next to each other stabilise each other, so a weak site is bound when a partner is there.
TF concentration and competition with other proteins set how many sites are occupied.


Each panel is a determinant that explains part of the gap on the previous slide. Nucleosomes: DNA on the octamer is bent and one face is blocked; access needs a pioneer factor or a remodeller (next slide). Methylation: the CTCF motif often contains CpGs (positions 13–14 of the JASPAR consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC); methylation there blocks binding, as at the H19 imprinting control region. Methyl-CpG can also increase binding for some TFs (the methyl-SELEX work of Yin et al. 2017). Cooperativity can be direct (protein–protein contacts, e.g. PU.1 with IRF4 or IRF8 on composite ETS–IRF elements in B cells) or indirect, through competition with the same nucleosome. TF concentration: a TF at higher levels occupies weaker sites; this is how dosage-sensitive TFs act.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Pioneer factors open closed chromatin


Pioneer factors bind their motif on nucleosomal DNA, recruit remodellers (SWI/SNF/BAF), and make the site accessible for other TFs.
Classic example: FOXA1/FOXA2 in liver; its forkhead domain resembles linker histone H1. In B cells PU.1 and EBF1 act as pioneers.
Pioneers set up competence: which enhancers can become active in a lineage. Signal-dependent TFs (NF-κB, steroid receptors) mostly bind where pioneers already opened the chromatin.


Zaret and Carroll 2011 is the review. FOXA binds its site on the nucleosome surface and can open compacted chromatin in vitro without ATP-dependent remodellers (Cirillo et al. 2002), though in cells it works with remodellers. Pioneering is a spectrum, not a binary class: many TFs can bind partial motifs on nucleosomes to some degree. The definition is operational: a TF that binds closed chromatin and is needed for its opening. PU.1 opens thousands of sites in macrophages and B cells (Heinz et al. 2010); EBF1 opens chromatin at B-cell genes during B-cell commitment (Boller et al. 2016). The steps in the figure map onto assays: step 1 has a ChIP peak but little ATAC; step 3 has ATAC, H3K27ac and other TFs. For the ML units: pioneers are exactly where sequence alone predicts accessibility best.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Combinatorial control: the B-cell example


B-cell identity rests on a few TFs: PU.1 and E2A induce EBF1, EBF1 and PAX5 activate each other and the B-cell programme, PAX5 represses other lineages.
An enhancer is active only with the right combination of TFs. PU.1 is in both B cells and macrophages, but binds different sites with different partners.
Combinations of ~1600 TFs give far more cell types than single TFs could.


The hierarchy is from mouse genetics: mice without E2A or EBF1 have no B cells, and Pax5-deficient pro-B cells can still become macrophages or T cells, so PAX5 is the commitment factor (Nutt et al. 1999). PAX5 targets include CD19 and CD79A (activated) and CSF1R (repressed). Heinz et al. 2010 is the key paper on the right panel: PU.1 binds tens of thousands of sites in macrophages and in B cells, but largely different ones, next to C/EBP motifs in macrophages and EBF/E2A/OCT motifs in B cells; collaboratively they choose which sites become enhancers. GM12878 is an Epstein–Barr-virus-transformed B cell, so in addition to the B-cell factors it has very active NF-κB and IRF4 (EBV activates them), relevant when you look at its motif enrichment.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin
text:
Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin


Distal ATAC peaks (summit more than 2 kb from a protein-coding TSS), 200 bp around the summit, against GC-matched genomic windows.
IRF4 (3.4×), CTCF (2.6×) and PU.1 (1.8×) motifs are the most enriched; OCT2, RUNX3 and EBF1 modestly (1.3–1.4×). Motifs of liver and erythroid TFs (HNF4A, FOXA1, GATA1) are not (≈1×).
The open chromatin of a cell type tells you its TFs: the basis of motif enrichment analysis and chromVAR.


Numbers next to the bars are the fraction of peaks with a match and the fraction of background windows with a match; 116 758 distal peaks of 155 151. Enrichments of 1.3–3-fold are typical: each motif occurs in only a minority of peaks, and many matches in either set are chance hits. IRF4 at the top fits an EBV-transformed B cell, where EBV drives IRF4; IRF and PU.1 motifs also occur together as composite ETS–IRF elements. Two honest caveats: PAX5’s JASPAR matrix is short (8 bp) and captures only part of its long bipartite site, so its enrichment is underestimated; and MEF2B, a germinal-centre B-cell TF, is depleted, a reminder that motif enrichment depends on the matrix, the background and the window, and that absence of enrichment does not mean absence of function. Formal motif enrichment (HOMER, MEME-SEA, chromVAR) and footprinting are taught in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting; here the point is qualitative. Made with motifmatchr and JASPAR 2024 matrices in make-generegulation-figs.R.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Co-activators turn binding into activity


Activation domains recruit p300/CBP, which acetylates H3K27 (and TFs): the H3K27ac you map at active enhancers and promoters.
BRD4 reads acetyl-lysine with its bromodomains and, with Mediator, helps recruit and release RNA polymerase II.
Repressors recruit the opposite: HDACs, Polycomb, H3K9 methyltransferases.


This closes the loop with the writers/readers/erasers framing of What is epigenetics?: TF binding at a sequence leads to the writing of a mark (H3K27ac by p300/CBP), which is read by BRD4, which helps the transcription machinery. It also explains why H3K27ac is such a good marker of active enhancers, and why p300 ChIP-seq was one of the first ways enhancers were mapped (Visel et al. 2009). Drugs: BET inhibitors (JQ1) displace BRD4 and hit super-enhancer-driven oncogenes such as MYC; p300/CBP inhibitors and degraders are in development. Pol II often pauses about 50 bp downstream of the TSS; release requires P-TEFb, which BRD4 recruits. Repressive co-factors are the other half: HDAC-containing complexes, Polycomb (H3K27me3) and SETDB1 (H3K9me3).

title: Gene regulation
text:
From mechanism to assay


ATAC-seq finds the open, TF-bound cores of promoters, enhancers and CTCF sites. ChIP-seq of a TF finds its bound sites, motif at the summit.
Histone ChIP / CUT&Tag shows the marks on flanking nucleosomes. Hi-C shows the loops between CTCF sites and between enhancers and promoters.
Motif analysis links the peaks back to the TFs that explain them.


This is the map for the rest of the course. Each assay sees one layer of what we discussed: accessibility (a consequence of TF binding), the TF itself, the co-activator footprint as histone marks, and the 3D contacts. A useful exercise for students is to predict, for an element of their choice, what each track should look like, and then check it in the data. Note the bimodal histone signal: the marks are on the nucleosomes flanking the NDR, so a histone ChIP peak often has a dip where the ATAC peak is. Motif enrichment and footprinting have their own unit; the ML units train models that read the sequence directly.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




cis-regulatory elements
core promoter, enhancers, silencers, insulators: clusters of TF sites


core promoter
about −40 to +40; TATA, Inr, DPE; CpG-island (about half, broad, housekeeping) vs non-CpG (tissue-specific)


enhancer
activates at a distance (up to ~1 Mb), either orientation; often not the nearest gene


active enhancer
open core with TFs; H3K4me1 + H3K27ac on flanking nucleosomes; eRNAs


insulator
CTCF; loops between convergent CTCF sites by cohesin extrusion


TF
DNA-binding domain + effector domain; ~1600 in human


PWM
counts → frequencies (pseudocount) → log-odds \log_2(p/q); score = sum over positions


information content
2 + \sum p \log_2 p per column; logo; chance match ≈ every 2^{IC} bp


binding
motif ≈ necessary, not sufficient: 4% of chr21 CTCF matches bound; accessibility, pioneers, partners


B cells
PU.1, E2A → EBF1 ↔︎ PAX5; combinations select enhancers




Students should be able to: build a PWM from a few aligned sites and score a sequence by hand; compute information content of a column; estimate the number of chance matches of a motif in a genome; explain why most matches are unbound; describe the marks of an active enhancer; and predict what ATAC-seq, TF ChIP-seq, histone ChIP-seq and Hi-C show at a promoter, an enhancer and a CTCF site. Next units: Genomic intervals (if not yet done), then the assay blocks, starting with ATAC-seq.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Banerji, Rusconi & Schaffner 1981, Cell. Expression of a β-globin gene is enhanced by remote SV40 DNA sequences. The discovery of enhancers.
Spitz & Furlong 2012, Nat Rev Genet. Transcription factors: from enhancer binding to developmental control. A clear review of enhancers, TF binding and combinatorial control.
Lambert et al. 2018, Cell. The human transcription factors. The census of ~1600 human TFs, their domains and motifs.
Wasserman & Sandelin 2004, Nat Rev Genet. Applied bioinformatics for the identification of regulatory elements. PWMs, information content and why most predicted sites are not functional (“the futility theorem”).
Zaret & Carroll 2011, Genes Dev. Pioneer transcription factors: establishing competence for gene expression. The pioneer factor concept.
Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities. PU.1 and its partners choose enhancers; also introduced HOMER.

After this exercise you will be able to:
