title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Background
Contact map. The genome is cut into bins (1 Mb to 1 kb). Pixel \((i, j)\) counts the read pairs that join bin \(i\) to bin \(j\), summed over millions of cells; the matrix is symmetric. “Balanced” maps have been corrected so that every bin has the same total (Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices).
Distance decay. The average contact frequency at genomic distance \(s\), \(P(s)\), falls roughly as \(s^{-1}\) between about 100 kb and a few Mb. Enrichment is measured against it: O/E = observed / expected at the same distance.
Features. Compartments: a checkerboard of A (active) and B (inactive) chromatin. Domains (TADs): squares on the diagonal, 0.1–1 Mb. Loops: dots off the diagonal, mostly between convergent CTCF sites (→ … ←), made by cohesin loop extrusion.
Depletion. Without CTCF, most domains and loops are lost and compartments stay; without cohesin, all loop domains are lost and compartments get stronger; without WAPL, loops get longer.

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Data
All from GM12878 in situ Hi-C (Rao et al. 2014, all replicates combined), as reprocessed by ENCODE on GRCh38 (experiment ENCSR410MDC, file ENCFF555ISR):







file

You need cooler and bedtools on the command line and, in Python, cooler, cooltools, numpy, pandas and matplotlib (see Install the software you need; one conda line: conda create -n hic -c conda-forge -c bioconda python=3.11 cooler=0.10 cooltools=0.7 pairtools=1.1 bwa samtools bedtools pybigwig pyfaidx bioframe matplotlib). Everything runs in a few minutes on a laptop.
Simplification: we use two chromosomes, a published matrix, and the published loop and domain calls. Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices makes a matrix from reads; Calling compartments, TADs and loops calls the features yourself.

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
By hand
B1. Read a map. A balanced contact map of eight 50-kb bins (only the upper triangle is shown; the matrix is symmetric):
        1     2     3     4     5     6     7     8
1     100    40    22    15     4     3     3     2
2           100    42    20     5     4     3     3
3                 100    41     6     4     3     2
4                       100     7     5     4     3
5                             100    45    25    18
6                                   100    43    24
7                                         100    44
8                                               100

Where are the domains (TADs)? Where is the boundary between them?
Pixel (1, 4) is 15, pixel (4, 7) is 4. Both are 150 kb apart. Why so different?
Pixel (5, 8) = 18 is the highest of all pixels 150 kb from the diagonal. Is it a loop? What would make you call it one?

B2. Distance decay. Take \(P(s) \propto s^{-1}\).

How much less often do two loci 1 Mb apart contact each other than two loci 100 kb apart? And 10 Mb apart?
A pixel 500 kb from the diagonal has 60 contacts. The average of all pixels 500 kb from the diagonal on that chromosome is 20. What is \(O/E\)? Why is the raw count alone not enough to say a contact is special?
The diagonal of every Hi-C map is bright. Is that biology?

B3. CTCF orientation. Four CTCF sites lie along a chromosome (motif orientation in brackets). A gene promoter lies at 200 kb and an enhancer at 600 kb:
site            A     B     C     D
position (kb)  100   300   450   700
orientation     →     ←     →     ←
promoter at 200 kb, enhancer at 600 kb

Cohesin can be loaded anywhere. Which loops do you expect? Which are the main domains, and where is the boundary between them?
Are the promoter and the enhancer in the same domain? Do you expect the enhancer to activate the gene strongly?
Site C is deleted. What changes? (d) Instead, site C is inverted (→ becomes ←). What changes?

B4. Remove CTCF, remove cohesin. Sketch, for one chromosome arm, a control Hi-C map with two domains, a loop and a checkerboard.

Sketch it after acute CTCF depletion, and after acute cohesin depletion. Which features remain in each?
A paper concludes: “CTCF depletion lost most TADs but changed expression of only ~200 genes, so 3D organisation is irrelevant for gene regulation.” Give three reasons this conclusion is too strong.

B5. Territories. A toy genome has three chromosomes of 100, 50 and 50 Mb.

If contact partners were picked at random from the whole genome, what fraction of contacts would be within a chromosome?
A Hi-C library has 80% of contacts within chromosomes. What does that say about the nucleus? A second library from the same cells has 45%. What might have gone wrong?

B6. One cell versus millions. Two loci are 300 kb apart. DNA-FISH in 200 cells finds them within 200 nm of each other in 20 cells (10%) and more than 600 nm apart in most others. Hi-C shows a strong dot between them.

Are the two results in conflict?
A student writes “the enhancer and promoter are in a stable loop”. Rewrite the sentence so it matches the data.

B7. Choose the assay. For each question, name the most suitable method from the 3C family (or imaging) and say why:

Does one candidate enhancer contact one promoter, in 30 patient samples, cheaply?
All contacts of 2 000 gene promoters at high resolution, to link GWAS variants to genes.
Compartments in a new cell type, genome-wide.
Loops anchored by cohesin, genome-wide, with a limited sequencing budget.
Enhancer–promoter contacts at nucleosome resolution.
How variable a domain’s shape is from cell to cell.

B8. A patient’s structural variant. A child with a limb malformation carries a 250-kb deletion. Before the deletion, the region looks like this:
[ domain 1: gene X (expressed in brain) ] | CTCF boundary | [ domain 2: limb enhancers, gene Y (expressed in limb) ]
                                        deletion: ─────────────── (removes the boundary and gene Y)

Predict what happens to gene X in the developing limb, and why.
Which data would you collect to test your prediction, in patient cells or in a mouse model?
A second patient has a deletion of the same size inside domain 2 that does not touch the boundary. Would you expect the same phenotype?

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
On the command line

C1 — What is in a .cool file?
cooler info $D/gm12878_hic_genome_1mb.cool
cooler ls $D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool
cooler info $D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/10000 | grep -E 'nbins|nnz|sum'
cooler dump --join -r chr21:33,000,000-33,500,000 $D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/100000 | head
cooler dump --join --balanced -r chr21:33,000,000-33,500,000 $D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/100000 | head -3

How many bins, non-zero pixels and contacts does the 1-Mb genome-wide matrix have? And the 10-kb matrix of chr19 + chr21?
What are the columns of cooler dump --join? Why is there no line with the first bin later than the second?
What does the extra column of --balanced contain?



C2 — Territories in numbers
cooler dump --join $D/gm12878_hic_genome_1mb.cool \
  | awk '{ t += $7; if ($1 == $4) c += $7 } END { printf "%d contacts, %.3f within a chromosome\n", t, c / t }'
for chr in chr1 chr19 chr21 chrX; do
  cooler dump --join $D/gm12878_hic_genome_1mb.cool \
    | awk -v c=$chr '$1 == c || $4 == c { t += $7; if ($1 == $4) w += $7 } END { printf "%s %.3f\n", c, w / t }'
done

What fraction of all contacts is within a chromosome? Compare with your answer to B5.
Which of the four chromosomes keeps the largest share of its contacts to itself, and which the smallest? Suggest a reason.



C3 — Loops and domains
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz | grep -v '^#' | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz | awk '$1 == "chr21"' | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz | grep -v '^#' \
  | awk '{ print ($5 + $6) / 2 - ($2 + $3) / 2 }' | sort -n | awk '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print "median loop size:", a[int(NR / 2)] }'
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_domains_arrowhead.bedpe.gz | grep -v '^#' \
  | awk '{ print $3 - $2 }' | sort -n | awk '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print NR, "domains, median size:", a[int(NR / 2)] }'

How many loops and domains did ENCODE call, and how many loops are on chr21?
What are the median loop size and domain size? Compare with the sizes on the Folding at many scales slide.



C4 — Are loop anchors CTCF sites?
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz | grep -v '^#' \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, $2, $3, "L" NR "_a"; print $4, $5, $6, "L" NR "_b" }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > anchors.bed
wc -l < anchors.bed
bedtools intersect -u -a anchors.bed -b $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz | wc -l
bedtools shuffle -i anchors.bed -g <(grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes) -chrom -seed 1 \
  | bedtools intersect -u -a - -b $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz | wc -l

What fraction of loop anchors overlaps a CTCF peak? What fraction of shuffled anchors?
How wide is an anchor in this file, and why does that width matter for (a)?

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
In Python
Start Python (or a Jupyter notebook) in ~/epi/genome3d:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
import cooler, cooltools
D = "/path/to/course/data"
MC = f"{D}/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/"

P1 — The whole genome
g = cooler.Cooler(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_genome_1mb.cool")
print(g.chromnames[:5], len(g.bins()[:]), g.info["sum"])
A = g.matrix(balance=True)[:]
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
plt.imshow(A, cmap="Reds", norm=LogNorm(vmin=np.nanpercentile(A[A > 0], 20), vmax=np.nanpercentile(A, 99.5)))
plt.colorbar(label="balanced contacts"); plt.title("GM12878, 1 Mb"); plt.savefig("p1_genome.png", dpi=120)

pix = g.pixels(join=True)[:]
cis = {c: pix["count"][((pix.chrom1 == c) | (pix.chrom2 == c)) & (pix.chrom1 == pix.chrom2)].sum()
          / pix["count"][(pix.chrom1 == c) | (pix.chrom2 == c)].sum() for c in g.chromnames}
cis = pd.Series(cis).round(3)
print(cis.sort_values())

Do the numbers agree with C2?
Which chromosomes have the lowest and highest cis fractions? Relate this to their size and gene density (chr17, chr19 and chr22 are small and gene-rich; chr18 is small and gene-poor). In the map, which off-diagonal blocks are brightest?



P2 — Compartments by eye
for chrom in ["chr19", "chr21"]:
    c = cooler.Cooler(MC + "250000")
    m = c.matrix(balance=True).fetch(chrom)
    L = c.chromsizes[chrom] / 1e6
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5.5))
    plt.imshow(m, cmap="Reds", norm=LogNorm(vmin=np.nanpercentile(m[m > 0], 5), vmax=np.nanpercentile(m, 99)),
               extent=[0, L, L, 0])
    plt.title(f"{chrom}, 250 kb"); plt.xlabel("Mb"); plt.savefig(f"p2_{chrom}.png", dpi=120)

Describe the checkerboard on chr19. Is it visible on chr21?
The first 14 Mb of the chr21 plot are empty (white). Why? (Hint: what is the short arm of chr21 made of?)



P3 — Distance decay
c = cooler.Cooler(MC + "10000")
view = pd.DataFrame({"chrom": ["chr19", "chr21"], "start": 0,
                     "end": [c.chromsizes["chr19"], c.chromsizes["chr21"]], "name": ["chr19", "chr21"]})
exp = cooltools.expected_cis(c, view_df=view, nproc=2)
exp["s"] = exp["dist"] * 10000
for chrom in ["chr19", "chr21"]:
    e = exp[(exp.region1 == chrom) & (exp.dist >= 2)]
    plt.loglog(e.s, e["balanced.avg"], label=chrom)
    sel = (e.s >= 1e5) & (e.s <= 1e6)
    print(chrom, "slope 100 kb - 1 Mb:", round(np.polyfit(np.log10(e.s[sel]), np.log10(e["balanced.avg"][sel]), 1)[0], 2))
plt.xlabel("distance (bp)"); plt.ylabel("P(s)"); plt.legend(); plt.savefig("p3_ps.png", dpi=120)
e = exp[exp.region1 == "chr21"].set_index("s")["balanced.avg"]
print("P(100 kb) / P(1 Mb) on chr21:", round(e[100000] / e[1000000], 1))

What slopes do you find? Compare with B2.
How many times more often do loci 100 kb apart contact than loci 1 Mb apart on chr21? Compare with the \(s^{-1}\) prediction.



P4 — Domains and loops in one window
res, chrom, s0, s1 = 10000, "chr21", 24_750_000, 26_250_000
c = cooler.Cooler(MC + str(res))
m = c.matrix(balance=True).fetch(f"{chrom}:{s0}-{s1}")
loops = pd.read_csv(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz", sep="\t", comment="#", header=None)
lp = loops[(loops[0] == chrom) & (loops[1] >= s0) & (loops[5] <= s1)]
dom = pd.read_csv(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_domains_arrowhead.bedpe.gz", sep="\t", comment="#", header=None)
dm = dom[(dom[0] == chrom) & (dom[1] >= s0) & (dom[2] <= s1)]
ext = np.array([s0, s1, s1, s0]) / 1e6
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6.5))
plt.imshow(m, cmap="Reds", extent=ext, norm=LogNorm(vmin=np.nanpercentile(m[m > 0], 30), vmax=np.nanpercentile(m, 99.7)))
plt.scatter((lp[4] + lp[5]) / 2e6, (lp[1] + lp[2]) / 2e6, s=150, facecolors="none", edgecolors="blue")
for _, d in dm.iterrows():
    a, b = d[1] / 1e6, d[2] / 1e6
    plt.plot([a, b, b], [a, a, b], color="black", lw=1, ls="--")
plt.title(f"{chrom}:{s0:,}-{s1:,}, {res // 1000} kb"); plt.savefig("p4_window.png", dpi=120)
print(len(lp), "loops and", len(dm), "domains in the window")

How many loops and domains are in the window? Do the loops sit at the corners of domains?
Pick one loop and read off its two anchor positions. Use the CTCF peak file (or a genome browser with the CTCF track) to check whether both anchors have a CTCF peak.
Change res to 5000 and to 50000. What can you see at each resolution, and what do you lose?

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Explore: loop extrusion
The demo simulates loop extrusion on 1 Mb of chromosome, cut into 200 bins of 5 kb. Cohesin complexes are loaded at random positions (loads per 100 steps), extrude a loop by moving both legs outward by one bin per time step, and are released after a random time (mean lifetime, in steps). A leg stops at a CTCF site whose motif points into the loop (▶ stops legs moving left, ◀ stops legs moving right) with the CTCF stop probability; a site in the other orientation is passed. Two legs cannot pass each other. The track under the map shows the loops of one cell (filled circle: leg stopped at CTCF). The triangle above is the contact map averaged over 1 200 snapshots (30 cells × 40 time points), in the same coordinates as the track. In each snapshot two bins contact each other with frequency 1/d, where d is their distance along the folded chain: the two legs of a cohesin hold the chain together, so a loop is a shortcut. Without cohesin, d is the genomic distance and the map is pure distance decay, P(s) = s−1 (the dashed line in the P(s) plot). Click the chain to add a ▶ site, turn ▶ into ◀, or remove a ◀ site; click the map to read one pixel; show obs/exp divides every pixel by the mean of its diagonal. The readout lists the strongest observed/expected pixels between pairs of CTCF sites. Simulated data: every change restarts the simulation from the same seed, so the same settings always give the same numbers.



E1. Start with Two domains + stripe. Which two pairs of CTCF sites give the strongest dots, how are their motifs oriented, and how strong are they (obs/exp)? Where are the two domains? The third pair in the list, 150 kb ▶ – 410 kb ▶, is in tandem: one cohesin cannot be stopped by both sites. Why does its pixel still light up? (Hint: where is 410 kb relative to 400 kb?)
E2. Press Flip one site: the site at 400 kb now points ▶. What happens to the 150–400 kb dot, and which new pair of sites makes a dot? Compare with the CTCF inversion experiment of the lecture.
E3. Press Delete one site (the 400 kb site is gone), then No CTCF, then No cohesin. For each, describe the dots and domains, and note the readout “P(s) at 250 kb”. Which depletion experiment of the lecture does each of the last two mimic, and what does P(s) tell you that the dots do not?
E4. Go back to Two domains + stripe. Lower the CTCF stop probability to 0.5, then to 0. Then set it to 0.9 again and tick one-sided extrusion. What happens to the dots, to the fraction of legs stopped at CTCF, and to the mean loop size? Where do you now see stripes?






Solutions





E1. The two strongest pixels are both convergent pairs: 150 kb ▶ – 400 kb ◀ (obs/exp 8.6) and 410 kb ▶ – 650 kb ◀ (7.4). They are the apexes of two triangles, the domains 150–400 kb and 410–650 kb; inside each, contacts are raised along the edges (the anchors keep reeling in DNA) and the domains are separated by the divergent pair at 400/410 kb. The tandem pair 150 ▶ – 410 ▶ reaches 4.1 because 410 kb is only two bins from 400 kb: in a cell where the 150–400 loop is held, 150 kb sits next to 400 kb and therefore also close to 410 kb. Neighbouring loop anchors cluster; this is also seen in real maps. (The model has 7.9 cohesins per cell, one per 127 kb, and 21% of legs stopped at CTCF.)
E2. The 150–400 kb pixel drops from 8.6 to 3.4 and leaves the top of the list. Legs coming from 150 kb now pass the site at 400 kb (it points away from them) and the next site that stops them is 650 kb ◀: a new dot appears at 150 ▶ – 650 ◀ (4.5, up from 3.2), the apex of a larger domain. This is the inversion experiment: the A–B loop is lost and an A–C loop forms with the next site in the right orientation. What remains at 150–400 kb comes from cohesins stacked against each other near 400/410 kb.
E3. Delete one site: the two domains merge; the strongest pixels are 410–650 kb (5.3) and 150–650 kb (3.9). No CTCF: no dots and no domains (the list is empty; any pixel you click is close to 1), but P(s) at 250 kb is still 2.7× the no-cohesin line: cohesin still extrudes loops, only at random places. This is the CTCF degron (Nora et al. 2017): loops and domains go, extrusion goes on. No cohesin: every pixel has obs/exp 1 and P(s) is exactly s−1 (1.0×): the cohesin degron (Rao et al. 2017), all loop domains gone. With cohesin, P(s) at 250 kb is 3.1× the no-cohesin value (default). P(s) shows whether loops are being extruded at all, even when no single position stands out. (Compartments are not part of this model.)
E4. With stop probability 0.5, the dots weaken (410–650 kb 4.5, 150–400 kb 3.9) and 14% of the legs are stopped (21% at 0.9). At 0 nothing is stopped (0%), the dots are gone (≤ 1.1) and the domains disappear, although cohesin still makes loops. With one-sided extrusion (stop probability 0.9) only one leg moves, and a dot needs a cohesin that was loaded right at one anchor: the dots almost vanish (150–400 kb 1.9, 410–650 kb 1.5), 10% of the legs are stopped and the mean loop size halves (73 kb, against 136 kb). What remains are stripes: lines running from the CTCF sites along the edges of the domains, e.g. from the ▶ site at 800 kb towards the upper right (click the pixel 800 kb – 900 kb: about 1.4 one-sided against 1.1 two-sided). Purely one-sided extrusion struggles to make dots between convergent sites; this is one argument that cohesin extrudes in both directions, at least on average.

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — reading maps and distance decay (B1, B2)





A domain is a block of high values near the diagonal with a sharp drop outside it. Compare pixels at the same distance from the diagonal (the same off-diagonal): only those are comparable. \(P(s) \propto s^{-1}\) means \(P(s_1)/P(s_2) = s_2/s_1\). For the bright diagonal, think of what the bin of a pixel \((i, i)\) contains. Background: Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009, Lajoie et al. 2015.









Hint 2 — CTCF and extrusion (B3, B4)





Cohesin extrudes in both directions and stops at a CTCF site whose motif points towards it, i.e. into the loop: a → site on the left, a ← site on the right. A loop needs a → site to the left of a ← site with no intervening site of the right orientation that would stop cohesin first (in most cells). Fudenberg et al. 2016, Sanborn et al. 2015, Nora et al. 2017, Rao et al. 2017.









Hint 3 — assays, imaging and disease (B5–B8)





The expected cis fraction for random partners is \(\sum_k L_k^2 / (\sum_k L_k)^2\). For assays, ask: how many viewpoints, genome-wide or targeted, how deep, is a protein involved, single cells or population? Reviews: Lajoie et al. 2015; single cells: Bintu et al. 2018; disease: Lupiáñez et al. 2015.









Hint 4 — command line (C1–C4)





cooler info, cooler ls, cooler dump: --join writes chromosome names and positions instead of bin IDs, -r selects a region, --balanced adds the balanced value. A .mcool holds several resolutions; address one as file.mcool::resolutions/10000. BEDPE has two intervals per line; columns 1–3 and 4–6 are the two loop anchors. bedtools shuffle with -chrom keeps each interval on its chromosome.









Hint 5 — Python (P1–P4)





cooler Python API: Cooler.matrix(balance=True).fetch(region) returns a NumPy array; Cooler.pixels(join=True)[:] a table of non-zero pixels. cooltools.expected_cis averages each diagonal (columns dist in bins and balanced.avg). matplotlib imshow with LogNorm gives the usual log colour scale; NaN (masked) bins are white.

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Two domains: bins 1–4 and bins 5–8, with the boundary between bins 4 and 5. Within each block the values fall slowly (40 → 22 → 15), between the blocks they are low (≤ 7). (b) Pixel (1, 4) is inside domain 1; pixel (4, 7) crosses the boundary. At the same distance (150 kb), contacts within a domain are about four times more frequent than across a boundary: that is what insulation means. (c) No. At its distance it is high because it is inside a domain, like (1, 4) = 15. A loop is a pixel enriched over its local neighbourhood, including the pixels next to it closer to the diagonal. Here (5, 8) = 18 is lower than its neighbours (5, 7) = 25 and (6, 8) = 24: it is just the far corner of domain 2. A loop would show as a local maximum, e.g. (5, 8) = 40 with (5, 7) and (6, 8) near 25: a dot at the corner of the domain.
B2. (a) 10 times less at 1 Mb, 100 times less at 10 Mb. (b) \(O/E = 60/20 = 3\). The raw count depends mostly on distance: a 500-kb pixel with 60 contacts is special, a 20-kb pixel with 60 contacts may be below average. (c) Mostly not: two positions in the same bin are linearly adjacent, so they are always close. It also collects artefacts such as unligated and self-ligated fragments (removed in processing) and is excluded from most analyses.
B3. (a) Each side of an extruding cohesin stops at the first site pointing towards it: the left side at a → site, the right side at a ← site. Loaded between A and B: loop A–B. Loaded between C and D: loop C–D. Loaded between B and C: the left side passes B (←, wrong way) and stops at A, the right side passes C (→) and stops at D: a larger, weaker loop A–D. The main domains are A–B and C–D; the divergent pair B ← | → C is the boundary between them (a classic strong boundary). (b) The promoter (200 kb) is in domain A–B, the enhancer (600 kb) in domain C–D, on opposite sides of the boundary; they meet only within the weaker A–D loop. Expect little activation. (c) Without C, cohesin loaded anywhere between B and D extrudes until A and D: the C–D domain is replaced by an A–D domain that contains both the promoter and the enhancer (the A–B loop remains nested inside). The enhancer can now reach the gene. (d) With C inverted (←), the right side of cohesin loaded between B and C stops at C: loops A–B, A–C and A–D; there is no longer a → site between A and D apart from A itself, so the boundary between B and C is gone and promoter and enhancer again share a domain. Either change can switch the gene on, which is the logic of the limb malformations in the lecture.
B4. (a) CTCF depleted: domains and loops largely gone (the squares and dots fade, contacts spread across the old boundaries), checkerboard unchanged. Cohesin depleted: all loop domains and dots gone, the near-diagonal looks smooth, the checkerboard becomes stronger and finer. (b) (1) The experiment measures short-term effects (hours to days); maintenance of an existing state can be robust while establishing a new state (development, activation) needs the structure. (2) Many enhancer–promoter contacts are short-range or CTCF-independent and survive. (3) “~200 genes” can include key genes and still be a strong phenotype; a degron in one cell type does not test other cell types or development. Also: residual CTCF, compensation, and expression measured as steady-state RNA (slow) rather than nascent transcription.
B5. (a) \((100^2 + 50^2 + 50^2) / 200^2 = 15\,000 / 40\,000 = 0.375\). (b) 80% ≫ 37.5%: chromosomes form territories. 45% close to random suggests a technical problem: many random ligations between fragments from different nuclei or in solution (poor crosslinking, nuclei lysed before ligation). The cis fraction is a standard Hi-C QC metric.
B6. (a) No. Hi-C counts ligation events summed over cells; 10% of millions of cells in contact gives many reads, far more than at neighbouring pixels where contact is rarer, so a dot appears. FISH shows the same thing as a distribution: most cells far apart, a minority close. (b) “The enhancer and promoter come close (within 200 nm) in about 10% of cells at any moment, more often than neighbouring loci.” Contact is transient and in a minority of cells.
B7. (a) 3C (qPCR across the ligation junction) or 4C from the promoter as viewpoint; cheap per sample. (b) Promoter Capture Hi-C (or Capture-C): baits for 2 000 promoters, deep at those. (c) Hi-C at modest depth (compartments are visible at 100 kb–1 Mb with a few hundred million reads or less). (d) HiChIP or ChIA-PET for cohesin (SMC1/RAD21): reads concentrated at bound anchors. (e) Micro-C: MNase cuts at every linker, giving nucleosome-level resolution. (f) Imaging: DNA-FISH or chromatin tracing (or single-cell Hi-C), because Hi-C averages over cells.
B8. (a) The limb enhancers lose their boundary and gene Y; gene X is now in the same domain as the limb enhancers and can be activated ectopically in the limb (as PAX3 in brachydactyly). (b) Capture-C or 4C from the gene X promoter in patient fibroblasts or limb buds of a mouse model to show new contacts with the enhancers; RNA (RNA-seq or in situ hybridisation) to show ectopic X expression in the limb; a mouse with the same deletion made by CRISPR to test whether it causes the phenotype. (c) Probably not: a deletion inside domain 2 that keeps the boundary does not bring the enhancers to X (Lupiáñez et al.: rewiring only happened when the variant disrupted a CTCF-associated boundary). It could still cause a phenotype by deleting enhancers of Y.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 1-Mb genome-wide: 3044 bins, 4 221 149 non-zero pixels, 4 564 968 531 contacts. 10 kb chr19 + chr21: 10 533 bins, 11 989 547 pixels, 123 772 864 contacts (only contacts within chr19 and within chr21). (b) chrom1 start1 end1 chrom2 start2 end2 count. Only the upper triangle (bin1 ≤ bin2) is stored; the lower triangle is the same by symmetry. (c) The balanced value: count × weight(bin1) × weight(bin2). It is NaN for masked bins (too few contacts to balance).
C2. (a) 0.772 of all contacts are within a chromosome, 15 times the random expectation for the human genome (0.051: with 23 chromosomes of similar size, a random partner is on the same chromosome only about 1 time in 20). Compare 0.375 in the toy genome of B5. (b) chr1 0.648, chr19 0.594, chr21 0.543, chrX 0.673. (These per-chromosome fractions are lower than 0.772 because each trans contact counts for both chromosomes it joins.) Large chromosomes keep most of their contacts (chr1); small, gene-rich chromosomes in the nuclear interior (chr19) have a larger share of trans contacts, because they are small (fewer cis partners) and sit near other small, gene-rich chromosomes. chrX (one active and one inactive X in a female cell line) is near the top: the inactive X is compact and contacts little else.
C3. (a) 14 599 loops and 10 306 domains; 164 loops on chr21. (b) Median loop size 330 000 bp (330 kb), median domain size 185 000 bp (185 kb): both in the 0.1–1 Mb range.
C4. (a) 29 198 anchors; 18 763 overlap a CTCF peak (64%), against 3 691 shuffled anchors (13%): a fivefold enrichment. The rest may be anchored by weaker CTCF sites missing from the conservative peak set, or by other factors (promoters, enhancers, YY1). (b) Anchors are 5, 10 or 25 kb wide (the resolution at which the loop was called: 16 466, 7 216 and 5 516 anchors), so a random 10-kb window often overlaps one of the 44 000 CTCF peaks by chance; the shuffled control is essential.









Solutions — Python





P1. (a) Yes: the same pixels, counted in the same way. (b) Lowest: chr22 (0.539), chr21 (0.543), chr17 (0.556), chr20, chr15, chr16; highest chr2 (0.681), chrX (0.673), chr3. Small chromosomes have fewer cis partners, and the small gene-rich ones (16, 17, 19, 20, 22) sit together in the nuclear interior: their mutual off-diagonal blocks are among the brightest in the balanced map.
P2. (a) On chr19 the map is a fine checkerboard of alternating blocks a few Mb wide; on chr21 it is coarser: mostly B from about 16 to 32 Mb (a gene-poor stretch), mostly A from about 32 to 37 Mb and 41 to 46 Mb (the gene-rich end of the long arm). (b) The short arm and centromere of chr21 (0–14 Mb) are gaps and repeats (rDNA, satellites) in the assembly: no unique alignments, so those bins are masked (NaN, white). Two more masked bins near 43–44 Mb are segmental duplications.
P3. (a) chr19 −1.14, chr21 −0.97: close to −1. (b) 8.7 times, close to the factor 10 predicted by \(s^{-1}\).
P4. (a) 15 loops and 9 domains; most loops sit at domain corners, some link the corners of nested domains. (b) Example: the loop chr21:24 890 000–24 900 000 × 25 310 000–25 320 000 has a CTCF peak at both anchors. With bedtools pairtobed -type both you find 6 of the 15 loops with peaks at both anchors and 11 with a peak at one or both; the strongest dot in the window (25.50 × 25.56 Mb, 858 contacts) has none, a reminder that not every loop is a CTCF loop. (c) At 5 kb the dots are sharp but the map is noisy away from the diagonal; at 50 kb the domains and checkerboard are clear but the loops blur into their domain corners.

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Where this leads

Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices turns raw read pairs into a .cool file like the ones used here, and explains balancing and \(P(s)\).
Calling compartments, TADs and loops computes the eigenvector, insulation scores and dots yourself on the same GM12878 data and tests them against ChIP-seq.
Linking regulatory elements to genes uses contacts to connect enhancers to target genes (the activity-by-contact model).

title: Exercise: 3D genome organisation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Dekker et al. 2002, Science. Capturing chromosome conformation.
Dixon et al. 2012, Nature. Topological domains in mammalian genomes identified by analysis of chromatin interactions.
Fudenberg et al. 2016, Cell Rep. Formation of chromosomal domains by loop extrusion.
Nora et al. 2017, Cell. Targeted degradation of CTCF decouples local insulation of chromosome domains from genomic compartmentalization.
Rao et al. 2017, Cell. Cohesin loss eliminates all loop domains.
Lupiáñez et al. 2015, Cell. Disruptions of topological chromatin domains cause pathogenic rewiring of gene-enhancer interactions.

title: Quiz: 3D genome organisation
text:
Short questions on territories, compartments, domains, loops and the assays that measure them. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Name the four features of a Hi-C map that correspond to territories, compartments, domains and loops, and the typical genomic size of each.






Answer





Territories: blocks on the genome-wide diagonal (contacts within a chromosome dominate), a whole chromosome (50–250 Mb). Compartments: a checkerboard away from the diagonal, ~1–10 Mb segments. Domains (TADs): squares on the diagonal, ~0.1–1 Mb (median 185 kb in GM12878). Loops: dots off the diagonal, anchors ~10 kb–1 Mb apart (median 330 kb).




Q2. With \(P(s) \propto s^{-1}\), two loci 50 kb apart have 400 contacts on average. How many do you expect for loci 500 kb apart? One pixel at 500 kb has 160 contacts: what is its observed/expected value?






Answer





Ten times farther, ten times fewer: 40 contacts. \(O/E = 160 / 40 = 4\): a strong enrichment, possibly a loop (check its local neighbourhood).




Q3. Two CTCF sites lie 400 kb apart: the left one points right (→), the right one points left (←). A Hi-C dot connects them. What happens to the dot if (a) the right site is deleted, (b) the right site is inverted, (c) cohesin is degraded?






Hint





Cohesin stops at a CTCF site whose motif points into the loop.









Answer






The dot disappears; cohesin continues to the next ← site further right, so a new, larger loop can form. (b) The same: a → site on the right does not stop cohesin coming from the left; the loop moves to the next convergent site. (c) The dot disappears (and so do the loop domains), because extrusion makes the loop; compartments remain and get stronger.





Q4. After acute CTCF depletion, domains and loops are largely lost, but the A/B checkerboard is unchanged. What does that tell you about how compartments form?






Answer





Compartments do not depend on CTCF (or on loop extrusion: they even strengthen without cohesin). They form by a separate mechanism, the preferential association of chromatin of the same type (affinity-driven segregation, e.g. heterochromatin with heterochromatin via HP1, Polycomb domains with each other), and are linked to nuclear position (lamina, nucleolus, speckles).




Q5. Compartment A correlates with which of these: H3K27ac, H3K9me3, early replication, the nuclear lamina, high GC content, high gene density?






Answer





A: H3K27ac, early replication, high GC content, high gene density, nuclear interior. B: H3K9me3 (and H3K27me3 in some subcompartments), late replication, the nuclear lamina (LADs) and the nucleolus. On GM12878 chr19, E1 correlates with H3K27ac (r = 0.50) and against H3K9me3 (r = −0.64).




Q6. In 4C from a promoter, a peak appears 250 kb away. DNA-FISH shows the two loci closer than 200 nm in only 15% of cells. Is this a contradiction? What does “contact” mean in each assay?






Answer





No contradiction. Hi-C/4C counts ligation events summed over millions of cells: a contact in 15% of cells is many more than at neighbouring positions, so a peak appears. FISH measures distances in single cells and shows the same thing as a distribution. Neither shows a stable loop in every cell; contact is transient and variable.




Q7. You want the contacts of 300 candidate disease-gene promoters at high resolution in 10 patient samples. Which method do you choose, and why not plain Hi-C?






Answer





Promoter Capture Hi-C (or Capture-C): baits for the 300 promoters concentrate the sequencing on their contacts. Plain Hi-C spreads reads over all pairs of the genome; reaching kilobase resolution at 300 promoters would need billions of reads per sample.




Q8. What do HiChIP and ChIA-PET add to Hi-C, and what bias do they introduce?






Answer





An immunoprecipitation (e.g. cohesin, CTCF, H3K27ac) after ligation keeps only contacts with at least one anchor bound by the protein: many fewer reads are needed for loops at those sites. But the signal mixes contact frequency with ChIP enrichment: a strong ChIP peak gives many reads and can look like many loops; anchors without the protein are invisible. Normalisation must account for this.




Q9. A patient has a deletion that removes a TAD boundary between a limb-enhancer cluster and gene PAX3; another has a deletion of similar size inside the enhancers’ domain that leaves the boundary intact. Which is more likely to cause ectopic PAX3 expression in the limb, and why?






Answer





The first. Removing the CTCF-associated boundary puts the limb enhancers and PAX3 in one domain, so the enhancers can contact and activate PAX3 (brachydactyly in Lupiáñez et al. 2015). A deletion inside the domain does not change which genes the enhancers can reach (though it may remove some enhancers).




Q10. In IDH-mutant gliomas, PDGFRA is activated without any mutation near it. Explain the chain of events.






Answer





Mutant IDH produces 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits TET demethylases, so CpG methylation rises genome-wide, including at CpGs in a CTCF motif at a domain boundary. CTCF cannot bind the methylated site, the boundary is lost, and a constitutive enhancer in the neighbouring domain (near FIP1L1) activates PDGFRA (Flavahan et al. 2016).

title: Genomic intervals
text:
About this lecture
In RNA-seq you counted reads per gene: the annotation told you where to count. In epigenomics there is no such list. Peaks, domains, CpG islands, loops and methylated regions are all intervals that you find in the data, and most of the analysis is arithmetic on intervals: which overlap, how far apart, how many more than by chance.

Coordinates: genome builds, and the two numbering systems (0-based and 1-based) that cause most off-by-one bugs.
File formats: BED and narrowPeak, GTF, bedGraph and bigWig.
Interval operations with bedtools on the command line.
Is an overlap meaningful? Comparing with shuffled intervals.
The same operations in R with GenomicRanges.


This is a technical unit, but every later unit depends on it. Students are comfortable on the command line and in R, so the new content is the coordinate conventions and the interval logic. The running example uses ENCODE peaks from GM12878 (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, CTCF) and the GENCODE annotation, the same files as in the exercise. By the end they should be able to answer “what fraction of my peaks are at promoters, and is that more than chance?” in a few lines, both with bedtools and in R.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Everything is an interval


A genomic interval is a chromosome, a start, an end and (sometimes) a strand: chr21:33,000,000–33,002,000 (+).
Genes, exons, promoters, peaks, CpG islands, methylated regions, reads, Hi-C loop anchors: all intervals.
Questions about biology become questions about intervals: do my peaks overlap promoters? which gene is nearest? how many reads fall in each peak?


The point of the figure: the same line (a stretch of chromosome) carries many different kinds of intervals, coming from annotation (genes, CpG islands) and from data (reads, peaks). Once everything is an interval, the same handful of operations answers most questions. Counting reads in peaks, which students will do for differential accessibility, is literally the same as counting reads in genes, which they did for RNA-seq; only the intervals differ.

title: Genomic intervals
section: A coordinate only means something with its genome build
text:
A coordinate only means something with its genome build


The reference genome is updated: GRCh37/hg19 (2009) and GRCh38/hg38 (2013) are both still used. The same gene has different coordinates in each.
Chromosome names differ too: UCSC writes chr1, Ensembl/NCBI write 1. Mitochondria: chrM vs MT.
Always check that all your files use the same build and the same naming. Mixing builds gives no error, just wrong answers.
This course uses GRCh38 with chr names throughout.


The most common silent error in interval analysis. bedtools will happily intersect hg19 peaks with hg38 genes and report a few random overlaps. Check the header of the file, the methods section, or test: does a well-known gene’s TSS fall where it should? Converting between builds is done with liftOver (later slide), which is lossy. Also mention the newer telomere-to-telomere T2T-CHM13 assembly, which fills the remaining gaps in GRCh38 and is gaining use, but most epigenomic resources (ENCODE, Roadmap) are still in GRCh38 or hg19.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Two ways to number the bases
text:
Two ways to number the bases


1-based, closed [s, e]: the first base is 1, and the end base is included. Used by GTF/GFF, SAM, VCF, and by genome browsers when they display a position.
0-based, half-open [s, e): count the gaps between bases from 0; the interval runs from gap s to gap e. Used by BED, bedGraph, BAM internally, and most programming languages.
The bases CGT above are chr1:3-5 in 1-based, chr1 2 5 in BED. Length: e - s + 1 in 1-based, e - s in BED.


Draw the ruler on the board. In the 0-based half-open system the numbers label the boundaries between bases, so an interval is “from boundary 2 to boundary 5”, which contains the 3rd, 4th and 5th bases. The advantages: length is end minus start, adjacent intervals share an end/start number, and an empty interval (an insertion point) has start = end. Rule for converting: BED start = 1-based start − 1, end is the same number. The UCSC browser displays 1-based but stores 0-based; that is why a BED line chr1 2 5 shows as chr1:3-5. This slide will be on the exam in some form.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Getting it wrong


Copy a 1-based position from a VCF into a BED file without subtracting 1 and your SNP sits one base to the right: next to the CpG you wanted, not on it.
For peaks of hundreds of bp an off-by-one hardly matters. For single bases (SNPs, CpGs, TSSs, Tn5 insertion sites) it changes the answer.
Tools convert for you when they read a format they know (rtracklayer::import adds 1 to BED starts). Trouble starts when you write files by hand with awk or paste.


A concrete failure, as in the figure: the VCF says the SNP is at 1043 (1-based), the G of a CpG. Written correctly to BED it is chr1 1042 1043; copied as chr1 1043 1044 it sits on the next base, outside the CpG, and an overlap with a CpG list misses it. The same happens to CpG positions from a methylation caller written to BED as pos, pos+1. The fix is boring but important: know which convention each file uses, and convert at the boundary. In the exercise, students make a TSS file with awk from the GTF and have to get exactly this right.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
BED and narrowPeak


BED: tab-separated; three required columns chrom start end (0-based), then optional name score strand and more.
narrowPeak (BED6+4): what peak callers like MACS write. Adds signalValue (enrichment), pValue and qValue (as -\log_{10}), and peak: the summit, as an offset from start.
broadPeak is the same without the summit column, for broad domains.


Walk through the example line (the numbers are illustrative; the exercise starts from real lines of the ENCODE CTCF file). Column 5 (score) is often a scaled integer for display (0–1000) and not a statistic; the statistics are in columns 7–9. pValue and qValue are already −log10, so 10 means 1e-10. Column 10 is easy to misread: it is not a genome coordinate; the summit is start + peak. Summits are useful because the binding site is usually within a few tens of bp of the summit, much narrower than the peak: motif analysis and footprinting use windows around summits. A value of −1 means “not available”: the ENCODE CTCF IDR peaks used in the exercise have pValue −1 in every line.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Annotation: GTF


Gene annotation (GENCODE, Ensembl) comes as GTF/GFF: one line per feature (gene, transcript, exon, CDS, …), 1-based closed.
Column 9 holds attributes: gene_id, gene_name, gene_type, transcript_id, ….
A gene has several transcripts, often with different start sites. “The TSS of a gene” is a choice: the gene start, every transcript start, or a canonical transcript.


Students met GTF files in RNA-seq when counting with featureCounts or building an index, but probably did not look inside. The hierarchy matters: gene lines span all their transcripts; transcripts are made of exons. GENCODE “basic” is a subset with the full-length, well-supported transcripts; we use it to keep files small. The TSS question is a real analysis choice: taking only the gene start can miss alternative promoters, and taking every transcript start counts some promoters many times. In the exercise students use transcript starts of protein-coding transcripts and collapse duplicates.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Strand: where is upstream?


Coordinates always increase left to right along the + strand. A gene on the − strand is read right to left.
TSS = start for a + gene, end for a − gene. Upstream of a − gene means higher coordinates.
“Promoter = 2 kb upstream to 500 bp downstream of the TSS” therefore needs the strand. GenomicRanges::promoters() handles it; bedtools slop -s -l 2000 -r 500 too.


The second classic bug after off-by-one. In the figure, gene A is on + and gene B on −; their promoters point in opposite directions. If you build promoters as start − 2000 to start + 500 for every gene, all minus-strand promoters are in the gene body near the 3’ end instead. In BED, strand is column 6; in GTF column 7. Peaks from ChIP or ATAC have no strand (“.” or “*“), because chromatin has no direction; but the genes they are near do.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Signal tracks: bedGraph and bigWig


A signal track gives a number for every position: reads piled up, divided by a normaliser (CPM, fold change over input).
bedGraph: a BED-like text file, chrom start end value, one line per run of constant value.
bigWig: the same data in a compressed, indexed binary file, with precomputed summaries at several zoom levels. A browser can fetch just the region on screen, even over the internet.


Pileup: count how many reads (or fragments) cover each base. bedGraph compresses runs of equal value into one line. bigWig (Kent et al. 2010) adds an index and zoom levels, which is why a 500 MB bigWig opens instantly in IGV: it reads only the blocks for the current window and the right zoom level. ENCODE provides fold-change and p-value bigWigs for every ChIP experiment; in the chromatin-intro exercise we read regions from them with rtracklayer. Making bigWigs from BAM files is in the reads-to-coverage unit (deepTools bamCoverage).

A reference slide. Rule of thumb: text formats are for small files and for reading with your eyes, indexed binary formats are for large files and random access. Any sorted, bgzip-compressed text file can be indexed with tabix for random access, which is how large BED and GTF files are often distributed. BAM stores 0-based positions internally, but samtools view prints 1-based POS in SAM text; again the tools convert for you.

title: Genomic intervals
section: A genome browser shows intervals and signals together
text:
A genome browser shows intervals and signals together


Real data: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq on chr21. Top: the fold-change bigWig. Middle: the narrowPeak intervals, with summits. Bottom: GENCODE genes.
Peaks are where the signal is high; a summit sits at the top of each peak.
IGV (desktop or igv.js in a browser) loads all of these formats directly.


This is a reconstruction of an IGV view in R (make-intervals-figs.R) so the exact files can be reproduced; in the exercise students load the same files in IGV. Point out a weak signal bump without a peak: the peak caller decided it was not significant. And point out how narrow CTCF peaks are: CTCF is a sequence-specific TF with a long motif, so its peaks are sharp, unlike the broad H3K27me3 domains in chromatin-intro.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
The basic interval operations


intersect: the parts of A that overlap B (or: the A intervals that overlap any B, -u).
subtract / -v: A minus B, or the A intervals that overlap no B.
merge: collapse overlapping (or nearby, -d) intervals into one.
closest: for each A, the nearest B and the distance.
slop / flank: grow intervals, or make windows next to them. complement: the gaps.


Go through each panel with the toy intervals. These six operations, plus coverage counting, cover most of what students will do. Every one exists in bedtools and in GenomicRanges, with slightly different names (table later). Insist on drawing toy intervals by hand when unsure what a command returns: it is faster than debugging.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
What counts as an overlap?


By default, one shared base is an overlap. A 1 bp touch between a 2 kb peak and a promoter counts.
Ask for a minimum: bedtools intersect -f 0.5 (at least 50% of A), -r (reciprocal), or a minimum number of bases (minoverlap in R).
Report choices: one line per pair (default), each A once (-u), or count of B per A (-c). These give different numbers of “overlapping peaks”.


Students are often surprised that “how many peaks overlap promoters” depends on these flags. Default intersect reports one line per overlapping pair, and each line is the overlapping piece, not the whole A interval (use -wa for whole intervals). A peak overlapping two promoters appears twice: if you count lines you overcount peaks. -u fixes that. In the figure the roles of A and B swap between the panels: in the left panel A is the promoters, because -f is a fraction of A. Fraction requirements matter most when comparing peak sets of different widths, for example narrow TF peaks against broad domains. There is no universally right choice; the rule is to state it in the methods.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Sorting and merging


Most tools that walk along the genome need input sorted by chromosome, then start: sort -k1,1 -k2,2n.
bedtools merge collapses overlapping intervals: e.g. peaks from two replicates into one consensus set.
Merging loses the per-interval information unless you ask for it (-c 5 -o max, keep the maximum score).


Sorting: -k1,1 sorts by the first column only (as text), -k2,2n by the second column numerically. Lexical chromosome order (chr1, chr10, chr11, …, chr2) is fine for bedtools, as long as all files use the same order; some tools (bedtools with -g, bigWig tools) want the order of a genome file. Merging peaks from replicates or conditions into a consensus set is the first step of differential accessibility: you need one common set of regions to count reads in.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Nearest feature and distance


bedtools closest -a peaks.bed -b tss.bed -d reports, for each peak, the nearest TSS and the distance (0 if they overlap).
Ties (two TSSs at the same distance) give several lines per peak; -t first keeps one.
The distribution of distances says what kind of element a mark labels: promoter marks sit at 0, enhancer marks kilobases away.


Both files must be sorted. For non-overlapping intervals bedtools reports one more than the number of bases between them (the toy A [900,950) and B [700,800) in the operations figure: 100 bases apart, reported as 101). A signed distance relative to the gene’s direction (-D b) tells upstream from downstream, useful for promoter analyses. Nearest gene is the naive way to assign a peak to a gene; it is right perhaps half the time for enhancers. The integration unit uses Hi-C contacts and activity to do better (ABC model).

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Windows around intervals


slop extends each interval (e.g. ±1 kb around a summit), flank makes windows next to it (e.g. the 2 kb upstream), both strand-aware with -s.
Near a chromosome end, a window would run off the end: these tools need a genome file with chromosome lengths (-g hg38.chrom.sizes) and clip at the end.


Note that flank needs both sides (-l 2000 -r 0); -l alone is an error. The genome file is a two-column text file: chromosome name and length. Download it from UCSC (hg38.chrom.sizes) or make it from a FASTA index (cut -f1,2 genome.fa.fai). The same file is needed for complement, shuffle and genomecov. In R, GRanges carries the chromosome lengths in its seqinfo, and trim() clips out-of-bound ranges.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
bedtools on the command line
# promoter windows: 1 kb either side of each protein-coding TSS
bedtools slop -i tss.bed -g hg38.chrom.sizes -b 1000 > promoters.bed

# H3K4me3 peaks at a promoter (each peak once) vs. not
bedtools intersect -u -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l

# candidate enhancers: H3K27ac peaks with no H3K4me3 peak and away from TSSs
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k27ac.bed -b h3k4me3.bed \
  | bedtools intersect -v -a - -b promoters.bed > enhancers.bed

# distance from every enhancer to its nearest TSS
sort -k1,1 -k2,2n enhancers.bed | bedtools closest -a - -b tss.bed -d -t first

Every command reads and writes plain text, so they chain with pipes (- means standard input).


These are the exact commands of the exercise, so students see the shape before they type them. The enhancer definition (H3K27ac without H3K4me3, distal from promoters) is a common heuristic and a useful example of building a biological category from interval operations. Point out that wc -l counts lines; with -u each peak appears once, so lines = peaks.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Real data: where do the peaks sit?
text:
Real data: where do the peaks sit?


Distance from each GM12878 peak to the nearest protein-coding TSS.
H3K4me3 peaks pile up at the TSS. H3K27ac is at TSSs and at distal enhancers. CTCF is mostly far from TSSs.


The x axis is log scale (distance + 1). Read the figure as the answer to “what does this mark label?”. The H3K4me3 distribution confirms the promoter mark from chromatin-intro with real data. H3K27ac is bimodal: active promoters and active enhancers. CTCF sites are insulators and loop anchors and are spread through the genome. Numbers on the plot (fraction within 1 kb) are computed in make-intervals-figs.R; students reproduce them in the exercise.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Is an overlap more than chance?
text:
Is an overlap more than chance?


Two sets of intervals will overlap somewhat by chance, more so if they are wide or numerous. A raw overlap count is not evidence.
Null by shuffling: place the same intervals (same widths) at random positions, count overlaps, repeat many times. Compare the observed count with this distribution.
Enrichment = observed / mean of shuffled. Empirical p-value = (number of shuffles with at least the observed overlap + 1) / (number of shuffles + 1).


This is a permutation test, the same idea as in any statistics course, applied to positions on the genome. bedtools shuffle does one shuffle; repeat it in a loop. The p-value can be no smaller than 1/(number of shuffles + 1), so 100 shuffles can at best give about 0.01. For large enrichments, report the fold enrichment and say that none of the N shuffles reached the observed value. Next slide: the real numbers.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Real data: H3K27ac and CTCF overlap more than chance
text:
Real data: H3K27ac and CTCF overlap more than chance


Grey: overlaps between CTCF peaks and shuffled H3K27ac peaks (100 shuffles, same chromosome, same widths). Red: the observed overlap.
The observed overlap is far outside the shuffled distribution: the two sets are associated.


Numbers in the figure come from make-intervals-figs.R. A good discussion point: why do CTCF and H3K27ac co-occur at all, when CTCF is an insulator? Some CTCF sites are at active promoters and enhancers; others are not. The overlap is significant but partial, which a single p-value hides: report the fraction too.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Shuffling has assumptions


A naive shuffle puts intervals in gaps (runs of N), centromeres and unmappable repeats, where real peaks can never be. This inflates enrichment.
Keep shuffled intervals on the same chromosome (-chrom) and inside the mappable, non-blacklisted genome (-incl / -excl).
Peaks also prefer GC-rich, gene-dense regions. The more of that structure the null ignores, the more “significant” everything looks. Choose the background with care; state it.


The general lesson: a p-value is only as good as its null. Here the null is “the intervals could have been anywhere”, and “anywhere” includes places where no assay can produce a peak. Better nulls restrict to the accessible genome, or match on GC content and distance to TSS. Tools such as regioneR (R) and LOLA formalise this; the idea is the same. The same issue comes back with motif enrichment (GC-matched background) and in the ML units (matched negatives).

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Intervals in R: GRanges


GRanges (package GenomicRanges): seqnames, ranges (start, end, width, 1-based closed), strand, and any metadata columns (mcols).
seqinfo holds chromosome names, lengths and genome build: R refuses to compare ranges from different builds if they are set.
rtracklayer::import() reads BED, narrowPeak, GTF and bigWig, and converts BED’s 0-based starts to 1-based.


GRanges is the Bioconductor container for intervals and is used under the hood by DESeq2’s rowRanges, ChIPseeker, DiffBind, csaw, minfi, and many more. Students used SummarizedExperiment through DESeq2; its rowRanges is a GRanges. The seqinfo check is a nice safety net: genome(gr) <- “hg38” on both objects and a comparison with an hg19 object fails loudly instead of silently.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
findOverlaps returns pairs

hits <- findOverlaps(peaks, promoters)      # one row per overlapping pair
queryHits(hits); subjectHits(hits)          # indices into peaks and promoters
peaks[unique(queryHits(hits))]              # each peak once
overlapsAny(peaks, promoters)               # TRUE/FALSE per peak (= bedtools -u)
countOverlaps(peaks, promoters)             # number of promoters per peak (= -c)

findOverlaps is the general operation; everything else is a convenience on top. The Hits object is a two-column table of indices, like a sparse matrix of overlaps. This is the same many-to-many issue as with bedtools default output: one peak can hit several promoters. subsetByOverlaps(peaks, promoters) is the R equivalent of intersect -u.

Use the command line for big files and pipelines, R for analysis, statistics and plots. The answers must agree (exercise R5).


A reference table; students do not need to memorise it. The key differences: GRanges is 1-based, bedtools 0-based (the numbers in the files differ by one at the start, the bases are the same); reduce() and findOverlaps() respect strand unless you say ignore.strand = TRUE (peaks have strand *, which overlaps both strands, so it rarely bites); distances differ by one: for two ranges that do not overlap, distanceToNearest reports the number of bases between them (0 for directly adjacent ranges), bedtools closest -d reports one more (1 for adjacent). Both report 0 for overlapping ranges. Small differences like these are why comparing the two in the exercise is instructive.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Same bases, different numbers


The BED line chr1  2  5 and the GRanges chr1:3-5 are the same three bases.
rtracklayer::import() and export() convert in both directions. If you read a BED file with read.table() and build a GRanges yourself, add 1 to the start.


The single most common bug when students mix R and the command line: reading a BED with read.table or fread and calling GRanges(chr, IRanges(start, end)) without adding 1. Then every range is 1 bp too long on the left. For peaks it is harmless; for CpGs or SNPs it is wrong. makeGRangesFromDataFrame has a starts.in.df.are.0based argument for exactly this.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Moving between builds: liftOver


liftOver maps intervals from one build to another using a chain file of aligned blocks (UCSC tool; rtracklayer::liftOver in R).
Some intervals fail (deleted or rearranged in the new build) or split into pieces. Check how many you lose.
Better, when possible: re-align the raw reads to the new build, or download the data already processed in the build you need.


Chain files list blocks of sequence that align between builds and the gaps between them. An interval that spans a gap in the alignment comes out split or not at all. For small intervals (SNPs, CpGs, narrow peaks) liftOver is usually fine; for broad domains and anything near rearranged regions, be careful. ENCODE has reprocessed its data on GRCh38, which is why we use their GRCh38 files directly.

Students should leave able to convert a coordinate between conventions by hand, read a narrowPeak line, build strand-aware promoter windows, answer an overlap question with both bedtools and GRanges, and explain why an overlap count needs a null. Next: from reads to coverage, where these intervals come from.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Quinlan & Hall 2010, Bioinformatics. BEDTools: a flexible suite of utilities for comparing genomic features. The tool of this unit.
Lawrence et al. 2013, PLoS Comput Biol. Software for computing and annotating genomic ranges. GenomicRanges and the Bioconductor interval infrastructure.
Li et al. 2009, Bioinformatics. The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools. The SAM/BAM formats.
Kent et al. 2010, Bioinformatics. BigWig and BigBed: enabling browsing of large distributed datasets. Why a bigWig opens instantly.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Compute observed/expected values, find the compartment pattern and choose the sign of the eigenvector, on a toy matrix by hand.
Compute an insulation score and an APA score by hand, and decide whether a bright pixel is a loop.
Call compartments, boundaries and dots on real GM12878 Hi-C with cooltools, and test them against GC content, histone marks, CTCF ChIP-seq and published calls.
Find the orientation of CTCF motifs at loop anchors in R, and judge claims about differential TADs and loops.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Compute observed/expected values, find the compartment pattern and choose the sign of the eigenvector, on a toy matrix by hand.
Compute an insulation score and an APA score by hand, and decide whether a bright pixel is a loop.
Call compartments, boundaries and dots on real GM12878 Hi-C with cooltools, and test them against GC content, histone marks, CTCF ChIP-seq and published calls.
Find the orientation of CTCF motifs at loop anchors in R, and judge claims about differential TADs and loops.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Background
Observed/expected. \(E(s)\) is the mean balanced contact frequency of all pixels at distance \(s\) (one diagonal); O/E = pixel / \(E(s)\).
Compartments. Correlate the rows of the O/E matrix (or centre it) and take the first eigenvector, E1. Bins with the same sign have similar contact profiles. The sign is arbitrary: flip E1 so that it is positive where GC content (or gene density) is high: that is compartment A. A saddle plot averages O/E over pairs of E1 groups; strength = (AA + BB)/(AB + BA).
Insulation. For each position, sum the contacts in a \(w \times w\) window that straddles it, just off the diagonal; the score is \(\log_2\)(sum / mean sum along the chromosome). Boundaries are local minima.
Dots. A loop pixel is tested against a local expected value: its distance-expected \(E\) scaled by observed/expected in a neighbourhood (donut, lower-left, horizontal, vertical), with a Poisson test. APA averages O/E submatrices around many loops; score = centre / mean of the lower-left corner.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Data
GM12878 in situ Hi-C (Rao et al. 2014), as reprocessed by ENCODE on GRCh38 (experiment ENCSR410MDC), reduced to chr19 and chr21, and ENCODE’s own calls; ChIP-seq from earlier units:

You need cooler, cooltools, samtools and bedtools on the command line; in Python cooler, cooltools, bioframe, pyfaidx, pyBigWig, numpy, pandas and matplotlib (one conda line: conda create -n hic -c conda-forge -c bioconda python=3.11 cooler=0.10 cooltools=0.7 pairtools=1.1 bwa samtools bedtools pybigwig pyfaidx bioframe matplotlib); in R GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, Rsamtools, JASPAR2024, TFBSTools and motifmatchr, as in Gene regulation. The whole exercise runs in about 10 minutes on a laptop; cooltools dots takes 1–3 minutes.
Simplification: we analyse two chromosomes of a published, very deep map, at one or a few resolutions. Calls on a whole genome, on shallower data, or with other callers will differ; that is part of the lesson.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
By hand
B1. Compartments on a toy chromosome. A balanced map of six 1-Mb bins (upper triangle):
        1     2     3     4     5     6
1       –    10    15     9     2     2
2             –    10     5    10     6
3                   –    30     5     3
4                         –    10     5
5                               –    30
6                                     –

Compute the expected value \(E(s)\) for distances of 1, 2 and 3 bins (the mean of each diagonal).
Compute O/E for pixels (1, 3), (2, 4), (1, 4), (2, 5) and (3, 6). Which bins seem to belong together?
Sort the six bins into two groups by eye from the O/E values.
An eigensolver returns E1 = (−0.41, 0.40, −0.42, −0.40, 0.41, 0.42). GC content of the bins is 0.48, 0.38, 0.50, 0.47, 0.40, 0.37. Which bins are compartment A? What would have happened in a genome-wide analysis if you had not checked the sign?

B2. Insulation by hand. In this 8-bin map, bins 1–4 and 5–8 are two domains. Contacts within a domain are 40, 22, 15 at distances 1, 2, 3 bins; across the boundary they are 8, 5, 4, 3 at distances 1, 2, 3, 4.

With a window of \(w = 2\) bins, the window for the gap after bin \(k\) covers pixels \((k-1, k+1)\), \((k-1, k+2)\), \((k, k+1)\), \((k, k+2)\). Compute the window sums for the gaps after bins 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
Compute the insulation score \(\log_2\)(sum / mean of the five sums) at each gap. Where is the boundary, and how deep is it?
What would happen with \(w = 1\), and with \(w = 4\), in a real map with nested domains?

B3. Read a saddle plot. Three E1 groups (B, middle, A), mean O/E:
            control                 cohesin depleted
         B     mid    A           B     mid    A
B       2.0    1.0   0.4         2.4    1.0   0.3
mid     1.0    1.1   0.9         1.0    1.1   0.9
A       0.4    0.9   1.5         0.3    0.9   1.9

Compute compartment strength in both conditions. (b) Is the change what you expect from 3D genome organisation? Why? (c) What must be the same in the two analyses for the comparison to be fair?

B4. Is it a loop? Two pixels are 200 kb from the diagonal, where the distance-expected count is \(E = 40\).




pixel count
donut: observed sum
donut: expected sum




pixel X
120
