Compute O/E against the distance-expected value for each pixel.
Compute the donut-corrected local expected value (\(E \times\) observed sum / expected sum) and O/E against it. Which pixel is a loop candidate?
Pixel Y lies at the corner of a strong domain. Explain why the distance-expected value alone would mislead you.
For pixel X, is a count of 120 surprising if the true mean is the local expected value? (A Poisson variable with mean 50 has standard deviation about 7.)

B5. APA. An APA pileup of 400 loops (O/E, 21 × 21 pixels) has a centre value of 3.2 and a lower-left 6 × 6 mean of 1.4. The same 400 loop positions piled up in a Hi-C map of a different cell type give 1.5 and 1.3.

Compute both APA scores. (b) What do you conclude about these loops in the second cell type? (c) Why use the lower-left corner rather than the whole pileup as background?

B6. CTCF orientation. At ten loops, the strongest CTCF motif at the left and right anchor lies on these strands:
+ −    + −    + +    + −    − −    + −    − +    + −    + −    + −

What fraction is convergent, tandem and divergent? What fractions would you expect if orientations were random? (b) Which model explains the excess of convergent pairs, and why are divergent pairs nearly absent at loop anchors although divergent CTCF pairs are common at domain boundaries?

B7. Judge the claims.

“Knockout cells have 30% fewer loops than wild type (6 900 vs 9 800, HiCCUPS).” The knockout map has 400 M contacts, the wild type 1.2 B, one replicate each.
“TADs are unchanged after the treatment: 95% of boundaries overlap between conditions.” The calls were made at 40-kb resolution with a single-scale caller.
“This enhancer forms a loop with gene X (HiChIP for H3K27ac), so it regulates X.”

B8. Resolution. A Hi-C experiment gives 300 million contacts genome-wide (about 60% within chromosomes). Which features can you analyse: compartments, domains, loops? At what bin size? (Rule of thumb from Rao et al. 2014: the resolution is the smallest bin size at which 80% of bins have at least 1 000 contacts.)

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
On the command line
cooltools also has a command-line interface. These steps write tables you can inspect with awk and bedtools.

C1 — Expected and insulation
M=$D/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool
cooltools expected-cis -p 4 -o expected_10kb.tsv $M::resolutions/10000
head -4 expected_10kb.tsv | cut -f1-8
cooltools insulation --threshold Li -o insulation_10kb.tsv $M::resolutions/10000 100000 200000 500000
head -2 insulation_10kb.tsv
for w in 100000 200000 500000; do
  awk -F'\t' -v c="is_boundary_$w" 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == c) k = i; next } $k == "True"' \
    insulation_10kb.tsv | wc -l
done

What do the columns of expected_10kb.tsv mean (the command shows the first eight)? Why is the expected value missing (NaN) for distances 0 and 1?
How many boundaries are there for each window size?



C2 — Boundaries and CTCF peaks
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "is_boundary_200000") k = i; next }
  $k == "True" { print $1, $2, $3 }' insulation_10kb.tsv > boundaries_200kb.bed
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz | awk -v OFS='\t' '$1 == "chr19" || $1 == "chr21" { s = $2 + $10; print $1, s, s + 1 }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > ctcf_summits.bed
wc -l < boundaries_200kb.bed
bedtools window -w 10000 -u -a boundaries_200kb.bed -b ctcf_summits.bed | wc -l
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 == "False" { print $1, $2, $3 }' insulation_10kb.tsv \
  | awk 'BEGIN { srand(1) } { print rand() "\t" $0 }' | sort -k1,1g | head -160 | cut -f2- | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n \
  | bedtools window -w 10000 -u -a - -b ctcf_summits.bed | wc -l

What fraction of boundaries lies within 10 kb of a CTCF summit, and what fraction of 160 random valid bins? (b) Why must the random bins be drawn from chr19 and chr21 and not from the whole genome?



C3 — Our boundaries and ENCODE’s domains
zcat $D/gm12878_hic_domains_arrowhead.bedpe.gz | awk -v OFS='\t' '$1 == "chr19" || $1 == "chr21" { print $1, $2, $2 + 1; print $1, $3 - 1, $3 }' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n -u > arrowhead_edges.bed
wc -l < arrowhead_edges.bed
bedtools window -w 20000 -u -a boundaries_200kb.bed -b arrowhead_edges.bed | wc -l
bedtools window -w 20000 -u -a arrowhead_edges.bed -b boundaries_200kb.bed | wc -l
What fraction of our boundaries is near an Arrowhead domain edge, and what fraction of Arrowhead edges is near one of our boundaries? Why are the two numbers so different?

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
section: Explore: compartments from a toy map
text:
Explore: compartments from a toy map
The demo simulates a balanced Hi-C map of a toy chromosome of 48 bins. You set the true compartment of every bin in the top track (click or drag to paint A or B). The contact frequency of two bins s bins apart is s−exponent (decay exponent), times √r if the two bins are of the same type and 1/√r if not (so same-type pairs contact r times more than A–B pairs at the same distance, A/B preference r), times random log-normal noise. The demo then follows the recipe of the lecture: divide by the expected value of each diagonal (O/E), correlate the rows, and find the first eigenvector E1 of the correlation matrix by power iteration (multiply a start vector by the matrix again and again, normalising each time, until it stops changing). Orient E1 with GC flips the sign if E1 correlates negatively with the GC track (A bins are GC-richer); E1 > 0 is called A, and black dots mark wrong calls. Skip O/E correlates the rows of the observed map instead. New start vector restarts power iteration from another random vector; New noise draws new noise. Simulated data.



E1. With the default settings (pattern blocks), how many power-iteration steps are needed, what are λ1 and λ2, and how many bins are called correctly? Now untick orient E1 with GC and press New start vector five times, noting the calls each time. What changes, what stays the same, and why? Which line of the readout would warn you in a real analysis?
E2. Tick orient E1 with GC again and tick skip O/E. What does E1 look like now, how many bins are called correctly, and how do λ1 and λ2 compare? Then set the decay exponent to 0. Finally untick skip O/E and move the decay exponent between 0 and 2: what happens to the calls, and why?
E3. Raise the noise step by step to 1.5. At which noise level do the first calls go wrong? What happens to λ1, to λ2 and to the number of power-iteration steps? Then set the noise back to 0.25 and r to 1. What does E1 show now?
E4. Press blocks, then paint a single B bin in the middle of the long A block (bins 25–34, the fifth run from the left). Is it called B? Is it still called B at noise 0.75? Why can the eigenvector call one isolated bin, where a smoothing method (such as the HMM of Chromatin states) might absorb it?






Solutions





E1. 10 steps; λ1 = 25.0 (52% of all variance; for a correlation matrix the eigenvalues sum to the number of bins, 48), λ2 = 2.4; all 48 of 48 bins are called correctly, and corr(E1, GC) = +0.83 (the solver’s sign happened to be right). Without orientation, the five new start vectors give: swapped (all 0 of 48 correct, corr(E1, GC) = −0.83), swapped, correct, swapped, swapped. λ1, the number of steps (10–12) and the pattern of E1 stay the same: v and −v are equally good eigenvectors, and which one power iteration lands on depends only on the start vector. The compartments (which bins go together) are found every time; only the labels A and B are arbitrary. The warning sign is a negative correlation of E1 with GC (or gene density, or active marks).
E2. E1 becomes a left–right split: bins 1–24 negative, 25–48 positive. Without O/E, every bin’s row is dominated by the distance decay, so neighbouring bins have similar rows and the strongest pattern in the correlation matrix is “where along the chromosome”. Only 27 of 48 calls are right (chance level), corr(E1, GC) = 0.04, and λ1 = 8.8 (18%) is barely larger than λ2 = 7.0 (so power iteration needs 94 steps). With decay exponent 0 there is no distance effect, and even without O/E E1 is right again (48 of 48, λ1 = 29.8). With O/E, the decay exponent makes no difference at all (the readout stays at 48 of 48, λ1 = 25.0 for exponents 0, 1 and 2): dividing by the expected value per diagonal removes the distance decay exactly, because in this model it multiplies every pixel at a given distance by the same factor. In real data, too, O/E is what makes compartments comparable across distances.
E3. At noise 0.5 all 48 calls are still right (λ1 = 11.6, 24%; 17 steps); at 0.75 the first 3 bins are wrong (45 of 48; λ1 = 6.6, λ2 = 3.5; 34 steps); at 1.0, 43 of 48 (λ1 = 4.8, λ2 = 3.7; 79 steps); at 1.5, 34 of 48 (λ1 = 3.9, λ2 = 3.8; 529 steps). As noise grows, λ1 shrinks towards λ2: there is no longer one dominant pattern, and power iteration converges slowly because each step separates the two eigenvectors only by the factor λ1/λ2. With r = 1 there are no compartments: E1 is a pattern of noise, 23 of 48 calls “right” by chance, corr(E1, GC) = 0.12, λ1 = 3.9 (8%). An eigenvector always exists; it only means something if it is clearly larger than the next and agrees with an independent track.
E4. Yes: the single B bin gets a negative E1 (−0.14, between neighbours at +0.14 and +0.16) and all 48 calls are right. At noise 0.75 it is still called B (45 of 48 correct overall; the errors are elsewhere). The eigenvector judges each bin by its whole row, that is by its contacts with all other bins, not by its neighbours along the chromosome; a B bin contacts the other B bins of the chromosome more, wherever they are. An HMM-style segmentation adds a cost for every switch between neighbours and could absorb a one-bin segment. (Real data are noisier per bin, which is why compartment calls are usually made at 50–250 kb, not at 5 kb.)

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
In R

R1 — CTCF motif orientation at loop anchors
As in Gene regulation, scan 100 bp around each CTCF peak summit with the JASPAR CTCF matrix, keep the strand of the best match, and give each loop anchor the motif of its strongest CTCF peak:
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
  library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite); library(motifmatchr)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
lp <- read.table(file.path(D, "gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz"), sep = "\t", comment.char = "#")[, 1:6]
names(lp) <- c("chrom1", "start1", "end1", "chrom2", "start2", "end2")
a1 <- GRanges(lp$chrom1, IRanges(lp$start1 + 1, lp$end1))
a2 <- GRanges(lp$chrom2, IRanges(lp$start2 + 1, lp$end2))
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
ctcf <- ctcf[overlapsAny(ctcf, c(a1, a2))]          # only peaks in loop anchors
win <- resize(GRanges(seqnames(ctcf), IRanges(start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak, width = 1)), 100, fix = "center")
ctcf_m <- getMatrixByID(dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024())), "MA0139.2")
pos <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, getSeq(FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz")), win), p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even",
                   out = "positions")[[1]]
ctcf$motif <- vapply(pos, function(x) if (length(x) == 0) NA_character_ else
                     as.character(mcols(x)$strand)[which.max(mcols(x)$score)], "")
c(peaks = length(ctcf), with_motif = sum(!is.na(ctcf$motif)))
anchor_motif <- function(a) {
  h <- findOverlaps(a, ctcf)
  d <- data.frame(q = queryHits(h), s = subjectHits(h), sig = ctcf$signalValue[subjectHits(h)])
  d <- d[!is.na(ctcf$motif[d$s]), ]
  d <- d[order(d$q, -d$sig), ]; d <- d[!duplicated(d$q), ]
  out <- rep(NA_character_, length(a)); out[d$q] <- ctcf$motif[d$s]; out
}
lp$motif1 <- anchor_motif(a1); lp$motif2 <- anchor_motif(a2)
write.table(lp, "loop_ctcf_orientation.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

How many CTCF peaks lie in loop anchors, and how many of them have a motif match?
Why take the strongest peak per anchor? What could go wrong with an anchor 25 kb wide?



R2 — Convergent, tandem, divergent
both <- lp[!is.na(lp$motif1) & !is.na(lp$motif2), ]
cls <- c("+-" = "convergent", "-+" = "divergent", "++" = "tandem", "--" = "tandem")[paste0(both$motif1, both$motif2)]
nrow(lp); nrow(both)
round(100 * prop.table(table(cls)), 1)
mean(!is.na(lp$motif1) | !is.na(lp$motif2))

What fraction of loops has a motif at both anchors? At least one?
What fractions are convergent, tandem and divergent? Compare with B6 and with Rao et al. 2014 (over 90% convergent for anchors with a single motif).

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
In Python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cooler, cooltools, bioframe, pyBigWig, subprocess
D = "/path/to/course/data"
MC = f"{D}/gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool::resolutions/"
CHROMS = ["chr19", "chr21"]
def view_of(clr):
    return pd.DataFrame({"chrom": CHROMS, "start": 0, "end": [clr.chromsizes[c] for c in CHROMS], "name": CHROMS})
def bw_mean(path, df):
    b = pyBigWig.open(path)
    v = [b.stats(r.chrom, int(r.start), int(min(r.end, b.chroms(r.chrom))), type="mean")[0] for r in df.itertuples()]
    return np.array([np.nan if x is None else x for x in v], dtype=float)

P1 — Compartments
c100 = cooler.Cooler(MC + "100000")
view = view_of(c100)
subprocess.run(f"samtools faidx {D}/hg38.fa.bgz chr19 chr21 > chr19_chr21.fa", shell=True, check=True)
bins = c100.bins()[:][["chrom", "start", "end"]]
gc = bioframe.frac_gc(bins, bioframe.load_fasta("chr19_chr21.fa"))
eigvals, eigs = cooltools.eigs_cis(c100, view_df=view, phasing_track=gc, n_eigs=3)
print(eigvals)
eigs["GC"] = gc["GC"].values
eigs["H3K27ac"] = bw_mean(f"{D}/gm12878_h3k27ac_fc.bigWig", eigs)
eigs["H3K9me3"] = bw_mean(f"{D}/gm12878_h3k9me3_fc.bigWig", eigs)
eigs["ENCODE"] = bw_mean(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_eigenvector_10kb.bigWig", eigs)
for ch in CHROMS:
    e = eigs[(eigs.chrom == ch) & eigs.E1.notna()]
    print(ch, len(e), "bins,", round((e.E1 > 0).mean() * 100), "% A;",
          {k: round(e.E1.corr(e[k], method="spearman"), 2) for k in ["GC", "H3K27ac", "H3K9me3", "ENCODE"]},
          "E2 vs GC:", round(e.E2.corr(e.GC, method="spearman"), 2))
e = eigs[eigs.chrom == "chr19"]
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 2.5))
plt.fill_between(e.start / 1e6, 0, e.E1, step="post")
plt.xlabel("chr19 (Mb)"); plt.ylabel("E1"); plt.savefig("p1_e1_chr19.png", dpi=120)

What fraction of each chromosome is A? How strongly does E1 correlate with GC, H3K27ac, H3K9me3 and ENCODE’s eigenvector?
Does E2 also correlate with GC? How would you notice if A/B had ended up in E2?
Run eigs_cis again without phasing_track and compare the sign of E1 on the two chromosomes.



P2 — Saddle plot
exp100 = cooltools.expected_cis(c100, view_df=view, nproc=2)
S, N = cooltools.saddle(c100, exp100, eigs[["chrom", "start", "end", "E1"]], "cis",
                        n_bins=5, qrange=(0.0, 1.0), view_df=view)
s5 = (S / N)[1:-1, 1:-1]                 # drop the two outlier rows/columns
print(np.round(s5, 2))
print("strength:", round((s5[0, 0] + s5[4, 4]) / (s5[0, 4] + s5[4, 0]), 2))

Which corner is strongest? Compute the strength. (b) Why does the middle group (3) show values near 1 with everything?



P3 — Insulation and boundaries
c10 = cooler.Cooler(MC + "10000")
v10 = view_of(c10)
ins = cooltools.insulation(c10, [100_000, 200_000, 500_000], view_df=v10, verbose=False)
for w in [100_000, 200_000, 500_000]:
    print(w // 1000, "kb window:", ins[f"is_boundary_{w}"].sum(), "boundaries")
ctcf = pd.read_csv(f"{D}/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz", sep="\t", header=None)
ctcf = ctcf[ctcf[0].isin(CHROMS)]
summits = pd.DataFrame({"chrom": ctcf[0], "start": ctcf[1] + ctcf[9], "end": ctcf[1] + ctcf[9] + 1})
near = lambda df: bioframe.overlap(df, bioframe.expand(summits, pad=10_000), how="left", return_index=True) \
    .groupby("index")["index_"].apply(lambda x: x.notna().any()).mean()
b200 = ins[ins["is_boundary_200000"]][["chrom", "start", "end"]]
valid = ins[~ins.is_bad_bin][["chrom", "start", "end"]]
print("boundaries near CTCF:", round(near(b200), 2), " random bins:", round(near(valid.sample(len(b200), random_state=1)), 2))
win = ins[(ins.chrom == "chr21") & (ins.start >= 37_000_000) & (ins.end <= 42_000_000)]
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))
for w in [100_000, 200_000, 500_000]:
    plt.plot(win.start / 1e6, win[f"log2_insulation_score_{w}"], label=f"{w // 1000} kb")
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel("chr21 (Mb)"); plt.savefig("p3_insulation.png", dpi=120)

How many boundaries for each window? Do the numbers match C1?
Compare the CTCF fractions with C2. (Random bins differ, so small differences are expected.)
In the plot, which dips appear at every window size?



P4 — Dots
exp10 = cooltools.expected_cis(c10, view_df=v10, nproc=4)
dots = cooltools.dots(c10, expected=exp10, view_df=v10, max_loci_separation=2_000_000, nproc=4)
print(len(dots), "dots;", dots.groupby("chrom1").size().to_dict())
hic = pd.read_csv(f"{D}/gm12878_hic_loops_hiccups.bedpe.gz", sep="\t", comment="#", header=None).iloc[:, :6]
hic.columns = ["chrom1", "start1", "end1", "chrom2", "start2", "end2"]
hic = hic[hic.chrom1.isin(CHROMS)]
def frac_matched(a, b, tol=20_000):
    hits = 0
    for r in a.itertuples():
        x = b[b.chrom1 == r.chrom1]
        d1 = np.abs((x.start1 + x.end1) / 2 - (r.start1 + r.end1) / 2)
        d2 = np.abs((x.start2 + x.end2) / 2 - (r.start2 + r.end2) / 2)
        hits += np.any((d1 <= tol) & (d2 <= tol))
    return hits / len(a)
hic2 = hic[hic.start2 - hic.start1 <= 2_000_000]
print("ours in HiCCUPS:", round(frac_matched(dots, hic), 2), " HiCCUPS (<= 2 Mb) in ours:", round(frac_matched(hic2, dots), 2))

How many dots does cooltools find, and how many HiCCUPS loops are on the two chromosomes?
What fraction of our dots is confirmed, and what fraction of HiCCUPS loops do we recover? Give three reasons for the difference.



P5 — APA by CTCF orientation
This uses the table written in R1.
lo = pd.read_csv("loop_ctcf_orientation.tsv", sep="\t")
lo = lo[lo.chrom1.isin(CHROMS)]
lo["cls"] = lo.motif1.fillna("0") + lo.motif2.fillna("0")
def to_feat(t):
    m1, m2 = (t.start1 + t.end1) // 2, (t.start2 + t.end2) // 2
    f = pd.DataFrame({"chrom1": t.chrom1, "start1": m1 - 5000, "end1": m1 + 5000,
                      "chrom2": t.chrom2, "start2": m2 - 5000, "end2": m2 + 5000})
    return f[(f.start2 - f.start1) >= 150_000]
sets = {"convergent": to_feat(lo[lo.cls == "+-"]), "other": to_feat(lo[lo.cls != "+-"])}
shifted = to_feat(lo).copy()
for k in ["start1", "end1", "start2", "end2"]:
    shifted[k] += 500_000
sets["shifted 500 kb"] = shifted[shifted.end2 < shifted.chrom2.map(c10.chromsizes)]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, (name, f) in zip(axs, sets.items()):
    st = cooltools.pileup(c10, f, view_df=v10, expected_df=exp10, flank=100_000)
    P = np.nanmean(st, axis=0)
    apa = P[10, 10] / np.nanmean(P[-6:, :6])
    print(name, len(f), "loops: centre", round(P[10, 10], 2), "APA", round(apa, 2))
    ax.imshow(np.log2(P), cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1.2, vmax=1.2); ax.set_title(f"{name}: APA {apa:.1f}")
plt.savefig("p5_apa.png", dpi=120)

What are the APA scores of the three sets? (b) What does the shifted control show? (c) Why pile up O/E rather than balanced counts?

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — compartments and saddles (B1, B3, P1, P2)





\(E(s)\) is the mean of one diagonal. Bins in the same compartment have O/E > 1 with each other at every distance. Check the sign of E1 against a track: here, bins with higher GC must get E1 > 0. Strength = (AA + BB) / (AB + BA) from the corners of the saddle. Papers: Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009; tools: cooltools.eigs_cis, cooltools.saddle, bioframe.frac_gc, and the compartments tutorial.









Hint 2 — insulation (B2, C1–C3, P3)





Write out the four pixels of each window, look them up, add. \(\log_2(x) = \ln x / \ln 2\). The original insulation score: Crane et al. 2015; cooltools.insulation and its tutorial; the cooltools CLI; bedtools window reports features within a distance. Caller comparisons: Forcato et al. 2017.









Hint 3 — dots and APA (B4, B5, P4, P5)





Local expected = \(E \times\) (observed in kernel / expected in kernel). For a Poisson mean \(\lambda\), the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\). APA score = centre / lower-left mean. HiCCUPS and APA: Rao et al. 2014; cooltools.dots and its tutorial; cooltools.pileup and the pileup tutorial.









Hint 4 — CTCF orientation (B6, R1, R2)





“+−” means the left anchor’s motif is on the + strand and the right anchor’s on the − strand: they point towards each other. With random strands each of +−, −+, ++, −− has probability 1/4. The R tools are those of Gene regulation: motifmatchr::matchMotifs with out = "positions" (a list per sequence with start, strand and score), JASPAR2024, GenomicRanges::findOverlaps. Loop extrusion: Fudenberg et al. 2016.









Hint 5 — judging claims (B7, B8)





Ask: equal depth? replicates? which caller, which resolution? is the statistic continuous (insulation, APA) or a binary call? does the assay itself enrich for the feature (HiChIP)? does the claim need a perturbation? For B8, count bins: the genome is 3.1 Gb; each contact adds to the row sums of two bins. Review: Lajoie et al. 2015.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Distance 1: (10 + 10 + 30 + 10 + 30) / 5 = 18. Distance 2: (15 + 5 + 5 + 5) / 4 = 7.5. Distance 3: (9 + 10 + 3) / 3 = 7.33. (b) (1, 3) = 15 / 7.5 = 2.0; (2, 4) = 5 / 7.5 = 0.67; (1, 4) = 9 / 7.33 = 1.23; (2, 5) = 10 / 7.33 = 1.36; (3, 6) = 3 / 7.33 = 0.41. Bins 1, 3, 4 attract each other, and 2, 5, 6 attract each other. (c) {1, 3, 4} and {2, 5, 6}: also (3, 4) = 30 and (5, 6) = 30 are high against 18, while (1, 2), (2, 3), (4, 5) are low. (d) GC is high in bins 1, 3, 4 (0.47–0.50), where E1 is negative: flip the sign. A = bins 1, 3, 4, B = 2, 5, 6. Without the check, chromosomes would be labelled at random: about half of them would have A and B swapped, and genome-wide statistics (e.g. “A is gene-rich”) would be diluted or reversed.
B2. (a) After bin 2: (1, 3) 22 + (1, 4) 15 + (2, 3) 40 + (2, 4) 22 = 99. After 3: (2, 4) 22 + (2, 5) 4 + (3, 4) 40 + (3, 5) 5 = 71. After 4: (3, 5) 5 + (3, 6) 4 + (4, 5) 8 + (4, 6) 5 = 22. After 5: (4, 6) 5 + (4, 7) 4 + (5, 6) 40 + (5, 7) 22 = 71. After 6: (5, 7) 22 + (5, 8) 15 + (6, 7) 40 + (6, 8) 22 = 99. (b) Mean = 362 / 5 = 72.4. Scores: log2(99/72.4) = +0.45, log2(71/72.4) = −0.03, log2(22/72.4) = −1.72, −0.03, +0.45. The boundary is between bins 4 and 5, a dip of about 1.7 below its neighbours (2.2 in log2 units against the flanks at +0.45). (c) \(w = 1\) uses one pixel per position: noisy, and it finds sub-domain boundaries; \(w = 4\) (as large as the domains) smooths over small domains and only shows the main boundaries; with nested domains each window size gives a different, valid set (the lecture’s 261 / 160 / 98 boundaries).
B3. (a) Control: (2.0 + 1.5) / (0.4 + 0.4) = 4.4. Cohesin depleted: (2.4 + 1.9) / (0.3 + 0.3) = 7.2. (b) Yes: without cohesin, loop extrusion no longer mixes neighbouring A and B segments, so compartmentalisation strengthens (Rao et al. 2017; Schwarzer et al. 2017). (c) The same resolution and E1 groups (ideally E1 from one condition or from both pooled), similar depth, the same distance range (excluding the diagonal), and the same expected-value normalisation for each condition.
B4. (a) X: 120 / 40 = 3.0; Y: 70 / 40 = 1.75. (b) X: local expected = 40 × 400/320 = 50; O/E = 120/50 = 2.4. Y: local expected = 40 × 1 120/700 = 64; O/E = 70/64 = 1.09. X is a loop candidate; Y is not. (c) Y sits in a region (a domain) where every pixel is enriched, so it is above the distance-expected value but not above its neighbours: a domain corner without a dot. (d) Very: 120 is (120 − 50)/7 ≈ 10 standard deviations above the mean; the Poisson p-value is far below any threshold, even after correcting for millions of tests.
B5. (a) 3.2 / 1.4 = 2.3 in the first cell type; 1.5 / 1.3 = 1.15 in the second. (b) The loops are much weaker or absent in the second cell type on average (or the second map has lower quality or resolution: check its APA at its own loops before concluding). Some may persist: an average hides heterogeneity, so look at subsets or at individual strong loops. (c) The whole pileup includes the stripes and domain signal around the loop; the lower-left corner (towards the diagonal) is the strongest background, so the score is conservative: a high score means a point-like enrichment, not just a domain.
B6. (a) Convergent (+−): 7 of 10 = 70%; tandem (++, −−): 2 = 20%; divergent (−+): 1 = 10%. Random expectation: 25% convergent, 50% tandem, 25% divergent. (b) Loop extrusion: cohesin stops at CTCF bound with its N-terminus facing the loop, i.e. motifs pointing into the loop; so loops form between convergent sites. Divergent sites (← →) point away from each other: each stops cohesin coming from outside, so a divergent pair separates two domains (a strong boundary) rather than anchoring a loop between them.
B7. (a) Not comparable: the knockout map has a third of the depth, and loop calls depend strongly on depth; one replicate gives no variance. Downsample the wild type to 400 M and call again, use replicates, and compare loop strength at a common loop set (APA, or counts at fixed loop positions) rather than numbers of calls. (b) At 40 kb with one scale, boundary positions are coarse and the call is binary: insulation strength can drop by half while the boundary is still “called”. Compare insulation scores or boundary strengths quantitatively at higher resolution, with replicates, and check several window sizes. (c) H3K27ac HiChIP enriches contacts at acetylated anchors, so active elements look connected partly because they are acetylated; and a contact is not regulation. Test with a perturbation: CRISPRi or deletion of the enhancer and measure X (and other genes).
B8. About 180 M cis contacts. Compartments at 100 kb–1 Mb: easily (3.1 Gb / 100 kb = 31 000 bins, about 10 000 contacts per bin). Domains at 25–50 kb: possible (62 000–124 000 bins, a few thousand contacts each). Loops at 5–10 kb need ~1 000+ contacts in 80% of bins: at 10 kb there are 310 000 bins and 600 M row-sum entries (2 × 300 M), about 1 900 per bin on average, so 10 kb is borderline and 5 kb out of reach; Rao et al. needed billions of contacts for 1–5 kb. Use APA at known loops rather than calling loops de novo.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) region1 region2 dist dist_bp contact_frequency n_total n_valid count.sum balanced.sum count.avg balanced.avg: for each chromosome and distance (in bins and bp), the number of pixels and of valid (not masked) pixels, the sums of raw and balanced counts, and their means; contact_frequency is the same as balanced.avg, i.e. \(E(s)\). Distances 0 and 1 are ignored (ignore_diags=2 by default, the same as balancing) because they are dominated by short-range artefacts and the polymer itself. (b) 261 / 160 / 98 boundaries for 100, 200 and 500 kb.
C2. (a) 106 of 160 boundaries (66%) are within 10 kb of a CTCF summit, against 63 of 160 random valid bins (39%). (b) chr19 is very gene- and CTCF-rich, chr21 less so; random bins elsewhere in the genome would have a different CTCF density and are not covered by our matrix, so the comparison would be biased.
C3. 843 distinct Arrowhead edges; 129 of our 160 boundaries (81%) lie within 20 kb of an edge, but only 267 of the edges (32%) near one of ours. Arrowhead calls nested domains of many sizes, so it has many more edges; most of our single-scale (200-kb window) boundaries are among them, but most of its edges are sub-domain or nested-domain edges that a 200-kb window does not resolve.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 15 172 CTCF peaks lie in loop anchors; 12 761 (84%) of them have a motif match at \(p < 10^{-4}\) within 50 bp of the summit. (b) An anchor of 5–25 kb can contain several CTCF peaks, sometimes in opposite orientations; the strongest peak is the most likely to be the one stopping cohesin, but not always. Peaks without a match, or matches in both orientations, add noise; the true fraction of convergent loops is therefore higher than what we measure.
R2. (a) 5 716 of 14 599 loops (39%) have a motif at both anchors; 76% at least one. (b) 83.9% convergent, 14.9% tandem, 1.2% divergent: far from the 25 / 50 / 25 of random orientations, close to the lecture figure. Rao et al. report over 90% convergent when restricting to anchors with exactly one motif.









Solutions — Python





P1. (a) chr19: 57% A; chr21: 46%. Spearman ρ of E1 with GC 0.78 / 0.64, H3K27ac 0.68 / 0.84, H3K9me3 −0.71 / −0.31, ENCODE’s eigenvector 0.97 / 0.90 (chr19 / chr21). (b) E2 vs GC: 0.15 / 0.11: E2 does not carry the A/B pattern here. If A/B had ended up in E2, E2 (not E1) would correlate with GC and the marks, and the E1 track would follow something else, e.g. a step at the centromere (one arm against the other). (c) Without phasing the sign is whatever the solver returns; in our run chr19 came out with the right sign (ρ with GC = +0.78) but chr21 flipped (ρ = −0.64): exactly the bug described in B1(d).
P2. (a) B–B (top left) 2.46, A–A 1.56, A–B 0.31: strength (2.46 + 1.56) / (0.31 + 0.31) = 6.6. (b) Group 3 holds bins with E1 near 0: bins at A/B transitions, bins that are A in some cells and B in others, or mixed bins at 100 kb; their contacts are close to the expectation with everything.
P3. (a) 261, 160 and 98 boundaries; the same as the CLI (both call cooltools.insulation with the same defaults). (b) 66% of the 200-kb boundaries are near a CTCF summit, against 45% of random valid bins in this draw (39% in C2: a sample of 160 random bins varies by several percentage points). (c) The dips at about 39.5 and 41.1 Mb appear at every window size: strong boundaries.
P4. (a) 178 dots (118 on chr19, 60 on chr21); HiCCUPS has 533 loops on the two chromosomes, 486 of them spanning ≤ 2 Mb. (b) 96% of our dots match a HiCCUPS loop; we recover 35% of HiCCUPS loops. Reasons: HiCCUPS merged calls from 5, 10 and 25 kb, we used only 10 kb; different thresholds (cooltools’ default FDR and clustering are conservative); HiCCUPS also calls dots up to 8 Mb; and nearby loops can be merged differently. Neither set is “the” loops of GM12878.
P5. (a) Convergent (102 loops longer than 150 kb): centre O/E 3.89, APA 2.8; other (223): centre 3.71, APA 2.8; shifted (324): centre 1.07, APA 1.0. The two loop classes are equally strong on average: every called loop passed the same threshold, and “other” contains many CTCF loops whose motif we missed. (b) The shifted control has no dot (APA ≈ 1): the enrichment belongs to the anchor positions, not to the distance or the domain. (c) Loops differ in length; balanced counts fall with distance, so averaging them mixes very different scales and is dominated by the shortest loops. O/E puts every loop on the same scale (1 = expected).

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Where this leads

Linking regulatory elements to genes uses contact frequencies (and the activity-by-contact model) to assign enhancers to target genes.
Epigenomics and genetic variation asks whether disease variants fall in loop anchors and domain boundaries.
For a new Hi-C or Micro-C data set, the same steps run genome-wide with the open2c distiller pipeline, or nf-core/hic, followed by cooltools.

title: Exercise: Calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Rao et al. 2014, Cell. A 3D map of the human genome at kilobase resolution reveals principles of chromatin looping.
Crane et al. 2015, Nature. Condensin-driven remodelling of X chromosome topology during dosage compensation.
Open2C et al. 2024, PLoS Comput Biol. Cooltools: enabling high-resolution Hi-C analysis in Python.
Forcato et al. 2017, Nat Methods. Comparison of computational methods for Hi-C data analysis.
Hsieh et al. 2015, Cell. Mapping nucleosome resolution chromosome folding in yeast by Micro-C.
Mumbach et al. 2016, Nat Methods. HiChIP: efficient and sensitive analysis of protein-directed genome architecture.

title: Quiz: calling compartments, TADs and loops
text:
Short questions on eigenvectors, saddle plots, insulation, dot calling and APA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why is the eigenvector computed on observed/expected values (or their correlation) rather than on the balanced matrix itself?






Answer





The balanced matrix is dominated by distance decay: every row looks like a peak around the diagonal, so the main pattern of variation would be distance, not compartment type. Dividing by the expected value at each distance removes that, leaving the preference of A for A and B for B; correlating rows sharpens it into a checkerboard.




Q2. An analysis of 23 chromosomes reports that compartment A is gene-poor on 11 of them and gene-rich on 12. What went wrong?






Answer





The sign of the eigenvector was not fixed. It is arbitrary for each chromosome (or arm); it must be oriented with a phasing track such as GC content, gene density or an active mark, so that A (E1 > 0) is the gene-rich, active compartment everywhere.




Q3. A saddle plot gives mean O/E of 2.0 for B–B, 1.6 for A–A and 0.4 for both A–B corners. Compute the compartment strength. After a treatment, the values are 1.6, 1.4 and 0.6. What happened?






Answer





Before: (2.0 + 1.6) / (0.4 + 0.4) = 4.5. After: (1.6 + 1.4) / (0.6 + 0.6) = 2.5. Compartmentalisation is weaker: A and B mix more (as after WAPL loss, when cohesin stays longer on DNA and extrudes larger loops). Check that the two maps had similar depth and were analysed with the same E1 groups.




Q4. An insulation profile has window sums 120, 118, 30, 115 and 125 at five consecutive positions. Compute the insulation score at the third position. Is it a boundary?






Hint





Score = log2(sum / mean of the sums); a boundary is a local minimum.









Answer





Mean = 508 / 5 = 101.6. Score = log2(30 / 101.6) = −1.76, a deep local minimum (neighbours at +0.22 and +0.18): a strong boundary.




Q5. Insulation with a 100-kb window finds 261 boundaries on chr19 + chr21; with a 500-kb window, 98. Which is correct?






Answer





Both. Domains are nested; a small window finds sub-domain boundaries, a large window only the boundaries of large domains. Report the window and resolution, and compare conditions with the same parameters, preferably using boundary strength rather than presence or absence.




Q6. A pixel has 70 contacts; the distance-expected value is 40, but its donut neighbourhood has 1 120 observed against 700 expected. Is it a loop?






Answer





Local expected = 40 × 1 120/700 = 64; O/E = 70/64 ≈ 1.1. No: it is enriched only because its whole neighbourhood (a domain) is enriched. A loop must stand out against its local background.




Q7. Why does HiCCUPS use a “lower-left” background in addition to the donut?






Answer





Pixels towards the lower left of a candidate loop pixel are closer to the diagonal, where contacts are higher. A pixel must also beat that stronger neighbourhood, which protects against calling a point on the edge of a domain or a stripe as a loop.




Q8. At 5 716 loops with a CTCF motif at both anchors, 84% are convergent and 1% divergent. What would you expect if orientation did not matter? Which model explains the result?






Answer





Random strands: 25% convergent (+−), 25% divergent (−+), 50% tandem. The strong excess of convergent pairs is explained by loop extrusion: cohesin is stopped by CTCF whose N-terminus faces the loop, i.e. motifs pointing into the loop.




Q9. An APA pileup gives a centre O/E of 3.9 and a lower-left mean of 1.4. The same loops shifted by 500 kb give 1.07 and 1.05. Compute both APA scores and interpret.






Answer





3.9 / 1.4 = 2.8 at the loops; 1.07 / 1.05 = 1.0 for the shifted control. The enrichment is specific to the anchor positions, not a property of the distance between them.




Q10. A paper compares a knockout and wild type: “the knockout loses 2 000 loops”. The knockout map has 300 M contacts, the wild type 1 B; one replicate each. What would you ask for?






Answer





Equal depth (downsample the wild type) before calling loops; replicates for each condition; a quantitative comparison at a common set of loop positions (APA or per-loop counts with a count model, e.g. diffHic/multiHiCcompare) instead of differences in the number of calls; and a check that P(s) is similar, or a distance-aware normalisation.

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
About this lecture
3D genome organisation showed what a Hi-C map contains. This lecture shows how a map is made from sequencing reads, and what can go wrong on the way.

The chemistry: in situ Hi-C, restriction enzymes and the ligation junction that every valid read pair carries.
Reads to pairs: mapping the two ends separately, chimeric reads, pair types, artefacts (dangling ends, self-circles) and duplicates.
Pairs to a matrix: binning, resolution versus depth, the .pairs, .cool, .mcool and .hic formats.
Normalisation: why maps are balanced (ICE), the distance decay P(s) and observed/expected.


The running example is real: GM12878 in situ Hi-C from Rao et al. 2014, library HIC001 (SRA run SRR1658570), 2 × 101 bp, MboI. We took the first 30 million read pairs of that run and aligned them to the whole genome: those statistics are on the slides. For the exercise we kept the read pairs that fall on chr21, so students can run the whole pipeline on a laptop in minutes; at the end we compare their chr21 map with ENCODE’s map of the same experiment built from all replicates (4.6 billion contacts). The tools are the open2c ones (bwa, pairtools, cooler, cooltools), which are what the 4DN consortium and the distiller pipeline use; Juicer and HiC-Pro do the same steps differently. Figures from make-hicproc-figs.py.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
The pipeline


The wet-lab steps decide which artefacts appear; each computational step removes or corrects one of them.
Output: a contact matrix with balancing weights, and its expected contact frequency at each distance.


Point out the file produced by each step, because the files are what students handle: FASTQ, SAM (never stored, streamed into pairtools), .pairs (text, one line per read pair), deduplicated .pairs, .cool (binned), .cool with a weight column after balancing, and tables of expected values. The same structure is shared with every assay in the course (reads, alignment, filtering, counting, normalisation); what is new here is that each read pair reports two positions, and the counting is in two dimensions.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
In situ Hi-C


Crosslink with formaldehyde, cut with a restriction enzyme, fill in the overhangs with a biotinylated nucleotide, ligate the blunt ends, shear, pull down biotin, sequence paired-end.
Ligation happens inside intact nuclei (in situ), which reduces random ligations between molecules from different complexes or nuclei.


Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009 ligated in dilute solution after lysing the nuclei (“dilution Hi-C”); Rao et al. 2014 kept the nuclei intact for digestion and ligation (“in situ Hi-C”), which gave fewer spurious interchromosomal ligations, a faster protocol and higher resolution. Biotin marks the ligation junctions so that, after shearing, fragments that contain a junction can be enriched on streptavidin beads; unligated fragment ends with biotin are a known artefact (dangling ends) and are removed in some protocols with an exonuclease step. Each sequenced fragment should contain one junction somewhere between its two ends.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
The ligation junction


MboI (and DpnII) cut ^GATC; fill-in and blunt ligation duplicate the overhang: the junction reads GATCGATC.
15% of our 101-bp reads contain GATCGATC: they read through a junction and are chimeric.
The enzyme sets the finest possible resolution: one site every ~256 bp (4-cutter) or ~4 kb (6-cutter).


The junction sequence is a fingerprint of a real ligation product, and it is the reason Hi-C reads need special alignment. HindIII (a 6-cutter, used in the original 2009 protocol) gives AAGCTAGCTT; Arima kits combine two enzymes (^GATC and G^ANTC), so four junction sequences occur. Some pipelines (HiC-Pro, Juicer) search for the junction and trim reads there; the pairtools approach instead lets bwa split the read into two alignments. A fragment that has no junction between its read ends is either a dangling end (never ligated) or a pair whose junction lies between the reads, in the unsequenced middle: both are common.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Restriction fragments on chr21


chr21 has 91 397 GATC sites (157 000 expected at random) and 11 263 HindIII sites: median fragments 282 bp and 2 284 bp.
Hi-C cannot resolve contacts within one fragment, so a 4-cutter allows kilobase maps; a 6-cutter limits them to ~5–10 kb.


Computed from the chr21 sequence in make-hicproc-figs.py; only fragments without assembly gaps are counted. The real distribution is broad because sites are not uniformly spaced: GATC is depleted in some sequence contexts and enriched in others, and repeats cluster. The resolution argument: the smallest unit of a contact is a pair of restriction fragments, and a bin must contain several fragments to average over their different ligation efficiencies. Micro-C replaces the enzyme by MNase, which cuts every linker, so its unit is a nucleosome (about 150 bp of DNA): the finest resolution available.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Read pairs, chimeras and walks


Each side of a pair is represented by the 5′ end of its read’s first (5′-most) alignment: that is the position closest to the junction’s partner fragment.
A read that crosses the junction gives two alignments; if both sides agree, the pair is rescued. Several junctions in one molecule make a walk.


Why the 5′ end: in a ligation product the junction lies between the two reads; the 5′ end of each read is the outer end of the molecule, i.e. the position in the fragment that was sequenced first, and its 5′-most alignment belongs to the fragment of that side. With 101-bp reads and fragments around 300–500 bp, a sizeable fraction of reads reach the junction (case 2). Walks (case 3) arise when three or more fragments were ligated together; they are informative about multi-way contacts (and are the basis of methods like Pore-C, which sequence whole concatemers with long reads), for a pairwise map we let pairtools report the 5′-most unique alignment of each side (–walks-policy 5unique); the alternative is to mask them (pair type WW).
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
section: Mapping: each end on its own
text:
Mapping: each end on its own
bwa mem -SP5M -t 8 chr21.fa R1.fastq.gz R2.fastq.gz \
  | pairtools parse --min-mapq 30 --walks-policy 5unique --max-inter-align-gap 30 \
      --drop-sam --drop-seq -c chr21.sizes -o chr21.pairs.gz

-SP: do not pair the mates: no mate rescue (-S), no pairing (-P). The two ends are expected to come from anywhere in the genome.
-5: for a split read, the 5′-most alignment is the primary one. -M: mark the other parts as secondary.
No trimming at the junction is needed: bwa mem’s local alignment splits chimeric reads itself.


Flags are not examined; the idea is. A normal paired-end aligner assumes the two reads face each other within a few hundred bp, penalises other placements and “rescues” a poorly aligned mate near the other; in Hi-C those assumptions are wrong for most pairs. bwa mem in local mode soft-clips the part of a read that crosses the junction and reports it as a supplementary alignment, which is exactly the split we want. Bowtie2 end-to-end (as in HiC-Pro) cannot do this and therefore needs the junction-trimming step. Our reference is chr21 only: an honest shortcut, because the reads were preselected as those that map to chr21 in the whole genome (see the last slides).

UU 70%, rescued UR + RU 9%; pairs with an unmapped or multi-mapped side (NU, MU, MM, …) are dropped.


All 30 million read pairs aligned to the whole genome (GRCh38 primary chromosomes and unplaced contigs, no alternative haplotypes), parsed with pairtools parse with the options on the previous slide; duplicates (1.5% of pairs, type DD) are left out of the chart. The pair type is two letters, one per side. M sides are mostly reads in repeats, segmental duplications and centromeric satellites. N sides include reads that are too short after a junction to align. About 5% of pairs have both sides multi-mapped or unmapped. In a typical library, 70–85% of pairs end up UU/UR/RU. The exercise does the same on chr21.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Ligation artefacts


Dangling ends (unligated fragments) and re-ligations of neighbours: reads point inward (+ −), less than ~1 kb apart.
Self-circles (a fragment ligated to itself): reads point outward (− +), within one fragment.
At large distances all four orientations are equally likely, so an excess of one orientation at short range marks artefacts.


These are the classic Hi-C artefacts (Imakaev et al. 2012; HiC-Pro classifies them explicitly using a restriction-fragment map). A dangling end looks like a normal short paired-end fragment, the kind of pair any library has; it carries no 3D information. A self-circle can only arise if the fragment is short enough to circularise. pairtools does not need the restriction map: the orientation-by-distance plot on the next slide shows where the artefacts stop, and the simplest filter is to ignore contacts closer than about 1–2 kb, which balancing and expected calculations do by skipping the first diagonals.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Real data: orientation versus distance


Between ~200 and 600 bp, 96% of pairs point inward (+ −): dangling ends and re-ligated neighbours. Outward self-circles are rare in this in situ library.
Above ~1 kb, all four orientations are within a few percent of 25%: the pairs are genuine ligation products.


From the dist_freq section of the pairtools stats file (30 M pairs, whole genome, after deduplication), the fraction of each orientation in logarithmic distance bins from 100 bp. Strand of the left side first, as in the .pairs file. The inward peak at 200–600 bp is the size distribution of sheared, unligated fragments (dangling ends). Below about 200 bp the tandem orientations (+ +, − −) dominate; these very short pairs are further artefacts of short molecules and are discarded with everything under 1 kb. From 1 kb the four orientations are within 3 percentage points of 25%. This plot is a standard QC figure (the “4DN orientation plot”); it also shows where to set the minimum distance for analyses. Students make it in the exercise from the stats file.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Duplicates

PCR and optical duplicates: two read pairs with the same two 5′ positions and strands. Two independent ligations producing exactly the same pair of ends are very unlikely.
pairtools dedup removes pairs whose both sides match within 3 bp (--max-mismatch 3).
Our 30 M pairs: 1.9% duplicates among mapped pairs; in the deep libraries of the full experiment the rate rises with depth (library complexity).

pairtools sort --nproc 4 -o chr21.sorted.pairs.gz chr21.pairs.gz
pairtools dedup --max-mismatch 3 --output-stats dedup.stats -o chr21.nodups.pairs.gz chr21.sorted.pairs.gz

Exactly the logic of duplicate marking for paired-end ATAC-seq: a pair is defined by both ends, so true duplicates are rare. Sorting first puts identical pairs next to each other. The tolerance allows for small position shifts (e.g. soft-clipping differences). The duplication rate grows as you sequence a library deeper; pairtools stats estimates library complexity (the number of distinct molecules) from it, which tells you whether more sequencing of the same library is worthwhile. Our rate (1.9%, 448 270 of 23.8 M) is low because 30 M pairs is a small fraction of a complex library; on the chr21 subset it is the same (1.9%).
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
section: Real data: where the read pairs go
text:
Real data: where the read pairs go


Of 30 M read pairs, 23.8 M (79%) have both sides uniquely mapped; 16.9 M are contacts on the same chromosome more than 1 kb apart.
84% of unique pairs are cis and 16% trans; 56% are cis and more than 20 kb apart.


pairtools stats of the deduplicated pairs (data/gm12878_hic_fullgenome_stats.txt). QC rules of thumb from 4DN and Rao et al.: a good in situ library has a high cis fraction, more than about 40% of pairs cis and more than 20 kb apart (“long-range cis”), and a trans fraction that is not too high (high trans suggests random ligation). Our library passes comfortably. The fraction of short-range cis pairs (< 1 kb) is mostly the artefacts of the previous slides and is not used.

Exact thresholds differ between consortia and protocols, so present them as orders of magnitude. The 4DN QC report and the ENCODE Hi-C pipeline compute these numbers. Two practical consequences: a shallow test sequencing run (a few million pairs) is enough to measure all of these before deciding to sequence deeply; and these metrics are the first thing to check in a paper’s supplementary data.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
From pairs to a matrix


Cut the genome into bins of fixed size; each valid pair adds 1 to pixel (bin of side 1, bin of side 2).
The matrix is symmetric and sparse: store only the upper triangle and only non-zero pixels.

cooler cload pairs -c1 2 -p1 3 -c2 4 -p2 5 chr21.sizes:10000 chr21.valid.pairs.gz chr21_10kb.cool

This is the “count matrix” step, the Hi-C equivalent of counting reads in peaks or genes, but in two dimensions. The columns -c1 -p1 -c2 -p2 tell cooler where chromosome and position of each side are in the .pairs file. Binning at 10 kb and then aggregating to coarser resolutions (cooler zoomify) is faster than re-reading the pairs. Bin by restriction fragments is possible too (Juicer offers fragment-resolution maps), but fixed-size bins are the norm because they make comparisons easy.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
File formats


.pairs: the 4DN text standard, one line per contact; keep it, you can re-bin it at any resolution.
.cool / .mcool (HDF5, cooler): one or many resolutions; .hic (Juicer): all resolutions plus normalisation vectors.
Convert with hictk or hic2cool; both are read by HiGlass, Juicebox (.hic) and the Python and R ecosystems.


The two big ecosystems are Juicer/Juicebox (Aiden lab: .hic, Java) and open2c/4DN (cooler, pairtools, cooltools, HiGlass: .cool, Python). ENCODE distributes .hic files; 4DN distributes .mcool and .hic. Our course matrix gm12878_hic_chr19_chr21.mcool was made by reading ENCODE’s 55-GB .hic file remotely with hic-straw (only the needed blocks are transferred), writing raw counts for chr19 and chr21 at 5 kb into a .cool, and running cooler zoomify with balancing: data/prepare-hic.sh. In R, the HiCExperiment package reads .cool, .mcool, .hic and .pairs.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Resolution and depth


Our 217 499 chr21 contacts against ENCODE’s 35.2 million (162×): at 250 kb the maps look alike; at 10 kb ours is mostly empty.
Rule of thumb (Rao et al. 2014): resolution = the smallest bin size at which 80% of bins have ≥ 1 000 contacts. Ours: 250 kb (82% of bins; 43% at 100 kb); ENCODE: 10 kb or finer (93% at 10 kb).


The number of pixels grows with the square of the number of bins, so halving the bin size needs roughly four times the reads for the same counts per pixel (within a fixed distance band, about twice as many). This is why compartments are studied at 100 kb–1 Mb with a few hundred million reads, while loops need billions. Same region (chr21:33–38 Mb), same colour scale rule (percentiles of each map), three resolutions. Our map is 273 200 read pairs, of which 217 499 valid contacts. The numbers for the 80% rule are printed by make-hicproc-figs.py for several bin sizes.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Why balance?


Bins differ in how visible they are: restriction-site density, GC content, mappability, copy number.
Model: observed O_{ij} = b_i\, b_j\, T_{ij}, with a bias b per bin and true contacts T.
Assumption: every bin is equally visible in truth (equal row sums of T). Bins with too few contacts are masked, not corrected.


These biases are multiplicative and specific to each bin, which shows as horizontal and vertical stripes in a raw map. Explicit models (Yaffe and Tanay 2011; HiCNorm) fit them from known covariates; matrix balancing does it implicitly, without knowing the causes. The equal-visibility assumption is wrong for copy-number changes (a duplicated region in a cancer genome really has more contacts), which is why cancer Hi-C needs special care (e.g. OneD, or CNV-aware methods). The masked bins are white in balanced maps: low-mappability regions, centromeres, and bins with too few non-zero pixels (cooler’s default filters: at least 10 non-zero pixels, and median absolute deviation filtering of row sums).
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Iterative correction (ICE)


Divide each row and column by its relative sum; repeat until all sums are equal. The product of the factors is the bias of each bin; cooler balance stores 1/bias as the weight column.
Balanced value = count × weight_i × weight_j. KR, VC and SCALE (Juicer) are variants of the same idea.


ICE (Imakaev et al. 2012) is an instance of matrix balancing (Sinkhorn–Knopp). In the toy example the raw row sums are 12, 20 and 8; after one iteration 13.1, 13.3, 13.7; at convergence all are 13.4. The bin with the most contacts gets the largest bias (1.50) and is scaled down most. Students do one iteration by hand in the exercise. Knight–Ruiz (KR) converges faster to the same solution; vanilla coverage (VC) is a single iteration; Juicer’s SCALE is a fast balancing designed for very large matrices. In practice: balance per chromosome (cis-only) when you only analyse cis contacts, as we did for the course .mcool; genome-wide when you need trans.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Real data: raw versus balanced


Raw: stripes where bins are seen too often or too rarely; row sums vary from 399 to 3 587 contacts per 250-kb bin.
Balanced: equal row sums (bottom), the stripes are gone, and 50 of 187 bins (the short arm and centromere, a few repeat bins) are masked.


Our chr21 map at 250 kb, from the students’ own pipeline (exercise C5–C6). The bars under the raw map are the row sums (coverage); under the balanced map, the balanced row sums, flat by construction. The masked region from 0 to about 14 Mb is the short arm and centromere of chr21, which is mostly gaps and satellite repeats in the assembly. Balancing does not remove distance decay, which remains the dominant signal; the next slide.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
The distance decay P(s)


Average the balanced matrix along each diagonal: P(s), the expected contact frequency at distance s.
Our chr21 map (217 499 contacts) and ENCODE’s give the same curve: slopes −1.02 and −0.97 between 100 kb and 1 Mb.


cooltools expected_cis computes, for each diagonal, the sum of balanced values divided by the number of valid pixels; with smoothing for display. Both curves are normalised to sum 1 so they can be compared. That two maps 162-fold apart in depth give the same P(s) shows that the expected is a robust statistic that needs few reads, unlike loops. P(s) is used as a QC (a library with too much random ligation has a flattened curve) and as biology: its shape reports on loop extrusion (cohesin loss removes the excess of contacts between about 100 kb and 1 Mb) and the curve of mitotic chromosomes is different again.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Observed / expected


Divide each pixel by P(s) at its distance: O/E removes the distance decay and shows what is special about a pair of loci.
On chr19 the balanced map (left) is dominated by the diagonal; O/E (right) shows the compartment checkerboard over the whole arm.


ENCODE’s chr19 map, 100 kb, q-arm (30 Mb to the end). Red: more contacts than expected at that distance, blue: fewer. The O/E matrix is the starting point of compartment calling (its correlation and eigenvector), of APA and of dot calling (which refines the expected locally): Calling compartments, TADs and loops. A by-hand O/E calculation is in the exercise.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
section: Pipelines and the shortcut used here
text:
Pipelines and the shortcut used here

Production pipelines: distiller (open2c, Nextflow: bwa + pairtools + cooler), nf-core/hic (HiC-Pro logic), Juicer (Aiden lab, .hic), the 4DN and ENCODE Hi-C pipelines. Same steps, different defaults.
Our shortcut: 30 M read pairs of one run were aligned to the whole genome; the pairs with a side on chr21 (and the other on chr21 or unplaced) were kept as FASTQ, so the exercise aligns to chr21 only. Contacts to other chromosomes and true multi-mappers elsewhere are therefore missing.
Our map: 217 499 contacts on chr21; ENCODE’s map of the full experiment: 4.6 billion genome-wide. The features unit uses ENCODE’s.


Be explicit about the shortcut (designprinciples §10). Running the full pipeline on a deep Hi-C experiment takes hundreds of CPU hours and terabytes of temporary space; the steps are the same as in the exercise, wrapped in a workflow manager on a cluster (SLURM). The whole-genome statistics on the slides come from our full alignment of 30 M pairs (data/prepare-hic.sh), so the pair-type and cis/trans numbers are real whole-genome values. A side effect of preselecting chr21 reads: a read that was multi-mapped in the whole genome may look unique on chr21 alone, so the chr21-only run slightly overestimates mappability.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Summary







step
key idea




chemistry
crosslink, digest (^GATC), biotin fill-in, ligate in situ; junction GATCGATC


mapping
each end alone (bwa mem -SP5M); split reads; 5′-most alignment represents a side


pairs
types UU/UR/RU kept; NU/MU/MM dropped; walks masked or reduced


artefacts
dangling ends (+ −) and self-circles (− +) below ~1–2 kb; PCR duplicates by both ends


QC
cis fraction, cis > 20 kb, duplicates, orientation convergence


matrix
fixed bins; symmetric, sparse; resolution limited by depth and enzyme


balancing
ICE: equal visibility; weight per bin; mask poor bins


expected
P(s) per diagonal; O/E removes distance decay




Students should be able to: write the ligation junction for an enzyme; explain why Hi-C ends are mapped separately; classify a read pair as dangling end, self-circle or valid from positions and strands; put pairs into bins and fill a matrix; run one ICE iteration by hand; compute an expected value and O/E; and judge a library from its QC numbers. Next: Calling compartments, TADs and loops.
crumbs: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices

title: Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009, Science. Comprehensive mapping of long-range interactions reveals folding principles of the human genome. Hi-C, compartments and the distance decay.
Rao et al. 2014, Cell. A 3D map of the human genome at kilobase resolution reveals principles of chromatin looping. In situ Hi-C, and the data used here.
Imakaev et al. 2012, Nat Methods. Iterative correction of Hi-C data reveals hallmarks of chromosome organization. ICE balancing.
Lajoie, Dekker & Kaplan 2015, Methods. The Hitchhiker’s guide to Hi-C analysis: practical guidelines. Every processing step and its pitfalls.
Open2C et al. 2024, PLoS Comput Biol. Pairtools: from sequencing data to chromosome contacts. Parsing, pair types and deduplication.
Abdennur & Mirny 2020, Bioinformatics. Cooler: scalable storage for Hi-C data and other genomically labeled arrays. The .cool format.
