title: Epigenetics
text: A second-cycle course at Umeå University on the biology of chromatin and DNA methylation, the sequencing assays that measure them, and how to analyse the data: from raw reads on the command line to interpretation in R.

title: Epigenetics
text:
Where to start

Course plan: the draft syllabus and current course information.
Learning outcomes: what we are trying to teach.

title: Epigenetics
text:
Before you start

Install the software you need: do this before you start the first unit.

title: Epigenetics
text:
Topics
Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Each unit lists its lecture, quiz and exercises in teaching order.

Foundations: what epigenetics is (chromatin, histone marks, DNA methylation), genomic intervals, gene regulation and transcription factors, from reads to coverage, and experimental design and QC.
Chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq): the assay, processing and peak calling, differential accessibility, and motifs and footprinting.
Protein–DNA binding and histone marks: ChIP-seq, peak calling, CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag, annotation and differential binding, and chromatin states.
DNA methylation: the biology, bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing, differential methylation, methylation arrays, epigenetic clocks and biomarkers, and long-read methylation and chromatin.
3D genome: genome organisation, Hi-C processing, and compartments, TADs and loops.
Integration and interpretation: linking regulatory elements to genes, and epigenomics and genetic variation.
Machine learning for prediction: machine learning from scratch, what people try to predict, how a CNN reads DNA, and what the model learned.

The material is under construction: more blocks are added as they are written.
See Canvas for the most up to date study instructions.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
About this lecture
Differential accessibility ended with tens of thousands of peaks that differ between cell types, most of them distal, and a nearest gene written next to each. This lecture asks how to find the gene (or genes) an element actually regulates, and how to tell whether a method works.

Why the nearest gene is often wrong, with numbers from CRISPR screens.
Correlation of accessibility and expression across samples, and its null.
Contact: the power law of distance, and Hi-C.
The activity-by-contact (ABC) model: activity × contact, normalised per gene.
Ground truth: CRISPRi enhancer screens, and precision–recall to compare methods.
Running example: K562 (CRISPRi benchmark) and GM12878 (course data).


This unit connects the chromatin units with the RNA-seq the students already know. The question is simple to state and hard to answer: which gene does this enhancer regulate? It matters for every downstream interpretation, from “the B-cell enhancers we found are near PAX5” to “this disease variant acts through gene X” (the next unit, Epigenomics and genetic variation). We use a real benchmark: about ten thousand enhancer–gene pairs tested by CRISPR interference in K562 cells, of which 471 are true regulatory links. Every method in the lecture is scored on the same table, so the students see that simple rules are surprisingly strong and that ABC is better but far from perfect. All numbers are from make-integ-figs.R and the exercise.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
The question


An enhancer is a peak of ATAC-seq and H3K27ac. Nothing in the peak says which promoter it talks to.
Candidate targets: every gene within about a megabase. The nearest TSS is the obvious guess, and the one most papers report.
We need a target to interpret a differential peak, a motif in it, or a disease variant in it.


Read the figure from the enhancer outwards: four genes within 500 kb on either side, the nearest TSS 140 kb away, the next one 150 kb away. Which gene would you pick? Students usually pick gene C. Ask what information they would want: is gene C expressed in these cells, is the enhancer in contact with its promoter, does the enhancer’s activity rise and fall with the gene’s expression across cell types, and what happens to each gene when the enhancer is switched off? These are exactly the four kinds of evidence of the lecture. One enhancer can also regulate several genes, and one gene usually has several enhancers; the question is about pairs, not about a single answer per enhancer.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Enhancers skip genes


ZRS: the limb enhancer of SHH sits about 1 Mb away, inside an intron of LMBR1; point mutations in it cause polydactyly.
FTO: the strongest obesity GWAS signal lies in an FTO intron but acts on IRX3 and IRX5, 0.5 and 1.2 Mb away.
BENC: a cluster of blood enhancers 1.7 Mb downstream of MYC; deleting it in mice removes Myc from haematopoietic stem cells.


Three classic cases, each discovered the hard way. The ZRS (zone of polarising activity regulatory sequence) controls Shh in the posterior limb bud; it is about a megabase from Shh and inside a gene that has nothing to do with limb patterning. The FTO story is the cautionary tale of GWAS interpretation: years of work on FTO before Smemo et al. 2014 showed that the obesity-associated region contacts and regulates IRX3, and Claussnitzer et al. 2015 traced one variant (rs1421085) to IRX3 and IRX5 in adipocyte progenitors. BENC (Bahr et al. 2018) is a blood-specific enhancer cluster 1.7 Mb from MYC; in K562 and in leukaemias, other distant MYC enhancers are used. The examples are extreme on purpose. The next slides show how often this happens in a systematic experiment.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
section: How far away are real targets?
text:
How far away are real targets?


10 356 element–gene pairs tested by CRISPRi in K562; 471 are positive (silencing the element lowers the gene).
Positives: median 26 kb from the TSS, 90% within 207 kb. Negatives: median 387 kb.
Within 10 kb, 60% of tested pairs are positive; at 200–500 kb, 0.9%.


This is the benchmark used throughout the lecture (Gschwind et al. 2023 combined several published screens, details later). Left: the tested pairs; right: the fraction positive by distance bin. Two lessons. First, distance is a very strong predictor: most real links are short-range, tens of kilobases. Second, the tail is real: some positives are hundreds of kilobases away (the K562 set includes MYC enhancers 1.8–2.0 Mb away). Be careful with the right panel: it describes what the screens tested, which was mostly elements within about 1 Mb of each gene; it is not the probability that a random element regulates a random gene. And a negative here means “no effect detected”, which for small effects can be a false negative.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
section: The nearest gene is right about half the time
text:
The nearest gene is right about half the time


Of 425 positive pairs whose target is expressed, the target is the closest expressed gene for 67%; for 33% it is the 2nd, 3rd … or a gene further away.
As a predictor, “nearest gene” has precision 0.41, recall 0.54 (all protein-coding genes): it misses half of the links and half of its calls are wrong.


How to read the bar chart: for each validated pair, rank the expressed genes (TPM ≥ 1 in K562) by the distance of their TSS from the element; the bar shows where the true target falls. Two thirds of the targets are the nearest expressed gene, 12% the second nearest, and one in ten is beyond the fifth. (46 positive targets have TPM < 1 in our K562 RNA-seq and are left out of the chart: a reminder that “expressed” depends on the threshold and the dataset.) As a rule applied to all 10 356 tested pairs, “the element regulates its nearest protein-coding gene” calls 630 links, 256 of them right: precision 0.41. It finds 256 of the 471 true links: recall 0.54. Restricting to expressed genes raises recall to 0.60 but lowers precision to 0.35, because more elements are now assigned to some expressed gene. Note also that an element can regulate more than one gene; nearest-gene allows only one. Keep these two numbers: every better method should beat them.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Four kinds of evidence


They fail in different ways, so they are most useful combined.
Only perturbation tests regulation directly; the others are predictions that perturbations are used to evaluate.


Proximity is free and always available. Correlation uses natural variation between samples: if an element is open in exactly the cell types that express a gene, that is evidence for a link, but correlated programmes produce many false links (next slides). Contact asks whether the element and the promoter touch in 3D: Hi-C and its variants, covered in 3D genome organisation and Hi-C: from reads to contact matrices; contact is necessary in most models of enhancer function, but not sufficient (a contacted element can be inactive). Perturbation (CRISPR interference, deletion) tests the causal question in the cell type of interest but scales to thousands of pairs, not the millions of candidate pairs in a genome. A fifth source, human genetics (a variant in the element changes the gene’s expression across people), is the topic of Epigenomics and genetic variation.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Correlation across samples


Measure accessibility (ATAC) and expression (RNA-seq) in the same set of samples, and correlate each element with each gene nearby.
With two groups of samples, everything specific to one group correlates with everything else specific to that group: co-variation is not regulation.
Test only pairs within a window (e.g. ±500 kb), use many diverse samples, and compare with a null of random pairs.


The idea is the same as an eQTL with cell types or individuals instead of genotypes. It needs no 3D data and uses data the students already have (the Corces atlas, Differential accessibility). The danger is in the figure: gene G3 on another chromosome correlates as well as the true target, because both belong to the cell-type-1 programme. With only two cell types the correlation is just a group difference, and every group-specific element is linked to every group-specific gene. More and more varied samples help: dozens of cell types, hundreds of individuals, or thousands of single cells (next slide). Gene G2 shows the opposite failure: a gene expressed everywhere gives no correlation, even if the element contributes to it. Correlation finds regulation that varies across the samples, nothing else.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Real data: 13 blood cell types


Corces et al. 2016: ATAC and RNA for 13 sorted cell types. Left: a CRISPRi-validated enhancer of GATA1 (14 kb), r = 0.97 across the cell types.
Right: the same element against GMPR, on another chromosome: also r = 0.97. 118 of 15 660 genes on other chromosomes reach r > 0.8.


Each point is a cell type: mean accessibility of the element (log2 CPM over donors) against mean expression of the gene. The GATA1 enhancer is open in MEPs, CMPs and erythroblasts, where GATA1 is expressed, and closed in lymphocytes: a textbook correlation, and a real link (silencing it in K562 lowers GATA1 by 33%). But GMPR, an erythroid-expressed gene on chromosome 6, correlates just as well, and so do about a hundred other genes elsewhere in the genome. With 13 points that fall into an erythroid group and a non-erythroid group, r ≈ 1 is easy to get. This is why correlation-based methods restrict to a cis window, compare with a null and, ideally, use many more samples than cell types.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Correlation needs a null


Positive pairs have higher r (median 0.39) than negative pairs (0.09). But for random peak–gene pairs, 5% have r > 0.59 and 1% r > 0.77.
As a score on the benchmark, correlation alone reaches AUPRC 0.14: three times random, far below distance (0.44).
Single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC in the same cells) gives thousands of samples; tools such as ArchR and Signac use the same test with a background of trans or GC-matched peaks.


The correlation distribution of random pairs is the null: it is wide because 13 cell types give 13 points, and cell-type programmes make many unrelated pairs co-vary. A p-value from the usual correlation test assumes independent samples and would be badly anti-conservative here; an empirical null (random or trans pairs, or permuted cell-type labels) is the honest comparison. Single-cell multiome data (10x Multiome, SHARE-seq) are the modern version: correlation across thousands of cells or “metacells”, with a background of peaks matched for GC and accessibility, as in ArchR’s peak-to-gene links and Signac’s LinkPeaks. More samples narrow the null, but the confounding by cell-type programme remains: it is still correlation. On our benchmark the correlation was computed in normal blood cell types and evaluated in K562 cells, which is part of why it is weak; see the exercise for how it combines with distance.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Contact falls with distance


In Hi-C, contact frequency falls roughly as a power law of genomic distance: C(d) \propto d^{-\gamma} with \gamma \approx 1 (3D genome organisation).
ABC can use measured Hi-C or this curve; the published average is \gamma = 1.02, flat below 5 kb (Hi-C cannot resolve shorter distances), and elements beyond 5 Mb are ignored.


Students meet the distance decay properly in the 3D units, where they compute it from a contact matrix. Here we only need its shape: on a log–log plot it is a straight line with slope about −1, so an element 10 times farther from the promoter has about 10 times fewer contacts. The ABC code (Fulco et al. 2019, Nasser et al. 2021) fits the power law to an average of Hi-C maps from several cell types: contact = exp(5.96 − 1.024 × ln(d + 1)); the scale factor cancels in ABC, only the exponent matters. Below 5 kb the curve is held flat. A power law is cell-type agnostic and has no domains, boundaries or loops: everything specific to the cell type then has to come from the activity term. That is a simplification we return to after the benchmark.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
The activity-by-contact model


An element’s effect on a gene ∝ its activity × its contact with the promoter; ABC is that product as a fraction of all such products near the gene (including the promoter itself).
Predict a link when ABC ≥ about 0.02 (2% of the gene’s regulatory input).


Go through the table: the promoter of G has the largest share, 72% (promoters are active and at distance 0). E1 is moderately active and close: 18%. E2 is the most active element but five times farther: 9%. E3 is weak and far: 0.5%. The denominator makes ABC a relative measure: a moderately active element near a gene with few other elements can score higher than a very active one near a gene with many. That is the model’s main idea: an element competes with all other elements for the gene. Fulco et al. 2019 tested the idea against thousands of CRISPRi perturbations; the published thresholds are 0.016–0.027 depending on the inputs (the 2% we use is in that range). Activity in the original paper is the geometric mean of DNase-seq and H3K27ac read counts; ATAC-seq can replace DNase-seq.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Activity: accessibility and acetylation


Candidate elements: ATAC peaks (summit ± 250 bp, merged) plus all protein-coding promoters: 85 273 in GM12878.
Activity A = \sqrt{\text{ATAC} \times \text{H3K27ac}}: an element needs both to score high. The geometric mean damps the noise of either assay.
Promoters are on or off: 2 337 promoters have no signal at all (genes silent in B cells); active promoters are the most active elements.


The two marks are correlated but far from redundant (Spearman 0.37 in GM12878). An open element without acetylation may be bound by CTCF, a repressor or a poised factor; acetylation without accessibility is mostly the flanks of active elements. The geometric mean penalises elements weak in either. Two technical points that matter in the exercise. First, our ATAC signal is ENCODE’s fold change over the local background; the strongest sites saturate (the vertical edge at the right of the scatter) because the local background rises around them. ABC uses read counts, which do not saturate; with K562 DNase-seq read-depth signal instead of ATAC fold change the benchmark improves (0.52 vs 0.48 AUPRC). Second, the H3K27ac signal is taken in a window 250 bp wider on each side, because the acetylated nucleosomes flank the open site.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
section: Real data: ABC at the PPIF locus in GM12878
text:
Real data: ABC at the PPIF locus in GM12878


ABC for PPIF from the course GM12878 ATAC and H3K27ac, against CRISPRi of 52 elements (Nasser et al. 2021).
All 6 positives (red) have ABC ≥ 0.02; they lie 15–62 kb upstream, inside ZMIZ1. The nearest gene of four of them is ZMIZ1, not PPIF.
Of the 46 negatives, 2 pass the threshold (80 kb, effects of 1%).


This locus matters for disease: Nasser et al. 2021 linked an inflammatory bowel disease risk variant to one of these enhancers and showed that it regulates PPIF, which affects mitochondrial membrane potential in macrophages. Here we compute ABC ourselves from course data (ENCODE GM12878 ATAC and H3K27ac fold-change tracks, the power law), and compare with the CRISPRi effects measured on PPIF in GM12878. Read top to bottom: the H3K27ac track already points to the cluster of strong elements between 79.24 and 79.33 Mb; ABC ranks them; the CRISPRi panel confirms the six closest strong ones and shows no effect for the many elements further away, including active ones in ZMIZ1. Over all 68 GM12878 pairs in the benchmark (9 genes), ABC ≥ 0.02 gives 13 true positives, 3 false positives and 3 false negatives (a MYC enhancer 525 kb away is one of them). A small sample, but a real test on course data.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Ground truth: CRISPRi screens


dCas9-KRAB (CRISPR interference) deposits H3K9me3 at the guide’s target and silences an enhancer without cutting DNA.
A: tile every element near one gene, sort cells by the gene’s RNA (FlowFISH), see which guides are depleted from the high bin.
B: many random guides per cell, single-cell RNA-seq, compare every nearby gene between cells with and without each guide.


Two designs give most of the data. In CRISPRi-FlowFISH (Fulco et al. 2019) one gene is measured by RNA FISH; a library of guides tiles all accessible elements within a few hundred kb; cells are sorted into bins of FISH signal; guides that silence an enhancer of the gene are depleted from the high-expression bin. It tests every element near one gene, but one gene at a time: 3500 pairs for 30 genes. In the single-cell design (Gasperini et al. 2019) each cell receives tens of random guides (a high multiplicity of infection), and single-cell RNA-seq reads out the whole transcriptome plus the guides: 5920 candidate enhancers in 254 974 cells, 664 significant pairs. Every gene within 1 Mb is tested against every element, but with less power per pair. KRAB silences roughly a 1–2 kb region, so a guide can also hit a nearby element; and an effect could in principle be indirect (the element regulates a TF that regulates the gene), which is why benchmarks keep only pairs within a few Mb.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
The benchmark


Combined and re-processed by Gschwind et al. (ENCODE-rE2G): 10 356 pairs in K562, 471 positives = significant decrease (FDR 5%).
Most effects are modest: median 10% decrease; 77% of positives below 20%.
A negative is “no effect detected”: pairs without power for a 25% effect were removed, but small effects are missed.


The table is in the course data (crispr_benchmark_k562.tsv.gz) with element coordinates, gene, effect size, adjusted p-value and power. “Regulated” = significant and negative; 75 significant positive effects (silencing an element raised a gene) are not counted as links: they can be real (a silencer, or competition between promoters) but most models do not predict them. Small effects dominate: a typical enhancer contributes 10–20% of a gene’s expression, because genes have several enhancers that act partly additively. That is one reason the benchmark is hard: an element can regulate a gene by 5% and still be called negative. Imbalance matters too: 4.5% positives means that a useless score already has 4.5% precision, the baseline of the next slide. The paper also provides a held-out set in five other cell types, including the 68 GM12878 pairs of the previous slide.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Precision and recall


Precision: of the links I call, how many are real? Recall: of the real links, how many do I find?
Any score + a threshold gives one point; all thresholds give the PR curve. Its area (AUPRC) summarises it; random = the fraction of positives.
With 4.5% positives, prefer PR to ROC: a ROC curve looks good even when most calls are wrong.


These numbers are for ABC at 0.02 on the K562 benchmark: 602 calls, 294 correct. Precision 0.49, recall 0.62: half of the links we call are real, and we find six in ten real links. For comparison, the nearest gene had 0.41 and 0.54. Why not a ROC curve? Its x axis is the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN); with 9885 negatives, 308 false positives are only 3% of the negatives, so the ROC point looks excellent even though half of the calls are wrong. The precision is what a biologist experiences when following up predictions. The same reasoning appears in the machine-learning units, which also stress comparing with a simple baseline: here the baseline is distance.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
section: Real data: which score finds the links?
text:
Real data: which score finds the links?


Distance alone is a strong baseline (AUPRC 0.44). Activity alone is useless (0.10): strong elements are not more likely to regulate a given gene.
ABC beats distance (0.48 with ATAC, 0.52 with DNase) and beats the nearest gene at both precision and recall.
At high recall all methods converge: 19% of positives overlap no candidate element at all.


Each curve ranks all 10 356 pairs by one score. Distance (1/distance to the TSS) is what most papers implicitly use; it is hard to beat because, as we saw, real links are mostly close. Activity alone ranks pairs by how strong the element is, regardless of the gene: an active element is tested against many genes and regulates at most a few. ABC combines the two and normalises per gene, and gains most at moderate recall: at the left of the plot, its top-ranked pairs are right about 80–90% of the time. Precision at 70% recall: distance 0.32, ABC 0.35. Our ABC is a simplified re-implementation (no quantile normalisation, fold-change tracks, ATAC peaks as candidates); the published ABC and the supervised ENCODE-rE2G do better on this benchmark. The flat end of the ABC curves: 87 positive pairs have ABC = 0 because the tested element overlaps none of our candidate elements (not called as an ATAC peak), so no threshold can find them.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
section: What ABC captures, and what it misses
text:
What ABC captures, and what it misses


ABC falls with distance; activity moves a pair up or down by up to 100-fold at a given distance.
Missed positives (ABC < 0.02) are farther away (median 51 kb vs 22 kb for those found) and often weakly marked.
Not modelled: silencers, insulation by CTCF boundaries, promoter–promoter competition, which TFs bind, and cell-type-specific 3D structure (when the power law is used).


Each point is a tested pair with a non-zero ABC score. Above the dashed line ABC predicts a link. Most positives (red) are close and above the line; the far ones are mostly below it. ABC assumes that an element’s contribution is additive and proportional to its activity and contact: strong evidence from CRISPRi supports this on average, but there are well-known exceptions. Elements with H3K27me3 or CTCF binding rarely behave as ABC predicts (the benchmark annotates these categories, and they are almost never positive). Housekeeping and ubiquitously expressed genes depend less on distal enhancers, so ABC over-predicts links to them; the ABC authors handle this partly by also reporting promoter class. Finally, ABC predicts which elements regulate a gene, not how strongly the gene will respond to a change in the element.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Hi-C or a power law?


A power law knows only distance. Measured contacts know domains: elements in the same TAD contact more, across a CTCF boundary less.
ABC with Hi-C uses the contact of each element with the promoter (at 5 kb resolution, normalised and scaled to the power law).
In the published comparisons, Hi-C improves ABC modestly; distance carries most of the information. Your own Hi-C of the 3D genome units can be plugged in.


The cartoon shows the case where the two disagree: G2 is closer but across a boundary, G1 is farther but in the same domain. Domains and boundaries are covered in Calling compartments, TADs and loops. In practice, ABC with cell-type-specific Hi-C and ABC with an average Hi-C map or the power law perform similarly on the CRISPR benchmarks, with Hi-C ahead mainly at large distances; deep Hi-C (or Micro-C, HiChIP for H3K27ac) is expensive, while a power law is free. Two cautions when using Hi-C directly. A loop called between an enhancer and a promoter is not proof of regulation (many contacts are structural, from CTCF/cohesin), and absence of a called loop is not proof against it (most enhancer–promoter contacts are weaker than loop-calling thresholds). The resolution also matters: at 5 kb, all elements within a bin share the same contact.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Computing ABC in R
el[, activity := sqrt(dnase * h3k27ac)]                         # one row per candidate element
win <- GRanges(genes$chr, IRanges(pmax(genes$tss - 5e6, 1), genes$tss + 5e6))
hw  <- findOverlaps(win, elg)                                   # every element within 5 Mb of each gene
abc <- data.table(gene = genes$gene[queryHits(hw)], e = subjectHits(hw))
abc[, d   := abs(el$mid[e] - genes$tss[queryHits(hw)])]
abc[, C   := (pmax(d, 5000) + 1)^-1.024]                        # power-law contact, flat below 5 kb
abc[, ABC := el$activity[e] * C / sum(el$activity[e] * C), by = gene]
abc[ABC >= 0.02]                                                # predicted enhancer–gene links

Ten lines on top of Genomic intervals: a window per gene, an overlap, a weighted share.
The full pipeline (ABC on GitHub, Snakemake) adds peak calling, read counting, quantile normalisation and Hi-C.


This is the code of the exercise (R5). el is a table of candidate elements with their signals, elg the same as GRanges, genes one row per gene with chromosome and TSS. findOverlaps gives all element–gene pairs within 5 Mb (about 760 000 for the 2113 genes of the benchmark); the rest is arithmetic in data.table, with sum(…) by = gene giving the denominator per gene. On a laptop the whole computation takes seconds. Compared with this, the production ABC pipeline calls peaks with MACS2 on DNase or ATAC, keeps the 150 000 strongest, counts reads (not fold change), quantile-normalises activity to a reference, and optionally reads Hi-C at 5 kb. The idea is unchanged. The output, genome-wide predictions for a cell type, is what you would intersect with your differential peaks or with disease variants.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Beyond ABC


Supervised models learn how to weigh ABC, distance and other features from CRISPRi data (ENCODE-rE2G, Gschwind et al.).
Single-cell multiome brings correlation to thousands of cells; sequence models predict expression from DNA; genetics asks whether a variant in the element changes the gene across people.


ENCODE-rE2G trains a logistic regression on the CRISPRi benchmark with ABC-like features (accessibility, contact, distance, numbers of nearby elements, promoter class) and is the current reference predictor; the risk is overfitting to the few cell types and loci that have been screened, so it is evaluated on held-out cell types (the GM12878 set we used is one of them). Sequence-based deep learning models (Enformer-type networks, see What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works) predict expression or chromatin tracks from DNA and can score the effect of deleting an element in silico; their accuracy at distances beyond tens of kilobases is still limited. Human genetics, the topic of the next unit, provides an independent kind of evidence: an eQTL in the element, colocalised with the GWAS signal. None of these replaces a perturbation, but each is cheaper.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
In your own study


Link differential peaks to genes with an ABC-type score (or contacts), keep the distance in the table, and report the method.
Test concordance with RNA-seq: do genes linked to opening elements go up, more than expected? A promoter peak and its gene agree better than a distal peak and its nearest gene (Differential accessibility: Spearman 0.69 vs 0.42).


This is how the pieces of the course fit together in an applied project with two conditions. The differential accessibility analysis gives the regions; a linking method turns them into candidate genes; RNA-seq from the same samples tests whether the predicted targets move in the expected direction. Concordance is evidence that the links are mostly right, not proof for any single pair. Keep the distance and the score in the result table, so a reader can see that “target of peak 1234” means “ABC 0.03, 180 kb”, not “nearest gene, 5 kb”. For the few pairs that matter (a disease variant, a key regulator), test them: CRISPRi of the element in the relevant cells, or a deletion. Without that, write “predicted target”.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Judging claims

“The enhancer regulates its nearest gene.” Correct about half the time; say “nearest gene” and give the distance.
“Hi-C shows a loop between the enhancer and the promoter, so the enhancer regulates the gene.” Contact is necessary in most models but not sufficient; many loops are structural (CTCF–CTCF).
“Accessibility of the element correlates with expression of the gene across 20 cell types (r = 0.9).” Compare with the correlation of random pairs; check genes on other chromosomes.
“CRISPRi of the element had no effect, so it is not an enhancer of the gene.” Check the power: a 10% effect is easy to miss; the element may be redundant with others (shadow enhancers).
“ABC predicts 40 000 enhancer–gene links.” A prediction with about 50% precision on benchmarks; useful for prioritisation, not proof.


These are the questions to ask when reading papers, and the kind of question the written exam asks (judge the claim). The last two are often forgotten. Negative CRISPRi results depend on power and redundancy: many genes have several enhancers with overlapping function, and silencing one may have little effect while silencing two has a large one (Osterwalder et al. 2018 showed this for limb enhancers in mice). Positive results can also be indirect if the element regulates a transcription factor that then regulates the measured gene; distance filters reduce, but do not remove, this possibility.

title: Linking regulatory elements to genes
text:
Summary







idea

the problem
enhancers act over tens of kb, sometimes Mb; the target is not written in the peak


nearest gene
right for about half of CRISPRi links (precision 0.41, recall 0.54 in K562)


correlation

contact
Hi-C contact ∝ distance^−1 (power law); domains and boundaries modify it


ABC
activity (√(ATAC or DNase × H3K27ac)) × contact, as a share of all elements of the gene; link if ≥ ~0.02


ground truth
CRISPRi screens (FlowFISH, single-cell); 471 of 10 356 K562 pairs positive, effects mostly 5–20%


evaluation

this benchmark
AUPRC: activity 0.10, correlation 0.14, distance 0.44, ABC 0.48–0.52




Students should leave able to: compute an ABC score by hand for a small locus; compute precision and recall from a confusion matrix and read a PR curve; explain why correlation across a handful of cell types links unrelated genes; and judge a claim that an enhancer regulates a gene. Next: Epigenomics and genetic variation, where the elements carry disease variants and these links become the bridge from a GWAS signal to a gene.

text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
About this lecture
Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing reads methylation from converted, short DNA fragments. Long-read sequencers read the native molecule, so the modification itself is part of the signal, on reads of 10 to 100 kb.

How a nanopore and a PacBio instrument see 5mC, 5hmC and 6mA without conversion.
The modBAM: MM and ML tags, call probabilities, and modkit pileup to a bedMethyl table.
Agreement with WGBS on the same cell line.
Haplotype-resolved methylation: phasing reads, imprinted loci, X inactivation.
Chromatin accessibility on single molecules: Fiber-seq and its nanopore relatives.
Running example: HG001 = GM12878 (nanopore, ~80×) and an EcoGII-treated nanopore run of HG002.


This lecture builds on two others: DNA methylation biology (imprinting, X inactivation, 5mC and 5hmC) and Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing (what a bedMethyl file is, how WGBS measures methylation). Here the question is what changes when the instrument reads the original DNA strand. Three things change. First, there is no conversion, so 5mC and 5hmC can be told apart and the reference genome stays a four-letter genome. Second, reads are long, so one read carries many CpGs and usually several SNPs, which lets us assign each read to a parental chromosome. Third, any other modification on the same molecule is read at the same time, including adenine methylation that we add on purpose to mark accessible chromatin. The data are real: Oxford Nanopore’s open data for HG001, which is the Genome in a Bottle name for NA12878, the woman whose cells are the GM12878 cell line used throughout this course, and a 2025 nanopore chromatin-accessibility release on HG002.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: Short converted reads vs long native molecules
text:
Short converted reads vs long native molecules


WGBS and EM-seq: reads of 150 bp, converted, aligned to a three-letter genome; 5mC and 5hmC both read as C.
Long reads: tens of kilobases of native DNA; every CpG on the molecule, its SNP alleles and other modifications in one record.


Walk through panel A: a region with a heterozygous SNP and an allele-specific methylated stretch. With 150-bp reads only the reads that happen to overlap the SNP can be assigned to an allele, and those reads usually do not reach the CpGs we care about. In panel B every read spans both the SNP and the CpGs, so every methylation call is labelled with a haplotype. This is the main scientific advantage; the practical advantages are no bisulfite damage (bisulfite fragments DNA heavily), no conversion-related biases, and the ability to map into repeats that short reads cannot place. The costs: more DNA input (micrograms of high-molecular-weight DNA), higher cost per genome than arrays, and calls that come from a neural network rather than from a chemical conversion we can count directly.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: Two ways to see a modification without conversion
text:
Two ways to see a modification without conversion


Nanopore: the ionic current through the pore depends on the few bases inside it; a methyl group changes it slightly. A neural network (dorado) turns the signal into bases and, for each candidate base, modification probabilities.
PacBio HiFi: the polymerase pauses longer at a modified template base (inter-pulse duration). 6mA gives a strong signal; 5mC at CpG is learned from the kinetics around it.


Nanopore: a single strand of DNA is pulled through a protein pore by a motor protein at about 400 bases per second; the current is sampled thousands of times per second. Because several bases sit in the constriction at once, the current reflects a k-mer, and a 5mC in that k-mer shifts the level by a few picoamperes. Modern basecallers (dorado) are neural networks that output bases plus modification calls in one pass; separate models exist for 5mC and 5hmC in CpG context, 5mC in all contexts, 6mA in all contexts and 4mC (bacteria). PacBio: the polymerase copies a circular molecule many times; each incorporated base gives a fluorescent pulse. The time between pulses (IPD) and the pulse width depend on the template base and its modifications. 6mA slows the polymerase a lot, which is why the original Fiber-seq used PacBio. 5mC is subtle and is called by a model (jasmine) over a window of kinetics. Both platforms report the result in the same way, which is the next topic.

Every call is a probability per base per read, from a model trained on control DNA (unmethylated PCR products, fully methylated by M.SssI, synthetic oligos).
Model and basecaller versions matter: always report them, and compare samples called with the same model.


The table is a snapshot (2025–2026); models are added frequently. Two consequences for analysis. First, a modification call is only as good as the model’s training data: models are trained on DNA of known state, for example PCR-amplified DNA (all unmethylated) and DNA treated with the CpG methyltransferase M.SssI (all CpGs methylated), so accuracy is best for contexts and modification densities that resemble the training data. Second, because calls come from a model, a new basecaller version can shift methylation levels by a few percent. Comparing a patient called with model v4 to controls called with v5 is like comparing arrays from two different platforms without normalisation. The HG001 data in this lecture were called in 2023 with a 5mCG_5hmCG model; the EcoGII data in 2025 with dorado 1.0 and the 5mCG_5hmCG and 6mA models (both recorded in the BAM header @PG and @RG lines).

10 462 reads, median length 4.6 kb (mean 11 kb) in the slices; about 80× coverage. The reads were cut out of the genome-wide CRAMs by indexed remote access (samtools view -M -L regions.bed https://...cram).


HG001 is the Genome in a Bottle reference sample made from a large batch of GM12878 cells, so these nanopore data come from the same cell line as the ENCODE data used elsewhere in the course. The 1000 Genomes high-coverage release includes NA12878’s parents (NA12891, the father, and NA12892, the mother), which lets us label haplotypes as paternal and maternal: rare and valuable, because most individuals do not have parents sequenced. The read lengths in a regional slice underestimate the run’s read lengths, because long reads that start outside the slice are kept but short reads are more numerous. Remote access: CRAM and BAM files with an index can be queried over https without downloading the whole file, which is how a 60-GB CRAM becomes a 120-MB teaching file. The HG002 chromatin data are a different person (HG002 is a man, NA24385, also from a lymphoblastoid cell line), so we compare with GM12878 ATAC peaks only as a rough guide.

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: The modBAM: MM and ML tags
text:
The modBAM: MM and ML tags


MM lists which bases carry calls (as skip counts); ML gives one probability per call, scaled to 0–255.
Calls refer to the read sequence as sequenced (SEQ is reverse-complemented for reverse-strand alignments: tools handle this).


The SAM tags specification defines MM and ML so that modification calls travel with the read through alignment, sorting and merging. Decode the example: C+m? says the calls are for C, on the top strand of the read, modification code m (5mC). The question mark means that Cs without a call are unknown, not unmethylated: the model only calls Cs in a CpG context, so the C in CA is simply skipped. The numbers 0,1,0 are skip counts over the Cs of the read: call the first C, skip one and call the third, skip none and call the fourth. ML gives one byte per call: 242/256 is about 0.95, so the first CpG is confidently methylated, the second (13) confidently unmethylated, and the third (128) is a coin flip, which modkit will filter. Real nanopore reads carry two lists, C+h? for 5hmC and C+m? for 5mC, with one ML value per call for each; the probability of plain C is what is left over. You will decode one by hand in the exercise; in practice nobody parses these strings, modkit and pysam do.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Probabilities, and the threshold


Most calls are confident (probability > 0.95). modkit estimates a threshold so that the least confident 10% of calls are discarded: 0.865 for these reads.
A methylation level is then a count: methylated calls / valid calls, exactly like C/(C+T) in WGBS.


Every CpG call has a probability for each state (C, 5mC, 5hmC); the call is the most likely state and its probability is the confidence. modkit samples reads, takes the 10th percentile of the confidence values, and drops calls below it as “fail”. Here that threshold is 0.865 for cytosines (computed from all 1.36 million calls in the region BAM; on a whole genome modkit samples a subset). Why not just average the probabilities? You could (some tools do), but thresholded counts behave like the binomial counts of bisulfite data and can be fed into the same statistics (Differential methylation). Dropping 10% of calls costs a little coverage but removes the calls that are most likely wrong, often at the read ends, in homopolymers or near other modifications. In the exercise you will compute a methylation level from a handful of read calls with a threshold by hand.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

text:
From reads to a bedMethyl table

modkit pileup $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam hg001_cpg.bed --ref hg38_lr.fa \
  --cpg --modified-bases 5mC 5hmC --combine-strands --sampling-frac 1 -t 4
grep -w m hg001_cpg.bed | head -2

This is the long-read counterpart of the Bismark methylation extractor from Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing. –cpg restricts to CpG sites in the reference, –combine-strands adds the two Cs of a CpG together (the methylation of the two strands is almost always the same, and it doubles the coverage), –sampling-frac 1 makes the threshold estimate use every read so that the result is reproducible. The output is bedMethyl: one row per CpG and modification code. For the m row, percent modified = N modified / N valid. Note that the 5hmC calls are counted in “N other” for the m row and vice versa, and that the denominator includes them: 5mC% + 5hmC% + C% = 100%. The first example line: 45 valid calls, 6 methylated, 39 unmethylated, no 5hmC, so 13.33%; 3 more calls failed the threshold and are not in the denominator. The second CpG, 27 bp away, is 94% methylated: neighbouring CpGs can differ, and both are at the edge of a region. On a laptop this step takes under a minute for the course data. The first line prepares an uncompressed reference for the four chromosomes we need: modkit and WhatsHap read random positions of the reference many times, and that is much faster from an uncompressed file.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Nanopore and WGBS agree


9 779 CpGs with ≥ 10 calls in nanopore and in each of two ENCODE WGBS replicates: nanopore vs pooled WGBS r = 0.92 (median absolute difference 0.05).
The two WGBS replicates agree less with each other (r = 0.80) than nanopore agrees with them. Along the chromosome the profiles are almost identical.


Left: per-CpG comparison of the nanopore level (5mC + 5hmC, because bisulfite cannot separate them) with ENCODE WGBS of GM12878 (two replicates pooled) in our regions. Most CpGs sit in the corners: fully methylated or unmethylated in both. Middle: the two WGBS replicates against each other on the same CpGs: more scatter, including CpGs that read 0 in one replicate and 1 in the other. Nanopore agrees with replicate 2 at r = 0.94 and with replicate 1 at r = 0.82: replicate 1 is the noisier library. The lesson is not that one technology is “right”: a correlation between two assays is limited by the noisier of the two, and a replicate-to-replicate comparison tells you what agreement to expect. Right: along 70 kb of chr21 around GART, SON and DONSON, both show the same unmethylated CpG islands at the promoters. Remember also that the samples are different DNA preparations of the same cell line, made years apart; a cell line that keeps dividing can change its methylation.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
5mC and 5hmC: what bisulfite cannot separate

In our HG001 slices: mean 5mC 55%, mean 5hmC 0.8% of CpG calls. Blood cells and cell lines have little 5hmC; brain has 10–20 times more.
Bisulfite (and EM-seq) report 5mC + 5hmC as “methylated”. TAB-seq, oxBS or 5hmC-specific enzymatic methods are needed to split them; the nanopore model does it in the same run.
Caution: at 1% the 5hmC calls are close to the false-positive rate of the model. Small 5hmC differences between samples need validation.


5hmC is the first oxidation product of TET enzymes (DNA methylation biology). In most cell types it is a small fraction of the modified cytosines; in neurons it can be 20–40% of the modified CpGs in gene bodies. A nanopore 5hmC call is a model prediction between three classes; for a class that is rare, even a small error rate produces many false calls relative to the true ones, the same base-rate problem as a screening test for a rare disease. The practical rule: 5hmC levels from nanopore are useful in tissues where 5hmC is abundant, and should be interpreted with care where it is not. For comparison with WGBS, always add 5mC and 5hmC (as in the previous slide).
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Haplotypes: which copy is methylated?


A level of 0.5 can mean half of the cells, or one of the two alleles in every cell. Only reads assigned to haplotypes tell them apart.
With the parents’ genotypes (a trio) the haplotypes get parental labels; without them they are just 1 and 2.


Step 1, Mendelian logic: at s1 the father is C/C and the child C/T, so the child’s T came from the mother. At s2 the mother is A/A, so the child’s G is paternal. At s3 both parents are heterozygous and the child is too: we cannot tell which allele came from whom. Step 2: a read that carries C at s1 and G at s2 is on the paternal chromosome. WhatsHap does this assignment for every read and writes the tag HP:i:1 or HP:i:2. Step 3: count calls per haplotype. In the toy example the paternal copy is fully methylated and the maternal copy unmethylated: the pattern of an imprinting control region. In most studies there are no parents: then SNPs are phased from the long reads themselves (read-based phasing, WhatsHap or LongPhase); haplotypes are consistent within a phase block (often hundreds of kilobases) but carry no parental label and may flip between blocks.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Phasing in practice
# child heterozygous, phase by transmission -> VCF with GT = paternal|maternal (awk in the exercise)
bcftools query -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT[\t%GT]\n' $D/hg001_trio_regions.vcf.gz | awk '...' > trio_phased.vcf
bgzip trio_phased.vcf && tabix -p vcf trio_phased.vcf.gz
whatshap haplotag --ignore-read-groups --reference hg38_lr.fa \
  --output-haplotag-list haplotags.tsv -o hg001_tagged.bam trio_phased.vcf.gz $D/hg001_ont_regions.bam
samtools index hg001_tagged.bam
modkit pileup hg001_tagged.bam phased/ --phased --ref hg38_lr.fa \
  --cpg --modified-bases 5mC 5hmC --combine-strands --sampling-frac 1 -t 4

562 heterozygous SNPs informative in the trio; 5 575 of 10 462 reads (53%) carry at least one and get a tag: 2 880 paternal, 2 695 maternal.
phased/hp1.bedmethyl and phased/hp2.bedmethyl: one bedMethyl per haplotype.


The awk program (written out in the exercise) keeps the child’s heterozygous SNPs and writes the paternal allele first in the genotype (for example 1|0 when the father passed on the ALT allele). WhatsHap haplotag reads that VCF and assigns each read to haplotype 1 (here: the first allele = paternal) or 2, using the alleles the read carries at those SNPs; reads that cover no informative SNP stay untagged. Half the reads are tagged here: the SNPs are not dense enough near some loci for reads of a few kb (the median read in our slice is 4.6 kb). Longer reads tag more. modkit pileup –phased then writes three bedMethyl files: hp1, hp2 and combined. In a production pipeline (ONT wf-human-variation) the SNPs come from the same reads (Clair3), are phased by WhatsHap or LongPhase, and the pileup is done per haplotype automatically.

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: Single molecules at the H19 imprinting control region
text:
Single molecules at the H19 imprinting control region


Paternal reads: 67% of CpG calls methylated; maternal reads: 8%, and across the 5-kb ICR 0.72 vs 0.01. The methylated copy is the paternal one, as the textbook says.
Outside the ICR (left, over the H19 gene) both alleles are partly methylated.


Each row is one nanopore read assigned to a parent; each circle a CpG call (filled = 5mC). The shaded region is the H19/IGF2 imprinting control region (ICR, also called IC1), about 2–7 kb upstream of the H19 transcription start. On the paternal allele the ICR is methylated, CTCF cannot bind, and the downstream enhancers reach IGF2 (expressed from the paternal allele); on the maternal allele the ICR is unmethylated, CTCF binds and insulates IGF2, and H19 is expressed. Recap from DNA methylation biology. The maternal reads are not completely unmethylated: a few isolated filled circles are either real (the ICR edges) or false-positive calls. Note that only 15 reads are shown: few reads reach both the ICR and an informative SNP (the nearest is 6 kb away), a real limitation of phasing in SNP-poor regions.

The three ICRs behave exactly as expected, and in both directions: H19 is methylated on the paternal copy, KvDMR and the Prader–Willi imprinting centre on the maternal copy. Look also at the gene bodies: downstream of the SNRPN promoter the paternal allele (the expressed one) is highly methylated over the gene body while the maternal allele is not. Gene-body methylation follows transcription (DNMT3B is recruited by H3K36me3), so the silent maternal copy has a methylation-free promoter-to-body pattern turned inside out. This is the same assay that clinical labs now use to diagnose imprinting disorders (Prader–Willi, Angelman, Beckwith–Wiedemann, Silver–Russell) and to see the parent of origin of a deletion in one run.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Three reasons for allele-specific methylation


Phasing finds allele-specific methylation (ASM); the cause must be inferred: parent of origin, random X choice, or the DNA sequence.
Test: does the methylated allele follow the parent (imprinting) or the SNP allele across people (meQTL)?


Panel A: imprinting. In every person, the paternal (or maternal) copy is methylated, whatever the SNP alleles on it. Panel B: X inactivation. Each cell of the early female embryo chooses one X; its descendants keep the choice. In a tissue, half the cells silenced each X, so each haplotype looks half methylated; in a clonal population such as a cell line, all cells made the same choice and the inactive X is the same haplotype everywhere. Panel C: sequence-dependent ASM. A SNP changes a TF binding site or removes the CpG itself; the methylated allele is the one carrying a particular base, regardless of which parent passed it on. Sequence-dependent ASM is the most common type genome-wide and is the molecular basis of methylation QTLs (meQTLs, Epigenomics and genetic variation). With one person you cannot tell A from C; with trios or many people you can.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: X inactivation, on one cell line’s two X chromosomes
text:
X inactivation, on one cell line’s two X chromosomes


62% of 399 chrX promoter CpG islands are methylated on one haplotype only (difference > 0.5), against 1.5% of 330 on chr20; the chr20 exceptions include the imprinted GNAS and MCTS2.
37 chrX islands are unmethylated on both: KDM5C, KDM6A, DDX3X, EIF2S3, ZFX, USP9X, STS, the PAR1 genes, all known to escape X inactivation.


ONT’s own haplotype-resolved pileups of HG001 (another flow cell, 2025), one point per promoter CpG island, averaged over its CpGs. On chr20 nearly all islands lie on the diagonal near zero: promoter CpG islands are unmethylated on both alleles. On chrX most islands are off the diagonal: one copy unmethylated (the active X) and one methylated (the inactive X). That GM12878 shows this so clearly means most of its cells inactivated the same X, as expected for a clonal (or nearly clonal) cell line (Three reasons, panel B). The points at the origin of the chrX panel are the escape genes; the pseudoautosomal genes (SHOX, CD99, SLC25A6, ASMTL…) have a Y-linked copy in males and are not subject to X inactivation, and genes like KDM5C, KDM6A and DDX3X are the classic escapees with Y homologues. A cluster near the diagonal at high methylation are islands methylated on both X chromosomes, not promoters of expressed genes in lymphoblasts. Caveat: here the haplotypes come from read-based phasing within phase blocks, so we cannot say whether the paternal or the maternal X is inactive.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: Accessibility on the same molecules: Fiber-seq
text:
Accessibility on the same molecules: Fiber-seq


Treat nuclei with a non-specific adenine methyltransferase (Hia5, EcoGII): it methylates A wherever the DNA is reachable. Then sequence the native DNA.
One read = one chromatin fibre: nucleosome footprints (~147 bp without m6A), linkers, and nucleosome-free regulatory elements, plus the read’s own 5mC and SNP alleles.


Fiber-seq (Stergachis et al. 2020, PacBio) and its relatives (SAMOSA with EcoGII on PacBio, NanoNOMe with a GpC methyltransferase on nanopore, SMAC-seq with several enzymes on nanopore, and the ONT EcoGII protocol used here) all write accessibility into the DNA as a modification that mammalian cells do not make themselves. Human DNA has essentially no 6mA of its own, so (apart from false-positive calls) every m6A is a mark left by the enzyme. Compare with ATAC-seq (ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder): ATAC counts cuts in a population of cells; Fiber-seq shows on each molecule whether this element was open, how its neighbouring nucleosomes were placed, and whether the CpGs of the same molecule were methylated. That allows questions ATAC cannot answer: are two enhancers open on the same molecule? Is the open copy the unmethylated allele?
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Real fibres at a promoter


At the ATP5PO promoter (an LCL ATAC peak), 12.9% of adenines are m6A in the nucleosome-free region, against 0.5% in the flanks; the CpG island on the same reads is unmethylated (9.5% vs 82%).
Fibres differ: some are open over the whole element, some only partly, a few not at all.


30 reads that span the 6-kb window, one per row. Red: adenines called m6A (EcoGII marks); black: CpGs called 5mC. Two things are visible on the same molecules. The promoter of ATP5PO, a mitochondrial ATP synthase subunit expressed in every cell, is nucleosome-free and accessible (dense red), and its CpG island has no methylation (no black). Away from the promoter, CpGs are methylated and m6A is sparse: here the DNA is wrapped in nucleosomes. The green band is the GM12878 ATAC peak; HG002 is a different person but also a lymphoblastoid cell line, and housekeeping promoters are open in both. Note the efficiency: even in the open region only about one adenine in eight is marked, because the enzyme is used at a limited dose and each A is a chance event. Footprint calling therefore uses the spacing of marks, not individual bases.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
The signal in aggregate


Over 116 ATAC summits on chr21 (33–34 Mb): m6A peaks at the summit (~8.5% of A), on a plateau of ~3% that extends ±400 bp.
Treated: 4.8% in peaks vs 0.37% outside (13-fold). Untreated control: 0.04% and 0.02%, the false-positive background of the 6mA model.


Left: the fraction of adenines called m6A as a function of distance to GM12878 ATAC summits, in the treated sample (red) and the untreated native DNA of the same individual (grey). Right: totals inside and outside peaks. Three lessons. First, the treated sample reproduces the accessibility landscape of ATAC-seq from a completely different chemistry. Second, the background outside peaks (0.37%) is ten times higher than in untreated DNA: linker DNA between nucleosomes is accessible too, so closed chromatin is not unmarked, only sparsely marked. Third, the untreated control is essential: 0.02–0.04% of adenines are called m6A in DNA that never saw the enzyme, which is the model’s false-positive rate. Claims of naturally occurring 6mA in mammalian genomes have been made with methods that could not exclude such artefacts, bacterial contamination or RNA; a control like this is the minimum.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: From m6A marks to footprints and elements
text:
From m6A marks to footprints and elements

Nucleosomes: stretches of ~100–200 bp without m6A between marked linkers. Methyltransferase-sensitive patches (MSPs): longer marked stretches, i.e. nucleosome-free regions.
Accessible regulatory elements per fibre (e.g. FIREs in the fibertools pipeline), then aggregated into peaks, like ATAC peaks but with a per-molecule fraction: “this element is open on 62% of fibres”.
TF footprints: short protected stretches inside an open element (CTCF, ~40 bp).
Tools: fibertools (PacBio and nanopore), modkit open-chromatin predict (nanopore EcoGII), NanoNOMe/nanopolish for GpC data.


The raw calls are sparse and noisy, so footprinting uses a hidden Markov model or a classifier over the pattern of marks along each read: long unmarked runs are nucleosomes, runs with dense marks are open. This is the long-read version of the nucleosome ladder from MNase-seq and ATAC fragment sizes (ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder), but per molecule. Two caveats: the methyltransferases are not perfectly uniform (both EcoGII and Hia5 methylate A in almost any sequence context, but with some preferences), and AT-rich DNA has more targets, so raw m6A density must be normalised by the number of As. And a “closed” fibre at a peak can be a molecule from a cell where the element is closed, or a molecule where the enzyme simply did not act: the per-fibre fraction is a lower bound.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Caveats and pitfalls

Models: accuracy depends on context and on the training data; compare samples called with the same basecaller and model version.
Thresholds: modkit drops the least confident 10% of calls; low-confidence regions (homopolymers, read ends) lose more coverage.
Strand and context: CpG models do not call CpH methylation; --combine-strands assumes symmetric CpG methylation (not true for hemimethylated DNA).
Mapping: long reads map into repeats short reads cannot, but MAPQ still matters; supplementary and secondary alignments are skipped by default.
Phasing: only reads with informative SNPs get a haplotype; switch errors between phase blocks mix haplotypes; parental labels need a trio or a known ICR.
Coverage: 30× genome ≈ 15× per haplotype: allele-specific calls are noisy at single CpGs, average over regions.


These are the questions to ask of any long-read methylation paper. The model point is the most common source of artefacts in published comparisons: a disease cohort sequenced in 2022 and controls sequenced in 2024 with a different basecaller is a batch effect by design. Hemimethylation: right after replication the new strand is unmethylated until DNMT1 catches up; strand-specific calling (without –combine-strands) can show this. Phasing switch errors: if the haplotype assignment flips halfway along a region, each “haplotype” becomes a mixture and allele-specific differences shrink. For per-haplotype analysis at 30× you have about 15 reads per allele, so binomial noise at a single CpG is large (standard deviation 0.13 at a level of 0.5); region-level averages or a DMR caller (modkit dmr, DSS on per-haplotype counts, Differential methylation) are the way to go.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
The workflow, end to end


Basecalling with modification models needs the raw signal and a GPU; most users start from the modBAM.
Production pipelines run every box: ONT wf-human-variation, PacBio HiFi-human-WGS.


The raw nanopore signal (POD5) of a 30× human genome is on the order of a terabyte, and basecalling with the most accurate models takes hours to days on GPUs. That is why public data and most core facilities hand out modBAMs: basecalled, aligned reads with MM/ML tags. From there the steps are the ones in the exercise: modkit pileup for aggregate levels, modkit extract for per-read calls, SNP calling and phasing for haplotypes, and pileup per haplotype. The Nextflow workflow wf-human-variation does it all (and calls structural variants, copy number and repeat expansions from the same reads); the bedMethyl files per haplotype we used for the chrX analysis come from that workflow. modkit dmr compares two samples or two haplotypes; for replicated designs, the beta-binomial models of Differential methylation (DSS, methylKit) take modkit counts as input.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
section: Where long reads change the answer
text:
Where long reads change the answer

Repeats and centromeres: the first complete human genome (T2T-CHM13) came with a complete methylome, including centromeric satellites invisible to short reads (Gershman et al. 2022).
Imprinting disorders: parent-of-origin methylation and the variant in one test.
X inactivation, escape and erosion in female cells and cell lines.
Allele-specific methylation and meQTLs without population arrays.
Single-molecule co-occurrence: is the open enhancer on the unmethylated copy? Are two elements open together?
Cancer: haplotype-specific methylation at amplified or deleted alleles; structural variants and their methylation from the same reads.


A short tour of where the long-read view is not just a cheaper or more convenient WGBS but answers questions short reads cannot. Gershman et al. (2022) mapped methylation across the centromeres of CHM13, which consist of megabases of near-identical alpha-satellite repeats, and found a hypomethylated “centromere dip region” that marks where the kinetochore assembles. Clinical genetics is moving towards a single long-read test that reports SNVs, structural variants, repeat expansions and imprinting methylation together. For the rest of this course: the chromatin accessibility from Fiber-seq connects to ATAC-seq and Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting; the per-haplotype methylation to Epigenomics and genetic variation; cfDNA methylation from nanopore to Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers.
crumbs: Methylation and chromatin from long reads

title: Methylation and chromatin from long reads
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




detection
nanopore: current through a pore; PacBio: polymerase kinetics; no conversion


what is called
5mC and 5hmC at CpG, 6mA, 4mC; probabilities per base per read from a model


modBAM
MM: which bases (skip counts); ML: probability × 256; ? vs . for skipped bases


pileup
modkit drops the least confident 10%; level = modified / valid calls (bedMethyl)


vs WGBS
r = 0.92 per CpG (WGBS rep vs rep: 0.80); compare 5mC + 5hmC with bisulfite


phasing
het SNPs on reads → HP tags (WhatsHap); trio gives parental labels


imprinting
H19 ICR paternal 0.72 / maternal 0.01; KvDMR and PWS-IC maternal


X inactivation
62% of chrX promoter CGIs methylated on one haplotype vs 1.5% on chr20; escapees on neither


Fiber-seq
m6A from an added methyltransferase marks accessible DNA on each fibre; untreated control essential




Students should leave able to: explain how each platform detects a modification without bisulfite; decode an MM/ML pair by hand; compute a methylation level from thresholded read calls; phase a SNP by Mendelian logic and say what a haplotag is; read a single-molecule plot and a per-haplotype methylation profile; distinguish imprinting, X inactivation and sequence-dependent ASM; and say why Fiber-seq needs an untreated control. In the exercise you run all of this on the course data: modkit pileup, trio phasing, haplotagging, per-haplotype pileups, the chrX analysis and the m6A analysis.

text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Flusberg et al. 2010, Nat Methods. Direct detection of DNA methylation during single-molecule, real-time sequencing. Polymerase kinetics reveal modified bases.
Simpson et al. 2017, Nat Methods. Detecting DNA cytosine methylation using nanopore sequencing. The first 5mC calls from nanopore current.

title: Exercise: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)

After this exercise you will be able to:

title: Exercise: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Background
Signals. For each CpG the array gives a methylated signal \(M\) and an unmethylated signal \(U\). Infinium I: \(M\) and \(U\) are the intensities of two bead types, read in the same colour (red or green, set by the base after the CpG). Infinium II: one bead; \(M\) is its green and \(U\) its red intensity.
\[ \beta = \frac{M}{M + U + 100}, \qquad M\text{-value} = \log_2\frac{M + 1}{U + 1} \approx \log_2 \frac{\beta}{1 - \beta}, \qquad \beta = \frac{2^{M\text{-value}}}{1 + 2^{M\text{-value}}}. \]
Detection p-value (minfi): the probability that background alone gives a total signal \(M + U\) at least as large as observed; background is modelled as a normal distribution with the mean and SD of the ~600 negative control probes (for the probe’s colour channel). Probes with \(p > 0.01\) “fail”.
Mixtures. A bulk sample’s β at a CpG is the fraction-weighted average of the cell types’ β: \(\beta = \sum_k w_k \beta_k\). Reference-based deconvolution (Houseman) estimates \(w\) from a reference of sorted cells at marker CpGs.
EWAS. A linear model per CpG on M-values with the same design for all CpGs (limma). Covariates go into the design formula, as in RNA-seq. Because fractions sum to about 1, one cell type is left out.
Genomic inflation. Convert each p-value to a 1-df chi-square statistic, \(\chi^2 = F^{-1}_{\chi^2_1}(1 - p)\), and divide the median by its expected value under the null, 0.455: \(\lambda = \text{median}(\chi^2)/0.455\). λ ≈ 1: most CpGs behave as null; λ ≫ 1: confounding, batch, or a very widespread true effect.

title: Exercise: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
Data
From data/prepare-meth2.sh arrays:
mkdir -p ~/epi/arrays && cd ~/epi/arrays
D=/path/to/course/data                     # where the course data are



file
what




gse42861_samples.tsv

gse42861_idat/

Shortcuts, said plainly. We use the 151 samples on the 14 BeadChips that hold both patients and controls (the full study has 689); the RA analysis therefore has less power than the original. The 450k is an older array than EPIC, with the same chemistry; EPIC v2 needs newer manifests (sesame handles them).
You need minfi, IlluminaHumanMethylation450kmanifest, IlluminaHumanMethylation450kanno.ilmn12.hg19, FlowSorted.Blood.450k, limma, data.table and ggplot2 (see Install the software you need). The R part takes about 25 minutes and needs about 10 GB of memory (run it on the cluster in an interactive job or with Rscript in an sbatch script). If preprocessFunnorm stops with return code from pthread_create() is 22, reinstall preprocessCore without threading: BiocManager::install("preprocessCore", configure.args = "--disable-threading", force = TRUE).

title: Exercise: Methylation arrays (Illumina EPIC)
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. β and M. (a) A probe has M = 3 000 and U = 1 000. Compute β and the M-value. (b) Another has M = 200, U = 5 000. (c) Convert β = 0.9 to an M-value, and an M-value of −2 to β. (d) Two groups differ by Δβ = 0.05 at two CpGs: from 0.50 to 0.55, and from 0.90 to 0.95. Compute the difference in M-values in each case. Why does this matter for a linear model?
B2. Two probe designs. (a) A Type II probe has green intensity 4 200 and red intensity 900. What is β? (b) A Type I probe designed for the red channel has red intensities 3 000 (M bead) and 800 (U bead), and green intensities 260 (M bead) and 240 (U bead). What is β, and what are the green values useful for? (c) Why are Type I and Type II β distributions different, and what does SWAN or BMIQ do about it?
B3. Detection p-value. In one array the negative control probes have mean 600 and SD 150 (both channels together). (a) A probe has M = 500 and U = 400. Using a normal approximation, what is its detection p-value (one-sided)? Does it fail at 0.01? (b) Another probe has M = 100, U = 2 900: p-value? (c) Why should a probe that fails in many samples be removed from all of them?
B4. A CpG that only measures cell composition. At a CpG, β = 0.85 in granulocytes and 0.15 in lymphocytes (all lymphocytes alike), in every person; no other cell types.

Controls have 58% granulocytes, patients 70%. Compute the expected β in each group and the difference.
The patients’ β is also 0.03 higher at a second CpG where granulocytes and lymphocytes are both 0.60. Which of the two differences can be explained by composition?
Write the design formula of an EWAS that adjusts for granulocytes, CD4 and CD8 T cells, NK cells, B cells and monocytes (six estimated fractions that sum to ~1). Why leave one out?

B5. Genomic inflation. (a) If the median p-value across 400 000 CpGs is 0.5, what is λ? (b) If it is 0.05? (The 95th percentile of \(\chi^2_1\) is 3.84.) (c) Look at the QQ plots of the lecture:

What changes between the second and the third panel, and why does adding five covariates remove 97% of the hits?
B6. Batch and design. In the full GSE42861 study, 36 of the 72 BeadChips (12 positions each) hold only patients or only controls.

Why is this a problem that statistics cannot fix afterwards?
You plan a new study of 96 patients and 96 controls on EPIC arrays (8 positions per BeadChip). How would you assign samples to chips and positions?

B7. A SNP in the probe. At a CpG, β across 300 people clusters at 0.02, 0.48 and 0.93, with 180, 100 and 20 people.

What is the most likely explanation? (b) Estimate the allele frequency of the “unmethylated” allele (Hardy–Weinberg). (c) Why would this CpG show up as associated with ancestry, and possibly with disease?

B8. Judge the claims.

“Patients with RA have 102 938 differentially methylated CpGs in blood (FDR 5%).”
“After adjusting for cell composition, methylation at CpG X is lower in RA; therefore hypomethylation at X causes RA.”
“Smokers have lower methylation at AHRR cg05575921; this CpG can be used to verify self-reported smoking.”

text:
In R

R1 — Read the arrays
