title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
On the command line
export PATH=/path/to/Bismark:$PATH      # only if Bismark is not installed with conda

C1 — Look at the reads
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_reads.fastq.gz | head -8
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_reads.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | wc -l
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_reads.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 { print length($0) }' | sort -n | uniq -c
zcat $D/gm12878_wgbs_reads.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | head -100000 | fold -w1 | sort | uniq -c
zcat $D/hg38_chr21.fa.gz | grep -v '>' | tr 'acgtn' 'ACGTN' | tr -d 'N\n' | fold -w1 | sort | uniq -c

How many reads, and how long? (b) Compare the base composition of the reads with that of chr21. Which strands do these reads come from? (The last command takes about a minute.)



C2 — Trim
fastp -i $D/gm12878_wgbs_reads.fastq.gz -o trimmed.fastq.gz \
  --adapter_sequence AGATCGGAAGAGC --length_required 30 -w 4 -j fastp.json -h fastp.html
How many reads pass, how many fail on quality, and in how many was an adapter trimmed? Why do we give the adapter sequence instead of relying on fastp’s auto-detection for single-end reads?


C3 — Bisulfite index
mkdir -p genome && zcat $D/hg38_chr21.fa.gz > genome/chr21.fa
bismark_genome_preparation --parallel 4 genome > genome_prep.log 2>&1
ls genome/Bisulfite_Genome/*
head -c 300 genome/Bisulfite_Genome/CT_conversion/genome_mfa.CT_conversion.fa; echo
What two genomes did Bismark make, and what does the first line of sequence look like?


C4 — Align
bismark --genome genome --parallel 2 -p 2 trimmed.fastq.gz > bismark.log 2>&1
grep -E "analysed|unique best|Mapping efficiency|no alignments|did not map uniquely|CT/CT|CT/GA|GA/CT|GA/GA" \
  trimmed_bismark_bt2_SE_report.txt

What is the mapping efficiency, and how many reads aligned to each strand? (b) Why are there no CTOT/CTOB alignments? (c) Is 93% a realistic alignment rate for WGBS? (See the Data section.)



C5 — Look inside the BAM
samtools view trimmed_bismark_bt2.bam | head -2 | cut -f 1-6,12-
samtools view trimmed_bismark_bt2.bam | grep -o 'XG:Z:..' | sort | uniq -c
samtools view trimmed_bismark_bt2.bam | head -1000 | grep -o 'XM:Z:[^[:space:]]*' | cut -c6- | fold -w1 | sort | uniq -c

What do the XR and XG tags record? (b) In the first 1000 reads, what fraction of CpG calls is methylated, and what fraction of CHH calls?



C6 — Deduplicate
deduplicate_bismark --single --bam trimmed_bismark_bt2.bam > dedup.log 2>&1
grep -E "analysed|removed|leftover" trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplication_report.txt
How many reads were removed?


C7 — Extract methylation calls
bismark_methylation_extractor --single-end --gzip --bedGraph --parallel 4 \
  trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated.bam > extract.log 2>&1
ls
grep -E "C methylated in|Total methylated C|Total C to T" trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated_splitting_report.txt
zcat trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated.bismark.cov.gz | head -3

What are the methylation levels in CpG, CHG and CHH context? (b) What are the columns of the .cov file?



C8 — One row per CpG, and ENCODE’s calls for the same region
coverage2cytosine --merge_CpG --zero_based --genome_folder genome -o gm_cpg \
  trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated.bismark.cov.gz > c2c.log 2>&1
head -3 gm_cpg.CpG_report.merged_CpG_evidence.cov
wc -l < gm_cpg.CpG_report.merged_CpG_evidence.cov
tabix $D/gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz chr21:33000001-35000000 \
  | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$13 == "CG" { s = ($6 == "+") ? $2 : $2 - 1
        N[s] += $10; M[s] += int($10 * $11 / 100 + 0.5) }
      END { for (s in N) print "chr21", s, s + 2, M[s], N[s] }' | sort -k2,2n > encode_region.bed
wc -l < encode_region.bed

How many CpGs have at least one read in our run, and how many in ENCODE’s file for the region? (b) Why are the start coordinates of the two files directly comparable here?

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
section: Explore: bisulfite conversion, alignment and calls
text:
Explore: bisulfite conversion, alignment and calls
The demo follows one short piece of simulated genome through the whole pipeline. (a) The two strands, with a lollipop on each C of a CpG: click one to cycle it through unmethylated (open), methylated (filled) and methylated in 50% of molecules (half filled); all other Cs are unmethylated, and their context (CHG, CHH) is written next to them. You can type your own top strand (6–30 bases). (b) The reads each strand gives after conversion and PCR, written 5’→3’ as the sequencer reports them, converted bases in red; tick non-directional library to add CTOT and CTOB. (c) Bismark’s three-letter alignment: each read converted in silico and placed under the converted genome it matches, with the number of mismatches there, at the next-best candidate, and in an ordinary (“plain”) alignment. (d) The original read against the original genome, with the methylation call letters of the XM tag. (e) Many simulated reads: a pileup of calls (dark = C kept, light = converted to T, orange = a non-CpG C that was not converted) and the β of each CpG with its 95% interval. The sliders set the number of reads and the conversion efficiency; C/T and T/T put a C→T SNP at the C of CpG 3.



E1. (links to B1) Click B1 (by hand) and compare panel (b) with your answer to B1(b). Then read panel (c): which converted genome, on which strand, does each read match? How many mismatches would an ordinary aligner see for the OT and the OB read, and why does Bismark convert the read before aligning?
E2. Go back to default. How many Cs are left in the OT read of 20 bases (b)? In (c), how many mismatches does the OT read have at the next-best candidate? Now tick non-directional library: how many candidate alignments does Bismark try per read, and what happens to the margin between the best and the next-best hit? What does this mean for reads from repetitive or low-complexity DNA?
E3. (links to B4, B6) Untick non-directional, set reads to 100 and conversion to 100%: what β do CpG 2 (unmethylated) and the non-CpG Cs show? Now set conversion to 95%, then 90%. What β does CpG 2 get, and what non-conversion rate do the non-CpG Cs estimate? Compare with \(\beta_\text{obs} = \beta + (1-\beta) f\). Then set conversion back to 99.5%, click CpG 2 twice (50%), and compare its 95% interval at 10 and at 100 reads.
E4. (links to B8, R5) Back at default (CpG 3 is methylated), with 100 reads and 99.5% conversion, choose C/T. What β does CpG 3 get, and why do its top-strand reads look exactly like unmethylated ones? Where in the pileup can you see the SNP? Then choose T/T. Why does the β of the bottom-strand C (opposite the G) drop too, although that C is not changed by the SNP?






Solutions (E1–E4)





E1. OT = ACGTTTGATTAG and OB = TTGATTGGACGT, as in B1. After C→T conversion in silico the OT read matches the C→T genome on the + strand with 0 mismatches (6 at the other candidate); the OB read matches the G→A genome on the − strand (its reverse complement is the G→A-converted top strand), 0 mismatches against 6. An ordinary aligner sees 3 mismatches for the OT read (the three converted Cs) and 2 for OB, in a read of 12 bases: every unmethylated C would count as an error, and the number of errors would depend on the methylation level, so methylated and unmethylated reads would align differently. Converting both read and genome removes the methylation information from the alignment step; it is put back in step (d), where the original read is compared with the original genome (OT calls Zxzx, OB calls Zzx).
E2. The OT read has only 2 Cs of 20 bases (the two methylated CpGs): bisulfite reads are mostly A, G and T (the lecture’s 1.5% C). In directional mode the next-best candidate is 14 mismatches away. In non-directional mode Bismark tries 4 alignments per read (C→T and G→A versions of the read against both converted genomes), and the next-best is only 3 mismatches away for every read type. In a three-letter genome many more sequences look alike, and with four candidates instead of two the chance that a second hit is as good as the first is higher: more reads are ambiguous and are discarded, especially in repeats and low-complexity DNA. This is why directional libraries are the default.
E3. At 100% conversion CpG 2 is 0.00 (0/100) and no non-CpG C is kept (0 of 200 calls). At 95%, CpG 2 shows 0.05 (5/100) and the non-CpG Cs 6.0% (12 of 200); at 90%, 0.08 (8/100) and 10.0% (20 of 200). With β = 0 the formula gives \(\beta_\text{obs} = f\), so CpG 2 and the non-CpG Cs estimate the same non-conversion rate, with sampling noise; this is why CHH calls (or a lambda spike-in) are used to measure conversion. The methylated CpGs stay at 1.00, since 5mC is never converted. At 50% and 99.5% conversion, CpG 2 is 0.50 (5/10), 95% interval 0.24–0.76 with 10 reads, and 0.47 (47/100), 0.38–0.57 with 100 reads: ten times the reads makes the interval about three times narrower (\(\sqrt{10}\)), as in B6.
E4. With C/T, CpG 3 drops from 1.00 to 0.52 (52/100), although no molecule lost methylation. Molecules with the T allele have TG instead of CG on the top strand: an OT read shows T at the C, exactly what an unmethylated, converted C gives, so Bismark calls it unmethylated. The SNP is visible only on the bottom-strand reads: at that position the bottom strand has G (C allele) or A (T allele), which bisulfite does not change, so the T allele shows up on the + strand as a T that conversion cannot explain (the red T, in 18 of the 42 bottom reads). With T/T, CpG 3 is 0.00 (0/100). On the T allele the bottom C is now in CpA context, not CpG: it is not maintained as methylated, so it is converted too. Both strands therefore report “unmethylated”, which is what B8 and the real data in R5 (heterozygous C/T sites at 0.38, homozygous at 0.01) show. Remove known SNPs at CpGs, or call genotypes from the reads (Bis-SNP, gemBS, BISCUIT).

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
In R
You need data.table and ggplot2.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(ggplot2) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — M-bias
read_mbias <- function(file) {
  l <- readLines(file); out <- list(); section <- NA
  for (x in l) {
    if (grepl("context", x)) { section <- x; next }
    if (grepl("^[0-9]+\t", x)) {
      v <- as.numeric(strsplit(x, "\t")[[1]][1:3])
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.table(section, pos = v[1], meth = v[2], unmeth = v[3])
    }
  }
  x <- rbindlist(out)
  x[, context := sub(" context.*", "", section)][, read := ifelse(grepl("R2", section), "R2", "R1")]
  x[, pct := 100 * meth / (meth + unmeth)][]
}
pe <- read_mbias(file.path(D, "gm12878_wgbs_pe_mbias.txt"))
se <- read_mbias("trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated.M-bias.txt")
pe[context == "CpG" & pos <= 6, .(read, pos, pct = round(pct, 1))]
pe[context == "CpG" & pos %in% 30:100, .(plateau = median(pct)), by = read]
ggplot(pe[context == "CpG" & meth + unmeth > 2000], aes(pos, pct, colour = read)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "position in read", y = "% CpG methylated")
ggplot(se[context == "CpG"], aes(pos, pct)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "position in read 1", y = "% CpG methylated")
se[context == "CHH" & pos <= 3, .(pos, pct = round(pct, 2))]

Which positions deviate from the plateau in each read of the paired-end library? (b) Is there any M-bias in our single-end read 1? Look at both CpG and CHH. (c) Write the Bismark option you would add to the extractor for the paired-end library.



R2 — Conversion
sp <- readLines("trimmed_bismark_bt2.deduplicated_splitting_report.txt")
get <- function(pat) as.numeric(sub(".*:\\s*", "", grep(pat, sp, value = TRUE)))
chh_m <- get("Total methylated C's in CHH"); chh_u <- get("Total C to T conversions in CHH")
f <- chh_m / (chh_m + chh_u)
c(non_conversion = f, conversion = 1 - f)
beta_obs <- function(beta, f) beta + (1 - beta) * f
beta_obs(c(0, 0.5, 1), f)
beta_obs(c(0, 0.5, 1), 0.05)
What is the conversion rate? How much does it change β at 0 and at 0.5? What if it were only 95%?


R3 — The per-CpG table and its precision
ours <- fread("gm_cpg.CpG_report.merged_CpG_evidence.cov",
              col.names = c("chr", "start", "end", "pct", "M", "U"))
ours[, N := M + U][, beta := M / N]
nrow(ours); nrow(ours[start >= 33e6 & start < 35e6])
summary(ours$N); mean(ours$N >= 10)
ours[N >= 10, .(mean_beta = mean(beta), low = mean(beta < 0.2), high = mean(beta > 0.8))]
ggplot(ours[start >= 33e6 & start < 35e6], aes(pmin(N, 50))) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)
# exact binomial 95% intervals for two CpGs with beta = 0.75
binom.test(3, 4)$conf.int; binom.test(30, 40)$conf.int

How many CpGs, what median coverage, what fraction with at least 10 reads? (b) Why are there CpGs outside 33–35 Mb? (c) Compare the binomial intervals with your answer to B6.



R4 — Compare with ENCODE
enc <- fread("encode_region.bed", col.names = c("chr", "start", "end", "M", "N"))
m <- merge(ours[, .(start, Mo = M, No = N)], enc[, .(start, Me = M, Ne = N)], by = "start")
nrow(m)
mean(m$Mo == m$Me & m$No == m$Ne)
fm <- m[No >= 10 & Ne >= 10]
nrow(fm)
cor(fm$Mo / fm$No, fm$Me / fm$Ne)
mean(abs(fm$Mo / fm$No - fm$Me / fm$Ne))
c(ours = sum(m$Mo) / sum(m$No), encode = sum(m$Me) / sum(m$Ne))
ggplot(fm, aes(Me / Ne, Mo / No)) + geom_bin2d(bins = 40) + geom_abline(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "ENCODE (gemBS)", y = "this exercise (Bismark)")

How well do the two pipelines agree? (b) Why are the counts not identical, although the reads are the same?



R5 — SNPs that look like unmethylated CpGs
x <- fread(cmd = paste("tabix", file.path(D, "gm12878_wgbs_rep1_chr21.bed.gz"), "chr21:33000001-35000000"),
           header = FALSE, select = c(2, 6, 13), col.names = c("s0", "strand", "call"))
x[, start := ifelse(strand == "+", s0, s0 - 1L)]
snp <- x[call != "CG", .(calls = paste(sort(unique(call)), collapse = ",")), by = start]
snp[, type := ifelse(grepl("TG|CA", calls), "homozygous C>T",
              ifelse(grepl("YG|CR", calls), "heterozygous C/T", "other SNP"))]
table(snp$type)
o <- merge(ours[N >= 8], snp[, .(start, type)], by = "start", all.x = TRUE)
o[is.na(type), type := "no SNP"]
o[, .(CpGs = .N, beta = sum(M) / sum(N)), by = type]

What does ENCODE’s genotype code YG mean (IUPAC: Y = C or T)? And TG? (b) Compare the methylation that Bismark reports at each type of site. Explain the numbers. (c) Why do “other” SNPs (e.g. G/T at the G) lower β less?

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — conversion by hand (B1, B2, B3)





Write the bottom strand as the reverse complement of the top. Then, on each strand separately, replace every C that is not methylated by T. A CpG on the top strand at positions \(i, i+1\) has its bottom-strand C opposite position \(i+1\). The Bismark user guide explains the XM characters and the four strands (alignment modes).









Hint 2 — conversion rate and M-bias (B4, B5, R1, R2)





Non-conversion = methylated CHH / all CHH calls. A spike-in of unmethylated lambda DNA gives the same estimate where CHH methylation is real. The M-bias plot was introduced with BSmooth (Hansen et al. 2012); Bismark’s extractor has --ignore, --ignore_r2, --ignore_3prime and --ignore_3prime_r2 (manual).









Hint 3 — precision (B6, R3)





95% interval ≈ \(\hat\beta \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat\beta(1-\hat\beta)/N}\); for small \(N\) use the exact interval (binom.test). Solve \(\sqrt{0.25/N} = 0.05\) for \(N\).









Hint 4 — tools (C2–C8)





fastp trims adapters and low-quality reads; Bismark documents bismark_genome_preparation, bismark, deduplicate_bismark, bismark_methylation_extractor and coverage2cytosine. tabix extracts a region from an indexed file. XR and XG are explained in the Bismark output description.









Hint 5 — SNPs and assay choice (B8, B9, R5)





IUPAC codes: Y = C/T, R = A/G, K = G/T, M = A/C, S = C/G. Bisulfite cannot create an A or a G, or turn a G into anything else. The lecture’s “Choosing an assay” table and Methylation arrays help with B9.

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Bottom strand 5’→3’: CTGATCGGACGT. (b) OT: ACGTTTGATTAG (the C at position 2 stays C, the Cs at 5, 6 and 10 become T). OB: TTGATTGGACGT (bottom-strand Cs at its positions 1 and 6 become T; the C at position 10, which pairs with the G of the methylated first CpG, stays C). (c) OT, after C→T, matches the C→T genome (top strand); OB, after C→T, matches the G→A genome (the top strand with G→A is the reverse complement of the C→T-converted bottom strand).
B2. (a) 101: 5 C of 6 = 0.83; 112: 4 of 6 = 0.67. (b) Incomplete conversion of that molecule (or a sequencing error); in mammals CHH methylation is near 0. A read with several unconverted non-CpG Cs is usually removed (Bismark’s filter_non_conversion). (c) r2: Z, h, z.
B3. One methylated CpG (Z), one unmethylated CpG (z), three unmethylated CHG (x), one unmethylated CHH (h); six C calls, of which 2/6 = 33% in CpG context.
B4. (a) \(f = 30\,824/4\,644\,038 = 0.66\%\); conversion 99.34%. (b) \(0 + 1 \times 0.0066 = 0.0066\); \(0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.0066 = 0.503\). (c) \(30/2000 = 1.5\%\), conversion 98.5%: acceptable by ENCODE’s ≥ 98%, but unmethylated islands would read about 1.5% vs 0.7% in the two libraries, a small systematic difference. Fine for most purposes; correct for it or treat library as a covariate if you compare low-methylation regions between batches. (d) Neurons have real non-CpG (mostly CpA) methylation, and plants methylate CHG and CHH: methylated CHH calls are then biology, not failed conversion. Use an unmethylated spike-in.
B5. (a) Read 2: ignore positions 1–4 (1 is too high, 2–4 too low; from 5 on it is near the 48% plateau): --ignore_r2 4. Read 1: position 1 is slightly high (52.3) and 4–5 slightly noisy; ignoring the first 1–2 bases is a cautious choice (--ignore 2). (b) End repair fills in the fragment end that read 2 starts from with unmethylated C; read 1 starts at the other end. (c) The methylation of a CpG cannot depend on where in a read it happens to be observed; averaged over millions of reads, every position should show the same level.
B6. (a) 3/4: \(0.75 \pm 1.96\sqrt{0.1875/4} = 0.75 \pm 0.42\) (the normal approximation fails here; the exact interval is 0.19–0.99). 30/40: \(0.75 \pm 1.96\sqrt{0.1875/40} = 0.75 \pm 0.13\) (0.62–0.88). (b) \(\sqrt{0.25/N} = 0.05 \Rightarrow N = 100\). (c) \(\sqrt{0.25/30} = 0.091\).
B7. (a) Copies of one molecule count as independent observations: coverage and confidence are inflated, and one molecule’s methylation is over-weighted (pseudo-replication, as in differential accessibility). (b) No: RRBS fragments all start at MspI sites, so identical starts are expected and removing them would remove most real data (UMIs can identify true duplicates).
B8. (a) Person A is heterozygous for a C→T SNP at the CpG: the T allele reads as “unmethylated”, halving β. (b) Look at reads from the other strand (OB if the SNP is at the top-strand C): at the opposite base they show G (reference) vs A (SNP), unchanged by bisulfite. A SNP caller for bisulfite data (Bis-SNP, BISCUIT, gemBS) does this systematically; or check dbSNP. (c) Remove CpGs that overlap known common SNPs or SNPs called in the samples before testing, or analyse them as meQTLs with genotype in the model.
B9. (a) EPIC array: cheapest per sample, standardised, 900 000 CpGs chosen for relevance; good statistical power from many samples. (b) EM-seq: works on picograms to nanograms with little damage (bisulfite would destroy much of 2 ng). (c) Nanopore or PacBio long reads: one read spans the region and heterozygous SNPs, so methylation is assigned to each parental haplotype. (d) oxBS together with BS (or TAB-seq), or nanopore: bisulfite or EM-seq alone report 5mC + 5hmC. (e) RRBS (or a targeted panel): covers most CpG-island promoters at single-CpG resolution cheaply; arrays are an alternative if the promoters of interest are on the array.









Solutions — command line





Run times on 8 server threads.
C1. (a) 360 142 reads: 335 040 of 125 bp and 25 102 of 151 bp (two sequencing runs). (b) Reads: about 28.8% A, 1.5% C, 21.2% G, 48.5% T. chr21: 11.8 M A, 8.2 M C, 8.2 M G, 11.9 M T (about 29.5%, 20.4%, 20.5%, 29.6%). C is almost gone and T much increased, G unchanged: read 1 of a directional library comes from the converted original strands (OT, OB). The remaining Cs are methylated CpGs.
C2. 338 087 reads pass; 21 908 fail on quality, 57 are too short, 90 have too many N; adapters trimmed in 36 808 reads (1.09 M bases). For single-end data fastp detects adapters by overrepresented sequences, which bisulfite’s skewed composition makes unreliable; the standard Illumina adapter start (AGATCGGAAGAGC) is safer. (3 s.)
C3. Two copies of chr21: one with every C converted to T (CT_conversion) and one with every G converted to A (GA_conversion), each with a bowtie2 index. The sequence starts with N (the unassembled start of chr21). (48 s.)
C4. (a) 338 087 analysed, 315 951 unique best hits (93.5%); 21 757 without alignment, 379 not unique; 158 877 OT (CT/CT) and 157 074 OB (CT/GA). (b) The library is directional: Bismark does not even try CTOT/CTOB (GA/CT, GA/GA = 0). (c) No: the reads were pre-selected as ENCODE-aligned to this region; real WGBS gives 60–80% unique alignment to the whole genome. (59 s.)
C5. (a) XR is the conversion of the read (always CT for read 1 here), XG the conversion of the genome strand it matched: CT = top strand (OT), GA = bottom (OB); 158 877 CT, 157 074 GA. (b) In the first 1000 reads: 795 Z and 648 z (55% of CpG calls methylated); 125 H and 18 455 h (0.7% of CHH calls methylated).
C6. 61 418 of 315 951 removed (19.4%), 254 533 left. (11 s.)
C7. (a) CpG 61.0%, CHG 0.7%, CHH 0.7% (209 721 methylated / 134 141 unmethylated CpG calls; 30 824 / 4 613 214 CHH). (b) chromosome, start, end (the same 1-based position), % methylated, count methylated, count unmethylated; one line per cytosine and strand, no strand column. (26 s.)
C8. (a) 24 675 CpGs in our merged file; 23 583 in ENCODE’s file for the region. (b) Both are BED-style: --zero_based makes Bismark’s start the 0-based position of the C on the + strand, and the awk command assigns the − strand C to the CpG start (position − 1), as ENCODE’s + strand line does. (coverage2cytosine 69 s.)









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Paired-end: read 2 positions 1–4 (66.0, 40.2, 43.0, 43.2% against a plateau of 48.0%); read 1 is close to its plateau (47.5%) except position 1 (52.3%). (b) Our read 1 is flat around 61% for CpG (only the last two positions dip slightly, to 58% and 57%), but CHH is 1.76% at position 1 vs about 0.65% further in: a small 5’ artefact, too small to matter for CpG calls. (c) --ignore_r2 4 (and perhaps --ignore 1) for bismark_methylation_extractor --paired-end.
R2. Non-conversion 0.66%, conversion 99.34%. β of 0 becomes 0.0066, 0.5 becomes 0.503, 1 stays 1. At 95% conversion: 0.05 and 0.525: every unmethylated CpG looks 5% methylated.
R3. (a) 24 675 CpGs (24 355 in 33–35 Mb), median 14 reads, 74.8% with ≥ 10; among those, mean β 0.62, 24% below 0.2 and 52% above 0.8 (this region is not in a partially methylated domain). (b) Reads that ENCODE placed in 33–35 Mb but Bismark placed elsewhere on chr21 (repeats, paralogous sequence), and reads overhanging the region boundaries. (c) binom.test(3, 4): 0.19–0.99; binom.test(30, 40): 0.59–0.87; close to the normal approximation for 40 reads, very different for 4.
R4. (a) 23 567 shared CpGs; 17 483 with ≥ 10 reads in both; Pearson r = 0.997, mean |Δβ| 0.016; overall 0.618 (ours) vs 0.616 (ENCODE). (b) Only 28% of CpGs have identical counts: different trimming (fastp vs gemBS), alignment filters (MAPQ, soft-clipping), duplicate removal, and treatment of read ends and low-quality bases change a few reads per CpG.
R5. (a) YG: at the C of this CpG the cell line is heterozygous C/T (the CpG exists on one allele only). TG: homozygous T: there is no CpG on either allele. (CR and CA are the same SNPs seen from the other strand.) In the region ENCODE called 328 heterozygous, 84 homozygous and 343 other SNP CpGs. (b) With ≥ 8 reads: no SNP 0.63 (19 991 CpGs); heterozygous C/T 0.38 (301); homozygous 0.01 (67); other 0.52 (182). The T allele produces T in the read, exactly like an unmethylated C, so heterozygous sites lose about half their signal and homozygous ones look completely unmethylated. (c) A G/T or C/A change produces a base that bisulfite conversion cannot produce (A at a C, or T at the G read on the other strand): Bismark treats it as a mismatch and does not count it as an unmethylated call, so β drops less.

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
Where this leads

Differential methylation takes per-CpG counts like those of C8 from several samples (ENCODE’s GM12878 and K562 replicates) and tests where they differ.
Methylation arrays measure selected CpGs with bisulfite conversion and hybridisation instead of sequencing.
Methylation and chromatin from long reads reads methylation without conversion, on single molecules and haplotypes.
At scale, nf-core/methylseq runs the same steps (trim, Bismark or bwa-meth, deduplicate, extract, MultiQC) on a cluster.

title: Exercise: Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Frommer et al. 1992, PNAS. A genomic sequencing protocol that yields a positive display of 5-methylcytosine residues in individual DNA strands.
Meissner et al. 2005, Nucleic Acids Res. Reduced representation bisulfite sequencing for comparative high-resolution DNA methylation analysis.
Lister et al. 2009, Nature. Human DNA methylomes at base resolution show widespread epigenomic differences.
Krueger & Andrews 2011, Bioinformatics. Bismark: a flexible aligner and methylation caller for Bisulfite-Seq applications.
Vaisvila et al. 2021, Genome Res. Enzymatic methyl sequencing detects DNA methylation at single-base resolution from picograms of DNA.
Liu et al. 2019, Nat Biotechnol. Bisulfite-free direct detection of 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine at base resolution.

title: Quiz: bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing
text:
Short questions on bisulfite chemistry, alignment, QC and the alternatives. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What do C, 5mC, 5hmC and 5caC read as after bisulfite treatment and PCR? What does that mean for “methylation” measured by WGBS?






Answer





C → T; 5mC → C; 5hmC → C (it forms a stable sulfonate adduct, CMS); 5caC (and 5fC) → T. WGBS therefore measures 5mC + 5hmC together; in tissues with much 5hmC (brain) “methylation” is partly 5hmC.




Q2. The top strand of a genomic segment is 5’-TCGACA-3’ and its CpG is methylated. Write the OT read after bisulfite conversion.






Hint





Only the C of the CpG is protected.









Answer





5’-TCGATA-3’: the C in CG stays C, the C in CA becomes T.




Q3. Why can bisulfite reads not be aligned well with a normal aligner, and how does Bismark solve it?






Answer





Every unmethylated C appears as a T, so reads carry many C/T mismatches that depend on methylation (biasing alignment against unmethylated reads), and the reads are low-complexity. Bismark converts all Cs to Ts in the read, aligns it with bowtie2 to a C→T and a G→A converted genome, keeps reads with a unique best hit, and then compares the original read with the original genome to call methylation.




Q4. In a directional WGBS library, from which strands does read 1 come? What happens if you align a four-strand non-directional library in directional mode? How does standard PBAT differ?






Answer





Read 1 comes from the original top (OT) or original bottom (OB) strand. A four-strand non-directional library also contains reads from CTOT and CTOB; in directional mode those are not tried, so roughly half of the reads fail to align. Standard PBAT yields read 1 from CTOT and CTOB, searched with --pbat; using default directional mode can lose nearly all of those reads. Some modified PBAT protocols are non-directional, so check the library protocol. See Bismark’s library options.




Q5. A mammalian WGBS library has 0.8% methylated CHH calls. What is the conversion rate, and what β would a truly unmethylated CpG show? When would this estimate be wrong?






Answer





Conversion 99.2%; an unmethylated CpG shows β ≈ 0.008. The estimate is wrong where non-CpG methylation is real (neurons, embryonic stem cells, plants); there use an unmethylated spike-in such as lambda DNA.




Q6. An M-bias plot of read 2 shows 40% CpG methylation at positions 1–3 and a flat 70% after position 5. Read 1 is flat at 70%. What causes this and what do you do?






Answer





End repair before adapter ligation fills the fragment ends with unmethylated C; read 2 starts in that filled-in DNA, so its first bases look unmethylated. Ignore the first ~4–5 positions of read 2 when extracting calls (--ignore_r2 5), then check the plot again. Do not discard the reads.




Q7. A CpG has 6 methylated reads out of 8. Another has 60 of 80. Give β and an approximate 95% interval for each.






Answer





Both β = 0.75. SE = \(\sqrt{0.75 \cdot 0.25/N}\): 0.153 for 8 reads (interval about 0.45–1.0; the exact binomial interval is 0.35–0.97), 0.048 for 80 reads (0.65–0.85). Ten times more reads, about three times narrower.




Q8. Should you remove PCR duplicates from (a) a WGBS library and (b) an RRBS library? Explain.






Answer






Yes: reads with the same start and strand are likely copies of one molecule and would be counted as independent observations, inflating confidence. (b) No: RRBS fragments all start at MspI sites, so identical starts are expected; deduplication would discard most of the data.





Q9. In GM12878, CpGs where the cell line is homozygous for a C>T SNP show β ≈ 0.01 in Bismark output. Explain, and say how such sites can be detected from the bisulfite data themselves.






Answer





There is no C at the site, so every read has T, exactly what an unmethylated C gives: the pipeline reports an unmethylated CpG that does not exist. Reads from the opposite strand show A instead of G at the paired position, which bisulfite cannot cause; SNP-aware callers (Bis-SNP, BISCUIT, gemBS) use this to call the genotype. Otherwise, filter CpGs that overlap known SNPs.




Q10. Give one advantage of EM-seq and one of TAPS over bisulfite sequencing.






Answer





EM-seq: much less DNA damage, so it works from very little input (cell-free DNA) with more even coverage, and it gives the same readout as bisulfite so the same pipeline works. TAPS: only modified cytosines change (to T), so reads keep four letters, align better and waste less sequencing; variants separate 5mC from 5hmC.

title: Differential methylation
text:
About this lecture
Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing turned reads into a table of methylated and total reads per CpG. This lecture compares such tables between groups of samples.

The data: two count matrices, methylated reads and all reads, CpGs × samples.
The models: binomial sampling and beta-binomial biological variation, the analogue of Poisson and negative binomial in RNA-seq.
Smoothing: borrowing strength from neighbouring CpGs.
DMLs and DMRs: single CpGs vs regions; multiple testing; effect sizes in Δβ.
Real data: ENCODE GM12878 vs K562, two replicates each, chr21, with DSS; annotation and expression.
Design: what replicates of a cell line can and cannot tell you.


Students know DESeq2. The structure of this unit mirrors Differential accessibility: a count model with a dispersion parameter, shrinkage of that parameter across features, a Wald test, multiple testing, then annotation. What is different: the data are proportions with known denominators (no library-size normalisation), neighbouring features are strongly correlated (so smoothing and regions make sense), and global differences between samples are common and biologically meaningful. The data are the same four ENCODE files used in DNA methylation biology; DSS runs on chr21 in about a minute.

title: Differential methylation
section: The data: methylated reads out of all reads
text:
The data: methylated reads out of all reads


For every CpG and sample: M methylated reads and N reads in total (both strands combined).
β = M/N is the level, but its precision depends on N: 6/8 and 60/80 are both 0.75.
No library-size normalisation is needed: each CpG is its own denominator.


Compared with RNA-seq, each entry of the matrix is a pair, and that pair already contains its own normalisation: sequencing depth changes N, not the expected β. This is why methylation analyses do not use size factors. They do need coverage filters (too few reads give no information; extreme coverage suggests copy-number changes or repeats) and they need to keep N in the model rather than analysing β alone. The toy numbers are illustrative; the real matrix has 366 640 CpGs that are covered in at least one of our four samples.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Two sources of variation


Biological: each sample has its own true level around the group mean (cell mix, individual, culture history).
Sampling: given the true level, reads are a binomial draw; this noise shrinks as N grows, the biological part does not.
The beta-binomial combines them, with an overdispersion parameter φ per CpG.


The hierarchy is exactly that of the negative binomial in RNA-seq: there a gamma-distributed true expression and Poisson counts; here a beta-distributed true proportion and binomial counts. φ (DSS uses φ, other papers ρ) is the intra-class correlation: the variance of the count is N p (1−p) [1 + (N − 1) φ]. With φ = 0 we are back at the binomial. Two practical consequences. First, sequencing deeper does not reduce the biological part: beyond about 10–20 reads per CpG, more replicates help more than more depth (Ziller et al. 2015). Second, tests that ignore φ, such as Fisher’s exact test on pooled reads, treat the reads as the replicates.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Binomial and beta-binomial


With 20 reads and a mean level of 0.5: the binomial gives SD 2.2 reads (β ± 0.11).
With φ = 0.2 the SD is 4.9 reads (β ± 0.24): the same mean, more than twice the spread, and 0 or 20 of 20 is no longer rare.


Read the numbers off the variance formula N p (1−p) [1 + (N − 1) φ]. With N = 20 and p = 0.5, N p (1−p) = 5, so the binomial SD is √5 = 2.2 reads. With φ = 0.05 the variance is 5 × 1.95 = 9.75 (SD 3.1 reads); with φ = 0.2 it is 5 × 4.8 = 24 (SD 4.9 reads, or 0.24 in β). The point for students: a test that assumes the black bars will call many CpGs significant whose difference is well within the orange spread. Exam calculations use the variance formula, not the density.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Real replicates are overdispersed


Compare the two replicates of each cell line, CpG by CpG, scaled by the binomial standard error. Pure sampling noise would give a variance of 1.
K562: 1.05, close to binomial. GM12878: 3.44: the two cultures really differ.
The spiky shape comes from small integer counts (10–20 reads).


z = (β1 − β2) / sqrt(p(1−p)(1/N1 + 1/N2)) with p the pooled level; CpGs with at least 10 reads in both replicates and 0 < p < 1 (169 163 for GM12878, 137 943 for K562). K562’s two replicates behave like two sequencing runs of one sample. The GM12878 replicates are independent growths of a lymphoblastoid line, and rep2 is about 0.07 more methylated than rep1 across most of chr21 (next slide). This is the biological variation of the previous slides in action: estimating it requires replicates, and a test that ignores it is anticonservative.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Replicates in 100-kb bins


K562 replicates agree almost perfectly (r = 0.999). GM12878 rep2 is 0.067 higher on average than rep1, most in partially methylated domains.
A global shift between replicates is real variation between cultures, not noise. In human samples it can come from age, cell composition or proliferation.


Correlations of bin means: GM12878 replicates 0.957, K562 replicates 0.999, GM12878 vs K562 about 0.64. Global shifts matter in two ways. They inflate dispersion and so reduce power; and if they are confounded with the groups (for example all cases processed in one batch, or cases older than controls), they create thousands of “DMRs” that are not about the question asked. Note that β needs no normalisation, but that does not protect against biological or technical global shifts; there is no “median of ratios” fix for them, only design.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Testing one CpG


Fisher’s exact test on pooled reads treats reads as independent: between the two GM12878 replicates, where there is no group difference, it calls 20 902 CpGs at FDR < 0.05.
DSS fits a beta-binomial per CpG, shrinks φ towards a common prior (empirical Bayes, as DESeq2 does), and uses a Wald test.
Smoothing (next slide) adds information from neighbours and raises the number of significant CpGs.


The bar chart compares three tests of GM12878 vs K562 on chr21 at FDR < 0.05. All three find very many CpGs, because the two cell lines differ in about two thirds of chr21’s 100-kb bins. The telling number is in the bullet: the same Fisher test applied to rep1 vs rep2 of GM12878 calls 20 902 CpGs (7% of those tested), which are false positives by construction. With only two replicates per group the dispersion of a single CpG cannot be estimated well; DSS borrows information across CpGs with a prior on φ, just like DESeq2’s dispersion shrinkage. methylKit offers logistic regression with an overdispersion correction; RADmeth and MACAU use beta-binomial regression with covariates.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Neighbouring CpGs are correlated: smoothing


Methylation changes over hundreds of bp, but each CpG has only 10–20 reads. Averaging neighbours trades resolution for precision.
BSmooth fits a local likelihood smoother per sample; DSS smooths with a moving average (default window 500 bp) before testing.
Smoothing assumes neighbours share a level: it blurs sharp boundaries and single-CpG events (e.g. at a TF site).


Dots are raw per-CpG levels (CpGs with at least 5 reads) of all four samples, lines are DSS’s smoothed group means (mu1, mu2 of DMLtest). The raw values of one sample jump between 0 and 1 because 1 of 2 and 9 of 10 are both possible; the smoothed curve recovers the regional level. Hansen, Langmead & Irizarry 2012 (key paper) showed that smoothing lets 4x coverage WGBS detect DMRs reliably, which made large WGBS studies affordable. Smoothing should be switched off when the question is about single CpGs (e.g. a CpG in a TF motif or an imprinting control CpG) or when CpGs are sparse (RRBS, arrays).

title: Differential methylation
text:
DSS in a few lines
library(DSS)
dat <- lapply(files, fread)                      # each: chr, pos, N, X (X = methylated reads)
bs  <- makeBSseqData(dat, c("gm1", "gm2", "k1", "k2"))
dml <- DMLtest(bs, group1 = c("gm1", "gm2"), group2 = c("k1", "k2"), smoothing = TRUE)
dmls <- callDML(dml, delta = 0.2, p.threshold = 1e-5)    # single CpGs
dmrs <- callDMR(dml, delta = 0.2, p.threshold = 1e-5)    # regions
DMLfit.multiFactor(bs, design = df, formula = ~ group + sex)  # general designs

delta: test |Δβ| > delta rather than Δβ ≠ 0 (an effect-size threshold built into the test).
Run time for chr21 (366 640 CpGs, 4 samples): under 1 minute.


DSS (Feng, Conneely & Wu 2014, key paper) is light to install and fast. The input is one table per sample with chromosome, position, total reads (N) and methylated reads (X): exactly what the command-line part of the exercise builds from the ENCODE files. DMLtest handles two groups; DMLfit.multiFactor handles designs with covariates (Park & Wu 2016), the equivalent of a DESeq2 design formula. With delta set, callDML reports the posterior probability that |Δβ| exceeds delta, which avoids calling tiny but significant differences. The p threshold of 1e-5 is DSS’s default for callDMR.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Single CpGs: the volcano


87 108 differential CpGs (|Δβ| > 0.2, p < 10⁻⁵); 82 788 (95%) are lower in K562.
The asymmetry is biology: K562 lost methylation in large domains; gains are few and focal.


A volcano plot of DSS’s Wald test, x axis K562 minus GM12878 (smoothed), 60 000 random CpGs shown. The left arm is dense because large domains lost methylation together; the right arm is sparse. Unlike an RNA-seq volcano there is a hard limit at ±1. With so many CpGs, p-values become tiny for small Δβ; the vertical lines at ±0.2 are the effect-size threshold. What Δβ is “biologically relevant” depends on the question: 0.05 can matter in a population study of blood (Methylation arrays), while cell-type differences are typically 0.3 or more.

title: Differential methylation
text:
From CpGs to regions


A DMR is a run of nearby differential CpGs: fewer, more interpretable units than single CpGs, closer to the scale of regulatory elements.
Each tool has its own rules (gap, minimum CpGs, minimum length, fraction significant) and the results depend on them.


Why regions: biological changes in methylation usually span many CpGs (an enhancer, a CGI shore, a PMD); single-CpG calls are noisy and redundant; and regions can be annotated and validated. DSS merges CpGs below the p threshold that are less than 100 bp apart, then keeps regions with at least 3 CpGs, 50 bp and 50% significant CpGs. BSmooth uses runs of t-statistics above a cutoff; metilene uses a segmentation algorithm; dmrseq (next slides) defines candidate regions and tests them as units.

title: Differential methylation
text:
DMRs between GM12878 and K562


5 061 DMRs on chr21: 4 803 lower in K562 (3.3 Mb in total) and 258 higher.
68% of the losses lie in K562’s hypomethylated domains (46% of tested CpGs do). Gains are enriched at CpG islands (9.7% vs 7.1% of CpGs) and promoters (6.6% vs 4.9%).


Median DMR: 416 bp and 10 CpGs for losses, 495 bp and 7 CpGs for gains. Many of the “losses” are pieces of the same megabase domains, cut into hundreds of DMRs by DSS’s 100-bp merging rule: counting DMRs inflates the number of “events”. Report the total length and the domain structure, or call large-scale blocks separately (BSmooth’s block finder; PMD callers such as MethylSeekR). The gains at CpG islands are the classic cancer pattern, CGI hypermethylation on a background of global hypomethylation (Epigenetics in disease and therapy), visible even on one chromosome of a leukaemia cell line.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Multiple testing: CpGs vs regions

Whole genome: ~28 million CpGs. At p < 0.001 you expect ~28 000 false positives: control the FDR (Benjamini–Hochberg), as in RNA-seq.
But an FDR over CpGs is not an FDR over regions: one false region can contain 10 false CpGs, and regions are defined after looking at the data.
dmrseq defines candidate regions, scores each as a unit, and estimates a pooled regional null from permuted sample labels: region-level FDR with as few as two samples per group.


No figure. With 2 vs 2 samples there are only three distinct unlabelled splits, so a separate permutation test for each fixed region has very coarse p-values. dmrseq overcomes this by pooling null region statistics across the genome and permutations; its documentation supports at least two samples per group. It fits generalised least squares to transformed methylation proportions, accounting for spatial correlation. The DMR list from DSS here has no calibrated region-level FDR because callDMR merges CpG-level calls; that limitation is not a prohibition on region-level inference with 2 vs 2. More biological replicates still improve power and robustness.

title: Differential methylation
text:
A promoter DMR


ITGB2 (integrin β2, CD18, a leukocyte gene): CpG-island promoter at 0.04 in GM12878 and 0.40 in K562 (DMR of 399 bp).
Expression: 16.8 TPM in GM12878, 0.2 in K562. Gain of promoter methylation, loss of expression.


Chosen by a rule in the figure script, not by eye: among genes whose CpG-island promoter overlaps a DMR higher in K562 and that are expressed in GM12878 (TPM > 2), the one with the largest drop in K562. Dots: per-CpG levels of the four samples (at least 5 reads); lines: DSS smoothed means; shaded: DSS DMRs. ITGB2 encodes the β chain of the leukocyte integrins (LFA-1), expressed in lymphocytes, so silence in an erythroleukaemia line is expected. The methylation in K562 is partial (0.4): the island may be methylated on one allele or in a subset of cells, which bulk data cannot tell apart (Methylation and chromatin from long reads). As always, this is consistent with methylation silencing ITGB2 in K562, and equally with methylation following silencing caused by lineage.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Do promoter DMRs change expression?


Promoters higher in K562: 5 of 11 genes are down more than 2-fold in K562, 1 up.
Promoters lower in K562: 7 up, 7 down of 63: no consistent direction (many are silent genes in domains that lost methylation).
Expression is weakly linked to promoter methylation genome-wide; strongly at CGI promoters that become methylated.


ENCODE total RNA-seq, two replicates per cell line (mean TPM), log2 (TPM + 1) ratio; promoter = TSS ± 1 kb. On one chromosome the numbers are small and the conclusions are tentative. The pattern is the one expected from DNA methylation biology: a methylated CpG-island promoter is a stable silent state, so gains at CGI promoters go with loss of expression; losses of methylation in PMDs happen at genes that are silent in both cell lines and stay silent, so they are not followed by activation. Never conclude causality from this kind of plot: methylation could follow silencing (most likely for many CGIs), and the two cell lines differ in everything (lineage, transformation, karyotype).

title: Differential methylation
text:
Design: what are the replicates?

Cell-line replicates (our data) measure technical and culture variation. The p-values say “these two cultures differ”, not “B cells differ from erythroleukaemia”.
In human samples, differences can come from cell-type composition, age, sex, genotype (SNPs, meQTLs), smoking, batch and conversion efficiency. Put them in the model or in the design.
Methylation differences between cell types are large (Δβ 0.3–1); between exposed and unexposed people often small (Δβ 0.01–0.05): they need many samples, which is why population studies use arrays.


The judgement slide. Cell-type composition is the classic confounder of methylation studies in blood and tissue: if cases have more neutrophils, every neutrophil-specific CpG looks differentially methylated (Houseman et al. 2012; Jaffe & Irizarry 2014; covered in Methylation arrays). Sex matters for chrX (and chrY) CpGs; age changes thousands of CpGs (Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers); genotype changes methylation at CpG-SNPs and meQTLs (Bisulfite and enzymatic sequencing, Epigenomics and genetic variation). Our GM12878 vs K562 comparison is a teaching example of the method only: the two lines come from different people, different lineages, and one was immortalised by EBV while the other is a leukaemia. Any DMR could be due to any of these differences.

Students should leave able to: write the beta-binomial variance and compute it; explain why pooling reads over replicates is wrong; say what smoothing buys and costs; apply DMR merging rules to a list of CpGs; interpret a DMR table with Δβ and length; list the confounders of a methylation study. Next: Methylation arrays, the platform of most human population studies, where the same questions are asked with a linear model on M-values.

title: Differential methylation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Hansen, Langmead & Irizarry 2012, Genome Biol. BSmooth: from whole genome bisulfite sequencing reads to differentially methylated regions. Smoothing; low coverage, many samples.
Feng, Conneely & Wu 2014, Nucleic Acids Res. A Bayesian hierarchical model to detect differentially methylated loci from single nucleotide resolution sequencing data. DSS: beta-binomial with shrunken dispersion.
Akalin et al. 2012, Genome Biol. methylKit: a comprehensive R package for the analysis of genome-wide DNA methylation profiles. A widely used alternative, especially for RRBS.
Korthauer et al. 2019, Biostatistics. Detection and accurate false discovery rate control of differentially methylated regions from whole genome bisulfite sequencing. dmrseq: region-level FDR.
Hansen et al. 2011, Nat Genet. Increased methylation variation in epigenetic domains across cancer types. Large hypomethylated blocks in cancer.
Ziller et al. 2015, Nat Methods. Coverage recommendations for methylation analysis by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing. Replicates vs depth.

text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Turn a biological question into a supervised learning problem: examples, features, labels, parameters.
Fit a logistic regression with glm, interpret its coefficients as log-odds and odds ratios, and fit the same model yourself by gradient descent.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Background
Supervised learning. Each example (here a 500-bp window of the genome) has a label (open = 1, closed = 0) and a set of features computed from it (GC fraction, CpG observed/expected, motif counts). A model maps features to a prediction and has parameters that are chosen to make the predictions match the labels on the training examples. Its quality is measured on test examples that played no part in fitting.
Logistic regression. \(\text{score} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \dots + b_p x_p\) is the log-odds of being open; \(P(\text{open}) = 1 / (1 + e^{-\text{score}})\). A coefficient \(b\) adds \(b\) to the log-odds per unit of its feature, i.e. multiplies the odds by \(e^b\), with the other features held fixed.
Loss and fitting. The log-loss of one window is \(-\log p\) if it is open and \(-\log(1-p)\) if it is closed, where \(p\) is the predicted P(open). Fitting minimises the mean log-loss over the training set (= maximum likelihood). Gradient descent does this by repeated small steps against the slope; for logistic regression the slope for coefficient \(j\) is the mean of \((p_i - y_i)\,x_{ij}\).
Overfitting and regularisation. With many parameters and few examples a model can fit the training data perfectly and new data badly. Ridge (L2) and lasso (L1) add a penalty \(\lambda \sum b_j^2\) or \(\lambda \sum |b_j|\) to the loss; the lasso sets many coefficients exactly to 0. \(\lambda\) is chosen by cross-validation within the training set.
Metrics. At a threshold: TP, FP, FN, TN; accuracy \(=(TP+TN)/n\), precision \(=TP/(TP+FP)\), recall \(=TPR=TP/(TP+FN)\), \(FPR=FP/(FP+TN)\). Over all thresholds: the ROC curve (TPR against FPR; AUC = probability that a random positive scores above a random negative) and the PR curve (precision against recall; a random model sits at the fraction of positives).

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Data
The exercise uses the GM12878 ATAC-seq peaks (ENCODE ENCSR095QNB, IDR thresholded peaks, GRCh38), the ENCODE blacklist, and the hg38 genome as a bgzipped, indexed FASTA (the same files as in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting). From the course repository:
data/download.sh ml-basics              # about 1 GB, mostly the genome
mkdir -p ~/epi/ml && cd ~/epi/ml
You need R with GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, Rsamtools, Biostrings, JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, RSQLite, motifmatchr (Bioconductor) and glmnet, pROC (CRAN); see Install the software you need. Building the data set (R1) takes one to two minutes; every other step runs in seconds, except R9 (about a minute). A laptop is enough.
Simplification. The labels are one cell line’s peak calls, the negatives are random genomic windows, and the features are five numbers chosen by hand. The next unit shows how the choice of negatives changes the answer; How a CNN reads DNA lets the model learn its own features from the sequence.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
By hand
Do these on paper. A calculator is fine.
B1. Framing a prediction problem. A study predicts, for every CpG in blood, whether it is methylated (β > 0.5), from three numbers: the GC fraction of the 500 bp around it, whether it lies in a CpG island (0/1), and the log distance to the nearest TSS. It uses 400 000 CpGs measured on arrays in 10 people.

What are the examples, the features and the label? How many parameters does a logistic regression with these features have?
A 500-bp window has 130 C, 120 G and 18 CG dinucleotides. Compute its GC fraction and its CpG o/e \(= \#CG \times 500 / (\#C \times \#G)\). Another has 100 C, 105 G and 5 CG. Which looks like a CpG island?
A colleague proposes adding a fourth feature: the methylation of the same CpG measured on the 450K array of the same person. Why is that a bad idea if the goal is to predict methylation where it has not been measured?

B2. Logistic regression. The five-feature model fitted in R7 is
\[\text{score} = -4.20 + 8.04\,\text{GC} + 0.97\,\text{CpG o/e} + 1.41\,\text{CTCF} + 0.60\,\text{SPI1} + 0.24\,\text{EBF1}\]
with motif features counting matches in the window.

Compute the score and P(open) for a window with GC 0.45, CpG o/e 0.30 and no motif matches.
The same window with one CTCF match. By what factor do the odds change? By what factor does the probability change? Why are these different?
How many PU.1 (SPI1) matches raise the score as much as one CTCF match?
By what factor do the odds change when GC rises by 0.1?

B3. Log-loss. A model predicts P(open) = 0.8 for an open window, 0.3 for a closed window and 0.1 for an open window.

Compute the log-loss of each window (natural log) and the mean.
Compare with a model that predicts 0.5 for everything. Which window is responsible for most of the first model’s loss?

B4. Confusion matrix. A classifier is tested on 1000 windows, 200 open and 800 closed. At its threshold it calls 250 windows open, of which 150 are truly open.

Fill in TP, FP, FN, TN.
Compute accuracy, precision, recall, FPR and \(F_1 = 2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall} / (\text{precision} + \text{recall})\).
What accuracy does a “model” get that calls every window closed? What does this say about accuracy as a metric here?

B5. ROC and PR by hand. Eight test windows, sorted by score:
