Walk down the list and write the (FPR, TPR) point after each window. Draw the ROC curve.
Compute the ROC AUC by counting (open, closed) pairs in which the open window has the higher score.
At threshold 0.6, what are precision and recall?
Compute the precision at the rank of each open window, and their mean (the average precision, an estimate of the PR AUC).

B6. Class imbalance. A model has TPR 0.8 and FPR 0.05 at its chosen threshold.

On a balanced test set with 1000 open and 1000 closed windows: how many TP and FP, and what precision?
Genome-wide, with 1000 open and 99 000 closed windows: how many TP and FP, and what precision?
Does the ROC curve of the model change between (a) and (b)? Does its PR curve?

B7. Judge the design.

Three models on the same data: A (2 features) training AUC 0.74, test 0.73; B (60 features) 0.86 and 0.79; C (5000 features) 1.00 and 0.61. Which overfits? Which would you choose?
A student tries 40 feature sets, keeps the one with the highest test AUC (0.81), and reports 0.81 as the expected performance on new data. What is wrong, and what should they have done?
A paper splits 1 million 200-bp genomic windows at random into 80% training and 20% test. Why might its test AUC be too optimistic? (Hint: how far apart are neighbouring windows, and are they independent?)

B8. Regularisation and cross-validation.

A lasso and a ridge model are fitted to the same 256 4-mer features. One keeps 47 non-zero coefficients, the other 256. Which is which, and why?
In 5-fold cross-validation on 36 000 training windows, how many windows is each model fitted on, and how many models are fitted to choose among 100 values of λ?
Horvath’s methylation clock used elastic net on about 21 000 CpGs and selected 353. Why is regularisation essential when the number of CpGs is comparable to, or larger than, the number of samples?

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
section: Explore: thresholds, ROC and PR under imbalance
text:
Explore: thresholds, ROC and PR under imbalance
The demo simulates the scores of a classifier as two normal distributions with the same spread: closed windows (crimson) around 0 and open windows (green) around the separation. Drag the green circle to change the separation and the green square to change the spread (or use the sliders). Each curve is drawn as a number of windows, so a rare class is a small curve. Drag the black threshold line: windows to its right are called open. On the right are the confusion matrix (expected counts in 10 000 test windows) and the metrics at that threshold. Below are the ROC and PR curves; the circle on each is the current threshold, and you can drag it along either curve. Fraction open sets the class balance from 1% to 50%. The presets give the balanced test set of R6 (46% open), the subsampled test set of R10 (7.7%) and a genome-wide scan (about 1%). Pin these curves keeps a dotted copy for comparison. Simulated test set draws 2000 windows from the model and adds their stepped curves. The default separation (1.53 standard deviations) gives ROC AUC 0.86, about the same as the lasso model of R9.



E1. (links to B4, R5) At the default settings (46% open, threshold 0.77), read TP, FP, FN and TN, and compute precision, recall and FPR from them yourself. Then set the threshold to 0 and to 2. Which metrics go up and which go down? Do the ROC and PR curves change?
E2. (links to B6, R10) Click pin these curves, then subsampled: 7.7% open and genome-wide: 1% open. Note the ROC AUC, the average precision (AP) and, at threshold 0.77, precision and recall. What happens to the ROC curve compared with the pinned one, and to the PR curve? Compare with what the real model did in R10.
E3. (links to B4c, R10b) At 1% open, compare the accuracy at threshold 0.77 with the accuracy of calling every window closed. Then move the threshold to get the highest accuracy you can. What is the recall there?
E4. Go back to 46% open, tick simulated test set and press new sample four times, noting the sample AUC and AP. Then do the same at 1% open (20 open windows among 2000). How much do the two numbers vary from sample to sample?
E5. At 1% open, how large must the separation be for AP to reach 0.5? What ROC AUC does that model have?






Solutions (E1–E5)





E1. TP 3571, FN 1029, FP 1192, TN 4208. Precision \(3571/4763 = 0.750\), recall \(3571/4600 = 0.776\), FPR \(1192/5400 = 0.221\), accuracy 0.778. Threshold 0: recall 0.937, FPR 0.500, precision 0.615, accuracy 0.701. Threshold 2: recall 0.319, FPR 0.023, precision 0.923, accuracy 0.675. A lower threshold calls more windows open: recall and FPR rise and precision falls. A higher threshold does the opposite. The curves do not change: they already contain every threshold, and only the circle moves along them.
E2. The ROC AUC stays 0.860 at all three balances, and the ROC curve lies exactly on the pinned one: TPR is computed among open windows only and FPR among closed windows only, so the ratio between the classes cancels. AP falls from 0.840 to 0.433 to 0.122. At threshold 0.77 recall stays 0.776, but precision falls from 0.750 to 0.227 to 0.034, because the same FPR of 0.221 now applies to many more closed windows (2184 false positives against 78 true ones at 1%). In R10 the real model went from ROC AUC 0.861 and PR AUC 0.835 to 0.871 and 0.412 at 7.7% open: the same pattern, and close to the 0.433 that this model predicts. Always read AP against its baseline, the fraction open (dashed line: 0.46, 0.077, 0.01). An AP of 0.122 at 1% open is 12 times better than random, and still means that most calls are wrong.
E3. At threshold 0.77, accuracy is 0.779, below the 0.990 of calling everything closed (the demo warns you). Accuracy rises as the threshold goes up. It reaches 0.990 at a threshold of about 3.8, where only about 1 of the 100 open windows is called (recall about 0.01). The “most accurate” classifier finds almost nothing, because at 1% open, accuracy mostly counts closed windows.
E4. At 46% open (about 920 open windows), seeds 1–5 give sample AUC 0.856–0.866 and AP 0.828–0.844, close to the exact 0.860 and 0.840. At 1% open (20 open windows) they give AUC 0.836–0.910 and AP 0.084–0.283: the curves are coarse staircases, and AP varies more than threefold. Your numbers depend on how many times you pressed new sample, but the spread will be similar. With few positives, report their number and a confidence interval. The change from 0.861 to 0.871 in R10 (167 open windows) is noise of this kind.
E5. A separation of about 2.56 standard deviations, i.e. ROC AUC 0.965 (and AP 0.96 on a balanced test set). For genome-wide predictions to be mostly right, the ROC AUC must be very high. A model with ROC AUC 0.86, which looks good on a balanced test set, gives AP 0.12 at 1% open.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
In R

R1 — Build the data set: open and closed windows
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
  library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite); library(motifmatchr)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
fa   <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))          # bgzipped + indexed genome
auto <- paste0("chr", 1:22)
bl   <- import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz"))
atac <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")

# positives: 500 bp centred on the summit of each distinct peak (keep the strongest summit)
pk  <- atac[seqnames(atac) %in% auto]
pk  <- pk[order(-pk$signalValue)]
pk  <- pk[!duplicated(paste(seqnames(pk), start(pk), end(pk)))]
pos <- resize(GRanges(seqnames(pk), IRanges(start(pk) + pk$peak, width = 1)), 500, fix = "center")
pos <- pos[!overlapsAny(pos, bl) & countOverlaps(pos, pos) == 1]   # no overlapping windows
set.seed(1)
pos <- sort(pos[sample(length(pos), 20000)])

# negatives: random 500 bp windows, at least 500 bp from any ATAC peak, no blacklist, no N
len <- seqlengths(seqinfo(fa))[auto]
set.seed(2)
chr <- sample(auto, 60000, replace = TRUE, prob = len)
neg <- GRanges(chr, IRanges(floor(runif(60000, 1, len[chr] - 500)), width = 500))
neg <- neg[!overlapsAny(neg, atac, maxgap = 500) & !overlapsAny(neg, bl)]
neg <- neg[letterFrequency(getSeq(fa, neg), "N")[, 1] == 0]
neg <- sort(neg[1:20000])
c(positives = length(pos), negatives = length(neg))
# features: GC fraction, CpG observed/expected, and motif counts for three TFs
jdb  <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
pwms <- do.call(PFMatrixList, lapply(c("MA0139.2", "MA0080.7", "MA0154.5"),
                                     function(id) getMatrixByID(jdb, id)))
names(pwms) <- c("ctcf", "spi1", "ebf1")
features <- function(gr) {
  s  <- getSeq(fa, gr)
  L  <- width(s)
  nc <- letterFrequency(s, "C")[, 1]; ng <- letterFrequency(s, "G")[, 1]
  cg <- vcountPattern("CG", s)
  mc <- as.matrix(motifCounts(matchMotifs(pwms, s, p.cutoff = 5e-5, bg = "even", out = "scores")))
  colnames(mc) <- names(pwms)
  data.frame(chrom = as.character(seqnames(gr)), start = start(gr) - 1, end = end(gr),
             gc = (nc + ng) / L, cpg_oe = cg * L / pmax(nc * ng, 1), mc)
}
dat <- rbind(cbind(features(pos), open = 1), cbind(features(neg), open = 0))
saveRDS(dat, "ml_atac.rds")
head(dat, 3)
This takes one to two minutes. It is the only step that needs the genome; everything after it reads ml_atac.rds.

Explain each filter applied to the positives and to the negatives. Why are negatives kept at least 500 bp away from any ATAC peak, and why are windows that overlap another window dropped?
Why is the summit start(pk) + pk$peak and not start(pk) + pk$peak + 1? (Recall Genomic intervals, R1.)
Look at the three rows printed. Compute GC and CpG o/e for a window yourself from getSeq(fa, ...) for the first row and check them against the table.

The motif features are deliberately counts of matches at a strict cutoff (motifCounts, p < 5 × 10⁻⁵). If you want a continuous motif score instead, use motifScores with p.cutoff = 1: with a strict cutoff every window without a match gets score 0, and the ranking is lost (see What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works, R2, and How a CNN reads DNA).


R2 — Look at the data before modelling
dat <- readRDS("ml_atac.rds")
table(dat$open)
aggregate(cbind(gc, cpg_oe, ctcf, spi1, ebf1) ~ open, data = dat, FUN = mean)
aggregate(cbind(ctcf > 0, spi1 > 0, ebf1 > 0) ~ open, data = dat, FUN = mean)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
boxplot(gc ~ open, dat, names = c("closed", "open"), main = "GC fraction")
boxplot(cpg_oe ~ open, dat, names = c("closed", "open"), main = "CpG o/e")
barplot(t(as.matrix(aggregate(cbind(ctcf, spi1, ebf1) ~ open, dat, mean)[, -1])),
        beside = TRUE, names.arg = c("closed", "open"), legend.text = c("CTCF", "SPI1", "EBF1"),
        main = "motif matches per window")

Which feature differs most between open and closed windows, judged by eye? Which motif is most enriched in open windows (ratio of the fractions)?
About three quarters of open windows have no CTCF match. Does that make CTCF a poor feature?



R3 — Split by chromosome and fit a logistic regression
test  <- dat$chrom %in% c("chr8", "chr9")
train <- dat[!test, ]
tst   <- dat[test, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(tst))

m1 <- glm(open ~ gc, family = binomial, data = train)
coef(m1)
p1 <- predict(m1, newdata = tst, type = "response")     # P(open) for the test windows
summary(p1)

How many training and test windows are there? What fraction of the test windows is open?
Write the fitted model as an equation. Use it to compute, by hand, P(open) for a window with GC 0.40 and one with GC 0.60. Check with predict(m1, data.frame(gc = c(0.4, 0.6)), type = "response").



R4 — Fitting by hand: gradient descent
X <- cbind(1, train$gc)                        # design matrix: intercept and GC
y <- train$open
sigmoid  <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
log_loss <- function(b) { p <- sigmoid(X %*% b); -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p)) }

b  <- c(0, 0)                                  # start somewhere
lr <- 5                                        # learning rate: the step size
for (i in 1:2000) {
  grad <- crossprod(X, sigmoid(X %*% b) - y) / nrow(X)   # slope of the loss
  b    <- b - lr * grad                                  # step downhill
  if (i %in% c(1, 10, 100, 500, 2000)) cat(i, round(b, 3), round(log_loss(b), 4), "\n")
}
c(gradient_descent = b, glm = coef(m1))

How does the loss change over the iterations? After how many steps are the coefficients within 0.01 of glm’s?
Rerun with lr <- 50 and with lr <- 0.5. What happens in each case, and why?
The loss at the start, with both coefficients 0, is 0.693. Why exactly that number?



R5 — From probabilities to calls: the confusion matrix
call <- as.integer(p1 >= 0.5)
table(true = tst$open, predicted = call)
TP <- sum(call == 1 & tst$open == 1); FP <- sum(call == 1 & tst$open == 0)
FN <- sum(call == 0 & tst$open == 1); TN <- sum(call == 0 & tst$open == 0)
round(c(accuracy  = (TP + TN) / nrow(tst),
        precision = TP / (TP + FP),
        recall    = TP / (TP + FN),
        FPR       = FP / (FP + TN)), 3)

Fill in the confusion matrix and check the four metrics by hand.
Change the threshold to 0.3 and to 0.7. Which metrics go up and which go down?



R6 — ROC and precision–recall curves, coded by hand
curves <- function(score, label) {
  o  <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)         # walk down the ranked list
  s  <- score[o]; l <- label[o]
  tp <- cumsum(l); fp <- cumsum(1 - l)
  k  <- c(diff(s) != 0, TRUE)                   # tied scores: one threshold, one point
  data.frame(threshold = s[k], tpr = tp[k] / sum(l), fpr = fp[k] / sum(1 - l),
             precision = tp[k] / (tp[k] + fp[k]))
}
auc_roc  <- function(cv) sum(diff(c(0, cv$fpr)) * (cv$tpr + c(0, head(cv$tpr, -1))) / 2)  # trapezoids
avg_prec <- function(cv) sum(diff(c(0, cv$tpr)) * cv$precision)   # area under the PR steps
c1 <- curves(p1, tst$open)
c(ROC_AUC = auc_roc(c1), PR_AUC = avg_prec(c1))
pROC::auc(tst$open, p1, quiet = TRUE)                          # check with a package
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(c1$fpr, c1$tpr, type = "l", xlab = "FPR", ylab = "TPR", main = "ROC"); abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
plot(c1$tpr, c1$precision, type = "l", xlab = "recall", ylab = "precision", main = "PR", ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(h = mean(tst$open), lty = 2)

What are the ROC AUC and PR AUC of the GC model? Does your ROC AUC agree with pROC::auc?
Ties: GC is a count divided by 500, so many windows have exactly the same GC. Remove the line k <- c(diff(s) != 0, TRUE) (and the [k]s) to break ties by row order instead, and recompute. Why does the AUC go up? (Look at the order of the rows in dat.)
Where on the PR plot does the dashed line sit, and what does it represent?



R7 — More features, and baselines
models <- list(gc = open ~ gc, gc_cpg = open ~ gc + cpg_oe, motifs = open ~ ctcf + spi1 + ebf1,
               all = open ~ gc + cpg_oe + ctcf + spi1 + ebf1)
set.seed(7)
scores <- c(list(coin_flip = runif(nrow(tst))),
            lapply(models, function(f) predict(glm(f, binomial, train), tst)))
t(sapply(scores, function(s) { cv <- curves(s, tst$open)
  round(c(ROC_AUC = auc_roc(cv), PR_AUC = avg_prec(cv)), 3) }))
m_all <- glm(models$all, binomial, train)
round(summary(m_all)$coefficients, 3)
round(exp(coef(m_all)), 2)                     # odds ratios

Rank the models by ROC AUC. How much does CpG o/e add to GC? How much do the motifs add?
The three-motif model has a lower AUC than GC alone, but its coefficients are large. Explain how both can be true.
Interpret the odds ratio for ctcf in one sentence. Why is the odds ratio for gc so large (3105), and what is it per 0.1 increase in GC?



R8 — Overfitting: many features, few examples
s4  <- getSeq(fa, GRanges(dat$chrom, IRanges(dat$start + 1, dat$end)))
kmr <- lapply(1:4, function(k) oligonucleotideFrequency(s4, k, as.prob = TRUE))
sapply(kmr, ncol)                              # 4, 16, 64, 256 features
set.seed(3)
small <- sample(which(!test), 500)             # only 500 training windows
over <- t(sapply(1:4, function(k) {
  d <- data.frame(open = dat$open, kmr[[k]])
  m <- suppressWarnings(glm(open ~ ., binomial, d[small, ]))
  c(k = k, features = ncol(kmr[[k]]),
    train_AUC = auc_roc(curves(predict(m, d[small, ]), dat$open[small])),
    test_AUC  = auc_roc(curves(suppressWarnings(predict(m, d[test, ])), dat$open[test])))
}))
round(over, 3)

Describe how training and test AUC change as the number of features grows. Which model would you choose, and which would you have chosen if you had looked only at training AUC?
Why does the 256-feature model fit the training data perfectly? (Count parameters and examples.)
Ignore the glm.fit warnings for k = 4 and say what they mean: “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”.



R9 — Regularisation and cross-validation with glmnet
library(glmnet)
X4   <- kmr[[4]]
fold <- match(dat$chrom, paste0("chr", 1:22)) %% 5 + 1     # 5 folds = 5 groups of chromosomes
table(fold[!test])
ridge <- cv.glmnet(X4[small, ], dat$open[small], family = "binomial", alpha = 0, foldid = fold[small])
lasso <- cv.glmnet(X4[small, ], dat$open[small], family = "binomial", alpha = 1, foldid = fold[small])
c(ridge = auc_roc(curves(as.numeric(predict(ridge, X4[test, ], s = "lambda.min")), dat$open[test])),
  lasso = auc_roc(curves(as.numeric(predict(lasso, X4[test, ], s = "lambda.min")), dat$open[test])))
c(ridge_nonzero = sum(coef(ridge, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0),
  lasso_nonzero = sum(coef(lasso, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot(lasso); plot(lasso$glmnet.fit, xvar = "lambda")
# all training windows, 4-mers plus the five hand-made features
Xall <- cbind(X4, as.matrix(dat[, c("gc", "cpg_oe", "ctcf", "spi1", "ebf1")]))
big <- cv.glmnet(Xall[!test, ], dat$open[!test], family = "binomial", alpha = 1, foldid = fold[!test])
p_big <- as.numeric(predict(big, Xall[test, ], s = "lambda.min"))
c1b <- curves(p_big, dat$open[test])
c(ROC_AUC = auc_roc(c1b), PR_AUC = avg_prec(c1b), nonzero = sum(coef(big, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0))

Compare the test AUC of ridge and lasso on the 500 windows with the unpenalised 256-feature model of R8. How many 4-mers does the lasso keep?
Look at plot(lasso): which λ does cross-validation choose, and how does the curve behave at the extremes?
The second chunk uses all 36 317 training windows. Compare its test ROC AUC with the five-feature glm of R7. Which of the two would you report as your model, and with which baseline next to it?



R10 — Class imbalance
set.seed(6)
keep <- which(tst$open == 0 | runif(nrow(tst)) < 0.1)   # keep all closed, 10% of open windows
mean(tst$open[keep])                                     # new fraction of positives
ci <- curves(p_big[keep], tst$open[keep])
rbind(balanced = c(ROC_AUC = auc_roc(c1b), PR_AUC = avg_prec(c1b)),
      imbalanced = c(auc_roc(ci), avg_prec(ci)))
mean(tst$open[keep] == 0)                                # accuracy of "always closed"

What fraction of the windows are open after subsampling? How do ROC AUC and PR AUC change, compared with the balanced test set?
What is the accuracy of a “model” that calls every window closed? Would you be impressed by a paper reporting 92% accuracy on this test set?

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — logistic regression (B2, R3, R7)





\(P = 1/(1 + e^{-\text{score}})\); odds \(= P/(1-P) = e^{\text{score}}\). Adding \(b\) to the score multiplies the odds by \(e^b\), whatever the starting point; the change in probability depends on where you start. In R, glm(..., family = binomial) fits the model and predict(..., type = "response") returns probabilities (the default, type = "link", returns the score). A friendly introduction: chapter 4 of An Introduction to Statistical Learning, free online.









Hint 2 — loss and gradient descent (B3, R4)





Use natural logarithms: \(-\log(0.5) = 0.693\). In gradient descent the step is learning rate × slope: too large and each step jumps over the valley to a higher point on the other side; too small and progress is slow. crossprod(X, r) is \(X^\top r\).









Hint 3 — confusion matrix and curves (B4–B6, R5, R6, R10)





Write the 2 × 2 table first, with row sums P and N. ROC: each open window moves the curve up by \(1/P\), each closed window right by \(1/N\). AUC by pairs: for each open window, count the closed windows with a lower score; add up; divide by \(P \times N\) (a tie counts ½). Precision depends on how many closed windows there are; TPR and FPR do not. Background: Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015; pROC::auc.









Hint 4 — overfitting, regularisation, CV (B7, B8, R8, R9)





Count parameters (one per feature, plus the intercept) and compare with the number of training examples. cv.glmnet fits the lasso (alpha = 1) or ridge (alpha = 0) for a sequence of λ values on each fold; foldid sets which fold each example belongs to; s = "lambda.min" uses the λ with the best cross-validated score. See the glmnet vignette.









Hint 5 — building the data (R1)





resize(..., fix = "center") makes a window around a point; overlapsAny(..., maxgap = 500) counts ranges within 500 bp as overlapping; getSeq on a FaFile reads only the windows you ask for; letterFrequency, vcountPattern and oligonucleotideFrequency count letters, a pattern and all k-mers; matchMotifs scans PWMs as in Gene regulation.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Examples: CpGs in individuals (400 000 CpGs × 10 people, or 400 000 if averaged). Features: window GC, CpG island (0/1), log distance to TSS. Label: methylated (β > 0.5) or not. Parameters: 4 (intercept + one per feature). Note that all three features are the same for every person: such a model can predict which CpGs are methylated, but nothing about differences between people. (b) GC \(= 250/500 = 0.50\), CpG o/e \(= 18 \times 500 / (130 \times 120) = 0.58\): close to the classic CpG island criteria (GC > 0.5, o/e > 0.6). The second: GC 0.41, o/e \(= 5 \times 500 / (100 \times 105) = 0.24\), typical bulk genome. (c) The feature is a measurement of the label itself. It would make the model look excellent, but it is not available for the CpGs and people we want to predict: leakage.
B2. (a) \(-4.20 + 8.04 \times 0.45 + 0.97 \times 0.30 = -0.29\); \(P = 1/(1 + e^{0.29}) = 0.43\). (b) Score \(-0.29 + 1.41 = 1.12\), \(P = 0.75\). The odds are multiplied by \(e^{1.41} = 4.1\) (from 0.75 to 3.1); the probability by only \(0.75/0.43 = 1.76\), because the logistic curve flattens towards 1. The odds ratio is the same for every window; the change in probability is not. (c) \(1.41 / 0.60 = 2.35\): two matches add 1.20, three add 1.80, so three. (d) \(e^{8.04 \times 0.1} = e^{0.80} = 2.2\).
B3. (a) \(-\log 0.8 = 0.22\), \(-\log 0.7 = 0.36\), \(-\log 0.1 = 2.30\); mean 0.96. (b) The constant model has loss 0.69 for each window, mean 0.69: better than our model, because of the third window, where the model was confident and wrong. Log-loss punishes overconfidence.
B4. (a) TP 150, FP 100, FN 50, TN 700. (b) Accuracy 0.85, precision 0.60, recall 0.75, FPR 0.125, \(F_1 = 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.75 / 1.35 = 0.67\). (c) 800/1000 = 0.80: almost as good as the model by accuracy, while finding no open window at all. With imbalanced classes, accuracy mostly measures the majority class.
B5. (a) (0, 0.25), (0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.5), (0.25, 0.75), (0.5, 0.75), (0.5, 1), (0.75, 1), (1, 1), starting from (0, 0). (b) The open window at 0.92 beats all 4 closed; 0.77 beats 3 (0.50, 0.33, 0.12); 0.64 beats 3; 0.41 beats 2: \(12/16 = 0.75\). (c) Calls 0.92, 0.85, 0.77, 0.64: TP 3, FP 1, FN 1: precision 0.75, recall 0.75. (d) Open windows at ranks 1, 3, 4, 6: precision 1/1, 2/3, 3/4, 4/6; mean \((1 + 0.667 + 0.75 + 0.667)/4 = 0.77\).
B6. (a) TP \(0.8 \times 1000 = 800\), FP \(0.05 \times 1000 = 50\), precision \(800/850 = 0.94\). (b) TP 800, FP \(0.05 \times 99\,000 = 4950\), precision \(800/5750 = 0.14\): six of seven calls are wrong. (c) The ROC curve is the same (TPR and FPR are each computed within one class). The PR curve drops, because precision depends on how many negatives there are.
B7. (a) C overfits badly (perfect training, worst test); B overfits a little (gap 0.07) but generalises best. Choose B, but the choice should be made on validation data or by cross-validation, keeping the test set for the final number. (b) The test set has become part of model selection: picking the best of 40 rewards luck as well as quality, so 0.81 is optimistic. Select with cross-validation or a validation set, then evaluate the single chosen model once on the test set. (c) Neighbouring windows overlap or share their surroundings (same peak, same domain, similar GC), and their labels are correlated. A random split puts near-copies on both sides, so the test set is not new. Split by chromosome (or by region).
B8. (a) The lasso keeps 47: the absolute-value penalty has a corner at 0, so it sets weak coefficients exactly to 0. Ridge shrinks all 256 towards 0 but none to exactly 0. (b) Each fit uses 4/5 of the data, 28 800 windows; 5 folds × 100 λ = 500 fits (glmnet computes each fold’s whole λ path in one go), plus a final fit on all training data at the chosen λ. (c) With as many or more CpGs than samples, there are infinitely many coefficient vectors that fit the training data perfectly; the penalty picks a small, stable one and, with L1, a short list of CpGs. Neighbouring CpGs are also strongly correlated, which makes unpenalised coefficients unstable.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Positives: one summit per distinct peak region (the ENCODE file lists many regions several times with different summits), autosomes only, no blacklist overlap, and no window overlapping another, so that no two examples share sequence. Negatives: random windows on the same chromosomes, in proportion to their length, at least 500 bp from any ATAC peak (so that the flanks of peaks are not labelled closed), not blacklisted, and without N (unsequenced gaps would give meaningless features). Of 60 000 candidates, about 53 000 pass; the first 20 000 are kept. (b) import() already added 1 to the BED start, so start(pk) + pk$peak is the 1-based position of the summit base (file start + peak + 1). (c) s <- getSeq(fa, GRanges("chr9", IRanges(88582, 89081))), then letterFrequency(s, "GC") / 500 gives 0.44 and vcountPattern("CG", s) * 500 / (letterFrequency(s, "C") * letterFrequency(s, "G")) gives 0.374.
R2. (a) GC (mean 0.50 open vs 0.41 closed) and CpG o/e (0.34 vs 0.20) shift most. CTCF is the most enriched motif: 26% of open windows vs 5.2% of closed (5×); EBF1 12% vs 5.2% (2.4×); SPI1 28% vs 16% (1.7×). (b) No. A feature can be informative without being present in every positive: among windows with a CTCF match, \(0.26/(0.26 + 0.052) = 83\%\) are open (in this balanced set). Open chromatin has many causes; CTCF is one.
R3. (a) 36 317 training and 3683 test windows; 1692 test windows are open (46%). (b) \(\text{score} = -4.57 + 10.28\,\text{GC}\). GC 0.40: score \(-0.46\), \(P = 0.39\); GC 0.60: score 1.60, \(P = 0.83\).
R4. (a) The loss falls from 0.693 to 0.6907 after one step, 0.607 after 100, 0.590 after 500, and stays at 0.5898; the coefficients are within 0.01 of glm’s after 1111 steps and equal to four digits after 2000 (−4.5744, 10.2845). (b) lr <- 50: the steps overshoot. After one step the loss is 0.735, after two 4.8, after three 10.4; the coefficients jump back and forth across the valley and never settle (after 2000 steps −52, 91, loss 4.5). lr <- 0.5: every step is ten times smaller; after 2000 steps the coefficients are −3.56 and 8.00, loss 0.594, still on the way down. Choosing the learning rate is a real problem when training neural networks. (c) With \(b = (0, 0)\) every window gets \(P = 0.5\), and \(-\log 0.5 = \log 2 = 0.693\).
R5. (a) TN 1441, FP 550, FN 756, TP 936: accuracy \(2377/3683 = 0.645\), precision \(936/1486 = 0.630\), recall \(936/1692 = 0.553\), FPR \(550/1991 = 0.276\). (b) Threshold 0.3: recall 0.907 and FPR 0.696 rise, precision falls to 0.526, accuracy 0.581. Threshold 0.7: recall 0.302 and FPR 0.070 fall, precision rises to 0.786, accuracy 0.642. Precision and recall pull in opposite directions.
R6. (a) ROC AUC 0.712, PR AUC 0.698; pROC::auc gives 0.7124, the same. (b) GC takes only 284 distinct values among the 3683 test windows, so ties are common. Broken by row order, the AUC of the GC model rises to 0.715, and that of the motif model in R7 from 0.667 to 0.856: 62% of test windows have no motif match and the same score, and because all open windows come first in dat, every tie is broken in favour of the positives. Tied scores must move the curve up and right together (a diagonal step), which is what k does. (c) At 0.46, the fraction of open windows: the precision of a model that ranks at random.
R7. (a) ROC AUC (PR AUC): coin flip 0.507 (0.463), motifs 0.667 (0.617), GC 0.712 (0.698), GC + CpG 0.713 (0.703), all five 0.764 (0.748). CpG o/e adds almost nothing once GC is known (they are correlated); the motifs add 0.05 on top of GC. (b) A motif match is strong evidence (odds × 4 for CTCF), but 62% of windows have no match for any of the three motifs, and the model can say nothing about them. Large coefficients on rare features give confident predictions for few windows; AUC measures the ranking of all windows. (c) “Each additional CTCF match multiplies the odds that a window is open by 4.1, at fixed GC, CpG o/e and other motif counts.” The GC odds ratio (3105) is per unit of GC, i.e. from 0 to 1, a range no window spans; per 0.1 it is \(e^{0.804} = 2.2\).
R8. (a) Training AUC rises steadily: 0.716, 0.779, 0.857, 1.000. Test AUC: 0.713, 0.740, 0.738, 0.618: best at 16–64 features, worst at 256. Training AUC would have picked the 256-feature model, the worst on new data. (b) 257 parameters for 500 windows: enough freedom to find coefficients that put every training window on the right side of the boundary (the classes are linearly separable in the training set). (c) The warning means perfect separation: the likelihood keeps improving as the coefficients grow, so they run off towards ±∞ and the fit has no finite optimum. A sign of overfitting.
R9. (a) Ridge 0.779 and lasso 0.761 on the test chromosomes, against 0.618 for the unpenalised fit with the same 256 features and 500 windows. The lasso keeps 47 of 256 4-mers. (b) plot(lasso) shows the cross-validated binomial deviance (lower is better) against \(\log \lambda\), with dashed lines at lambda.min and lambda.1se. It is high at large λ (all coefficients 0: too simple), falls to a minimum, and rises again at small λ (overfitting). (c) All training data, 4-mers plus the five features: ROC AUC 0.861, PR AUC 0.835, with 204 non-zero coefficients, against 0.764 for the five-feature glm. Report the lasso model, with the GC-only model (0.712) and the coin flip as baselines.
R10. (a) 7.7% open. ROC AUC 0.861 → 0.871 (the difference is sampling noise: only 167 open windows remain); PR AUC 0.835 → 0.412. (b) 92.3%. Not impressive at all: it is the fraction of closed windows. Ask for the PR AUC, precision at a useful recall, and the prevalence.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Where this leads

What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works asks what changes when the negatives are GC-matched, when windows overlap, and when the test cell type is different.
How a CNN reads DNA replaces the hand-made features by filters that the network learns, trained by the same gradient descent (R4).
Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers uses the elastic net (R9) to predict age from methylation.

title: Exercise: Machine learning from scratch
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Libbrecht & Noble 2015, Nat Rev Genet. Machine learning applications in genetics and genomics.
Greener et al. 2022, Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol. A guide to machine learning for biologists.
Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, J Stat Softw. Regularization paths for generalized linear models via coordinate descent.
Horvath 2013, Genome Biol. DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types.
Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015, PLoS ONE. The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets.

title: Quiz: machine learning from scratch
text:
Short questions on supervised learning, logistic regression, overfitting and classifier metrics. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A study predicts whether each 200-bp window of the genome is bound by CTCF in K562, from the counts of all 6-mers in the window. Name the examples, the features, the label and the parameters of a logistic regression. How many parameters are there?






Hint





How many different 6-mers are there? Do not forget the intercept.









Answer





Examples: the 200-bp windows. Features: the 6-mer counts, \(4^6 = 4096\) of them. Label: bound (1) or not (0), from CTCF ChIP-seq peaks in K562. Parameters: one coefficient per 6-mer plus the intercept, 4097.




Q2. A logistic regression gives a window the score \(-1\). What is P(bound)? A feature with coefficient 0.7 increases by 1. What happens to the odds, and what is the new probability?






Answer





\(P = 1/(1 + e^{1}) = 0.27\). The odds are multiplied by \(e^{0.7} = 2.0\) (from 0.37 to 0.74); the new score is \(-0.3\) and \(P = 1/(1 + e^{0.3}) = 0.43\).




Q3. A model predicts P(open) = 0.95 for a window that is closed. What is its log-loss? Compare with the log-loss of predicting 0.5.






Answer





\(-\log(1 - 0.95) = -\log 0.05 = 3.0\), against \(-\log 0.5 = 0.69\). Being confidently wrong costs more than four times as much as saying “I don’t know”.




Q4. On 500 test windows (100 bound, 400 unbound) a classifier calls 120 windows bound, 80 of them correctly. Give TP, FP, FN, TN, precision, recall, FPR and accuracy.






Answer





TP 80, FP 40, FN 20, TN 360. Precision \(80/120 = 0.67\), recall \(80/100 = 0.80\), FPR \(40/400 = 0.10\), accuracy \(440/500 = 0.88\).




Q5. Six test windows, sorted by score: open, open, closed, open, closed, closed. Draw the ROC curve and give its AUC.






Hint





Up by 1/3 for each open window, right by 1/3 for each closed one. Or count (open, closed) pairs in the right order.









Answer





Points (0, 0), (0, 1/3), (0, 2/3), (1/3, 2/3), (1/3, 1), (2/3, 1), (1, 1). Pairs: the first two open windows beat all 3 closed ones (6 pairs), the third open beats 2: 8 of 9, AUC \(= 0.89\).




Q6. Two papers predict enhancers. Paper A reports ROC AUC 0.92 on a test set with one enhancer per non-enhancer; paper B reports ROC AUC 0.90 and PR AUC 0.35 on a test set with one enhancer per 50 non-enhancers. Can you say which model is better? What would you ask for?






Answer





Not from these numbers. ROC AUCs are roughly comparable across class ratios (0.92 vs 0.90 is a small difference, and the test sets differ in other ways too). PR AUCs depend strongly on the fraction of positives: paper B’s 0.35 is far above its baseline of 1/51 = 0.02, and paper A’s PR AUC is not given (its baseline would be 0.5). Ask for both models evaluated on the same test set, with the same class ratio, ideally the realistic one, and with a simple baseline (GC, motif presence).




Q7. A model with 10 000 features is trained on 300 samples. Training accuracy is 100%, test accuracy 58%, in a balanced two-class problem. What happened, and name two remedies.






Answer





Overfitting: with far more parameters than samples the model can fit the training labels perfectly, including noise, and the fit does not generalise (58% is barely above the 50% of guessing). Remedies: regularisation (lasso, ridge or elastic net, with λ chosen by cross-validation), fewer features (chosen inside the cross-validation, not on all data), or more samples.




Q8. What is the difference between the lasso (L1) and ridge (L2) penalties in what they do to the coefficients? Which one would you use to obtain a short list of CpGs for an epigenetic clock?






Answer





Both shrink coefficients towards 0; the lasso sets many of them exactly to 0 (feature selection), ridge keeps all of them small but non-zero. For a short list of CpGs: the lasso, or the elastic net (a mix of both, as in Horvath’s clock), which keeps the selection but behaves better when CpGs are correlated.




Q9. A student tunes λ by trying 50 values and picking the one with the best AUC on the test chromosomes, then reports that AUC. What is wrong? How should λ be chosen?






Answer





The test set was used to choose the model, so the reported AUC is optimistically biased: it is the best of 50 tries, partly by luck. Choose λ by cross-validation within the training chromosomes (folds made of whole chromosomes), then evaluate the chosen model once on the test chromosomes.




Q10. In the lecture, the GC-only model had ROC AUC 0.71 for open vs closed windows. A new model reaches 0.73. Is that a good result? What is the baseline here, and what other information would you want?






Answer





It is only 0.02 above a one-feature baseline, so it adds little beyond GC content; whether that difference is real needs an uncertainty estimate (e.g. a bootstrap of the test windows, or several held-out chromosomes). Also ask how the negatives were chosen: with random-genome negatives, GC alone separates the classes well, and a model can look good by learning GC. With GC-matched negatives the comparison would be fairer (next unit).

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
About this lecture
Machine learning from scratch fitted a logistic regression on features we chose (GC content, motif counts). A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns its own features directly from the DNA sequence. This lecture opens the box:

One-hot encoding: DNA as a matrix of numbers.
A convolutional filter is a PWM that slides along the sequence; ReLU and max pooling turn its scores into “is the motif there?”.
A dense layer with a sigmoid on top: logistic regression on learned features.
Training: loss, gradient descent, epochs, validation, early stopping, in pictures.
Real data: a small CNN that tells GM12878 CTCF peaks from GC-matched background, its test performance, and what its filters learned.


This is the third unit of the machine-learning block. Students have seen supervised learning, logistic regression, train/validation/test splits by chromosome, overfitting and ROC curves in Machine learning from scratch, and the map of prediction tasks and the evaluation traps in What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works. Here we take one task, TF binding from sequence, and one model class, the CNN, and look inside it. No equations beyond what they know from logistic regression: the point is that every piece of a CNN maps onto something from the motif units (Gene regulation; Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting). The exercise trains exactly the model described here, in R with the torch package, on a laptop CPU in about five minutes. The next unit, What did the model learn? Variant effects, interprets this trained model and uses it to score genetic variants.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: The task: is this 200 bp bound by CTCF?
text:
The task: is this 200 bp bound by CTCF?


Positives: 200 bp centred on each of the 44 217 GM12878 CTCF peak summits. Negatives: random windows with the same GC distribution, more than 1 kb from any peak.
Split by chromosome: train on 20, validate on chr7, test on chr8 + chr9, as in Machine learning from scratch.
Balanced classes: 44 217 positives, 43 586 negatives.


Same framing as the earlier ML units: GM12878, held-out chromosomes, GC-matched negatives. Why GC-matched: CTCF peaks are GC-rich (51% against a genome average of 41%), so with random background a model can score well by learning GC content alone; What people try to predict showed this with logistic regression. With matched negatives, GC content has a test AUC of 0.51: whatever the model learns must be sequence beyond composition. Why whole chromosomes: neighbouring windows share sequence and repeats; splitting by chromosome keeps any test sequence far from every training sequence. Numbers per split: train 38 270 positives and 37 745 negatives, validation (chr7) 2169 and 2141, test (chr8 + chr9) 3778 and 3700. A few GC bins have fewer candidate background windows than peaks, which is why there are 631 fewer negatives than positives. Simplification: the labels come from one ChIP-seq experiment thresholded by IDR, so some “negatives” are weakly bound sites and some peaks are noise; every model inherits this label noise.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: The baseline: scan with the CTCF PWM
text:
The baseline: scan with the CTCF PWM


Score each window by its best match to the JASPAR CTCF matrix (both strands): test AUC 0.93.
A strong baseline, but the distributions overlap: some peaks have only a weak match, and some background windows a good one.
Can a model that learns its motifs from the 76 000 training sequences do better?


This is the PWM from Gene regulation: log-odds weights summed over 15 positions, maximum over all windows and both strands. motifmatchr reports that maximum with out = “scores”, but only for windows that contain a match above its p-value cutoff, unless p.cutoff = 1: with the default, 62% of test windows get a score of 0 and the AUC drops to 0.84, a trap the exercise shows. Medians: 13.1 in peaks and 2.0 in background. The AUC of 0.93 is the number to beat; any CNN result should be reported next to such a simple baseline, as the earlier ML units insisted. Why the PWM is imperfect: it was built from 913 sites and summarises CTCF in 15 independent columns; it ignores the flanks (CTCF has an upstream motif module bound by more zinc fingers), it cannot use any other sequence features of bound sites, and a peak without a strong match may be bound through a weaker site or indirectly. A model trained on these peaks can learn all of that, but it can also learn the biases of this experiment; we come back to that.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
DNA as numbers: one-hot encoding


Each base becomes a column with one 1 and three 0s: a 200-bp sequence is a 4 × 200 matrix.
No base is “bigger” than another (coding A = 1, C = 2, G = 3, T = 4 would invent an order).
This is the input to every sequence model in this lecture, from our 2 500-parameter CNN to AlphaGenome.


One-hot encoding is the same idea as dummy variables for a factor in a linear model: a factor with four levels becomes indicator columns. Here we keep all four (no reference level) because we never fit an intercept per position. An N is either all zeros (Enformer) or 0.25 in every row; we removed windows with N. The order of rows does not matter, but must be fixed: A, C, G, T in this course, like a PWM. A batch of sequences is a 3-dimensional array: sequences × 4 × positions. In torch this is the layout that nn_conv1d expects (batch, channels, length): the four bases are the input channels, like the red, green and blue channels of an image.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: A convolutional filter is a PWM
text:
A convolutional filter is a PWM


A filter is a 4 × k matrix of weights, like a PWM. Multiply it element-wise with a one-hot window and add everything up.
Only the weight of the base that is present survives in each column: the result is the PWM score of the window.
Difference: a PWM is computed from known sites; a filter’s weights are learned from labelled sequences.


Work through the figure: the toy filter prefers C, C, A, G (+2 each), and every other base costs −1. The window CCAG scores 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, the maximum. This is the scalar product of two 4 × 4 matrices, which is why a convolutional layer is just many such products. The link to Gene regulation is exact: there, a PWM weight was log2(p/q) from counts; here the weights can be any real numbers, chosen by training so that the network’s predictions are good. Nothing forces them to look like log-odds, and they are on an arbitrary scale; that is why, to compare a filter with JASPAR, we later look at the sequences that activate it rather than at the raw weights. The exercise B2 does this calculation by hand.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Sliding the filter: convolution


Slide the filter one base at a time and record the score at each position: an activation track. A width-19 filter on 200 bp gives 182 scores.
A match scores high (CCAG: 8); one mismatch scores less (CCTG: 5); unrelated sequence is negative.
A filter reads one strand. A site on the other strand needs another filter (the reverse complement), which the network learns too.


“Convolution” is the name from signal processing (strictly, deep-learning libraries compute a cross-correlation; the difference is only whether the filter is flipped and does not matter when the weights are learned). The same weights are used at every position: this weight sharing is why a CNN can find a motif anywhere in the window with few parameters, and it is exactly what a PWM scan does. Length: L − k + 1 positions without padding. Strands: the toy filter does not see CTGG, the reverse complement of CCAG. CTCF sites occur in both orientations, so the trained network ends up with filters for both: we will see that in its filters. Some models build in strand symmetry (for example by scoring the reverse complement too and averaging); ours simply learns both.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Bias, ReLU and max pooling


Add a bias (one per filter): a learned threshold. ReLU, max(0, x), keeps only the positions that pass it.
Max pooling keeps the largest value: with global max pooling, one number per filter says how well its motif is present anywhere in the window.
This is a PWM scan with a threshold, as in Gene regulation, except that threshold and weights are learned.


ReLU (rectified linear unit) is the simplest non-linearity: without it, stacking layers would collapse into one linear function. The bias of −5 makes the toy filter strict: only a perfect CCAG passes. With −4, the one-mismatch CCTG would also count, with activation 1. Max pooling over a short window (say 4 or 10 positions) keeps rough positions and is used between layers in deeper networks (DeepSEA, Basset); global max pooling throws position away completely, which suits a question like “is there a CTCF site anywhere in these 200 bp?”. Our exercise model uses global max pooling. Other choices: average pooling (how much motif overall), or keeping all positions for a dense layer (position-specific, more parameters).

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
The whole network


32 filters of width 19 → ReLU → global max pool → 32 numbers → a dense layer with a sigmoid → P(bound).
The last step is logistic regression, with the 32 filter outputs as its features. Training learns the filters and the regression weights together.
2 497 parameters, trained on 76 015 sequences.


This is the exact model of the exercise. Count the parameters: each filter has 4 × 19 = 76 weights and one bias, so 32 × 77 = 2464; the dense layer has 32 weights and one bias. That is tiny by deep-learning standards (DeepSEA had tens of millions, Enformer about 250 million), which is why it trains on a laptop. Compare with Machine learning from scratch: there, the features were chosen by hand (GC, CpG o/e, three motif counts, or 256 4-mer counts) and only the regression weights were fitted. Here the features themselves are fitted. The word “deep” means more layers between the input and the final regression; each layer is the same kind of operation. The output is a logit z (log-odds of being bound), turned into a probability by the sigmoid, exactly as in logistic regression; in the next unit we will work on the logit scale.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Deeper layers combine motifs


A second convolutional layer reads the activation tracks of the first layer: its filters respond to combinations of motifs at a given spacing and orientation.
That is the “motif grammar” a PWM cannot represent: pairs of TFs, helical spacing, a required partner.
More layers also see further: each layer widens the stretch of DNA that one output depends on (its receptive field).


Layer 1 learns motifs; layer 2 learns arrangements of motifs; further layers, arrangements of arrangements. This is the general architecture of DeepSEA, Basset and their successors (three or more convolutional layers with pooling in between). For CTCF a second layer could, for example, learn the core motif together with the upstream motif module that some CTCF sites have about 20 bp away. Our exercise model has a single convolutional layer on purpose: it is easy to interpret (each filter is a motif, and the output is a weighted sum of motif presence), and for CTCF most of the information is in one long motif. The receptive field of a stack of layers grows with depth and with pooling; BPNet and Enformer grow it with dilated convolutions or attention, as we will see at the end and in the next unit.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: How wrong is a prediction? The loss
text:
How wrong is a prediction? The loss


The binary cross-entropy (log loss) from Machine learning from scratch: small when confident and right, very large when confident and wrong.
The network’s loss is the average over the sequences. Training = finding weights that make it small.
Reference values: 0.693 for always predicting 0.5; our trained CNN reaches about 0.20 on the validation chromosome.


This is the same loss that glm() minimises for logistic regression (it is minus the log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model). Two examples: a bound site predicted at 0.9 costs −log 0.9 = 0.11; predicted at 0.1 it costs 2.30. A balanced data set predicted at 0.5 everywhere costs log 2 = 0.693 per sequence: the starting point of training, since an untrained network predicts close to 0.5. The validation loss of the trained model is 0.197 (exercise R5). In torch the sigmoid and the loss are computed together (nn_bce_with_logits_loss) because that is numerically more stable than computing p first and then its logarithm. Logistic regression has a unique optimum; a neural network has many, which is the next slide.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Gradient descent


Compute the slope of the loss with respect to each weight (the gradient) and take a small step downhill. Repeat.
The learning rate η sets the step size: too small is slow, too large overshoots and never settles.
Backpropagation computes all 2 497 slopes in one pass backwards through the network: the chain rule, done by the computer.


For logistic regression the gradient has a simple form that students can compute by hand: for one sequence, the derivative of the loss with respect to the logit is p − y (prediction minus label), and with respect to a weight w_j it is (p − y) x_j. The exercise B4 does one update by hand. In a CNN the same chain rule passes this error signal back through the dense layer, the max pooling (only the winning position gets a gradient), the ReLU (only positions above the threshold) and into the filter weights: the filter weights at the bases of the best-scoring window move towards “more of this” in bound sequences and “less of this” in background. torch records the operations of the forward pass and computes all gradients with loss$backward(). We use Adam, a variant of gradient descent that adapts the step size for each weight; the idea is the same. Because the loss surface of a network is not a bowl, the result depends on the random starting weights; we fix the seed so that everyone gets the same model.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Training: mini-batches and epochs


Each step uses a random mini-batch of 128 sequences: cheap, slightly noisy gradient steps. One epoch is one pass over all training sequences.
After each epoch, compute the loss on the validation chromosome; keep the best model; stop when it no longer improves (early stopping).
The test chromosomes are not touched until the very end.


Why mini-batches: the gradient over all 76 000 sequences would be exact but expensive, and the noise of small batches even helps to escape poor regions of the loss surface. Batch size, learning rate, number of filters and filter width are hyperparameters: they are set by us, not by gradient descent, and are chosen on the validation set (or with cross-validation over chromosomes). In the exercise: Adam with learning rate 0.001, batches of 128, at most 20 epochs, patience 3. One epoch is 594 steps; on four CPU threads an epoch takes about 15–20 seconds. Early stopping is a form of regularisation: it stops before the network starts to memorise the training sequences. Saving the best model (torch_save) is also how we pass the model to the next unit.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Real data: learning curves


Left: with 76 015 training sequences the validation loss follows the training loss; best at epoch 13 (validation loss 0.197), stopped at epoch 16.
Right: the same network with only 500 training sequences memorises them (training loss → 0.02) while validation stalls at about 0.36: overfitting.
The gap between the curves, not the training loss, tells you how well the model will do on new DNA.


Both runs use the same seed and architecture (exercise R5 and R7). Left: training and validation loss start at about 0.30 after the first epoch and drop to 0.19 and 0.20; the curves stay together because 2 497 parameters are few compared with 76 000 training sequences. The model stopped at epoch 16 after three epochs without improvement and the saved model is the one from epoch 13. Right: with 500 sequences the network has five training sequences per parameter; it can fit them almost perfectly (training loss 0.016 at epoch 150) but the validation loss levels off around 0.36 and creeps up again after its minimum at epoch 85 (0.354; 0.372 at epoch 150); the test AUC of this model is 0.919 against 0.972. Students should read this plot in the exam: which curve is which, where to stop, is the model overfitting? This is the same picture as the overfitting slide of Machine learning from scratch, now for a neural network.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Choices you make (hyperparameters)








choice
in our model
what it controls

32

19 bp

0.001, 128
speed and stability of training

early stopping
dropout, weight decay are common alternatives

200 bp

Choose them on the validation set, never on the test set. The data (positives, negatives, splits) matter more than most of these.


A text slide to collect the knobs. Dropout randomly switches off units during training so that the network cannot rely on any single one; weight decay adds an L2 penalty to the weights, exactly the ridge penalty of Machine learning from scratch. More filters than motifs is normal: the network learns redundant copies and some filters that are barely used, as we will see. A practical rule from the literature (Koo and Eddy 2019): first-layer filters are most interpretable as motifs when the network pools heavily after the first layer, as ours does; deeper networks with little pooling spread a motif over several filters. The single most important choice is the data: what counts as a positive (IDR threshold, peak width), which negatives (What people try to predict showed how they change the task), and which chromosomes are held out.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Real data: test performance


On the held-out chr8 and chr9: CNN AUC 0.972, CTCF PWM 0.929, GC content 0.511.
At a 5% false positive rate the CNN recovers 87% of the peaks, the PWM 74%.
The CNN learns more than the core motif; the next slides show what.


The ROC curves are drawn with ties handled (GC content has many tied values), as in Machine learning from scratch. The test set was used exactly once, after the model was chosen on chr7. The validation AUC of the saved model was 0.977, close to the test AUC: no sign that the choice of epoch overfitted the validation chromosome. GC content at 0.51 confirms that the negatives are matched: the gain of the CNN over the PWM comes from sequence, not composition. Is 0.97 “good”? Relative to the PWM, clearly; in absolute terms it says that a 200-bp window around a strong CTCF summit is easy to recognise. It does not mean the model can find CTCF peaks in the whole genome: there, unbound motif matches outnumber bound ones many times (Gene regulation: 4% of chr21 CTCF matches are bound), the classes are very imbalanced, and precision would be much lower (precision–recall curves, Machine learning from scratch).

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: Real data: the filters learned the CTCF motif
text:
Real data: the filters learned the CTCF motif


For each filter, collect the 19-bp windows where it fires strongly in the test sequences and draw them as a logo.
The filters with the largest output weights are the CTCF motif, on both strands, matched to JASPAR by correlation (as TOMTOM does).
The network was never told about CTCF: it found the motif from labelled sequences alone.


Method (exercise R8): for filter k, take every test sequence whose maximum activation exceeds half of the filter’s overall maximum, cut out the 19 bases at the best position, and count bases: a position frequency matrix, drawn as an information-content logo. Comparing it with all 879 JASPAR 2024 vertebrate CORE matrices by Pearson correlation of the columns, trying all offsets and both strands (universalmotif::compare_motifs, the same idea as TOMTOM in the MEME suite), the top matches are CTCF or its paralogue CTCFL (BORIS), which binds the same motif. The logos are drawn aligned to the JASPAR matrix; some filters are the reverse complement, which is why the alignment flips them. Filters often cover only part of the motif or are shifted, because the 19-bp window does not need to be centred on it. The filter weights themselves can also be drawn as a logo, but they are on an arbitrary scale; activation-based logos are easier to compare with databases (Alipanahi et al. 2015; Koo and Eddy 2019).

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Real data: all 32 filters


9 of 32 filters match CTCF or CTCFL (correlation ≥ 0.9), all with positive output weights: they are the evidence for “bound”.
Most others are short, GC-rich, low-information patterns with negative weights: “GC-rich, but no CTCF motif” points to background.
Their best JASPAR matches (ZIC, KLF, PLAGL2 …) are weak; with 879 matrices to compare, some match is always found.


The x axis is the information content of each filter’s activation logo, the y axis its weight in the dense layer. Interpretation of the negative-weight filters: because the negatives have the same GC content as the peaks, GC-rich windows without a CTCF motif are mostly background, and the network uses generic GC-rich patterns as evidence against binding. That is a property of how we built the data set, not a discovery about B cells. Two filters with AT-rich patterns get small positive weights. A filter matching ZIC4 with p = 1e-4 among 879 comparisons is not a new motif: multiple testing applies to motif matching too (exam question). Redundancy is normal: nine filters learn variants and shifts of one motif in both orientations. If you want one filter per motif, use fewer filters or tools that cluster learned patterns (TF-MoDISco, next unit).

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: Real data: where and which filters matter
text:
Real data: where and which filters matter


Left: the strongest CTCF filter fires at the summit, like the motif scan in Gene regulation. The network was not given positions.
Right: the 9 CTCF-like filters alone give AUC 0.945, a little better than the JASPAR PWM; the other 23 together only 0.660.


Left: positions of the strongest match of the top filter, relative to the summit, in the test peaks where it fires (numbers printed by make-mlcnn-figs.R). The centrality is the same signature as the CTCF motif-centrality plot of Gene regulation, here rediscovered by the network. Right: an ablation. We compute the max-pooled outputs of all 32 filters, then recompute the network’s logit using only a subset of filters (the contribution of the others set to zero) and measure the test AUC. Only the CTCF-like filters: 0.945, between the JASPAR PWM (0.929) and the full model (0.972): nine learned filters cover the motif and its variants a little better than one matrix, and the remaining gain comes from the other filters working together with them. Without the CTCF-like filters the rest reach only 0.660 (GC-rich background patterns). The strongest filter fires in about a fifth of test peaks at our strict threshold (half its maximum) and almost never in background (0.2%), with a median distance of 4 bp from the summit. Ablation is the simplest way to ask what a model relies on; the next unit asks the same question for single bases.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: What this model does not know
text:
What this model does not know

Cell type: trained on GM12878 only. CTCF binding is largely shared between cell types; most TFs’ binding is not.
Chromatin: it sees 200 bp of sequence, not accessibility or DNA methylation. Two copies of the same motif, one methylated, get the same score.
Context: nothing beyond ±100 bp; no information on where the window lies in the genome.
The labels: peaks above an IDR threshold of one experiment, and negatives chosen by us. It learns the boundary we drew, including our biases.
Prediction ≠ mechanism: high accuracy does not show that the learned features cause binding.


A text slide on honest limits, worth a minute in the video. The methylation example connects to Gene regulation (CTCF does not bind methylated CpGs in its motif, as at the H19/IGF2 imprinting control region): a sequence model cannot see an epigenetic state, so the same DNA in two cell types or on two alleles gets the same prediction. Models that add accessibility as an input, or that are trained per cell type (Basset, chromBPNet), address part of this. Labels: changing the negatives changes the task; random genomic background teaches GC content, accessible-but-unbound background teaches what distinguishes CTCF sites from other open chromatin (What people try to predict). Finally, a classifier with AUC 0.97 can still rely on features that merely correlate with binding in this data set; whether a feature matters causally needs experiments (mutating the site), which the next unit mimics in silico.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: The models that made this popular
text:
The models that made this popular


DeepBind and DeepSEA (2015) showed that CNNs learn TF specificities from data and can score non-coding variants.
Basset (2016) did the same for accessibility in 164 cell types; BPNet (2021) predicts base-resolution binding profiles.


DeepBind (Alipanahi et al. 2015) trained one small CNN per protein on in vitro (protein-binding microarrays, HT-SELEX) and in vivo (ChIP-seq, CLIP-seq) data and visualised what a model learned as “mutation maps”, the in-silico mutagenesis of the next unit. DeepSEA (Zhou and Troyanskaya 2015) trained one network on 1 kb of sequence to predict 919 chromatin profiles at once (TF ChIP-seq, DNase-seq and histone marks from ENCODE and Roadmap): multi-task learning, where the filters are shared between all outputs, and showed that the model scores single-nucleotide changes. Basset (Kelley et al. 2016) predicted DNase-seq accessibility in 164 cell types from 600 bp and found that likely causal GWAS SNPs had larger predicted effects than the SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with them. BPNet (Avsec et al. 2021) is on the next slide. Note the held-out chromosomes in all of them: DeepSEA used chr8 and chr9 as test chromosomes, the convention we follow.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
section: BPNet: predicting the profile, not just “bound”
text:
BPNet: predicting the profile, not just “bound”


BPNet predicts the number and positions of reads at every base (ChIP-nexus), not a yes/no label.
Dilated convolutions see 1 kb with few parameters. Interpreting the model revealed soft motif syntax, tested by CRISPR point mutations.
The same design, applied to ATAC-seq, is chromBPNet (next unit).


Avsec et al. 2021 trained BPNet on ChIP-nexus (ChIP-exo-like, base-resolution) profiles of Oct4, Sox2, Nanog and Klf4 in mouse embryonic stem cells. Each output is the read coverage on both strands at every base of the central 1 kb: the strand-specific shape (reads stack on either side of the bound protein) contains the exact position of binding, and the total count says how strongly the region is bound. Predicting profiles gives far more training signal per region than one label. Dilated convolutions skip inputs (spacing 1, 2, 4, 8 …) so the receptive field doubles with each layer. With the interpretation methods of the next unit (contribution scores, TF-MoDISco) the authors found that Nanog binds preferentially to sites spaced by about 10.5 bp (a helical turn) and that some TF pairs cooperate only in one direction, and confirmed predictions with CRISPR-induced point mutations in the motifs. This is the model family to which chromBPNet belongs; the next unit uses it as an example of variant-effect prediction for accessibility.

Students should be able to: one-hot encode a sequence; compute a filter’s activation track, apply a bias and ReLU, and max-pool, by hand; explain why the last layer is a logistic regression; compute a log loss and one gradient step for a weight of the last layer; read learning curves and say where to stop and whether a model overfits; explain why the test set must be held out by chromosome and used once; interpret first-layer filters as motifs and judge a claimed motif match. Next: What did the model learn? Variant effects, where we ask which bases in a sequence drive the prediction, and what happens when we change one of them.

title: How a CNN reads DNA
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Alipanahi et al. 2015, Nat Biotechnol. Predicting the sequence specificities of DNA- and RNA-binding proteins by deep learning. DeepBind: CNNs as learned motif scanners.
Zhou & Troyanskaya 2015, Nat Methods. Predicting effects of noncoding variants with deep learning–based sequence model. DeepSEA: one network, 919 chromatin profiles, variant effects.
Kelley, Snoek & Rinn 2016, Genome Res. Basset: learning the regulatory code of the accessible genome with deep convolutional neural networks. Accessibility in 164 cell types from sequence.
Avsec et al. 2021, Nat Genet. Base-resolution models of transcription-factor binding reveal soft motif syntax. BPNet: profiles, interpretation, motif syntax.
Koo & Eddy 2019, PLoS Comput Biol. Representation learning of genomic sequence motifs with convolutional neural networks. When first-layer filters are (and are not) interpretable as motifs.
Eraslan et al. 2019, Nat Rev Genet. Deep learning: new computational modelling techniques for genomics. A readable review of the whole field.

title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
Background
ISM. For a sequence \(s\) with prediction \(z(s)\) (the logit, log-odds of “bound”), change each position \(i\) to each other base \(b\) and record \(\Delta_{i,b} = z(s_{i \to b}) - z(s)\). The importance of position \(i\) is \(-\frac{1}{3}\sum_b \Delta_{i,b}\): positive if the reference base is better than the alternatives on average.
Gradients. \(\partial z / \partial x_{b,i}\) is the slope of the output with respect to input base \(b\) at position \(i\), for all positions at once (one backward pass). Gradient × input keeps the slope at the reference base. It is a linear approximation of ISM and can miss effects when the model is non-linear (a ReLU switching, a different window winning the max pooling, saturation).
Reference-based attribution. DeepLIFT and SHAP explain \(z(s) - z(\text{reference})\), with a reference such as shuffled sequence; contributions sum to that difference, so redundant motifs share credit.
Variant effect. \(\Delta = z(\text{alt}) - z(\text{ref})\), with the variant in the same sequence context. It is a log odds ratio: the odds of binding are multiplied by \(e^{\Delta}\). To convert to probabilities use \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\).
Allele-specific binding (ASB). In a heterozygous individual, ChIP-seq reads over a SNP come from both alleles; a significant imbalance (after controlling for copy number and mapping bias) means one allele is bound more. ADASTRA (Abramov et al. 2021) has called ASB SNPs for hundreds of TFs from public ChIP-seq data. Epigenomics and genetic variation covers allele-specific signals and QTLs in detail.

Data
The trained model and the data set from How a CNN reads DNA (files ctcf_cnn.pt and ctcf_dataset.rds in ~/epi/ml-cnn), the hg38 genome (hg38.fa.bgz) and a table of CTCF allele-specific binding SNPs from ADASTRA (release Mabel v6.1, FDR < 0.05, all cell types; hg38, 1-based positions):
data/download.sh ml-interpretation-variants
cd ~/epi/ml-cnn                 # the folder of the previous exercise
If you did not save the model, the course data contain the same files, made with the same code and seed: ml_ctcf_dataset.rds and ml_ctcf_cnn.pt (see the comment in R0).
You need, in R: torch, Rsamtools, GenomicRanges, Biostrings, JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, ggplot2 and the CRAN package ggseqlogo (install.packages("ggseqlogo")). The R part takes about two minutes.
Simplifications. A one-layer model on 200 bp; ISM and gradient × input only (DeepLIFT/SHAP and TF-MoDISco need Python tooling and are described, not run); ASB SNPs from many cell types scored with a model of one cell line; only SNPs, no indels; the SNP is placed at the centre of a 200-bp window.

title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
By hand
The toy model of the lecture: one filter of width 4 with weights (rows A, C, G, T; columns 1–4)
      1    2    3    4
A    -1   -1   +2    0
C    +2   +2   -1   -1
G    -1   -2   +1   +2
T    +1   -1   -2   -1
bias −4, ReLU, global max pooling, and output \(z = -2 + 1 \times (\text{max activation})\).
B1. In-silico mutagenesis. The sequence is TCCGGA.

Score the three windows, apply the bias and ReLU, and compute \(z\) and \(p\).
Compute Δ for every mutation at positions 2, 3, 4 and 5 (12 mutations). Then the importance of each of the six positions.
One mutation increases \(z\). Which, and why?
Mutating C to A at position 3 gives Δ = 0, although position 3 lies in the best window. Why? (Look at all windows of the mutant.)

B2. Redundancy. The sequence is CCAGTTCCAG.

Compute \(z\).
What is Δ for every single-base mutation? What does ISM say about which bases matter?
Mutate the A in both copies to T. What is Δ now? What does this tell you about the motifs?
An enhancer has two binding sites for the same TF. Deleting either one in mice has no phenotype; deleting both does. Relate this to (b) and (c).

B3. Gradient × input. For the toy model with TCCGGA the gradient of \(z\) with respect to the input is non-zero only in the winning window, where it equals the filter weights (because the ReLU is active there and max pooling passes the gradient only to the winning window).

Write gradient × input for the six positions.
Compare with your ISM importances from B1. Where do they agree, and where not?
The gradient predicts Δ for C→A at position 3 as \(w_{A,2} - w_{C,2}\) (the weight change in the filter’s second column). What is that prediction, and what did ISM give? Why do they differ?

B4. Variant effects on the logit scale.

A model gives \(z = 3.0\) for the reference allele and \(z = 0.5\) for the alternative. Compute Δ, both probabilities, and the factor by which the odds of binding change.
At another site, \(z\) goes from 9 to 7. Compute Δ and the two probabilities. Which variant has the larger effect: (a) or (b)? On which scale does the answer look different, and why?
A paper reports predicted probabilities 0.60 (ref) and 0.40 (alt). What is Δ on the logit scale?

B5. Allele-specific binding.

A heterozygous SNP (G/T) is covered by 60 CTCF ChIP-seq reads: 42 G and 18 T. In the input DNA, 31 G and 29 T. A binomial test of 42 of 60 against 0.5 gives \(p = 0.003\). Which allele is preferred, and why do you look at the input?
Our model predicts Δ = −2.5 for G>T. Is that concordant with the ChIP-seq?
A model is tested on 200 ASB SNPs, 120 of which prefer the reference allele. It predicts the right direction for 118. Is it better than a model that always says “the reference binds better”? For the 40 SNPs where it predicts |Δ| > 2, it is right for 37. What do you conclude?

B6. Judge the claims.

“ISM shows that position 120 of this enhancer has zero importance, so mutating it in the genome will not change binding.”
“Our model predicts expression across genes with ρ = 0.6. We therefore used it to predict which patients carry expression-lowering variants.”
“The variant has a predicted effect of Δ = −4 on CTCF binding in GM12878, so it causes the disease associated with this locus.”
“Gradient × input and ISM agree with r = 0.93, so the attribution is correct.”
