title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
In R

R0 — The model and the data from How a CNN reads DNA
library(Rsamtools); library(GenomicRanges); library(Biostrings)
library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite); library(motifmatchr)
library(torch); library(ggplot2); library(ggseqlogo)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
ds    <- readRDS("ctcf_dataset.rds")       # from How a CNN reads DNA, R1
model <- torch_load("ctcf_cnn.pt")         # from How a CNN reads DNA, R5
# no files? use the prepared copies (same code, same seed):
# ds <- readRDS(file.path(D, "ml_ctcf_dataset.rds")); model <- torch_load(file.path(D, "ml_ctcf_cnn.pt"))
model$eval()
one_hot <- function(s) {
  m <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(s, ""))
  x <- array(0, c(length(s), 4, ncol(m)))
  for (k in 1:4) x[, k, ] <- m == c("A", "C", "G", "T")[k]
  x
}
logit <- function(seqs) with_no_grad(as.numeric(model(torch_tensor(one_hot(seqs), dtype = torch_float()))))
test <- ds[ds$split == "test", ]
test$cnn <- logit(test$seq)
jaspar <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf_m <- getMatrixByID(jaspar, "MA0139.2")
pwm_score <- function(seqs)          # best log-odds score of the CTCF PWM in each sequence
  motifScores(matchMotifs(ctcf_m, DNAStringSet(seqs), out = "scores", bg = "even", p.cutoff = 1))[, 1]
summary(test$cnn[test$label == 1]); summary(test$cnn[test$label == 0])
What are the median logits of test peaks and background windows? What probabilities are they?


R1 — In-silico mutagenesis of one peak
ism <- function(s) {                 # in-silico mutagenesis: every position, every other base
  b   <- strsplit(s, "")[[1]]
  mut <- expand.grid(alt = c("A", "C", "G", "T"), pos = seq_along(b), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  mut <- mut[mut$alt != b[mut$pos], ]                       # 3 alternatives per position
  mutants <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(mut)), function(i) {
    x <- b; x[mut$pos[i]] <- mut$alt[i]; paste(x, collapse = "") }, "")
  mut$ref   <- b[mut$pos]
  mut$delta <- logit(mutants) - logit(s)                    # change in log-odds of "bound"
  mut
}
pos_test <- test[test$label == 1, ]
ex <- pos_test[which.min(abs(pos_test$cnn - median(pos_test$cnn))), ]   # a typical peak
ex[, c("chr", "start", "cnn")]
r <- ism(ex$seq)
nrow(r)
head(r[order(r$delta), ], 10)
ggplot(r, aes(pos, alt, fill = delta)) + geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2a6f97", mid = "white", high = "#c0392b") +
  labs(x = "position in the 200-bp window", y = "mutated to", fill = "delta logit")
imp <- -tapply(r$delta, r$pos, mean)         # importance of the reference base at each position
imp_mat <- one_hot(ex$seq)[1, , ] * rep(imp, each = 4)
rownames(imp_mat) <- c("A", "C", "G", "T")
ggseqlogo(imp_mat[, 60:140], method = "custom", seq_type = "dna") + labs(y = "importance (-mean delta logit)")

How many mutants does ISM need for a 200-bp sequence, and how many predictions in total?
Which mutations have the largest effects, and where are they relative to the summit (position 100)? Read the motif in the logo: which strand is it on? (Compare with the JASPAR consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC.)
Find a base with negative importance. What would happen to the prediction if you mutated it?



R2 — Gradient × input
x <- torch_tensor(one_hot(ex$seq), dtype = torch_float(), requires_grad = TRUE)
z <- model(x)
z$backward()                                         # gradient of the logit w.r.t. every input
grad <- as.array(x$grad)[1, , ]                      # 4 x 200
gxi  <- colSums(grad * one_hot(ex$seq)[1, , ])       # gradient x input: one value per position
cor(gxi, imp)
plot(imp, gxi, xlab = "ISM importance", ylab = "gradient x input", pch = 19, col = "#2a6f97")

How well do the two attributions agree? How many forward/backward passes did each need?
Look at the points furthest from the diagonal. Using B3, suggest why they differ.



R3 — What the model uses around the motif
set.seed(2)
peaks <- pos_test[pwm_score(pos_test$seq) > 12, ]           # peaks with a good CTCF match
peaks <- peaks[sample(nrow(peaks), 200), ]
hits  <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, DNAStringSet(peaks$seq), out = "positions", bg = "even", p.cutoff = 1e-4)[[1]]
best  <- t(sapply(hits, function(h) { h <- h[which.max(mcols(h)$score)]
                                       c(start = start(h), minus = mcols(h)$strand == "-") }))
prof <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(peaks)), function(i) {
  r   <- ism(peaks$seq[i])
  imp <- -tapply(r$delta, r$pos, mean)                       # importance per position
  idx <- best[i, "start"] + (-20):34                         # 20 bp flank, 15-bp motif, 20 bp flank
  if (best[i, "minus"]) idx <- rev(idx)                      # read minus-strand sites backwards
  imp[pmin(pmax(idx, 1), 200)] * (idx >= 1 & idx <= 200)
}))
mean_imp <- colMeans(prof)
p   <- (Matrix(ctcf_m) + 0.25) / colSums(Matrix(ctcf_m) + 0.25)
ic  <- 2 + colSums(p * log2(p))                              # information content per column
plot(-20:34, mean_imp, type = "h", lwd = 4, col = "#8c564b",
     xlab = "position relative to the start of the CTCF motif", ylab = "mean ISM importance")
round(cor(mean_imp[21:35], ic), 2)

Why do we align the peaks on their best PWM match, and why reverse minus-strand sites?
Which motif positions does the model rely on most? Compare with the information content of the JASPAR columns (round(ic, 2)) and with the CTCF logo of Gene regulation.
The 200 peaks were chosen because they have a good PWM match. How does that choice bias the comparison?



R4 — Core versus flanks
core <- 21:35
data.frame(where = c("motif, high-information positions (IC > 1 bit)", "motif, other positions",
                     "flanks 1-10 bp", "flanks 11-20 bp"),
           mean_importance = round(c(mean(mean_imp[core][ic > 1]), mean(mean_imp[core][ic <= 1]),
                                     mean(mean_imp[c(11:20, 36:45)]), mean(mean_imp[c(1:10, 46:55)])), 3))
How much does mutating a core position cost on average, compared with a flanking base? Express the core effect as a factor on the odds of binding.


R5 — Real SNPs with allele-specific CTCF binding
asb <- read.delim(file.path(D, "ctcf_asb_adastra.tsv"))
names(asb) <- c("chr", "pos", "ref", "alt", "rsid", "tfs", "cell_types",
                "fdr_ref", "fdr_alt", "es_ref", "es_alt")              # FDRs are -log10
asb <- asb[asb$chr %in% c("chr8", "chr9"), ]                           # test chromosomes only
sig_ref <- !is.na(asb$fdr_ref) & asb$fdr_ref > -log10(0.05)
sig_alt <- !is.na(asb$fdr_alt) & asb$fdr_alt > -log10(0.05)
keep <- xor(sig_ref, sig_alt)                                          # exactly one preferred allele
asb <- asb[keep, ]
asb$preferred <- ifelse(sig_ref[keep], "ref", "alt")
table(asb$preferred)

genome <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))
ref_seq <- as.character(getSeq(genome, GRanges(asb$chr, IRanges(asb$pos - 99, width = 200))))
stopifnot(substr(ref_seq, 100, 100) == asb$ref)                        # the SNP is base 100
alt_seq <- ref_seq; substr(alt_seq, 100, 100) <- asb$alt
asb$d_cnn <- logit(alt_seq) - logit(ref_seq)                           # variant effect, log-odds
asb$d_pwm <- pwm_score(alt_seq) - pwm_score(ref_seq)
observed <- ifelse(asb$preferred == "alt", 1, -1)                      # +1: alt allele bound more
concordance <- function(d, min_abs) {
  k <- abs(d) > min_abs
  c(n = sum(k), concordant = round(mean(sign(d[k]) == observed[k]), 3))
}
rbind(cnn_all = concordance(asb$d_cnn, 0),   cnn_0.5 = concordance(asb$d_cnn, 0.5),
      cnn_1   = concordance(asb$d_cnn, 1),   cnn_2   = concordance(asb$d_cnn, 2),
      pwm_all = concordance(asb$d_pwm, 0),   pwm_1   = concordance(asb$d_pwm, 1),
      pwm_2   = concordance(asb$d_pwm, 2),   always_ref = c(nrow(asb), mean(observed == -1)))
cor(asb$d_cnn, asb$d_pwm)
sum(asb$d_cnn == 0); sum(asb$d_pwm == 0)

How many ASB SNPs are on the test chromosomes, and how many prefer each allele? Why use only chr8 and chr9?
How often does the CNN predict the right direction overall, and compared with “always the reference”? And when it predicts a large effect?
For how many SNPs is the predicted effect exactly 0, for the CNN and for the PWM? Explain both numbers.
Give three reasons why most ASB SNPs are not predicted well (see the lecture).



R6 — One SNP up close
big <- asb[order(-abs(asb$d_cnn)), c("rsid", "chr", "pos", "ref", "alt", "preferred", "d_cnn", "d_pwm")]
head(big, 8)
i <- which(asb$rsid == big$rsid[1])
show_ism <- function(s, title) {
  r <- ism(s); imp <- -tapply(r$delta, r$pos, mean)
  m <- one_hot(s)[1, , ] * rep(imp, each = 4); rownames(m) <- c("A", "C", "G", "T")
  ggseqlogo(m[, 75:125], method = "custom", seq_type = "dna") + ggtitle(title)
}
show_ism(ref_seq[i], paste(asb$rsid[i], "reference allele", asb$ref[i]))
show_ism(alt_seq[i], paste(asb$rsid[i], "alternative allele", asb$alt[i]))

Which SNP has the largest predicted effect? Do the model, the PWM and ADASTRA agree on its direction?
In the logos, find the SNP (column 26 of the plot, base 100 of the window). Which motif position does it hit?
Look the SNP up in the ADASTRA web interface (search by rs ID). In which cell types was the imbalance seen?

title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — ISM and redundancy by hand (B1, B2)





For each mutant, rescore all windows: a mutation can destroy the best window but also create a new one. Activation = max(0, score − 4); \(z = -2 + \max\). Δ is mutant minus reference. Importance is minus the mean of the three Δ at a position. With two identical best windows, max pooling returns the same value as long as one survives. Alipanahi et al. 2015 introduced mutation maps for CNNs; Novakovsky et al. 2022 reviews ISM and its pitfalls.









Hint 2 — gradients (B3, R2)





The gradient is the local slope: it predicts the change for small changes of the input as if the model were linear. A one-hot base change is not small; whenever a ReLU switches, or another window wins the max pooling, the linear prediction is wrong. In torch, set requires_grad = TRUE on the input tensor and call $backward() on the output (autograd). Integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al. 2017) integrates gradients along a path from a reference input. DeepLIFT (Shrikumar et al. 2017) instead backpropagates contributions based on differences between activations and their reference values.









Hint 3 — logits, probabilities and odds (B4)





\(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) and \(z = \ln(p/(1-p))\). Useful values: \(e^{-2.5} = 0.082\), \(e^{-3} = 0.050\), \(e^{0.5} = 1.65\), \(\ln(1.5) = 0.405\). A difference of logits is the log of an odds ratio.









Hint 4 — allele-specific binding (B5, R5)





In ADASTRA tables fdr_ref and fdr_alt are −log10 FDRs for preferential binding of the reference and of the alternative allele (readme of the release); Abramov et al. 2021 describes how copy number and mapping bias are handled. A concordance is only meaningful next to the trivial baseline: the fraction of SNPs in the majority class.









Hint 5 — R functions (R0–R6)





ggseqlogo draws logos from a matrix with method = "custom" (letter heights = matrix values, negative values below the axis). motifmatchr::matchMotifs with out = "positions" gives the start, strand and score of every match; with out = "scores" and p.cutoff = 1 the best score of every sequence. Rsamtools::FaFile and getSeq read the windows around the SNPs; substr<- replaces one base. xor() is TRUE when exactly one of two conditions holds.









Hint 6 — judging claims (B6)





Ask: what does the model predict (which readout, which cell type)? How was it evaluated (across genes or across individuals; on variants at all)? Is a large predicted molecular effect evidence for a phenotype? Does agreement between two attribution methods show that either is right about biology? See the last slides of the lecture, Huang et al. 2023 and Sasse et al. 2023.

title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Windows: TCCG = 1 + 2 − 1 + 2 = 4, CCGG = 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7, CGGA = 2 − 2 + 1 + 0 = 1. After bias and ReLU: 0, 3, 0. Max 3, \(z = -2 + 3 = 1.0\), \(p = 0.73\).

Δ (rows: mutated to):

position    2: C    3: C    4: G    5: G
→ A          -3      0      +1      -2
→ C          ref    ref     -2      -3
→ G          -3     -1      ref     ref
→ T          -1     -3      -3      -3
Positions 1 and 6 lie outside every window that can win, so all their Δ are 0. Importances (−mean Δ): position 1: 0, 2: 2.33, 3: 1.33, 4: 1.33, 5: 2.67, 6: 0.

G→A at position 4 gives TCCAGA: CCAG scores 8, activation 4, \(z = 2\), Δ = +1. The reference has G at the filter’s third column (+1), while A is the preferred base (+2): the reference site is not optimal, so its importance at that position is reduced.
The mutant TCAGGA loses CCGG but gains a new window TCAG = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7, as good as the old best window. Max pooling takes the new one and \(z\) is unchanged. ISM measures the model’s output, whatever window produces it.

B2. (a) Windows CCAG (8), CAGT, AGTT, GTTC, TTCC, TCCA, CCAG (8): two activations of 4, max 4, \(z = 2\).

Every single mutation leaves at least one intact CCAG, so the max stays 4 and every Δ is 0: ISM says no base matters.
CCTGTTCCTG: both copies broken (CCTG = 2 + 2 − 2 + 2 = 4, activation 0); no other window passes. \(z = -2\), Δ = −4. The motifs matter, but they are redundant: each can replace the other.
The same logic in vivo: redundant (shadow) enhancers or binding sites buffer each other, so single deletions show no effect. Testing pairs (or a reference without any copy, as in DeepLIFT/SHAP) reveals the effect.

B3. (a) The winning window is CCGG at positions 2–5, so the gradient at the reference base is the filter weight for that base: position 2 (C, column 1) +2, position 3 (C, column 2) +2, position 4 (G, column 3) +1, position 5 (G, column 4) +2; positions 1 and 6: 0. Gradient × input: 0, 2, 2, 1, 2, 0.

Both give 0 outside the window and rank positions 2 and 5 high. They disagree at position 3 (gradient 2, ISM 1.33) and somewhat elsewhere, because ISM averages real effects that include ReLU clipping (Δ cannot go below −3 here: the activation cannot drop below 0) and new windows.
Linear prediction: $w_{A,2} - w_{C,2} = -1 - 2 = $ −3. ISM: 0, because a new window (TCAG) takes over (B1d). The gradient sees only the current winning window and assumes everything else stays the same.

B4. (a) Δ = 0.5 − 3.0 = −2.5. \(p_{ref} = 1/(1 + e^{-3}) = 0.953\), \(p_{alt} = 1/(1 + e^{-0.5}) = 0.622\). The odds are multiplied by \(e^{-2.5} = 0.082\) (about 12 times lower). (b) Δ = −2; \(p\) goes from 0.99988 to 0.99909. On the logit scale (a) is the larger effect (−2.5 vs −2), and both are substantial; on the probability scale (b) looks negligible (0.0008) because the sigmoid is saturated near 1. Log-odds compare sites of different strength fairly. (c) $(0.4) - (0.6) = (0.4/0.6) - (0.6/0.4) = -0.405 - 0.405 = $ −0.81.
B5. (a) G (the allele with 70% of the reads). The nearly balanced input (31/29) gives no evidence of a large allelic dosage difference and helps assess mapping bias. With only 60 input reads it does not rule either out; compare ChIP with input statistically and use bias-aware mapping before claiming ASB.
The tests answer different questions. The binomial test asks whether the ChIP counts differ from an assumed 50:50 ratio (\(p = 0.0027\)). A two-sided Fisher exact test of the ChIP counts (42 G, 18 T) against the input counts (31 G, 29 T) asks whether the allele proportions differ between ChIP and input, accounting for sampling uncertainty in both; it gives \(p = 0.061\). G is over-represented in the observed ChIP reads, but this direct comparison does not establish enrichment relative to input at the 5% threshold. That is not evidence that the alleles bind equally; more informative data and control of mapping bias are needed.

Δ = −2.5 means the model predicts G>T reduces binding, i.e. G is bound more: concordant. (c) 118/200 = 59% vs 120/200 = 60% for “always reference”: no better than the baseline overall. For large predicted effects 37/40 = 92.5%: the model is informative when it predicts a strong effect (typically a SNP in a motif), not otherwise. This is the pattern of our real data in R5.

B6. (a) Zero ISM importance can mean redundancy (another site compensates, B2), saturation of the output, or simply that this model, with its 200-bp view and its training data, ignores that base. It does not show that the base is irrelevant in the genome, in another cell type, or for another readout. (b) Predicting which genes are high or low (across genes) is a different task from predicting differences between people (across individuals); current models do poorly at the second (Huang et al. 2023; Sasse et al. 2023). The model must be validated across individuals before such use. (c) A predicted change in CTCF binding in one cell line is a molecular hypothesis. Causality for the disease needs genetic evidence (fine-mapping: is this variant, and not one in LD, responsible?), evidence that CTCF binding matters at this locus in the relevant cell type, and experiments (allele-specific binding, editing). (d) Agreement between two attribution methods shows they describe the model consistently. Whether the model is right about biology needs independent data: motif databases, mutagenesis experiments, allele-specific binding.









Solutions — R





R0. Median logit of test peaks 4.26 (\(p = 0.986\)) and of background windows −3.43 (\(p = 0.031\)).
R1. (a) 3 × 200 = 600 mutants, plus the reference: 601 predictions. (b) The example is chr8:65 143 411–65 143 610 (\(z = 4.26\)). The largest effects are at positions 103–114: C→T at 105 (Δ = −5.77), C→A and C→G at 105, G→C at 114, G→A at 113 and 114, G→C at 110 (all below −3.5). They lie 3–14 bp to the right of the summit, in the best CTCF match: ACCCCTCCTGGTGGC at positions 101–115 on the plus strand, whose reverse complement GCCACCAGGAGGGGT is close to the JASPAR consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. The motif is on the minus strand, and the logo shows it as the reverse complement. 48 of the 600 mutations change \(z\) by more than 1. (c) Bases drawn below the axis (for example around positions 99–104) have negative importance: mutating them would, on average, increase the predicted binding, because the reference base is worse than the alternatives at a motif position.
R2. (a) Correlation 0.955. ISM: 601 forward passes; gradient: 1 forward and 1 backward pass. (b) The outlying points are positions where a mutation changes which window wins the max pooling of a filter, or pushes a filter’s activation below its ReLU threshold: non-linear effects that the local gradient cannot see (B3c). Over 200 peaks the median correlation is 0.93 (lecture).
R3. (a) Each peak has its motif at a different position and on either strand; aligning on the best match puts the same motif position in the same column, and reversing minus-strand sites makes column 1 always the first base of the motif as written in JASPAR. (b) Correlation with information content 0.94. The largest importances (about 4.5) are at motif positions 3, 8 and 11 (0-based 2, 7, 10 on the plot), the C, G and G with about 1.9 bits in JASPAR; the low-information positions 1, 6 and 15 have the lowest importance. The importance profile has the shape of the logo. (c) Peaks were selected because their sequence matches the PWM well (score > 12; 2236 of 3778 test peaks), and aligned with the PWM. This favours agreement with the PWM; peaks bound through weaker or different sites are excluded, so the analysis says nothing about them.
R4. High-information motif positions 3.17, other motif positions 1.31, flanks 1–10 bp 0.074, 11–20 bp 0.013. A core mutation costs about 3.2 logit units on average: the odds of binding fall by a factor \(e^{3.2} \approx 25\). Flanking bases matter about 40 times less, and almost not at all beyond 10 bp.
R5. (a) 2611 ASB SNPs on chr8 and chr9; for 2 both alleles are significant and they are dropped, leaving 2609: 1526 prefer the reference allele, 1083 the alternative. Only the test chromosomes, so that no SNP lies in a sequence the model was trained on. (b) Overall the CNN is right for 58.2% of the 2462 SNPs with a non-zero prediction, the same as always guessing the reference (58.5%). With |Δ| > 0.5: 73.6% (531 SNPs); > 1: 82.1% (280); > 2: 94.8% (115). The PWM: 74.0% (385 SNPs), 79.8% (262) for |Δ| > 1 and 81.6% (206) for |Δ| > 2. The predicted effects of the two methods correlate with r = 0.70. (c) 147 SNPs have Δ = 0 exactly for the CNN: the SNP does not touch the best-scoring window of any filter, so no max-pooled value changes. 2224 for the PWM: it changes only if the SNP is inside the best-scoring 15-bp window (or creates a better one). (d) The SNP is not the causal variant (another variant on the same haplotype); the effect works outside the 200-bp window or through other factors or DNA methylation; the imbalance is small and the predicted Δ is within the model’s noise; the model was trained on one cell line, without any variants; and ASB calls carry mapping-bias, copy-number and cell-type differences.
R6. (a) rs12237222 (chr9:83 219 828, G>T): Δ = −6.23 for the CNN (\(z\) from 6.35 to 0.12) and −8.14 for the PWM; ADASTRA reports the reference G as preferred. All three agree. (b) The best CTCF match in the reference window is CCCACTGGGGGGCAG at positions 93–107 on the plus strand; the SNP (position 100) is motif position 8, the G with about 1.9 bits in JASPAR, one of the three most informative positions. In the reference logo it is one of the tallest letters; in the alternative logo the T is drawn below the axis and the importance of the neighbouring core bases drops. (c) ADASTRA lists the imbalance in many cell types and tissues (for example adrenal gland, liver, hepatocytes, glioblastoma cells, LNCaP, MCF-7, HUVEC and a lymphoblastoid line): a strong, cell-type-independent CTCF site whose motif is broken by the T allele.

title: Exercise: What did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
Where this leads

Epigenomics and genetic variation shows how allele-specific signals, chromatin QTLs and methylation QTLs are measured, the data that variant-effect models are tested against.
The 3D genome units show what a CTCF site does: loop anchors, whose loss can rewire contacts between enhancers and promoters.
The models of the last slides (Enformer, Borzoi, chromBPNet, AlphaGenome) are used through their authors’ software or web services; the ideas here (Δ on the logit scale, attribution, validation against allelic data and across individuals) are what to look for in their results.

title: Quiz: what did the model learn? Variant effects
text:
Short questions on attribution, in-silico mutagenesis and variant effects. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is in-silico mutagenesis? How many model evaluations does it need for a 1-kb sequence?






Answer





Change each base of the sequence to each of the three other bases, run the model on every mutant, and record the change in the output, Δ = z(mutant) − z(reference). For 1000 bp: 3 × 1000 = 3000 mutants, plus the reference: 3001 evaluations.




Q2. A model gives \(z = 2.5\) for a sequence. The three mutants at position 40 give \(z = 0.5\), \(1.5\) and \(2.5\). What are the three Δ values and the importance of position 40?






Answer





Δ = −2.0, −1.0 and 0.0. Importance = −mean Δ = 1.0. The reference base is better than two of the alternatives and equivalent to the third.




Q3. A sequence contains two copies of a CTCF motif. ISM gives importance close to zero at every base, although the model predicts strong binding. Explain, and suggest how to reveal the motifs.






Answer





Redundancy (saturation): each copy alone is enough for the prediction (for example through max pooling), so destroying one leaves the other and the output barely changes. Mutate both copies together (pairs or whole motifs), or use a reference-based method (DeepLIFT, SHAP, integrated gradients) that measures contributions against a sequence without the motifs, so the two copies share the credit.




Q4. Why is gradient × input much cheaper than ISM, and when can the two disagree?






Answer





One backward pass gives the gradient with respect to all inputs at once, instead of one forward pass per mutant. The gradient is a local, linear slope: it disagrees with ISM when a mutation changes the model non-linearly, for example when a ReLU switches on or off, another window wins the max pooling, or the output is saturated.




Q5. A variant has \(z_{ref} = 1.0\) and \(z_{alt} = -1.0\). What is the variant effect, by how much do the odds of binding change, and what are the two probabilities?






Answer





Δ = −2.0. The odds are multiplied by \(e^{-2} = 0.135\) (about 7.4 times lower). \(p_{ref} = 1/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.73\), \(p_{alt} = 1/(1 + e^{1}) = 0.27\).




Q6. Two variants: one changes \(z\) from 8 to 6, the other from 0 to −2. Which has the larger effect on the probability scale, and which on the logit scale? Which scale would you use to compare them?






Answer





On the logit scale both are Δ = −2. On the probability scale the first moves from 0.9997 to 0.9975 (hardly at all), the second from 0.50 to 0.12. The logit scale compares relative changes in the odds of binding regardless of how strong the site is, which is what a variant effect should measure; the probability scale is compressed near 0 and 1.




Q7. In ChIP-seq of a heterozygous individual, 45 reads carry the reference allele and 15 the alternative; in the input DNA the split is 30/30. What does this show, and why is it called a natural experiment?






Answer





The ChIP reads show a 3:1 allelic ratio (75% reference), consistent with allele-specific binding. The balanced input argues against a large dosage difference or shared mapping bias, but 60 input reads cannot rule these out. After technical biases and dosage are controlled, a within-person comparison controls the trans environment and supports a cis effect of the two haplotypes (the SNP itself, another variant in phase, or a haplotype-specific epigenetic state).




Q8. A sequence model predicts the direction of 2609 allele-specific CTCF SNPs correctly 58% of the time; 58.5% of these SNPs prefer the reference allele. For the 115 SNPs with |Δ| > 2 it is right 95% of the time. Summarise what the model can and cannot do.






Answer





Overall it is no better than always guessing the reference allele: for most allele-specific SNPs (not in a motif, or not causal) its predictions carry no information. When it predicts a large effect, typically for a SNP that breaks or creates a strong motif, it is usually right. Use its large predicted effects, and compare every concordance with the trivial majority-class baseline.




Q9. Enformer predicts gene expression across genes with a correlation of about 0.57 in lymphoblastoid cells. Why can it still fail to predict which people have high or low expression of a given gene?






Answer





Across genes, expression differs because of large differences in promoters, CpG islands, enhancers and gene structure, which the model learned from the reference genome. Across people, for one gene, the differences come from a few common variants with small effects; the model must get the effect and direction of each variant right, and it was never trained on variation between individuals. Huang et al. 2023 and Sasse et al. 2023 found cross-individual correlations centred near zero and often the wrong sign.




Q10. “Our deep-learning model predicts that this non-coding variant reduces CTCF binding (Δ = −4), so the variant causes the patient’s disease.” List what is missing.






Answer





The prediction is a molecular hypothesis for one readout in the model’s cell type. Missing: evidence that this variant (not one in linkage disequilibrium) is causal (fine-mapping, segregation in a family); evidence that binding changes in the relevant cell type (allele-specific binding, reporter or editing experiments); evidence that the CTCF site matters for a gene relevant to the disease (contacts, expression); and functional evidence that the gene change causes the phenotype.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
About this lecture
Machine learning from scratch built a small classifier and measured it. This unit looks outward: what does the field try to predict from sequence, chromatin and methylation, and how do we know whether a reported performance is real?

A map of tasks: binding and accessibility, expression, variant effects, enhancer–gene links, imputation, 3D contacts, age and tumour type. The big models appear as examples, not as tools.
Traps specific to genomic data: leakage between overlapping or similar sequences, held-out chromosomes, the choice of negatives, baselines, other cell types, other individuals.
Each trap demonstrated with real data from GM12878 and K562.


The first half is a tour: for each task, what is the input, where do the labels come from, what has been achieved. Students do not need to remember model names; they need to recognise the shape of each problem so they can read a paper about it. The second half is the critical part and the exam-relevant part: judging whether an evaluation is sound. Every claim is backed by a small experiment that students repeat in the exercise, using the same data framing as the two following units (How a CNN reads DNA, and What did the model learn? Variant effects): positives are GM12878 peaks, negatives are matched genomic windows, and whole chromosomes (8 and 9) are held out for testing.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
A map of prediction tasks


Inputs: DNA sequence, epigenomic tracks of a cell type, or DNA methylation. Labels: what an assay measured.
Same structure as in the last unit: examples, features, labels, a model with parameters, a held-out test.


Read the map from left to right. Sequence-based models are the most active area: from a window of reference sequence they predict what assays would measure there. Models that take epigenomic tracks as input predict things that are expensive to measure directly (enhancer–gene links, 3D contacts) or fill in experiments that were never done. Methylation-based predictors are the oldest and most used in practice: epigenetic clocks and the methylation classifier for brain tumours are used clinically or in large cohort studies. The ABC model in the enhancer–gene box is not machine learning in the strict sense (it is a formula: activity × contact), but it is the baseline that learned models are compared against. C.Origami takes sequence plus ATAC and CTCF tracks, hence the dashed arrow.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Binding and accessibility from sequence


Input: a window of reference sequence (0.5–2 kb), one-hot encoded. Output: is there a peak in the centre, for hundreds of assays at once (multi-task).
DeepSEA (2015) and Basset (2016) started this with CNNs; BPNet and chromBPNet predict the base-resolution profile.
The same sequence gives different labels in different cells: the cell type enters only through the label, as a separate output per cell type.


This is the task of the next two units, in miniature: students will train a CNN to tell CTCF peaks from background. DeepSEA predicted 919 chromatin features (TF ChIP, DNase, histone marks across ENCODE and Roadmap cell types) from 1 kb; Basset predicted DNase accessibility in 164 cell types from 600 bp. Multi-task training shares one sequence model across many outputs, which helps when some outputs have few positives. A key limitation is on the slide: the model sees only the reference sequence, so differences between cell types must be learned as separate outputs; it cannot predict a cell type it has never seen. The numbers in the bars are illustrative.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Expression from sequence: long context


Genes are regulated by enhancers tens to hundreds of kb away. Basenji, Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome read 131 kb to 1 Mb and predict thousands of tracks at once: CAGE, RNA-seq coverage, ChIP, ATAC, contacts.
Trained on the reference genome, across many cell types; evaluated on held-out chromosomal regions.


The trend over ten years has been longer input and more outputs. Enformer (2021) added attention layers so that distant positions can interact, with a 196 kb input; Borzoi (2025, preprint 2023) predicts RNA-seq coverage from 524 kb, and so also splicing and polyadenylation; AlphaGenome (2026) reads 1 Mb and predicts several thousand human tracks at up to base-pair resolution. These are large models trained on hundreds of GPU/TPU-days; nobody in this course will train one, and that is not the point. What students should take away: these models predict how much a gene is expressed, in a given cell type, from the reference sequence around it, and they are good at it across genes (for example, Sasse et al. 2023 found r = 0.58 between Enformer’s predictions and measured brain expression across 13 000 genes). Later in this lecture: what they are not good at. The ZRS limb enhancer of SHH sits about 1 Mb from its gene, at the edge of even the longest model.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: Variant effects: one model, two sequences
text:
Variant effects: one model, two sequences


A trained sequence model can score any variant: predict the reference and the alternative sequence, take the difference.
Used to prioritise non-coding GWAS variants, rare variants in patients, and to design experiments.


This is the main practical use of sequence models today, and the topic of What did the model learn? Variant effects. The appeal is that no experiment is needed for the particular variant: the model has learned general rules (motifs, their spacing, GC preferences) and applies them to the new sequence. In the illustrative example the alternative base destroys a high-information position of the CTCF motif, and the predicted binding drops. Whether these predicted effects match measured effects (allele-specific binding, eQTLs, massively parallel reporter assays) is an empirical question; the answer is “often for strong effects at strong motifs, much less for subtle effects”, and the last part of this lecture shows the most striking failure.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Which enhancer regulates which gene?


One example = one (enhancer, gene) pair; features from chromatin (activity, contact, distance); labels from CRISPRi screens, eQTLs or Hi-C loops.
The task the nearest-gene rule does badly. Covered in Linking regulatory elements to genes.


Most GWAS hits are in enhancers, so connecting enhancers to their target genes is central to interpreting them. The best labels come from CRISPR interference screens that silence each candidate enhancer and measure expression of nearby genes; there are a few thousand tested pairs, mostly in K562. The ABC model (Fulco et al. 2019) multiplies enhancer activity by Hi-C contact frequency and normalises over all enhancers near the gene; it is a simple formula, and learned models have to beat it. This task is also the source of one of the best-known evaluation failures, which we look at below (TargetFinder).

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Imputation: experiments nobody did


Large consortia measure many marks in many cell types, but the matrix is mostly empty. Imputation predicts a missing track from the same mark in other cells and other marks in the same cell.
ChromImpute (2015), Avocado (2020). Evaluated by hiding tracks that were measured.


Roadmap Epigenomics (127 epigenomes) and ENCODE measured only a few marks in most cell types. ChromImpute trained one regression model per target track using features from related tracks; Avocado factorises the whole three-dimensional tensor (cell type × assay × genomic position) into learned embeddings. Imputed tracks were good enough that Roadmap used them for chromatin-state annotation. Two cautions to discuss: an imputed track is a prediction, not a measurement, and is most reliable where the cell type resembles others in the training set; and imputation is evaluated on tracks that exist, which are the commonly measured marks in commonly studied cells, so the hardest cases are the least tested.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
3D contacts from sequence


Akita predicts a Hi-C / Micro-C contact map from ~1 Mb of sequence; C.Origami adds a cell type’s ATAC and CTCF tracks to predict cell-type-specific maps.
Use: in-silico experiments, e.g. delete a CTCF site and predict whether a TAD boundary disappears.


The 3D genome units show how CTCF and cohesin form loops and domains through loop extrusion, which depends on CTCF motif orientation. Akita (Fudenberg et al. 2020) learned much of this from sequence alone, including the importance of CTCF motifs. Because a sequence-only model cannot know which cell type it is in, C.Origami (Tan et al. 2023) adds cell-type-specific inputs. The appeal of both is the in-silico screen: mutate thousands of sites computationally and predict which matter, then test the few interesting ones in cells.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Predictions from DNA methylation


Epigenetic clocks: elastic-net regression of age on CpG methylation (Horvath 2013: 353 CpGs). The difference between predicted and real age is studied as “age acceleration”.
Tumour classification: a random forest on array methylation assigns brain tumours to 82 classes (Capper et al. 2018), now part of diagnosis.


These are the oldest and most clinically used predictors in epigenetics, and they are covered in Epigenetic clocks and biomarkers and in Epigenetics in disease and therapy. They are not sequence models: the input is a methylation profile measured in a sample. Both have many more features (hundreds of thousands of CpGs) than samples (thousands), so regularisation and careful validation are essential: the clock was validated in independent data sets; the tumour classifier in a prospective cohort, where it changed the diagnosis for about 12% of cases. A point for discussion: the clock’s prediction error is partly what makes it interesting (age acceleration), which is unusual for a predictor.

The last column is the important one, and is the bridge to the second half. A test is only meaningful if it resembles the use we have in mind. If we want to predict expression for a person’s genome, the test must contain people the model has not seen. If we want to apply an enhancer–gene model genome-wide, the test must contain genes and enhancers not in the training set. The general principle: decide what “new” means for the intended use, and make the test set new in exactly that sense.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: How do we know a prediction is real?
text:
How do we know a prediction is real?


Leakage: information about the test examples reached the training. The model looks better than it is.
In genomics the usual routes: overlapping or duplicated regions, similar sequences on different chromosomes, and decisions made using the test set.


Three questions to ask of every evaluation: Is the test set really unseen (leakage)? Is the comparison fair (what are the negatives)? Is there a baseline? The figure shows the leakage question. Gold examples are pairs of near-identical examples, one on each side of the split. A model that can memorise, such as a nearest-neighbour classifier, a random forest or a deep network, will recognise the test copy and get it right without having learned anything general. The third arrow is the subtle one: choosing features, architectures or thresholds by looking at test performance also leaks.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Overlapping windows leak


Shifting windows to create more training data (augmentation), tiling the genome with overlapping inputs, or a peak listed twice: all create near-copies.
If near-copies are split at random, the test set contains copies of the training set.


These are not exotic mistakes. Shifting a window by a few bases and adding the reverse complement are standard ways to augment training data for CNNs; the trap is doing it before splitting. Tiling the genome into 200-bp bins with 1 kb of context, as DeepSEA and many later models do, makes neighbouring inputs share 800 bp; it is safe only because those models split by chromosome. The ENCODE IDR peak files list many peaks several times, once per summit: the GM12878 ATAC file has 155 153 lines but only 75 409 distinct regions. The rule: define the groups of related examples first (a region with all its shifted copies; a chromosome), and split by group.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Leakage, measured


6000 GM12878 open/closed regions, each as three windows shifted by 150 bp; 4-mer counts as features. Test sets: random windows, whole regions, or whole chromosomes (8, 9).
1-nearest neighbour: 96% accuracy with a random split, 65% when whole regions are held out. For 87% of test windows, the nearest training window is a shifted copy of itself.


This is the experiment of exercise R1. The 1-nearest-neighbour classifier gives each test window the label of the most similar training window; it is the purest memoriser. With a random split it looks excellent, because a shifted copy of almost every test window is in the training set. Holding out whole regions or whole chromosomes removes the copies, and its accuracy collapses to 64–65%. The 25-nearest-neighbour model is less extreme (AUC 0.86 vs 0.79 vs 0.78), ridge regression on 4-mers moves least (0.85 vs 0.82), and the GC model hardly at all. The lesson: leakage inflates flexible models most, which is exactly why it matters for deep learning. A second lesson hides in the last group: GC drops from 0.75 to 0.72 between the region split and the chromosome split, without any leakage, simply because chromosomes 8 and 9 differ from the genome average. Test sets differ; compare models on the same test set.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Held-out chromosomes, and their limit


Holding out whole chromosomes is the field’s standard: overlapping windows, neighbouring peaks and shared domains all stay on one side.
It does not stop similar sequences on other chromosomes: repeats (half of the genome), segmental duplications, paralogous genes.


A held-out chromosome is a good test for most purposes, and it is what students do in the exercises and in the CNN units (chr8 and chr9). The remaining leak is sequence similarity across chromosomes. A model can learn to recognise an Alu or L1 subfamily, or a duplicated promoter, from training copies on other chromosomes. Whether this matters depends on the claim: if the claim is “the model learned regulatory grammar”, test also on unique sequence or on clusters of similar sequences held out together. Two more points: in a cross-species setting (training on mouse, testing on human), orthologous regions play the same role; and a held-out chromosome is not a held-out cell type or a held-out individual, which come next.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Case study: enhancer–promoter prediction


TargetFinder (2016) predicted which enhancer–promoter pairs interact, F1 ≈ 0.83 with random cross-validation.
With pairs split by chromosome, F1 fell to 0.13 in K562 (Xi & Beer 2018): the model had learned which promoters interact, from pairs that shared them.


The example in the figure: four enhancers of one promoter, three in training and one in test. The promoter’s features are identical in all four pairs, and the “window” features between enhancer and promoter overlap heavily. The model learns that this promoter has many interactions, and correctly guesses that the test pair interacts, without learning anything about which enhancer is used. Xi and Beer showed that more than 92% of training pairs shared a promoter with another pair. With a 1:20 ratio of positive to negative pairs, random guessing gives F1 = 1/11 ≈ 0.09, so the chromosome-split result is barely above chance. This is a published, well-cited model, which is why it is a good warning: the original authors were careful in many respects, and the leak was still there.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
The negatives decide the question


Random genome as negatives: “is this a CTCF site or any piece of DNA?” GC content alone helps a lot.
GC-matched negatives remove that shortcut. Accessible but unbound negatives ask what makes a site CTCF rather than just open.


A classifier learns whatever separates the positives from the negatives, including differences we did not intend. Random genomic windows are AT-rich and gene-poor; peaks are GC-rich and near genes. So “GC content” can do much of the work, and a model can report a high AUC by learning GC. Matching the negatives on GC (sampling negatives with the same GC distribution, as in the motif-enrichment unit) or on accessibility forces the model to use other information. None of the three is wrong: they answer different questions. The questions to ask of a paper: what were the negatives, and does the conclusion match that question? The curves in the figure are schematic; the real ones are on the next slide.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Negatives, measured: CTCF in GM12878


10 000 CTCF peaks against 10 000 windows of each kind; models trained on chr1–22 except 8 and 9, tested on 8 and 9.
GC only: ROC AUC 0.71 with random negatives, 0.49 with GC-matched (chance), 0.51 with accessible ones. The best CTCF PWM score in the window: 0.91–0.94 whatever the negatives. 256 4-mers: 0.80 → 0.70.


Left: the GC distributions. Random windows have mean GC 0.41, CTCF peaks 0.49; the GC-matched set has the same distribution as the peaks by construction, so its curve hides the peaks’ curve; ATAC peaks without CTCF are GC-rich too (0.50). Right: three models, each trained and tested separately against each negative set. The GC model is useful only against random negatives. The PWM model, which uses one number (the best CTCF motif score in the window), is barely affected (0.94, 0.91, 0.92), because it measures what actually distinguishes CTCF sites. One technical trap: motifmatchr reports a score of 0 for any window without a match passing p.cutoff, so with the usual cutoff of 5e-5 most negatives tie at 0 and this baseline drops to about 0.84; the continuous score needs p.cutoff = 1 (How a CNN reads DNA discusses the same trap). The 4-mer ridge model is the interesting one: it loses 0.1 of AUC when GC is matched, which shows that a good part of what it had learned was GC content, not CTCF. A CNN trained against random negatives can make the same mistake, which is why the CNN units use GC-matched negatives. Accessible negatives are slightly easier for the 4-mer model than GC-matched ones (0.73 vs 0.70): open regions without CTCF have their own sequence character (other TF motifs) that the model can use to reject them.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: The simplest baseline is often strong
text:
The simplest baseline is often strong


One known motif, scored with one PWM: 72% of CTCF peaks have a match (p < 5 × 10⁻⁵), against 5% of random, 9% of GC-matched and 8% of accessible windows.
Ranked by its best score in each window, the PWM reaches ROC AUC 0.91 against GC-matched negatives. Trap: motifmatchr gives score 0 to windows without a match at the cutoff; use p.cutoff = 1 for a continuous score (else 0.83; see How a CNN reads DNA).
Any model of CTCF binding must be compared with this. The CNN in How a CNN reads DNA is: same kind of data, same test chromosomes.


CTCF is the easiest TF for this kind of baseline: its motif is long (the MA0139.2 matrix used here spans 15 bp) and highly informative, and most of its peaks contain it. So the best PWM score gets an AUC above 0.9 against any negatives, and the 4-mer model, with 256 parameters, is far worse than this single number once GC is matched (0.70 vs 0.91). Two things limit the PWM: 28% of peaks have no match at this threshold (weaker or non-canonical sites, or indirect binding), and 5–9% of non-peak windows do have a match (sites that are methylated, in closed chromatin, or simply not bound in this cell type; compare Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting). A model that improves on the PWM has to learn something about these cases: flanking sequence, motif strength beyond a threshold, co-occurring motifs. For TFs with short, degenerate motifs the PWM baseline is much weaker and learned models gain more. The right panel shows the best score in every window (scanned with p.cutoff = 1, so that windows without a significant match keep their best, weak score): median 13.3 in CTCF peaks against 3–5 in the negative sets. Ranking by this continuous score is what gives the baseline its AUC of 0.91; using only presence at p < 5e-5, or a score that is 0 below the cutoff, throws most of that information away.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: Does the model work in another cell type?
text:
Does the model work in another cell type?


4-mer models of “open vs closed” trained in GM12878 or in K562, tested on chr8–9 on regions open in both, only in GM12878, or only in K562.
Regions open in both are easy for either model (0.91–0.92). Each model is best on its own cell type’s specific regions and loses 0.05–0.06 on the other’s (0.87 → 0.82 for K562-only; 0.79 → 0.73 for GM12878-only).


Two ridge models on 4-mer counts: one trained on GM12878 open regions, one on K562 open regions, both against the same closed-in-both windows, on all chromosomes except 8 and 9. Test sets on chr8–9: GM12878 peaks not overlapping any K562 peak (4070), GM12878 peaks overlapping a K562 peak (2039), K562 peaks not overlapping a GM12878 peak (1925), against 1965 windows closed in both. The shared regions are mostly CpG-island promoters and CTCF sites, whose sequence is distinctive in any cell type. The drop for the cell-type-specific regions is real but smaller than one might expect, for an honest reason: much of what a sequence model learns about “open” is generic (GC, CpG, AT-rich closed DNA), and both cell types’ specific regions share it. The cell-type-specific part (PU.1, EBF1 and IRF motifs in GM12878; GATA1 and TAL1 motifs in K562) is what is lost. Note the negatives here are random genome; with GC-matched negatives the cell-type-specific part would be a larger share and the drop larger. The general lesson: a model can only predict cell types like those it was trained on, and a held-out chromosome in the training cell type does not test this.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: Across genes is not across people
text:
Across genes is not across people


Expression models predict which genes are highly expressed well (Enformer: r ≈ 0.55–0.6 across genes).
But for one gene across people, with each person’s own variants inserted, predictions barely correlate with measured expression (mean r ≈ 0), and often have the wrong sign (Sasse et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023).


This is the best-documented failure of the large sequence models, published in two papers in the same issue of Nature Genetics. Both inserted each individual’s variants into the reference sequence, predicted expression with Enformer (and other models), and correlated predicted with measured expression across people. Sasse et al. used 839 individuals with whole-genome sequencing and brain RNA-seq (ROSMAP): across genes the correlation was good, but across individuals the mean correlation was about zero; where it was significant, about a third of genes had the wrong sign, while PrediXcan (a simple elastic net trained on genotypes and expression of people) did much better on the same genes and was never anti-correlated. Huang et al. found the same for four models with 421 Geuvadis individuals (lymphoblastoid cell lines, close relatives of GM12878): cross-individual correlations centred near zero, and frequent disagreement on the direction of effect. Why? The models were trained across genes in one reference genome, so they learned what makes genes differ, which is dominated by promoters and large-scale features, not the small effects of common variants. The test that matters for personal genomics (new individuals) was not the test used in training. Newer models (Borzoi, AlphaGenome) improve variant-effect benchmarks, but this remains the standard check.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
section: Reading a machine-learning paper: a checklist
text:
Reading a machine-learning paper: a checklist







question
warning signs




What exactly is predicted, and for what use?
test set does not match the intended use (new cell type, new person)


How were the data split?
random windows; shifted or overlapping windows; features chosen on all data


What are the negatives?
random genome for a GC-rich target; negatives from other experiments or batches


Which baselines?
no GC / k-mer / known-motif / nearest-gene baseline; only other deep models


Which metric, at which class balance?
accuracy on imbalanced data; PR AUC without the prevalence; balanced test sets only


Was the test set used once?
many architectures tried on the test set; no independent validation


Does it generalise?
one cell type, one cohort, one lab; no external data set




This is the practical summary of the second half and a good template for exam questions of the “judge the design” kind. It is adapted from Whalen et al. 2022 (Navigating the pitfalls of applying machine learning in genomics), which is the recommended further reading for this unit. Students should be able to take a methods paragraph and say which of these questions it answers and which it does not.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




sequence → binding, accessibility
CNNs on 0.5–2 kb; one output per assay and cell type (DeepSEA, Basset, BPNet)


sequence → expression
long context (131 kb – 1 Mb): Basenji, Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome


variant effects
predict(alt) − predict(ref) with any trained sequence model


other tasks
enhancer–gene links (ABC, CRISPRi labels), imputation, 3D contacts, clocks, tumour classes


leakage
near-copies across the split; memorising models gain most (1-NN: 96% → 65%)


splits
group related examples; hold out chromosomes; mind repeats and paralogs


negatives
define the question; GC-matched negatives remove the GC shortcut


baselines
GC, k-mers, one PWM, nearest gene; report them


generalisation
other cell types and other individuals are harder tests than other chromosomes




Students should leave able to place a new paper on the map (input, labels, intended use), to spot the main evaluation traps in a methods section, and to explain with an example why a high AUC can be meaningless (leakage, easy negatives, no baseline). Next: How a CNN reads DNA, where they train their own sequence model on CTCF peaks against GC-matched background and compare it with the PWM baseline from this unit.

title: What people try to predict, and how to tell if it works
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Whalen, Schreiber, Noble & Pollard 2022, Nat Rev Genet. Navigating the pitfalls of applying machine learning in genomics. The evaluation traps of this unit, with many examples.
Zhou & Troyanskaya 2015, Nat Methods. Predicting effects of noncoding variants with deep learning–based sequence model. DeepSEA: chromatin features and variant effects from sequence.
Avsec et al. 2021, Nat Methods. Effective gene expression prediction from sequence by integrating long-range interactions. Enformer: long-context expression prediction.
Xi & Beer 2018, PLoS Comput Biol. Local epigenomic state cannot discriminate interacting and non-interacting enhancer–promoter pairs with high accuracy. A clear case of leakage in a published model.
Sasse et al. 2023, Nat Genet. Benchmarking of deep neural networks for predicting personal gene expression from DNA sequence highlights shortcomings. Good across genes, poor across individuals.
Huang et al. 2023, Nat Genet. Personal transcriptome variation is poorly explained by current genomic deep learning models. The same finding in lymphoblastoid cell lines.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Background
Motif matches. A position weight matrix (PWM, from Gene regulation) gives each window of DNA a log-odds score; a window is a match when its score would be reached by chance with probability below a threshold \(p\) (motifmatchr uses \(p < 5 \times 10^{-5}\)). A region of length \(L\) has about \(2L\) windows (both strands), so it contains on average \(2Lp\) chance matches.
Enrichment. For a target set of peaks (for example B-up) and a background set (here the ns peaks, which are not differential by the course thresholds):




with match
without




target
\(a\)
\(b\)


background
\(c\)
\(d\)



Odds ratio \(\mathrm{OR} = ad / bc\). Under the null, the target is a random draw of \(a + b\) peaks from all \(N = a + b + c + d\) peaks, of which \(K = a + c\) have a match; the expected number in the target is \((a+b)K/N\). The one-sided p-value is the hypergeometric upper tail \(P(X \ge a)\), which equals the one-sided Fisher’s exact test.
Multiple testing. With \(m\) motifs, Bonferroni rejects when \(p < 0.05/m\). Benjamini–Hochberg (BH): sort the p-values, find the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le 0.05\, i/m\), and reject the \(i\) smallest.
chromVAR computes, for each motif and sample, the fraction of reads in peaks with the motif, compares it with the expected fraction (all samples pooled), and standardises it against background peak sets matched for GC content and average accessibility: a deviation z-score. Variability is the standard deviation of a motif’s z-scores across samples.
Footprints. Each read end marks one Tn5 insertion: in BED coordinates, read start + 4 on the + strand and read end − 5 on the − strand. With 1-based closed R coordinates, use start + 4 and end − 4. Averaging insertions around many motif sites, oriented by motif strand, gives an aggregate footprint: a dip where the bound protein blocks Tn5, flanked by high insertion rates in the open DNA next to it.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Data

Saved differential peaks: ~/epi/diffacc/differential_peaks.tsv, written in R11 of Differential accessibility. Its B_up, T_up and ns classes use adjusted \(p < 0.05\) and absolute apeglm-shrunken log2 fold change > 1. We reuse these classes and compare each differential group with ns.
Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis ATAC-seq (GEO GSE74912): read counts in 590 650 fixed 500-bp peaks (hg19) for 132 samples. The 77 samples from healthy donors cover 13 cell types; the sample names encode donor and cell type (decoded below from the GEO sample table). The same file as in Differential accessibility, with the UCSC hg19 → hg38 chain file; these are used for chromVAR in R6. Motif enrichment in R1–R5 uses the saved differential-peak table.
hg38 genome as a bgzip-compressed, indexed FASTA (hg38.fa.bgz, .fai, .gzi), so R can read any region quickly.
GM12878 ATAC-seq, ENCODE ENCSR095QNB replicate 1, paired-end 2 × 101: the 6.1 million read pairs that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, as raw FASTQ, and a bowtie2 index of chr21 + chrM. Plus the ENCODE GM12878 ATAC peaks and CTCF ChIP-seq peaks (from Genomic intervals).

data/download.sh motifs-footprinting      # about 2 GB, mostly the hg38 genome and the reads
D=/path/to/course/data                    # where download.sh put the files
mkdir -p ~/epi/motifs && cd ~/epi/motifs
# only if your data folder has hg38.fa.gz but not hg38.fa.bgz:
# zcat $D/hg38.fa.gz | bgzip -@ 4 > $D/hg38.fa.bgz && samtools faidx $D/hg38.fa.bgz
Shortcuts, said plainly. The footprint uses one chromosome (chr21) of one replicate: aggregate footprints work at this depth, single-site footprints do not. chromVAR uses the 100 000 most-read peaks rather than all 589 000, and sums technical replicates per donor. Motif enrichment is done in R with motifmatchr; HOMER and the MEME suite, the usual command-line tools, are shown in the lecture and under Where this leads but not installed in this course.
You need fastp, bowtie2 and samtools (≥ 1.10) on the command line, and the R packages listed in Install the software you need, including JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, chromVAR and universalmotif. Total running time on a laptop with 4–8 cores: about 25 minutes, most of it alignment and motif matching. Complete Differential accessibility first and keep its saved table; we do not rerun DESeq2 here.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Chance matches. You scan 300-bp peaks with a motif at threshold \(p = 10^{-4}\).

How many windows does one peak have (both strands, ignore the ends)? How many chance matches do you expect per peak?
In 50 000 peaks, how many chance matches do you expect in total?
Chance matches are rare events, so the number per peak is roughly Poisson. What fraction of peaks has at least one chance match? (\(P(\ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\).)
A paper reports “a GATA motif in 25% of our peaks”. What do you need to know before this means anything?

B2. A 2×2 table. 400 target peaks, 120 with a match to motif M. 9600 background peaks, 1440 with a match.

Write the 2×2 table and the fraction with a match in each group.
Compute the odds ratio.
How many target peaks would you expect to have a match if the target were a random draw from all 10 000 peaks? Is the observation higher or lower?
In the real data, an EBF1 match is in 2728 of 19 404 B-up peaks and in 22 271 of 175 523 ns peaks; \(p \approx 4.5 \times 10^{-8}\). Compute the two fractions and the odds ratio. Is EBF1 “the TF that drives B-cell chromatin”? What else would you look at?

B3. Many motifs. You test 800 motifs. The eight smallest p-values are
\(1\times10^{-40}\), \(3\times10^{-12}\), \(2\times10^{-6}\), \(4\times10^{-5}\), \(9\times10^{-5}\), \(1.5\times10^{-4}\), \(2.5\times10^{-4}\), \(6\times10^{-4}\).

What is the Bonferroni threshold at 5%, and how many of these motifs pass?
Apply Benjamini–Hochberg at FDR 5%. How many pass?
If none of the 800 motifs were truly enriched, how many would you expect below \(p = 0.05\)?
The top 30 motifs include 12 ETS motifs (ELF1, ELF3, ETV1, GABPA, …). How many independent findings is that?

B4. Background and GC. Your target peaks are promoters (mean GC 0.62). You compare them with (i) random 500-bp windows of the genome (mean GC 0.41) and (ii) GC-matched peaks from the same cells.

With background (i), which kinds of motifs will look enriched only because of base composition? Give an example.
Why does the comparison with (ii) answer a more useful question?
In the real B-up peaks (mean GC 0.48, ns peaks 0.51), the SP1 motif has OR 0.58 against ns and 0.95 against GC-matched ns peaks. Which number would you report, and what do you conclude about SP1?

B5. One motif, many TFs. In B-up peaks the three most enriched motifs are SPIB (OR 2.95), SPI1 (PU.1, OR 2.64) and SPIC (OR 2.85).

Can you tell from these numbers which of the three TFs binds the B-cell peaks? Why not?
Name two kinds of data that would help.
In T-up peaks, ETS1 has OR 2.66 but SPI1 only 1.33. How can two ETS motifs behave so differently? (Hint: look at the logos in the lecture.)

B6. Read a chromVAR heatmap. Part of a deviation z-score table (mean over donors):

For each motif, name the cell types where peaks with the motif are more accessible than expected.
What does a z-score of −22 for GATA1::TAL1 in monocytes mean? Does it mean GATA1 represses those peaks in monocytes?
chromVAR reports a motif named “GATA3” with almost the same z-scores as GATA1::TAL1, highest in MEPs and erythroblasts, although GATA3 is a T-cell factor. Explain.
Why does chromVAR compare with background peaks of matched GC content and accessibility instead of just using the raw deviation?

B7. Read an aggregate footprint. Mean Tn5 insertions per site around 1000 CTCF motif sites inside CTCF ChIP peaks: about 0.70 at ±30–60 bp from the motif centre, 0.25 within ±10 bp of the centre, and 0.30 at ±100 bp.

Sketch the profile. Which features are the flanks and which is the footprint?
Compute the ratio centre/flank. What would it be for a motif without any protection?
For 5000 CTCF motif sites in closed chromatin the profile is flat at 0.01. Why flat, and why so low?
A colleague finds no footprint for the glucocorticoid receptor at its ChIP-seq peaks and concludes that it does not bind there. What is wrong with this conclusion?
An aggregate footprint of motif X shows a sharp 3-bp dip at the same position in cells with and without the TF. What is the likely explanation, and how would you correct for it?

B8. Judge the claim. “Peaks gained after stimulation are enriched for AP-1 motifs (p < 10⁻¹⁰⁰ against random genomic regions), so AP-1 opens these regions.” List three problems or missing controls.

On the command line

C1 — Trim and align the GM12878 ATAC-seq reads
This is the pipeline of ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, run on the chr21 + chrM subset. It keeps properly paired fragments with MAPQ ≥ 30 and removes duplicates.
fastp -i $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R2.fastq.gz \
  -o R1.trim.fq.gz -O R2.trim.fq.gz --detect_adapter_for_pe -w 4 -j fastp.json -h fastp.html

    -1 R1.trim.fq.gz -2 R2.trim.fq.gz 2> bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
  | samtools view -u -f 2 -q 30 - \
  | samtools sort -u - \
  | samtools markdup -r -s - gm12878_atac_rep1.bam 2> markdup.log
samtools index gm12878_atac_rep1.bam
tail -1 bowtie2.log
samtools idxstats gm12878_atac_rep1.bam

What fraction of the read pairs aligned? How many reads are left on chr21 and on chrM after filtering?
What fraction of the filtered reads is on chrM? Why is it so high in ATAC-seq, and why does it not matter for footprinting on chr21?
markdup.log reports the duplicates removed. Why are duplicates a particular problem when you count insertions at single bases?

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Explore: a 2×2 motif table, the threshold and the background
text:
Explore: a 2×2 motif table, the threshold and the background
The demo simulates 1000 target peaks and 8000 other peaks of 300 bp (random bases at each peak’s GC content). A PU.1-like motif is planted in a fraction of the target peaks (and in 5% of the other peaks, because bound sites occur there too). A GC box (SP1-like) is planted nowhere. Both motifs are scanned on both strands; a peak has a match when its best window passes the threshold, given as a p-value per window (motifmatchr’s default is \(5 \times 10^{-5}\)). Target GC − background GC makes the target peaks GC-richer (or AT-richer) than the others. Background compares the target with all other peaks or with a GC-matched set (two other peaks from the same 1%-GC bin per target peak; R5 applies the same matching idea to ns peaks using 2%-GC bins). Panel (a) shows the two 2×2 tables with the odds ratio and the exact one-sided Fisher / hypergeometric p-value (computed on the log scale, as in R4), and whether it passes Bonferroni for 879 motifs. Panel (b) shows GC content, panel (c) the odds ratio against the threshold.



E1. At the defaults, read the PU.1 table. Compute the two fractions and the odds ratio by hand, and the number of target matches expected if the target were a random draw from all 9000 peaks. Compare with the demo.
E2. Move the threshold from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-6}\) (watch the note under the controls and panel c). How do the number of PU.1 matches in the target, the odds ratio and the p-value change? Why is neither the most lenient nor the strictest threshold best?
E3. The GC box is not bound anywhere. What odds ratio and p-value does it get against all other peaks? Would it survive Bonferroni for 879 motifs? Switch to the GC-matched background: what happens to the GC box, and to PU.1? Then set the GC difference to 0 and to +0.12 (the data are re-simulated when you release the slider).
E4. Set target peaks with a PU.1 site to 0%. Why is the PU.1 odds ratio now below 1? Finally: a correction for multiple testing would not have stopped the GC box in E3. Why not, and what else in this demo is a hidden multiple-testing problem?






Solutions





E1. \(a = 136\), \(b = 864\), \(c = 456\), \(d = 7544\): 13.6% of target peaks against 5.7% of the other peaks have a match. \(\mathrm{OR} = (136 \cdot 7544)/(864 \cdot 456) = 2.60\). Expected under the null: \(1000 \times (136 + 456)/9000 = 66\), observed 136, \(p = 9.3 \times 10^{-18}\). Note that the fraction of bound target peaks is 25%, but only 13.6% have a match: half of the planted sites score below the threshold, and some matches in the target are chance matches (about 3% of peaks have one at this threshold: 0.029 per peak).
E2. At \(10^{-3}\): 538 target matches (54% against 48%), OR 1.24, \(p \approx 10^{-3.2}\): almost every second peak has a chance match, and the real sites drown in them. At \(10^{-4}\): 177, OR 2.23, \(p \approx 10^{-15.8}\); at \(5 \times 10^{-5}\): 136, OR 2.60, \(p \approx 10^{-17.0}\); at \(10^{-5}\): 76, OR 3.88, \(p \approx 10^{-17.3}\); at \(10^{-6}\): 22, OR 3.2, \(p \approx 10^{-4.6}\). A stricter threshold removes chance matches faster than true sites, so the odds ratio rises, but it also loses true sites (weak matches), and with few counts the estimate becomes noisy and the p-value weak. The threshold trades counts (sensitivity) against specificity.
E3. Against all other peaks the GC box has OR 2.24 (4.1% vs 1.9%), \(p = 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\): it passes Bonferroni (\(p < 5.7 \times 10^{-5}\)). It is enriched only because the target peaks are GC-richer (mean GC 0.52 vs 0.44), and a GC-rich word matches more often by chance in GC-rich DNA. Against GC-matched peaks: OR 0.99, \(p = 0.56\). PU.1 hardly changes (OR 2.60 → 2.63), because its enrichment is real. With no GC difference the GC box gets OR 1.12 against all peaks; at +0.12 it gets OR 4.55, \(p \approx 4 \times 10^{-22}\), and 1.23 against GC-matched peaks. The background decides the question you ask; in the real data (lecture, R5) the same effect works in the other direction, because B-up peaks are AT-richer than the ns peaks.
E4. With no bound target peaks, PU.1 has OR 0.49 (2.9% vs 5.7%): the background still contains 5% of peaks with a bound site, so the target is depleted relative to it. “Depleted” means “less than in the background”, not “avoided”. Multiple-testing corrections control errors made by chance; the GC box is a bias that gets more significant with more data. Only a better background (or a GC-aware test) removes it. The hidden multiple testing: trying several thresholds or backgrounds and reporting the one that gives the best p-value.
