title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
In R
Start R in ~/epi/motifs (where the BAM file is) and load the packages:
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(SummarizedExperiment); library(rtracklayer); library(GenomicRanges); library(Rsamtools)
  library(GenomicAlignments); library(Biostrings); library(Matrix)
  library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(motifmatchr); library(chromVAR)
  library(universalmotif); library(BiocParallel); library(ggplot2); library(pheatmap)
})
register(MulticoreParam(4))         # on Windows: register(SerialParam())
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
genome <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))
set.seed(1)

R1 — Reuse the saved differential peaks
Read the table written in R11 of Differential accessibility. Set diff_file to that file if you used another working folder. Coordinates are already GRCh38, 1-based closed: do not add 1 to the start. The saved class column preserves the paired DESeq2 analysis and its apeglm-shrunken fold-change threshold.
diff_file <- path.expand("~/epi/diffacc/differential_peaks.tsv")
tab <- read.delim(diff_file, check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(tab$peak_id), all(tab$class %in% c("B_up", "T_up", "ns")))
tested <- GRanges(tab$chr, IRanges(tab$start, tab$end))
names(tested) <- tab$peak_id
tested$lfc <- tab$log2FoldChange; tested$padj <- tab$padj
tested$class <- tab$class
stopifnot(all(width(tested) == 500))
b_up <- tested$class == "B_up"
t_up <- tested$class == "T_up"
ns <- tested$class == "ns"
c(tested = length(tested), B_up = sum(b_up), T_up = sum(t_up), ns = sum(ns))

How many peaks were tested, and how many belong to each class? Check that the counts agree with the saved table from Differential accessibility.
Why reuse the class column instead of applying the cutoff to the unshrunk maximum-likelihood fold changes? Does ns prove that a peak is unchanged?



R2 — JASPAR motifs
jdb <- RSQLite::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
pfms <- getMatrixSet(jdb, opts = list(collection = "CORE", tax_group = "vertebrates",
                                      all_versions = FALSE))
names(pfms) <- paste(name(pfms), ID(pfms), sep = "_")
length(pfms)
fam <- sapply(pfms, function(p) paste(tags(p)$family, collapse = "; "))
head(sort(table(fam), decreasing = TRUE), 8)
TFBSTools::Matrix(pfms[["CTCF_MA0139.2"]])
view_motifs(convert_motifs(pfms[c("Spi1_MA0080.7", "SPIB_MA0081.3", "ETS1_MA0098.4")]))

How many motifs are there? Which TF families have the most motifs?
The CTCF matrix is a table of counts. How many binding sites was it built from? (Sum a column.)
Look at the three ETS logos. What do they share, and where do they differ?



R3 — Motif matches in all tested peaks
system.time(hit <- motifMatches(matchMotifs(pfms, tested, genome = genome, p.cutoff = 5e-5)))
dim(hit)
summary(colMeans(hit))
sort(colMeans(hit), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]

What is the median fraction of peaks that match a motif? Compare with your answer to B1 for a 500-bp peak at \(p = 5 \times 10^{-5}\).
Which motifs match the most peaks? Why might short or low-information motifs match far more peaks than the median?



R4 — Enrichment in B-up and T-up peaks
Compare B-up with ns, and T-up with the same ns background. The opposite differential group is excluded from each comparison. First one motif with fisher.test, then all motifs at once with the hypergeometric distribution (identical to one-sided Fisher, but vectorised and on the log scale, so that p-values below \(10^{-308}\) do not become 0):
selected <- b_up | ns
tab <- table(B_up = b_up[selected], SPIB = hit[selected, "SPIB_MA0081.3"])
tab
fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")

enrich <- function(target, hit, bg) {
  stopifnot(!any(target & bg))
  a <- colSums(hit[target, , drop = FALSE]); b <- sum(target) - a
  c <- colSums(hit[bg, , drop = FALSE]);     d <- sum(bg) - c
  lp <- phyper(a - 1, a + c, b + d, a + b, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
  data.frame(tf = sub("_MA.*", "", colnames(hit)), family = fam[colnames(hit)],
             frac_target = a / (a + b), frac_bg = c / (c + d), OR = (a * d) / (b * c),
             log10p = lp, padj = p.adjust(10^lp, "BH"))
}
eB <- enrich(b_up, hit, bg = ns); eT <- enrich(t_up, hit, bg = ns)
head(eB[order(eB$log10p), -2], 15)
head(eT[order(eT$log10p), -2], 15)
c(B = sum(eB$padj < 0.05 & eB$OR > 1), T = sum(eT$padj < 0.05 & eT$OR > 1))
sel <- c("EBF1_MA0154.5", "PAX5_MA0014.4", "PAX2_MA0067.3", "POU2F2_MA0507.3", "Runx1_MA0002.3",
         "TCF7_MA0769.3", "Gata3_MA0037.5", "ETS1_MA0098.4", "Spi1_MA0080.7", "CTCF_MA0139.2")
round(cbind(B = eB[sel, c("OR", "log10p")], T = eT[sel, c("OR", "log10p")]), 2)

From tab, compute the odds ratio by hand and compare with fisher.test. Why does fisher.test report \(p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) while enrich() gives \(10^{-966}\)?
Which TF families dominate the top of each list? Do they match what you know about B and T cells?
How many motifs are significant at FDR 5%? Is that a useful number?
Look at EBF1, PAX5 and PAX2 in B-up peaks. What do you conclude about the B-cell master regulators EBF1 and PAX5, and about the PAX5 matrix?
CTCF has OR < 1 in both lists. Explain.



R5 — A GC-matched background
gc <- as.numeric(letterFrequency(getSeq(genome, tested), "GC") / 500)
tapply(gc, tested$class, mean)
bin <- cut(gc, seq(0, 1, 0.02), include.lowest = TRUE)
pool <- split(which(ns), bin[ns])
set.seed(1)
gcm <- unlist(lapply(split(which(b_up), bin[b_up]), function(i) {
  p <- pool[[as.character(bin[i[1]])]]
  n <- min(length(p), length(i))
  if (n == 0) integer(0) else p[sample.int(length(p), n)]
}))
c(background_peaks = length(gcm), mean_gc = mean(gc[gcm]))
eB_gc <- enrich(b_up, hit, bg = seq_along(tested) %in% gcm)
sel2 <- c("SPIB_MA0081.3", "EBF1_MA0154.5", "SP1_MA0079.5", "KLF4_MA0039.5", "Nrf1_MA0506.3",
          "CTCF_MA0139.2")
data.frame(OR_ns = eB[sel2, "OR"], OR_gc = eB_gc[sel2, "OR"], row.names = sel2)

Are B-up peaks more or less GC-rich than the ns peaks? How many background peaks were sampled?
Which motifs change most when the background is GC-matched, and in which direction? Explain using (a). The matching samples without replacement from ns in each 2%-GC bin. If a bin has too few ns peaks, it contributes fewer partners, so the background may be smaller than the target. Why is it useful to report its size and GC distribution?



R6 — chromVAR across 13 cell types
chromVAR needs the count matrix across all healthy donors and cell types, rather than the differential-peak table alone. Load and lift that matrix here, preserving the same coordinate filters as Differential accessibility. This prepares counts for chromVAR without fitting another differential model.
cnt <- read.delim(file.path(D, "corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz"), check.names = FALSE)
peaks19 <- GRanges(cnt$Chr, IRanges(cnt$Start + 1, cnt$End))        # BED-like 0-based starts
cnt <- as.matrix(cnt[, -(1:3)])

# sample names -> donor and cell type (codes from the GEO sample table, GSE74912)
code <- c("1" = "HSC", "2" = "MPP", "3" = "LMPP", "4" = "CMP", "5" = "GMP", "6" = "MEP",
          "7" = "Mono", "9" = "CD4", "10" = "CD8", "11" = "NK", "13" = "B", "14" = "CLP",
          "15" = "Ery")
nm <- colnames(cnt)
ok <- grepl("^(Donor)?[0-9]{4}-", nm)                                # healthy donors only
info <- data.frame(sample = nm[ok],
                   donor = sub("^(Donor)?([0-9]{4})-.*", "\\2", nm[ok]),
                   celltype = code[sub(".*-([0-9]{1,2})[A-C]?(-[0-9]{6})?$", "\\1", nm[ok])])

# lift to hg38; keep peaks that map in one piece of 500 bp
chain <- tempfile(fileext = ".chain")
writeLines(readLines(file.path(D, "hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz")), chain)
lo <- liftOver(peaks19, import.chain(chain))
keep <- which(lengths(lo) == 1)
peaks <- unlist(lo[keep])
ok <- width(peaks) == 500 & as.character(seqnames(peaks)) == as.character(seqnames(peaks19)[keep])
keep <- keep[ok]; peaks <- peaks[ok]
cnt <- cnt[keep, info$sample]

table(info$celltype)
length(peaks)

grp <- paste(info$celltype, info$donor, sep = "_")                 # one column per donor x cell type
cm <- sapply(split(info$sample, grp), function(s) rowSums(cnt[, s, drop = FALSE]))
top <- order(rowSums(cm), decreasing = TRUE)[1:100000]              # the 100 000 most-read peaks
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = cm[top, ]), rowRanges = peaks[top],
                           colData = DataFrame(celltype = sub("_.*", "", colnames(cm))))
se <- addGCBias(se, genome = genome)
mm <- matchMotifs(pfms, se, genome = genome, p.cutoff = 5e-5)
bg <- getBackgroundPeaks(se, niterations = 50)
system.time(dev <- computeDeviations(se, annotations = mm, background_peaks = bg))
z <- deviationScores(dev)
dim(z)
v <- computeVariability(dev)
head(v[order(-v$variability), c("name", "variability")], 15)

show <- c("GATA1::TAL1_MA0140.3", "Gata3_MA0037.5", "KLF1_MA0493.3", "CEBPA_MA0102.5",
          "Spi1_MA0080.7", "EBF1_MA0154.5", "TCF3_MA0522.4", "POU2F2_MA0507.3", "Runx1_MA0002.3",
          "TCF7_MA0769.3", "TBX21_MA0690.3", "CTCF_MA0139.2")
ord <- c("HSC", "MPP", "LMPP", "CMP", "GMP", "MEP", "Ery", "Mono", "CLP", "B", "CD4", "CD8", "NK")
zm <- sapply(ord, function(ct) rowMeans(z[show, dev$celltype == ct, drop = FALSE]))
round(zm)
pheatmap(pmax(pmin(zm, 15), -15), cluster_cols = FALSE,
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#2a6f97", "white", "#c0392b"))(101))

How many healthy libraries, donor × cell-type samples and cell types are there? How many peaks pass the liftOver filters? Which motifs are the most variable?
Read the table zm: in which cell types is each motif most accessible? Do they fit the known regulators of each lineage (GATA1 and KLF1 for erythroid cells, C/EBPα for myeloid cells, PU.1, EBF1 and E2A (TCF3) for B cells, RUNX, TCF7 and T-bet (TBX21) for T and NK cells)?
Compare GATA1::TAL1 and Gata3. What does this tell you about naming a TF from a chromVAR result?
Some highly variable motifs have names like FIGLA, ASCL1 or TBR1, factors not expressed in blood. Look at their family in fam and suggest which blood TF they stand for.



R7 — Tn5 insertions and a CTCF footprint
The offsets below use 1-based closed coordinates, as in BRGenomics ATAC-seq import.
ga <- readGAlignments("gm12878_atac_rep1.bam",
                      param = ScanBamParam(which = GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))))
# GRanges is 1-based closed: the BED end - 5 base is end(ga) - 4 in R.
ins <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(ifelse(strand(ga) == "+", start(ga) + 4, end(ga) - 4), width = 1),
               seqinfo = Seqinfo("chr21", 46709983))
length(ins)
cov_ins <- coverage(ins)$chr21                     # insertions per base along chr21 (an Rle)

ctcf_pk <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
atac_pk <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
sites <- matchMotifs(pfms[["CTCF_MA0139.2"]], chr21, genome = genome,
                     out = "positions", p.cutoff = 1e-4)[[1]]
sites <- sites[!overlapsAny(sites, import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz")))]
grp <- ifelse(overlapsAny(sites, ctcf_pk), "bound (ChIP peak)",
       ifelse(overlapsAny(sites, atac_pk), "open, no ChIP peak", "closed, no ChIP peak"))
table(grp)
mean(overlapsAny(ctcf_pk[seqnames(ctcf_pk) == "chr21"], sites))   # ChIP peaks with a motif

profile <- function(s) {                                          # mean insertions, motif-oriented
  w <- promoters(resize(s, 1, fix = "center"), upstream = 100, downstream = 101)
  x <- as.matrix(Views(cov_ins, ranges(w)))
  minus <- as.logical(strand(w) == "-")
  x[minus, ] <- x[minus, ncol(x):1]
  colMeans(x)
}
fp <- data.frame(pos = rep(-100:100, 3), grp = rep(sort(unique(grp)), each = 201),
                 ins = unlist(lapply(sort(unique(grp)), function(g) profile(sites[grp == g]))))
ggplot(fp, aes(pos, ins, colour = grp)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "bp from CTCF motif centre", y = "Tn5 insertions per site")

b <- fp[fp$grp == "bound (ChIP peak)", ]
c(flank = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) >= 30 & abs(b$pos) <= 60]),
  centre = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) <= 10]), far = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) >= 90]))

How many insertions are there on chr21? How many CTCF motif sites, and what fraction of them lies in a CTCF ChIP peak? What fraction of the chr21 ChIP peaks contains a motif site?
Describe the three profiles. Compute centre/flank for the bound sites (compare with B7).
Why are the “open, no ChIP peak” sites so much lower than the bound sites, although they are in ATAC peaks?
Replace upstream = 100, downstream = 101 by a window that is not strand-aware (resize(s, 201, fix = "center") and no flipping). What happens to the profile, and why?



R8 — Tn5 sequence preference
set.seed(2)
k <- sample(length(ga), 200000)
st <- as.character(strand(ga))[k]
pos <- ifelse(st == "+", start(ga)[k] + 4, end(ga)[k] - 4)
win <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(pos - 10, pos + 10), strand = st)
freq <- consensusMatrix(getSeq(genome, win), as.prob = TRUE)[c("A", "C", "G", "T"), ]
colnames(freq) <- -10:10
round(freq, 2)

chr21 is about 41% GC. At which positions near the insertion is the base composition clearly not random?
Why does this matter for footprints of a motif whose sequence is the same at every site?

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — chance matches and the 2×2 table (B1, B2, R3, R4)





Windows per peak ≈ \(2L\); expected matches \(\lambda = 2Lp\); \(P(\ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\). Odds ratio \(ad/bc\); expected target matches \((a+b)(a+c)/N\). R: fisher.test, phyper with lower.tail = FALSE gives \(P(X > q)\), so use \(q = a - 1\) for \(P(X \ge a)\). matchMotifs returns a sparse peaks × motifs matrix via motifMatches().









Hint 2 — multiple testing (B3)





Bonferroni: \(p < \alpha / m\). BH: compare \(p_{(i)}\) with \(\alpha\, i / m\) and find the largest \(i\) that passes; all smaller p-values pass too. R: p.adjust.









Hint 3 — motif databases (R2, B5)





JASPAR 2024 (paper: Rauluseviciute et al. 2024); in R the JASPAR2024 package with TFBSTools::getMatrixSet. The family and class of each matrix are in tags(pfm). universalmotif::view_motifs draws and aligns logos. Other collections: CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO.









Hint 4 — chromVAR (B6, R6)





The chromVAR vignette explains addGCBias, getBackgroundPeaks, computeDeviations, deviationScores (z) and computeVariability; method in Schep et al. 2017. A negative z means the motif’s peaks are less accessible than expected in that sample, relative to matched background peaks; it says nothing about the mechanism.









Hint 5 — insertions and footprints (B7, R7, R8)





readGAlignments reads the BAM; start()/end() are the leftmost/rightmost aligned base, so the 5’ end of a − strand read is its end(). coverage of 1-bp ranges counts insertions per base; indexing an Rle with a GRanges and as.matrix gives one row per window. promoters builds strand-aware windows. Residence time and footprints: Sung et al. 2014; bias correction: TOBIAS (Bentsen et al. 2020).









Hint 6 — alignment (C1)





fastp detects and trims the Nextera adapters; bowtie2 -X 2000 allows fragments up to 2 kb; samtools fixmate -m adds the mate tags that samtools markdup needs; samtools idxstats gives reads per chromosome.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) About \(2 \times 300 = 600\) windows; \(\lambda = 600 \times 10^{-4} = 0.06\) chance matches per peak. (b) \(50\,000 \times 0.06 = 3000\). (c) \(1 - e^{-0.06} = 0.058\): about 6% of peaks contain a chance match. (d) What fraction of peaks would contain a GATA match by chance (the GATA motif is short, so at a lenient threshold this can be 10–20%), the match threshold and peak width, and above all a comparison with a background set of peaks. “25%” alone is not evidence of anything.
B2. (a)




with match
without
fraction




target
120
280
30%

1440
8160
15%




\(\mathrm{OR} = (120 \times 8160)/(280 \times 1440) = 979\,200 / 403\,200 = 2.43\). (c) \(400 \times 1560 / 10\,000 = 62.4\) expected; 120 observed, about twice as many. (d) \(2728 / 19\,404 = 14.1\%\) vs \(22\,271 / 175\,523 = 12.7\%\); \(\mathrm{OR} = (2728 \times 153\,252)/(16\,676 \times 22\,271) = 1.13\). Highly significant because the sets are large, but a weak effect: on this evidence EBF1 is not a major distinguishing motif. Before concluding, check a GC-matched background (EBF1’s motif is GC-rich and B-up peaks are AT-rich; with GC matching the OR rises to about 1.44, R5), the quality of the matrix, EBF1 expression, EBF1 ChIP-seq, and chromVAR (R6: the EBF1 motif is most accessible in lymphoid progenitors). EBF1 is in fact a B-cell master regulator; motif enrichment just measures it poorly here.

B3. (a) \(0.05 / 800 = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\): four motifs pass (\(10^{-40}\), \(3 \times 10^{-12}\), \(2 \times 10^{-6}\), \(4 \times 10^{-5}\)). (b) BH thresholds \(0.05\,i/800 = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\, i\): \(6.25 \times 10^{-5}\), \(1.25 \times 10^{-4}\), \(1.9 \times 10^{-4}\), \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\), \(3.1 \times 10^{-4}\), \(3.75 \times 10^{-4}\), \(4.4 \times 10^{-4}\), \(5 \times 10^{-4}\). The 7th p-value (\(2.5 \times 10^{-4} \le 4.4 \times 10^{-4}\)) passes, the 8th (\(6 \times 10^{-4} > 5 \times 10^{-4}\)) does not: 7 motifs. (c) \(800 \times 0.05 = 40\). (d) Essentially one: all ETS motifs share the GGAA core, so they are 12 correlated tests of one signal (perhaps two, if PU.1-type and ETS1-type sites separate).
B4. (a) GC-rich and CpG-containing motifs: SP/KLF (GGGCGG), NRF1, E2F, ETS motifs typical of promoters (GABPA), CTCF. They are enriched in promoters against AT-rich random DNA because of composition and because promoters are open, not because they explain anything specific. (b) GC-matched peaks are also open chromatin with the same base composition, so a motif that remains enriched is more frequent in the target than composition and openness alone predict. (c) Report the GC-matched OR of 0.95 alongside the ns-background OR of 0.58, naming both backgrounds. The apparent strong depletion largely disappears after matching GC: the B-up peaks are AT-richer (distal elements) than the ns background, which contains many GC-rich promoters. Neither result establishes whether SP1 binds or drives accessibility.
B5. (a) No. SPIB, PU.1 and SPIC have nearly identical motifs (one family, one DNA-binding domain); the small differences in OR reflect the matrices, not which protein binds. (b) Expression (RNA-seq of B and T cells: PU.1 and SPIB are expressed in B cells; SPIC mainly in red-pulp macrophages), ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for each candidate, and perturbation (knock-out or degradation followed by ATAC-seq). (c) The ETS core GGAA is shared, but the flanks differ: PU.1/SPIB prefer an A-rich 5’ flank (AAAGAGGAAGT), ETS1/GABPA prefer CCGGAAGT. T-cell-specific peaks contain ETS1-type sites, B-cell-specific peaks PU.1-type sites, and each matrix detects mostly its own subtype.
B6. (a) GATA1::TAL1: MEPs (and erythroblasts); SPI1: monocytes and B cells; CEBPA: monocytes; TCF7: CD4 T cells. (b) In monocytes, reads in peaks with a GATA motif are much less frequent than expected from the average sample and from matched background peaks: those peaks are relatively closed. It says nothing about repression: most likely no GATA factor is active in monocytes, and the peaks are open only in other cell types. (c) GATA1 and GATA3 bind the same WGATAR motif. chromVAR measures the motif, not the protein; in erythroid cells the GATA-motif peaks are open because of GATA1, whatever name the matrix carries. (d) Samples differ technically (GC bias of the library, fraction of reads in peaks); these shift all peaks with a given GC content or accessibility, motif or not. Background peaks matched on these properties move the same way, so the z-score keeps only the motif-specific part.
B7. (a) Two flanking maxima (≈ 0.7 at ±30–60 bp), a dip over the motif (≈ 0.25, the footprint), lower values further out (≈ 0.3 at ±100 bp). (b) \(0.25 / 0.70 \approx 0.36\). Without protection about 1 (a flat profile, apart from sequence bias). (c) Closed chromatin is inaccessible to Tn5 along the whole window, so there are almost no insertions (0.01 per base per site) and nothing to protect. No open region, no flanks, no dip. (d) The glucocorticoid receptor has a short residence time (about 10 s): it binds and leaves many times during tagmentation, so Tn5 mostly finds the site free. No footprint even though ChIP shows binding (Sung et al. 2014). (e) Tn5 sequence bias at the motif sequence: it is present whether or not the TF is there. Correct with a bias model (TOBIAS ATACorrect, chromBPNet), compare with naked-DNA Tn5 data, or compare bound with unbound sites of the same motif.
B8. (1) The background: random genomic regions are closed and AT-rich, so any set of open regions is enriched for the motifs of open chromatin; AP-1 is the classic motif of active enhancers. Compare with peaks that did not change (GC-matched). (2) The p-value: with thousands of peaks any small difference is significant; report the odds ratio and the fractions. (3) Causality and identity: enrichment is a correlation; the AP-1 family (FOS, JUN, ATF, BATF, …) has many members; to show that AP-1 opens the regions, measure binding (ChIP/CUT&RUN for the stimulated factor) and perturb it (inhibitor, knock-out) to see whether the peaks fail to open. chromVAR or footprinting changes are supportive, not proof.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 5 993 179 read pairs passed fastp; 99.65% aligned (94.5% concordantly once, 4.4% more than once). The rate is so high because the reads were selected as those ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM: a real full library would give a lower number, with reads from all chromosomes. After filtering (proper pairs, MAPQ ≥ 30) and duplicate removal: 504 974 reads on chr21 and 2 125 212 on chrM. (b) \(2\,125\,212 / 2\,630\,186 = 81\%\) of the filtered reads are mitochondrial. Mitochondrial DNA is not packed in nucleosomes, and a cell has hundreds of copies, so Tn5 cuts it eagerly (see ATAC-seq). Our subset exaggerates it (only chr21 of the nuclear genome is kept), but 20–50% chrM is common in full ATAC libraries. It does not matter here because we only look at insertions on chr21; it does waste sequencing depth. (c) markdup removed 8 720 088 of 11 350 274 reads (77%), most of them on the tiny chrM, where so many fragments share both ends by chance. On chr21, a PCR duplicate would count the same insertion twice: at single-base resolution this adds spikes that look like signal, so footprinting always uses deduplicated reads.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 211 824 tested peaks: 19 404 B_up, 16 897 T_up and 175 523 ns, exactly as saved in Differential accessibility. (b) The class column retains that analysis’s apeglm-shrunken effect sizes and adjusted-p threshold. Reapplying the cutoff to MLE fold changes would admit some borderline peaks and change the target sets. The ns class includes nonsignificant peaks and peaks below the effect-size threshold; it is not evidence that every ns peak is unchanged.
R2. (a) 879 motifs. The largest families are zinc-finger proteins with more than 3 adjacent fingers (124), HOX (49), NK homeodomain (40), paired-related homeodomain (39), FOX (33), dispersed zinc fingers (32), Tal-related bHLH (32) and ETS (28). (b) Each column sums to 903: the matrix was built from 903 aligned sites. (c) All three have the GGAA core. PU.1 and SPIB add an A-rich 5’ flank (AAAGAGGAAGT), ETS1 prefers CC before the core (ACCGGAAGT).
R3. The matching takes about 3 minutes. (a) Median 6.4% of peaks (range 0.4–65%), close to the 5% expected by chance for a 500-bp peak at \(p = 5 \times 10^{-5}\) (\(2 \times 500 \times 5 \times 10^{-5} = 0.05\)). Most motifs are present in a few percent of peaks, real sites and chance matches together. (b) MEIS1 (65%), SP5 (55%), IKZF2 (53%), FIGLA and ZEB1 (41%). These are short matrices with little information (MEIS1: TGACAG; IKZF: GGGAA; E-box: CAGCTG). A short matrix has few distinct scores, so the score cut-off that corresponds to \(p < 5 \times 10^{-5}\) cannot be set precisely, and many windows reach it. Treat enrichment results for such motifs with extra care.
R4. (a) \(\mathrm{OR} = (8227 \times 140\,448)/(11\,177 \times 35\,075) = 2.95\), the same as fisher.test’s estimate (about 2.95; Fisher reports a conditional maximum-likelihood estimate, which is almost identical for large tables). fisher.test uses a default print format that displays very small p-values as < 2.2e-16; the probability here is about \(10^{-966}\) and underflows on the ordinary probability scale, so enrich() evaluates the hypergeometric tail on the log scale. (b) B-up: ETS of the PU.1 type (SPIB, SPI1, SPIC), IRF/STAT (ETS–IRF composite elements and interferon-response elements), IKZF1, and POU/OCT (POU2F1/2/3, the OCT2 motif). T-up: BCL11B, ETS of the ETS1/ERG/GABPA type, IKZF3, RUNX (Runx1 OR 2.13, ETS1 OR 2.66), and further down TCF7/LEF (TCF7 OR 2.11). Both fit: PU.1, SPIB, OCT2, IRF4/8 and IKAROS are B-cell regulators; RUNX1/3, ETS1, TCF1 and BCL11B are T-cell regulators. (c) 511 (B-up) and 507 (T-up) of 879. Not useful by itself: half of all motifs, mostly redundant family members and composition effects. Rank by odds ratio and group by family. (d) B-up: EBF1 OR 1.13 (\(p \approx 4.5 \times 10^{-8}\)), PAX5 OR 0.90 (not enriched), PAX2 OR 1.86 (\(p \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-35}\)). Both are B-cell master regulators, so absence of enrichment is not absence of function. For EBF1 the effect is weak with this background (see R5); for PAX5 the JASPAR matrix MA0014.4 is short and matches only 1.8% of peaks, while the longer PAX2 matrix (same paired domain) detects the enrichment. Matrix choice and background matter; lack of enrichment does not show that the TF is inactive. In T-up peaks EBF1 is clearly depleted (OR 0.51). (e) Many CTCF sites are shared between B and T cells, so they are not differential in this comparison: they are under-represented in any set of cell-type-specific peaks compared with the ns peaks (OR 0.51 and 0.59).
R5. (a) Less GC-rich: mean GC 0.477 in B-up versus 0.513 in ns peaks. All 19 404 B-up peaks find partners in their 2%-GC bins, giving 19 404 distinct ns background peaks with mean GC 0.477. (b) GC-rich motifs move towards 1: SP1 0.58 → 0.95, KLF4 0.73 → 1.07, NRF1 0.38 → 0.73; their apparent depletion was largely composition. EBF1 rises from 1.13 to 1.44. SPIB hardly changes (2.95 → 2.89) and CTCF stays depleted (0.51 → 0.54): those effects survive GC matching. Reporting the background size and GC distribution makes a shortage of partners or an imperfect match visible. The values above use set.seed(1); other random draws vary slightly.
R6. (a) 77 healthy libraries become 47 donor × cell-type samples across 13 cell types after summing technical replicates. The liftOver filters retain 589 070 peaks; chromVAR uses the 100 000 most-read. dim(z) is 879 × 47; computeDeviations takes about 25 s on 4 cores after the motif matching (whole block about 3 minutes). The most variable motifs are GATA (GATA1::TAL1 34, then GATA4, Gata3, GATA6, GATA2), the PU.1-type ETS motifs (SPIC, Spi1, SPIB, 14–16) and E-box motifs (ERF::FIGLA, FIGLA, ZEB1, 13–15). (b) GATA1::TAL1: MEP 77, Ery 50, CMP 37, MPP 12, negative in all lymphoid and myeloid cells. KLF1: weak (Mono 12, Ery 5): the KLF motif is GC-rich and shared with many KLF/SP factors. CEBPA: GMP 21, Mono 22. Spi1: LMPP 19, GMP 25, Mono 22, B 19; negative in MEP, Ery, T and NK. EBF1: CLP 20, B 6. TCF3 (E2A): CLP 27, LMPP 19, B 17, CD4 9. POU2F2: B 13. Runx1: LMPP 18. TCF7: CD4 11, CD8 8. TBX21: NK 21, CD8 15. CTCF: high only in GMPs (26), a pattern without an obvious biological explanation; worth checking for a technical batch. Overall, the known regulators of each lineage come out where expected. (c) Gata3 follows GATA1::TAL1 (MEP 46, Ery 27, CMP 36) and is negative in CD4 T cells (−17), where GATA3 is the active GATA factor. The motif cannot tell family members apart; in erythroid cells the open GATA sites are bound by GATA1. (d) fam["FIGLA_MA0820.2"] and BHLHE22 are “Tal-related” and ASCL1 “MyoD/ASC-related”: bHLH factors binding E-boxes (CANNTG). In blood the E-box factors are E2A (TCF3), HEB (TCF12) and E2-2 (TCF4) in lymphoid cells, and TAL1 with GATA1 in erythroid cells. TBR1 (“TBrain-related”) is a T-box motif: in blood it stands for T-bet (TBX21) and Eomes, high in NK and CD8 T cells.
R7. (a) 504 974 insertions on chr21. 15 684 CTCF motif matches at \(p < 10^{-4}\): 400 (2.6%) in a CTCF ChIP peak, 427 in an ATAC peak without ChIP peak, 14 857 in closed chromatin. 82% of the 405 chr21 ChIP peaks contain a motif match. (b) Bound sites: flanks rise to about 0.7 insertions per site at −23 and +34 bp (5-bp smoothed), a dip over the motif (about 0.2 on either side of the centre) with a narrow spike at the centre, and lower values far out. Averages: flank (30–60 bp) 0.48, centre (±10 bp) 0.34, far (≥ 90 bp) 0.20; centre/flank = 0.69 (the central spike raises the ±10-bp average; without it the dip is deeper). Open but unbound sites: flat at about 0.45, no flanks, no dip, but the same central spike. Closed sites: flat near 0.01. (c) Being in an ATAC peak only means the site lies somewhere in an open region, typically not at its centre and not bound: no protein protects it and no CTCF-positioned nucleosome-free region surrounds it. Without binding there is neither a footprint nor the flank pattern. (d) Without orientation, + and − strand sites are averaged in opposite directions: the profile becomes nearly symmetric (flank maxima at −31 and +33 instead of −23 and +34) and the central dip slightly shallower (minimum of the 5-bp-smoothed profile within ±10 bp: 0.24 instead of 0.21). Real asymmetric features of the CTCF footprint are smeared out.
R8. (a) The strongest deviations occur near the insertion: C is enriched at −6 and +4 (0.44) and −1 (0.41), G at −4 (0.48), +1 (0.40) and +6 (0.41), while T is depleted at −4 (0.09) and A at +4 (0.12). Further out the composition settles at the GC-rich level of open chromatin (about 0.3 for each of C and G), above the chr21 average of 41% GC. (b) The sequence of a motif is nearly the same at every site, so Tn5’s preference for or against it repeats at every site. Averaged over thousands of sites this gives a reproducible spike or dip that has nothing to do with binding, as in the central spike of R7. Footprints must be compared with unbound sites of the same motif or corrected with a bias model.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Where this leads

HOMER and MEME do known and de novo motif enrichment from the command line: findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa out/ -size 200 -bg ns.bed, or sea --p b_up.fa --n ns.fa --m JASPAR2024.meme and streme (see the lecture).
TOBIAS corrects Tn5 bias and compares footprints between conditions: TOBIAS ATACorrect --bam atac.bam --genome hg38.fa --peaks peaks.bed, then ScoreBigwig and BINDetect --motifs JASPAR.meme.
chromVAR on single cells (ArchR, Signac) gives each cell a motif z-score; the same idea as R6 with cells as columns.
ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag measure the binding of one TF directly and give the ground truth that motifs and footprints only suggest.
How a CNN reads DNA shows that a convolutional filter is a motif scanner, and models like chromBPNet learn motifs and Tn5 bias from the sequence.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities.
Bailey et al. 2015, Nucleic Acids Res. The MEME Suite.
Rauluseviciute et al. 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles.
Schep et al. 2017, Nat Methods. chromVAR: inferring transcription-factor-associated accessibility from single-cell epigenomic data.
Sung et al. 2014, Mol Cell. DNase footprint signatures are dictated by factor dynamics and DNA sequence.
Bentsen et al. 2020, Nat Commun. ATAC-seq footprinting unravels kinetics of transcription factor binding during zygotic genome activation.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Short questions on motif matches, enrichment, chromVAR and footprints. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You scan 200-bp peaks for a motif at a match threshold of \(p = 10^{-4}\). How many chance matches do you expect per peak, and in 20 000 peaks?






Hint





Count the windows on both strands.









Answer





About \(2 \times 200 = 400\) windows per peak, so \(400 \times 10^{-4} = 0.04\) chance matches per peak, and about \(0.04 \times 20\,000 = 800\) in 20 000 peaks. A motif in 4% of peaks is therefore what chance alone gives.




Q2. 1000 target peaks, 200 with a match; 9000 background peaks, 900 with a match. Compute the odds ratio and the number of target matches expected under the null.






Hint





\(\mathrm{OR} = ad / bc\). Under the null the target is a random draw from all 10 000 peaks.









Answer





\(a = 200, b = 800, c = 900, d = 8100\). \(\mathrm{OR} = (200 \times 8100) / (800 \times 900) = 1\,620\,000 / 720\,000 = 2.25\). Expected: \(1000 \times 1100 / 10\,000 = 110\); observed 200, so the motif is enriched (20% vs 10%). The p-value comes from Fisher’s exact test, equivalently the hypergeometric distribution.




Q3. You test 900 motifs. What p-value threshold does Bonferroni give at 5%? Why is “612 motifs significant at FDR 5%” from 20 000 target peaks not a useful result on its own?






Answer





\(0.05 / 900 \approx 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\). With 20 000 target peaks, tiny differences in motif frequency become significant, and motifs of one family (and GC-rich or AT-rich motifs) are counted many times over. Rank by effect size (odds ratio, fractions with a match), group motifs by family, and check the background.




Q4. Peaks that gain accessibility after a treatment are compared with random genomic windows, and CTCF, SP1 and NRF1 motifs come out as highly enriched. Is the treatment acting through these TFs? What background would you use instead?






Answer





Those results alone do not show that. These motifs are typical of open chromatin and GC-rich promoters in general; random genomic windows are mostly closed and AT-rich, so any set of peaks is “enriched” for them. Use the tested ns peaks (not differential by the chosen significance and effect-size thresholds) as background, ideally GC-matched. Exclude both differential groups from this background; ns is not proof that a peak is unchanged. Then CTCF in particular usually comes out depleted, because many of its sites are shared across conditions.




Q5. The top motifs in B-cell-specific peaks are SPIB, SPI1 (PU.1) and SPIC, all ETS factors with nearly the same motif. Which TF binds? How would you find out?






Answer





The motif cannot tell: family members share a DNA-binding domain and motif. Check which family members are expressed (RNA-seq of the same cells; in B cells both PU.1 and SPIB are), and measure binding directly (ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for the candidates), or perturb them (knock-out, degradation) and see which peaks close.




Q6. In a chromVAR analysis the motif GATA1::TAL1 has z = +60 in erythroblasts and z = −20 in B cells. What does each value mean?






Answer





In erythroblasts, reads in peaks with the GATA motif are far more frequent than expected from the average sample and from background peaks with the same GC content and accessibility: GATA-motif peaks are specifically open, consistent with GATA1 activity. In B cells they are less accessible than expected relative to background peaks. A negative z says nothing about mechanism: it does not mean that a GATA factor represses those peaks in B cells, only that they are relatively closed.




Q7. Why does chromVAR compare each motif with background peaks matched for GC content and average accessibility?






Answer





Samples differ technically: one library may have more reads in GC-rich peaks (PCR) or in strong peaks (better signal-to-noise). These effects would change the reads in a motif’s peaks without any change in TF activity. Background peaks with the same GC and accessibility are affected in the same way, so standardising against them (the z-score) removes the technical part.




Q8. An aggregate ATAC-seq profile around 2000 bound CTCF motif sites shows about 0.8 insertions per site at ±30 bp, 0.3 over the motif, and 0.4 at ±100 bp. Sketch it and name the features. What would the profile look like at 2000 CTCF motif sites in closed chromatin?






Answer





Two flanking peaks at ±30 bp (open, nucleosome-free DNA next to the bound protein), a dip over the motif (the footprint: CTCF blocks Tn5), and a lower level further out (decreasing accessibility towards the nucleosomes). Centre/flank \(\approx 0.3/0.8 \approx 0.4\). At closed sites: flat and close to zero, because Tn5 hardly inserts in closed chromatin. There is no peak to have a footprint in.




Q9. A narrow 2-bp spike in the middle of a footprint is seen at bound sites and equally at unbound sites with the same motif. What is it, and how is it handled?






Answer





Tn5 sequence bias: Tn5 prefers to insert at certain sequences, and the motif has the same sequence at every site, so the preference repeats at every site and adds up in the aggregate. It is not caused by the protein. Correct by comparing with insertions expected from sequence alone (Tn5 on naked DNA, a k-mer bias model as in TOBIAS ATACorrect, or a learned bias model as in chromBPNet), or always compare bound with unbound sites of the same motif.




Q10. “ChIP-seq shows that the glucocorticoid receptor binds 5000 sites, but ATAC-seq shows no footprint at them, so the ChIP-seq peaks must be false.” Is the conclusion justified?






Answer





No. A footprint needs the TF to occupy the site for a large part of the tagmentation reaction. Factors with short residence times (seconds), such as the glucocorticoid receptor, bind and leave quickly, so Tn5 mostly finds the site free and no dip forms, although the TF binds and opens the region (Sung et al. 2014). Absence of a footprint is not evidence of absence of binding.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
About this lecture
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have found tens of thousands of loci for diseases and traits. Almost all of them are non-coding. This lecture shows how chromatin maps turn such a locus into a testable hypothesis.

GWAS in one slide; why the lead SNP is a tag, not the cause (linkage disequilibrium).
Enrichment of disease loci in cell-type regulatory elements: the 2×2 test, the background, windows vs LD, partitioned heritability.
Fine-mapping, and functional priors from chromatin.
Mechanisms: a variant in a TF motif; chromatin QTLs; allele-specific accessibility in one person.
From variant to gene: colocalisation and enhancer–gene links.


This unit is the meeting point of human genetics and epigenomics, and the reason a lot of chromatin data is generated today. Students know what a SNP is and probably what a GWAS is; we recap the minimum and spend the time on what chromatin adds. All real-data figures come from make-variants-figs.R: the GWAS Catalog (one file of genome-wide significant associations), ENCODE ATAC-seq peaks of GM12878, K562 and HepG2, the Corces et al. 2016 blood cell types, JASPAR motifs, and the GM12878 ATAC reads the students aligned in ATAC-seq processing and peak calling. The links from elements to genes come from the previous unit, Linking regulatory elements to genes.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
A GWAS in one slide


Genotype millions of SNPs in many people; test each SNP for association with the trait; plot −log10 p along the genome.
Genome-wide significance: p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ (about one million independent tests). Typical odds ratios are 1.05–1.3.
A significant locus contains many associated SNPs; the most significant one is reported as the lead SNP.


A case–control GWAS compares allele frequencies between cases and controls (here 35% vs 30%, an odds ratio of about 1.26); quantitative traits use regression. The 5 × 10⁻⁸ threshold is a Bonferroni correction for roughly one million independent common variants in European genomes. Effects are small, so GWAS need tens to hundreds of thousands of people, and the result is a list of loci, each a peak of correlated SNPs. The GWAS Catalog (EBI/NHGRI) collects the reported associations from published studies: about 845 000 genome-wide significant SNP–trait associations, 334 000 unique SNPs, in the release we use. It records lead SNPs as reported by the authors, not the full summary statistics; for most analyses in research you would use full summary statistics.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Most GWAS hits are non-coding


Only 3.3% of the 333 556 genome-wide significant SNPs in the GWAS Catalog change a protein or a splice site; 65% are intronic, 23% intergenic.
Fine-mapping of 21 autoimmune diseases came to the same conclusion: about 90% of causal variants are non-coding (Farh et al. 2015).
So most disease variants must act by changing gene regulation: which elements, in which cells, controlling which genes?


Context is the annotation of the reported SNP relative to genes (Ensembl variant consequence). Intronic does not mean “in the gene that matters”: introns contain enhancers for distant genes (FTO and IRX3 in the previous unit). Two caveats make 3.3% an underestimate of coding mechanisms: the reported SNP is a tag, and a coding variant in LD with it may be the cause; and coding variants with large effects are rare and often missed by GWAS arrays. Even so, careful fine-mapping (Farh et al. 2015) finds that about 90% of causal autoimmune variants are non-coding, and about 60% fall in immune-cell enhancers. This is why epigenomic maps are now a standard part of interpreting GWAS.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: The lead SNP is a tag
text:
The lead SNP is a tag


Nearby variants are inherited together on haplotypes: linkage disequilibrium (LD), measured by r^2.
A causal variant makes every SNP in LD with it look associated. The lead SNP is the best-measured tag, often not the cause.
In Europeans, LD blocks span tens of kb (sometimes > 100 kb), so a locus holds 10–100 candidate variants.


Walk through the haplotypes: “causal”, s4 and “lead” carry the minor allele on exactly the same haplotypes, so their correlation is 1 and no association test can tell them apart; s2 is correlated with them (r² = 0.6) and will also be associated, more weakly. LD comes from shared ancestry: recombination has not yet separated nearby variants. It depends on the population (African genomes have shorter LD blocks, which is why multi-ancestry GWAS help fine-mapping). For annotation this means: checking whether the lead SNP lies in a peak is not enough; we must consider all the variants in LD with it. We will use a crude stand-in for this (a window around the lead SNP), and name the real tools (fine-mapping, S-LDSC).

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: From a locus to a mechanism
text:
From a locus to a mechanism


The questions are distinct, and each uses different data. Chromatin maps enter at almost every step (green).
The end point is a hypothesis: variant → element → TF → gene → cell type, which an experiment can test.


This is the map of the lecture. “Which variant” is statistical fine-mapping, helped by functional priors. “Which cell type” is enrichment: are the loci of a disease concentrated in the open chromatin of a particular cell type? “Which element” is the overlap of candidate variants with peaks. “How” asks what the variant does to the element: break a motif, change accessibility (a chromatin QTL), and whether we can see that within one person (allelic imbalance). “Which gene” uses the enhancer–gene methods of Linking regulatory elements to genes plus eQTL colocalisation. Experiments at the end: base editing of the variant, CRISPRi of the element, massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) of both alleles.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: GWAS SNPs sit in open chromatin
text:
GWAS SNPs sit in open chromatin


Fraction of SNPs within 1 kb of the 50 000 strongest GM12878 ATAC peaks: random positions 3.6%, all GWAS SNPs 6.6%, autoimmune loci 11.8%.
GWAS SNPs of any trait are near open chromatin more often than random positions: they sit in gene-rich, active regions. The right background is other GWAS SNPs, not the genome.


This is Maurano et al. 2012 in miniature: disease and trait variants are concentrated in DNase I hypersensitive sites. But the second bar is the important one. All GWAS SNPs together are 1.8 times more often near a GM12878 peak than random positions, because GWAS arrays and associations concentrate near genes and in active regions, and because many traits involve blood. A test of “autoimmune loci vs random positions” would give 3.3-fold enrichment and would overstate the specificity; “autoimmune vs other GWAS SNPs” gives 1.8-fold for all GM12878 peaks, and more for cell-type-specific ones (next slides). LDL, schizophrenia and height loci are close to the background: their relevant cells are liver, brain and growth plate, not B cells. Loci are pruned so that each counts once (the strongest SNP; others within 250 kb dropped).

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Enrichment is a 2×2 table


Count loci near and not near the annotation; compare with the background rate. Binomial or Fisher test; report the enrichment and its uncertainty.
The test is only as good as its background: matched for allele frequency, LD and distance to genes, or modelled genome-wide (S-LDSC).


The same 2×2 logic as motif enrichment in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting: a property is more frequent in the foreground than in a background. Expected 21.6 of 770 loci near a GM12878-specific peak; observed 51. The binomial test treats loci as independent, which is why we prune them first. Tools: GREGOR and SNPsnap pick background SNPs matched for allele frequency, number of LD proxies and distance to the nearest gene; GARFIELD and S-LDSC (next slides) model LD explicitly. In a research project, use one of these rather than the crude version we run in the exercise; the crude version is good for understanding what the tools do.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: Real data: which cell’s open chromatin?
text:
Real data: which cell’s open chromatin?


Peaks among the 50 000 strongest that are found only in GM12878 (B cells), only in K562 (erythroid) or only in HepG2 (liver).
Autoimmune loci: 2.3× in GM12878-only peaks (p = 4 × 10⁻⁸). LDL loci: 1.8× in HepG2-only peaks (p = 4 × 10⁻⁴). Peaks shared by all three: no enrichment.


A double dissociation: autoimmune loci prefer B-cell-specific elements, LDL-cholesterol loci prefer liver-specific elements, schizophrenia and height prefer neither (their cell types are not here). Shared elements, mostly promoters and CTCF sites active everywhere, carry little cell-type information and no enrichment. LDL loci show a weaker signal in K562-only peaks (1.5×, p = 0.02); hepatocyte-like and erythroid cells share some programmes, and with ~40 loci per cell, the numbers are small. This is the logic Maurano et al. used to identify pathogenic cell types without prior knowledge, and Finucane et al. 2015 did systematically with heritability.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Real data: 13 blood cell types


The 25 000 most specific peaks of each cell type (Corces et al. 2016). Lymphocytes light up for all four autoimmune diseases: MS 5.3× and RA 3.6× in CD4 T cells, SLE 3.4× in B cells.
IBD also in monocytes (2.4×); LDL, schizophrenia and height: nothing in blood.


The cell-type pattern matches what is known about these diseases: multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis loci are strongest in T cells (and MS also in B cells, consistent with the effect of B-cell depletion therapy); lupus is a B-cell disease with autoantibodies; IBD involves innate immune cells, and its monocyte signal fits Nasser et al.’s finding of the strongest enrichment in dendritic cells and macrophages. Progenitors show weak, mostly non-significant enrichment. Stars mark binomial p < 0.05/91. Two warnings. Enrichment says where the variants act, not where the disease starts: a T-cell enrichment in MS does not prove that T cells initiate MS. And resting sorted cells miss states: many autoimmune variants act in stimulated T cells (Farh et al. 2015), which were not profiled here.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Windows instead of LD


The lead SNP itself in a peak: few loci (16 of 770), strongest enrichment (3.4×). A ±20 kb window: 46% of loci, enrichment 1.4×.
A window is a crude proxy for LD: it includes unlinked SNPs and misses distant ones. Proper analyses use the LD proxies of each lead SNP (r² > 0.8 in a reference panel) or fine-mapped credible sets.


Why the trade-off: a narrow window misses causal variants that are in LD with the lead SNP but a few kb away, so the counts are small and noisy; a wide window catches them but also many peaks that are near by chance (the dashed background curve rises fast because peaks are common), so the enrichment drops towards 1. Every published method has to deal with this: Maurano et al. used LD proxies from the 1000 Genomes project; S-LDSC uses LD scores of all SNPs; fine-mapping replaces the lead SNP with a set of candidates and their probabilities. In the exercise we use ±1 kb and say so. A reference panel such as 1000 Genomes or the LDlink web service gives the r² of each proxy, ancestry by ancestry.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Partitioned heritability (S-LDSC)


Under polygenicity, a SNP’s association statistic grows with how many SNPs it tags (its LD score). Split the LD score by annotation to estimate the share of heritability from each.
Uses all SNPs (summary statistics), conditions on ~50 baseline annotations, and reports enrichment = % heritability / % SNPs.


This is the method behind most “which cell type” results in modern papers (Finucane et al. 2015). Instead of counting lead SNPs, it regresses the chi-square statistics of all SNPs on their LD scores, split into annotation categories; the coefficient τ of an annotation measures the extra heritability per SNP. Because the model includes a baseline of general annotations (coding, conserved, promoters, all enhancers…), a cell-type-specific annotation must add information beyond “active chromatin in general”. Finucane et al. found large enrichment for conserved regions across traits, very large immune-disease enrichment in FANTOM5 enhancers, and central nervous system enrichment for traits such as BMI and educational attainment. The bars here are toy numbers to show the definition. The software (ldsc) needs full summary statistics and an LD reference, beyond the scope of the exercise.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Fine-mapping


Assume one causal variant: its posterior inclusion probability PIP = BF / Σ BF over the SNPs in the locus. A 95% credible set collects the top SNPs until their PIPs sum to 0.95.
A functional prior (higher prior for SNPs in open, acetylated elements of the relevant cells) can shrink the set. Here: 4 SNPs → 3, and SNP c gets PIP 0.79.


The Bayes factor of a SNP compares the data under “this SNP is causal” with “no SNP is causal”, computed from the effect estimate and its standard error (Wakefield’s approximate Bayes factor). With a single causal variant and equal priors, PIPs are the Bayes factors normalised to sum to one. Methods such as SuSiE and FINEMAP allow several causal variants per locus; PAINTOR and PolyFun bring in functional annotations as priors, learned from data (for example from S-LDSC enrichment). Caution: if you then report “the fine-mapped variant lies in an enhancer”, part of that came from the prior; say how the prior was chosen. The by-hand exercise repeats this computation.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: A variant can change a TF motif
text:
A variant can change a TF motif


Score the window with each allele, on both strands, over all windows that contain the variant; compare the best scores: Δ = alt − ref.
A difference of −2.5 bits means the alternative allele matches 2^{2.5} \approx 6 times worse (in odds against the background).
Tools: motifbreakR, FIMO on both alleles; the PWMs and their scoring are from Gene regulation and the cis-regulatory code.


This is the PWM scoring students did by hand in Gene regulation and the cis-regulatory code, applied twice. Only windows that overlap the variant can change; a motif of width w has w such windows per strand. A change from a strong match to a weak one suggests loss of binding, from no match to a match a gain. The log-odds difference is not a binding energy, but it correlates with changes in binding measured in allele-specific ChIP-seq. motifbreakR implements exactly this for a list of variants and a motif database, with thresholds on the relative score of the better allele. In the next two slides: one famous success, and a sober look at how often motif changes happen by chance.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: A classic: rs12740374 at the SORT1 locus
text:
A classic: rs12740374 at the SORT1 locus


The minor allele T of rs12740374 (chr1:109 274 968, 3′ UTR region of CELSR2) creates a C/EBP binding site in a liver enhancer.
More C/EBP binding → more SORT1 in hepatocytes → lower LDL cholesterol and less myocardial infarction (Musunuru et al. 2010).


This was one of the first complete stories from a non-coding GWAS signal to a mechanism. The 1p13 locus is strongly associated with LDL cholesterol and coronary disease. Musunuru et al. showed that the minor allele creates a C/EBP site, increases enhancer activity and SORT1 expression in liver, and that changing SORT1 levels in mouse liver changes plasma LDL. The bars show the best score of five JASPAR C/EBP matrices over the windows containing the SNP: the T allele scores 7–13 bits higher than G (our motif scan in the exercise also calls it a gained C/EBP match at p < 10⁻⁴). Note the gene: the variant lies in the 3′ UTR of CELSR2, next to PSRC1, but the target was SORT1, whose TSS is about 120 kb away; the link needed eQTL data in liver and experiments.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: Real data: motif changes are everywhere
text:
Real data: motif changes are everywhere


211 autoimmune GWAS SNPs in GM12878 ATAC peaks, against 879 JASPAR motifs (p < 10⁻⁴): 85% gain or lose at least one match. Random positions in the same peaks: 81%.
With 23 blood TF motifs: 15% vs 11% (not significantly different). Farh et al.: only 10–20% of fine-mapped causal variants change a recognisable motif.


The left panel is the sobering control. A single base change in a 50-bp neighbourhood will almost always create or destroy a match for some of 879 motifs, many of them similar (TF families share motifs). So “the risk allele disrupts a motif for X” means little unless X is expressed and bound in the relevant cells, the change is large, and there is evidence that the variant changes binding or accessibility (the QTL and allelic data of the next slides). Restricting to TFs that matter in B cells (ETS, IRF, NF-κB, RUNX, EBF1, POU2F2, CTCF…) gives smaller numbers, but still no clear excess over random sites with this sample size. The right panel lists the blood-TF changes; CTCF dominates because its long motif has many near-matches. Note that the lead SNPs are tags: with credible sets instead of lead SNPs, the picture would be cleaner.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Chromatin QTLs


Measure a molecular trait in many genotyped people and test each nearby SNP: caQTL/dsQTL (accessibility), hQTL (histone marks), meQTL (DNA methylation), eQTL (expression).
Degner et al. 2012: 8902 dsQTLs in 70 lymphoblastoid cell lines; 16% are also eQTLs, and up to 55% of eQTL SNPs are dsQTLs.


A chromatin QTL turns “the variant might change binding” into a measurement: across people, those with the GG genotype have a more open element. Lymphoblastoid cell lines like GM12878 were the workhorse because hundreds of genotyped lines exist (1000 Genomes, HapMap). Degner et al. measured DNase-seq in 70 Yoruba LCLs; dsQTLs were enriched in TF binding sites and often showed allele-specific binding, and many eQTLs could be explained by a change in accessibility. Kumasaka et al. 2016 did the same with ATAC-seq (2707 caQTLs from a modest sample) and introduced RASQUAL, which combines differences between people with allelic imbalance within people. meQTLs are common too, and methylation often follows accessibility (a TF that cannot bind no longer protects its site from methylation); the methylation units return to this. QTLs are correlational at the level of the variant, LD again blurs which SNP is causal.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Allele-specific accessibility in one person


At a heterozygous SNP in a peak, reads from the two haplotypes are counted in one sample: same cells, same nucleus, only the allele differs. Imbalance → a cis effect.
Test against 0.5 (binomial), but beware reference mapping bias: reads carrying the non-reference allele map less well.


Allelic imbalance is the within-person version of a QTL, and it controls for everything that differs between people (environment, cell composition, batch). It needs only one heterozygous individual, which is why GM12878, with its high-quality phased genome (NA12878, Genome in a Bottle), is ideal. The pitfall is technical: a read that carries the alternative allele has one mismatch to the reference genome, so it is somewhat more likely to fail alignment or be filtered for low MAPQ, especially if another variant lies nearby. The result is a genome-wide excess of reference reads. WASP (van de Geijn et al. 2015) re-maps each read with the allele flipped and discards reads that do not map to the same place; a personal diploid genome can reduce reference mismatches but still needs checks for unequal allelic mappability. Copy-number changes and imprinting also cause imbalance unrelated to the variant.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
section: Real data: allelic imbalance in GM12878
text:
Real data: allelic imbalance in GM12878


437 heterozygous SNPs (GIAB) in chr21 ATAC peaks with ≥ 10 reads, from the replicates you aligned in ATAC-seq processing. Pooled reference fraction 0.516: mapping bias.
62 SNPs at FDR < 10%. Neighbouring SNPs in the same peak agree (e.g. 3 SNPs at 42.1 Mb, all reference-biased), as expected for a haplotype-level effect.


The histogram is centred slightly above 0.5 (red line, 0.516), the signature of reference bias; with WASP it would move back towards 0.5. A test against the pooled fraction instead of 0.5 is a quick correction. Sixty-two significant SNPs is many for 437: some are real cis effects on accessibility, but several are complete (79 reference reads, 0 alternative at 44.196 Mb): that pattern suggests a deletion or loss of one haplotype in this cell line, or a genotyping error, rather than a regulatory variant. Lymphoblastoid lines are EBV-transformed and can carry copy-number changes, so check neighbouring SNPs and copy number before claiming a regulatory variant. The exercise reproduces these counts with bcftools and a binomial test in R.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Colocalisation


A GWAS locus and an eQTL (or caQTL) for a gene in the same region: is it one causal variant, or two different ones in LD?
coloc compares the association patterns and gives a posterior for “shared variant” vs “distinct variants”. A shared variant links the disease signal to the gene (or element).


Overlap of two association peaks is not enough: in a region with long LD, a disease variant and an independent eQTL variant can produce overlapping peaks by chance, and many loci contain several eQTLs for different genes. Colocalisation methods (coloc, Giambartolomei et al. 2014; eCAVIAR; SMR-HEIDI) test whether the two signals have the same shape, which they do only if one variant drives both. They need full summary statistics from both studies and the right tissue: an eQTL measured in whole blood may not exist in the relevant immune cell state. Large eQTL resources (GTEx for tissues, eQTL Catalogue, DICE and others for immune cell types) make this routine; the fraction of GWAS loci that colocalise with an eQTL is still surprisingly modest, one argument for context-specific regulation.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
From variant to gene


The gene containing or nearest to the variant is a guess (Linking regulatory elements to genes: right about half the time).
Combine: fine-mapping, overlap with an element active in the enriched cell type, enhancer–gene links (ABC), colocalised eQTL, and a perturbation.


The figure is a composite of the kinds of evidence. Nasser et al. 2021 used ABC maps in 131 cell types to connect 5036 GWAS signals for 72 traits to genes, and showed that ABC links were more precise than nearest gene or eQTL alone for genes with known causal roles. One of their examples is an IBD risk variant in an enhancer that regulates PPIF in macrophages, the locus we analysed in GM12878 in the previous unit. Variant-to-gene pipelines such as Open Targets Genetics combine distance, QTLs, chromatin interactions and functional annotations into one score per gene, trained on gold-standard genes. Each line of evidence has false positives; agreement between independent ones is what makes an assignment credible.

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
The enrichment test in R
near <- function(chr, pos, peaks, w = 1000)                       # SNP within w bp of a peak?
  overlapsAny(GRanges(chr, IRanges(pmax(pos - w, 1), pos + w)), peaks)
loci <- leads[set == "autoimmune"]                                # one lead SNP per locus
k  <- sum(near(loci$chr, loci$pos, gm_only))                      # 51 of 770
p0 <- mean(near(bg$chr, bg$pos, gm_only))                         # 0.028 for all GWAS SNPs
c(enrichment = k / nrow(loci) / p0,
  p = binom.test(k, nrow(loci), p0, alternative = "greater")$p.value)

Pruning, peaks and backgrounds as in Genomic intervals: one overlapsAny per question.
Production tools: GREGOR, GARFIELD, S-LDSC (ldsc), with LD panels and matched backgrounds.


This is the core of the exercise (R2). The loci were pruned first: within each trait set, keep the most significant SNP and drop any SNP within 250 kb of a kept one, a crude replacement for LD clumping (plink –clump does the same with r² from a reference panel). gm_only are the GM12878 peaks absent from the K562 and HepG2 top-50 000 sets; bg are all unique SNPs in the GWAS Catalog. The binomial test asks whether 51 successes in 770 trials is surprising when the success probability is 0.028. Everything here can be done with bedtools as well (the exercise’s command-line part).

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Judging claims

“The lead SNP lies in an enhancer, so it is the causal variant.” It is a tag; check all SNPs in LD, fine-map, and look for QTL or allelic evidence.
“Disease loci are enriched in T-cell enhancers, so the disease starts in T cells.” Enrichment shows where variants act, not where the disease is initiated; other cell types and states may not have been profiled.
“The risk allele disrupts a motif for TF X.” About as many random sites do; is X expressed and bound there, and does the variant change accessibility or binding?
“40% of our loci overlap open chromatin (vs 4% of random positions).” Compare with other GWAS SNPs and matched backgrounds, and consider the window used.
“This allele shows 3:1 imbalance in one sample.” Mapping bias, copy number and coverage first; replicate across individuals.


These claims all appear in papers. Ask students to identify which slide of the lecture addresses each. Common thread: each piece of evidence is weak alone (LD, enrichment backgrounds, chance motif matches, technical imbalance), and convincing stories combine several independent lines, ideally ending with an experiment on the variant itself (base editing or a reporter assay of both alleles).

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




GWAS hits
~3% coding or splice; most act through gene regulation


LD
the lead SNP tags a block of correlated variants; it is often not causal


enrichment
2×2 against other GWAS SNPs (matched), not random positions


this data
autoimmune loci 2.3× in B-cell-specific peaks; LDL 1.8× in liver-specific; MS 5.3× in CD4 T cells


windows
narrow = few loci, strong enrichment; wide = more loci, diluted


S-LDSC
heritability enrichment from all SNPs, conditional on a baseline


fine-mapping
PIP = BF / Σ BF (one causal variant); functional priors sharpen credible sets


motifs
Δ score of two alleles; most sites change some motif by chance


QTLs, allelic
caQTL across people, imbalance within one person; beware mapping bias


variant → gene
colocalisation + enhancer–gene links + perturbation




Students should be able to: compute r² from haplotype frequencies; set up and evaluate an enrichment 2×2 table with an appropriate background; compute PIPs and a credible set from Bayes factors; score both alleles with a PWM; test allelic imbalance with a binomial test and recognise mapping bias; and judge claims about causal variants. The next units take a different angle on the same problem: machine-learning models that predict the effect of a variant directly from sequence (What did the model learn? Variant effects).

title: Epigenomics and genetic variation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Musunuru et al. 2010, Nature. From noncoding variant to phenotype via SORT1 at the 1p13 cholesterol locus. A complete mechanism, from GWAS signal to C/EBP site to liver gene.
Maurano et al. 2012, Science. Systematic localization of common disease-associated variation in regulatory DNA. Disease variants concentrate in DNase I hypersensitive sites of relevant cells.
Degner et al. 2012, Nature. DNase I sensitivity QTLs are a major determinant of human expression variation. Chromatin QTLs in lymphoblastoid cell lines.
Finucane et al. 2015, Nat Genet. Partitioning heritability by functional annotation using genome-wide association summary statistics. Stratified LD score regression.
Farh et al. 2015, Nature. Genetic and epigenetic fine mapping of causal autoimmune disease variants. 90% non-coding, 60% in immune enhancers, few in motifs.
Schaid, Chen & Larson 2018, Nat Rev Genet. From genome-wide associations to candidate causal variants by statistical fine-mapping. Review of fine-mapping methods.
